title: Vilnius
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
Vilnius, the Grand Duchy’s capital since at least 1323 (Gediminas’s letters), sits where the Vilnia meets the Neris. In the 1380s it has three castles: the brick Upper Castle on Gediminas hill; the walled Lower Castle on the flat below, with the ducal residence and the site of the later cathedral; and the wooden Crooked Castle on the Bald Hill across the Vilnia. The town is mostly timber and mixed: Lithuanian pagans, an Orthodox Ruthenian quarter, a German-Catholic merchant colony with Franciscans. The Order attacked it in 1365, 1375, 1377, 1383, 1390, 1392, 1394 and 1402.
Key dates: Kęstutis took the city in autumn 1381; Hanulas and the townsfolk handed it to Jogaila on 12 June 1382; the baptism of Lithuania came in early 1387, with the Vilnius bishopric (charter 17 Feb) and Magdeburg rights (22 Mar); the siege of 11 Sep to 7 Oct 1390 destroyed the Crooked Castle (fell 16 Sep; it was never rebuilt) and killed Jogaila’s brother Karigaila; Union of Vilnius and Radom, 18 Jan 1401; a fire in 1419 burned the cathedral and castle, and Vytautas rebuilt the Upper Castle (finished 1422). Vytautas was buried in the cathedral beside Ona (St Michael’s altar). Casimir was proclaimed Grand Duke here on 29 June 1440 and issued his privilege on 2 May 1447 (VLE: 5 May). Sources: VLE, en.wikipedia (Vilnius Castle Complex, Siege of Vilnius).

title: Vilnius
text:
Sensory sketch
Hills above rivers: mist in the Vilnia valley, the Neris running broad and brown below the Upper Castle, the smell of wood smoke, flax-retting, tanneries on the stream, tallow and beeswax. A city of timber with brick only in the castles; before 1387 pagan groves stand inside it, and the sound is the Orthodox bells of the Ruthenian quarter, a Franciscan bell, and a crowd speaking three tongues. In winter the Neris freezes and sledges cross it; autumn brings rain and mud, and in spring the thaw. After 1387 comes the ring of masons, lime and scaffolding at the new cathedral. After the siege of 1390 the Crooked Castle’s hill is charred.

title: Vilnius
text:
In the saga
The city of the Šventaragis flame until 1387, then the city of the White Silence. In Book I the Crooked Castle is only “the third castle,” old and wooden, so that in Book II it can burn: Vytautas’s own fire against his own city. The Iron Wolf of the founding legend howls on Gediminas hill. After the baptism the Silence lies over court and cathedral, and under the cathedral the old grove’s ashes and, in Book V, the crypt where Vytautas lies. Hanulas, who opens the city to Jogaila in 1382, is the Shadow-Seller’s first mask. The record’s “seven hills” Rome echo is avoided: the saga names Gediminas hill, the Bald Hill and Table Hill.

title: Vilnius
text:
Getting there
Trakai is 25 km west (28-32 km by road, half a day on horse); Kernavė about 35 km north-west on the Neris. Vilnius to Krėva is about 77 km straight, 90-105 km by road via Medininkai (30 km) and Ašmena: two days by horse, or one long day at best; a prisoner convoy takes two to three. To Kaunas, 95 km (100 km by road, two and a half days; by the Neris, 180-200 km of river, four to five days downstream). To Marienburg, 550-650 km via Kaunas, Insterburg, Königsberg and Elbing: 13-16 days. To Kraków 750-850 km (three to four weeks); to Kyiv 750-800 km (three to four weeks); to Palanga 350-400 km (eight to ten days, four with relays).

title: Vilnius
text:

title: Tapiau (Tepliava)
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
Tapiau (Lith. Tepliava; Rus. Gvardeysk) is an Order castle about 38 km east of Königsberg on the Pregel, where the Deime branches north to the Curonian Lagoon. The Order built a wooden fort here between 1283 and 1290 to guard Sambia; a stone castle replaced it in 1351. Vytautas was baptised here as “Wigand” on 21 October 1383 (VLE and lt/en Wikipedia; the pl Wikipedia gives 12 October and names the godfather as Wigand von Beldersheim, komtur of Ragnit; one en.wikipedia entry says 1385). His brother Tautvilas was baptised Kondrat the same day. The act is the first of several pledges to the Order: the vassalage treaty is the later Königsberg treaty of 30 January 1384. Sources: VLE (Vytautas), en.wikipedia (Gvardeysk, Tapiau Castle).

title: Tapiau (Tepliava)
text:
Sensory sketch
A river-junction castle on a green floodplain, boats at the quay, swans in the reeds, a chapel with high narrow windows. In late October the light is white and cold, the leaves falling, the smell of wet stone, tallow and Latin incense. Inside the chapel the sounds are the creak of the font cover, the priest’s voice speaking a name the baptised does not understand, and water that is deeply cold. Outside: gulls, boats, bells, a long wind from the lagoon.

title: Tapiau (Tepliava)
text:
In the saga
The lying baptism. Vytautas takes the Order’s name and the amber in his pouch dies at once (magic §5.4), “like a smothered bird”; the saga uses the junction as an image of water that runs two ways. The chapter makes the oath an alliance oath and the title vassal come later. The silence of the amber is recalled again at Krėva (1385) and in Book II.

title: Tapiau (Tepliava)
text:
Getting there
Tapiau lies 38 km east of Königsberg: a day’s ride, or one day downstream by boat. It is about 70 km from Ragnit and about 40 km from the lagoon. By water from Kaunas, via the Nemunas, the lagoon and the Deime, it is on the route of 300-320 km (six to nine days downstream), which is how Vytautas arrives in the saga: by boat from the Nemunas. From Marienburg about 190 km, six or seven days.

title: Tapiau (Tepliava)
text:

Book I ch. 19 Velnio sandėris (21 Oct 1383, the chapel), ch. 20 Svetimi dievai (the aftermath); recalled in ch. 28b and 29, Book II ch. 20, Book III ch. 2 and ch. 28.

title: Salynas (island in the Nemunas)
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
An islet of the Nemunas, probably between Kulautuva and the mouth of the Nevėžis; the treaty was signed here on 12 Oct 1398 (event).

title: Salynas (island in the Nemunas)
text:
Sensory sketch
A long, low island in the Nemunas, pine and oak on sand, a meadow in the middle, willows and reeds on the shoreline. In mid-October the weather is cold and wet; the river runs high and brown from autumn rain, the leaves of the oaks are rusted, and mists lie on the water in the morning. The saga’s feast hall is a huge open-sided timber pavilion on posts, white cloths on three long tables, a black-cross banner and a red rider banner snapping in the wind, the smell of roasted meat, wet wool, pine smoke and river. The island is neutral ground because it belongs to nobody; boats, not horses, are the sound of arrival.

title: Salynas (island in the Nemunas)
text:
In the saga
Eglė’s price comes due here: “never sell the forest”.

title: Salynas (island in the Nemunas)
text:
Getting there
The islet lay on the middle Nemunas, probably between Kulautuva and the mouth of the Nevėžis, a short way downstream of Kaunas (about 15-25 km). From Kaunas it is half a day by boat downriver (40-60 km per day), or a day’s ride along the bank. From Vilnius it is about 120 km, three days on horse, or four to five on the Neris and Nemunas. From Ragnit, the Order’s launch point for the middle Nemunas, upstream is some 130 km and takes several days of towing (upstream rates are 10-20 km per day). From Marienburg, Konrad von Jungingen’s party would have ridden to Königsberg and then taken the river route, about two weeks. As in other treaty sites on this river, both sides could arrive by water without stepping on the other’s bank.

title: Ritterswerder (Nemunas island near Lampėdžiai)
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
A Nemunas island near Lampėdžiai where the Order built a fort in autumn 1391; its guests were seized and the fort destroyed in summer 1392 (event).

title: Ritterswerder (Nemunas island near Lampėdžiai)
text:
Sensory sketch
A newly raised timber fortress on a low Nemunas island, so green wood sweats resin in the sun, with pine-pitch and fresh-hewn sawdust underfoot, and the harbour smell of river mud and hemp rope. A festival night in early summer (the saga puts it on St John’s) brings drums, torches along the bank, and beer; the broad river reflects bonfires, and the wooden palisade is the only brightness that is not water. Mosquitoes near the reed-beds. After the fire the sound is a flat crackle and a river that goes on as before.

title: Ritterswerder (Nemunas island near Lampėdžiai)
text:
In the saga
The wooden fort smells of resin and Order ale; Vytautas’s name hangs over its gate: “dar viena dovana, kuri buvo paskola”.

title: Ritterswerder (Nemunas island near Lampėdžiai)
text:
Getting there
The island lies in the Nemunas just below Kaunas near Lampėdžiai, in the stretch of river the Order held as a line of forts. From Vilnius, Kaunas is about 95 km (2.5 days by horse; the Neris is also navigable downstream in four or five days). To Jurbarkas by the Nemunas is about 85 km (two days downstream; upstream four to eight). To Königsberg by water it is 300-320 km (six to nine days downstream; two to four weeks the other way). Because the fort stood on an island and was reachable only by boat or ford, guests could be gathered inside it by invitation and then cut off: the island was both bait and trap.

title: Raciążek (Vistula island)
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
Raciążek on an island of the Vistula at the confluence with the Drwęca, where the Peace of Raciąż was made on 22-23 May 1404 (event).

title: Raciążek (Vistula island)
text:
Sensory sketch
A small riverside stronghold and a Vistula island in late May: reed beds, braided channels, heavy water carrying spring flood, lush meadow, willows in leaf, and the first heat. The stage is a tented camp, Masovian guards, Polish envoys, Order retainers, dogs and horses, so the smell is tar, wet canvas, horse dung and river. The Vistula is wide here and runs quietly with a brown, silty smell, and you can hear the sandbars. In the saga’s chapter the peace is also a feast in a pavilion with the Order’s wine, and the only sound that matters is a toast.

title: Raciążek (Vistula island)
text:
In the saga
The evening feast where Marquard insults Birutė.

title: Raciążek (Vistula island)
text:
Getting there
Raciążek lies on the lower Vistula upstream of Toruń (Thorn), about 130 km from Marienburg in a straight line. River travel is the realistic way: downstream from Raciążek to Marienburg is about 2-3 days by boat at 40-60 km per day; upstream, ten to twenty km a day. The Masovian town of Płock is some 120 km upstream by water. By land, Toruń is a day’s ride. From Vilnius the distance is about 500 km (650 km by road, two and a half weeks by horse; envoys carrying documents would take a little over two weeks, as for Vilnius-Marienburg). From Kraków it is about 330 km (ten days). Plenipotentiaries from three courts could assemble here by water without crossing hostile territory.

title: Pabaiskas
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
Pabaiskas lies near the Šventoji river about 9 km south of Ukmergė (Vilkmergė, Pol. Wiłkomierz). The battle of 1 September 1435 (also the Battle of Wiłkomierz or of the Šventoji) was fought here between Švitrigaila’s army (about 11,000, including the Livonian knights, at least 500 Tatars, and some Teutonic Knights) and the forces of Žygimantas Kęstutaitis under his son Mykolas Žygimantaitis with about 4,000 Poles under Jakub Kobylański. Lake Žirnajai and a marshy creek (Žirnaja or Vintara) first separated the armies; two days later, when Švitrigaila and the Livonian master Franke Kerskorff moved toward Ukmergė, Žygimantas’s side attacked while a rivulet had split the enemy host, which broke in panic; many drowned in the Šventoji. Kerskorff, his marshal and several komturs were killed; Žygimantas Kaributaitis was wounded, captured and died days later; Švitrigaila fled to Polotsk with about 30 followers; the winners hunted survivors for 15 days. It was the last big battle of the Lithuanian crusade and broke the Livonian Order. Sources: en.wikipedia (Battle of Wiłkomierz); VLE.

title: Pabaiskas
text:
Sensory sketch
A river valley of lakes, reed-fringed creeks and rye stubble on the first day of September: damp mist at dawn burning off to heat, the dull sound of bridle chains, drums and horn, the smell of river mud, wet wool and rotting reeds. After the rout the Šventoji is full of drowned horses and men; the dead are not buried for days, and crows, ravens and wolves arrive in the same hour.

title: Pabaiskas
text:
In the saga
Kin-slaughter, worse than the crusades. The unburned dead and the Unbinding at its height. In Book V ch. 13 Pilkoji and twelve wolves watch from the pines; the rule that a wolf does not shed Gediminid blood keeps them out of a battle between two Gediminid hosts. Afterwards (ch. 16) she burns the dead on the slope, hundreds of pyres, and a Polish captain asks who allowed her to burn Christians. The Livonian knights’ defeat ends the Order’s long century of war on Lithuania.

title: Pabaiskas
text:
Getting there
Ukmergė is 9 km north. Vilnius is about 75 km south-east (95 km by road, two to three days). Kernavė about 40 km, Kaunas about 70 km. Polotsk, where Švitrigaila fled, lies some 250 km north-east (six or seven days with a few followers). Riga is about 200 km north.

title: Noteć ford (Neumark / Greater Poland border)
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
The Noteć (Ger. Netze) formed the frontier between the Neumark and Greater Poland. The Neumark had belonged to the Order since 1402. In August 1430 Sigismund of Luxembourg sent two courtiers ahead, the jurist Baptista Cigala and the Silesian Sigismund Roth (they left Vienna on 4 July) with letters and goods for the intended coronation of Vytautas; they were robbed and beaten before 19 August on the Neumark-Greater Poland border by the royal guards under Jan Czarnkowski, who took their letters, horses and about 1,000 ducats’ worth of valuables. The embassy waited at Frankfurt (Oder) and turned back. The crown itself was never seized: the Order’s komtur of Schlochau wrote on 19 August that the crown had not been taken, because the courtiers never had it. The seizure is a later legend. Sources: Bar 2017 and Szybkowski 2010 via Book IV’s fact-check; en.wikipedia.

title: Noteć ford (Neumark / Greater Poland border)
text:
Sensory sketch
A low river on a sandy frontier: reeds and willow, brown water running shallow in late August, flat fields stripped by harvest, pine woods on the sand. Merchants’ carts line up because the ford is free while the bridge below charges toll. Dry heat, dust, wasps, cart-grease and horse sweat; at the water’s edge, the silence of men waiting for a ruler who is not coming.

title: Noteć ford (Neumark / Greater Poland border)
text:
In the saga
The false-crown scene. A chest is opened and dry leaves tumble out; the Hungarian goldsmith’s apprentice Pál swears he held real gold. In the saga Henė’s bargain had turned the crown to leaves, and Vytautas refuses it: “I never offered a lie; it was my most honest bargain, and I lost it.” The record gives only a robbery; the saga gives it a meaning.

title: Noteć ford (Neumark / Greater Poland border)
text:
Getting there
Frankfurt (Oder) is some 80-120 km west (three to four days for couriers). Poznań, the Greater Poland capital, about 80 km east. From Vienna the road runs through Silesia and the Neumark: about 500 km straight, c. 700 km by road. To Vilnius it is about 650 km straight; two to three weeks by road, eight to ten days with relays.

title: Noteć ford (Neumark / Greater Poland border)

title: Naujapilis (Marienwerder)
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
The Order’s castle at Kaunas in 1384: Marienwerder, also Naujasis Marienburgas or Lithuanian Naujapilis (“New castle”), built on the Nemunas for the Order’s vassal Vytautas on the site of old Kaunas (whose brick castle the Order had destroyed at Easter 1362); the exact site (right bank or an island) is uncertain. The VLE and Acta Baltico-Slavica 2017 call it the Order’s furthest eastern point. Vytautas reconfirmed the Königsberg treaty here in June or July 1384. In July 1384 he reconciled secretly with Jogaila, took the Order’s castles at Kaunas and Jurbarkas and burned them, capturing their garrisons; the Order’s Marquard von Salzbach, later komtur of Ragnit, is said to have been captured then. It is not Marienwerder (Kwidzyn) in Prussia, seat of the Pomesanian bishop, and not Georgenburg near Insterburg. Sources: VLE (Jurgenburg, Vytautas), en.wikipedia (Lithuanian Civil War).

title: Naujapilis (Marienwerder)
text:
Sensory sketch
Fresh-hewn oak, lime, river mud, new timber ramps, barges grinding at the quay under loads of bombards, powder and oil. In July the heat is heavy and the air storm-grey; the Nemunas runs broad and low. The garrison drinks Königsberg wine and sings hymns by fires; in the saga’s night the camp is full of the clink of armour, snoring, and the sizzle of oil. When the castle burns it makes a long red column under the river sky, and the dawn smells of tar.

title: Naujapilis (Marienwerder)
text:
In the saga
The “Išdavikų išdavikas” set piece (Book I ch. 22-25): a castle opened from inside by its own lord at a feast, guests become captives, the traitor’s hospitality mirrors Krėva. The Iron Saint’s men burn as Kęstutis did not. Vytautas thinks of the warmth of Perkūnas’s mark “as at Marienwerder” (Book III ch. 21) and Book II ch. 26 recalls the fire. The record gives only the burning: the staging (the sword in the fire, the Kaunas depot) is invention.

title: Naujapilis (Marienwerder)
text:
Getting there
Kaunas is 95 km from Vilnius (100 km by road, two and a half days on horse; 180-200 km on the Neris, four to five days downstream). To Jurbarkas by the Nemunas is about 85 km, two days downstream; Vytautas burned both castles within days of each other (the record gives 9 July for Jurbarkas). To Königsberg by water, 300-320 km, six to nine days downstream; two to four weeks back up. To Salynas, a few hours by boat downstream.

title: Lyck (Ełk)
text:
Sensory sketch
In January 1390 the place is a wooden fortress on a narrow neck of land between two lakes, with plank ramparts and palisades heavy with rime, ice thick on both waters, and the smoke from the timber hall hanging flat in frozen air. A winter castle smells of tallow, wet felt and smoked fish; the lakes boom at night as the ice contracts. The silence of the Masurian lake country in deep winter makes small sounds carry: a latch, a horse blowing, the creak of the sentry’s boots on the walkway. The Order’s brick castle is documented only from 1398, so in the winter of 1390 there is no stone to speak of; the consecrated relic the chaplain holds is the one hard, cold thing in the place.

title: Lyck (Ełk)
text:
In the saga
A consecrated stone dims the pebble.

title: Lyck (Ełk)
text:
Getting there
Lyck (Ełk) lies in Sudovia, on the Order’s side of the old Wildnis, a little over 100 km from Grodno (straight line) and about 190 km from Trakai (route 250-280 km, seven to eight days by horse, much of it through the border forest). To Königsberg it is about 160 km straight (5-6 days), to Marienburg 220 km (280-320 km by route, seven or eight days), and to Rastenburg (Kętrzyn) about 80 km. Vytautas’s winter ride from Grodno across the frozen marsh belt would take four days; a sledge on lake ice could do it faster. Treaties were signed here because it lay inside Order territory yet close enough to Lithuania that Vytautas could come and go without announcing himself.

title: Lake Ublik (Wobel), Masuria
text:
Sensory sketch
A lake in the Masurian lake country, in the border forest of southern Prussia: pine, spruce and birch round a long, narrow water, reedy margins and cold black bog. In March the ice is grey and rotting at the edges, with open leads; the air smells of wet earth, snow-melt and resin; the forest drips. Sound is the problem: nothing carries, the ice groans at night, and the camp fires are small. A raiding camp pitched here would hear nothing until the horsemen were on it. The saga’s chapter makes that absence the warning.

title: Lake Ublik (Wobel), Masuria
text:
In the saga
Frost and thaw; the hidden nine arrive too late.

title: Lake Ublik (Wobel), Masuria
text:
Getting there
Ublik (Wobel) lies near Johannisburg (Pisz) in the Order’s border country, about 230 km in a straight line from Trakai, in the southern reaches of the Wildnis. By road from Trakai it is some 300-330 km (8-10 days on horse; the Order’s Wegeberichte routes counted it as a long Reise). It is about 190 km straight to Marienburg, or 230-250 km by road (six to seven days for a mounted escort; the prisoner was held there for about half a year). The raid of 1361 had taken Kęstutis and Algirdas to Eckersberg and Johannisburg, so the camp was a few days’ march inside the Order’s frontier. The Masovian border is only about 60-80 km south.

title: Krėva
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
Krėva (Pol. Krewo; Bel. Kreva) lies about 75-80 km east-south-east of Vilnius, now in Belarus. It was Algirdas’s patrimony and then Jogaila’s. It is a stone-and-brick enclosure castle of irregular plan on low, marshy ground, with a big corner tower and a smaller tower, among the oldest masonry castles in the Grand Duchy; scholars date it to the first half of the 14th century under Gediminas, others to Algirdas’s time. After the arrest on 3 August 1382 Jogaila held Kęstutis and Vytautas here. Kęstutis was found dead on 15 August (the Assumption). Most sources, including VLE, say he was strangled; Jogaila’s official version was that he hanged himself, which few believed. Vytautas was held until autumn 1382, when he escaped in a woman’s clothes (the maid’s name is not recorded). The Union of Krėva was signed here on 14 August 1385. The castle was sacked by Crimean Tatars in the early 16th century and ruined in the First World War; Poland conserved the remains in 1929. Sources: VLE (Kęstutis, Krėva), en.wikipedia.

title: Krėva
text:
Sensory sketch
A castle that hides rather than protects: thick walls of big fieldstone and brick, small windows, and below them cells that never dry. The air is damp stone, old straw, tallow and the sweat of long confinement; in August, hot masonry, harvest dust and horse sweat (rye harvest). Low ground between streams gives mist at dawn and mosquitoes by dusk, and frost arrives early. Sound is thin: footfalls on stone stairs, keys, and the distance from one wall to the next. In the saga the silence here is not an absence but a weight.

title: Krėva
text:
In the saga
The wound in the map. Kęstutis’s death is Henė’s Breath of the Void, a silence that took the sound out of the castle; the White Silence first touches Krėva as frost in November 1382 and settles over it at the 1385 union. The cell holds a residue (magic rules): seers feel it for a century, and Žygimantas feels it in Book V. The silver wolf passes from Kęstutis to Vytautas through the Krėva stones (Book I ch. 8). Perkūnas marks Vytautas here. The Union of 1385 is staged in the room above the death cell. Krėva sits on the edge of the eastern Dykra: the first forest Vytautas reaches after the escape.

title: Krėva
text:
Getting there
From Vilnius, 90-105 km by road via Medininkai and Ašmena: two days on horse, or a long day at best; a prisoner convoy takes two to three days. From Trakai 110-125 km, two and a half days. The Dykra (Naliboki edge) begins 30-60 km south, half a day to a day by horse. To Palanga is 470-520 km (10-13 days; five to six with relays), which is the key news route. To the Prussian border 330-400 km (eight to ten days); to Masovia (Czersk) 480-520 km, ten to twelve days.

title: Krėva
text:

Book I ch. 8 Krėvos požemiai, ch. 9 Paskutinė giesmė, ch. 10 Šaltas rytas (the Assumption morning), ch. 12-14 (the weeks of mourning, the exchange, the night escape), ch. 28b Krėvos sutartis (14 Aug 1385), ch. 30 (epilogue); Book II ch. 10 (recalled); Book IV ch. 26, 29 (recalled); Book V ch. 6, ch. 19 Išdavystės aidas (14 Aug 1438, Žygimantas at Krėva).

title: Königsberg (Karaliaučius)
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
Königsberg (Lith. Karaliaučius; Pol. Królewiec) was founded in 1255 on the Pregel and was the seat of the Order’s Marshal, who led the Reisen into Lithuania. It was three towns, Altstadt, Löbenicht and the Kneiphof, with the brick castle on the old hill; the cathedral on the Kneiphof was building from the 1330s and completed c. 1380. It was the mustering point for western crusader-guests: English, French, German and Bohemian knights joined the summer and winter Reise here (Henry Bolingbroke in 1390).
Key events: the Treaty of Königsberg, 30 January 1384, in which Vytautas ceded Samogitia up to the Nevėžis and became the Order’s vassal (the Treaty of Lyck confirmed it in 1390). Vytautas’s wife Ona and children were kept here as sureties (1383-84), and after the treaty moved to Marienburg. His second flight to the Order in 1389 and, in later tradition (Simon Grunau, 16th century; en.wikipedia calls it a false rumour), the poisoning of two young sons in July 1392 are tied to Königsberg, but the record is thin. After Salynas (1398) the Order took Samogitian elders’ sons as hostages; the saga sends them to Königsberg. Sources: VLE; en.wikipedia (Treaty of Königsberg, Treaty of Lyck).

title: Königsberg (Karaliaučius)
text:
Sensory sketch
A river port in the Prussian lowlands: boats at the Pregel quays, timber stacked high, hemp and tar, herring, amber, wax and furs in the warehouses, brick churches over timber lanes. In summer, banners, tents and horses before the Reise, English and French voices, drinking songs, the Order’s Mass at dawn. In winter, heavy snow on the castle gates, ice on the river, and the dull sound of sleighs. The air is damp and salty; the lagoon fog rolls up the Pregel.

title: Königsberg (Karaliaučius)
text:
In the saga
The Iron Saint’s barracks. Heraldry, drinking and pious brutality; the saga’s Table of Honour for the best crusader guests. Here Vytautas meets the western knighthood, and here the treaty that sells Samogitia is sealed in the January cold; the “Amber Debt” is signed into the record. Ona’s wing of the castle is a polite prison. Book III shows its other face: forty-one Samogitian children learning “a civilised language” in the same town.

title: Königsberg (Karaliaučius)
text:
Getting there
From Tapiau, 38 km east along the Pregel (a day on horse, or a boat downstream from Tapiau in about a day). From Marienburg about 165 km straight, c. 200 km by road (five to six days). From Kaunas it is 220 km straight: 6-8 days on horse overland across the Wildnis (about 250 km), or 300-320 km by water (Nemunas, lagoon, Deime, Pregel), six to nine days downstream, two to four weeks upstream. From Vilnius 410 km straight, on the Order’s own road to the capital.

title: Kamianets (Podolia)
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
Kamianets (Pol. Kamieniec, today Kamianets-Podilskyi) sits on a peninsula wound by the Smotrych river, with a castle traditionally dated to the second half of the 14th century on a site occupied since the 12th-13th. The Koriatovych (Karijotaičiai) brothers, sons of Gediminas’s son Karijotas, held Podolia as Lithuanian vassals; a document of 1374 by Yuriy Koriatovych promises Magdeburg rights to the town. Fyodor Koriatovych was expelled in 1393, after which Lithuanian and Polish governors held Podolia in turn; Spytek of Melsztyn, a Polish magnate, modernised the castle c. 1400, adding ten towers. From the mid-14th to mid-15th century it lay on the Polish-Lithuanian frontier with the steppe. After Vytautas’s death (27 Oct 1430) the Polish lords seized Podolia in the next weeks; Kamianets, according to the lt.wikipedia account the Book V fact-check used, refused to surrender. Poland organised the Podolian Voivodeship in 1434 with Kamianets as its seat. Sources: en.wikipedia (Kamianets-Podilskyi Castle); VLE; lt.wikipedia (Švitrigaila).

title: Kamianets (Podolia)
text:
Sensory sketch
A fortress on a rock island in a canyon: limestone cliffs, a green river far below the walls, a single bridge to the mainland. Stone castle, thick walls, new towers around the courtyard; Armenian, Ruthenian, Polish and Wallachian traders in the town. Autumn mist in the canyon, steppe wind overhead, cold stone in November, the smell of horses and tanneries. The frontier is audible as a hush of watchers on the walls.

title: Kamianets (Podolia)
text:
In the saga
Podolia is Vytautas’s southern shield; its loss within weeks of his death is the first sign that the empire will not outlive him. Book V ch. 3 has an envoy ride twelve days through the first frost to tell Švitrigaila that the Polish lords “took Kamianets”, which matches the record: Polish and Podolian lords took the castle in Oct-Nov 1430 and the Poles then declined to return it to Lithuania as the truce required. No mythic overlay of its own.

title: Kamianets (Podolia)
text:
Getting there
Kamianets is some 670 km south of Vilnius in a straight line (850-900 km by road, about four weeks on horse). The saga’s messengers from Podolia took twelve days to reach Švitrigaila in the late-autumn frost. From Lutsk about 250 km; from Lviv about 225 km; from Kraków about 500 km. The Dniester lies 30 km south-west; the steppe edge lies a few days’ ride east.

text:

title: Jogaila’s camp near Trakai
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
On 20 July 1382 Trakai fell to Jogaila and the Order; the armies then stood facing each other near the town for two weeks. On 3 August Kęstutis and Vytautas were persuaded by Skirgaila to come to talks at Jogaila’s camp, where both were arrested (VLE, Skirgaila; en.wikipedia).

title: Jogaila’s camp near Trakai
text:
Sensory sketch
A summer camp in a lake and pine country: sandy ground under pine, birch and aspen, long evenings off the water, the smell of tar, horse dung, cook-smoke and resin, and in the night a faint damp from the lakes. In early August the days are hot and the nights cool; mosquitoes and midges near the reeds. The sound of an army camp is large (smiths, farriers, drilling, dogs), which is why the saga’s camp is eerie: the loudest noises have been taken out and the field feels padded, as if the camp itself is listening. The palisade is raw yellow timber still oozing sap, the gate fresh-sawn oak with iron straps, the manor a low timber house with a shingle roof and a barn behind it.

title: Jogaila’s camp near Trakai
text:
In the saga
Book I’s camp: a palisaded field between the lakes and the pines, a requisitioned Trakai manor as the negotiating hall, tents beyond the manor fence, an iron-bound gate made by the Order’s carpenters in a few days (the “Iron Gates”). Sound dies inside it.

title: Jogaila’s camp near Trakai
text:
Getting there
The camp stood outside Trakai, on the Vilnius side, a short ride from the lake town. Trakai to Vilnius is about 25 km straight (28-32 km by road), half a day on horseback; the camp is then within a morning’s ride of Jogaila’s capital and of the Order’s marching route down the Neris. From Kęstutis’s pine hill beyond the lake it was an afternoon’s ride. After the arrest the prisoners were taken to Krėva: Trakai to Krėva is about 90 km (110-125 km by route), about two and a half days on horseback with a guard, three with a captive convoy through Vilnius, Medininkai and Ašmena. Kęstutis was found dead there on 15 August, twelve days after the arrest.

title: Jogaila’s camp near Trakai
text:

The arrest; Book I ch. 5-7.

text:
In the 1380s [Record]
Horodło on the Bug, where the union was signed on 2 Oct 1413 (event).

title: Horodło (on the Bug)
text:
Sensory sketch
A river town on the Bug in mid-autumn: wet meadows beside the water, tents standing in rows by the castle, the smell of damp wool, woodsmoke, horses and cooked game for hundreds of guests. Rain, mud, and a thin autumn light. The ceremony is built of sound as much as sight: heralds calling Polish noble houses by name, the clank of coats-of-arms being hung, Latin Masses, and the dry rustle of charters. A wooden royal manor, a church, and a modest hill castle are the only buildings; nothing is large enough to hold the crowd, so the union is sworn half in the open.

title: Horodło (on the Bug)
text:
In the saga
A heraldry ceremony that is a declaration of civil war twenty years early.

title: Horodło (on the Bug)
text:
Getting there
Horodło stands on the western bank of the Bug, the frontier between Lesser Poland (Lublin land) and Lithuanian Volhynia. From Lutsk it is about 100 km in a straight line, roughly two and a half days on horseback; from Brest-Litovsk (Brasta) about a day and a half. From Kraków the route is 420-450 km (ten to twelve days for a court), from Lublin about three days. From Vilnius it is 550-600 km by road, two to three weeks. Because the Bug is a navigable border river, boat traffic could carry baggage down toward the Vistula. The place was chosen precisely because it is neither Polish nor Lithuanian ground in the mind of either side: it is where the two courts could meet halfway.

title: Grodno
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
Grodno (Lith. Gardinas; Bel. Hrodna) is an old Ruthenian town on the high bank of the Nemunas, with the oldest surviving church of the region, the Kalozha church (before 1183). It was part of the Trakai duchy under Kęstutis; a convention here in 1358 settled the border with Masovia. VLE says Vytautas received it (with Brest and Podlasie) in 1384; en.wikipedia says he was prince of Grodno 1376-92, and that Jogaila took it in 1390 and Vytautas in 1391. Anna (Ona) was in Grodno in 1389. Vytautas later built a brick castle (dating uncertain). Jewish privileges: Brest 1 July 1388, Grodno 1389. Talks for the Union of Vilnius and Radom began here in December 1400. In 1413 it became the centre of a powiat of the Trakai voivodeship; Polish-Order border talks met here in 1425; on 15 October 1432 Bishop Oleśnicki’s delegation received Žygimantas Kęstutaitis’s oath and proclaimed him Grand Duke for life, with Jogaila absent (his own act came from Lwów on 30 Oct). Magdeburg law came in 1441. Sources: VLE; en.wikipedia (Hrodna).

title: Grodno
text:
Sensory sketch
A high bank over a broad river, a timber castle and wooden town with a stone church of ancient make, mixed Ruthenian, Lithuanian, Jewish and Tatar traders, Orthodox bells, flax and furs. The Nemunas runs wide and cold below; frost on the cobbles in October, snow by December. Smoke, tar and river fog; in summer meadows and storks.

title: Grodno
text:
In the saga
Vytautas’s consolation prize and first court at home: the Nemunas here is the same river that runs past Ragnit and Georgenburg, tying his small domain to his enemy. The saga’s Gardinas is where Ona waits in 1389 while the wedding-wagon plot ripens (Book II ch. 4-5), and, in Book V ch. 10, where the agreement that makes Žygimantas Grand Duke “for life”, without a crown, is sworn.

title: Grodno
text:
Getting there
From Vilnius about 150 km straight (180-190 km by road, four to five days on horse). From Krėva about 175 km straight, 225-250 km by road (five to six days), by Lida (about 100 km from Grodno), which is why Vytautas’s escape route avoided it. From Trakai about 130 km straight. From Lyck about 100 km (three days); from Brest on the Bug about 200 km; to Marienburg about 340 km. The Biebrza marshes and Masovian frontier lie 60 km south-west.

title: Grodno
text:
Scenes set here
Book I ch. 17 Pasienis (the Gardinas forests); Book II ch. 4 Gardino kiemas (1388-89), ch. 5 Vestuvių vežimai (1389); Book V ch. 10 Gardino sutartis (15 Oct 1432), ch. 18 (recalled, 1438).

title: Dykra (swamp-forest wilderness)
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
The Wildnis (German Wiltnis; Lithuanian historiography: dykra) was a deliberately depopulated border belt between Prussia and Livonia and settled Lithuania, formed after the conquest of Prussia (1283) and Sudovia (1277-83) and a century of raiding. It lay south of the Nemunas over old Sudovia-Yotvingia, up to c. 150 km deep; along the west and north of Samogitia, c. 60 km; and in patches on the Livonian border. Some old population survived there and some trails were known: the Order recorded them in about 100 route reports, the Wegeberichte, compiled between 1384 and 1402 from the accounts of Lithuanian and Prussian guides, listing fords, night camps and villages. For 1341-1450 it is the real war-zone: raids of both sides, winter and summer Reisen, and refugees like Vytautas (1382) crossed it. The Treaty of Melno (1422) at last fixed the frontier. Sources: VLE (Dykra), Wegeberichte editions.

title: Dykra (swamp-forest wilderness)
text:
Sensory sketch
Alder carr and peat, black water, sphagnum moss with cranberries, birch stands drowned at the roots, pine on sand islands. Cranes in spring, bitterns in the reeds, the howl of wolves. Midges and horseflies in summer, dense mist in autumn, a smell of rot and iron-rich water. Winter freezes the bog and makes a hard road; thaw drowns it. Few people, no bells: just stray hunters, beekeepers with tree-hives, and the faint smoke of a hidden hamlet. The ground quakes underfoot where it looks solid.

title: Dykra (swamp-forest wilderness)
text:
In the saga
The saga’s Dykra is larger than the historical Wildnis: the western Dykra is the real border belt; the eastern Dykra is the swamp-forests of the upper Nemunas, the Naliboki and the Biebrza marshes, the territory “between Krėva and the Neman”. It is the Root-Mother’s own country, the map of what the crusade cost, and it grows as the books go on. It is the one country the Pact still fully protects after 1384. Pelkių Eglė speaks for it. It never lies about where you end, only about how long it takes: paths shorten for those she favours and lengthen without end for those she does not. It is also the hiding place of the surviving wolves.

title: Dykra (swamp-forest wilderness)
text:
Getting there
The Dykra begins within a day’s ride of Krėva: 30-60 km to the Naliboki edge, half a day to a day on horse, one to two days on foot (a starving fugitive in bog does 10-15 km a day). From Krėva to the Prussian border is 330-400 km (eight to ten days, four to five with remounts); the direct road is watched, which is why Vytautas went in. The Order’s raiders cross it from Insterburg and Lyck; a winter Reise on ice makes 40-60 km a day. Across Sudovia from Kaunas to Königsberg it is some 250 km overland.

title: Dykra (swamp-forest wilderness)
text:
Scenes set here
Book I ch. 15 Pabėgimas, ch. 16 Pelkės vaikai (Eglė’s bog), ch. 17 (the Gardinas forests and the Biebrza marsh), ch. 23; Book II ch. 14 Vilkų medžioklė (the Dykra’s edge, winter 1395-96); Book III ch. 7 Pilkoji and ch. 9 (1404-06), ch. 29 (Rasos night 1411); Book IV ch. 6; Book V ch. 7 (Christmas Eve 1430), ch. 11, ch. 28 (the oldest bog, 1449); Book VI ch. 5 (an island in the swamp, 1345), ch. 9 Dykros gimimas (Sūduva, 1348).

title: Christmemel (Skirsnemunė)
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
Christmemel (now Skirsnemunė) lies on the Nemunas about 9 km from Jurbarkas. The Order built a wood-and-earth castle on a hill fort here between 8 and 22 April 1313 as a base against Samogitia; Vytenis besieged it in 1315 for 17 days without success, and it was abandoned in 1328. A Christmemel is again among the Order’s Samogitian castles in 1409, when the Samogitian uprising took and burned it (this is the account in en.wikipedia; whether the site is the same is not established). The Treaty of Christmemel was concluded here on 19 June 1431: Švitrigaila, Grand Master Paul von Rusdorf and the Livonian Master Zisse von Rutenberg agreed to mutual aid if attacked, war only by joint consent, and shared spoils; witnesses included Švitrigaila’s brother Lengvenis, Žygimantas Kęstutaitis, Jonas Goštautas, Kristinas Astikas and other nobles. The Polish invasion of Volhynia began six days later. Sources: VLE (Skirsnemunė); en.wikipedia (Treaty of Christmemel, Skirsnemunė).

title: Christmemel (Skirsnemunė)
text:
Sensory sketch
A river meadow on the bank of the Nemunas under old trees in mid-June, grass high, leaves new, the river smell of mud and fish; a pavilion or tent of the Order’s colours, banners snapping, a cluster of horses. Mosquitoes at dusk. Behind the chancery sounds there is the continuous sound of the river itself, the oldest speaker present.

title: Christmemel (Skirsnemunė)
text:
In the saga
A treaty sworn on the Order’s river that is really a declaration that Lithuania is at war with itself: the saga places the signing on the bank beneath trees (Book V ch. 3). The treaty binds Švitrigaila to the Order; Žygimantas Kęstutaitis stands among the witnesses and will overthrow him in 1432.

title: Christmemel (Skirsnemunė)
text:
Getting there
From Jurbarkas, 9 km (a morning’s ride). From Kaunas about 90 km (two days by horse). From Vilnius 185 km, four to five days. From Marienburg, a fortnight by route; from Königsberg, 250 km across the Wildnis. Lutsk, where Švitrigaila’s war went next, is about 500 km south-east.

title: Christmemel (Skirsnemunė)
text:
Scenes set here
Book V ch. 3 Švitrigailos pakilimas (dateline “1430 Oct to 1431 Sep, Vilnius, Christmemelis, Luckas”); recalled in ch. 4.

title: Ašmena
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
Ašmena (Bel. Ašmiany, Pol. Oszmiana) lies on the Ašmena river (now the Ashmyanka), on the Vilnius-Krėva road about 25 km from Krėva. First mentioned in the 1350s as a town of the Vilnius duchy; the Lithuanian chronicles give it to Jaunutis after Gediminas died in 1341. The Order destroyed the town in 1384 and was repelled in 1402. By 1384 a ducal manor stood here, and a Franciscan church was founded after 1387. In the saga’s period the places that mattered were the manor and the ford. Key events: Žygimantas Kęstutaitis’s coup against Švitrigaila in the night of 31 August to 1 September 1432, and the battle of 8 December 1432 (one battle only, not two) in which Žygimantas defeated Švitrigaila’s army, which had come from Polotsk with Tatar help and taken Minsk, Krėva and Ašmena. Hanseatic routes crossed here in the 15th century. Sources: VLE (Ašmenos mūšis), en.wikipedia (Ashmyany, Battle of Ashmyany).

title: Ašmena
text:
Sensory sketch
A small town in a rolling, wooded plain: timber houses, a manor yard, a ford, rye fields, flax. The sounds are hooves on a plank bridge, geese, carts, the clack of a mill. Autumn turns the roads to clay and the first snow falls in December; the 8 December battle was fought on cold, hard ground. A night coup is noise and torchlight in a quiet place: a ducal manor in the dark, dogs barking, and doors opened by men who know the house.

title: Ašmena
text:
In the saga
The place where the 1382 road and the 1432 road cross: the same inn and ford, fifty years apart. The coup of 1432 is Henė’s whispering in a kinsman’s ear; Švitrigaila’s pregnant wife is seized and he flees to Polotsk. The ground has no mythic residue of its own: its weight is that it lies at the edge of the eastern Dykra, so the Root-Mother’s forest returns after the battle (Book V ch. 11). The word ašmenys (blade) in Book I’s prologue and ch. 2 is not this town.

title: Ašmena
text:
Getting there
Ašmena is between Vilnius and Krėva on the same road: Medininkai is the stop 30 km from Vilnius, then Ašmena, some 25 km short of Krėva. From Vilnius it is about 65-75 km by road, a long day or one and a half days on horse. From Krėva, a half-day ride. Polotsk (where Švitrigaila fled) is some 300 km north-east. Minsk about 120 km south-east. A courier on relay can run Vilnius to Ašmena in a day.

title: Ašmena
text:
Scenes set here
Book V ch. 9 Ašmenos naktis (31 Aug-1 Sep 1432); ch. 11 (the roads to Ašmena, autumn-winter 1432, the December battle); mentions in ch. 16, 18, 19; Book IV ch. 2 (two small castles near Ašmena in the Horodło exchange) and ch. 9 (Ona’s silver sent through Ašmena).

title: Ženklai (signs)
text:
What it is
Carved signs: stored intention, the way to enchant objects. A sign is carved, burned, woven or embroidered, then fed: blood for a strong sign, milk for a gentle one, ash for a binding one.

title: Ženklai (signs)
text:
Who can use it (path & tier)
Tier 0 can use a fed sign; tier 2 (the burtininkas or sign-carver) makes warded objects; a bound object (signs plus Kalba plus blood) becomes an artifact. The Trakai smith, Kęstutis and the Flame-Keeper (from 1410) all carve.

title: Ženklai (signs)
text:
How it works (medium, words, timing)
Common signs: the saulutė (sun-wheel; repels night spirits; milk at dawn); perkūnėlis (thunder-cross; wards lightning, breaks curses on a threshold, marks an oath; blood once); žalčiukas (zigzag; house-luck, warns of poison; milk weekly); Laimos medis (eases childbirth); žvaigždutė (helps sight-workings); žirgeliai (roof-horses turn aside unbound spirits); mėnulio pjautuvas (hides things by distraction, not illusion; ash).

title: Ženklai (signs)
text:
Costs
The feed (blood, milk, ash). A sign fades if not fed; a broken sign reverses for a night; Kęstutis’s sword rusts as the sign under its grip fails when the Pact cracks (Book I ch. 2, the sword).

title: Ženklai (signs)
text:
Limits & counters
Signs on iron are twice as strong but anger the laumės. A sign carved by a baptised hand works only if the carver means it (Law of Truth). Inside consecrated stone it works at half strength if meant: masons’ saulutės in Gothic vaults are the last ward on Vilnius (Book II ch. 11; Book V ch. 20, eight on the cathedral crypt’s vault keys).

title: Ženklai (signs)
text:
Folk basis [Record]
[Record]. Baltic folk ornament carries sun-wheels, the perkūnėlis (“Perkūno cross”), grass-snake zigzags, Laima’s tree and the Austras tree, carved on lintels, spindles, cradles, beehives, belts and the horse-head gables (žirgeliai) of roof-ridges. The identifications with gods and the idea of “feeding” a sign are later reconstruction.

title: Ženklai (signs)
text:
Notable practitioners
Kęstutis burns a perkūnėlis under his sword’s grip; the Trakai smith fits one on every sword and “feeds it once with the prince’s blood” (Book VI ch. 1, 4, 16, 30). Vytautas feeds it with his own palm blood before the oath (Book III ch. 17). Elena’s tow-knot (Book I ch. 12) and Galminas’s warding face-marks (Book III ch. 1) are the Root-Mother’s signs.

title: White Silence’s frost-touch
text:
What it is
The White Silence’s frost-touch: granted power from the White Silence. A healer’s touch that heals by frost: holy calm, closed wounds, the ending of fever. It is also a cold that spreads.

title: White Silence’s frost-touch
text:
Who can use it (path & tier)
A vessel only (tier 5): Jadvyga from 1386, whom the Force uses as a conduit. She is “a saint” by acclaim, not decree.

title: White Silence’s frost-touch
text:
How it works (medium, words, timing)
She lays on a hand: her touch closes a leper’s sore overnight (Book II ch. 21). Frost fern-patterns grow where her hands lie, and on a baby’s lips. Warmth leaves the healer; sound dies around her.

title: White Silence’s frost-touch
text:
Costs
Warmth leaves the healer: a week of being unable to get warm, two days of an aura of cold around her (Book II ch. 21, as she tells her confessor). The child’s lips go white. Frost passes into those who kiss her hand (Jogaila). Sound dies: at the 1385 union the quill makes no noise (Book I ch. 28b).

title: White Silence’s frost-touch
text:
Limits & counters
It is not hers to command; it is a Force’s will wearing her hands. A žaltys warns her that “the Silence will freeze your heart while it saves your soul” (Book II ch. 21). Counters: warmth, such as tears (Book IV ch. 14), and a living flame; its own touch smothers Wind and freezes Water.

title: White Silence’s frost-touch
text:
Folk basis [Record]
[Record]. Jadwiga of Poland (c. 1373–17 July 1399) was crowned king (rex) in 1384, married Jogaila in 1386 after being betrothed to Wilhelm of Habsburg, and died days after her infant daughter Elizabeth Bonifacia. She was canonised in 1997. The frost-touch is saga overlay; her reputation for charity and piety is historical.

title: White Silence’s frost-touch
text:
Notable practitioners
Jadvyga (Book II ch. 21, the night her child is ill, July 1399). In the world bible her body “does not decay but turns to salt and silver” (hidden_immortals §5), an anchor for the Force in the Polish heartland. Jogaila carries its frost afterwards (Book III ch. 3; Book IV ch. 19).

title: Birutė’s Senovės Sutartis over Vytautas
text:
Terms
[Saga invention], made in Book I ch. 3 (1382): the Senovės Sutartis by which Birutė binds her son Vytautas. Four requirements, all on the page: amber charged by the binder (the pebble); the binder’s blood on it (a crescent vaidilutė knife across her left palm); the bound one’s true name (slaptas vardas), a name he has never heard, spoken by her; and an unbreakable promise both ways. Hers: “Jo skola — mano skola” (“his debt is my debt”). His: “Kol aš gyvas, paskutinė ugnis neužges.” (the flame promise).

title: Birutė’s Senovės Sutartis over Vytautas
text:
Parties & witnesses
Binder and surety: Birutė, who stands laidas for the bound. Bound: Vytautas (“surištas”, the third path to Kalba). Witness: the elements, and the Amber Queen, to whose request Birutė answers “if someone must pay, let it be me, not him.” She comes to it half-blind from the Praurimė vision at Dagotuvės. The pebble (Motinos gintaras) is the token; see the event.

title: Birutė’s Senovės Sutartis over Vytautas
text:
Breaches
Penalties are unchanged from the old doc: loss of gift, curse of the elements, memory loss, madness, death in the extreme. A cost can be deferred, not refused, and deferred costs compound. Failure of the promise: letting the flame die while he lives.

title: Birutė’s Senovės Sutartis over Vytautas
text:
Consequences
Surety. Part of every price Vytautas incurs is paid by Birutė wherever she is: his costs look light in Book I while her voice and sight fail (the Krėva fog, ch. 14, 25). In ch. 27 (1384) she pays the whole remaining debt at once at Palanga (the sacrifice), and from Book II there is no surety: at the foundations of the island castle “the spring damp doubled it, and Birutė was not beside him” (Book II ch. 2); Vorskla has no mother’s fog, only shame. The pebble stays the bond’s token and barometer.

title: Priesaika (oath-binding)
text:
What it is
Oath-binding: an oath sworn with the right form is literally binding. It is the old law of the land turned into magic: the oath-breaker pays, physically.

title: Priesaika (oath-binding)
text:
Who can use it (path & tier)
Anyone who swears with the right form. The Krivis (tier 4) and tier 3 priests conduct oaths. Patrons: Perkūnas and Žemyna.

title: Priesaika (oath-binding)
text:
How it works (medium, words, timing)
Earth oath (kissing or eating soil): the oath-breaker’s own land rejects him; crops fail, horses throw him, the forest loses him. Thunder oath (on an axe, or by an oak struck by lightning): Perkūnas enforces it. Blood-brotherhood (susibroliavimas): shared fate; one feels the other’s death. Safe-conduct oaths count. Christian oaths on relics are enforced by the Iron Saint among the Order’s men, so the Order distrusts converts who swore on pagan forms first. An oath sworn on a claimed person’s name binds the Force too.

title: Priesaika (oath-binding)
text:
Costs
The breaker’s: lightning, a rejecting land, the loss of the god’s favour. The keeper’s: Kęstutis pays for every word he has sworn since the ox oath (Book VI ch. 28). A precise oath pleases Perkūnas, who reads the words and finds them exact, not because he forgives but because exactness pleases him (Book VI ch. 13).

title: Priesaika (oath-binding)
text:
Limits & counters
Oaths are kept to the letter by gods: Perkūnas and Gabija are exact, and what is deceived by the letter is still taken by the spirit (Book VI ch. 11). An oath cannot be sworn by one who does not mean it, or it rings false (the pebble dies at the false baptism, Book I ch. 19).

title: Priesaika (oath-binding)
text:
Folk basis [Record]
[Record]. Pagan Lithuanians swore on the gods or the earth, with animal sacrifice; treaties were sworn in pagan form. In 1351 Kęstutis swore a pagan oath to Louis of Hungary with an ox, promised baptism, and left without keeping it (Polish chroniclers; verify Jan of Czarnków). Earth-oaths and thunder-oaths are later folklore and reconstruction. The Rus’ swore by Perun in the 10th century.

title: Priesaika (oath-binding)
text:
Notable practitioners
The Krivis; Kęstutis (the ox oath, Book VI ch. 13, 17; Rudau, ch. 24); Skirgaila (the broken safe-conduct, Book I ch. 1, 2, 8); Vytautas (Ostrów, Book II ch. 11; the renewal, Book III ch. 17).

title: Iron Saint’s fearlessness
text:
What it is
The Iron Saint’s fearlessness: granted power from the Iron Saint. It gives tireless marching, immunity to terror and absence of pity.

title: Iron Saint’s fearlessness
text:
Who can use it (path & tier)
Order knights and their commanders who are “real enough”: Zöllner (tier 3, from 1382) and Jungingen (tier 3, from 1407). It comes when thousands of prayers, indulgences and Reise marches are poured into one battle so that the fight is easy for all who truly believe.

title: Iron Saint’s fearlessness
text:
How it works (medium, words, timing)
No words are needed from the knight; the prayers do the work. Signs: furnace heat in winter, quench-water smell, crosses that ring like anvils, ice melting on the shields, snow blackening under their steps (Book VI ch. 24). The ranks narrow and thicken; faces “of men who feel nothing” (Book VI ch. 7).

title: Iron Saint’s fearlessness
text:
Costs
Pity dies; such knights cannot weep. The Force’s nature binds the bearer, and the gift can be withdrawn all at once: at Grunwald a knight lowers his sword and tears come, then another and a third (Book III ch. 20).

title: Iron Saint’s fearlessness
text:
Limits & counters
It counters Earth’s Unmovable Will and Fire’s terror (magic rules §9): neither has a grip on the knights. Against it: the only counter in the books is the Force’s own death, at Grunwald (Book III ch. 20), and the weeping that follows. The gift does not care what creed the bearer has; it needs only appetite and an institution to feed it.

title: Iron Saint’s fearlessness
text:
Folk basis [Record]
[Record]. The Order was a religious order of monk-knights under a Rule, with Marian devotion, and its Reise campaigns (with Western “guests”, indulgences and the Ehrentisch feast) were preached as crusades. Chroniclers (Dusburg, Wigand) recorded real discipline and real brutality. The “fearlessness” is saga overlay.

title: Iron Saint’s fearlessness
text:
Notable practitioners
Zöllner (Book I ch. 17–18), Jungingen (Book III ch. 11, 20), and the nameless knights of the Strėva (1348) and Rudau (1370) fights in Book VI ch. 7 and 24. Brother Hartmann, Marienburg’s stove-keeper, notices the cellar stone warming (Book III ch. 11).

title: Gintarystė (amber-craft)
text:
What it is
Amber-craft: Saulė’s grief as the universal medium. Amber stores memory and carries workings, and it is the only medium that all five elements accept (Kalba).

title: Gintarystė (amber-craft)
text:
Who can use it (path & tier)
Tier 4 amber priestesses (the Palanga line, Birutė) work it fully; any bearer, even ungifted, can release charged amber with the right word (tier 0). Patron: Saulė.

title: Gintarystė (amber-craft)
text:
How it works (medium, words, timing)
Raw amber carries any working. Charged amber holds a working breathed into it, released later by the bearer. Anchored amber carries the caster’s blood and links caster and bearer across any distance, only one anchor per caster at a time (a second breaks the first). Memory amber takes a last memory from one who dies holding it, and may show it to a seer. Amber answers to the truth of the bearer: the pebble is warm when freely given (Book I ch. 3), cold at the false baptism (ch. 19), burning at Žemyna’s price (ch. 20), hot at an honest choice (ch. 23), glowing at the baptism honest about its dishonesty (ch. 29).

title: Gintarystė (amber-craft)
text:
Costs
The anchoring caster pays for every working done through the anchor; when Birutė cast from Palanga she paid in her voice and sight (Book I ch. 14–25). Amber taken from the shore after a storm without an offering goes cold for its life.

title: Gintarystė (amber-craft)
text:
Limits & counters
One anchor at a time. Consecrated stone chills it: the pebble dies in the Order’s fortress (Book I ch. 19) and cannot be used while Vytautas carries the Order’s sword. The Order’s Bernsteinmeister burn charged amber. It does not flatter its bearer (Book III ch. 21, 25).

title: Gintarystė (amber-craft)
text:
Folk basis [Record]
[Record]. Baltic amber has been traded since antiquity (Tacitus, Germania 45, has the Aestii gathering it), and amber was a grave good. The Teutonic Order controlled the Prussian amber trade and punished private gathering harshly. That amber remembers, or that it is Saulė’s tears, is saga overlay; the folk record ties amber to Jūratė’s shattered palace.

title: Gintarystė (amber-craft)
text:
Notable practitioners
Birutė and the Palanga priestesses; Vytautas (the pebble: Book I ch. 3–29; it cracks at his death, Book IV ch. 29); the kneeling statue (kneeling woman); the Flame-Keeper (Book V ch. 29, the last speaking through amber).

title: Vėjas (Wind)
text:
Deity & zenith
Deity: Vėjopatis. Incantation: Vėjas tau neš (“Wind for you shall carry”), man for oneself. Medium: open air with wind. Zenith: storms and Vėlinės (late October–2 November, when the vėlės travel): cost halved; doubled in caves and still air.

title: Vėjas (Wind)
text:
Boon
Shadow Speed and far-speech: fog, swiftness and carried words. The fog is real fog, never an illusion (Law of Truth). It carries speech to the dead through the god and a message across distance, with an amber anchor making distance free.

title: Vėjas (Wind)
text:
Minor / major cost
Minor: vertigo. Major: loss of voice: only whistling, for days, and permanently with repeated use. In Book VI ch. 16 the cost is small but present: Birutė, casting for Kęstutis before his 1361 capture, leans on the table “as if the ground had become far”. Birutė’s voice fails after the Krėva fog (Book I ch. 14–25), and the vessel’s declining body is the bill. The Five-Voice cost, a little of every price at once, is cumulative (magic rules §4.2).

title: Vėjas (Wind)
text:
Limits
The White Silence smothers Wind (no sound, no far-speech). It cannot be cast in a cave or still air without doubling. A wind-cast “man” in Book II ch. 27 helps Vytautas move unseen after a defeat. Without the surety the cost is paid in full.

title: Vėjas (Wind)
text:
Uses in the books
Book I ch. 11: Birutė at the sea: “Vėjas tau neš… Vėjopati, let the fog be his shield.” Ch. 14: the Krėva fog, white, thick, real. Ch. 15: the Five-Voice in the swamp. Ch. 25: a thinner fog, her last mortal strength. Book II ch. 27: Vytautas, after Vorskla (Vėjas man neš). Book VI ch. 16: far-listening for Kęstutis (Vėjas tau neš: “I will hear”).

title: Žvaigždės (Stars)
text:
Deity & zenith
Deity: Praurimė, with Laima, whose spinning the seer reads. Incantation: Žvaigždės tau švytės (“Stars for you shall shine”). Medium: a starlit sky. Zenith: Kūčios, winter-solstice midnight (~13 December in 1382, not the Christian 24th): cost halved; doubled in daylight; impossible under overcast.

title: Žvaigždės (Stars)
text:
Boon
Clear Sight: seeing at distance, through time (as possibility, never certainty) and into the truth. Every Praurimė vision shows the seer something about herself (Law of Truth).

title: Žvaigždės (Stars)
text:
Minor / major cost
Minor: hours of blindness. Major: blind for days, or the permanent loss of one beloved face from memory. At the wrong hour the price doubles: Birutė’s ch. 3 vision at Dagotuvės costs “two days, maybe three” of blindness (Book I). At the right hour: Book V ch. 29, “Praurimė shone highest, and the price was half. Half. Still everything.”

title: Žvaigždės (Stars)
text:
Limits
It shows branches, never a fixed trunk: prophecy is not fate. Overcast sky makes it impossible. A Praurimė seer can see through the Shadow-Seller’s illusions at the cost of blindness, the only such counter besides wit. Consecrated stone doubles the cost.

title: Žvaigždės (Stars)
text:
Uses in the books
Book I ch. 3 (the Ship of swords and the first Sutartis); ch. 9 (the vault of Praurimė’s night as Kęstutis’s torch fades); ch. 15 (the Five-Voice ends in “the cold brightness of Praurimė’s eyes”, and he faints); ch. 27 (Birutė sees the small flame in the stone vault). Book V ch. 29 (the Queen’s last working, for the dying Flame-Keeper, at the Kūčios zenith: afterwards she can no longer speak through the amber).

title: Žemė (Earth)

Deity & zenith
Deity: Žemyna. Incantation: Žemė tau laikys (“Earth for you shall hold”), man for oneself. Medium: bare earth. Zenith: Dagotuvės, autumn-equinox dusk (~14–15 September): cost halved. Off zenith: the working is impossible at sea or in the air. Her price for desecration (Book I ch. 20) is a separate matter: an earth-debt, not a working.

title: Žemė (Earth)
text:
Boon
Unmovable Will: stillness and endurance, a will that does not bend. Cast on another (tau) it holds him; cast on oneself (man) it “holds more firmly, but only me” (Book II ch. 19).

title: Žemė (Earth)
text:
Minor / major cost
Minor: stiffness. Major: petrification for the length of the effect, and a permanent loss of grace. In Book II ch. 19 the last Samogitian žynys Kantaudas turns to river-stone from the hand upward, before the oak the axemen fell at Salynas: “let it take me; let them see what they are cutting”. In ch. 27 Vytautas, fleeing after Vorskla, says Žemė man laikys and goes rooted and heavy; his horse freezes and a patrol’s eyes slide off him.

title: Žemė (Earth)
text:
Limits
Impossible at sea or in the air. The Iron Saint’s knights are immune to Earth’s terror. The earth also remembers the working as residue (Memory, magic §5.3).

text:
Uses in the books
Book I ch. 3 (as one of the five lines); ch. 20 (Žemyna’s price for a burned village is a red blister under the pouch, and the pebble goes cold); Book III ch. 8 (Henė: blood spilled “where a debt is owed” at Dagotuvės is heard); Book II ch. 19, 27 above.

title: Sandėris (bargain)
text:
What it is
Sandėris: bought power. A deal worded precisely, with the Shadow-Seller (a shard of Velnias) or a lesser spirit, binding the parties only by the letter, never by the Three Laws.

title: Sandėris (bargain)
text:
Who can use it (path & tier)
Anyone desperate (tier 0). Canon bargainers: Jogaila (1380: the “easy way” of the trap), Skirgaila (Krėva), and later Vytautas (Book II’s Vorskla vision; Book IV’s crown). Either party may initiate; the human is rarely informed.

title: Sandėris (bargain)
text:
How it works (medium, words, timing)
Velnias never cheats; he drafts. The deal is free at first; the “thread” comes later, a small favour then a larger one. Signs of a bargain in progress: sounds die (the Breath of the Void), warm coins, a figure at the edge of the firelight, the three black stones.

title: Sandėris (bargain)
text:
Costs
Paid later, with interest. The price is “something worth more than you thought”. For Jogaila: his line inherits the crown and loses the land. For Skirgaila: to be used and discarded. Deferred costs compound.

title: Sandėris (bargain)
text:
Limits & counters
Beatable only by cleverness, never strength or faith: the folk crop-division tale (ATU 1030) is the model, with the peasant planting turnips and rye. A Praurimė seer can see through the Shadow-Seller’s illusions, at the cost of blindness. The Shadow-Seller alone can lie; mortals cannot.

title: Sandėris (bargain)
text:
Folk basis [Record]
[Record]. There is no recorded “bargain” system. The folk base is tales of the devil’s contract, the clever peasant who cheats Velnias (ATU 1030) and the aitvaras-keeper whose house burns if the spirit is not fed; the treasure that is Velnias’s. The saga makes the folk figure literal.

title: Sandėris (bargain)
text:
Notable practitioners
Jogaila, Skirgaila (graph tier 0); Vytautas’s Vorskla vision (1399); Žygimantas (Book V ch. 19). Henė admires the 1411 Toruń clause “for the lifetimes of king and prince” as a sentence the Devil himself could not draft more cleanly (Book III ch. 25). Book I ch. 19 is titled “Velnio Sandėris”; Book IV ch. 22 “Paskutinis Sandėris” (Lutsk).

text:
House card



Seat

A drop of amber with a flame inside. [Saga invention]

Patron / burden

title: Palanga amber-priestess line (Gintaro vaidilutės)
text:
Lineage
Basis [Record]: Birutė’s Palanga origin is a strong Lithuanian tradition (Birutė Hill, her role as a vaidilutė guarding a sacred fire). Długosz has her drowned in 1382; Lithuanian tradition has her living to c. 1416. Everything else is invention. The gift runs through the mothers, and each generation gives one daughter to the shore flame. Birutė is the last vessel. Her maternal kin stay unnamed and few; a grandmother who was a vessel before her is the cleanest invention. The tradition that Birutė’s relatives were killed in 1382 can mean that Jogaila’s men tried to end the line (source to verify).

title: Palanga amber-priestess line (Gintaro vaidilutės)
text:
Feuds & alliances
Allied to the Kęstutaičiai by Birutė’s marriage; patron of Kęstutaičiai through the Amber Queen. Opposed in the saga by the Polish clergy who come to break the statue in 1417–18.

title: Palanga amber-priestess line (Gintaro vaidilutės)
text:
Fate across the books

VI: Birutė is chosen; the “abduction” (Būk paimta) places the Amber Queen’s vessel in the Gediminid bed; Vytautas is born under the three spinners.
I: Birutė becomes the Queen (1384); the kneeling amber statue stands at Palanga (the pebble; the statue).
IV: the clergy try to break the idol; their boat goes down.
V: a remnant of women keeps a hidden fire without a vessel. The statue no longer glows in 1445 (ch. 25) and the sea takes it in 1450 (ch. 29).

title: House of Luxembourg
text:
House card



Seat
Buda (Hungary), Prague (Bohemia) and the imperial court. [Record]


Arms / sigil
The Luxembourg lion; Sigismund’s arms combine Hungary, Bohemia and the imperial eagle. He founded the Order of the Dragon in 1408. [Record]


Words

Patron / burden
The Shadow-Seller serves him in 1429–30; the Gold-Glutton flatters him. [Saga]

title: House of Luxembourg
text:
Lineage
Sigismund (1368–1437), son of Emperor Charles IV: King of Hungary 1387, King of the Romans 1411, of Bohemia 1419/1436, Emperor 1433. Married Mary of Hungary (1385), then Barbara of Celje (1405/08), a cousin of Jogaila’s second queen Anna of Celje (relationship to verify). [Record]

title: House of Luxembourg
text:
Feuds & alliances
Arbiter between Poland and the Order (the Breslau award of 1420 went against Poland); host of the Council of Constance; ally of the Order in 1409–10; opponent of the Polish–Lithuanian union, which a Lithuanian crown could split.

title: House of Luxembourg
text:
Fate across the books

III: a reigning king of forty-one, not a “younger” figure, who takes the Order’s money before Grunwald.
IV: at the Congress of Lutsk (Jan 1429) he offers Vytautas a crown, then sends it by couriers who are robbed on the Polish border in August 1430. In the saga, Henė is his jester and the crown turns to leaves.
V: dead by 1437; his daughter’s marriage to Albert II of Habsburg carries his claims to the Habsburgs. [Record]

title: Jogailaičiai (Jagiellonians)
text:
House card



Seat
Vilnius (as Grand Dukes), Krėva (Algirdas’s patrimonial castle, Jogaila’s refuge and prison of 1381–82), Vitebsk (Uliana’s dower lands), later Kraków (Wawel). [Record]


Arms / sigil
The Vytis for the Grand Duchy; Jogaila’s personal double cross on his seals after his baptism (1386); the Polish White Eagle quartered with the Vytis on royal seals (arrangement to verify). [Record] Saga sigil: a crow on a crown, the Shadow-Seller’s eyes. [Saga invention]


Words
Tyla toliau nueina. “Silence goes further.” [Saga invention]


Patron / burden
The Shadow-Seller (Jogaila’s 1382 bargain: his line inherits the crown and loses the land); the White Silence where baptisms are bought; later the Gold-Glutton. [Saga]

title: Jogailaičiai (Jagiellonians)
text:
Lineage
Algirdas’s second marriage (1350) to Uliana of Tver produced the inner dynasty: Jogaila (c. 1362 – 1 Jun 1434; Władysław from 1386), Skirgaila, Kaributas, Lengvenis, Karigaila, Vygantas and Švitrigaila. [Record]
Jogaila’s four marriages: Jadwiga of Anjou (1386; one daughter, who died in infancy in 1399), Anna of Celje (1402; Jadwiga, 1408–31), Elżbieta Granowska (1417; none) and Sophia of Halshany (1422), mother of Władysław III (1424–44), Casimir IV (1427–92) and a short-lived Kazimierz. [Record] Sophia’s family is the Alšėniškiai. Casimir was elected Grand Duke on 29 Jun 1440, aged 12, and crowned King of Poland on 25 Jun 1447.

title: Jogailaičiai (Jagiellonians)
text:
Feuds & alliances
Jogaila against Kęstutis (1380–82) and Vytautas (1382–84, 1389–92); Švitrigaila against everyone (1393, 1402, 1408, 1430–32); Skirgaila’s resentment of Jogaila’s ingratitude. Marriage web: Moscow (Lengvenis, Elena), Masovia (Aleksandra and Siemowit IV), Pomerania, Mecklenburg. After 1386 the house is also the Polish crown, and the Lesser Poland lords rule through it.

title: Jogailaičiai (Jagiellonians)
text:
Fate across the books

I: Jogaila, bought by Henė, kills his uncle and agrees the Krėva Union (1385); baptised 1386. II: distant in Kraków; Skirgaila rules for him. III: reconciliation at Grunwald.
IV: outlives Vytautas, still guilty; his sons come only from the last wife, and the lords sell their succession for privileges.
V: Jogaila dies at Gródek (1 Jun 1434), Henė’s last stone dropping. Casimir inherits both realms, and the Grand Duchy becomes a province of his house, as the bargain’s letter said. [Saga]

title: Žemyna
text:
Folk sources [Record]
Žemyna (“earth”, from žemė) is the Baltic earth goddess. The first written naming is Jan Łasicki’s De diis Samagitarum (c. 1582, printed 1615; “Zemina”), followed by Daukša, Daniel Klein (1666) and Matthäus Prätorius (1690s). Prätorius describes the household rite of žemyneliauti: beer poured on the ground, a cock or hen cooked and eaten, the remains offered to the goddess. Other recorded practices: bread of the last harvest buried before sowing, a black piglet sacrificed, and kissing the earth in prayer. She is the wife of Perkūnas in later folklore (hence no ploughing before the first thunder), though the pairing is a reconstruction.
Earth-oaths (kissing or eating soil) come from later ethnography; medieval treaties name gods, not the earth. Dagotuvės as an equinox feast is a modern Romuva reconstruction.

title: Žemyna
text:
In the saga
Domain: earth, fertility, oaths sworn on soil. Element: Earth (“Žemė tau laikys”), zenith Dagotuvės (autumn-equinox dusk). Force-face: with Medeina’s grief she hardened into the Root-Mother (canon D8: not a synonym). She patronises Priesaika: an earth-oath is binding physically, and the oath-breaker’s land rejects him.
Book I: the Pebble’s first working is “the old power of Gabija and Žemyna, passed through a mother’s hands” (ch. 3); Kęstutis says “Žemyna still holds us” (ch. 4) and, dying, calls his nephews the greatest cowards “this Žemyna ever carried” (ch. 9). After Vytautas’s army burns a village, Žemyna “took the first part of the debt” (ch. 20): a red blister under the pouch and a cold pebble. Henė notes that Žemyna has her hour at Dagotuvės and that blood spilled on owed ground is heard then (Book III ch. 8). Samogitian baptism puts one God above “Perkūnas and Žemyna” (Book IV ch. 3). Weakness: she turns away from the one who burns the land, and she cannot work at sea or in the air.

title: Žemyna
text:
Offerings & taboos
Bread and beer given to the ground; the kissed soil of oaths. Taboos: ploughing or sowing before the first thunder (later folk rule), and breaking an earth-oath, for the land will refuse the breaker.

title: Žemyna

Pronunciation

title: Vėjopatis
text:
Folk sources [Record]
Vėjopatis (“lord of the wind”, vėjas + patis, as in Žemėpatis) is the Lithuanian wind god. The only early witness is Matthäus Prätorius (1690s); he is not in the medieval chronicles. Later writers add that he is master of Dausos, the afterlife meadow, and that he blows wicked souls into oblivion; those details lack early sources, and Bangpūtys is sometimes made his father or double. The -patis form (“lord of…”) recurs in Łasicki’s Zemopacios and is a pattern some scholars suspect of being artificial. His role as carrier of souls along the Birds’ Way is the saga’s synthesis, not a recorded belief.

title: Vėjopatis
text:
In the saga
Domain: the four winds, messenger between worlds. Element: Wind (“Vėjas tau neš”), zenith Vėlinės and storms. Force-face: none. He carries the vėlės along the Birds’ Way, and speech with the dead goes through him: a fed vėlė can be asked for help through him (veles).
Book I ch. 3: Birutė’s Sutartis promises that “the winds in Vėjopatis’s lips will whisper betrayals” to Vytautas. Ch. 11: “Vėjopati, let the fog become his shield.” Ch. 15: the Five-Voice cry in the swamp is answered, the fog thickens until he is unseen. Ch. 25: the fog is “visibly weaker”, Birutė’s last mortal strength. The Krėva fog (ch. 14) is real fog (Law of Truth), cast from Palanga through the amber anchor at his zenith, since the escape falls on Vėlinės. Costs: vertigo for a minor working, loss of voice (only whistling) for days for a major one, permanent with repeated use. Limits: doubled in caves or still air; the White Silence smothers Wind altogether.

title: Vėjopatis
text:
Offerings & taboos
The vėlės are fed at Vėlinės (late October to 2 November in later folk custom): food left out overnight, the bathhouse heated, graves visited with fire, quiet kept in the house. A fed vėlė can be asked for help through him.

title: Praurimė
text:
Folk sources [Record]
Praurimė is said to be the goddess of the sacred fire, served by vaidilutės. She is the most doubtful of the saga’s gods. The name is not in Łasicki, the Volhynian Chronicle, Prätorius or the early lists; the standard source is the 19th-century mythographer Teodor Narbutt (1835), whose reconstructions are often called inventions, and Vėlius and others discard many of his names. Stryjkowski (1582) does describe a perpetual fire in the Vilnius valley, and Dusburg a priest-kept fire at Romowe, but neither names Praurimė. Modern writers often equate Praurimė with Gabija and disagree about which the priestesses served. Her etymology is unknown. The saga’s vaidilutė as a vestal of an eternal flame is also shaped by Romantic historiography, though sacred fires themselves are attested (Długosz).

title: Praurimė
text:
In the saga
Domain: the fire of the stars, the sky-twin of the eternal flame. Element: Stars (“Žvaigždės tau švytės”), zenith Kūčios (winter-solstice midnight). Force-face: none. Folk memory has her as a goddess of sacred fire, while the saga’s seers know her as the fire above, the stars read as the threads Laima spins. Both are true (cosmology §3.1).
Book I ch. 3 is her textbook scene: Birutė opens a shutter at Dagotuvės, off her zenith, and sees a ship that “might not appear”; “Praurimė shows always a possibility, not a doom”; the cost is doubled, blindness of two or three days. Ch. 9: “the icy vault of Praurimė’s night” as Kęstutis’s torch fades. Ch. 15: the Five-Voice ends in “the cold brightness of Praurimė’s eyes”. Book V ch. 29 at Kūčios: “Praurimė shone highest, and the price was half. Half. Still everything.” Costs: hours of blindness, or days of it, or a beloved face lost from memory. Limits: impossible under overcast and doubled in daylight.

title: Praurimė
text:
Offerings & taboos
Kūčios is the seer’s night: shadows on the wall, firelight in amber, the lots. A starry sky is the medium; no altar. Rule (Law of Truth): ask only for what you truly want, or you get nothing, or what you do want.

title: Mėnuo
text:
Folk sources [Record]
Mėnuo is both “the Moon” and “month” (cognate with English moon and month). He is a dievaitis, a son of Dievas, in folk reckoning; the Baltic moon is male. The main source is a mythological daina (“Mėnuo Saulužę vedė / Pirmą pavasarėlį”), printed in Rhesa’s collection (1825; verify) and variants: in the first spring the Moon married the Sun; he wandered off at night and fell in love with Aušrinė, the morning star; Perkūnas, enraged, cut the Moon in two with his sword. The waxing and waning are the wound. Other variants have the couple divorce, with their daughter Žemyna seen by sun by day and moon by night, or the Moon’s face disfigured by Dievas or Saulė. No medieval source names him as an object of cult; his reconstructed role is folkloric. The myth is usually read as a law of marital and oath fidelity.

title: Mėnuo
text:
In the saga
Domain: the Moon, tides, the faithless husband. Element: none, but he is patron of Water: the tides and the full moon fix Bangpūtys‘s zenith. Force-face: none. In the legend the Moon is the oath-breaker whom Perkūnas cuts; the saga uses this as nursery-law for Perkūnas’s claim and as the amber-priestesses’ picture of Jogaila (“a Mėnuo”; the seducer Aušrinė goes unpunished). Amber washes ashore at the full moon: Saulė’s tears returned monthly by her husband.
The books never name him as a speaker. He is a calendar and a law: Book I ch. 27’s Water working at the full moon is correctly timed, and the saga’s reading (legends §7) makes Vytautas’s false baptism (ch. 19) “Mėnuo’s sin” against his oath. Weakness: none; he is the lesson, not the actor, and he heals monthly only to be cut again.

title: Mėnuo
text:
Offerings & taboos
No cult or offering is recorded, and the saga adds none. His only observances are the calendar ones: the full moon and spring ice-break as Water’s zenith, and Perkūnas’s law that the oath-breaker is cut.
