title: Laima
text:
Folk sources [Record]
Laima decides each person’s fate at birth (Laima lėmė, “Laima decreed”), and she appears in songs at births and weddings. The earliest written name is “Laimelea” in Wilhelm Martini’s Latin preface to Daniel Klein’s Lithuanian songs (1666); Prätorius and later 17th–18th-century writers follow. Latvian Laima has two sisters, Kārta and Dēkla. Nineteenth-century birth rites, performed by women in the bathhouse (pirtis), offered her a hen, linen or towels. The cuckoo is her bird in later folklore.
Contested: Lithuanian Laima is sometimes one goddess and sometimes three, and she is often confused with laimė (“luck”) and laumė (“fairy”). Dalia (“share”) and Giltinė as Laima’s sisters, and the seven spinning deivės valdytojos (Gimbutas’s reconstruction), are largely folk or modern. Greimas argued that Laima knows fate rather than imposes it, against the old label of a “fatalistic” religion.

title: Laima
text:
In the saga
Domain: fate, share, death. Element: none. Force-face: none. She spins every thread at birth; Dalia measures it and Giltinė cuts it (cosmology §3.1, bestiary). Laima’s spinning is why seers see possibilities, never certainties, and she is patron of Užkalbėjimai and of Stars (Praurimė reads her threads).
Her scene is Book VI ch. 12 (“Laima prie Lopšio”): at Vytautas’s birth (1350), three women come to Birutė’s lamplit room, a spinner who says “we are not gods; we only read the thread”, a merry younger sister, and a tall grey one with sheep-shears. They foretell three baptisms, a crown that will follow him all his life, and that he will outlive his heirs. Birutė stops the shears with the word “Dar ne” (“not yet”). Laima warns that “not yet” is paid for, and Birutė answers “I will pay”: the first sign of her surety. Book I ch. 3’s vision, “a possibility, not a doom”, is the same law. Weakness: she keeps her ledger to the letter, yet a thread can be asked to be re-tied, and every re-tying shortens another.

title: Laima
text:
Offerings & taboos
Linen, a towel or a hen left for her in the bathhouse at a birth, women only. Fates spun without a gift are plainer after 1387, with fewer surprises.

title: Gabija
text:
Folk sources [Record]
Gabija is the hearth fire and its guardian spirit. The name is tied (uncertainly) to gaubti, “to cover”, for banking the coals. In the old lists she appears only in Jan Łasicki’s De diis Samagitarum (c. 1582, 1615), as the household-fire spirit (“Gabie”). Narbutt (19th century) split her into hearth and bread aspects; treat with caution. Hearth custom is later ethnography: bread and salt given to the fire; coals covered with ash at night so the fire does not “wander”; a bowl of water left so she can wash; no spitting, stamping on or urinating on the fire, or the house will burn.
Not Gabija: the great sacred fires. The record is: Dusburg’s Romowe flame (1326), Jerome of Prague’s household snakes and a “perpetual fire” (via Piccolomini), Stryjkowski’s fire in the Vilnius valley, and Długosz’s account of Jogaila extinguishing it in 1387. None names Gabija. Modern writers often identify Gabija with the sacred-fire goddess Praurimė, and scholars disagree about which the vaidilutės served.

title: Gabija
text:
In the saga
Domain: the hearth and sacred fire. Element: Fire (“Ugnis tau degs”), zenith Rasos (summer-solstice noon). Force-face: none; she does not hunger, she guards. Every household fire is a small shrine. Her sparks, cut off when a sacred flame is killed, are the užgesilės.
The saga identifies her with the Šventaragis flame: “Gabijos liepsna” is put out by the king’s buckets and the Krivis does not resist (Book I ch. 29, the baptism). In Book III ch. 17 a lantern flame the size of a palm silences the rain, “Gabija’s work”. In Book VI ch. 11 the old priestess says the vow-fire “is not a fool, only exact”: Birutė swore “I will not give myself” and Kęstutis found a loophole; the gods one cheats by the letter still take by the spirit. Weakness: she punishes insult and desecration, and she cannot defend a flame no one tends.

title: Gabija
text:
Offerings & taboos
Bread and salt, a bowl of water by the hearth, ashes over the coals at night; fire-leaping at Rasos. Taboo: spitting into the fire or stepping over it.

title: Gabija
text:
Pronunciation
gah-BIH-yah (IPA [ɡɐˈbʲɪjɐ]), stress ga-BI-ja.

title: Bangpūtys
text:
Folk sources [Record]
Bangpūtys is the Lithuanian god of waves, sea and storms. The name is read as banga (“wave”) plus pūsti (“to blow”). He is late and thinly attested: the early lists give him only through Matthäus Prätorius (1690s), who reports a single rite; he is absent from the medieval chronicles. Later authors made him the father of the four winds (Rytys, Pietys, Šiaurys, Vakaris) and sometimes link him to Vėjopatis.

title: Bangpūtys
text:
In the saga
Domain: the sea, storms, waves. Element: Water (“Vanduo tau teks”), zenith at full moon, high tide and the spring ice-break. Force-face: none. He is in an old feud with Perkūnas over Jūratė, and Mėnuo sets his tides.
Book I ch. 11: Birutė throws her wedding ring into the waves, “Gabija’s fire in this metal went out, giving way to Bangpūtys’s depth”; the sea returns it three times (the ring-thrice motif, canon D3). Ch. 27 (1384): her full-moon working pays Vytautas’s surety in full. Book VI ch. 10: before the ice-break, the old priestess says “tonight Bangpūtys is strongest, the ice just broke; the cost is lower”. Costs per the magic rules: a minor Water working brings raging thirst; a major one makes the caster take part of the patient’s wound. Limits: it can pull a soul back from the gate but cannot heal a mortal wound, it is doubled away from living water, and the White Silence freezes it.

title: Bangpūtys
text:
Offerings & taboos
Prätorius reports a single sea-rite, and its details are not reliable. In the saga the offering is amber, or a ring given to the water (Birutė’s, Book I ch. 11); the sea may refuse it.

title: Baltoji Tyla (White Silence)
text:
Nature
Egregore (cosmology §3.3): Baltoji Tyla. It is fed by purchased purity: baptisms bought or sold for land and crowns. It gathers wherever a baptism is being bought, which is why it settles on Jogaila’s Vilnius in 1382 (he is already pricing a crown) and on Krėva, where the 1385 union will be signed. Jadvyga at her best is its victim, not its servant.

title: Baltoji Tyla (White Silence)
text:
Wants
The Order’s absolute dominion; the world “bleached” of pagan colour. Quiet and stillness as a state of grace.

title: Baltoji Tyla (White Silence)
text:
Takes (its price)
Fearlessness, holy calm, healing with frost, and the “Crusader’s Winter” of early snows that starve defenders. The healer gives up warmth and sound dies around them (the frost-touch).

title: Baltoji Tyla (White Silence)
text:
Signs & manifestations
Frost flowers on blades and windows that grow slowly “like someone writing”; sound dying; lilies on frozen fields; breath white in summer. Krėva first (Book I ch. 14, November 1382), and then at the 1385 union, where frost ferns grow on the glass while the Latin is read and the quill makes no sound (ch. 28b). Frost around the shoes of a boyar family given vaidilutės in marriage (Book II ch. 3); on Jadvyga’s hands and her child’s lips (ch. 21); on Jogaila’s brows when he kisses her hand.

title: Baltoji Tyla (White Silence)
text:
Vessels, servants, claims
Vessel: Jadvyga (1386–99), a “saint” only because it uses her as a conduit; at her death, per the world bible (hidden_immortals §5), her body does not decay. Fed by: Poland and the Algirdaičiai (from 1382). Servants: the bebalsiai (“the voiceless”, hollowed by bought baptisms).

title: Baltoji Tyla (White Silence)
text:
Weaknesses
It smothers Wind (no sound, no far-speech) and freezes Water workings. Warmth beats it: frost melts when a man weeps (Book IV ch. 14). A žaltys tells Jadvyga that “the Silence will freeze your heart while it saves your soul” (Book II ch. 21).

title: Baltoji Tyla (White Silence)
text:
Arc across the books
I: Krėva (ch. 14), the 1385 union (ch. 28b). II: the church at Vilnius (ch. 3), Jadvyga’s frost (ch. 21). III: Jogaila’s frozen hand on the stone (ch. 3). IV: frost in Jogaila’s rooms (ch. 19). V: after the Last Flame goes out, an unnamed cold fills Trakai (ch. 4). It is the last of the four to become pure institution.

title: Šešėlių Pardavėjas / Henė
text:
Nature
Native Force: a splinter of Velnias that “learned to enjoy the trade” (cosmology §3.2; canon D2). He wears mortal masks: first Hanulas, the Riga-born Vilnius merchant who opened Vilnius to Jogaila in 1382, then Henė the jester (the English docs write “Henne”). He is the only being in the saga who can lie and make illusions; no mortal can (magic rules §1).

title: Šešėlių Pardavėjas / Henė
text:
Wants
Deals, and through deals the dead (the past) to outweigh the living (the future). He serves the deal, never the man.

title: Šešėlių Pardavėjas / Henė
text:
Takes (its price)
Threads: small obligations that compound. Every bargain is kept to the letter, is free at first, and is paid later with interest (magic rules §8). The price for Jogaila: his line inherits the crown and loses the land; for Skirgaila: to be used and discarded.

title: Šešėlių Pardavėjas / Henė
text:
Signs & manifestations
A figure at the edge of the firelight; a voice like your own conscience (the Echo); sounds that die; warm coins; three blackened stones he juggles, one dropped for each bargain collected (three stones). The Krėva silence is his Breath of the Void (Book I ch. 14). The void under his mask is “the hollow where the dead keep the past” (ch. 30).

title: Šešėlių Pardavėjas / Henė
text:
Vessels, servants, claims
Masks and masters: Hanulas; Jogaila’s court (1382), Skirgaila (1387–97), Vytautas’s court (from 1392), Sigismund (1429–30). Bargains: Jogaila, Skirgaila, Vytautas (the Vorskla vision), Žygimantas. Servants: pinčiukas, the aitvaras; objects: the golden chain and the Lutsk crown.

title: Šešėlių Pardavėjas / Henė
text:
Weaknesses
He is beatable only by cleverness, never strength or faith, like the folk peasant who plants turnips then rye. A Praurimė seer can see through his illusions, at the cost of blindness. He fears Perkūnas, and he can be refused: Vytautas’s refusal at Lutsk is the point where the crown turns to leaves.

title: Šešėlių Pardavėjas / Henė
text:
Arc across the books
I: Hanulas and the 1382 trap, the stones, the Breath at Krėva (ch. 5, 12, 14, 28, 30). II: Skirgaila (ch. 1, 10, 16). III: the offer of the cousins (ch. 8). IV: Sigismund’s court, the crown, the last bargain refused (ch. 17, 21–22, 30). V: the chain to Žygimantas; the last unmasking (ch. 19, 24).

title: Perkūno Rūstybė
text:
Nature
Native Force: Perkūnas after a thousand sworn oaths. It is the god’s attention hardened by human worship, war and oath-taking into appetite and agenda (cosmology §2.1, §3.2). It is saga invention built on the folk figure of the oath-keeping thunderer.

title: Perkūno Rūstybė
text:
Wants
Oaths kept; cowards punished. Justice without mercy: it strikes its own as readily as the foe.

title: Perkūno Rūstybė
text:
Takes (its price)
Claims on warriors. Marked Kęstutis, and Vytautas at Krėva in 1382 (Book I ch. 10, the mark): a heavy rhythm in the fingers, a smell of ozone, eyes that catch lightning. It acts through the claimed at moments of its choosing and punishes them when they break their own oath (magic rules §7). It does not empower at will.

title: Perkūno Rūstybė
text:
Signs & manifestations
Lightning that strikes only banners and oaks; thunder that sounds like a traitor’s name; dry storms with no cloud (Book I ch. 6, ch. 21; Book V ch. 2). A single sourceless lightning stroke over Samogitia at Rasos 1411 closes the war (Book III ch. 29). A cracked window (Book I ch. 19) is a warning.

title: Perkūno Rūstybė
text:
Vessels, servants, claims
Claimed: Kęstutis (Book VI), Vytautas. Instruments: the perkūnėlis carved under a sword’s grip (Book III ch. 2, 17; Book VI ch. 1, 16, 30); the oath over a claimed name binds the Force too. Feud with Jūratė and Bangpūtys.

title: Perkūno Rūstybė
text:
Weaknesses
It can be bound by oath: “an oath on a claimed person’s name binds the Force too” (power systems §7), so Vytautas can swear to it and make it act. It cannot be bargained with, only kept faith with, and its claims are contested by the Root-Mother. It is silent when nothing is owed.

title: Perkūno Rūstybė
text:
Arc across the books
VI: marks Kęstutis (ch. 13, 24). I: Krėva (ch. 10), the cracked window (ch. 19), the oak (ch. 21). II: an unspoken debt on the road (ch. 5), Skirgaila’s death “too late” (ch. 16), the Vorskla verdict (ch. 26). III: the renewed oath over the rusted sword (ch. 17); rewards a kept oath at Grunwald. IV: silent after the war (ch. 1). V: thunder at Vytautas’s funeral (ch. 2), once.

title: Gintaro Karalienė (Amber Queen)
text:
Nature
Native Force, and an office, not a goddess (canon D1; cosmology §3.4). It is the sea’s memory of everything gods and men have destroyed, born of Jūratė’s grief when Perkūnas shattered her amber palace. It needs a mortal vessel to act on land. The vessels come from the Palanga amber-priestess line and each ends by giving her mortality back to the sea.

title: Gintaro Karalienė (Amber Queen)
text:
Wants
Memory kept. She preserves the stories of those the other gods forgot, and the sea tells her priestess one thing for forty years: “the Queen lacks land” (Book VI ch. 11).

title: Gintaro Karalienė (Amber Queen)
text:
Takes (its price)
The vessel’s mortality. Birutė, the last vessel, “gave everything” so that Vytautas’s sword should never be powerless (Book I prologue, ch. 27). The Queen never raises the dead; she keeps them, in memory and in amber.

title: Gintaro Karalienė (Amber Queen)
text:
Signs & manifestations
Surf-whisper that comes only through amber (Book I ch. 3); foam on the waves; amber appearing in the hands of the lost; eyes gone sea-dark (ch. 11); the sea refusing to drown her and returning her ring three times (ch. 11; canon D3). After ch. 27 she acts only through amber Birutė touched.

title: Gintaro Karalienė (Amber Queen)
text:
Vessels, servants, claims
Vessels: Jūratė (mythic first holder), Birutė (1382–84). Anchors: the kneeling woman at Palanga (whoever moves her dies at sea) and Vytautas’s pebble. Patron of the Kęstutaičiai and the Palanga vaidilutės. Place: Palanga.

title: Gintaro Karalienė (Amber Queen)
text:
Weaknesses
Once Birutė is spent she cannot walk again, and her reach is only through touched amber. Consecrated stone dampens amber workings; Church men want the statue gone (“remove the idol they call Jūratė”, Book IV ch. 8). A vessel is mortal and her price is final.

title: Gintaro Karalienė (Amber Queen)
text:
Arc across the books
VI: Birutė chosen at Palanga (ch. 10–11). I: frame narration (prologue), the Queen heard through amber (ch. 3), the widow’s eyes (ch. 11), the amber kneeling woman (ch. 27). II: only the pebble remains. III: her voice at sea before Grunwald (ch. 14). IV: Polish clergy come for the statue (ch. 8). title: Teutonic Order
text:
Overview
[Record] A crusading order that settled in Prussia in 1226-30 and ruled it from Marienburg. In this saga’s years it is the Grand Duchy’s chief enemy and its main source of hostages and treaties. Grand Masters: Winrich von Kniprode (1351-24 Jun 1382), Konrad Zöllner von Rotenstein (elected 5 Oct 1382, d. 20 Aug 1390), Konrad von Wallenrode (1391-93), Konrad von Jungingen (1393-1407), Ulrich von Jungingen (1407, killed at Grunwald 15 Jul 1410), Heinrich von Plauen (1410-13), Michael Küchmeister (1414-22), Paul von Rusdorf (1422-41). Key dates: Dovydiškės 31 May 1380; Dubysa 31 Oct 1382; Königsberg 30 Jan 1384; Salynas 12 Oct 1398; First Peace of Thorn 1 Feb 1411; Melno 27 Sep 1422; Christmemel 19 Jun 1431; Brest 31 Dec 1435; the Prussian Confederation, 1440.

title: Kingdom of Poland (Lesser Poland lords)
text:
Overview
[Record] After Louis I of Hungary and Poland died on 10 Sep 1382, the Lesser Poland lords crowned his daughter Jadwiga King (16 Oct 1384) and chose Jogaila as her husband at Krėva (14 Aug 1385). Jogaila was baptised Władysław at Kraków on 15 Feb 1386, married Jadwiga on 18 Feb and was crowned on 4 Mar. Jadwiga died on 17 Jul 1399; Jogaila reigned until 1 Jun 1434. Milestones: Vilnius-Radom (1401), Grunwald (15 Jul 1410), Horodło (2 Oct 1413), the crown affair (1429-30), the Jedlnia privilege (4 Mar 1430), Władysław III at Varna (10 Nov 1444), Casimir crowned 25 Jun 1447.

Overview
[Record] Rurikid princes of Moscow, rising as the Horde’s tribute-collectors. Dmitry Donskoy (1359-89) won Kulikovo (1380), but Tokhtamysh burned Moscow in Aug 1382. Vasily I (1389-1425) married Sofija, Vytautas’s daughter, in 1391; he stood off Vytautas on the Ugra in 1408 and made Vytautas guardian of his son in his 1423 testament. Vasily II (1425-62) was blinded in the civil war of 1446 and restored.

title: Vilkatai (Iron Wolves)
text:
Overview
[Saga invention] The sworn wolf-brotherhood (Brolija; each pack a gauja of five to nine), which calls itself Dievo šunys, “God’s dogs”. Folk sources: Baltic werewolf belief and the 1692 Thiess trial. The packs hold the Iron Wolf’s skull (since 1323) and give Kęstutis the silver wolf in 1345. About 120 in 1382; about 40 after the Vilnius massacre (Book I ch. 7) and the schism; 14 at Kūčios 1430 (V ch. 7); a dozen at Pabaiskas, 1 Sep 1435; Pilkoji lies down with the skull on 2 Nov 1449 (V ch. 28). The Flame-Keeper, burned at Palanga in March 1450, is the last (V ch. 29).

title: Vilkatai (Iron Wolves)
text:
Internal tensions
The 1382 schism split Vilnius packs (loyal to Jogaila’s flame) from Kęstutis’s nine: seven of the nine died in the tents at Jogaila’s camp near Trakai and were buried in the bog; Jonas’s men stayed in Kęstutis’s own camp. The order of the dead after 1430 is a ledger: four taken at Pabaiskas (V ch. 13), five that winter (V ch. 16), then Dobilas, Uosis and Pilkoji. The Order puts a bounty on their hides; the Church hunts them.

Overview
[Record] The German merchant league. The Prussian towns (Danzig, Thorn, Elbing, Königsberg) are the Order’s subjects and increasingly its opponents: the Prussian Confederation of 1440. title: Grand Duchy of Lithuania
text:
Overview
[Record] A pagan realm, the last in Europe, stretching from the Baltic coast to the Rus’ lands. Mindaugas was crowned King in 1253; Gediminas (c. 1316-1341) made Vilnius its capital in 1323; Algirdas (east) and Kęstutis (west) ruled as a diarchy from 1345 to 1377. Grand Dukes in the saga’s years: Jogaila (1377-81; 1382-92), Kęstutis (1381-82), Vytautas (1392-1430, by the Ostrów agreement, 4-5 Aug 1392), Švitrigaila (1430-32), Žygimantas (1432-40) and Casimir (elected 29 Jun 1440, aged 12). Baptism came with Jogaila in 1387 and Samogitia in 1413-17.

On the longest night by the drifted calendar (12 Dec 1449; the calendar has drifted twelve days from Kūčios; Praurimė’s zenith halves Birutė’s cost) Žiežirba lights an ordinary driftwood fire on the Palanga shore, the first fire of his own in forty-four years (green-blue with salt). title: Battle of the Vorskla
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Fought on 12 August 1399 on the Vorskla near present-day Poltava. Vytautas’s coalition (Lithuanians, Ruthenian princes, Poles, Moldavians and Wallachians, some Order knights under Marquard von Salzbach, and the exiled khan Tokhtamysh) was defeated by the army of Edigu and Khan Temür Qutlugh. About 50 princes fought under Vytautas and about 20 were killed, an estimate from Zenonas Ivinskis (1978); later accounts give far higher figures. The dead included Andrei of Polotsk and Dmitry (Demetrius) Starshy, Algirdas’s sons, and Spytko II of Melsztyn. Temür Qutlugh proposed a three-day truce that was a trick to gain time and feigned a retreat to draw the Lithuanians from their wagon-fort; Tokhtamysh fled when he judged it lost. Vytautas barely escaped. Marquard, komtur of Ragnit, brought an Order contingent (en.wikipedia’s 1,600 horse is unconfirmed); Posilge lists nine members of the Order killed and names Marquard among the rescued, and a Marienburg treasurer’s entry of 2 Nov 1399 records the return of the money given for the unit. Consequences: Lithuanian expansion into southern Ruthenia was blocked, Smolensk, Novgorod and Pskov rebelled (Smolensk was recaptured in 1404), he reaffirmed the union with Jogaila and turned east to Moscow and west to the Order; he may have learned the feigned-retreat tactic he used at Grunwald. Sources: Długosz, Posilge, the Itinerarium Witolda, Ivinskis (Wikipedia, Battle of the Vorskla River). Treat the casualty numbers with caution.

title: Battle of the Vorskla
text:
What really happened [Saga]
Henė appeared to Vytautas as a messenger of the East with a vision of a golden throne and a crown at Sarai, and he accepted it in the winter, at which the pebble went cold. The Steppe-Hunger fed: dust devils walked beside the columns and horse-hair turned up in wells. The Root-Mother could not follow, so the wolves did not come; Kalvis and a few loyal wolves went anyway and died on the field. Perkūnas’s verdict on a man who broke his oaths: Form 5 breaks. Vytautas escapes with a handful and no fog from his mother, shame only; he speaks the Five-Voice alone and pays the whole bill: sight and hearing dim, a face goes from memory. The Steppe-Hunger feeds on the field behind him.

title: Battle of the Vorskla
text:
Consequences
Caused by the Treaty of Salynas (which freed his western flank) and leading to the Union of Vilnius and Radom. Jadwiga’s death on 17 July, a month earlier, is the last warning he ignored (her death).

title: Battle of the Vorskla
text:
Dramatisation
Book II ch. 22 “Geležinis Maršas” (Spytko II), ch. 23 “Raudonas Dangus” (Vytautas), ch. 24 “Edigėjus” (Edigu; 11 August), ch. 25 “Dulkės ir Kraujas” (Spytko), ch. 26 “Skerdynės prie Upės” (Vytautas; 12 August), ch. 27 “Antrasis Bėgimas” (Vytautas) and ch. 28 “Kijevo Išpirka” (a Kyivan monk). High summer; the Book II climax.

title: Hanulas and the townsfolk take Vilnius for Jogaila
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
On 12 June 1382, while Kęstutis was in the Severian land against Dymitr Korybut (Kaributas) and Vytautas was at Trakai, the Vilnius townspeople led by the merchant Hanul of Riga took the castle and city and handed them to Jogaila (Wikipedia, Lithuanian Civil War 1381–84; VLE, Hanulas). Hanul (Hennecke, Hannike, Hanulas) was a German-origin merchant from Riga who had become a burgher of Vilnius. He did not “open a gate”: he took the castle and handed over castle and city (the silver is kept only as rumour). He served as the first elder (namiestnik) of Vilnius from 1382 to 1387, took part in diplomatic missions (including the delegation that preceded the Act of Krėva) and died in Kraków c. 1417–18. On 6 July Jogaila signed the two-month Truce of Bražuolė with the Order; on 20 July Trakai surrendered to the joint forces.

title: Hanulas and the townsfolk take Vilnius for Jogaila
text:
What really happened [Saga]
Hanulas is Henė’s first mask (canon D2): a Riga-born merchant of Vilnius whom the Shadow-Seller possessed for a time (Q12 suggests a real man, possessed 1380–82, who never remembers it). The silver is a rumour that the saga keeps as a price: a sack of Riga silver. The same crossed-key mark of Riga appears on the golden chain that later strangles Kęstutis.

title: Hanulas and the townsfolk take Vilnius for Jogaila
text:
Consequences
Caused by Kęstutis’s coup. It leads to the arrest of Kęstutis and Vytautas.

title: Hanulas and the townsfolk take Vilnius for Jogaila
text:
Dramatisation
Book I ch. 1 “Senasis Šernas” (Kęstutis, Trakai: in June the Riga merchant Hanulas and the townspeople took Vilnius castle and handed it over, “už Rygos sidabrą” the people whispered), ch. 2 (Vytautas’s men saw Hanulas’s wagons) and ch. 5 “Dvigubas Veidas” (Jogaila; the silver of Hanulas’s promises in his pockets). The event itself is backstory: 12 June 1382.

title: Truce in the ashes with Jogaila
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
In spring 1384 Jogaila had offered Volhynia with Lutsk, which Vytautas refused, demanding his Trakai patrimony; in July 1384 the two reconciled and Vytautas abandoned the Order, burning its castles (see the burnings). The terms: Grodno, Brest and Podlasie for Vytautas; Trakai stayed with Skirgaila, who had held it since 1382 (Jogaila had promised it to Vytautas in spring 1384 once Skirgaila was settled in Polotsk). Marquard von Salzbach was captured in July 1384. The meeting itself has no documented place or witnesses. Sources: Posilge, Wigand, the Lithuanian chronicles; Kiaupa and Ivinskis in modern writing.

title: Truce in the ashes with Jogaila
text:
What really happened [Saga]
A secret parley in a roofless burnt church at the edge of the Šventaragis grove, with a red dot of fire in the valley below. Jogaila arrives with four guards, no banners or trumpets; Vytautas comes alone in the Order’s battered armour with the cross torn off. Between them lies Kęstutis’s blood. Jogaila says that the Order stood at Trakai: it was the cross or the fire. No forgiveness, only a truce of necessity. Henė knocks two stones together in the dark; Vytautas shows the silver wolf amulet and does not kill. It is the first time since Krėva they have looked each other in the eye.

title: Truce in the ashes with Jogaila
text:
Consequences
Caused by the burnings of 1384. It leads to Birutė’s Amber Sacrifice; the autumn settlement confirms Skirgaila’s hold on Trakai.

title: Vytautas baptised ‘Wigand’ (a lie)
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Vytautas was baptised in the Catholic rite at Tapiau (Tepliava) on 21 October 1383 and took the name Wigand. The Order and Jogaila’s alliance (the Treaty of Dubysa of 31 October 1382) collapsed in June 1383, and in early September the Knights and Vytautas briefly took Trakai and unsuccessfully attacked Vilnius. Konrad Zöllner von Rotenstein had been elected Grand Master after Kniprode’s death on 24 June 1382. The date is attested in the Order’s records (the chronicler is not identified in my sources; verify). The Königsberg treaty followed on 30 January 1384.

title: Vytautas baptised ‘Wigand’ (a lie)
text:
What really happened [Saga]
A lying baptism. Vytautas kneels before the bishop of Sambia in a chapel full of incense that smells of cellars; every “Amen” is a nail driven into his ancestors. The stained glass cracks at the promise: Perkūnas’s warning. His amber pebble dies, cold, a plain stone: the lie breaks the connection to the elements, and the baptismal font is a consecrated place (magic §5.4). He receives the Order’s sword. Henė is among the knights in German furs.

title: Vytautas baptised ‘Wigand’ (a lie)
text:
Consequences
Caused by the audience at Marienburg, which follows the Dykra rescue and the refuge in Masovia. It leads to the Treaty of Königsberg.

title: Vytautas’s hostage sons poisoned (a contested tradition)
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Contested; a late tradition, not a recorded fact. The story that Vytautas’s two sons, held as hostages by the Order, were poisoned rests on Simon Grunau, a 16th-century Prussian chronicler, who has a knight poison “Iwan and Georg” in revenge for the father’s betrayal. The English Wikipedia (Ostrów Agreement, citing Jonynas 1984) calls it a false rumour and notes that no reliable source knows of the sons; Sofija is the only child in the record. Vytautas’s own letters name only his sister and brother as hostages and never accuse the Order of killing sons; a “Jurgis and Jonas” on the 1390–92 hostage list were kinsmen who came back alive. The tradition puts the poisoning after the break (the real break is July 1392, no day known) and before Ostrów (4 August). His wife Ona was released by the Order in May 1392.

title: Vytautas’s hostage sons poisoned (a contested tradition)
text:
What really happened [Saga]
Adopted as canon for Book II as a tradition, with the doubt voiced in-world (Q11): the sons are not on the Order’s written hostage list (“the household’s escort, nobody writes those down”), and Henrik’s “kai kurie sako, kad ne” keeps the doubt alive. After the burned forts the Order’s cook vanishes and the boys sicken at Balga. Šešiapirštis carries a Sambian ragana’s offer to draw the poison for the blood of an Order child; Vytautas says “Ne” (the forbidden transfer of the wound). The boys die that morning, herb-lore, mundane. Šešiapirštis dies afterwards. This ends Form 4 and deepens Ona’s silence.

title: Vytautas’s hostage sons poisoned (a contested tradition)
text:
Consequences
Caused by the break at Ritterswerder (the Order’s revenge, per the tradition). The graph no longer puts it after Ostrów: it precedes the Agreement of Ostrów, as in the book.

title: Vytautas’s hostage sons poisoned (a contested tradition)
text:
Dramatisation
Book II ch. 9 “Kraujo Puta” (Vytautas and Šešiapirštis; spring to summer 1392; the Neman and Prussia), with ch. 6 (the hostage list) and ch. 10 (Henrik: “some say no”). Ona’s grief is in ch. 10 and ch. 20. The afterword says plainly that the tradition is Grunau’s and that the saga chose it.

title: Vytautas flees to the Order again
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
In May 1389 at Lublin Jogaila mediated between Skirgaila and Vytautas; Vytautas signed a declaration of loyalty to Skirgaila, but his position as Duke of Lutsk was not formally recognised. In 1389 a plot to seize Vilnius castle using armed men in supply wagons “sent for his sister’s wedding” was betrayed by a spy (Wikipedia, Lithuanian Civil War 1389–92, citing Urban and Ivinskis) and the conspirators were executed; Vytautas’s allies Tautvilas and Ivan Olshanski lost Navahrudak and Halshany. (The wedding detail may be a Narbutt-type embellishment.) Vytautas fled to the Teutonic Order and on 19 January 1390 signed the Treaty of Lyck (Ełk), reaffirming the 1384 Königsberg terms; the Order demanded hostages: his brother Žygimantas (Sigismund), wife Ona, daughter Sofija, sister Rymgajla and other nobles. Žygimantas was a hostage from 1390 to 1398 (VLE gives 1389–98).

title: Vytautas flees to the Order again
text:
What really happened [Saga]
The wedding wagons of the Book II ch. 5 plot (forty-two wagons, a real wedding, arms beneath the oat sacks; bride Daumantė and her father Rimgaudas are the saga’s) are the saga’s elaboration of the supply-wagon plot. Pinčiukas sold the plan to Skirgaila for a miller’s debt. Perkūnas’s claim tightens: thunder without rain over the road. At Lyck the oaths are sworn on relics, and the Iron Saint keeps Christian oaths. Marquard von Salzbach, Vytautas’s old captive and friend, signs for the Order and offers a velvet threat to the hostages (“grąžinu skolą”); Vytautas says “Aš tai prisiminsiu”. (The insult to Birutė belongs to Raciąż, 1404, not to Lyck.)

title: Vytautas flees to the Order again
text:
Consequences
Caused by Trakai being Skirgaila’s. It leads to the Treaty of Lyck and the siege of Vilnius in September 1390, where Vytautas stands with the Order against the city he saved in 1384.

title: Vytautas flees to the Order again
text:
Dramatisation
Book II ch. 5 “Vestuvių Vežimai” (Vytautas; autumn 1389, Vilnius, then the road to Prussia in winter) and ch. 6 “Įkaitų Pilis” (Ona; January to August 1390, Lyck and Rastenburg; the hostages are Ona, Sofija, Žygimantas, Rymgailė, Jonas Alšėniškis and others). The graph places the event at Königsberg.

title: The break: Ritterswerder guests seized, Order forts burned
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Ritterswerder was built by the Order in autumn 1391 on a Nemunas island near Lampėdžiai. In summer 1392 (July) Vytautas invited the Knights to festivities there, took most of the prominent guests prisoner, and destroyed Ritterswerder, Metenburg and Neugarten near Grodno (en.wikipedia, Civil War 1389-92 and Ostrów Agreement). No source gives a day. In May the Order had released Ona so that she could travel to Lithuania and spread pro-Lithuanian rumours; Žygimantas stayed a hostage.

title: The break: Ritterswerder guests seized, Order forts burned

What really happened [Saga]
The important guests are seized and the rest of the garrison is put out alive. The Rasos (St John’s) night of the burning is the saga’s invention. The Order hears of the burned forts; by a contested tradition it takes its revenge on the hostage sons.

title: Casimir’s privilege for Lithuania
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Casimir Jagiellon, born 30 November 1427, was proclaimed Grand Duke by the lords in Vilnius on 29 June 1440 (aged twelve) and issued his privilege for Lithuania in Vilnius on 2 May 1447 (the VLE says 5 May). It gave offices only to locals, forbade the arrest or confiscation of a noble without trial, allowed free travel abroad, promised no reduction of Lithuania’s territory, gave landowners jurisdiction over their peasants and secured the rights of townspeople and of nobles regardless of rite. He was crowned King of Poland at Wawel by Archbishop Wincenty Kot on 25 June 1447 (pl.wikipedia, Kazimierz IV). Casimir died on 7 June 1492.

title: Casimir’s privilege for Lithuania
text:
What really happened [Saga]
Laws, seals and charters replace oath and omen. A jester at the feast offers the young king a deal and Casimir looks straight through him. The old world becomes folklore; the gods do not die but are written out.

title: Casimir’s privilege for Lithuania
text:
Consequences
The graph records no causes edges; the privilege follows the murder of Žygimantas and the raising of Casimir, and the Lithuanian lords’ bargain it records is the end-point of Book V’s slow drift from oath to ledger.

title: Perkūnas claims Vytautas
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Nothing in the record: a private event of the night of 15 August 1382 in the Krėva cell, with no witnesses beyond the jailer. The record gives only that Vytautas, on learning of his father’s death, lived through the next weeks in the same castle until the escape in autumn.

title: Perkūnas claims Vytautas
text:
What really happened [Saga]
In the morning Vytautas sees the body in the yard on a cart under a fur. Perkūnas touches him: “the first true touch of Perkūnas”. It is a claim, not a gift: Perkūnas, keeper of oaths and justice, marks the warrior whose oaths he will hold to account. Canon’s reason is that Vytautas is the Amber Queen’s vessel’s son, and the god’s old feud with Jūratė is unfinished. Vytautas shaves and strips his insignia, with a dulled knife kept by a miracle. Ona arrives. The claim will tighten when he breaks his oaths (the second defection, the Vorskla), relent when he keeps one (Grunwald), and fall silent at his death.

title: Perkūnas claims Vytautas
text:
Consequences
Caused by the death of Kęstutis. It is the first marker on Thread E of the series arc (Perkūnas’s claim).

title: Battle of Pabaiskas
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Fought on 1 September 1435 near Pabaiskas, about nine kilometres south of Ukmergė, on the Šventoji (hence also the Battle of Šventoji or Wiłkomierz). Lithuanians under Mykolas Žygimantaitis, with about 4,000 Poles under Jakub Kobylański, defeated Švitrigaila’s host and the Livonian Order. The Livonian Master Franke Kerskorff was killed with his marshal and several komturs; Žygimantas Kaributaitis was wounded, captured and died days later; Švitrigaila fled to Polotsk with about thirty riders (Wikipedia, Battle of Wiłkomierz). The graph lists Mykolas Žygimantaitis, Žygimantas Kęstutaitis’s son, as the commander (Žygimantas himself was not at the battle).

title: Battle of Pabaiskas
text:
What really happened [Saga]
Kin-slaughter worse than the crusades, which leaves thousands of unburned dead on the field. The Riders of the Reise ride their last raid and break at the unfrozen river they cannot cross: the Iron Saint is silenced in the North. At the Vėlinės the living cannot feed so many; Pilkoji’s dozen burn the dead all winter with the keeper’s lightning-fire and most of the wolves die doing it. The Root-Mother’s shadow lies over the field.

title: Battle of Pabaiskas
text:
Consequences
Caused by the coup at Ašmena. It leads to the Peace of Brest, at which the Order abandons Švitrigaila.

title: Battle of Pabaiskas
text:
Dramatisation
Book V ch. 13 “Pabaisko Laukas” (Žiežirba), ch. 14 “Mirštantis Ordinas” (a Livonian Order brother; both 1 September 1435, late summer) and ch. 16 “Nedegintųjų Žiema” (Pilkoji; Vėlinės 1435 to spring 1436).

title: Ona dies
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Anna (Ona), Vytautas’s wife, died on 31 July 1418 at Trakai and was buried in Vilnius cathedral (en.wikipedia, Anna, Grand Duchess of Lithuania; pl.wikipedia, Witold Kiejstutowicz; the Lithuanian Wikipedia gives 31 August, a minority date). She is remembered for helping Vytautas escape Krėva in 1382. Her birth year and origins are uncertain. Vytautas married Julijona of Alšėnai, Ona’s niece, on 13 November 1418; the Bishop of Vilnius refused for kinship and the Bishop of Włocławek, Jan Kropidło, officiated. Švitrigaila had escaped from Kremenets in March of that year.

title: Ona dies
text:
What really happened [Saga]
The book moves her death to the eve of the rye harvest. Her last words show she always knew about the vault and kept it from everyone, as she kept the swap at Krėva. She is the last person who knew Vytautas before the Krėva night. Her last letter, found in a copper-bound box, is read aloud by Julijona at his deathbed: “Grįžk, jei gali. Jei negali, žinok, kad aš žinau.”

title: Ona dies
text:
Consequences
The graph records no outgoing edge. The saga’s consequences are her husband’s second marriage and, in 1430, her letter at his deathbed.

title: Ona dies

Dramatisation

title: Kęstutis marries Birutė
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Tradition dates the marriage of Kęstutis and Birutė to about 1350 (the English Wikipedia says c. 1344; the saga picks 1349) and the birth of Vytautas to about 1350 (a minority puts it at 1354–55). The story that she was a Palanga vaidilutė, a priestess of the sacred fire, whom Kęstutis carried off, rests on the 16th-century chronicle tradition (Bychowiec chronicle; Stryjkowski; verify) and is open to question. His elder sons Vaidotas and Butautas belonged to an earlier marriage. Kęstutis’s later oath to Louis of Hungary (1351) and the 1361 capture are separate events. See Wikipedia, Birutė.

title: Kęstutis marries Birutė
text:
What really happened [Saga]
Birutė, sworn at thirteen to the shore-fire, will not give herself to any man. The old priestess, the Amber Queen’s vessel, tells her: “Then don’t give. Be taken.” A vow not to give herself is not broken if she is carried off. Birutė struggles loudly where the fishermen can see, so that the chroniclers have their abduction and the gods their letter kept. Palanga’s flame, the second flame of the Pact, needs a husband for its last keeper. The old woman dies on the shore in the autumn. At Senieji Trakai the spinners of Laima sit on the sill when Vytautas is born in 1350: a crown will travel toward him all his life; he will be baptised three times; he will outlive every heir. Birutė says “Dar ne”, and Laima: for “not yet” you pay.

title: Kęstutis marries Birutė
text:
Consequences
The graph attaches no outgoing ‘causes’ edge. The marriage brings the amber-priestess line into the Gediminids and gives Vytautas the pebble; it also seeds the 1365 treason of Butautas.

title: Kęstutis marries Birutė
text:
Dramatisation
Book VI ch. 10 “Palangos Ugnis” (Birutė; April 1349), ch. 11 “Būk Paimta” (the old priestess and Birutė; spring and summer 1349), ch. 12 “Laima prie Lopšio” (Birutė; spring 1349 to February 1350; the birth in Senieji Trakai).

title: Treaty of Lyck; hostages demanded
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Signed at Lyck (Ełk) on 19 January 1390 by Marquard von Salzbach, komtur Arnold von Bürglen and Thomas son of Survila; it confirmed the 1384 Königsberg treaty (Samogitia to the Nevėžis, vassalage). Hostages demanded: his brother Sigismund (Žygimantas), wife Anna (Ona), daughter Sofija, sister Rymgajla, brother-in-law Ivan Olshanski and other nobles. Sofija was a hostage; the Moscow embassy reached Prussia at the end of the summer and she left from Marienburg by ship via Danzig and Pskov (Grala, citing Posilge). The marshal is not attested; some doubt the treaty’s originality.

title: Treaty of Lyck; hostages demanded
text:
What really happened [Saga]
Vytautas swears “honestly”, to keep faith as long as the Order does; the pebble is dim in the consecrated stone. Marquard von Salzbach, his old captive and friend, offers a velvet threat to the hostages. The Order lets mother and daughter spend a day together before Sofija’s autumn departure.

title: Treaty of Lyck; hostages demanded
text:
Consequences
Caused by the second defection. Leads to the siege of Vilnius.

title: Treaty of Lyck; hostages demanded
text:
Dramatisation

title: Baptism of Lithuania; Šventaragis flame put out
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Jogaila returned to Vilnius at the end of 1386 (the formal steps fall in February–March 1387), established the first parishes and began mass baptisms of nobles and their peasants; in Aukštaitija the nobility followed in spring. Długosz reports that Jogaila put out the sacred fire, felled the sacred groves and had the sacred snakes killed; modern historians treat Długosz’s information on this episode as of disputed accuracy (Wikipedia, Christianization of Lithuania; the extinguished fire is not corroborated there). Vilnius Cathedral was begun in 1387 on the site of the pagan shrine; a decree of 17 February 1387 provided for it and the diocese; Magdeburg law was granted to the city on 22 March 1387. Urban VI’s bull of 12 March 1388 addressed the destruction of pagan objects; on 19 April 1389 he recognised Lithuania as a Catholic state. Vytautas, baptised twice already, was a witness.

title: Baptism of Lithuania; Šventaragis flame put out
text:
What really happened [Saga]
Before dawn the king’s men carry buckets to the Šventaragis fire. The Krivis does not resist; as the water hits the embers he says “Sutartis baigta” (the Pact is ended) so that the spirits of place hear it from a man and not from a priest, then walks into the grove and is never seen again. The vaidilutės are led to carts where Catholic nobles wait. Galminas watches from the hill. In the icy Neris the baptised are frightened and doing it to save their children. Vytautas’s double accuses him; the pebble glows. Clause 1 of the Silent Pact is broken and the Pact ends. The Unbinding begins: the spirits are no longer owed courtesy and no longer give it.

title: Baptism of Lithuania; Šventaragis flame put out
text:
Consequences
Caused by the Kraków baptism and marriage. It ends the Silent Pact (the graph’s ‘ends’ edge) and leads to Vytautas lighting the Last Flame the same night. Its long consequence is the Unburned of Book II.

title: Baptism of Lithuania; Šventaragis flame put out
text:
Dramatisation
Book I ch. 29 “Krikštas” (Vytautas; February 1387, Vilnius, Šventaragis and the Neris), plus Book II ch. 3 “Kas Ugnį Gesina” (a Franciscan of Vilnius; winter 1387–88; the first Unburned and Quenched).

title: Vytautas escapes Krėva in the maid’s clothes
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Vytautas escaped from Krėva in the autumn of 1382 with the help of his wife Ona. The accounts disagree on how. In the Lithuanian chronicles she brings two maids and persuades one to exchange clothes with Vytautas; Wigand of Marburg has him wearing Ona’s own clothes; other versions have him lowered in a wicker basket from a window. Ona’s role never varies. The fate of the maid, and of Ona, is unclear; Ona probably stayed in Krėva. Vytautas fled to Masovia, to his sister Danutė and her husband Janusz I of Warsaw (the English Wikipedia adds Siemowit IV), and finally to the Teutonic Knights.

title: Vytautas escapes Krėva in the maid’s clothes
text:
What really happened [Saga]
On the eve of Vėlinės, with the Wind at its zenith, Birutė in Palanga raises a real sea-fog over the Krėva yard, through the amber pebble she anchored with her blood. The Law of Truth forbids illusion, so no one is deceived: they simply cannot see. The fog costs her voice. The maid is called Elena in the saga; she takes his bed and stays, and is executed. Ona plays the broken widow, smuggling in the dress and a draught, and when a drunk guard stops Vytautas in the yard the fog does the rest.

title: Vytautas escapes Krėva in the maid’s clothes
text:
Consequences
Caused by the death of Kęstutis. It leads to the rescue through the Dykra and the refuge in Masovia.

title: Vytautas escapes Krėva in the maid’s clothes
text:
Dramatisation
Book I ch. 12 “Gedulo Skraistė” (Ona, Krėva), ch. 13 “Keitimas” (Vytautas; the dress and the haircut), ch. 14 “Šešėlis Naktyje” (Vytautas; the fog), autumn 1382. The text places ch. 12 on the day of the death, the record some weeks later.

title: Treaty of Königsberg (Samogitia ceded)
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Signed at Königsberg on 30 January 1384: Vytautas promised to become the Order’s vassal and ceded Samogitia up to the Nevėžis, including Kaunas (Wikipedia, Treaty of Königsberg). The Dubysa line was a different promise, Jogaila’s of 31 October 1382 at Dubysa, which was never ratified. In February 1384 several Samogitian districts acknowledged Vytautas and the Knights; the Order began New Marienwerder near Kaunas in May and Vytautas renewed the treaty there in the summer (14 June or 16 July, sources differ). Vytautas was baptised at Tapiau as Wigand on 21 October 1383.

title: Treaty of Königsberg (Samogitia ceded)
text:
What really happened [Saga]
The Amber Debt comes due. Samogitia, the land of the Hidden Groves, goes to the Iron Saint’s servants on a piece of parchment. The Order gives its new vassal a Neman castle that he does not hold except on paper: the keys are carried by the Order’s vaitas. Ona and the children are lodged at Königsberg as honoured guests.

title: Treaty of Königsberg (Samogitia ceded)
text:
Consequences
Caused by the Tapiau baptism; it leads to the burnings of 1384 when he turns the Order’s own fortress against it.

title: Treaty of Königsberg (Samogitia ceded)
text:
Dramatisation
Not dramatised. Book I ch. 19 “Velnio Sandėris” (Vytautas, autumn 1383; Ona and children at Königsberg) leads up to it; ch. 22 “Naujapilis” opens by recalling it (“sausio šaltyje”, the January frost) and moves on to the construction of Naujapilis. Winter.

title: Kęstutis strangled at Krėva
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Kęstutis was found dead at Krėva on 15 August 1382, the feast of the Assumption, about twelve days after the arrest of 3 August (some sources say “a week later”). Jogaila claimed that his uncle had hanged himself, which few believed. VLE says he was killed (strangled); the Lithuanian Wikipedia has him strangled on the orders of Julijona or Skirgaila, the body burned in Vilnius; the Order’s chronicler Wigand of Marburg is the main near-contemporary. Whether he died “naturally or was murdered” is stated as debated in the English Wikipedia; most historians accept murder. The body was cremated with pagan rites in Vilnius, according to tradition. Skirgaila found the body.

title: Kęstutis strangled at Krėva
text:
What really happened [Saga]
Henė‘s Breath of the Void muffled the tower so that no struggle was heard, and a shard of Velnias strangled the duke while the guards slept in unnatural stupor (mythic_gaps §1). Four Rus’ mercenaries, paid in Riga silver, strangle him with the golden chain whose clasp bears the Riga mark of two crossed keys under a cross. Kęstutis, who took the beggar’s coin knowing, says: Gabija will not shine on your masters today; the cowards are Skirgaila and Jogaila. Birutė appears as an apparition leading his soul. The wolves of the Dykra howl. It is the kin-murder that breaks clause 2 of the Silent Pact: no Gediminid sheds Gediminid blood. The gods’ protection lapses and the Shadow-Seller collects.

title: Kęstutis strangled at Krėva
text:
Consequences
Caused by the arrest. It breaks clause 2 of the Silent Pact and leads to Perkūnas claiming Vytautas and to the escape from Krėva. It also sets Skirgaila and Jogaila on the road that ends in the 1385 Union signed above the cell, and Žygimantas in the cell in 1438.

title: Kęstutis strangled at Krėva
text:
Dramatisation
Book I ch. 8 “Krėvos Požemiai” (Kęstutis and Vytautas, talking through the stones; about ten to fourteen August), ch. 9 “Paskutinė Giesmė” (Kęstutis, then Vytautas; the night of 14–15 August; Žolinė eve), ch. 10 “Šaltas Rytas” (Vytautas; the morning of 15 August). Echoes: ch. 28b (Vytautas in the cell, 1385), Book I ch. 30 (Skirgaila), Book V ch. 19 (Žygimantas).

title: Jadvyga dies
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Jadwiga of Poland (crowned “king” in Kraków on 16 October 1384, married to Jogaila on 18 February 1386) gave birth to a daughter, Elisabeth Bonifacia, on 22 June 1399; the child died on 13 July, and Jadwiga herself on 17 July 1399, aged about 25, of postpartum complications. They were buried together at Wawel on 24 August as her will required; she was canonised in 1997. Her death weakened Jogaila’s claim to the Polish crown, which rested on the marriage: he left for Ruthenia six days after the funeral, the Polish lords renewed their oaths, and he married Anna of Celje on 29 January 1402. See Wikipedia, Jadwiga of Poland. That she warned against the steppe war is in Długosz (verify).

title: Jadvyga dies
text:
What really happened [Saga]
She is the Relic of the White Silence, a saint by the cold, not by decree: her touch heals and leaves frost. In July there is frost on the sheets. Her body does not decay and her tomb becomes the White Silence’s anchor in the Polish heartland: a tragedy, not a villainy.

title: Jadvyga dies
text:
Consequences
The graph records no outgoing edge. In the saga her tomb frosts in March 1401 when Jogaila prays there, and the White Silence holds Poland while Lithuania’s flames go out.

Dramatisation

title: Battle of Grunwald / Žalgiris
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Fought on 15 July 1410 between the armies of Jogaila and Vytautas and the Teutonic Order under Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen near the villages of Grunwald, Stębark and Łodwigowo. Estimates of strength range from about 16,000 to 39,000 on the Polish-Lithuanian side and 11,000 to 27,000 on the Order’s side, and the sources are poor. Jungingen was killed; the Cronica conflictus says by Dobiesław of Oleśnica, Długosz says by Mszczuj of Skrzynno. Before the battle the Order’s heralds brought the king two naked swords as a taunt. Jogaila was heard at Mass after Mass; Długosz says Zbigniew Oleśnicki, the king’s secretary, saved him from the knight Lupold of Kökeritz. A Tatar contingent led by Jalal ad-Din fought beside the allies. The Lithuanian wing withdrew; historians disagree whether this was a planned feigned retreat (argued from a German letter published by Sven Ekdahl, 1963; disputed by Stephen Turnbull) or a rout, as Długosz presents it while crediting the Poles alone. Of the Order’s roughly 270 brothers on the field between 203 and 211 died. The siege of Marienburg was lifted on 19 September; the First Peace of Thorn of February 1411 gave Dobrzyń to Poland, Samogitia to Lithuania for the lifetimes of the two rulers, and a silver indemnity. See Wikipedia, Battle of Grunwald, and the Banderia Prutenorum.

title: Battle of Grunwald / Žalgiris
text:
What really happened [Saga]
The eve of the battle is the lantern: the flame leaves Trakai for the first time, in a horn lantern carried by Žiežirba, and Vytautas opens it before a single Medvėgalis žynys and swears the thunder-oath to Perkūnas on Kęstutis’s sword; an oath on a claimed man’s name binds the Force too. In the morning the wolves lead pursuing knights into bog and wood when the Lithuanian wing withdraws; Galminas becomes the wood-skinned beast and the Root-Mother takes her harvest. When Jungingen falls the Iron Saint breaks, the Riders of the Reise scream on every road, and lightning stands on the field. The Medvėgalis žynys dies. In autumn an oak and hazel grove grows through the graves.

title: Battle of Grunwald / Žalgiris
text:
Consequences
Caused by the Union of Vilnius and Radom, which allied the cousins. It leads, in the graph, to the Union of Horodło (1413). The saga’s price is that the victory changes nothing for the gods: the gods remain unbound and Samogitia will be baptised.

title: Battle of Grunwald / Žalgiris
text:
Dramatisation
Book III ch. 15 “Tiltas per Vyslą” (Žiežirba), ch. 16 (Eglė), ch. 17 “Žibintas” (the Medvėgalis žynys; night 14–15 July), ch. 18 “Du Kalavijai” (Zawisza Czarny; the morning), ch. 19 “Traukimasis?” (Rūdis), ch. 20 “Geležies Mirtis” (Vytautas; the afternoon), ch. 21 “Kruvini Laužai” (Ona by letter and Vytautas; the night), ch. 23 “Galmino Giraitė” (Eglė; autumn). Midsummer heat.

title: Goštautas gives the warm coin to a beggar
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Nothing in the record. Jonas Goštautas’s Vilnius feast (February 1437) is the saga’s; the Hanseatic loan for the bricks is invention on top of the real Hansa office at Kaunas (c. 1441).

title: Goštautas gives the warm coin to a beggar
text:
What really happened [Saga]
After the last guest leaves, a warm coin lies by the untouched sugar swan (a coin that warms from someone else, not from a hand). Goštautas gives it to an old beggar on the threshold without looking at it. Under the floor the Counter falls silent for three breaths; then: “Viena moneta pasiekė žmogų. Neįvertinta. Neužskaityta.” The beggar is not named in the text; read as Dievas Senelis, the same Beggar who turned Kęstutis’s coin to stone in 1382. The Counter then reads the term on Trakai: three years and a month.

title: Eglė leads Vytautas through the Dykra
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Nothing in the record. After the escape from Krėva in autumn 1382, the sources place Vytautas next at the court of his sister Danutė and her husband Janusz I of Masovia, then with the Teutonic Order. The route between Krėva and Masovia, through the Grodno forests and the Biebrza marshes, passed the empty belt that the Order called the Wildnis. Whether he travelled with a guide is unknown.

title: Eglė leads Vytautas through the Dykra
text:
What really happened [Saga]
The Dykra, the Root-Mother’s own country since 1348, swallows Skirgaila’s trackers. Vytautas’s horse dies; he speaks the Five-Voice for “man” (the cost is shown: his hearing and sight dull); Eglė appears with her žaltys and leads him through. He mistakes her for an amber priestess (“Tu esi Gintaro Šventikė”) and she corrects him: “Ne gintaro. Šaknų.” (not amber, roots). In the swamp the Root-Mother’s price is the offering: he lays a silver buckle and a scrap of silk on the stone. Eglė’s own price, “never sell the forest”, comes due at Salynas in 1398.

title: Eglė leads Vytautas through the Dykra
text:
Consequences
Caused by the escape from Krėva. It leads, in the graph, to Vytautas’s audience with Zöllner at Marienburg and so to the baptism at Tapiau: the flight ends in the Order’s service. The saga’s route also passes Masovia, which the graph links only to the escape.

title: Eglė leads Vytautas through the Dykra
text:
Dramatisation
Book I ch. 15 “Pabėgimas” and ch. 16 “Pelkės Vaikai” (Vytautas; late autumn 1382). Eglė’s earlier life is the prologue (her last night as a mortal vaidilutė). The wiki places the event at the Dykra.

title: Algirdas & Kęstutis depose Jaunutis
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
In 1345 Algirdas and Kęstutis removed their brother Jaunutis. Kęstutis, from Trakai, took Vilnius unexpectedly and called Algirdas, who took the Duchy of Vilnius and the Grand Duke’s title; the sources give the year but not the day. The brothers offered Jaunutis the Duchy of Zasłaŭje, which he refused; he was imprisoned at Vilnius, escaped and fled to Simeon of Moscow, where he was baptised Orthodox as Ioann, and was later reconciled and held Zasłaŭje; he last appears in 1366. The Bychowiec chronicle records that his mother Jaunė supported him. Algirdas ruled east from Vilnius, Kęstutis west from Trakai and Samogitia; the Order’s chroniclers treat Kęstutis as a ruler in his own right. A planned Order reise of 1345 may have prompted the move. Sources: Šapoka (1989), Kiaupa et al. (2000); Wikipedia, Jaunutis.

title: Algirdas & Kęstutis depose Jaunutis
text:
What really happened [Saga]
Kęstutis takes the city by night on All Souls’ Eve 1345, and the wolves at the doors of the Vilnius hall let him pass (“Ugnis nepasakė”). Jaunutis leaves east unharmed by the Smolensk road, and Kęstutis promises him that no Gediminid will shed his blood: the seed of clause 2 of the Pact. Algirdas rides in from Vitebsk at dawn and the brothers divide the realm. The wooden Crooked Castle on Bald Hill, taken without a blow, is left with thirty of Kęstutis’s men and forgotten.

title: Algirdas & Kęstutis depose Jaunutis
text:
Consequences
Leads to the Silent Pact, sworn the following night. The diarchy is the political frame of Book VI and of everything the sons will break.

title: Algirdas & Kęstutis depose Jaunutis
text:
Dramatisation
Book VI ch. 2 “Jaunučio Kėdė” (Kęstutis; 1342–44), ch. 3 “Vilniaus Užėmimas” (Kęstutis; the eve of Vėlinės, 1345, Vilnius; autumn).

title: Truce of Czartorysk
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
After the Polish invasion of Volhynia from 25 June 1431 the king crossed on 21 July; Švitrigaila was beaten on the Styr on 31 July; Lutsk castle was besieged from about 1 August and an assault repulsed on 13 August; an agreement was reached on 26 August and the Truce of Czartorysk, running to 24 June 1433, on 1 September 1431 (Wikipedia, Lithuanian Civil War 1431–35; Polish Wikipedia, Świdrygiełło). Goštautas was captured defending Lutsk (VLE).

title: Truce of Czartorysk
text:
What really happened [Saga]
The truce is the pause in which the lords turn against the new Grand Duke. Žygimantas watches from the edge of the Christmemel party and begins to count his chances.

title: Žygimantas’s coup at Ašmena
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
In the night of 31 August to 1 September 1432 the Lithuanian lords, among them Jonas Goštautas, Petras Mangirdaitis and Semen Olshanski, backed Žygimantas Kęstutaitis and overthrew Švitrigaila at Ašmena. Švitrigaila escaped half-dressed to Polotsk; his pregnant wife was captured (Wikipedia, Lithuanian Civil War, 1432–38; VLE, Žygimantas Kęstutaitis). Most sources give 31 August, some 1 September.

title: Žygimantas’s coup at Ašmena
text:
What really happened [Saga]
Henė, holding Jogaila’s last stone, whispers to Žygimantas anyway. The coup takes place at the same inn and ford Kęstutis passed on his way to Krėva fifty years before; the residue is still in the road. Žygimantas asks the keeper to relight the flame for him, and the keeper refuses.

title: Žygimantas’s coup at Ašmena
text:
Consequences
Caused by the death of Vytautas. It leads to three events: Grodno, where the Poles swear him in, the battle of Ašmena in December, and Pabaiskas in 1435.

title: Žygimantas’s coup at Ašmena
text:
Dramatisation
Book V ch. 8 “Sąmokslas Trakuose” (Žygimantas, July 1432, Trakai), ch. 9 “Ašmenos Naktis” (Žiežirba, the night of 31 August, Ašmena).

title: Treaty of Christmemel (Švitrigaila and the Order)
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Treaty of Christmemel (Skirsnemunė), 19 June 1431, between Švitrigaila, Grand Master Paul von Rusdorf and the Livonian Master Zisse von Rutenberg. Terms: mutual aid if attacked, war only by joint consent, shared spoils (Wikipedia; VLE, Skirsnemunės sutartis). Witnesses included Jonas Goštautas, Kristinas Astikas, Mykolas Kęsgaila and Žygimantas Kęstutaitis. Sources disagree on whether Palanga was ceded (the English Wikipedia says so; VLE says the Melno borders held); the saga keeps Palanga Lithuanian.

title: Treaty of Christmemel (Švitrigaila and the Order)
text:
What really happened [Saga]
The pact between Švitrigaila and the crusader Orders is the old enemy’s re-entry through the front door: the alliance that Vytautas refused to the end. Žygimantas rides with him as a witness, already watching.

title: Treaty of Christmemel (Švitrigaila and the Order)

Consequences
The graph records no outgoing edge. The treaty is the diplomatic root of the war that ends at Pabaiskas, and the Polish reply (the invasion of Volhynia) leads to the Czartorysk truce.

title: Peace of Brest (Brześć Kujawski): the Order drops Švitrigaila
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
The Peace of Brześć Kujawski, 31 December 1435, ended the war between Poland and the Teutonic Order. The Order dropped Švitrigaila and agreed to support only dukes of Lithuania chosen jointly by Poland and Lithuania (Wikipedia, Lithuanian Civil War of 1431–35; VLE, Bresto taika). It follows the defeat of Švitrigaila and the Livonian Order at Pabaiskas on 1 September.

title: Peace of Brest (Brześć Kujawski): the Order drops Švitrigaila
text:
What really happened [Saga]
The peace is the Iron Saint’s retreat in the North: the Order, shorn of Livonia’s leadership, cuts loose a client it can no longer afford. Švitrigaila, who is a man of the old realm in his own telling, loses Polotsk, Vitebsk and Smolensk piece by piece; the saga’s own judgement is that the dynasty’s id survives and its soul does not. His mother Uliana of Tver is remembered in the monastery she founded at Vitebsk.

title: Peace of Brest (Brześć Kujawski): the Order drops Švitrigaila
text:
Consequences
Caused by Pabaiskas. The graph attaches no outgoing edge: the saga uses it as the last act of the Order as Lithuania’s patron of civil war.

title: The Beggar turns Kęstutis’s coin to stone
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Nothing in the record. On 3 August 1382 Kęstutis and Vytautas rode to the talks at Jogaila’s camp near Trakai; that the old man gave alms to a beggar on the way is a motif of folk tale, not of chronicle.

title: The Beggar turns Kęstutis’s coin to stone
text:
What really happened [Saga]
The Beggar is Dievas Senelis, walking as a stranger with a staff. He asks Kęstutis for a coin, and the duke gives it. The silver turns to grey stone and the old man vanishes into a grey stone at the road’s edge. Rule of the cosmology (§5): those who give are not saved, they are seen; their road becomes clear to them even if it leads to death. Kęstutis rides on to the camp knowing. The Beggar calls Vytautas “Vyti”, an allowed exception to the intimate-vocative rule (Q7). The coin turning to stone says that what is paid for truth is worth nothing as money. (A second beggar turns up in Book V: Goštautas gives a warm coin to a beggar on his threshold.)

title: The Beggar turns Kęstutis’s coin to stone
text:
Consequences
The graph records no outgoing ‘causes’ edge. The beggar’s seeing is the first signal of Kęstutis’s walk into the arrest and death at Krėva; it is also the model for later epiphanies of Dievas in the saga.

title: Kęstutis & Vytautas lured to Jogaila’s camp near Trakai and arrested
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Modern accounts (Wikipedia’s civil-war article, citing Ivinskis, Urban, Kiaupa; VLE, Kęstutis and Skirgaila) put it on 3 August 1382. Trakai had surrendered to Jogaila and the Order on 20 July; the armies of Kęstutis and Jogaila then stood facing each other near Trakai. Skirgaila persuaded Kęstutis and Vytautas to come to the talks at Jogaila’s camp near Trakai, where both were treacherously arrested, and taken to Krėva. No battle was fought. Some accounts place the arrest closer to 10 August; the sources count from the arrest to Kęstutis’s death on 15 August (“a week later”, or two weeks). The tradition that Skirgaila guaranteed a safe-conduct is plausible but not in a named chronicle. Principal sources are the Order’s chroniclers (Wigand of Marburg, Johann von Posilge) and the later Lithuanian chronicles.

title: Kęstutis & Vytautas lured to Jogaila’s camp near Trakai and arrested
text:
What really happened [Saga]
A treachery under sworn safety is the oath-break Perkūnas notes: Skirgaila’s oath on Perkūnas, given at Trakai two weeks earlier, is the safe-conduct. Book I stages it where the record puts it. The camp’s iron-bound palisade gate, built by the Order’s carpenters, shuts behind the ducal retinue; sound dies in the camp (the Shadow-Seller’s Breath of the Void); hundreds of archers line the palisade; Skirgaila speaks from the wooden balcony of the negotiating hall (a requisitioned manor), Jogaila watches from the upper gallery, and Henė turns one blackened stone under the gate beams. The same night Skirgaila’s men massacre Kęstutis’s guard in the tents beyond the manor fence, blocking the tent openings while Jogaila sits alone at a feast; seven of the hidden nine die and are buried in the bog, while Jonas’s men stayed in Kęstutis’s own camp.

title: Kęstutis & Vytautas lured to Jogaila’s camp near Trakai and arrested
text:
Consequences
The arrest follows Jogaila’s retaking of Vilnius and leads directly to Kęstutis’s death at Krėva. Vytautas, who escapes Krėva in the autumn, carries the story forward.

title: Kęstutis & Vytautas lured to Jogaila’s camp near Trakai and arrested
text:
Dramatisation
Book I ch. 4 “Kelionė į stovyklą” (the ride to the camp; the Beggar on the road, 3 August), ch. 5 “Dvigubas Veidas” (Jogaila, same day, the requisitioned Trakai manor), ch. 6 “Geležiniai Vartai” (the “Iron Gates” are the camp palisade gate; late-summer afternoon), ch. 7 “Tylos Puota” (Jogaila and Skirgaila; the same night). Kęstutis’s body is still burned in Vilnius (ch. 10).

title: Žaltvykslės (bog-lights, treasure-flames)
text:
Folk source [Record]
Lights over bogs and meadows at night, believed to be souls that lead travellers astray (klystžvakės, “straying candles”); in Lithuanian tradition some are the souls of dishonest land-surveyors condemned to measure fields at night. Separately, hidden treasure was said to show itself as a flame (pinigai dega, “the money is burning”) on certain nights; a brave finder might claim it by throwing clothing onto the flame, though the devil or the dead guard it and demand a price.

Treasure-flames are wealth buried with a curse or bargain, still owed to the roots; taking one means taking on its debt.

title: Velnias’s small shapes (velniukai)
text:
Folk source [Record]
Velnias is one of the most vivid figures of Lithuanian folk tales. He often appears as a gentleman, frequently a “little German” (vokietukas) in a green or black coat with a hat hiding his horns and a goose- or horse-foot he cannot hide. He also takes the shapes of black cats and black dogs, haunts swamps, stones and mills, makes bargains (signed in blood in Christian-era tales) and is regularly cheated by clever peasants. He fears Perkūnas, who hunts him with lightning; in storms people chased cats and dogs out of the house.

title: Velnias’s small shapes (velniukai)
section: In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
text:
In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
Not the Shadow-Seller himself, but small change from the same purse: velniukai, minor shards of Velnias that do small deals in villages and serve as his eyes. The Shadow-Seller uses them as scouts; a black dog at the edge of the firelight is often how he learns what a prince will need. Velnias is hungry and fair: his small shapes keep every deal to the letter and lose to anyone cleverer.

title: Velnias’s small shapes (velniukai)
text:
Signs & habitat
A black cat that arrives the day before a quarrel; a stranger in a too-fine green coat at a wedding who will not dance (he would show his foot); a dog that will not leave during a thunderstorm.

title: Velnias’s small shapes (velniukai)
text:

Before: country tricksters. After 1387 the green-coated gentlemen move to towns, where the Gold-Glutton’s ledgers make better bargains than any peasant’s harvest.

title: Velnias’s small shapes (velniukai)
section: Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
text:
Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
Thunder-stones and, after 1387, the Candlemas thunder candle lit in storms (Perkūnas’s attention comes with them). Never shake his hand or accept the first gift (rudeness to strangers is itself a sin against custom). Out-think him by drafting the deal yourself; if you are less clever than you think, the letter is your ruin.

title: Vandenis and undinės (lake-keepers)
text:
Folk source [Record]
Many Baltic and Slavic communities believed certain lakes and rivers demand a drowning each year and house a water-spirit; vandenis is a Lithuanian name for a male water-spirit. Undinė (water-maiden) is probably a later borrowing shaped by German and literary tradition; older water-maidens overlap with laumės. People offered bread or animals to waters and floated a loaf with a candle to find a drowned body.

title: Vandenis and undinės (lake-keepers)
section: In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
text:
In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
Every lake is an eye of the World Tree, and an eye must be kept open: each year a lake takes one life to see through, and the drowned become its vandeniai, looking up at the world through the water. The folk are right about the annual drowning and wrong that it can be avoided; it can only be chosen. The sea’s jūrų mergelės are the remnants of Jūratė’s drowned court and answer, faintly, to the Amber Queen.

title: Vandenis and undinės (lake-keepers)
text:
Signs & habitat
Deep lakes no one has sounded; a spot where the ice never closes; a pale face just under the surface at dusk; a village avoiding one shore in early summer.

title: Vandenis and undinės (lake-keepers)
text:
Before / after the Unbinding
Before: one a year, and villages “gave” the lake a black rooster or a condemned thief. After: lakes take many, and at the spring ice-break whole carts go through.

title: Vandenis and undinės (lake-keepers)
section: Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
text:
Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
An offering at the ice-break (it shortens the wait but does not replace the death). A willing drowning: old people sometimes walked in to spare the young. A line of salt along the shore holds a vandenis for one night (a fortune in salt). The floating loaf finds the body so it can be burned, and the lake is then owed again.

title: Užgesėlės (the Quenched)
text:
Folk source [Record]
[Saga invention.] No folk source; it grows from the Baltic reverence for the sacred hearth-flame and from the historical putting-out of the Šventaragis flame at the baptism of 1387.

title: Užgesėlės (the Quenched)
section: In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
text:
In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
Born of killed sacred flames. When the Šventaragis flame was put out in 1387 the fire did not simply stop: its sparks, cut off from Gabija, scattered into Vilnius’s hearths as cold things that remember being fire. Tiny blue sparks like embers that nest in hearths and eat fire, so a house with užgesėlės cannot keep a hearth lit, which in winter is death. They are not malicious; they are trying to become fire again.

title: Užgesėlės (the Quenched)
text:
Signs & habitat
Hearths that go out every night; blue glints in cold ash; children who are always cold. Worst near Vilnius and around every grove-flame put out after 1387.

title: Užgesėlės (the Quenched)
text:
Before / after the Unbinding
They exist only after 1387 and multiply with every flame extinguished (the Samogitian alkai, 1413–17).

title: Užgesėlės (the Quenched)
section: Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
text:
Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
Live ash from a still-kept sacred flame, scattered in the hearth, gives them what they want, and they go out content; after 1387 the only kept flame is Vytautas’s secret one at Trakai, and every pinch is a risk to its keeper (the graph records the ember as their counter). Gabija’s own words, “Ugnis tau degs”, spoken by a caster at the hearth, cost exhaustion and soul-chill.

title: Slogutis (the presser)
text:
Folk source [Record]
The nightmare spirit (from slėgti, “to press”) that sits on sleepers’ chests so they cannot breathe or move, and rides horses at night, leaving manes tangled into braids. In some regions it is the wandering soul of a living person, often a witch. Defences across the region: stop keyholes, keep a blade by the bed, or invite the presser to come for something in the morning, so that whoever arrives to borrow it is unmasked.

title: Slogutis (the presser)
section: In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
text:
In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
A shard of a living person’s grudge. Anyone who falls asleep in envy or hatred may send one without knowing. The folk are right that it is a living soul and wrong that only witches send it: the jealous sister-in-law, the cheated neighbour and the bitter old soldier all do, and wake tired. In a court full of resentment (Jogaila’s Vilnius, 1382) the sloguciai are thick as moths.

title: Slogutis (the presser)
text:
Signs & habitat
A heavy weight on the chest at the edge of sleep; braided horse-manes; a neighbour who looks bruised and exhausted next day.

title: Slogutis (the presser)
text:

Before: frightening but rarely fatal. After: sloguciai kill, pressing infants and the old to death, and hatred concentrated in towns and camps produces ones that can be seen.

title: Slogutis (the presser)
section: Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
text:
Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
A knife or sickle at the bedside, blade up (children roll onto it). Stop every hole (in winter a sealed smoky hut is its own danger). Say in the dark “Ateik rytoj druskos”, “Come tomorrow for salt”: whoever comes to borrow salt is the sender, and now you have a feud and must give the salt.

title: Reizos raiteliai (Riders of the Reise)

[Saga invention.] Built on a historical practice: the Order’s crusading season, the Reise, brought guest-knights from across Europe each winter and summer to raid Lithuania.

title: Reizos raiteliai (Riders of the Reise)
section: In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
text:
In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
The Iron Saint’s creatures. Knights who died on Reise in a state of complete fearless conviction, the state the Iron Saint grants, did not stop. They ride the old raid-routes on the anniversary of their death: a column of armoured riders whose mail never rusts, smelling of quench-water and hot iron, who ride through villages without seeing them and kill everything in their path as they once did. They do not hunger; they repeat.

title: Reizos raiteliai (Riders of the Reise)
text:
Signs & habitat
Furnace heat in winter; crosses that ring like anvils; the Reise routes through the Wildnis, along the Neman and into Samogitia; hoof-prints that steam in snow.

title: Reizos raiteliai (Riders of the Reise)
text:
Before / after the Unbinding
Before 1387 they ride only in Prussia, harmlessly, on Order land. After: the Pact no longer bars them from Lithuanian soil.

title: Reizos raiteliai (Riders of the Reise)
section: Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
text:
Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
They cannot cross unfrozen running water (the Reise needed frozen ground and fords; in winter everything is frozen). Bog-iron does nothing and feast-day iron feeds them; only smith’s iron forged at a pagan hearth bites, and few such smiths remain. Stand still and do not fear: they see only fear and pass the fearless by.

Book III: the Riders strengthen before Grunwald and scream when the Iron Saint breaks. Book IV: Riders on the Samogitian roads as the Hidden Groves fall. Book V ch. 14: they break at the unfrozen river at Pabaiskas.

Folk source [Record]

section: In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
text:
In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
One named velniukas, the Shadow-Seller’s clerk. Where Henė makes the great deals with princes, Pinčiukas makes the small ones with millers, sextons and serving-maids and keeps the threads that bind them. Fussy, polite, fond of mills and millponds, always carrying a ledger: the reason Henė always knows who in a castle can be bought.

Make him write the bargain down, then read it back aloud (he cannot resist reading), and be able to spot the trick when he does. Never let him name the price “later”; he will refuse the bargain and you will not get what you came for.

title: Laumės (weavers by the water)
text:
Folk source [Record]
Supernatural women of meadows, rivers, lakes and swamps: beautiful, long-haired, betrayed by hen’s or goat’s feet. They spin, weave and wash linen at night, reward diligent and orphaned girls and punish the lazy. Women must not spin on Thursday evening, the laumės’ time. A laumė’s gift of linen never runs out unless the recipient measures it. They dance in moonlit meadows, marry mortal men (who lose them when a taboo is broken) and swap human babies for their own. The rainbow is laumės juosta, the laumė’s sash.

title: Laumės (weavers by the water)
section: In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
text:
In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
The laumės are the weavers of custom. Every courtesy between the land’s people and its spirits is a thread they spin, and the Silent Pact is their great tapestry; they are its most direct witnesses (the graph records them as surety for it). Neither kind nor cruel: they enforce a law of work and courtesy, which looks like kindness to the diligent and cruelty to the rest. The Thursday taboo is real: Thursday is Perkūnas’s day, and a woman spinning then spins against the laumės’ own wheel.

title: Laumės (weavers by the water)
text:
Signs & habitat
Paddle-beats by the river at midnight; wet linen spread on meadows at dawn with no one about; hen-tracks in the dew; a rainbow ending at a lake.

title: Laumės (weavers by the water)
text:
Before / after the Unbinding
Before: hard but fair. After: the tapestry tears. Laumės who once swapped babies now drown them, and their endless linen becomes shrouds.

title: Laumės (weavers by the water)
section: Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
text:
Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
Spin diligently, never on Thursday evening, and leave a hank of flax by the water at Rasos (the labour is a poor girl’s dowry). Never measure a laumė’s gift, so you can never sell it. Never watch laumės bathe (the curious are blinded or drowned). Iron does little; courtesy is the only real ward.

title: Laumės (weavers by the water)
text:
Danger level
II hazard → IV deadly.

title: Laumės (weavers by the water)
text:
Story hooks
Book I: Birutė’s women washing linen in the sea (ch. 11) echo them. Book II: a laumė-wife in a southern castle leaves when a Catholic priest blesses the bed. Book V: laumės’ shrouds wrapping the unburned dead of Pabaiskas.
