title: Geležinis Vilkas (the Iron Wolf omen)
text:
Folk source [Record]
In the legend recorded in the 16th-century Lithuanian chronicles, Grand Duke Gediminas, after hunting near the Šventaragis valley, slept on a hill and dreamt of an iron wolf howling with the voice of a hundred wolves. The pagan priest Lizdeika interpreted it: Gediminas should build a castle and city there, whose fame would carry like that howl. Thus Vilnius was founded.

title: Geležinis Vilkas (the Iron Wolf omen)
section: In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
text:
In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
Not a creature that can be met, fought or fed: an omen-entity, the bound spirit of the Gediminaičiai themselves. In the Krivis’s version of the legend it is iron because it is collared, and its hundred voices are the house’s own sons and grandsons tearing at one another. It howls at the turning points of Gediminid fate: a Gediminid betrayed, kneeling at a foreign altar, or dead. The thousands of wolves that answer it (Book I ch. 9) are the dead sworn vilkatai, laid in bogs and never burned. The brotherhood keeps the one physical relic of the dream, the wolf’s skull, on which every initiate swears.

title: Geležinis Vilkas (the Iron Wolf omen)
text:
Signs & habitat
Thousands of wolves howling at once in the deep forest; a wolf of grey iron glimpsed in mist on an island or hill; frost on iron in summer.

title: Geležinis Vilkas (the Iron Wolf omen)
text:
Before / after the Unbinding
Before: it howled once in Gediminas’s dream and seldom since. After 1382 it howls often: at the prologue’s prophecy, at Kęstutis’s death (ch. 9) and on through the series. When the last flame dies in 1430 it is seen dissolving into mist on Trakai island (Book V ch. 1), and its last howl rises from the Trakai lake in 1440 (Book V ch. 22).

title: Geležinis Vilkas (the Iron Wolf omen)
section: Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
text:
Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
None. Those who hear it learn their master’s fate, not their own; the cost is knowing.

title: Geležinis Vilkas (the Iron Wolf omen)
text:
Danger level
Omen (not rated).

title: Geležinis Vilkas (the Iron Wolf omen)
text:
Story hooks
Book I: the prologue; ch. 9; ch. 25’s rumour (the folk attach the omen to Vytautas, which is half right). Book V: the epilogue’s grandfather, “Kai miškai buvo žali, jis buvo.”

text:
Folk source [Record]

section: In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
text:
In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
The baubas is made of telling. Under the Pact told fears stayed stories. After the Unbinding, each time a mother says “the baubas will come”, a little fear settles in the dark corner of the house, and a family that threatens its children nightly feeds a real thing that eventually comes. The folk are right that it exists and wrong that they are only pretending.

Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
Laughter, light, and a small pet-name (baubiukas) cost nothing, which is why grown-ups forget. Stop using it as a threat; then you need another way to keep children from the well.

Origin [Record] the unmourned, unburied or unfed dead who return, kept busy with scattered poppy seed · [Saga] the same dead, no longer fed
Tier Revenant · the fed dead gone predator
Danger III dangerous → IV deadly
Habitat Unconsecrated graves near abandoned groves; cold houses
Wants Warmth, then memory, then life
Takes Warmth first, then the living's memory of the dead one's face, then life: the old and the sick die in its presence
Signs Houses that will not stay warm; a family that cannot remember a grandmother's name; cattle dead in the stall without a mark
Banes Burning the body (the only true cure); poppy seed; a ring of ash

TraitsHalf-wrong truth. The folk say the dead return until set right. The truth: a vėlė no longer fed does not fade. It starves, and starving makes it a predator. The worst are the unburned, who cannot climb at all.Legion. Rare before 1387 (bad deaths only). After it, abandoned groves breed them. This is the saga's central later-book threat.

CostsFeeding them late. Bread, kisielius or beer on the grave and the name spoken. The priest asks why you are feasting on a grave.Poppy seed. Scattered on the path from the grave; they must count it. Buys a night, not a cure.The ash ring. Renewed nightly. Ordinary ash thins fast; live ash is priceless.Burning the body. After 1387 a crime and a heresy, and someone always sees the smoke.

title: Alkanosios vėlės (the hungry dead)
text:
Folk source [Record]
Folk tradition across the region knows dead who return because they were not properly mourned, buried or fed: suicides, the murdered, the drowned, those buried without rites. They wander, harm livestock and trouble the living until set right. Scattering seed (poppy and others) to keep the dead busy counting is reported across the Slavic and Baltic region.

title: Alkanosios vėlės (the hungry dead)
section: In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
text:
In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
A vėlė no longer fed does not fade: it starves, and starving makes it a predator. It eats warmth first (cold houses), then memory (the living forget the dead person’s face), then life (the old and sick die in its presence). The worst are the unburned, the buried who cannot climb at all (see Nedegintieji).

title: Alkanosios vėlės (the hungry dead)
text:
Signs & habitat
Houses that will not stay warm; a family that cannot remember a grandmother’s name; cattle dead in the stall without a mark; graves in unconsecrated ground near abandoned groves.

title: Alkanosios vėlės (the hungry dead)
text:
Before / after the Unbinding
Before: rare (bad deaths only). After: legion; abandoned groves breed them. This is the saga’s central later-book threat.

title: Alkanosios vėlės (the hungry dead)
section: Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
text:
Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
Feed them late: bread, kisielius, beer on the grave and the name spoken (the priest asks why you feast on a grave). Poppy seed scattered on the path from the grave buys a night, not a cure. A ring of ash around the house, renewed nightly (live ash from a sacred flame is priceless after 1387). Burning the body is the only true cure, and after 1387 opening a grave and burning a corpse is a crime and a heresy.

title: The Iron Wolves
text:
Source: world_rules/iron_wolves.md
Canonical for the sworn wolf-brotherhood. Subordinate to canon_decisions.md, cosmology.md, magic_rules.md and master_chronology.md. It is consistent with power_systems.md (§3, the Wolf-Change; §5, Kęstutis’s silver wolf and the Iron Wolf’s skull) and bestiary.md (§12 werewolves; §23 the Iron Wolf omen). Labels: [Record] means historical or folkloric fact; [Saga invention] means ours.

title: The Iron Wolves
text:
1. At a glance







What peasants call them
vilkatai (werewolves), or “the grey ones”, never to their faces


What they call themselves
Dievo šunys, “God’s dogs”: the old folk name for wolves [Record], worn as a joke and a creed


What the Order calls them
Wolfsbrüder, wolf-brothers [Saga invention]; heathen werewolves, with a bounty on their hides


The brotherhood
Brolija; each band is a gauja (pack) of five to nine


Sworn to
The Root-Mother (body) and the Gediminid flame (name). See §3


Numbers
About 100 under Gediminas; about 120 in 1382; about 40 after the 1382 schism; a dozen by 1435; one (the Flame-Keeper) by the late 1440s [Saga invention]


Country
The Dykra (geography_gazetteer.md B.2): bog-island lairs (guoliai) reached by sunken paths


Power family
Granted power, not asked (power_systems.md §1). They are not casters and sit outside the practitioner tiers

title: The Iron Wolves
text:
2. What the record gives us [Record]
The brotherhood is invented, but every piece of it stands on something real.

The Indo-European wolf-warrior band. Scholars of early Indo-European society describe bands of young unmarried men who lived outside the settlement for a period, raided, and were ritually identified with wolves or dogs. This is the Männerbund (see Kris Kershaw, The One-Eyed God: Odin and the (Indo-)Germanic Männerbünde, 2000). Parallels often cited include the Old Norse úlfheðnar (“wolf-skins”, named beside the berserkers in skaldic verse) and the Irish fían war-bands. David Anthony and Dorcas Brown have interpreted midwinter dog and wolf sacrifices at the Bronze Age site of Krasnosamarskoe (Samara valley) as traces of such an initiation. The Proto-Indo-European name often reconstructed for the band is kóryos.
Baltic werewolves. Lithuanian folklore knows the vilkatas and vilkolakis (bestiary.md §12). Herodotus (Histories 4.105) says the Neuri, usually placed in this region, became wolves for a few days each year. Olaus Magnus (1555) describes werewolves gathering on Christmas night in Prussia, Livonia and Lithuania, breaking into cellars and drinking the beer.
The “hounds of God”. In 1692 at Jürgensburg in Livonia, an old man named Thiess told his judges that werewolves were the hounds of God. In his account they went down to hell three times a year to fight the witches and bring back the stolen seed-grain, so that the harvest would be good. Carlo Ginzburg made the case famous. Lithuanian peasants likewise called wolves Dievo šunys, God’s dogs, and folk custom made St Jurgis (George) the shepherd of wolves, feeding them on his feast day.
The Iron Wolf. Gediminas’s dream, interpreted by Lizdeika, is a 16th-century chronicle legend (legends_and_songs.md §3a).
Kęstutis’s war. Kęstutis fought the Teutonic Order on the western border for some four decades. He was captured in 1361 and escaped from Marienburg (master_chronology.md).
The Wildnis. A deliberately depopulated border belt crossed by raiders and by Lithuanian and Prussian guides (Wegeleute) whom the Order paid to lead its columns (geography_gazetteer.md B.2). Sudovia (Yotvingia) was conquered and largely emptied by 1283.
Sunken paths. Baltic peoples built kūlgrindos: paved causeways laid just below the water of a bog, invisible to strangers and used for defence.

title: The Iron Wolves
text:
3. Origins [Saga invention]

3.1 Before Gediminas: the Sudovian wolves
When the Order emptied Sudovia (1277–83), the last Sudovian warriors went into the new wilderness instead of into baptism or exile. They lived as wolf-bands in the bogs, raiding both sides. The Root-Mother, newly formed out of Žemyna’s and Medeina’s grief (cosmology.md §3.1), took some of them: the first men to lie down in the Dykra mud and get up changed. They had no master and no name. To the Lithuanians who traded with them, they were simply vilkatai.


3.2 Lizdeika’s hundred
The night of Gediminas’s dream, Lizdeika understood something he never told the Grand Duke (legends_and_songs.md §3b). The Iron Wolf was collared because the house would devour itself, and a collar needs a hand on the leash. In the morning he climbed the hill and found a wolf’s skull lying where the dream-wolf had stood, grown hard and grey as iron (Geležinio Vilko kaukolė, power_systems.md §5). He carried it into the Dykra and made the wolf-bands an offer. They would be given a place in the land’s order, food, honour and a fire to give their names to. In return they would guard the Gediminid hearth and the Pact’s peace, and they would be the house’s leash. A hundred came. That is the “hundred voices” in the folk version, read by the brotherhood their own way.
From then on, the brotherhood belonged to two masters: the Root-Mother, who made their bodies, and the Gediminid flame at Šventaragis, which kept their names. That double loyalty is the source of every tragedy below.


3.3 Kęstutis’s wolves (1345–1382)
After the Silent Pact of 1345 (cosmology.md §4.1), the brotherhood became the Pact’s teeth. Kęstutis, holding the west from Trakai, used them as his border raiders in the Wildnis. They burned Order supply-dumps, drowned Reise columns in the bogs, and guided Lithuanian raids into Prussia along routes no Wegeleute knew. He also kept a hidden guard of nine at his side, never named in any chronicle. Algirdas in Vilnius kept the other half of the brotherhood near the Šventaragis flame. When Algirdas died in 1377 those Vilnius packs passed to Jogaila with the city. This split is the root of the 1382 schism (§10).

title: The Iron Wolves
section: 4. Vilkų krikštas: the Wolves’ Baptism [Saga invention]
text:
4. Vilkų krikštas: the Wolves’ Baptism [Saga invention]
The rite is called krikštas, “baptism”, in mockery: the brotherhood took the Christian word and hung it on the oldest thing in the land. It is held in the twelve nights after Kūčios (the winter solstice), the time when the boundary between the living and the dead is thinnest and wolves are said to gather (compare Olaus Magnus and Krasnosamarskoe, §2).
Who is chosen. Unmarried men, usually 16 to 25 (the one exception is the Flame-Keeper, sworn at fourteen, nearly fifteen, in 1405): younger sons, outlaws, the last of burned villages, the occasional boyar’s bastard. Each must be sponsored by a sworn wolf (his vilktėvis, “wolf-father”), who answers for him with his own life.
The rite, in nine steps.

The funeral feast. The candidate’s family holds a šermenys (wake) for him as though he had died. He eats his last meal at his mother’s hearth. From then on he is dead to the household, and his kin may not speak his name.
The name to the fire. At a sacred flame (Šventaragis before 1387; Vytautas’s secret flame after), the candidate whispers his true name (magic_rules.md §6) into the fire. The fire keeps it. His name will go up to Dausos when he dies, without him.
The throat-mark. The sponsor draws a shallow cut across the candidate’s throat at the voice-box and rubs live ash from that same flame into it. It heals as a thin pale line, the gerklės žymė. It is the only mark the brotherhood bears.
Nine nights without fire. The candidate is taken into the Dykra naked but for a belt and a knife of bog-iron. For nine nights he may not light or approach a fire. The packs hunt him. If they catch him, they beat him and let him go; if he is caught three times, he is sent home, nameless and disgraced. Some do not survive the cold.
The drowning. On the ninth night he is led along a kūlgrinda to the oldest bog in the Dykra and pressed under the mud until he stops struggling. The Root-Mother decides. Most come up. Some do not, and they are left where they lie. What comes up has left part of its soul below (power_systems.md §3).
The oath on the skull. Dripping and blue with cold, he swears the Pack’s Word (§6) with both hands on the Iron Wolf’s skull. A lie spoken over the skull is heard by every wolf in the Dykra (power_systems.md §5).
First meat. He eats raw from the pack’s kill, in silence, beside the others.
The skin-name. The Vilkų Tėvas gives him a kailio vardas (skin-name): a nickname, a dead enemy’s name, or an object (Rūdis, Kirmėlė, Jonas). He answers to nothing else for the rest of his life.
The wolf-hide. He receives a wolf-hide from his sponsor, from a wolf the sponsor killed with his own hands. He will be laid in the bog in it.

Failure. About a third of candidates are sent home or die [Saga invention]. The families of those sent home have already held their funeral, so the failures live as ghosts in their own villages. Some become the hedge-folk who later help the brotherhood; some become its informers.

title: The Iron Wolves
section: 5. What it makes of a man
text:
5. What it makes of a man

5.1 Gifts (the Wolf-Change, power_systems.md §3)

The sight of the dvasios. The most important gift and the reason for everything after 1387: a vilkatas sees and hears spirits: laumės at the river, a slogutis on a sleeper’s chest, the hunger in an unfed grave. Priests cannot see them (cosmology.md §4.3).
Night-sight and scent. He sees by starlight as a man sees at dusk, and he can track by smell across a bog a day old.
The Root-Mother’s healing. Wounds packed with bog-moss and mud close in days instead of weeks; their blood is dark, runs slow, and smells of peat. This healing does not work on wounds made by feast-day iron.
Cold and wet are nothing. He can sleep in snow and lie in bog-water for hours.
Pack-sense. Sworn wolves know when a brother dies, wherever they are: they hear one more voice in the Iron Wolf’s chorus.
The iron hour (geležinė valanda). A battle-frenzy like the berserkers’ or úlfheðnar’s. For about an hour the wolf feels no pain or fear, and fights at a ferocity that has given the folk their tales of men becoming wolves. They do not change shape (see §5.4).



5.2 Flaws

No hearth. A vilkatas cannot sleep under a roof with a lit hearth. The fire that holds his name rejects his body, and he wakes choking, with a slogutis’s weight on his chest. They sleep in barns, byres and under the sky.
Feast-day iron burns them like any spirit (bestiary.md preface). Smith’s iron stings; bog-iron does not.
Consecrated stone sickens them: dizziness, nausea, their gifts dimmed (compare magic_rules.md §9).
The hungry dead hunt them (power_systems.md §3). A vilkatas smells of the roots, where the dead are going, and unfed vėlės are drawn to him like moths to a lantern. After 1387 this is both their worst danger and their main tool (§8.3).
The iron hour costs memory. Each frenzy takes a human memory: a face, a song, the way home. Old wolves are people with holes in them.
They cannot weep.



5.3 Physical tells (for prose)
The thin pale throat-scar. Cold skin even in summer. Dogs bristle and whine around them, and a farm-dog will not stay in a room with one (ch. 15–16’s fleeing hounds). A faint smell of peat and wet fur. Old wolves’ eye-teeth lengthen and their body-hair coarsens. No wolf-eyes, no glowing: they look like hard, weathered, quiet men.


5.4 The folk are half right: do they change?
Peasants are sure the vilkatai become wolves. In the iron hour they do not. But the Seniai (§7), wolves who have lived past twenty years sworn, can put on the wolf at need: real flesh, granted by the Root-Mother. Each time they come back less. The last time, they do not come back at all, and they run into the Dykra on four feet. Galminas’s beast-rage (persona/Galminas/) is a different thing again: the Root-Mother’s direct possession of her host, not the brotherhood’s gift.


5.5 The price under the Law of Balance
The Wolf-Change is granted power, bound by the Root-Mother’s nature rather than by the Three Laws. Even so, “Kiek paimi, tiek atiduok” still holds, because the Root-Mother keeps strict accounts.







Taken
Given




The true name (kept by the fire)
A place in the land’s order; the skin-name


The road up: a vilkatas is laid in the bog, never burned, and never climbs to Dausos. Only his name goes up
His voice joins the Iron Wolf’s pack at the roots (bestiary.md §23)


The hearth, and the household: he is dead to his kin
The pack


Part of the soul stays in the bog
The sight of the dvasios


Memory, a little each iron hour
The iron hour itself


Tears
Cold, wet and pain become nothing



Leaving. A vilkatas can return to human life once, if someone who knew his true name speaks it to him by a living fire and offers him bread on a knife-point (the folk cure for werewolves, half right as always). He loses every gift at once, ages the years he has spent sworn in a single winter, and the brotherhood treats him as dead. It is rare, and it is almost always a mother.

title: The Iron Wolves
section: 6. Gaujos žodis: the Pack’s Word [Saga invention]
text:
6. Gaujos žodis: the Pack’s Word [Saga invention]
Nine rules, sworn on the skull.

Duona už duoną (“Bread for bread”). Take nothing that was not given. Pay for every meal, with meat, labour or blood.
No Gediminid blood. A sworn wolf may not shed the blood of Gediminas’s house. This is the Pact’s second clause in the brotherhood’s own mouth. Breaking it gives the wolf to the Root-Mother at once: he goes into the bog alive.
No sleep under a lit roof.
The name stays in the fire. Never seek your own true name; never speak another wolf’s.
Žaltys, oak and flame are never harmed.
The dead go to the bog. A wolf is never burned and never buried in a churchyard. His brothers carry him home to the Dykra, however far.
Courtesy before iron. With spirits, ask first, bargain second, kill last.
Hunt what custom cannot hold. When the village’s charms, milk and salt fail, the wolf comes.
The pack answers the flame, not the man. The brotherhood serves whoever keeps the Gediminid flame, whatever they think of him.

Rule 9 and rule 2 together make the brotherhood’s tragedy. In 1382 the Šventaragis flame stands in Jogaila’s Vilnius, so by the letter the brotherhood owes Jogaila. And no wolf may lift a hand against Skirgaila, whatever he does.

title: The Iron Wolves
text:
8. Weapons and craft

8.1 Arms
Light gear for bog-country: no plate, little mail. Wolf-hide over quilted wool or leather. Their weapons are bog-iron spears, heavy fighting knives and axes, hunting bows, and crossbows taken from the Order. They fight from ambush, at night, in water and reeds, and they prefer drowning a knight in a bog to fighting him on dry ground.


8.2 Bog-craft
They know every kūlgrinda in the Dykra and have laid many themselves. Lairs (guoliai) are bog-islands reached only by these paths. Signals are howls (a whole vocabulary, which the Order’s guides learned to fear) and marks cut in birch-bark. They speak with Wegeleute on both sides, and some of them are Wegeleute (§13, Rūdis).


8.3 The spirit-hunter’s kit (after 1387)
Each pack carries a salt horn (bought dear from Hanseatic smugglers), linen thread spun by the wolves’ sisters, a poppy-seed pouch, juniper, a thunder-stone if they can find one, the ash-pot, flint and steel, and a pyre-axe.
Their method is grim and practical, and it turns their worst flaw into a tool.

Find it. They read the signs (bestiary.md) and talk to the village, the ragana and the dead.
Ask. Most spirits can be bargained with (rule 7). Most hunts end here, with a feast for a forgotten grandmother or a žaltys carried to the forest.
Bait. If asking fails, a wolf offers himself: the hungry dead are drawn to him (§5.2). He lies down inside a ring of live ash beside a prepared pyre.
Burn. When the thing comes, the pack drags the body it rose from onto the pyre. Burning is the only true cure for the unburned (bestiary.md §16, §24).
Leave before dawn, because after 1387 a pyre with a corpse on it is heresy, and someone always sees the smoke.

title: The Iron Wolves
text:
9. How they are seen

Peasants. Fear and need in equal measure. Mothers threaten children with them (feeding the baubas, bestiary.md §10). Yet the same mothers leave bread on a stump at the forest edge for them, as for wolves at Jurginės. After 1387 a village that needs them hangs a wolf’s jaw on its gatepost, and pays in bread, a night in the barn and silence. Nobody thanks them, and nobody tells the priest.
Boyars. Useful dogs: raiders, scouts and assassins of last resort. They are an embarrassment once the boyar is baptised, but boyars hire them secretly when the family’s own dead come for them.
Pagan priests (žyniai, the Krivis). Distrust. The vilkatai belong to the roots, the priests to the sky and fire. A man who is never burned is, to a žynys, half impure: his name goes up and he goes down. The Krivis keeps their names in his flame and does not invite them to his table. After 1387 the surviving žyniai and the wolves need each other and still do not like each other.
Christian clergy. Werewolves and devil-worshippers. The Order pays a bounty per hide. Yet the clergy are blind to the unbound spirits, and from Book III some Franciscans and parish priests quietly send for the wolves when their parishioners start dying. A medieval pun called the Dominicans Domini canes, “the Lord’s dogs” [Record]. The saga should let a friar notice that the Lord now has two kinds of dog.
The Order. The one enemy that does not fear them, because the Iron Saint grants its knights fearlessness (magic_rules.md §9). Wolves who face knights die like anyone else.
Vytautas. See §11.

title: The Iron Wolves
section: 10. Before the Unbinding: border raiders and the hidden guard (to 1387)
text:
10. Before the Unbinding: border raiders and the hidden guard (to 1387)
Until 1382 the brotherhood does three jobs: border war in the Wildnis for Kęstutis; guard (Kęstutis’s hidden nine; the Vilnius packs at the Šventaragis flame); and custom-keeping among the peasantry. That last job is the one the saga’s grey tone needs. A man who killed a žaltys or felled a sacred oak could expect a visit at night. The wolves were the Pact’s police, and the villages feared them for it.
The 1382 schism (Skilimas). When Jogaila took Vilnius in 1382, the Vilnius packs under their leader Kalvis (§13) obeyed rule 9: the flame was in Jogaila’s city, so they owed Jogaila. They did not kill Kęstutis’s men. They stood aside while Skirgaila’s killers did their work at Jogaila’s camp near Trakai (ch. 7), and they told themselves that this kept rule 2. Kęstutis’s packs went with their prince; seven of the hidden nine died in the camp slaughter and were buried in the bog, while Jonas’s men stayed in Kęstutis’s own camp and were not in the tents. The brotherhood has been at war with itself ever since. Wolves have eaten wolves, as ch. 21 puts it (“Vilkas pradėjo ėsti savo paties gaują”).

title: The Iron Wolves
section: 11. After the Unbinding: the only ones who hunt (1387–1450)
text:
11. After the Unbinding: the only ones who hunt (1387–1450)
In 1387 Jogaila puts out the Šventaragis flame (ch. 29). In one stroke:

The Vilnius packs’ master broke the Pact himself, and their loyalty to Jogaila is void.
The only Gediminid flame left is the one Vytautas lights in secret that night (magic_rules.md §6). By rule 9, the whole brotherhood now answers to Vytautas, including the men who held the doors at his father’s murder.
New initiations need a kept flame. Every future wolf must be named into Vytautas’s fire, so the brotherhood’s survival is tied to his. When his flame dies in 1430, so does the krikštas.
Live ash becomes priceless. It is the one ward that holds the unburned dead and calms the Quenched (bestiary.md §27). The ash-bearers make a dangerous journey to Trakai to refill their pots.

From then on the vilkatai are what cosmology.md §4.3 promises: the feared, needed hunters of unbound spirits. They are hated by the Church, used by boyars, paid by peasants in bread and silence, and dying out.

title: The Iron Wolves
section: 12. The wolves and Vytautas, Books I–V
text:
12. The wolves and Vytautas, Books I–V

12.1 Why he is never one of them
Vytautas is bound by his mother’s Sutartis and claimed by Perkūnas (magic_rules.md §2, §7). The Root-Mother cannot take a man already owned twice. Claims can be contested, and she would lose. So the wolves follow a man who is not a wolf. They call him Vilkų kunigaikštis, prince of the wolves, half in irony.


12.2 Book I hooks (for the revision)







Where
Hook




Ch. 2:67 (“Geriausius savo vyrus, kurie negeria Jogailos midaus”)
These “men who don’t drink Jogaila’s mead” are Kęstutis’s hidden nine, with Jonas among them. They literally will not drink from a hand that has not given bread (rule 1). Plant the silver wolf here: Kęstutis touches it on its thong at the door (Book I ch. 2). It passes to Vytautas through the Krėva wall in ch. 8 (D11), not in the armoury


Ch. 7:9 (the slaughter of Kęstutis’s guard at Jogaila’s camp near Trakai, in the tents beyond the manor fence: the killers block the tent openings)
The ordinary guard dies asleep or drinking. Of the hidden nine, seven die in their tents and are buried in the bog; Jonas’s men stayed in Kęstutis’s own camp, and Kirmėlė was not in the tent. They are shot with feast-day iron crossbow bolts (review H2: Order iron arriving with Order silver via Hanulas). Survivors: Jonas and Kirmėlė


Ch. 9:41 (the wolves howl)
The Iron Wolf and its pack of the dead, answered by the living wolves in the forest beyond Krėva


Ch. 13–14
The brotherhood does not storm Krėva. Šešiapirštis judges it impossible, and Birutė’s line in ch. 9 (“Miškas pats pasirūpins savo vilku”) is the Root-Mother’s word: the wolf must reach the forest on his own


Ch. 15 (review C4: the horse from nowhere)
Jonas leaves the horse at a named oak a night’s walk from Krėva. This fixes the continuity hole


Ch. 16:9–11 (skulls under the water; the trackers drowned)
The skulls and rusted armour include wolves laid in the bog (rule 6). The trackers do not just sink: the packs are in the reeds, and they drown Skirgaila’s men, who are not Gediminids. The stone of offering is the brotherhood’s own


Ch. 16 vs 17, 26 (review C3: the amulet)
Vytautas cannot give the silver wolf to the swamp, because it is not his to give: it carries the brotherhood’s sign (power_systems.md §5). Eglė’s silence on the stone accepts the buckle and refuses the wolf


Ch. 17
Rūdis, the Order’s guide at the border fort, recognises the sign on the silver wolf (a grey Prussian border guide; the book shows only his recognition, not his oath, and does not yet name him). That is why the guards stop laughing


Ch. 21:31
The wolves refuse to fight Lithuanians beside the Order. Vytautas loses his pack, and the line “Vilkas pradėjo ėsti savo paties gaują” becomes literal


Ch. 22–24 (recast as the July 1384 Neman castle burnings, review H7)
The wolves come back for this: they open the gates of Marienwerder and Georgenburg from inside


Ch. 25 (the band, Jonas, the “Iron Wolf” rumour)
The “small band” is the remnant of Kęstutis’s packs, led by Jonas as their vilkų vyresnysis. He dies under the oak. Add a scene: Vytautas does not burn him but carries him to a bog (rule 6), the first time he keeps a wolf’s law. The rumour at 25:17 is the folk seeing a ragged prince among men in wolf-hides who drown knights, and calling the whole thing the Iron Wolf. Šešiapirštis lets the rumour stand: it hides the brotherhood behind a man. Cost: everything the wolves do is now blamed on Vytautas


Ch. 26:19
Jogaila flinches from the silver wolf because he knows what the sign means: the wolves who held his doors in 1382 are watching


Ch. 29
After the flame is put out, Vytautas himself takes the one live grain from the wet ash and carries it across the Neris to Kęstutis’s old lodge, where he lights the Last Flame (D11). Kalvis guards that lodge flame from then on and, in Book II, asks to be judged





12.3 Books II–V

Book II (1387–99). The wolves guard the secret flame in the Trakai island vault. Vytautas must judge Kalvis (he spares him, and the old Kęstutis wolves never forgive either of them). 1392: Šešiapirštis goes into Prussia to save Vytautas’s hostage sons, finds them already poisoned (herb-lore, mundane: power_systems.md §2.4), and comes back to lay himself in the bog. 1399, Vorskla: the wolves will not follow Vytautas into the steppe, because the Root-Mother’s gifts fade far from forest. The few who go die. “No mother’s fog, only shame” (magic_rules.md §4.3), and no wolves either.
Book III (1399–1411). The Samogitian uprisings (1401, 1409) beside Galminas. On campaign an ash-bearer carries the secret flame in a lantern (books/series_arc.md, Book III). Grunwald, 1410: the wolves are Vytautas’s vanguard, and they run in the Lithuanian retreat, real or feigned (master_chronology.md), leading pursuing knights into the woods. The Riders of the Reise scream when the Iron Saint breaks (bestiary.md §25).
Book IV (1411–30). The Hidden Groves fall, and with Samogitia baptised the Church hunts the wolves in earnest. A second split: the krikštyti vilkai (baptised wolves) buy their lives by taking bishops’ coin to hunt the unbound in parishes, and by informing on the rest, while Pilkoji’s faction keeps the old way. Henė’s offer (the crown for the flame, magic_rules.md §6) threatens the brotherhood’s existence. If Vytautas lets the flame die, there will be no more wolves, and rule 2 forbids them to stop him by force. The key Book IV wolf scene: Pilkoji at the vault door, deciding whether to break rule 2. 1430: Vytautas dies and the flame goes out.
Book V (1430–50). See §14.

title: The Iron Wolves
text:
13. Notable members [Saga invention]
Skin-names are given; birth-names were pagan two-part names (in the style of Daugirdas, Rambaudas: houses_and_lineages.md) and are lost, by rule 4.

Šešiapirštis (Six-Fingers), Vilkų Tėvas, c. 1325–1392. Grandson of Sudovian wolves; sworn in the year of the Pact. Kęstutis’s oldest captain, who knew the man and not the prince. Dry, patient, merciless to his own. Book I: unseen in the Dykra (ch. 15–16); he meets Vytautas only after ch. 25, at the hunters’ hut. Dies in Book II.
Jonas, c. 1335–1384. Kęstutis’s armour-bearer and the vilkų vyresnysis (pack-elder) of the hidden nine, and so of the ch. 25 band (books/character_arcs.md §5). His skin-name is the baptismal name of an Order sergeant he killed in 1361 during Kęstutis’s escape from Marienburg: the brotherhood’s grim habit of wearing the enemy’s Christian name as a trophy. This explains why a pagan wolf has a saint’s name (ch. 25:7). He survives ch. 7, leaves the horse in ch. 15, and dies in ch. 25.
Kirmėlė (the Worm). One of the hidden nine. In 1382 he sold the hidden guard’s sleeping-place to Skirgaila through Pinčiukas (bestiary.md §21) to save his home village from burning; he was not in the tent that night. The village was burned anyway. He is exposed in Book II (ch. 11, the Trakai vault; Henė, Pušis), and Vytautas lets him live, because he needs every wolf. Grey to the bone.
Rūdis (Rust). A Sambian Prussian, an Order Wegeleute guide of long standing, and (in the canon, not yet on the page in Book I) a sworn wolf: the brotherhood’s eyes inside the Order. Book I ch. 17 shows only his recognition of the silver wolf (the “nineteen of twenty years” figure is unsupported by the text); a double agent through Books II–III; dies at Grunwald in Order colours, killed by a Lithuanian who never knew.
Kalvis (the Smith), leader of the Vilnius packs. He held the doors in 1382 by the letter of rule 9. He guards the lodge flame from 1387 (it is Vytautas, not Kalvis, who carries the ember out: D11) and asks Vytautas for judgement. Book II: spared, despised, loyal unto death.
Pilkoji (the Grey One), born c. 1365 (Book III ch. 7 has her 38 in 1404; Book V ch. 28 has her 84 in 1449; Q13 made her older than the Flame-Keeper). A Samogitian woman of thirty-eight whose village’s dead rose in 1404. She walked into the Dykra, and the Root-Mother took her into the krikštas against all custom: after the Unbinding, custom no longer binds even the Root-Mother. The first woman sworn. Books III–V; the only Vilkų Motina.
The Flame-Keeper (skin-name Žiežirba, D11), born c. 1390–91 (5 in winter 1395–96, 14 and nearly 15 at Kūčios 1405, 48 in 1438; Books II–V). Book V’s protagonist (books/character_arcs.md §4): a boy rescued during the first Unbinding hunts of Book II (winter 1395–96), raised in the Trakai vault as the secret flame’s guard (a boy tending the flame from 1399), and sworn at Kūčios 1405 at fourteen, nearly fifteen (Book III ch. 9): the one wolf named below the usual age of sixteen (§4), an exception the books make because he already lives at the flame. Pilkoji’s foster-son in all but name. After 1430 he wants to relight the flame and cannot, because the Pact cannot be re-sworn by one man. He is the brotherhood’s last wolf.

title: The Iron Wolves
section: 14. Their fate in Book V [Saga invention]
text:
14. Their fate in Book V [Saga invention]

1430. The flame dies with Vytautas. There will be no more krikštas. The Iron Wolf is seen dissolving into mist on Trakai island (Book V ch. 1). It is not leaving; the house it stood for has lost its last keeper of the fire.
1435, Pabaiskas. The field holds thousands of unburned dead (bestiary.md §24). The last dozen wolves, led by Pilkoji, spend a winter burning them. Most die doing it.
1440. Žygimantas Kęstutaitis, Kęstutis’s last son, is murdered at Trakai. The wolves, too few, fail him. The Iron Wolf’s last howl rises from the lake (Book V ch. 22): the pack of the dead mourning the last of the prince they were first sworn to.
Kūčios 1430. Pilkoji gives Kęstutis’s silver wolf (and the cracked pebble), kept from Vytautas’s body since 27 October, to the Flame-Keeper (the “Book V keeper” of power_systems.md §5), as D11 and Book IV have it, not at her death.- The end (Vėlinės, 2 Nov 1449). Pilkoji carries the Iron Wolf’s skull into the oldest bog in the Dykra and lies down beside it. The Flame-Keeper is now the last sworn wolf (he gives the silver wolf to Rimgailė at Palanga in 1450, Book V ch. 29–30). His arc ends when he lets the gods become stories (books/character_arcs.md §4) and, at the series’ close, chooses whether to lie down in the bog or to go home and be named by the fire one last time (§5.5, Leaving). The author decides.
The echo. The brotherhood leaves behind half-made wolves: failed candidates and the sons of wolves, throat-marked but never named into a flame. Their descendants are what Olaus Magnus heard about in 1555, Lithuanian and Livonian “werewolves” breaking into cellars on Christmas night for beer. They are the brotherhood dwindled into a drunken folk-tale, the way the giants dwindled into men (bestiary.md §13). The last trace is old Thiess of Jürgensburg in 1692, telling his judges he was one of God’s hounds, and believing it.
Epilogue (Book V ch. 30): the grandfather’s “Kai miškai buvo žali, jis buvo” is true of the brotherhood as well as the omen.

title: The Iron Wolves
text:
16. Open questions for the author

Is the schism (the Vilnius packs holding the doors in ch. 7) too dark for Book I’s reader? It makes ch. 21 and ch. 29 hit far harder.
(Settled, D11.) The silver wolf passes Kęstutis → Vytautas through the Krėva wall in ch. 8, not in the armoury or on the road.
(Settled, D11 and Book I ch. 29.) Vytautas himself carries the Šventaragis ember to Kęstutis’s lodge.
(Settled by Book III ch. 9.) The Flame-Keeper is sworn at Kūčios 1405, so he has the full gifts.

title: Powers & politics
text:
Source: world_rules/powers_and_politics.md
Canonical reference for factions, treaties and the political board, 1377–1450. Follows canon_decisions.md (D3: real dates, office-holders and outcomes are fixed), cosmology.md (Forces §3, the Silent Pact §4) and master_chronology.md. Genealogy, heraldry and the Teutonic Order’s offices are in houses_and_lineages.md.
Labels: [Record] = sources or standard scholarship. [Saga invention] = the series’ overlay. [Saga suggestion] = proposed, not yet canon; the author decides. (verify) = check before it goes into prose.

title: Powers & politics
section: 1. How power works in the Grand Duchy [Record]
text:
1. How power works in the Grand Duchy [Record]

The Grand Duke (didysis kunigaikštis) rules from Vilnius. Until 1392 the realm is effectively a family firm: Algirdas and Kęstutis’s diarchy (1345–77), then Jogaila with Kęstutis as senior partner (1377–81).
Appanages. Every son receives a city and its lands (Polotsk, Vitebsk, Kyiv, Grodno, Trakai…). The appanage prince owes service and loyalty but has his own court, men and ambitions. Vytautas’s reign (1392–1430) is the slow replacement of appanage princes by appointed governors (namiestniki), often boyars.
The council (later Ponų taryba) is informal before 1413 and powerful after it. Horodło (1413) creates the voivodes of Vilnius and Trakai; by 1440 the council elects grand dukes.
Samogitia governs itself through its elders and assemblies and owes the Grand Duke service, not obedience. It is the land everyone trades and nobody holds.
Religion as politics. A pagan dynastic core; an Orthodox majority in the Ruthenian lands; Catholic merchants and friars in Vilnius. Baptism is a bargaining chip: the Gediminids offer it to the Pope (1323), Louis of Hungary (1351), the Order (1380, 1382, 1383) and Moscow (1384), and finally give it to Poland (1385–87).
Oaths. Treaties are sworn with pagan rites (Kęstutis’s ox in 1351), on the cross, or both. [Saga invention] Every oath form is literally binding by a different power (power_systems §2.6), so the side that swears in the wrong form is the side that pays.

title: Powers & politics
text:
2. Factions inside the Grand Duchy

2.1 The Algirdaičiai (Jogaila’s party)
[Record] Uliana of Tver’s sons and their followers: Jogaila, Skirgaila, Kaributas, Lengvenis, Karigaila, Vygantas, Švitrigaila, with Uliana herself until c.1391. They hold Vilnius and the eastern appanages. After 1386 Jogaila is King of Poland and governs Lithuania through Skirgaila (governor from 13 Mar 1386; VLE gives 1387–92), then through Vytautas as lieutenant (1392 onward).







Book
What they want




I (1382–87)
Remove Kęstutis; get the Order off their backs (Dovydiškės 1380, Dubysa 1382); then trade baptism for a crown (Krėva 1385). Uliana’s alternative: an Orthodox marriage with Moscow (1384 draft with Dmitry Donskoy).


II (1387–99)
Hold Lithuania through Skirgaila; keep Vytautas small (Grodno, not Trakai). After 1392, accept Vytautas as lieutenant and keep overlordship.


III (1399–1411)
Secure Vilnius–Radom (1401): Lithuania reverts to the Crown when Vytautas dies. Then join him against the Order.


IV (1411–30)
Heirs for Jogaila (Sophia’s sons, 1424 and 1427); buy the lords’ consent with privileges; stop the Lithuanian crown without breaking with Vytautas.


V (1430–50)
Švitrigaila claims Lithuania for the Algirdaičiai alone; Casimir (1440) recovers it for the Jagiellonians through the Lithuanian council.




Leverage: the Polish crown, papal legitimacy after 1386, Polish knights and money, Jogaila’s patience, Skirgaila’s sword.
Red lines: Lithuania must remain Jagiellonian property, never a separate kingdom under a Kęstutaitis line.
Force patron: Šešėlių Pardavėjas (Jogaila’s 1382 bargain: the crown gained, the land lost; magic_rules §8); the White Silence settles where his baptism is bought (cosmology §3.3); the Gold-Glutton feeds on his heirs’ privileges. [Saga invention]



2.2 The Kęstutaičiai (Vytautas’s party)
[Record] Kęstutis (to 1382), Vytautas, his brothers Tautvilas and Žygimantas, his sisters’ Masovian husbands, the Samogitians, and the Trakai and Grodno boyars.







Book
What they want




I
Survive Krėva; avenge Kęstutis; recover Trakai and Samogitia. Vytautas uses the Order (1383–84) and then betrays it.


II
Trakai (held by Skirgaila until 1392); the grand-ducal throne (Ostrów 1392); then empire: Kyiv, Smolensk, Podolia, the steppe through Tokhtamysh.


III
Recover Samogitia and break the Order (Grunwald 1410); keep Vilnius–Radom’s reversion clause a dead letter.


IV
A crown to make Lithuania a kingdom equal to Poland; the succession, which he does not have (no son).


V
Žygimantas takes the throne (1432) to save the Kęstutaičiai inheritance from Švitrigaila; his son Mykolas is dispossessed in 1440.




Leverage: Vytautas’s generalship; the Samogitians’ loyalty to Kęstutis’s son; his marriage web (Masovia, Moscow through Sofija); his willingness to change sides.
Red lines: Samogitia for good (he trades it away three times, but always as a loan); never again a prisoner of his cousins.
Force patron: the Amber Queen through Birutė (D1; cosmology §3.4); Perkūnas’s claim (magic_rules §7), contested by the Root-Mother; the flame vow (magic_rules §6). [Saga invention]



2.3 The boyars
[Record] Lithuanian servitor nobility: before 1413 they are the duke’s men; after Horodło (1413), Catholic boyars hold Polish arms and the new offices; by the 1440s the council lords (Goštautas, Daugirdas, Kęsgaila) are the state.

Want: land grants, offices, privileges (1387, 1413, 1432, 1434, 1447 (verify each)), no Polish governors, and a grand duke of their choosing.
Book by book: I–II, they back whichever cousin can win and reward them (many Trakai men follow Vytautas into exile). III, Vytautas’s companions rise with his conquests. IV, Horodło makes them heraldic nobles; they fear the reversion clause and support the crown as Lithuanian independence. V, they make and unmake grand dukes: Švitrigaila (1430), Žygimantas (1432), Casimir (1440, against Kraków’s wishes).
Leverage: they run the castles; the grand duke cannot raise an army without them.
Red lines: Incorporation into Poland as a province; a tyrant who executes them (which is why Žygimantas dies in 1440).
Force patron: the Gold-Glutton (Book V outline ch. 17). [Saga invention]



2.4 The Orthodox Ruthenian princes
[Record] Algirdas’s elder sons (Andrius of Polotsk, Dmitrijus of Bryansk, Vladimiras of Kyiv), the Karijotaičiai of Podolia, the Volhynian houses (Ostrogski, Czartoryski), the Halshany princes, the Smolensk Rurikids. Orthodox, Ruthenian-speaking, the majority of the Grand Duchy’s population and land.

Want: their patrimonies; protection of Orthodoxy; equal access to office; a Kyivan metropolitan independent of Moscow (Vytautas had Gregory Tsamblak elected Metropolitan of Kyiv in 1415 (verify)).
Book by book: I, Andrius fights Jogaila with Moscow and the Livonian Order (to 1387). II, Vytautas removes appanage princes (Vladimiras, Kaributas, Fedor Koriatovich, 1393–95); many still die for him at the Vorskla. IV, Horodło bars the Orthodox from the highest offices, a lasting grievance. V, they are Švitrigaila’s army; Žygimantas’s privilege of 1434 tries to buy them back (verify); the Union of Florence (1439), signed by Metropolitan Isidore of Kyiv and repudiated in Moscow, splits them again.
Leverage: numbers, wealth, the eastern frontier, the Church.
Red lines: forced Catholicism; loss of patrimony.
Force patron: none canonical. Their dvoeverie (surrounding_folklore.md) keeps the household spirits fed after the gods fall silent. [Saga suggestion] the Unbinding is gentler in the Orthodox east because custom never stopped there.



2.5 The Samogitians (Žemaičiai) as a political actor
[Record] The western lowland between Prussia and Livonia: the land bridge the Order needs to join its two halves. Ceded on paper in 1382 (Dubysa), 1384 (Königsberg), 1390 (Lyck), 1398 (Salynas), 1404 (Raciąż); actually held by the Order only 1404–09 (and partly 1398–1401). It rose in 1401 and 1409 (the second rising triggered the Great War). Restored to Lithuania for the lifetimes of Jogaila and Vytautas at Thorn (1411) and permanently at Melno (1422). Baptised 1413 (with Jogaila and Vytautas present) and 1417 (bishopric of Medininkai). Samogitian delegates testified at Constance (1416) that the Order had never tried to convert them, only to conquer them. A revolt against the new clergy in 1418 (verify). In 1440–41 they negotiated their own terms with Casimir (verify).

Want: to be left alone by everyone: the Order, Vilnius and the Church.
Leverage: forests, swamps and men; the ability to make any treaty unworkable. They are the only actor who can veto a deal they never signed.
Red lines: the felling of their groves; being sold.
Force patron: Šaknų Motina and Perkūnas; the Hidden Groves bought by Birutė’s sacrifice (cosmology §4.2) are Samogitian. Galminas is their voice (persona). [Saga invention]



2.6 The pagan clergy
[Record] Little is certain. Długosz describes the Vilnius sacred fire, grove and snakes destroyed in 1387. Peter of Dusburg describes a Prussian high priest (Criwe) at Romuva; whether Lithuania had an equivalent Krivis is debated. Legend names Lizdeika, interpreter of Gediminas’s dream. Priestly titles (žynys, vaidilutė) survive in later sources and folklore.

[Saga invention]: the Krivis of Šventaragis witnessed the Silent Pact (1345). The flames of Šventaragis, Palanga and the Samogitian alkai are its collateral. After 1387 the priesthood breaks into lineages that are dying out (power_systems §4). The saga’s Galminas (a forest-keeper and sap-bleeding priest, invented) becomes a grove at Grunwald (1410, D11); he shares his name only with the historical Jurgis Galminas, Vytautas’s deputy in the 1409 rising and Samogitian elder 1432–34 (VLE). The last žynys of Book V ch. 27, who dies in the 1440s, is his pupil, the beekeeper-žynys, not Galminas.
Want: the flames kept; the Pact honoured; kin-killing punished.
Leverage: the commons’ belief; the oath ceremonies that treaties need; the ability to read signs in public (a priest who declares a lightning-struck oak a verdict can end a campaign).
Red lines: the extinguishing of a flame (1387 is the end of the world for them).
Force patron: the gods themselves: they are the Pact’s human party.

title: Powers & politics
text:
3. Factions outside the Grand Duchy

3.1 The Teutonic Order (Prussia)
[Record] A crusading corporation with an amber monopoly, grain exports, Hanse towns, papal and imperial privileges, and the Reise: seasonal raids into Lithuania with Western guests. Grand Masters: Kniprode (to 24 Jun 1382), Zöllner (1382–90), Wallenrode (1391–93), Konrad von Jungingen (1393–1407), Ulrich von Jungingen (1407–10), Plauen (1410–13), Küchmeister (1414–22), Rusdorf (1422–41).







Book
What the Order wants




I
Keep the cousins at war; buy Samogitia from each in turn (Dovydiškės, Dubysa, Königsberg); hold Vytautas as a puppet claimant and keep Ona and the children as surety.


II
Use Vytautas again (1389–92, the 1390 siege of Vilnius); after his second defection, win Samogitia by treaty (Salynas 1398).


III
Hold Samogitia; stop the Polish–Lithuanian alliance; decisive war (Ulrich von Jungingen). Lose at Grunwald; survive at Marienburg.


IV
Pay the Thorn indemnity; win the propaganda war at Constance (Falkenberg’s tract) and before Sigismund’s arbitration; support Vytautas’s crown to split the union.


V
Back Švitrigaila (Christmemel 1431); after Pabaiskas (1435), sign Brest; face the Prussian Confederation (1440).




Leverage: the best army in the Baltic; money; hostages; castles on the Neman; the claim that Lithuania’s baptism is fake; papal and imperial friends; guests from all over Christendom.
Red lines: Marienburg and Pomerelia (Danzig); the crusade’s legitimacy. A baptised Lithuania leaves the Order with no reason to exist, which is why it insists the baptism is false.
Force patron: Geležinis Šventasis (Iron Saint): Reise, forced baptism, furnace heat in winter (cosmology §3.3). Its “final screams” at Grunwald (series outline).



3.2 The Livonian Order
[Record] The Order’s autonomous northern branch (Riga, Wenden, Dünaburg) under its own Landmeister. Feuded with the archbishops of Riga and with Pskov and Novgorod. Supported Andrius of Polotsk against Jogaila (1380s (verify)). Raided Lithuania from the north. Allied with Švitrigaila and crushed at Pabaiskas (1 Sep 1435), where Master Franco Kerskorff and much of the Livonian leadership died.

Want: Samogitia (the land bridge to Prussia); Polotsk and the Daugava trade; to dominate Riga.
Leverage: northern raids; the Daugava; alliances with Ruthenian princes.
Red lines: Riga’s independence from the Order.
Force patron: the Iron Saint’s northern face. Book V ch. 14: “the Iron Saint is finally silenced in the North.” [Saga invention]



3.3 Poland: the Crown and the Lesser Poland lords
[Record] After Louis I’s death (Sep 1382), two years of interregnum. The Lesser Poland lords (Spytko II of Melsztyn, Jan of Tarnów, Dobiesław of Kurozwęki and others) crown Jadwiga (16 Oct 1384), reject Wilhelm of Habsburg and Siemowit IV, and choose Jogaila (Krėva 1385). Jadwiga recovers Red Ruthenia from Hungary (1387). Later the Oleśnicki generation fights the Lithuanian crown (1429–30) and the Hussite sympathisers (Spytko III, d. 1439).







Book
What Poland’s lords want




I
A king who brings an army against the Order and a realm to the Crown: Krėva’s ambiguous applicare (to “attach” Lithuania) (verify the term and its readings).


II
Lithuania governed for the Crown (Skirgaila, then Vytautas as lieutenant); Red Ruthenia; peace with the Order. Spytko II dies at the Vorskla with Vytautas.


III
Vilnius–Radom: Lithuania reverts to the Crown; recover Dobrzyń (Raciąż) and then Pomerelia (war, 1409–11).


IV
Horodło (union on Polish terms); privileges in return for Sophia’s sons’ succession; no Lithuanian crown. Oleśnicki’s guards block the crown embassy at the border (Aug 1430).


V
Podolia and Volhynia (from 1430); a Polish king in Lithuania (Władysław III’s governor Casimir). The Lithuanians outmanoeuvre them in 1440.




Leverage: the crown Jogaila wears; election of his heirs; papal law; Polish knights.
Red lines: a separate Lithuanian kingdom; Jogaila’s sons inheriting without new privileges.
Force patron: the Gold-Glutton (Oleśnicki, character_arcs) and the White Silence (purchased purity; Jadwiga’s anchor, written as its victim). [Saga invention]



3.4 Hungary and the Luxembourgs
[Record] Louis I (d. 1382) ruled Hungary and Poland. Sigismund of Luxembourg married Louis’s daughter Mary (1385), ruled Hungary from 1387, lost the crusade at Nicopolis (1396), sold the Neumark to the Order (1402) (verify), arbitrated between Poland and the Order (Buda 1412; Breslau 1420, which went in the Order’s favour), hosted Constance, and at Lutsk (1429) offered Vytautas a crown.

Want: Hungarian claims to Red Ruthenia and Moldavia; an anti-Ottoman coalition; to split Poland from Lithuania; money (often the Order’s).
Leverage: imperial authority to grant crowns; Council and arbitration; marriage (Barbara of Celje is kin to Jogaila’s second queen).
Red lines: a Polish–Lithuanian bloc dominating Central Europe; the Hussites (his Bohemian inheritance).
Force patron: the Shadow-Seller serves him in 1429–30 (D2); the Gold-Glutton flatters him. [Saga invention]



3.5 Masovia
[Record] The Piast duchies north of Poland: Janusz I (Warsaw, Czersk) ⚭ Danutė Kęstutaitė; Siemowit IV (Płock, Rawa) ⚭ Aleksandra Algirdaitė; Henryk, bishop-elect, ⚭ Rimgailė (1392). Vassals of the Polish crown, neighbours of the Order.

Want: survival as Piast duchies; to avoid both absorption by Kraków and Order raids.
Leverage: refuge (Vytautas runs here after Krėva, late 1382); mediation (Henryk at Ostrów 1392); marriage links to both Gediminid lines.
Red lines: incorporation into the Polish crown.
Force patron: none. Masovia is neutral ground in the saga.



3.6 The Golden Horde and its succession wars
[Record] Tokhtamysh reunited the Horde (1380), burned Moscow (Aug 1382), was broken by Timur (1391, 1395), and fled to Vytautas. Edigu, beglerbeg and kingmaker, with Temur Qutlugh, destroyed Vytautas’s coalition at the Vorskla (12 Aug 1399). Tokhtamysh’s sons (Jalal ad-Din at Grunwald) were Lithuania’s clients. The Horde fractured in the 1420s–40s: Ulugh Muhammad, and Hacı Giray’s Crimea, founded with Lithuanian backing (verify year).







Book
What the steppe wants




I
Tribute from the Rus’ lands; to punish Moscow (1382). Lithuania is a distant partner (Jogaila’s 1380 alliance with Mamai).


II
Tokhtamysh: restoration, paid for with rights over Rus’ (verify). Edigu: Tokhtamysh’s head and no Lithuanian protectorate over the steppe.


III
Edigu: punish Moscow (1408); keep Lithuania off the Black Sea. Tokhtamysh’s sons: Vytautas’s help to the throne; Jalal ad-Din’s Tatars ride at Grunwald.


IV
Rival khans court Vytautas (who makes and unmakes khans in the 1410s–20s (verify)).


V
Crimea breaks away under Hacı Giray with Lithuanian support; Kazan is founded (verify dates).




Leverage: cavalry; tribute; the ability to wreck Kyiv and Podolia.
Red lines: a Christian protectorate over the khan.
Force patron: Stepių Alkis (Steppe-Hunger), which is not Tengri (cosmology §2.2), but the hunger of horizon-kings. It feeds on Vytautas as much as on Edigu.



3.7 Muscovy
[Record] Dmitry Donskoy (to 1389): Kulikovo 1380; the 1384 marriage draft with Uliana. Vasily I (1389–1425) ⚭ Sofija Vytautaitė (1391); fought his father-in-law over Smolensk, Pskov and Novgorod in 1406–08, ending with the stand-off on the Ugra (1408). Received the defecting Švitrigaila (1408). Vasily II (1425–62) was placed under Vytautas’s protection (Vasily I’s testament (verify)), with Sofija as regent, and was blinded in 1446 in the Muscovite civil war.

Want: to “gather the Rus’ lands”: Smolensk, Novgorod, Tver; the Metropolitan of all Rus’ to sit in Moscow.
Leverage: Orthodoxy; Horde favour; marriage (Sofija).
Red lines: a Lithuanian metropolitan of Kyiv; Lithuanian control of Novgorod.
Force patron: none canonical. [Saga suggestion]: the Steppe-Hunger’s shadow, since Moscow learned rule as the Horde’s tribute-collector.



3.8 Novgorod and Pskov
[Record] Merchant republics that hire princes: Lithuanian Gediminids served them (Narimantas earlier, Lengvenis 1389–92 and again in the 1400s (verify)). Vytautas besieged Opochka (Pskov land, 1426) and Porkhov (Novgorod land, 1428), taking large ransoms (verify sums). Their trade runs through the Hanse’s Peterhof in Novgorod.

Want: independence; trade; a prince who protects without ruling.
Leverage: silver; the fur trade; playing Vilnius against Moscow.
Red lines: a resident overlord.
Force patron: [Saga suggestion]: the Gold-Glutton, through the Hanse.



3.9 The Hanse
[Record] The German merchant league. The Prussian towns (Danzig, Thorn, Elbing, Königsberg) are the Order’s subjects and increasingly its opponents (Prussian Confederation, 1440). Riga dominates Daugava trade and Polotsk. Hanseatic merchants in Vilnius (Hanulas of Riga led the townspeople who took Vilnius castle for Jogaila on 12 Jun 1382 and became first elder of Vilnius). A Hanseatic office (Kontor) at Kaunas from 1441 (verify).

Want: privileges, safe roads, an end to the Reise’s disruption, wax, furs, grain and amber.
Leverage: credit; ships; the Order’s tax base.
Red lines: monopoly breaches; war that closes the rivers.
Force patron: the Gold-Glutton: its envoys walk Trakai in Book I ch. 28 (cosmology §3.3). The Shadow-Seller’s first mask, Hanulas, is a Riga merchant (D2). [Saga invention]



3.10 The Papacy and the Councils
[Record] The Western Schism (1378–1417): Rome against Avignon (and Pisa from 1409). Poland and Lithuania follow Rome. The bishopric of Vilnius is founded in 1387–88. The Council of Constance (1414–18) ends the schism, burns Jan Hus (6 Jul 1415), and hears the Polish–Lithuanian case against the Order: Paulus Vladimiri (Paweł Włodkowic) argues that pagans have rights; the Samogitian delegation testifies (1416); the Order’s Johannes Falkenberg attacks Jogaila in a libel later condemned (verify outcome). The Council sets up the Samogitian bishopric (1417). Martin V (1417–31) presses Lithuania over the Hussites. The Council of Basel (1431–49) and the Union of Florence (1439) follow.

Want: unity, Church union with the Orthodox, crusade against the Ottomans, control over the Order’s crusade.
Leverage: legitimacy; crowns (no crown without Rome); bishoprics.
Red lines: heresy (the Hussites); schism.
Force patron: the White Silence gathers around purchased baptism and purity (cosmology §3.3). Honest clerics (Włodkowic, the Vilnius Franciscans) are its victims, never its agents (cosmology §2.2). [Saga invention]



3.11 Bohemia and the Hussites
[Record] After Hus’s burning, Bohemia revolts (1419). The Hussites offer their crown to Jogaila and then to Vytautas (1420–21), who sends his nephew Žygimantas Kaributaitis to Prague (1422; again 1424–27). Jogaila issues the anti-Hussite Edict of Wieluń (1424) under papal pressure. In 1433 a Polish–Hussite army raids the Order’s Pomerania to the Baltic (verify details). Lipany (1434) breaks the radicals. Hussite sympathy survives among Polish lords (Spytko III, killed at Grotniki in 1439).

Want: allies against Sigismund; recognition.
Leverage: the most feared infantry in Europe; a vacant crown to offer.
Red lines: Sigismund on the Bohemian throne.
Force patron: none canonical. [Saga suggestion]: Hussites scorn bought indulgences, so they starve the White Silence, which makes them the egregore’s enemies and the saga’s unexpected allies of the old gods’ logic.

title: Powers & politics
text:
6. Political story engines

Trakai in Skirgaila’s hands (1382–92). Vytautas must bow in his father’s hall to the man who held the rope. Every feast at Trakai is a provocation; Skirgaila drinks there with Henė (Book II opens here, series_arc). The engine burns until Ostrów.
Ona and the children as hostages (1383–84; c.1390). The Order’s surety for Vytautas’s loyalty. Each defection is a decision to risk his family; the second, by one tradition, costs him his sons (1392; contested). Ona stops looking at him (character_arcs).
Vytautas’s two defections (1384, 1392). Both times he holds Order castles when he turns (Georgenburg, Marienwerder; later Neman forts (verify)). The Order’s knights who trusted him burn; his name in Prussia becomes a curse. Perkūnas, keeper of oaths, keeps score (magic_rules §7).
The Samogitia-for-peace trades. Dubysa, Königsberg, Lyck, Salynas, Raciąż: five times the same land is sold by men who do not hold it. The Samogitians never sign and always pay. Each sale is a grove felled in the Hidden Groves.
Kęstutis’s mercy (1381). He held Jogaila, read the treaty, and let him go. Every Kęstutaitis afterwards must choose between mercy and survival; Žygimantas (Book V) chooses survival and becomes a tyrant.
The disinherited elder sons. Andrius and Dmitrijus fought for Moscow at Kulikovo while Jogaila marched for Mamai; Andrius rots in a Polish prison; both die for Vytautas at the Vorskla. Why would Algirdas’s first-born die for Kęstutis’s son? A Book II mystery with a political answer: Vytautas treated them as princes.
Brothers on both sides of the wall (Vilnius, 1390). Karigaila (Algirdaitis) dies defending; Tautvilas (Kęstutaitis) dies attacking. Henry Bolingbroke watches. One siege kills a cousin on each side: Gediminid blood shed by Gediminids, three years after the Pact that forbade it died, so no god intervenes and no one is punished.
Masovia’s two sisters-in-law. Danutė Kęstutaitė (Warsaw) and Aleksandra Algirdaitė (Płock) are married to brothers. Vytautas’s flight in 1382 runs through their courts. Henryk of Masovia mediates Ostrów, marries Rimgailė, and dies within a year: poison, or bad luck?
The heirless king and the reversion clause. Jadwiga’s death (1399) leaves Jogaila’s Polish crown legally exposed; Vilnius–Radom (1401) makes Vytautas’s realm revert to Jogaila. Vytautas’s only defence is to make Lithuania a kingdom, which leads to Book IV.
Sofija’s Moscow. Vytautas’s daughter rules Moscow’s court for thirty years; her son Vasily II is his ward (1425–30). The grandfather wars on the son-in-law (1406–08) and protects the grandson. The Kęstutaičiai blood survives only in Moscow.
Tokhtamysh’s yarlik. A deposed khan offers the Rus’ lands for an army. Vytautas’s empire dream is a contract with a ghost; the Vorskla collects (Steppe-Hunger, Henė’s vision).
Švitrigaila, the perpetual pretender. Rebels in 1393, 1402 and 1408; imprisoned at Kremenets for nine years; freed by an Orthodox prince’s raid (1418 (verify)); Grand Duke in 1430; loser at Pabaiskas. He is the dynasty’s id, and he outlives everyone.
Horodło’s two faces (1413). Catholic boyars adopt Polish arms and gain offices, and the Orthodox princes are shut out. The grievance becomes Švitrigaila’s army in 1432. A heraldry ceremony is a declaration of civil war twenty years early.
The Order’s insult to Birutė. Marquard von Salzbach insulted Vytautas’s murdered mother after the Peace of Raciąż (1404, not 1390: en.wikipedia after Ekdahl); after Grunwald Vytautas has him beheaded for refusing to apologise. Plant the insult early; let the Amber Queen’s son answer it on the field of the Iron Saint.
The propaganda war (Constance, 1414–18). Włodkowic against Falkenberg; Samogitian witnesses in a German city. The Order needs Lithuania’s baptism to be fake; Lithuania needs it to be real. Vytautas, who keeps a secret pagan flame, is the one man for whom the Order is right.
The crown affair (1429–30). Sigismund offers it to break the union; Oleśnicki stops it to save the union; Jogaila is caught between; Henė offers the last bargain (the crown for the flame, magic_rules §6). Vytautas refuses and dies uncrowned (series_arc).
The Hussite crown (1420–27). Lithuania flirts with heresy: Vytautas accepts the Bohemian offer and sends Kaributaitis, then abandons him under papal pressure. Kaributaitis ends at Pabaiskas on Švitrigaila’s side, captured by the Kęstutaitis army and dead soon after (verify how).
The Halshany women. Vytautas marries Julijona (1418); he proposes her niece Sophia to Jogaila (1422). Sophia’s sons become the Jagiellonian dynasty. Vytautas chose the mother of the kings who inherited his realm.
The Czartoryski knives (1440). Maria of Vitebsk’s descendants (if Konstantinas’s parentage holds) murder the last ruling Kęstutaitis, with council lords behind them (verify). The first Kęstutaitis grand duke was killed by Uliana’s line, the last by Maria’s: a closed circle.
The child elected against Kraków (1440). The Lithuanian council crowns a 12-year-old Jagiellonian to keep Lithuania from Poland, and the boy grows into the king who unites them on Lithuanian terms (1447). The cousins’ war ends with a grandson’s compromise.
