title: Peoples & cultures
text:
Source: world_rules/peoples_and_cultures.md
World-bible reference for Geležinio Vilko Saga. It sits below canon_decisions.md, cosmology.md, magic_rules.md and master_chronology.md, and does not override them. The companion volume is geography_gazetteer.md.
Labels. [Record] means attested in sources or archaeology, or the scholarly consensus. [Ethnographic] means known from later (16th–19th c.) folk custom and projected back, plausible but not proven for 1382. [Saga invention] is ours. (verify) means uncertain or contested.
A caution that governs this whole file. Much of what we “know” about 14th-century Lithuanian paganism comes from enemies (Order chroniclers such as Peter von Dusburg and Wigand of Marburg), from later Christians (Długosz, the 16th-c. Lithuanian chronicles), or from 19th-c. Romantic reconstruction. Treat every pagan detail as half record, half rumour. That suits the saga’s rule that the folk are only ever half right (cosmology, epigraph).

title: Peoples & cultures
text:
Part A. The peoples

A.1 Aukštaičiai (Highlanders)

Who [Record]: The Lithuanians of the eastern core: Vilnius, Trakai, Kernavė, Ukmergė, the lake country. The Gediminid dynasty’s home people.
Language: Lithuanian, Aukštaitian dialects. Unwritten in 1382: the court writes in Ruthenian (east) and Latin (west), and Lithuanian is spoken but never put on parchment [Record]. The first Lithuanian books are 16th-century.
Faith: Pagan, publicly and officially, in 1382 [Record]. Princes’ Orthodox wives keep churches in Vilnius, several Gediminids are baptised Orthodox, and Catholic friars minister to merchants. Lithuanian rulers tolerate all of it as long as it does not become politics (Gediminas’s letters make religious tolerance part of diplomacy [Record]).
Dress: Linen and wool; patterned woven belts; fur in winter. The elite blend Ruthenian and Western fashion (see C.7).
Food: Rye, barley, peas, dairy, pork, game, fish, honey (see C.6).
Status: The ruling people of an empire mostly made of others. A small warrior aristocracy (the bajorai) over a free and semi-free peasantry.
How others see them: To the Order, Litwini, “Saracens of the North”, obstinate idolaters, and also dangerous, brave, and (in Kęstutis’s case) honourable enemies (Order chroniclers praise his keeping of his word (verify specific passages)). To Ruthenians, rough pagan overlords who nevertheless protect Orthodoxy better than the Tatars did. To Poles, raiders who carried off whole villages in living memory.
Saga notes: Perkūno Rūstybė claims their warriors: oath and courage are his food. In Book I they are the people whose courtesy keeps the Pact alive. After 1387 they are the first to be baptised and the first to be haunted: their groves are nearest the capital, so their unfed dead rise first (the Unbinding, cosmology §4.3).



A.2 Žemaičiai (Samogitians, the Lowlanders)

Who [Record]: The western Lithuanians, between the Nevėžis and the sea, ruled by elders (seniūnai, Germ. Ältesten) under the Trakai duke’s overlordship rather than by resident princes.
Language: Samogitian, a Lithuanian dialect group distinct enough to sound foreign to a Vilnius courtier [Record].
Faith: The most stubbornly pagan people in Europe. They destroyed the Sword Brothers at Saulė (1236) and the Order at Durbe (1260) [Record]. Baptised only in 1413–17, and sent their own delegation to the Council of Constance in 1416 to accuse the Order of using baptism as a pretext for conquest [Record].
The Samogitian question [Record]: Samogitia is the land bridge between the Order’s Prussia and Livonia. Every Lithuanian ruler in the saga, when cornered, sells it: Jogaila at Dovydiškės (1380) and the Dubysa (1382), Vytautas at Königsberg (1384) and Salynas (1398), Vytautas and Jogaila at Raciąž (1404). The Samogitians keep refusing to be sold, rising in 1401 and 1409. It is the saga’s purest grey tragedy: their own princes are the brokers of their conquest.
Dress and food: As A.1, poorer and more archaic. More fish and coastal goods near the sea.
How others see them: To the Order, the most bestial pagans of all, beyond negotiation. To Vilnius, loyal, useful and expendable. To themselves, the free people.
Saga notes: The Root-Mother protects them. Their land holds the Hidden Groves bought by Birutė (cosmology §4.2), and Galminas is their priest (Book V). The Iron Saint hungers for them most. Kęstutis was “theirs”, which is why Samogitian loyalty to Vytautas is his to lose. Every time he signs Samogitia away, a grove should go quiet on the page.



A.3 The remnant Prussians (Prūsai)

Who [Record]: The West Baltic people conquered by the Order between 1230 and 1283, after the Great Prussian Uprising (1260–74). In 1382 they are a subject peasantry in their own country, with a minority of free Prussians who serve the Order.
Language: Old Prussian, a West Baltic language related to Lithuanian but not mutually intelligible. It survived as a peasant tongue into the 16th c. (catechisms of 1545 and 1561) and died out around 1700 [Record].
Faith: Officially Catholic. Pagan practice persisted in secret (16th-c. Order and Lutheran sources describe goat sacrifices, notably the Sudauerbüchlein (verify dating)) [Record].
Status: Most work under Prussian or German law as unfree or semi-free peasants. Some, the Witinge (Lith. vitingai), are free Prussian military servitors who hold land for service and act as the Order’s light cavalry, scouts and guides into Lithuania [Record (verify the term’s use in the 1380s)].
How others see them: To the Germans, peasants of doubtful faith. To Lithuanians, lost kin and also traitors who guide the Reise. To themselves, it depends whom you ask.
Saga notes: The orphaned people of the Pact: their flame (Romuva) went out a century ago, and their unburned dead are among the oldest ravenous vėlės in the Dykra. A Witing guide who leads Order raids into Samogitia by day and leaves milk for the žaltys by night is the best embodiment of the saga’s grey. A Prussian Witing would be the ideal guide (or betrayer) for the Order’s Book I campaign (ch. 20).



A.4 Yotvingians and Sudovians (Jotvingiai, Sūduviai)

Who [Record]: A West Baltic people of the lands south of the Nemunas (Sudovia/Sūduva), conquered by the Order in 1277–83. Some were resettled into Samland by the Order (the Sudauer Winkel) [Record]; others fled into Lithuania (verify: the Lithuanian chronicles and place-names suggest settlement around Grodno and elsewhere). Their homeland became the deepest part of the Wildnis [Record].
Language: West Baltic (Yotvingian), extinct. It survives in place-names and a disputed 17th-c. word list (verify).
Faith: Pagan until conquest. The remnant is half-Christian, half-nothing.
Status in 1382: Scattered families in the Dykra, in Lithuanian service, or as Order peasants in Samland. A people that has become a landscape.
Saga notes: The Dykra’s ghost-people. Their overgrown hillforts are its “old villages”. Eglė’s swamp-kin speak a language Vytautas almost understands, which could be Yotvingian [Saga invention]. The Root-Mother remembers them by name, and nobody else does.



A.5 Curonians (Kuršiai)

Who [Record]: A Baltic people of the coast from the Curonian Lagoon north into Courland. Conquered by the Livonian Order in the 1260s (verify). The Palanga area is a Curonian–Samogitian borderland, and Birutė’s hill was a Curonian settlement and hillfort [Record].
Language: Curonian, a Baltic tongue between Lithuanian and Latvian, absorbed by both. The later Kursenieki fishermen of the Curonian Spit spoke a Latvian-based dialect (verify).
Faith: Pagan, then nominally Christian under the Livonian Order; the coast stays semi-pagan.
Status: Fishermen, amber gatherers, coast-folk. The “Order’s” Curonians in Courland live a short ride from the “free” Samogitian ones at Palanga.
Saga notes: The Amber Queen’s people. The vaidilutės of the shore flame may have been Curonian-born [Saga invention], which makes Birutė a borderland woman, half of the sea. The servant girl “from the coastal village” in ch. 11 is Curonian. The Order’s amber monopoly (C.10) falls on their cousins in Samland.



A.6 Ruthenians (Rusėnai; Rus’, the Ruthenian lands)

Who [Record]: The East Slavic Orthodox majority of the Grand Duchy: Polotsk, Vitebsk, Kyiv, Volhynia, Podolia, Black Ruthenia, Siveria. The ancestors of today’s Belarusians and Ukrainians.
Language: East Slavic vernaculars. Writing uses Church Slavonic and the Ruthenian chancery language in Cyrillic. This is the GDL’s administrative language: charters, treaties with the east, and later the Lithuanian chronicles and statutes [Record].
Faith: Orthodox Christian, under the metropolitan of Kyiv and all Rus’. The metropolitan seat itself is contested between Lithuanian and Muscovite candidates (Cyprian is the key figure of the 1370s–80s (verify)). Folk practice keeps the old spirits: the domovoy, leshy and rusalki (surrounding_folklore.md: dvoeverie) [Ethnographic].
Dress: Long kaftans; boots; fur hats; women with covered heads (married) and embroidered linen. The elite wear Byzantine-influenced silks.
Food: Rye and buckwheat (verify buckwheat’s spread by the 1380s), kvass, mead, fish fasts on Orthodox calendar days. The strict Orthodox fasts set the rhythm of the year.
Status: Not a conquered people in their own eyes. Their princes (Rurikid and Gediminid) are part of the ruling elite. Their boyars serve in the grand duke’s armies. Their towns have churches, monasteries, icons and literate clergy. Pagan Lithuania ruled them partly by leaving them alone: “we do not change the old, we do not bring in the new” is a later formula attributed to GDL practice (verify).
How others see them: To Lithuanians, the clerks, priests and craftsmen of the realm, and wives of princes: Algirdas’s two wives were Orthodox princesses, and Jogaila’s mother is Julijona of Tver [Record]. To Catholics (Poles, the Order), “schismatics”, barely better than pagans. To Moscow, kin who chose the wrong master.
Saga notes: The Vulture Forces largely pass them by. No purchased baptism (they were baptised four centuries ago), no crusade aimed at them. Their danger is the Steppe-Hunger at their southern edge and the Gold-Glutton in tribute and trade. Their spirits are not Lithuanian dvasios, but they obey the same rule of courtesy (cosmology §2.3), which shows the old courtesy is wider than Lithuania. A Ruthenian chancery scribe at Jogaila’s court (who writes down what the pagans will not) makes a strong recurring point-of-view: the man who decides what history remembers.



A.7 Poles (Lenkai)

Who [Record]: The people of the Kingdom of Poland and the Masovian duchies.
Language: Polish; Latin for church, chancery and law.
Faith: Catholic, with a strong episcopate (Kraków, Gniezno). Old saints (Stanisław, Wojciech/Adalbert).
Dress: Western fashion filtered through Bohemia and Hungary (Louis of Hungary’s court): tight hose, short doublets for young men, long robes for the old and the clergy, mail and plate for knights.
Status in 1382: A kingless kingdom after September 1382, run by magnate clans (Toporczyk, Leliwa, Nałęcz, Grzymała (verify the civil-war factions)) and bishops, deciding whom to marry the child queen to. Masovia is separate, poorer and closer to Lithuania by blood (Danutė, then Aleksandra) [Record].
How others see them: To Lithuanians, old raid targets: Lithuanian raids took Polish and Masovian captives by the thousand in the 13th–14th centuries [Record], and Lithuanian captive-villages of Poles existed (verify). From 1385, partners of convenience. To the Order, rivals for Pomerania and Kulmerland.
Saga notes: The White Silence gathers around the 1385–86 bargain: a baptism bought with a crown. Poles themselves are not its servants. Jadwiga is its victim and later its anchor (hidden_immortals.md §5); Oleśnicki is the Gold-Glutton’s champion (outlines). Show decent Poles from the start (a Masovian priest at Danutė’s court; a Kraków knight at Grunwald), so that Book IV’s “the Poles stole the crown” stays one faction’s crime, not a nation’s.



A.8 German Order brethren and settlers

Who [Record]: The Teutonic Order (Ordo domus Sanctae Mariae Theutonicorum) is a military-religious order. Its brethren are knight-brothers (white mantle with black cross), priest-brothers, and sergeant or half-brothers (grey mantles, the Graumäntler). Most are recruited from the German lands of the Empire (Franconia, Thuringia, Swabia, the Rhineland), very rarely from Prussia itself. Under them are German settlers: towns under Kulm law (from the Kulmer Handfeste, 1233), German peasant villages, Hanseatic merchants.
Language: Middle High and Low German. Latin for liturgy and chancery. Knight-brothers are often barely literate; the chaplains write.
Faith: Catholic, of a militant devotional kind, centred on the Virgin Mary (Marienburg is her castle). Brethren take vows of poverty, chastity and obedience and live by a Rule: fixed hours of prayer, common meals, silence at table, fasting, no private property, no hunting except wolves and bears (verify the exact rule) [Record].
The Reise guests [Record]: Western knights come to Prussia for the summer or winter Reise to fight the “Saracens of the North”: English, French, Scots, Bohemians, Germans. Chaucer’s Knight “had reysed in Lettow” (Lithuania) [Record]. Henry Bolingbroke, the future Henry IV, joins the 1390 siege of Vilnius [Record]. For them it is chivalric tourism with salvation attached.
Dress and arms: In the 1380s, mail and a coat of plates, a bascinet, gauntlets; the mantle over it. Crossbows in quantity. Big horses, heavy lances.
How others see them: To Lithuanians, kryžiuočiai (“cross-men”), the iron enemy, and also the source of the best weapons, salt and silver, and of a refuge for every defeated Gediminid (Vytautas twice, Švitrigaila). To Poles, overmighty neighbours. To their own Prussian peasants, lords.
Saga notes: The Iron Saint feeds on the Reise (cosmology §3.3). Brethren range from sincere ascetics (a sergeant-brother who nurses Lithuanian captives in the Order’s hospital) to career killers for whom the Rule is cover. Konrad Zöllner von Rotenstein (Book I’s Grand Master) is an administrator, not a monster. The Order is also a builder of towns, schools and hospitals [Record]. Never let the Iron Saint wear every white mantle.



A.9 Hanseatic merchants

Who [Record]: Merchants of the German Hanse, the league of trading towns (Lübeck, Visby, Riga, Danzig, Elbing, Thorn, Königsberg, Reval). Kontors at Novgorod (Peterhof), Bruges, London and Bergen.
Language: Middle Low German, the Baltic’s lingua franca of trade [Record].
Faith: Catholic, practical. A merchant in a pagan town needs a priest and a church, and gets them.
Trade: Out of Lithuania and Rus’: furs, wax, honey, hides, timber, amber (from the Order’s monopoly), grain (Prussia). In: salt (Lüneburg and Biscay “bay salt”), Flemish and English cloth, metals and arms (when not embargoed), wine, herring, spices, silver [Record].
How others see them: To the Order, its tax base and allies (most Prussian towns are Hanse members). To Lithuanians, useful foreigners with too many scales. To Novgorod, rivals and partners.
Saga notes: The Gold-Glutton’s counting-houses (cosmology §3.3). Hanulas, the Riga merchant who opens Vilnius to Jogaila (1382) [Record], is Henė’s first mask (D2). Show a decent merchant too, one who smuggles salt to a starving Samogitian village because a debt is a debt. The Glutton feeds on the ledger, not the trader.



A.10 Tatars (Totoriai) [Books II–V]

Who [Record]: Turkic-speaking subjects of the Golden Horde (the Ulus of Jochi). After Vytautas’s steppe campaigns (from c. 1397) and Tokhtamysh’s exile in Lithuania, Tatar communities were settled in the GDL: given land for military service, allowed to keep their faith, later known as Lipka Tatars [Record].
Language: Kipchak Turkic. Later generations shift to Ruthenian and Polish while keeping Arabic-script religious books (kitabs) (verify dating).
Faith: Sunni Islam (the Horde converted under Özbeg in the 14th c.) over older steppe custom [Record].
Dress, food: Felt and leather, kaftans, horse-centred culture (mare’s milk kumis; horse meat). Settled Tatars adapt to the forest economy.
Status: Honoured military settlers under Vytautas, with a right to their own law in some matters (verify), and mosques in later centuries.
How others see them: To Lithuanians, terrifying enemies at Blue Waters and Vorskla, and excellent allies at Grunwald [Record: Tatar contingents fought at Grunwald under Jalal al-Din]. To the Order, proof that Vytautas brings infidels against Christians, which became propaganda at Constance (verify).
Saga notes: The Steppe-Hunger is not “the Tatars”. It feeds on conquest-without-end, and its most willing host in Book II is Vytautas. The Tatars settled in Lithuania are, if anything, its refugees. Tokhtamysh, a deposed khan seeking a home, is a mirror of Vytautas in 1382.



A.11 Karaims (Karaimai) [Books II–V]

Who [Record]: A Turkic-speaking people of Karaite Judaism brought from Crimea by Vytautas at the end of the 14th century (traditionally c. 1397–98; the exact year is not securely documented (verify)) and settled chiefly at Trakai, with other communities later (Lutsk, Halych, Biržai/Panevėžys) [Record].
Language: Karaim, Kipchak Turkic, written in Hebrew script; Hebrew in liturgy.
Faith: Karaite Judaism: scripture (the Tanakh) without the rabbinic Talmud. Their house of prayer is the kenesa [Record].
Status: Under ducal protection, with privileges (later charters (verify dates)). Tradition holds they served as guards of Trakai castle [Ethnographic/tradition (verify)]. In later centuries the Karaim street in Trakai has houses with three windows to the street (tradition (verify)), and they are famed for kibinai pastries (later (verify)).
Saga notes: Book II–IV’s Trakai garrison. Strangers who owe loyalty to one man, Vytautas, not to a church or a nation. [Saga invention, optional]: the Karaim guard captain is the only one who knows what burns in the island castle’s vault (magic_rules.md §6), and keeps silent because his own faith also keeps a lamp (do not go further than this parallel). Avoid exoticising them: they are soldiers, gardeners, scholars and householders.



A.12 Jews (Žydai) [Book II onward; possible earlier]

Who [Record]: Jewish communities in Brest, Grodno, Trakai, Lutsk and other towns. They came from the west (Ashkenazi, from German lands and Poland) and possibly earlier from the Byzantine and Kyivan east (verify). Vytautas’s privilege to the Jews of Brest (1 July 1388) and to Grodno (1389) (with Trakai and Lutsk following, or Trakai first (verify)) is usually cited as the founding charter of Lithuanian Jewry. Its authenticity has been questioned (verify the current consensus) [Record].
Language: Hebrew for scripture and learning; the vernaculars of their towns. Yiddish as a distinct Lithuanian Jewish tongue comes later (verify periodisation).
Faith: Rabbinic Judaism.
Status: Under the grand duke’s direct protection. The privileges promise judicial autonomy in their own disputes, freedom to travel and trade, and protection of synagogue and cemetery, with severe penalties for violence against them [Record, as summarised by the privilege texts]. Occupations: trade, crafts, toll- and customs-farming, medicine, lending.
How others see them: Varies. Catholic clergy are hostile; the grand duke protective, for reasons of policy; townspeople both.
Saga notes (important): Never link Jews to the Gold-Glutton, to money-magic, or to blood or poison rumours. These are the real medieval libels that killed real people, and putting them in the saga’s mythic layer would endorse them. If a Jewish character appears, give him the saga’s ordinary greyness: a Brest physician who treats Ona’s fever, a Grodno toll-farmer who is honest and resented for it, a scholar who argues with a Karaim about texts. The grand duke’s protection is one of the decencies Vytautas actually achieved: let it count.

Rules of thumb for scenes.

Status is personal and armed. A boyar is what his horse, retinue and ancestors make him. There are no coats of arms in pagan Lithuania: the Horodło union of 1413 gives 47 Lithuanian families Polish arms [Record]. Use personal signs (seal-marks, house-marks, horse brands) in Book I and heraldry from Book III.
Baptism becomes a class line in 1387. Jogaila’s 1387 privilege grants rights to Catholic boyars [Record], so after it, conversion buys status. That is exactly the “purchased baptism” the White Silence eats (cosmology §3.3).
Hostages (įkaitai) are the hinge of every treaty. Vytautas’s wife and children with the Order (1383–84, again 1390–92) are standard practice, and his sons’ deaths in 1392 (verify) are its cruellest result.

title: Peoples & cultures
text:
Part C. Daily life

C.1 Law and blood-feud

[Record] There is no written Lithuanian law until the First Statute (1529). In 1382 justice is customary, administered by the grand duke, princes and elders, with the duke as final judge. The statutes later preserve old principles: compensation for killing (head-money, galvapinigiai), graded by the victim’s status, and recognised private vengeance curbed by it.
[Ethnographic/Saga] Blood-feud between boyar kin-groups is a live threat: a killing obliges the kin to take vengeance or accept payment. Kęstutis’s murder is, in this frame, the ultimate unpaid blood-debt, and Vytautas’s whole life is the feud. The saga can treat the 1392 Ostrów settlement as head-money paid in land.
Ordeals and oaths decide what witnesses cannot. Treaties are secured by oaths plus hostages.



C.2 Oaths

[Record] In 1351 Kęstutis swore an oath to Louis of Hungary with a pagan rite, sacrificing an ox, promised baptism, and slipped away (chronology). Order and Rus’ sources show pagan Lithuanians swearing treaties by their own gods and rites (details are scanty (verify)).
[Saga, per cosmology]:

By earth (Žemyna): kneel and kiss the bare earth or take a handful into the mouth. Binding physically: the oath-breaker’s land rejects him (crops fail, horses balk at his threshold).
By Perkūnas: hand on an oak struck by lightning, or on a sword laid on the stone. Perkūnas punishes the breach in his own time (Skirgaila’s broken safe-conduct, 1382).
By fire (Gabija): swearing over the hearth; to break it is to have no fire that will light for you.

Christian oaths on relics and the Gospels arrive with baptism. [Saga] They bind nothing in the old cosmology, which is why the old gods regard Christian treaties as “unwitnessed” and why the Order’s treaties feel unreal to pagans.



C.3 Hospitality: bread and salt

[Ethnographic] Welcoming a guest with bread and salt is a deep Baltic and Slavic custom, recorded richly in later centuries. Projecting it to 1382 is reasonable (ch. 1 uses it well).
Salt is precious: Lithuania has no salt of its own and imports it from Prussia, the Hanse and Galicia [Record]. Offering salt is offering wealth.
[Saga rule] Bread-and-salt makes the guest sacred for three days, and harming him breaks custom (the dvasios notice). The Krėva arrest and the 1384 burnings are both violations of hospitality, from opposite sides. This is the grey symmetry: Vytautas repays Skirgaila’s betrayal with his own.



C.4 Marriage and women’s power

[Record] Gediminid women are instruments and agents of diplomacy. Danutė (Anna) Kęstutaitė married Janusz I of Masovia. Rimgailė married into Masovia too (verify). Algirdas’s daughters married into Rus’ and Poland. Julijona of Tver (Jogaila’s mother) is a political force in the 1370s–80s. Ona (Vytautas’s wife) manages the Krėva escape, endures years as hostage, and later travels to Prussia as Vytautas’s envoy (c. 1400 (verify)) [Record].
Pagan custom (verify): Order and Christian writers accuse pagan Lithuanian nobles of polygyny. Treat it as possible but unproven; the saga need not use it.
Bride-taking: The Birutė legend (16th-c. chronicles) has Kęstutis take the Palanga priestess by force, because she was vowed to the flame [Record as legend]. [Saga] That violence is part of the Amber Debt. Keep it uncomfortable, not romantic.
Priestesses: Vaidilutės (flame-keepers) are an attested later tradition. Their vows of chastity and the penalties for breaking them are from late or hostile sources (verify).
Models for the saga’s women:

Birutė: power by sacred office (the vessel; D1).
Ona: power by courage and management: the escape, the hostage years, diplomacy.
Danutė: power by marriage: the sister in a foreign court who can give tears but not troops.
Julijona: power by motherhood and faith: the Orthodox widow behind Jogaila’s throne.
Jadvyga: power by crown and sacrifice.




C.5 Death: cremation and burial

[Record] Pagan Lithuanian rulers were cremated. Kęstutis was burned in Vilnius in August 1382 with his horses, weapons, hounds and falcons, and with lynx and bear claws so that he could climb on Judgement Day (Długosz). Algirdas’s 1377 funeral is reported as a cremation with horses, though some Rus’ sources claim he died Orthodox (verify).
Ordinary Lithuanians in the 14th century used both cremation and inhumation. Samogitia kept cremation longest (into the 15th c. (verify)). Christians (Ruthenians, Catholics) bury.
[Record/Ethnographic] The dead are fed at autumn feasts (Vėlinės, the “souls’ days”, later fused with All Souls). Food is left on the table, a place is set, the doors are opened.
[Saga, cosmology §1] Fire is the fastest road to Dausos. An unburned pagan lingers as a vėlė. Every Order victory leaves unburned dead; every baptism ends a family’s cremations; the Unbinding is built from corpses that were buried instead of burned. The Order’s insistence on burial is, to pagans, an atrocity against the soul.
Pilėnai (1336) [Record, Order chronicles]: the defenders, under Margiris, burned themselves and their property rather than surrender. [Saga] A sacred memory: “the Pilėnai choice”. It is the place-name to invoke when a character chooses fire over the cross.



C.6 Food and drink

Staples [Record/archaeology]: rye (bread; sacred, never thrown away, a dropped crust is kissed [Ethnographic]), barley (groats, beer), oats, wheat for the elite, peas, beans, turnips, cabbage, onions, garlic, hemp and flax seed; dairy (curd cheese, butter, sour milk); pork, beef, mutton, poultry; game (venison, boar, wisent, beaver tail as a fast-day dish (verify)); fish (pike, bream, eel, salted herring imported via the Hanse); mushrooms and berries; honey.
Drink: alus (beer: everyday), midus (mead: festive, elite, ritual; famous abroad [Record]), gira (kvass-like), birch sap in spring [Ethnographic]; wine imported for church and high table.
Anachronism watch: no potatoes, tomatoes, maize, peppers, tobacco, coffee, tea, chocolate, or New World turkey. Sugar is a rare imported spice. Lemons are a miracle. Cucumbers (in references/daily_life_symbols.md line 7) are doubtful for 1380s Lithuania (verify). Beetroot soups belong to later centuries (verify). Buckwheat is spreading in the east (verify the period).
Feast rules [Saga + Ethnographic]: The first drops of every drink go to the earth (Žemyna). The first slice of bread goes to the hearth (Gabija). A guest is fed before he is questioned.



C.7 Clothing and arms

Common folk [Record/archaeology + Ethnographic]: linen shirts and wool overgarments (sermėga, rudinė), patterned woven belts (juostos: protective, gifted at weddings), leg-wraps and bast shoes (vyžos) or leather shoes, fur caps and sheepskins in winter. Married women cover their hair (linen headwraps, nuometas); maidens wear headbands or crowns [Ethnographic]. Bronze and silver jewellery; amber beads and amulets.
Boyars: Ruthenian-style kaftans and furs with Western touches; imported cloth (Flemish scarlet is a status marker); silver belts; good boots.
Arms, Lithuanian [Record]: mail shirts; conical or rounded helmets; lamellar and scale from the east; round shields and the large pavise (the “Lithuanian shield” is a possible origin of the pavise (verify)); spears, javelins (the sulica type), axes, swords (often imported), bows and increasingly crossbows. Light, hardy horses (ancestors of the žemaitukai) that cross bog where Western chargers founder.
Arms, Order: see A.8. Bombards are new and few in the 1380s (the Order uses guns in the 1380s–90s; their first use in the region is debated, and references/warfare.md line 12’s “early 14th century” is too early (verify)).



C.8 Housing

[Record/archaeology + Ethnographic] A Lithuanian homestead is timber, log-built:

troba / numas: the dwelling, often a smoke-hut without a chimney (the smoke finds the roof).
klėtis: storehouse and granary; the family’s valuables, the bride’s chest, summer sleeping for the young; [Ethnographic] a semi-sacred place.
jauja: the grain-drying and threshing barn, warm and dangerous (fires), a known haunt of spirits.
pirtis: the bath-house (sauna): steam, birch whisks, cold plunge. Used for washing, birth, healing and laying out the dead [Ethnographic]. [Saga] At night it belongs to the spirits; never bathe after dark, and leave water for the vėlės.
cattle sheds and a fenced yard; the žaltys under the threshold or behind the stove; the sacred corner (later the icon corner in Ruthenian houses).

Settlements cluster under hillforts (piliakalniai), which are refuges in raids. Towns are few: Vilnius, Kaunas, Trakai, Grodno; Ruthenian towns are older and larger.
Castles: most are wood and earth on hillforts; a handful are brick and stone (Vilnius, Trakai, Krėva, Medininkai, Lida, Kaunas before 1362). See the gazetteer.



C.9 Crafts and amber

Smiths are respected and feared. [Record] The 1261 Malalas gloss names a divine smith, Teliavelis, who forged the sun (verify). [Saga] Smiths stand between Gabija’s fire and the Iron Saint’s iron, and a smith’s oath is double.
Amber [Record]: The Order holds an amber monopoly (the Bernsteinregal) on the Samland coast. Coastal people must hand over what they gather, under oath and harsh penalties, with gallows on the shore remembered in later centuries (verify for the 14th c.). The Order sells raw amber to the rosary-makers’ guilds of Bruges and Lübeck (the Paternostermacher) [Record]. Saulė’s tears end up as Christian prayer beads. The irony writes itself; use it once, well.
At Palanga (outside the monopoly, in Samogitia) amber is gathered after storms, worked into beads and cone-shaped amulets, and offered to the sea [Saga + archaeology of amber ornaments].
Other crafts: weaving (belts, linen), pottery, bone and antler, leather and fur, beekeeping in tree-hives (drevininkai), carpentry (the whole world is wooden), boat-building on the rivers.



C.10 The economy

[Record] Exports: furs (squirrel by the hundred-thousand, marten, beaver, sable via the east), wax (one of the great exports: the Order and the Hanse pay well, and Lithuanian wax lights Western altars), honey, hides, timber, amber (via the Order).
Imports: salt (critical, and embargoable), cloth, iron and weapons (papal and Order bans on selling arms to pagans; smuggling is constant (verify specifics)), silver, wine, spices.
Tribute of the Ruthenian lands: silver, furs and grain flow from Polotsk, Vitebsk, Kyiv and Volhynia to Vilnius. The empire pays for the pagan core, an uncomfortable truth for saga Lithuanians who see themselves as the persecuted ones.
Money [Record]: Lithuanian “longs” (ilgieji): cast semicircular silver bars about 13 cm long, roughly 100–110 g (a half-mark standard, c. 104 g), chopped to the needed weight. One bar would buy roughly 15 sheep; a horse cost about a bar and a half (one popular source (verify)). Bars and hack-silver are being supplemented in the later 14th century by the first Lithuanian coins (small silver denars; attribution to particular rulers is debated (verify)). Prague groschen, Order schillings and Tatar dirhams circulate too.
Scene detail: A buyer snaps or chops a piece off a silver bar and weighs it on a folding balance. Every serious man carries scales. The sound of a chisel on silver is the sound of a deal (the Gold-Glutton’s music).
Ch. 2’s “Venetian wax” as a luxury gift to Lithuania (02_vilko_perspejimas.qmd:21; 03_gintaro_sapnas.qmd:7) is coals to Newcastle: Lithuania exports wax. Either make it an intended insult (Vytautas can say so) or swap it for Venetian glass, Flemish scarlet, or perfumed candles (the perfume, not the wax, being the luxury).



C.11 War customs

The raid (žygis, Germ. Reise) [Record]: Lithuanian and Order warfare in the 14th century is mostly raiding: fast columns that burn crops, drive off cattle and take captives. Set battles are rare (Strėva 1348, Rudau 1370). Castles are besieged in great campaigns.
The Reise from the other side [Record + Saga]: Smoke on the horizon three villages away, then horns from the hillfort. Cattle driven into the bog islands; the old, women and children into the hillfort or the forest; grain buried; the žaltys left to guard the empty house. The column arrives, burns, takes whoever is slow, and is gone in a day. Two weeks later the winter kills more than the raid did. Write the Reise once from a Samogitian girl’s point of view and every Order scene after it will carry weight.
Captives and ransom [Record]: Captives are wealth. Nobles are ransomed; commoners are settled as labour (Lithuanians) or sold or settled (the Order also takes Lithuanian captives to Prussia as peasants). Exchange of prisoners is part of every truce.
Hostages: see Part B.
Sacrifice of captives [Order sources, partly propaganda]: Order chroniclers report Lithuanians burning captured knights in armour on their horses as offerings to the gods (verify specific incidents). [Saga] Treat it as real and rare: the old faith’s own atrocity. Do not make it routine, and do not omit it.
The Order’s side: forced baptisms, villages burned with people inside (attested in Lithuanian complaints, e.g. at Constance 1416 [Record]), the Ehrentisch feasts celebrating the year’s best killers. Also: truces honoured, prisoners exchanged, courtesy between Kęstutis and particular Order commanders [Record (verify)].
Signals of war [Saga/Ethnographic]: the war-arrow (karo strėlė) or a club passed from homestead to homestead to call the levy is attested in later Baltic custom (verify). Beacon fires on hillforts.

title: Peoples & cultures
text:
Part D. Grey morality notes
For the author: how to keep every culture human, and avoid both the noble-savage and the evil-crusader cliché.

Pagan Lithuania was an empire, not a victim. It ruled millions of Orthodox Ruthenians and took tribute from them, and it raided Poland, Masovia, Prussia and Livonia for captives and cattle as eagerly as the Order raided it. The saga’s Lithuanians should know this and justify it the way all empires do. Kęstutis was a great raider. Romanticise his honour, never his innocence.
The old gods take blood too. Captive-burning, the Amber Debt (“royal blood for land lost”), bride-taking of a vowed priestess (Birutė), and the Pact itself, which binds the people’s safety to a dynasty’s crimes. The Root-Mother is not kind; she is angry, and she eats trackers (ch. 16) who were only obeying orders. Let a pagan character be ashamed of something his faith demands.
The Order is not “evil Christians”. Per cosmology §2.2, the Iron Saint is an egregore fed by the institution of crusade, not the Christian God, and the saga never judges the faith. Individual brethren can be devout, humane, homesick, curious, or monstrous. The Order also built towns, hospitals and law where it ruled. Its crime is structural: a war that needed pagans to exist, which is why it fought on after 1387 (the Samogitian question).
Conversion was both liberation and theft. Baptism ended the crusade’s pretext and brought Lithuania into Europe, literacy and law. It also burned the groves, made status depend on the right faith (the 1387 privileges), and handed the land to its own unfed dead (the Unbinding). The saga must let a character be genuinely, joyfully converted (a boyar’s daughter who loves the music in the new church), and another genuinely robbed.
Every ruler sells someone. Jogaila sells his uncle and his country’s independence. Vytautas sells Samogitia (three times) and his own people’s villages to the Order’s torches (ch. 20). Skirgaila sells his safe-conduct. Birutė sells her mortality, which is the only sale that costs only the seller. Measure characters by what they sell and what they refuse to.
Ruthenians are not background. They are the literate, Christian majority of the realm, with their own grievances (Catholic favouritism after 1387, which sparks Švitrigaila’s war in Book V). Give them faces: a priest, a scribe, a princess.
Minorities are not magic. Tatars, Karaims and Jews should never be the Forces’ instruments by virtue of who they are. Above all, no Jewish-money or poison tropes, no “steppe horde” dehumanising of Tatars, and no exotic-mystic Karaims. Their stories are refuge, service, protection and its price: the ducal privilege can be withdrawn by the next duke. That is grey enough.
Women act within constraints, not outside them. Birutė, Ona, Danutė and Julijona have power through office, marriage, management and motherhood. Do not hand them anachronistic freedom; do not reduce them to pawns either. The best scenes are where a woman uses the very constraint as the tool (Ona as “the silly grieving wife” at Krėva, ch. 12).
Atrocities on every side, decencies on every side. A useful exercise for each book: list one atrocity and one decency per culture on the page. Book I example:









Culture
Atrocity

Lithuanians (Jogaila’s party)
Murder under safe-conduct (Krėva)

Lithuanians (Kęstutis’s party)

Kęstutis’s mercy to Jogaila in 1381


Order
Burning villages on Vytautas’s march (ch. 20)

Masovians

Language does moral work. Avoid “savage”, “horde”, “infidel” and “heathen” in narration. Put them in characters’ mouths, where they reveal the speaker. Equally avoid “pure”, “innocent” and “noble” for pagans in narration. Let the reader do the judging.

The Three Laws (Balance, Truth, Memory) bind mortal craft. Gods and Forces are not bound by the Law of Truth. The Shadow-Seller can lie, deceive and create illusions; no mortal caster can. That asymmetry is why bargaining with him is so dangerous.

title: Magic rules
text:
2. Who can use Kalba

Prigimtis (born): the soul resonates with an element from birth. It usually runs down the maternal line (the Palanga amber priestesses; Birutė). Gifted children show it early: candle flames lean toward them, žalčiai come to their cradles.
Pažymėtas (noticed): a life event so large that an element notices the person: near-death, great sacrifice, a sacred deed. Usually grants one element, often temporarily.
Surištas (bound): someone else binds the person into a Senovės Sutartis. This is Vytautas’s path. Birutė binds him in ch. 3, and Krėva and his mother’s sacrifice later deepen the bond (they do not create it). This resolves the conflict with the old “key” wording.

The baptised can still use Kalba. The gods do not care about creed; they care about truth (§5.3).

title: Magic rules
text:
3. How a working is cast

3.1 The formula
Every working names an element, a recipient and a verb of giving, in Old Lithuanian:

[Element] [tau / man] [verb]. Žvaigždės tau švytės · Ugnis tau degs · Vanduo tau teks · Žemė tau laikys · Vėjas tau neš


“tau” (for you): cast on another. The caster pays.
“man” (for me): cast on oneself. The caster pays, but the cost is lighter (no transfer loss).
This is why Birutė says tau in ch. 3 and Vytautas says man in ch. 15. Both are correct.



3.2 Requirements

Contact with a sacred medium: amber (any element, the universal medium), living fire (Gabija), running or sea water (Bangpūtys), bare earth (Žemyna), open air with wind (Vėjopatis), a starlit sky (Praurimė).
The words aloud. A whisper is enough. Gagged casters cannot work; this is why the Order gags captured žyniai.
Intent that is true (Law of Truth). A caster who asks for what they do not truly want gets nothing, or gets what they do truly want.



3.3 Timing: zeniths

Full moon or high tide; strongest at the spring ice-break

Book I check: Birutė’s Praurimė vision in ch. 3 happens at Dagotuvės, off zenith, so it costs double. Show her fully blind afterwards (review M1/M11). Ch. 27’s Bangpūtys working at the full moon is correctly timed.


3.4 Range

With an amber anchor that the caster has touched and charged (Vytautas’s pebble), distance is free: Birutė can reach Krėva from Palanga.
Without an anchor, range is line of sight, and cost rises steeply beyond it.

title: Magic rules
section: 4. Costs (the Law of Balance made concrete)
text:
4. Costs (the Law of Balance made concrete)

4.1 Per element








Element
Minor working (a candle-length)
Major working (a night, an army, a life)




Stars (Clear Sight)
Hours of blindness
Blind for days, or the permanent loss of one beloved face from memory


Fire (Soul Armour, strength)
Exhaustion
Soul-chill: empathy gone for days; the caster can kill without feeling


Water (Life Spring, healing)
Raging thirst
The caster takes the patient’s wound in part. Moving the cost into another body (a second person, a child) is a forbidden, costly working: “the debt finds its owner.” Book II ch. 9 only offers* it: the Lagoon witch names the road (a small body to take the poison in her place) and Vytautas answers “Ne”; the boys die. The rule is stated there, never exercised.*


Earth (Unmovable Will)
Stiffness
Petrification for the length of the effect; permanent loss of grace


Wind (Shadow Speed, far-speech)
Vertigo
Loss of voice: only whistling, for days, and permanently with repeated use





4.2 The Five-Voice invocation (Penkių Balsų Šauksmas)
Speaking all five lines together (ch. 3, ch. 15) calls a little of every boon at once: sight, warmth, healing, endurance, concealment. It is a desperate act. Cost: a little of every price, permanent and cumulative: a dimming of sight and hearing, a fraying of memory (exactly what ch. 15 describes). It is the only permanent cost a minor working can carry. Each use leaves the caster a bit less present. By Book IV, an old Vytautas who has used it perhaps five times hears the world as if through water.


4.3 Surety: who pays when someone is bound
In a Senovės Sutartis, the binder may stand surety (laidas) for the bound: “Jo skola — mano skola” (“his debt is my debt”). Birutė stands surety for Vytautas. Consequences:

Part of every price Vytautas incurs is paid by Birutė, wherever she is.
This is why his costs look light in Book I and why Birutė declines: voice failing after the Krėva fog, sight going, until ch. 27, when she pays the whole remaining debt at once.
After ch. 27 there is no surety. From Book II, Vytautas pays full price himself. The Vorskla flight has “no mother’s fog, only shame” (Book II outline, ch. 18) because the surety is gone.



4.4 Unpaid debts
A cost cannot be refused, only deferred, and deferred costs compound: memory first, then health, then years of life, then madness, then death.

title: Magic rules
text:
5. The Three Laws, clarified

5.1 Balance: “Kiek paimi, tiek atiduok”
See §4. Write the bill on the page.


5.2 Truth: “Tiesa galingesnė už bet kokį burtą”

Allowed: hiding (real fog, real shadow), revealing, strengthening, healing, carrying messages, showing possibilities.
Forbidden: making anyone perceive what is not there. No glamours, no false faces, no illusions. The Krėva fog is real fog (ch. 14 is correct; mythic_gaps.md §2’s “distortion reflecting expectations” is wrong and is corrected there).
Corollary: magic always reveals some truth, often unwanted. Every Praurimė vision shows the seer something about herself.



5.3 Memory: “Atmintis amžina”

The land remembers every working done on it. Places of great working carry residue that seers feel (the Krėva cell; the Palanga stone).
Amber stores memory (it is Saulė’s grief). Amber that has carried a working answers to the truth of whoever holds it.



5.4 The amber barometer (canon rule)
Vytautas’s pebble responds to the truth of the bearer, not to his faith:








Chapter
State
Why




3
Warm, pulsing
Freely given in love

Faint light in the dark
He is true to his grief


19
Dead, cold stone
Baptised as a lie (he does not believe and does not intend to keep the oath)


20
Burning
Žemyna’s price for the burned village


23
Hot
He chooses truly (betray the Order to save Vilnius)


29

title: Magic rules
section: 6. The Senovės Sutartis (the Ancient Pact rite)
text:
6. The Senovės Sutartis (the Ancient Pact rite)
Four requirements, all on the page:

Amber charged by the binder.
The binder’s blood on the amber.
The bound person’s true name (slaptas vardas), the secret name the mother whispers at birth, known only to her and the elements (see languages_and_naming.md).
An unbreakable promise exchanged both ways.

Canon for ch. 3 (to be written into the revision):

Birutė cuts her palm and presses the pebble into Vytautas’s hand, so her blood is on the amber.
She speaks his true name, which he has never heard. This gives the reader a jolt and leaves a mystery to pay off later.
Her promise: “Jo skola — mano skola” (surety, §4.3).
His promise: “Kol aš gyvas, paskutinė ugnis neužges” (“While I live, the last fire will not go out”).
Consequence across the series: after Jogaila extinguishes Šventaragis in 1387, Vytautas secretly keeps one sacred flame burning, in the Trakai island castle’s deepest vault (Books II–IV). When he dies in 1430, it goes out. That is Book V ch. 1’s “massive, unnatural silence”. If he ever lets it die while he lives, the Pact’s penalties apply (madness, then death). Book IV temptation: Henė offers him the crown in exchange for letting the flame die.

Penalties for breaking the Sutartis: loss of gift, curse of the elements, memory loss, madness, and death in the extreme. These are unchanged from the old doc.

title: Magic rules
text:
7. Claims (Žymės)

A Force may mark a mortal as its instrument without consent. The mark is felt (a rhythm in the fingers, a smell of ozone or of sap) and sometimes seen (a scar, eyes that catch lightning).
A claimed mortal is not empowered at will. The Force acts through them at moments of its choosing, and punishes them for betraying its nature.
Perkūnas’s claim on Vytautas (ch. 10): Vytautas becomes the hand of justice and oath. Perkūnas rewards him when he keeps faith (the ch. 21 lightning is ambiguous by design) and strikes when he breaks an oath (the ch. 19 cracked window is a warning, because the baptism oath is false). Book II: the Vorskla defeat is partly Perkūnas’s verdict on Vytautas’s oath-breaking.
Claims can be contested. The Root-Mother and Perkūnas both want Vytautas. That is the “reluctant hero” tension in relationship_maps/mystical_connections.md.

title: Magic rules
text:
8. Bargains (Sandėriai) with the Shadow-Seller

Always kept to the letter. Velnias never cheats. He drafts.
Always free at first. The “thread” comes later: a small favour, then a larger one.
Beatable only by cleverness, never by strength or faith. The model is the folk crop-division tale (ATU 1030, widespread in Lithuanian variants): the peasant agrees to give Velnias “what grows above the ground” and plants turnips, then “what grows below” and plants rye. Velnias keeps the bargain to the letter and is ruined by it.
Signs of a bargain in progress: sounds die (his “Breath of the Void”, which resolves Krėva’s silence in mythic_gaps.md §1), warm coins, a figure at the edge of the firelight, three stones.
Who has bargained (canon): Jogaila (1382: the “easy way” of the trap; the price is that his line inherits the crown and loses the land, so the Jagiellonians end up ruling Poland), Skirgaila (Krėva; the price is to be used and discarded), and later Vytautas (Book II’s Vorskla vision; Book IV’s crown).

title: Magic rules
text:
9. Counter-forces

Consecrated stone (Order castles, cathedrals) dampens Kalba: costs double and amber goes cold. This is part of why the pebble dies at Marienburg in ch. 19 (both explanations hold).
The Iron Saint grants knights fearlessness, so Earth’s “Unmovable Will” and Fire’s terror have no grip on them.
The White Silence smothers Wind (no sound, no far-speech) and freezes Water workings.
Cold iron cut by a Christian smith on a feast day burns most spirits (bestiary). Peasants hang old Order horseshoes over doors after 1387, an irony the saga should enjoy.
Cremation and fire release the dead and close a vėlė’s road back.

title: Magic rules
text:
10. What magic cannot do

Raise the dead (the Amber Queen keeps the dead, she does not return them).
Create love or force a will (it can strengthen a will that is already there).
Change the past (prophecy shows branches, never a fixed trunk).
Win a war. At most it saves one person on one night. Battles are won by men, logistics and weather, sometimes weather that a Force has nudged.
Work on a person who knows your true name better than you do (the defence against a binder who would enslave).

title: Magic rules
section: 11. Quick checklist for writing a magic scene
text:
11. Quick checklist for writing a magic scene

Who is casting, and by which path (born, noticed, bound)?
Which mode: Kalba, Claim or Bargain?
Is it at the zenith or off it? What does that do to the cost?
What is the bill, and where on the page is it shown?
Does it obey the Law of Truth (no illusions)?
Does it leave residue (Memory) that a later chapter can find?
Does the political problem still have to be solved by mortals? (It must.)

title: Languages & naming
text:
Source: world_rules/languages_and_naming.md
Canonical reference for the languages spoken in the saga’s world, how its names are built, and the saga’s invented “true names” and incantation grammar. Pronunciation of the names below is in pronunciation_guide.md (and pronunciation_lexicon.json). Spelling decisions follow canon_decisions.md D4 and D8. The magic mechanics that use true names are in magic_rules.md §3 and §6.

title: Languages & naming
section: 1. The languages of the Grand Duchy in the 1380s [Record]
text:
1. The languages of the Grand Duchy in the 1380s [Record]

Speech, song, oath, prayer to the old gods. Never written in this period. Two main dialect groups, Aukštaitian (highland) and Samogitian (lowland), already distinct.
The language of every pagan scene. Kęstutis, Birutė and Vytautas think in it. The Senovės Kalba is its oldest register (§4).

Jewish communities, whose first known privileges came from Vytautas in 1388–89 (verify years)
Hebrew for liturgy and learning. In the 14th century the spoken vernacular may still have been Judeo-Slavic; Yiddish grew dominant later with Ashkenazi migration (debated; verify)
Book II onward (Brest, Grodno, Trakai, Lutsk).

Turkic-speaking Karaites brought from Crimea to Trakai c. 1397–98 (tradition)

Book II onward, at Trakai.


Old Prussian
Prussians under the Order
Speech only (an Order word list, the Elbing Vocabulary, survives in a c. 1400 copy)
Prussian peasants and guides in Order lands, ch. 17–19. Extinct by c. 1700.


Latvian, Livonian, Curonian
Peoples of Livonia and the coast
Speech
Coastal and Livonian scenes.



Interpreters. The Order employed professional interpreters, called Tolken in Order documents (verify term), many of them Prussians or Lithuanian converts. An interpreter in ch. 18–19 is both accurate and useful: the Grand Master hears Vytautas’s words after a stranger has chosen them.
Writing in Book I. The earliest surviving Lithuanian text is a handful of prayers handwritten into a book printed in Strasbourg in 1503 (date of the handwriting c. 1503–25; verify). The first printed Lithuanian book is Mažvydas’s catechism (Königsberg, 1547). So a written Lithuanian word, letter or inscription in 1382–87 is an anachronism. If the plot needs a written message between Lithuanians, it is in Ruthenian or Latin, or it is not written at all: a token, a knotted cord, an amber piece, a krivulė (the krivis’s crooked staff, carried as a summons).
Christian words are borrowed [Record]. Lithuanian took its Christian vocabulary from Ruthenian and Polish: krikštas (baptism), bažnyčia (church), kryžius (cross), griekas (sin), dūšia (soul), knyga (book). A pagan in 1382 hearing these words hears foreign words, which is a strong effect to use in POV. The native words for the sacred are older: dievas (god, cognate with Latin deus), šventas (holy), siela and vėlė (soul), auka (offering), alkas (grove). Even kunigaikštis (duke) is built on kunigas “lord”, an early loan from Germanic *kuningaz “king”.

2. How Lithuanian names are built

2.1 Two-part (dithematic) names [Record]
Old Lithuanian princely and boyar names are compounds of two elements, like Germanic Wil-helm or Slavic Vladi-mir. The same elements recur in many names, which is how scholars identify them. The meanings below are the ones commonly proposed in Lithuanian onomastics. Most are probable, few are certain, and the confidence column is honest.

A correction to the brief’s divisions. Algirdas divides Al-girdas, not Algi-rdas, because -girdas recurs as an element (Mantigirdas, Visgirdas). Gediminas is usually divided Gedi-minas, with a linking vowel.
Žygimantas is not native. It is the Lithuanian form of German Sigismund, folk-reshaped to look like žygis “campaign” + -mantas. Žygimantas Kęstutaitis’s name is therefore a sign of his Christian upbringing; his pagan name, if he had one, is unknown (verify).


2.2 Short and diminutive names [Record]
Alongside the compounds there are short names, often one element plus a suffix: -utis/-utė (Jaunutis “little young one”, Birutė, Danutė), -enis (Vytenis, Lengvenis), -ys, -elis/-ėlė. Many feminine names of the dynasty are of this kind. Medieval women’s names are poorly recorded. Most noblewomen appear in the sources only under their baptismal names (Ona, Elena, Marija, Sofija, Julijona, Eufemija, Kotryna).


2.3 Patronymics and family names [Record]

No surnames in the 14th century. A person is X, son/daughter of Y, or X of [place].
Lithuanian patronymic suffixes: -aitis (son: Žygimantas Kęstutaitis, Andrius Algirdaitis); -aitė (daughter: Danutė Kęstutaitė); -ėnas (son or descendant, especially in the east: compare sūnėnas “nephew”, “brother’s son”). The suffix -áitis is always stressed.
Ruthenian patronymics: -ovich/-evich (son), -ovna/-evna (daughter). Vytautas Kęstutaitis is Vitovt Keistutyevich in Ruthenian, and Jogaila Algirdaitis is Jagailo Olgerdovich (verify exact spellings).
Dynastic plurals (Gediminaičiai, Kęstutaičiai, Algirdaičiai, Jogailaičiai) are modern historians’ terms. They are fine in narration and anachronistic in dialogue.
Married names in -ienė (Kęstutienė) belong to the later surname system. Do not use them in Book I. Say Kęstučio žmona “Kęstutis’s wife”, or let the title carry it (kunigaikštienė “duchess”).

title: Languages & naming
text:
3. Spelling rules for the project

Always full diacritics (Kęstutis, not Kestutis). In English docs as well as Lithuanian text: the marks change the sounds.
D4 names: Vytautas, Jogaila, Kęstutis, Ona, Skirgaila, Birutė, Švitrigaila, Jadvyga (Jadwiga in Polish context), Henė (Henne in English docs). Vyti is a vocative used only by Birutė and Kęstutis. Vytis is the coat of arms.
One spelling per castle: Krėva (not Kreva, Krewa or Krewo); Astravas (Ostrów); Ašmena.
D8 terms: Aukso Rijūnas (not Auksinis Smauglys), Šaknų Motina (not a synonym for Žemyna), Dykra.
Latin epithets should be grammatical: Sanctus Ferrum mixed genders (ferrum is neuter), so it is corrected to Ferrum Sanctum (“Holy Iron”); Sanctus Ferreus (“the Iron Saint”) is the other grammatical option. Mercator-Rex is fine. (D8 now records Ferrum Sanctum.)
Persona files’ “True Name” field should be renamed “Historical name”, so that it does not collide with the saga’s true name (§5).

title: Languages & naming
section: 4. The Senovės Kalba as Old Lithuanian
text:
4. The Senovės Kalba as Old Lithuanian

4.1 What it is
[Saga invention] In the world, the Senovės Kalba (“the Ancient Speech”) is Lithuanian in its oldest register, the words the elements were first addressed in. It was handed down by mouth from krivis to žynys and from mother to daughter, and never written. Mortals ask in it, and the elements answer only to it.
[Record] In fact, the five incantations are standard modern Lithuanian. Real Old Lithuanian, as the 16th–17th-century texts preserve it, had features that modern Lithuanian has lost or reduced. The saga can draw on them for flavour:

Athematic verbs in -mi: esmi “I am”, eimi “I go”, duomi “I give” (modern esu, einu, duodu).
The permissive with te-: teesie “let it be”, teateinie “let it come”, tebūnie “let it be” (Daukša’s Lord’s Prayer, 1595).
A living dual number: mudu “we two”, judu “you two”, dvi žvaigždi “two stars”.

These are attested forms. Inventing new archaic forms (for example a permissive *tešvytie “let it shine”) should be checked with a historical linguist first (verify). A wrong “archaism” will jar a Lithuanian reader more than plain modern Lithuanian.


4.2 The formula (from magic_rules.md §3.1)

[Element] [tau / man] [verb].









Element
Line
Literal sense




Stars (Praurimė)
Žvaigždės tau švytės
“The stars will shine for you”


Fire (Gabija)
Ugnis tau degs
“Fire will burn for you”


Water (Bangpūtys)
Vanduo tau teks
“Water will fall to your lot” (see below)


Earth (Žemyna)
Žemė tau laikys
“Earth will hold (it) for you”


Wind (Vėjopatis)
Vėjas tau neš
“Wind will carry (it) for you”



The grammar, and why it matters to the magic:

The element comes first, in the nominative. Naming the power is the address, so the element is spoken first. Never reorder the words.
The pronoun comes second, in the dative. tau means “for you” (cast for another; the caster pays) and man means “for me” (cast on oneself; the caster pays, but less). These are unstressed clitics. (A possible extension, not canon: jam/jai “for him/her”, used only through a charged amber anchor for someone absent; mums “for us” for a joint working.)
The verb comes last, in the 3rd-person future. The appendices gloss it as a wish (“Tegul žvaigždės tau švytėtų”, “May the stars shine”). Grammatically it is a statement about the future: “the stars will shine.” This is the saga’s best hidden rule. A working is a prophecy the caster asks the element to make true. Under the Law of Truth a false statement fails, so a caster cannot ask for what they do not truly intend (magic_rules §3.2). The Lithuanian 3rd person is the same in singular and plural, which is why žvaigždės (plural) and ugnis (singular) take the same form of verb.
The verb is the element’s own natural act: stars shine, fire burns, earth holds, wind carries.
Every line ends on a stressed syllable (švy-TĖS, DEGS, TEKS, lai-KYS, NEŠ). New lines should keep this hard, falling-shut cadence.

The water line’s double sense. Teks is the future of tèkti “to fall to one’s share; to have to”, not of tekėti “to flow” (whose future is tekės). Read strictly, Vanduo tau teks means “water shall be your portion”. That is a fitting oath for the element that heals by taking the patient’s wound onto the healer (magic_rules §4.1). Keep the line as it is, and let a learned character (the krivis, Birutė) notice the double meaning once. If the author ever wants the plain sense “water will flow for you”, the line would be Vanduo tau tekės.
The Five-Voice invocation (Penkių Balsų Šauksmas) speaks the five lines in the order Stars, Fire, Water, Earth, Wind, from the sky down to the air around the caster.


4.3 Writing new workings [Saga invention]

Keep the three-word shape. A fourth word may be a direct object placed before the verb (Vėjas tau žodį neš “Wind will carry the word for you”) (proposal; check the rhythm aloud).
Candidate verbs (3rd-person future). These are suggestions; check stress before use:








Element
Verbs




Stars
švytės “will shine”, rodys “will show”


Fire
degs “will burn”, šildys “will warm”, saugos “will guard”


Water
teks “will fall to one’s lot”, plaus “will wash”


Earth
laikys “will hold”, slėps “will hide”


Wind
neš “will carry”, pūs “will blow”




No Christian or Slavic loanwords in the Kalba (dūšia, griekas, kryžius). The elements do not know them, which is a rule worth a scene.
No modern or abstract coinages. Regėjimo Aiška (the Stars boon) uses aiška, which is not a standard noun. It works as an archaic-sounding name for the boon, but avoid it inside an incantation.
Vows in Kalba scenes use plain, short sentences: Jo skola — mano skola (“His debt is my debt”); Kol aš gyvas, paskutinė ugnis neužges (“While I live, the last fire will not go out”).

title: Languages & naming
section: 5. The true name: slaptas vardas [Saga invention]
text:
5. The true name: slaptas vardas [Saga invention]
Required by the Senovės Sutartis (magic_rules.md §6, requirement 3).

What it is. At birth, before any public name is given, the mother whispers a secret name into the child’s ear. Only she and the elements know it. The public name (Vytautas, Eglė) is given later, at the naming feast.
How it is given. In the first hour, over the five media if she can manage it: a candle (fire), a bowl of water, a pinch of earth, an open window (wind), and starlight or amber (stars). Most mothers manage two or three. The elements present are the elements that will “know” the child.
What it sounds like. A single old word, never a two-part princely name. Often it is something the mother saw or felt at the birth (a bird, a weather, a tree), or a nature word with an old diminutive. The point is that it sounds nothing like a duke’s name. Do not invent Vytautas’s true name in the docs. Magic_rules §6 has Birutė speak it in ch. 3 and leaves it as a mystery for later. The reader should hear only that it was a word older than “Vytautas” (author’s decision).
Who may speak it. Only the mother; the bearer, if they ever learn it; a binder in a Senovės Sutartis; and an Iron Wolf candidate, who whispers his own to a sacred flame at his making (iron_wolves.md: “the name stays in the fire”). Speaking another’s true name to anyone else is the gravest breach of trust a Lithuanian of the saga can commit.

The skin-name. Distinct from the true name, an Iron Wolf also bears a kailio vardas (“skin-name”). It is a public nickname, a dead enemy’s name, or an object. Kęstutis’s armour-bearer Jonas wears the baptismal name of an Order sergeant he killed (persona/Jonas/description.md). The skin-name hides nothing and binds nothing.

What it does. It addresses the person beneath every title, baptism and mask. This is why baptism cannot overwrite it. Vytautas is Wigand and then Aleksandras to the Church, but his true name is unchanged, and this is why the amber answers to his truth, not his creed (magic_rules §5.4). Under magic_rules §10, someone who knows your true name better than you do is beyond your workings.
Hooks. The Shadow-Seller collects true names. A mother who dies in childbirth takes the name with her, and that child is unbindable, which is a blessing and a curse. When the Root-Mother takes Eglė, she names her anew (Pelkių Eglė), which is what “taken” means (D5).

title: Languages & naming
text:
6. Naming new characters

6.1 Lithuanian men
Attested 13th–15th-century names [Record]: Mindaugas, Treniota, Traidenis, Vaišvilkas, Daumantas, Vytenis, Gediminas, Jaunutis, Narimantas, Karijotas, Liubartas, Manvydas, Algirdas, Kęstutis, Vaidotas, Butautas, Tautvilas, Vygantas, Karigaila, Skirgaila, Lengvenis, Kaributas, Jogaila, Švitrigaila, Vaidila, Kęsgaila, Daugirdas, Rumbaudas (Valimantaitis), Astikas, Radvila, Goštautas, Mantigirdas (verify), Gedgaudas (verify), Survila (verify).
Constructed on the same patterns [Saga invention] (check with a Lithuanian reader; several also exist as 20th-century revival names, which is fine): Kęsmantas, Daugvilas, Narvydas, Rimgaudas, Tautgirdas, Butvilas, Skirmantas, Jogirdas, Vilgaudas, Gedmantas.


6.2 Lithuanian women
Attested [Record]: Birutė, Danutė, Rimgailė (Ringailė), Miklausė, Aigusta (Gediminas’s daughter, baptised Anastasia), Jaunė (Gediminas’s wife; verify), Aldona (Gediminas’s daughter, as named by Długosz; verify), Vilheida (per houses_and_lineages.md; verify).
Constructed [Saga invention]: Daumantė, Kęsgailė, Tautvilė, Rimvilė, Mingailė, Narvilė, Jogailė, Gedvilė.
Revival names: use with care. Eglė, Daiva, Rūta, Jūratė, Laima, Gintarė, Aušra, Vaiva are 19th–20th-century personal names drawn from words, myth or literature. They are fine for mythic figures (Eglė), but a Lithuanian reader will hear them as modern if they are given to ordinary 14th-century villagers.


6.3 Ruthenian (Orthodox) names [Record]

Men: Ivan, Andrei, Dmitry, Fyodor, Mikhail, Yury, Semyon, Vasily, Boris, Gleb, Konstantin, Lev, Roman, Danylo, Olelko (from Aleksandr).
Women: Uliana, Maria, Anna, Ofimia (Eufemia), Fedora, Elena, Anastasia, Feodosia.
Form: Ivan Olgerdovich, Maria Olgerdovna.
Lithuanian forms: Ivanas, Andrius, Dmitrijus, Fiodoras, Mykolas, Jurgis, Semionas, Vasilijus, Borisas, Konstantinas, Levas; Julijona, Marija, Ona, Eufemija, Elena.



6.4 Teutonic Order names [Record]

Given names common among the brethren: Konrad, Kuno, Heinrich, Ulrich, Friedrich, Werner, Dietrich, Johann, Hermann, Siegfried, Gottfried, Marquard, Günther, Wigand, Winrich, Ludolf, Burchard, Arnold, Thomas, Michael, Paul.
Real officers of the period (from houses_and_lineages.md): Kuno von Hattenstein, Konrad von Wallenrode, Friedrich von Wallenrode, Marquard von Salzbach, Kuno von Liebenstein (the 1381 informant; Günther von Hohenstein is the saga’s invented young brother, sharing a name with an older real komtur), Thomas von Merheim, Werner von Tettingen, Wilhelm von Friemersheim.
Inventing a brother. Use Bruder + given name + von + a place in Franconia, Swabia, Thuringia, Hesse or the Rhineland (the Order’s recruiting grounds). Brethren were German-born; natives of Prussia were not admitted.
Offices (German, then Lithuanian): Hochmeister (didysis magistras), Großkomtur (didysis komtūras), Marschall (maršalas), Komtur (komtūras), Vogt (vogtas), Tressler (iždininkas).



6.5 Polish names [Record]

Men: Jan, Mikołaj, Piotr, Zbigniew, Spytek, Dobiesław, Krystyn, Sędziwój, Jaśko, Zawisza, Wojciech.
Women: Jadwiga, Elżbieta, Anna, Zofia, Katarzyna, Małgorzata.
Form: Jan z Tarnowa (“of Tarnów”); Lithuanian Jonas iš Tarnuvo.



6.6 Tatar names [Record]
Tokhtamysh, Edigu, Temur Qutlugh, Jalal ad-Din, Kadir Berdi, Hacı Giray, Mamai. Titles: khan, emir, beg, mirza, beglerbeg.

Engine. The two marriages of Algirdas made two Algirdaičiai houses: Orthodox elder sons with no inheritance, and younger sons (Uliana’s) with everything. In 1377 Uliana’s party won. In 1440 the dispossessed line takes its revenge: the Czartoryski brothers, descendants of Algirdas’s first marriage (if Konstantinas’s parentage holds), kill Žygimantas Kęstutaitis at Trakai. The first Kęstutaitis to rule was murdered by Uliana’s sons; the last is murdered by Maria’s grandsons.


1.4 The Kęstutaičiai (children of Kęstutis and Birutė)

The eldest sons, Vaidotas and Butautas, were adults by the 1360s, which fits a c.1350 marriage only barely. Some historians suggest an earlier wife (verify). 1.5 Vytautas and Ona

Ona (Anna). Married Vytautas c.1370 (verify). Her parentage is unknown. One hypothesis makes her a princess of Smolensk, another a daughter of a Lithuanian boyar house (verify; leave her origin a mystery in prose). Died 1418 at Trakai. She organised the Krėva escape of autumn 1382, in which her maid (Elena (verify name)) stayed in Vytautas’s bed and was executed. Hostage of the Order in 1383–84 (saga) and, in the record, from the Treaty of Lyck (19 Jan 1390); the Order freed her in May 1392 to spread pro-Lithuanian rumours; she confirmed Ostrów in two letters. Born c. 1350–52 (the record has no date; Book IV’s ch. 9 makes her 66 in 1418).
Sofija (1371 – 1453). Betrothed to Vasily Dmitrievich of Moscow. By tradition the match was made when Vasily escaped from the Horde in 1386–87 and passed through Lithuanian lands (verify). Married 9 Jan 1391 (verify day). Grand Princess of Moscow 1391–1425; regent for her son Vasily II from 1425 in the Muscovite civil war. Her children include Vasily II the Blind (1415–62), Anna (1393–1417), who married the Byzantine heir John VIII Palaiologos in 1411 and died of plague, and Anastasija, who married Olelka of Kyiv, so Vytautas’s granddaughter married Algirdas’s great-grandson (verify).
The sons: a CONTESTED tradition. Sofija is the only child of Vytautas in the record. The late tradition (Simon Grunau, 16th c.) says that two young sons, Iwan and Georg (Jurgis and Ivanas: the names are the tradition’s, not the saga’s), were poisoned by a knight while hostages of the Order, as revenge for the betrayal (after the break, before Ostrów, summer 1392). en.wikipedia (Jonynas 1984) calls it a false rumour; Vytautas’s letters never accuse the Order of it; a “Jurgis and Jonas” on the 1390–92 hostage list were kinsmen who came back alive. The saga adopts the tradition (D3) and says so in Book II’s afterword.
Second wife: Julijona Alšėniškė (Uliana Olshanska), ⚭ 13 Nov 1418 at Grodno (en.wikipedia; VLE: “before Christmas 1418”), daughter of Prince Ivan of Halshany (Alšėnai) (verify). No children. [Record], with genealogy to verify: she was aunt of Sophia of Halshany, so Vytautas and Jogaila ended up married to an aunt and her niece.

Consequence [Record]. Vytautas died with no male heir. His blood survived only in Moscow: his grandson Vasily II. Vasily I’s testament (1423) placed the boy under Vytautas’s protection (verify date). The Kęstutaičiai line that the Order tried to wipe out ends up on the Muscovite throne, which is the bitterest irony in the series.

Casimir IV was elected Grand Duke of Lithuania on 29 June 1440, aged 12, by the Lithuanian council against Polish wishes, and crowned King of Poland on 25 June 1447. He is the founder of the Jagiellonian golden age.
