title: Houses & lineages
text:
2. House cards
Mottos are [Saga invention] unless stated. Heraldry follows the record where it exists and says so where it does not.

A note on Lithuanian heraldry [Record]

The Vytis (Pogonia, Pogoń): an armed rider charging, sword raised. Mounted-warrior seals appear among the Gediminids in the second half of the 14th century. Which duke used it first is debated (attributions to Algirdas’s era and to Narimantas or Kęstutis circulate) (verify before stating in prose). Under Jogaila and Vytautas it becomes the arms of the Grand Duchy. In the 1380s it is a princely seal, not yet a “national” flag.
The Columns (Gediminaičių stulpai): the “Gediminid” name is a 19th-century label. The sign is first attested on Vytautas’s coins and seals in the late 14th century (verify earliest date; c.1397 is often cited), and is used afterwards by Žygimantas Kęstutaitis. It is plausibly a family tamga (property mark) of the Kęstutaičiai. In the period the Columns are Vytautas’s mark, not Jogaila’s.
The double cross (Jagiellonian cross): appears on Jogaila’s seals after his baptism (1386) (verify). It is Jogaila’s personal sign as a Christian king.
Długosz on Grunwald [Record]: the Lithuanian banners bore mostly the rider, a minority the Columns (verify the exact count).
Horodło 1413 [Record]: 47 Catholic Lithuanian boyar families were “adopted” into Polish heraldic clans and took Polish arms (see §3). Before 1413, Lithuanian boyars used house-marks, not Western coats of arms.

Consequence for the books. In Book I (1382–87), no one should wear the Columns as a dynastic blazon on Jogaila’s side. That is an anachronism, and it also inverts the symbolism (books/1/prologue.qmd line 17 puts “Gediminaičių stulpai” on the armour of Jogaila’s captain; change it to the rider or to Jogaila’s own house-mark). The Vytis on a ducal seal or banner is acceptable, with care.



2.1 House of Gediminas (the dynasty as a whole)

Seat: Vilnius: the Upper Castle on the hill, the Lower Castle, and the wooden Crooked Castle (burnt 1390). Older seats: Kernavė and Trakai.
Arms: the Vytis [Record, with the dating caveats above].
Sigil (saga use): the Iron Wolf howling on the hill [Saga invention; the dream itself is Record as legend].
Words: Kol staugia vilkas, stovi miestas. “While the wolf howls, the city stands.” [Saga invention]
Character: pagan-pragmatic. They marry Orthodox, Catholic and steppe brides, accept baptism when it pays and drop it when it does not. They rule a mostly Ruthenian and Orthodox empire from a pagan Baltic core. Their genius is the appanage: every son gets a city, and every city gets a son who might rebel.
Feuds: Jaunutis against his brothers (1345); Algirdaičiai against Kęstutaičiai (1380–92, 1432–40); the elder Algirdaičiai against the younger (1377–99).
Mythic patron or burden: the Silent Pact (cosmology §4.1) is sworn by the house, not by one branch. Clause 2, no Gediminid sheds Gediminid blood, binds every branch, which is why every kin-killing in the tree above costs something in the Unbinding.



2.2 The Algirdaičiai of Uliana: Jogaila’s line (the Jogailaičiai)

Seats: Vilnius (as Grand Dukes), Krėva (Algirdas’s patrimonial castle; Jogaila’s refuge after 1381 and the prison of 1382), Vitebsk (Uliana’s dower lands), later Kraków (Wawel).
Arms: the Vytis for the Grand Duchy; Jogaila’s personal double cross after 1386 [Record]. After 1386 Jogaila quarters the Polish White Eagle with the Vytis on royal seals (verify the arrangement).
Sigil (saga use): a crow on a crown [Saga invention]. In persona notes, crows follow Jogaila as the Shadow-Seller’s eyes.
Words: Tyla toliau nueina. “Silence goes further.” [Saga invention] This echoes the chronicle tradition that Algirdas never told even his captains where an army was marching (record as tradition (verify source)).
Character: patient, calculating, Orthodox-raised by their mother and Catholic by necessity. They win by waiting. Jogaila outlives every rival: Kęstutis, Skirgaila, Jadwiga, Vytautas. The house’s virtue is endurance; its vice is that it lets others do the killing.
Feuds: Jogaila against Kęstutis (1380–82) and Vytautas (1382–84, 1389–92). Švitrigaila against everyone. Skirgaila’s resentment of Jogaila’s ingratitude. The Uliana sons against Maria’s sons.
Marriage web: Moscow (Lengvenis ⚭ Maria Dmitrievna; Elena ⚭ Serpukhov), Masovia (Aleksandra ⚭ Siemowit IV), Pomerania, Mecklenburg; Jogaila’s four queens (Anjou, Celje–Piast, Pilica, Halshany).
Mythic patron or burden: the Shadow-Seller (Šešėlių Pardavėjas). Jogaila’s 1382 bargain: his line inherits the crown and loses the land (magic_rules §8). The White Silence settles where his baptism is bought (cosmology §3.3: Vilnius 1382, Krėva 1385). Later, the Gold-Glutton feeds on his heirs’ Polish privileges. The Root-Mother treats him as “a tumour in her side” (persona). [Saga invention]



2.3 Skirgaila: “the hand that did the work” (cadet seat)

Seats: Trakai (1382, and by Jogaila’s grant after 1384), Polotsk (taken from Andrius, 1387), Kyiv (1395–97) [Record].
Arms: used the dynastic rider as Jogaila’s lieutenant (verify any personal seal).
Sigil (saga use): a mailed fist closing on a chain, the chain that strangled Kęstutis [Saga invention].
Words: Darbas nekalba. “The work does not speak.” [Saga invention]
Character: the family’s enforcer. Brave in the field (he took Polotsk and defended Vilnius in 1390), feared and drinking, never thanked. Historically he was Jogaila’s most capable lieutenant and the man Polish lords expected to govern Lithuania for the king.
Feuds: with Vytautas (Trakai is the open wound until Ostrów 1392); with Andrius of Polotsk (whom he captured); with Švitrigaila (whom he treats as a child).
Mythic patron or burden: the Shadow-Seller’s second stone. His price was to be used and then discarded (magic_rules §8). Perkūnas’s enmity follows his broken safe-conduct of August 1382 (power_systems §2.6). He dies in Kyiv in 1397 with no heir; the stone drops (character_arcs). [Saga invention]



2.4 The elder Algirdaičiai: Maria’s sons, the Orthodox princes

Seats: Polotsk (Andrius), Bryansk and Trubchevsk (Dmitrijus), Kyiv (Vladimiras), Chartoryisk (Konstantinas’s heirs).
Arms: the rider on Ruthenian-style princely seals (verify). Orthodox icons and princely signs.
Sigil (saga use): a church dome under a rider [Saga invention].
Words: Pirmasis kraujas neužmiršta. “First blood does not forget.” [Saga invention]
Character: the first-born, Orthodox and Russian-speaking, with Kyivan Rus’ manners. Loyal to their lands, not to Vilnius. They change sides (Moscow, the Livonian Order, Vytautas) to keep their patrimonies. Yet two of them die for Vytautas at the Vorskla (1399), which shows that the Kęstutaitis cousin treated them better than their half-brother had.
Feuds: Andrius against Jogaila and Skirgaila (1377–87); their descendants against the Kęstutaičiai (the Czartoryski murder of 1440).
Mythic patron or burden: no canonical Force. [Saga suggestion, not canon]: the Steppe-Hunger takes its price from them at the Vorskla; their dvoeverie (double faith, surrounding_folklore.md) keeps the domovoi fed even as the gods fall silent.



2.5 Švitrigaila: the storm-bringer

Seats: Vitebsk (1390s), Podolia and Chernihiv–Siverian lands (verify grants), Lutsk (his last seat).
Arms: the rider; as Grand Duke 1430–32 he sealed with the Vytis (verify).
Sigil (saga use): a black horse rearing in lightning [Saga invention].
Words: Audra neprašo leidimo. “A storm asks no leave.” [Saga invention]
Character: the youngest, Uliana’s favourite (persona), charming to Orthodox princes, Tatars and the Order alike. He rebels in every decade of his long life and dies in his bed at eighty, outliving every brother and cousin. He is the Gediminids’ last pure appanage prince.
Feuds: against Jogaila (1393, 1402, 1430–32); against Vytautas (1408 defection to Moscow; prisoner 1409–18); against Žygimantas Kęstutaitis (the civil war of 1432–38).
Mythic patron or burden: none canonical. [Saga suggestion, not canon]: in Book V the Root-Mother’s wolves attack only men carrying “foreign seals” (Book V ch. 11). Švitrigaila promises a “return to the Old GDL”, so the forest may briefly court him, then abandon him at Pabaiskas when his allies prove to be the Livonian Order, the Iron Saint’s own.



2.6 The Kęstutaičiai: Kęstutis’s line

Seats: Trakai, which includes Senieji Trakai (Old Trakai, Kęstutis’s early residence), the Peninsula Castle and the Island Castle (begun under Kęstutis, completed by Vytautas in the early 15th century) (verify phases). Also Kaunas (destroyed 1362, rebuilt), Grodno (Vytautas’s seat before 1382 and after 1384), and Samogitia as their sworn charge. [Record]
Arms: the Columns (Vytautas’s and Žygimantas’s mark [Record, late 14th century onward]); the Vytis as Grand Dukes after 1392.
Sigil (saga use): the boar for Kęstutis (“the Old Boar”, Senasis Šernas, the series’ own epithet); the wolf for Vytautas; amber for Birutė [Saga invention].
Words: Duotas žodis nerūdija. “A given word does not rust.” [Saga invention] This is grounded in Kęstutis’s real reputation among the Order’s own chroniclers for keeping faith, and ironic because his sons break their word to the Order again and again.
Character: soldiers, oath-swearers, frontiersmen. Western-facing (Prussia, Masovia, the Order) where the Algirdaičiai face east. Kęstutis himself was admired by his enemies; the knights told stories of his escape from Marienburg (1361) (verify details). His sons inherit the courage, not the honesty.
Feuds: Butautas’s betrayal (1365); Vytautas against Jogaila and Skirgaila; Žygimantas’s paranoia against the boyars and against Švitrigaila (Book V).
Marriage web: Masovia (Danutė ⚭ Janusz I; Rimgailė ⚭ Henryk), Moldavia (Rimgailė’s second marriage), Moscow (Sofija ⚭ Vasily I), Halshany (Julijona).
Mythic patron or burden: the Amber Queen’s line through Birutė (D1; cosmology §3.4), and claimed by Perkūnas (cosmology §3.2; magic_rules §7), because the feud between Perkūnas and Jūratė is unfinished, and Vytautas is the vessel’s son. The Root-Mother contests the claim (magic_rules §7). The house carries the flame vow (magic_rules §6): while I live, the last fire will not go out. [Saga invention]



2.7 Vytautas’s own line

Seat: Trakai (Island Castle) and Vilnius; the court at Lutsk for the 1429 congress.
Arms: the Columns on his seals and coins, the Vytis for the state [Record].
Sigil (saga use): the Iron Wolf with an amber eye [Saga invention].
Words: Kas atsimena, tas valdo. “Who remembers, rules.” [Saga invention] This is the Amber Queen’s office of memory turned into politics.
Character: the man of two baptisms (Wigand 1383, Aleksandras 1386) and two defections (1384, 1392). He builds an empire from the Baltic almost to the Black Sea, and dies without a son.
Feuds: with Skirgaila (Trakai); with Švitrigaila (Moscow, Kremenets); with Oleśnicki and the Lesser Poland lords (the crown, Book IV).
Burden: the sons poisoned (1392) as the price of defection (series_arc I). Sofija in Moscow as the only survivor. The flame vow, which costs him the crown in Book IV (series_arc). [Saga invention for the vow; Record for the heirlessness]



2.8 The Palanga amber-priestess line (Gintaro vaidilutės) [Saga invention]

Basis [Record]: Birutė’s Palanga origin is a strong Lithuanian tradition (Birutė Hill at Palanga, her legendary role as a vaidilutė guarding a sacred fire). Wigand of Marburg (c. 1394), not Długosz, has Jogaila drown her (en.wikipedia: at Brest, with relatives Vidimantas and Butrimas killed); VLE thinks Kęstutis sent her to Brest in 1382; at Constance (1416) delegates said she lived long and died a natural death; the Palanga burial first appears in Stryjkowski (1582). Her death date is unknown. Everything else below is invention.
Seat: Birutės kalnas (Birutė Hill), its shore flame and the sea-stone (Šventasis akmuo, ch. 11).
Sigil: a drop of amber with a flame inside [Saga invention].
Words: Jūra atsimena. “The sea remembers.” [Saga invention]
Inheritance: through mothers (magic_rules §2: the gift “usually runs down the maternal line”). Each generation gives one daughter to the shore flame. The line supplies the vessels of the Amber Queen (cosmology §3.4).
Birutė’s maternal kin: keep them unnamed and few. A grandmother who was a vessel before her (the last “walking” of the Queen before 1384) is the cleanest invention. The chronicle tradition that Birutė’s relatives were killed in 1382 (verify source and names before use) can mean, in the saga, that Jogaila’s men tried to end the line. Birutė is the last vessel (D1): after 1384 the Queen acts only through amber Birutė has touched.
Status after 1387: a remnant of women keeping a hidden fire at Palanga (the “Ghost-Fire of Palanga”, mythic_gaps.md §5) without a vessel. By Book V the statue no longer glows (Book V ch. 25).

title: Houses & lineages
text:
3. The great boyar families
Period rules. Before Horodło (1413) there are no “magnates” in the Polish sense: there are boyars (bajorai), servitors of the duke, rewarded with land and castles. The great families named below rise through Vytautas’s service and become magnates in the 1430s–40s. Use surnames sparingly before 1413; patronymics (Astikaitis, Valimantaitis) are more authentic.









Family
Founder(s) in our period
Polish arms after Horodło
Role and era




Goštautai (Gasztołd)
Jonas Goštautas (d. 1458)
Abdank (verify)
Rises under Vytautas. In the 1430s–40s the leading voice of the Lithuanian council: his role in the 1440 murder of Žygimantas is uncertain (VLE; the killers are recorded as the Czartoryski brothers, Švitrigaila’s partisans); leader of the council that elected Casimir Grand Duke in 1440. Voivode of Trakai, then of Vilnius (verify offices and years). Book V’s kingmaker.


Astikai (Ościk)
Kristinas Astikas (fl. 1390s–1430s; d. c.1442–44)
Trąby (verify)
Vytautas’s companion. His son Radvila Astikaitis (d. 1477) founds the Radvilos.


Radvilos (Radziwiłł)
Radvila Astikaitis
Trąby
Only beginning in Book V. The Radvilos are a late-15th-century power. In 1440–50 they are a young branch of the Astikai. Treat any “Radvila magnate” before 1450 as anachronistic (Book V outline ch. 17 should say “the Astikai and their sons”).


Kęsgailos (Kieżgajło)
Mykolas Kęsgaila (d. 1450), son of Valimantas
Zadora (verify)
Samogitian magnates. Elders (seniūnai) of Samogitia 1412–32, 1440–41 and 1443–50 (Švitrigaila’s man: imprisoned by Žygimantas after 1432, restored in 1440). The Valimantaičiai brothers, including Rumbaudas Valimantaitis, Vytautas’s man in Samogitia c.1409–11 (verify), are the bridge between Vilnius and the Samogitian assemblies.


Manvydai (Moniwid)
Albertas (Vaitiekus) Manvydas, first voivode of Vilnius (1413) (verify)
Leliwa (verify)
The first holders of the new Horodło offices. Unrelated to Prince Manvydas son of Gediminas (no evidence of descent (verify)).


Jaunius
Jaunius, first voivode of Trakai (1413) (verify)
—
Vytautas’s administrator.


Daugirdas (Dowgird)
Jonas Daugirdas, voivode of Vilnius in the 1430s–40s (verify)
—
Council lord of the Žygimantas years.


Alšėniškiai (Holszański, Halshany princes)
Ivan Olshansky (Jonas Alšėniškis); his son Andrei
(princely)
Lithuanian–Ruthenian princes. Ivan was one of Vytautas’s chief captains and governor of Kyiv after Skirgaila (verify). Julijona (Vytautas’s second wife) and Sophia (Jogaila’s fourth wife) are from this family. The house that married both cousins.


Ostrogski
Dashko (Danylo) Ostrozky; Fedir Ostrozky
(princely)
Volhynian Orthodox princes. Dashko freed Švitrigaila from Kremenets in 1418 (verify); Fedir fought alongside the Hussites and was a pillar of Švitrigaila’s party in the 1430s (verify).



Era notes

Book I (1382–87): name boyars by patronymic or personal name only. The Kęstutis loyalists massacred in ch. 7 can be the Iron Wolves (iron_wolves.md), invented retainers. Their names should be pagan dithematic (Dau-gird-as, Ram-baud-as).
Books II–III: Vytautas’s companions (Astikas, Goštautas’s father’s generation, Valimantas’s sons) rise. Many princes and boyars die at the Vorskla (1399), which makes room for new men.
Book IV (1413–30): Horodło makes the Catholic boyars a heraldic nobility. The new voivodes of Vilnius and Trakai become offices worth fighting over. Orthodox lords are excluded from the highest offices: a Record grievance that feeds Book V.
Book V (1430–50): the council lords (Goštautas, Daugirdas, Kęsgaila) are the state. They make and unmake grand dukes, as in 1440.

title: Houses & lineages
text:
4. The neighbouring houses

4.1 The Masovian Piasts [Record]

Seat: Warsaw and Czersk (Janusz I); Płock and Rawa (Siemowit IV).
Arms: the Masovian (Piast) eagle (verify tinctures).
Words: Między dwoma ogniami. “Between two fires.” (Polish) [Saga invention]
Key figures: Janusz I (c.1346–1429) ⚭ Danutė Kęstutaitė: Vytautas’s brother-in-law and steady ally. Siemowit IV (c.1352–1426) ⚭ Aleksandra Algirdaitė (1387): a failed candidate for the Polish crown in 1382–84, who tried to seize Kraków by force (verify details). Henryk (d. 1392/93), bishop-elect of Płock and Jogaila’s envoy at Ostrów, ⚭ Rimgailė Kęstutaitė in 1392 and was dead within a year (verify cause).
Character: small, proud, squeezed between the Order, Poland and Lithuania. Two brothers married the two Gediminid lines: Janusz to Kęstutis’s daughter, Siemowit to Algirdas’s.
Patron: none canonical. In the saga Masovia is the neutral ground where cousins meet and where Vytautas runs first after Krėva.



4.2 The Polish court and the Lesser Poland lords

The Anjou queen. Jadwiga (see 1.6). Daughter of Louis I of Hungary and Poland (d. 10/11 Sep 1382) and Elizabeth of Bosnia (murdered 1387). Persona patron: the White Silence (cosmology §2.2 says honest Christians are its victims, not its servants. Write her as used by it.)
The Lesser Poland (Małopolska) lords [Record]: the oligarchy that chose Jogaila over Wilhelm of Habsburg and Siemowit IV (1384–85). Key names: Spytko II of Melsztyn (Leliwa arms; voivode of Kraków; killed at the Vorskla, 1399); Jan of Tarnów (Leliwa); Dobiesław of Kurozwęki; Jan Tęczyński; Krystyn of Ostrów, castellan of Kraków (verify each office).
Two Spytkos, do not merge them. Spytko II (d. 1399), Jogaila’s backer, dies beside Vytautas at the Vorskla. Spytko III of Melsztyn, his son (d. 4 May 1439 at Grotniki), led the Hussite-leaning confederation against Oleśnicki (persona/Spytek is Spytko III) (verify dates).
Zbigniew Oleśnicki (1389–1455) [Record], Dębno arms. Royal secretary; at Grunwald he saved Jogaila from a German knight’s charge (Długosz). Bishop of Kraków (appointed 9 Jul 1423), cardinal (created 18 Dec 1439 by Eugene IV; the antipope Felix V also named him on 20 Jan 1440). Leader of the Polish party that blocked Vytautas’s coronation (1429–30). Patron in the saga: the Gold-Glutton (character_arcs), with Henė’s last bargain.
Words (Lesser Poland lords): Rex regnat, nos regimus. “The king reigns; we rule.” (Latin) [Saga invention]



4.3 The Luxembourgs [Record]

Seat: Buda (Hungary), Prague (Bohemia), the imperial court.
Arms: the Luxembourg lion; Sigismund’s arms combine Hungary, Bohemia and the imperial eagle. Sigismund founded the Order of the Dragon (1408) [Record].
Key figure: Sigismund (1368–1437). ⚭ Mary of Hungary (1385), then Barbara of Celje (1405/08). King of Hungary 1387, King of the Romans 1411, of Bohemia 1419/1436, Emperor 1433. Hosted the Council of Constance. Arbiter between Poland and the Order (the 1420 Breslau award went against Poland). Offered Vytautas a crown at Lutsk (1429).
Words: Divide et arbitra. “Divide, then arbitrate.” [Saga invention]
Patron: the Shadow-Seller serves him in 1429–30 (D2) and the Gold-Glutton flatters him.



4.4 The Rurikids of Moscow [Record]

Seat: the Moscow Kremlin.
Arms: the mounted St George appears on Moscow coins from the late 14th century (verify). Two riders, Lithuania’s and Moscow’s, facing each other across the Ugra.
Key figures: Dmitry Donskoy (1350–89), victor of Kulikovo (8 Sep 1380), negotiated with Uliana in 1384 to marry a daughter to Jogaila (an Orthodox alternative to Krėva). Vasily I (1371–1425) ⚭ Sofija Vytautaitė: three wars with his father-in-law (1406–08), ended by the stand-off on the Ugra (1408). Vasily II (1415–62), Vytautas’s grandson, under Vytautas’s protection from 1425.
Words: Sobirai i terpi. “Gather and endure.” (Russian) [Saga invention]
Patron: none canonical. [Saga suggestion]: Moscow is the realm the Horde taught to collect tribute, so the Steppe-Hunger’s shadow lies on it lightly.



4.5 The Horde khans [Record]

Tokhtamysh (khan c.1380–95; killed c.1406 near Tyumen (verify)). Reunited the Horde, burned Moscow in August 1382 (the same month Kęstutis died), was broken by Timur (1391, 1395), and fled to Vytautas, granting him rights over the Rus’ lands in exchange for restoration (verify terms). Sons Jalal ad-Din (fought beside Vytautas at Grunwald; briefly khan 1411–12) and Kadir Berdi (killed Edigu in 1419) (verify).
Temur Qutlugh (khan 1397/98–99). Nominal victor of the Vorskla; died months later.
Edigu (c.1352–1419). Manghit emir and beglerbeg, the kingmaker of khans; field commander at the Vorskla; raided Moscow (1408) and Kyiv (1416) (verify). Persona: “the Steppe Butcher”.
Hacı Giray (d. 1466): raised in Lithuania, made first khan of an independent Crimea with Lithuanian backing in the 1440s (verify year). Book V seed.
Arms: tamgas (clan marks).
Words: Tengri – dangus, žemė – arklio. “The sky is Tengri’s; the earth belongs to the horse.” [Saga invention, phrased in Lithuanian as heard at Vytautas’s court]
Patron: Stepių Alkis (Steppe-Hunger), which is not Tengri (cosmology §2.2) but the egregore of horizon-conquest.

title: Houses & lineages
section: 5. The Teutonic Order as an institution-house
text:
5. The Teutonic Order as an institution-house

5.1 House card

Seat: Marienburg (Malbork), the Grand Master’s seat since 1309. The Marshal at Königsberg. Frontier houses on the Neman: Ragnit, Georgenburg (Jurbarkas), Christmemel, Marienwerder (Naujapilis), built for Vytautas in 1384.
Arms: the black cross on white [Record]. The Grand Master’s arms add a gold cross over the black, with the imperial eagle on an inescutcheon (verify details). The fleur-de-lis ends attributed to St Louis are legend.
Words: no period motto. Helfen – Wehren – Heilen is a modern motto; do not use it in 14th-century scenes. Saga motto: Per crucem, ferro. “Through the cross, by iron.” [Saga invention]
Character: a corporation, not a family. Celibate brother-knights recruited mainly from the German lands, with no heirs, so the house never dies and never forgives. It is rich (amber monopoly, grain, the Prussian Hanse towns) and diplomatically skilled. It ran the Reisen, the winter and summer raids with Western “guests” (Henry Bolingbroke in 1390 among them).
Feuds: internal: the Grand Master against the Prussian estates (the Prussian Confederation, founded 1440); Heinrich von Plauen deposed by his own chapter (1413). External: Lithuania, Poland, the archbishops of Riga.
Patron: Geležinis Šventasis (Iron Saint) (cosmology §3.3), fed by the Reise and forced baptism. Not the Christian God.

Membership. Brother-knights (Ritterbrüder) took the three monastic vows of poverty, chastity and obedience; they had to be of knightly, legitimate birth and, in practice, from the German lands. Priest-brothers served as chaplains. Half-brothers (Graumäntler) and familiares were associates. Guests (Gäste) were Western crusaders on the Reise.


5.4 Why Vytautas could not be Marshal (review H5)

The Marshal was a professed brother-knight: a monk under vows. A married man could not take the vow of chastity without his wife’s consent and separation, and Vytautas was married to Ona, who was then a hostage in the Order’s hands.
The great offices were filled from senior brothers with decades in the Order. A convert of weeks (baptised at Tapiau on 21 Oct 1383) was not even a novice.
Recruitment was effectively German-only. No Lithuanian ever held a great office.
The Marshal led the Reisen against Lithuania. Handing the Order’s war against Lithuania to a Lithuanian claimant would have been absurd to the chapter, and the Order was suspicious of converts who had sworn first by pagan forms (power_systems §2.6).
What he really was [Record]: a baptised ally and vassal under the Treaty of Königsberg (30 Jan 1384). He pledged Samogitia to the Nevėžis and was entrusted with castles to hold (Marienwerder, Georgenburg) and with Order troops “lent” to his war. This is the correct Book I status: a vassal-prince with borrowed knights, not an officer. The Marshal of ch. 20 is a real Order brother. (The Marshal around 1383 may be Kuno von Hattenstein (verify) before naming him.)

title: Houses & lineages
text:
6. Quick genealogy rules for prose

Kinship terms are fixed by D9: Kęstutis is dėdė to Jogaila, Skirgaila and Švitrigaila; Vytautas and Jogaila are pusbroliai.
Baptismal names appear only after the baptisms: Vytautas is Wigand from Oct 1383 and Aleksandras from 1386; Jogaila is Władysław from 15 Feb 1386; Skirgaila is Kazimierz and Švitrigaila Bolesław from 1386.
No Columns on Jogaila’s men. The rider on seals and banners is fine.
Ona dies in 1418 (31 Jul), Sofija marries in 1391 (9 Jan), and the sons (a contested tradition) die in 1392 (master_chronology).
Radvilos are not a power before c.1450; Goštautai are a power from the 1430s.
Before 1413 no Lithuanian boyar has a Polish coat of arms.
When a date carries (verify) here, keep it out of chapter text until it is checked, or blur it (“that winter”, “the year the Order burned Kaunas”).

Source: world_rules/religion_and_clergy.md
Reference for Geležinio Vilko Saga, Book I era (1382–1387) and its aftermath. Subordinate to canon_decisions.md, cosmology.md, magic_rules.md and master_chronology.md. In-world tales mentioned here are in legends_and_songs.md.

title: Faiths & clergy
section: 1. The Baltic religion as practised in 1382 [Record]
text:
1. The Baltic religion as practised in 1382 [Record]

1.1 The sources and their problems
Almost everything written about Lithuanian paganism before 1387 was written by enemies, converts or later antiquarians. No Lithuanian pagan text survives.









Source
Date
Value
Problem




Peter of Dusburg, Chronicon terrae Prussiae
1326
Describes Prussian religion, the sanctuary of Romowe (Romuva) in Nadruvia and its high priest the Criwe, whom he likens to a pope
An Order priest writing crusade justification. The “pagan pope” may be built by analogy with Rome; Romuva’s location has never been found. Contested.


Livonian Rhymed Chronicle; Hermann von Wartberge; Wigand of Marburg
13th–14th c. (Wigand survives in a 15th-c. Latin version)
Raids, oaths, funerals, burnings of captives
Order perspective; details of rites are second-hand.


Jan Długosz, Annales
c. 1455–80
The 1387 extinction of the Vilnius flame, the felling of the grove, the killing of the sacred snakes; Samogitian conversion
Written seventy or more years later by a Polish canon with a case to make for Jogaila as apostle.


Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini, De Europa
c. 1458
Anecdotes from Jerome of Prague’s preaching in Lithuania: household snakes, sacred groves, a sacred fire (verify the dating of Jerome’s mission)
Hearsay, written decades later.


16th-c. Lithuanian chronicles (incl. Bychowiec)
16th c.
Šventaragis, Lizdeika, the Iron Wolf, Birutė the vaidilutė
Dynastic legend; Renaissance invention of a Roman origin for the nobility.


Jan Łasicki, De diis Samagitarum; Maciej Stryjkowski
c. 1580 (Łasicki published 1615)
Long lists of Samogitian gods
Many names are probably misunderstandings or inventions.


Archaeology
—
Cremation dominant; horse burials; hillforts; sacred hills (alkos kalnai)
Shows practice, not belief.



Consequence for the saga. The terms Krivis, Krivių Krivaitis, vaidilutė and the image of an organised pagan “church” with a hierarchy and a centre are partly a construct of hostile and Romantic sources. The saga is entitled to use them, since folklore taken literally is its premise, but docs should never present them as settled history.


1.2 The clergy








Role
What the sources say
Uncertainty




Krivis, Krivių Krivaitis (“Krivis of Krivises”)
Dusburg’s Criwe at Romuva, a high priest whose messenger carried his staff or another sign; the 16th-c. chronicles make Lizdeika a high priest under Gediminas. Later ethnography records the krivulė, a crooked staff carried from farm to farm to summon a village assembly.
High. Whether a single high priest existed in 14th-c. Lithuania is doubtful; the title Krivių Krivaitis is largely 16th-c. and later.


Žyniai (sing. žynys, “one who knows”, from žinoti)
General term for priests and seers: sacrificers, interpreters of omens, healers.
Medium. The word is genuine Lithuanian, but its use as a formal rank is largely modern.


Vaidilos / vaidilutės
Prussian sources (late, e.g. Grunau, 16th c.) mention Waidelotten; Lithuanian tradition makes Birutė a maiden keeper of the sacred fire at Palanga.
High. The vaidilutė as a vestal virgin of an eternal flame is shaped by Romantic historiography (19th c.), though sacred fires themselves are attested (Długosz).


Burtininkai (lot-casters, from burtai, lots)
Lots and omens before war and for choosing offerings are reported by Order chroniclers.
Low to medium. Divination is well attested in general terms.


Raganos (witches, seers; linked to regėti, “to see”, though the etymology is debated)
Folklore: women who see, heal, curse, fly to hilltop gatherings (Šatrija).
They belong to folk belief, not to any priesthood; witch-trial records are post-1500.





1.3 Sacred places

Alkai (sing. alkas): sacred groves, hills, stones or fields where no tree was cut and no plough went. The word survives in hundreds of place names (Alkos kalnas, Alkupis). Oaths were sworn and offerings left there. [Record]
Eternal flames: Długosz describes the perpetual fire in Vilnius, tended by priests and extinguished by Jogaila in 1387. Lithuanian tradition places another on Birutė’s hill at Palanga. Długosz and others describe Samogitian sacred fires extinguished during the 1413 conversion (verify sites). [Record, late sources]
Šventaragis: in the 16th-c. chronicles, a legendary prince who asked to be burned at the confluence of the Neris and the Vilnia; the valley took his name and later rulers were cremated there. The traditional site lies under or beside Vilnius Cathedral. [Record: legend]



1.4 Offerings and oaths

Offerings: grain, bread, beer, milk (for the žaltys), first fruits, animals (goats, oxen, horses, cocks); amber and weapons appear in graves. [Record]
Oaths: sworn on earth, by the gods, with an animal sacrifice. In 1351 Kęstutis swore a pagan oath to King Louis of Hungary, sacrificing an ox, promised baptism, and then left without keeping it (recorded by Polish chroniclers; verify Jan of Czarnków). The saga mirrors it in Vytautas’s 1383 false baptism (master chronology). [Record]
Human sacrifice: Order chroniclers repeatedly report captured knights burned as thank-offerings. Dusburg reports that after the 1320 battle at Medininkai the Samogitians burned a captured Order official, Gerhard Rude, mounted on his horse (verify name and details). These are hostile sources, but the reports are too frequent to dismiss. The saga keeps them (see §2.2).



1.5 Cremation

Practice: cremation was the normal rite of Lithuanian pagans into the 14th century; graves with horses, weapons and personal goods are common in the archaeology. [Record]
Algirdas, May 1377: cremated with his horses and goods in a pagan rite according to Order sources (the “eighteen horses” figure and the forest of Kukaveitis are often cited; verify Wigand of Marburg). Some Rus’ chronicles claim instead that he died an Orthodox monk. Contested. The saga takes the cremation (master chronology), and it can hint at the Orthodox rumour through his widow Uliana (§3). [Record, contested]
Kęstutis, August 1382: cremated with full pagan rites in Vilnius, with his horse, arms, hounds and falcons, by order of the nephew whose men killed him (the detailed list follows Długosz; verify). [Record] Saga use: review H4, and legends_and_songs.md §4 (Sovijus).



1.6 Sacred animals

Žalčiai (grass snakes): kept in houses and sanctuaries, fed milk, killing one a disaster. Długosz says the snakes of the Vilnius sanctuary were killed in 1387; Aeneas Silvius tells of households keeping snakes as guardian spirits (verify). [Record]
Horses: sacrificed and burned with their lords; white horses used in divination in Baltic sources (best attested for the Pomeranian Slavs and the Prussians; verify for Lithuania). [Record, partial]
Wolves, aurochs, bees, the cuckoo carry heavy folk symbolism (the Iron Wolf, the aurochs of Tauras hill, the cuckoo of the Eglė tale), but there is no reliable record of cult.



1.7 What the Order and the chroniclers saw
Western chivalric writers often called the Lithuanians “Saracens” (verify specific sources), and the Order presented them as worshippers of fire, groves, snakes and stones, so that the Reise could be preached as a crusade with indulgences. Its chroniclers were not stupid: they knew the land and its people well, recorded real oaths and real funerals, and negotiated with pagan dukes as equals when it suited them. Their descriptions are accurate observations framed by a purpose. The saga’s priests and knights should talk that way too: precise about the enemy’s rites and wrong about their meaning.

title: Faiths & clergy
section: 2. Saga overlay: the clergy and the Forces [Saga invention]
text:
2. Saga overlay: the clergy and the Forces [Saga invention]

2.1 Who does what, in the three-layer cosmology









Role
Relation to the gods and Forces
Relation to Senovės Kalba
Book I examples




Krivis
Keeper of the Silent Pact (cosmology §4.1). He does not command the gods; he witnesses and binds. The Krivis office moved from Romuva to Vilnius (Šventaragis) when Prussia fell in 1283 (master chronology). The line claims descent from Lizdeika (legends_and_songs.md §3).
Rarely casts. His power is the binding (Senovės Sutartis, magic §6) and the oath-memory of the flame. Carries the krivulė, the crooked staff that “remembers” every oath sworn while it was held.
The Krivis of 1382 (unnamed in Book I; offstage).


Žyniai
Petitioners of gods; negotiators with spirits of place.
Trained askers (tier 3 in power_systems.md §4), taught in a living lineage; the gift itself still comes by one of the three paths (born, noticed, bound; magic §2). The Order gags captured žyniai because Kalba needs words aloud (magic §3.2).
Galminas, “the last of the old žyniai” (ch. 29), also the Root-Mother’s host (hidden_immortals §4).


Vaidilutės
Keepers of the sacred flames that are clause 1 of the Pact. Gabija’s servants.
Born (prigimtis), usually down the maternal line. Fire workings.
Eglė of Šventaragis, before she becomes Pelkių Eglė (D5).


The Palanga amber line
A distinct sisterhood: vessels of the Amber Queen (cosmology §3.4). Not subordinate to the Krivis, and older than his office in Lithuania.
Born; amber as universal medium; Water and Stars.
Birutė (D1).


Burtininkai
Readers of Laima’s threads through lots.
Minor Stars workings. Their weakness: lots, like Laima’s words, admit many readings (legends_and_songs.md §10), so a lot-caster can always find the answer the paymaster wants without technically lying (Law of Truth, magic §5.2).
Jogaila’s court lot-caster (prologue context; see §2.2).


Raganos
Outside the Pact. Never sworn into it, so never protected by it and never bound by its courtesy. They bargain directly with Forces (the Root-Mother, sometimes the Shadow-Seller).
Born seers; the most dangerous independents.
None on the page in Book I; they rise after 1387.



Rule: the pagan clergy are not the gods’ servants in any simple sense. They are brokers between mortals and powers that are indifferent (gods) or hungry (Forces). Like all brokers, some are honest, some are frightened, and some take a cut.


2.2 Sympathetic and corrupt: the old faith

Sympathetic:

Eglė, who told Jogaila’s captain the truth to his face and paid for it with her mortality (prologue; D5).
Birutė, who used a priestess’s trick to marry for love and paid the bill herself (legends §5).
Galminas, who in ch. 29 does not curse, only watches. He is stern, unforgiving and honest.

Corrupt or grey:

The Krivis of 1345–82 (suggested name: Sirvydas; Saga invention). He bound two princes to a Pact whose price, royal children’s blood, the people were never told (legends §6). He kept the flame and the secret, and in 1382, when Jogaila’s captain came for a prophecy, he sent his youngest vaidilutė (Eglė) to give it rather than face the duke himself.
Jogaila’s court burtininkas (Saga invention). A lot-caster who has never once in twelve years cast an unfavourable lot for his master. He is not a liar; he is a good reader. Henė likes him.
The žyniai who burn captives (grounded in the record, §1.4). After the first Order raid of Book I, a captured young knight is burned on his horse as a thank-offering to Perkūnas. Vytautas does not stop it. The saga should show this without excuse: it is what the Order’s chroniclers said it was, and also what the Order did to Samogitian villages in reverse.




2.3 The fate of the pagan hierarchy after 1387
[Record] In February–March 1387, Jogaila, now King of Poland, came to Vilnius with Polish clergy. According to Długosz he had the perpetual fire extinguished, the sacred grove felled and the sacred snakes killed, while the people watched and wondered that the gods did nothing. Commoners were baptised in groups, each group given one Christian name, and the baptised received woollen garments, which drew many to the font (verify Długosz’s details). Few Polish priests spoke Lithuanian, and Długosz says Jogaila himself taught the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer in Lithuanian (verify). The Vilnius bishopric was founded, a cathedral begun on the sanctuary site, and privileges were issued favouring Catholic boyars (verify the terms of the 1387 privilege). Samogitia remained pagan until 1413–17.
[Saga invention] What happened to the clergy:

The Krivis stays by the flame as it is put out. He does not resist. When the water hits the embers, he speaks the Pact’s ending aloud (“Sutartis baigta”), so that the spirits of place hear it from a human mouth and not from a priest’s Latin. That is the moment the Unbinding begins (cosmology §4.3). He walks into the felled grove and is not seen again. (Option for the author: before the extinguishing he passes an ember to Galminas, who carries it to Vytautas that night. That would give Vytautas’s secret Trakai flame (magic §6) its source on the page.)
The vaidilutės of the city are baptised and married off to Catholic boyars, which is what the privileges reward. One or two go west to the Hidden Groves of Samogitia (D7). Their flames are the last legal pagan fires in Europe until 1413.
The žyniai scatter into the villages as healers, bone-setters and weather-askers. With no Krivis and no flames, nobody can bind new oaths with the gods, only bargains with Forces. That is the Unbinding in a sentence: after 1387, the only supernatural contracts left are bargains (magic §1), and bargains are Velnias’s trade.
The raganos rise. They were outside the Pact, so they lose nothing when it ends. In Books II–V the peasantry turns to them, quietly (cosmology §4.3).
The žalčiai. The snakes killed in Vilnius were the descendants of Žilvinas (legends §2). Eglė’s is the last of the line. The threshold lullaby (legends §12.3) begins to be sung that spring.



2.4 Christian clergy and the Forces

Christian priests cannot see the Baltic spirits, and holy water does nothing to things that do not believe in it (cosmology §4.3). This is not a verdict on Christianity. Two orders of meaning are passing each other without touching.
Consecrated stone dampens Kalba (magic §9): the old powers are strangers in a church, as a Franciscan would be a stranger in an alkas. Cold iron forged by a Christian smith on a feast day burns spirits (magic §9), the one point where the two orders collide, and the saga should enjoy the irony of peasants hanging Order horseshoes over their doors after 1387.
The egregores feed on appetite wearing faith’s clothes, not on faith. A Franciscan praying for a dying pagan feeds nothing. A Reise launched for indulgences and slaves feeds the Iron Saint. A baptism bought for a crown or a woollen shirt feeds the White Silence. A bishopric’s tithe-ledger, once it outweighs its almonry, feeds the Gold-Glutton.
Christian grace is never mocked and never explained. If an honest priest’s blessing seems to steady a frightened man, the saga does not say whether God did it or the man did. The camera does not go there.

title: Faiths & clergy
section: 3. Orthodox Christianity in the Grand Duchy [Record]
text:
3. Orthodox Christianity in the Grand Duchy [Record]

Most of the Grand Duchy was Orthodox. By 1382 the Ruthenian lands (Polotsk, Vitebsk, Kyiv, Volhynia, Chernihiv-Siversk, Smolensk’s borders) made up the greater part of the realm’s territory and population. Algirdas ruled them through Orthodox sons (e.g. Andrei of Polotsk, Dmitri of Bryansk). Ruthenian was the chancery language. [Record]
Algirdas’s wives were Orthodox: Maria of Vitebsk (died c. 1346) and Uliana of Tver (married 1350), Jogaila’s mother. Uliana was devout, politically formidable and a patron of monasteries, and she remained a power at court after 1377 (the extent of her influence on Jogaila is debated; verify). Whether Jogaila was baptised Orthodox as a child is disputed. [Record]
Orthodox Vilnius: the city had a Ruthenian quarter and several Orthodox churches by the mid-14th century; tradition ascribes St Paraskeva’s church to Maria of Vitebsk (verify). [Record, partly traditional]
The Vilnius martyrs. Tradition holds that in 1347 three Orthodox courtiers of Algirdas, Anthony, John and Eustathius, were executed for refusing to renounce their faith (the story includes a refusal to break the fast), and were hanged on an oak at an execution place where the Holy Trinity church and monastery later stood. They were venerated early and are saints of the Orthodox Church; their relics are kept in Vilnius (Church of the Holy Spirit) (verify dates, the stage of their canonisation and the relic history). [Record: tradition]
Church organisation: Constantinople at times appointed a separate metropolitan for Lithuania, against Moscow’s objections; Cyprian was consecrated in 1375 for Kyiv and Lithuania (verify). Orthodox Lithuania was therefore a diplomatic battlefield between the Grand Duke, Moscow and the Patriarchate. [Record]
Vytautas and Orthodoxy: Vytautas is often said to have taken Orthodox baptism (as Yuri / Jurgis) during his 1384 reconciliation (verify). Ona’s origins are uncertain; some identify her with a Smolensk princely family, which would make her Orthodox-born (verify).


3.1 Saga overlay [Saga invention]

Orthodoxy in Book I is a household faith, not a crusading one. It is the faith of mothers, wives and the eastern half of the realm. The Vulture Forces barely notice it in 1382, because nobody is buying a crown with it yet. That changes in Book II, when Sofija’s marriage to Vasily I of Moscow (1391) puts an Orthodox throne on the ledger.
Double faith (dvoeverie, surrounding_folklore.md): in Ruthenian Lithuania the žaltys gets milk and the icon gets a candle in the same house. The saga treats this as wisdom, not confusion.
Sympathetic:

The 1347 martyrs. Pagan Vilnius killed them. The saga does not soften that. Their oak is the first holy tree in Vilnius that the old gods did not plant.
Uliana, a pious woman who loved her son and taught him to hide what he wanted. She is grey, not corrupt.

Corrupt (Saga invention): the hegumen of Holy Trinity, who sells splinters of the “martyrs’ oak” to Hanseatic merchants at a price that rises each Lent, and whose counting-room has a warm coin on every shelf (a Gold-Glutton sign, cosmology §3.3).

title: Faiths & clergy
text:
4. Catholicism [Record unless marked]

4.1 The Franciscans in Vilnius

Gediminas’s letters (1323) invited merchants, craftsmen and clergy, mentioned friars (Franciscans and Dominicans) already serving in his realm, and spoke of churches built for them (verify which churches). Catholic merchants and friars had a quiet presence in Vilnius through the pagan period. [Record]
The Franciscan martyrs. Later Franciscan tradition remembers friars killed in Vilnius under the pagan dukes: two in Gediminas’s time and a larger group (often given as fourteen, sometimes dated 1369, sometimes 1341) under Algirdas. The accounts are late and partly legendary; dates, numbers and circumstances vary (verify). [Record: tradition, historicity debated]
The Franciscan church “on the Sand” (Church of the Assumption, Smėlynė) is traditionally the old Franciscan site of Vilnius (verify founding date).



4.2 The 1387 bishopric

Jogaila founded the Vilnius bishopric in 1387, endowed the cathedral (dedicated to St Stanislaus) on or beside the sanctuary site, and the papacy confirmed it (verify: Urban VI, 1388). The first bishop was Andrzej Wasilko (Andrew Jastrzębiec), a Franciscan (verify). The new parishes were few and their clergy mostly Polish.
Archaeology: excavations under Vilnius Cathedral (led by Napoleonas Kitkauskas from the 1980s (verify)) found earlier structures. Whether they include a pagan sanctuary, Mindaugas’s 13th-century cathedral, or both is debated. The saga may stack all three: the cathedral of 1387 on the ruins of Mindaugas’s church on the flame of Šventaragis. [Record, contested interpretation]



4.3 The Teutonic Order’s spirituality

A religious order: the Ordo fratrum domus hospitalis Sanctae Mariae Theutonicorum in Jerusalem (the Brothers of the German House of St Mary). Knight-brothers and priest-brothers took vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, kept the hours, and lived under a Rule. [Record]
Marian devotion: Mary was the Order’s patroness; its capital was Marienburg; Prussia itself was “Mary’s land”. The castle church carried a colossal image of the Virgin (verify date). The great campaigns were timed around Marian feasts, especially the Purification (2 Feb) for winter and the Assumption (15 Aug) for summer (verify how consistently). [Record]
The Reise: seasonal raids into Lithuania joined by Western “guests” (French, English, German, Scottish nobles) for honour and indulgence, sometimes celebrated by the Table of Honour (Ehrentisch) feast. Henry Bolingbroke rode in 1390 and 1392 (master chronology 1390). Chaucer’s Knight is the period’s own witness: “In Lettow hadde he reysed and in Ruce.” [Record]
Irony for the books: Kęstutis died on 15 August 1382, the Feast of the Assumption (master chronology), the Order’s high summer feast, when Marian hymns were being sung in Marienburg. The saga should let a knight remark on it, and should let the remark be devout rather than gloating.



4.4 Saga overlay [Saga invention]

Sympathetic Catholics:

Kuno von Liebenstein, komtur of Osterode, who historically warned Kęstutis of Jogaila’s treaty in 1381 (Ivinskis, via en.wikipedia; master chronology). He was a knight of the Order who kept faith with an enemy duke. Perkūnas would approve of him. (The saga’s Günther von Hohenstein is a different, invented young brother of Book VI, not the informant.)
Konrad Zöllner von Rotenstein (Grand Master 1382–90; H1): old, devout, a chess player. He believes honestly in Vytautas’s conversion, which makes Vytautas’s lie in ch. 19 cost something.
The Franciscans of Vilnius (cosmology §2.2): poor, Lithuanian-speaking in a few cases, and victims of both the pagan dukes and, later, of the bishops who arrive with money. A Franciscan in ch. 29 who baptises a frightened child by name, instead of by group, is the saga’s quiet answer to the White Silence.
Andrzej Wasilko, the first bishop: portray him as an honest Franciscan placed in a political job. He is a historical person; keep invention light.
Jadvyga, at her best (cosmology §2.2): a young queen who gave up the man she loved for a duty she believed in. The White Silence uses her (hidden_immortals §5); she is its victim, not its servant.

Corrupt or grey Catholics:

The amber wardens of Prussia, who hang poor gatherers for a pocket of sea-gold (verify period), all in the name of Mary’s land.
The commander who prices baptisms: in Book I, an Order Komtur who keeps a tariff of how many Lithuanian villages each converted boyar is worth. The Iron Saint walks behind him like heat from a forge.
The Polish clerk of 1387 (Saga invention): he counts woollen shirts against names at the Neris font. He is not cruel, only efficient, and frost forms on his ink.

title: Faiths & clergy
text:
5. Holy places gazetteer









#
Place
[Record]
[Saga] notes




1
Šventaragis valley, Vilnius (Neris–Vilnia confluence)
Legendary cremation site of dukes (16th-c. chronicles); site of the perpetual fire extinguished in 1387 (Długosz); now the cathedral square
Seat of the Krivis and the Silent Pact (1345). Eglė’s flame (prologue, after D5). The dead under the city are kept asleep by the fire (legends §3); the Unbinding starts here in 1387. The burnt-church meeting place of ch. 26 (review C9) belongs here.


2
Tauras hill, Vilnius
Named in the Iron Wolf legend as where Gediminas killed the aurochs (16th c.)
The price paid for the city (legends §3). No aurochs comes near it.


3
Holy Trinity, Vilnius (the martyrs’ oak)
Traditional execution site of the 1347 Orthodox martyrs
The first holy tree in Vilnius not planted by the old gods. Pagan and Orthodox Vilnians both avoid sitting under it, for different reasons.


4
Franciscan church “on the Sand”, Vilnius
Traditional Franciscan site (verify)
The friars’ bell is the one Christian sound the spirits of the Vilnia do not flee. Nobody knows why; the saga never says.


5
Birutė’s hill, Palanga
Traditional site of Birutė’s sanctuary and grave; archaeology found traces of a wooden structure, interpreted by some as a pagan sanctuary or observatory (verify dating). A chapel stands there now (19th c.).
The Palanga shore-fire of the amber line; the Šventasis akmuo of ch. 11 and 27; the amber kneeling woman on the beach below (ch. 27). The surf here speaks only through amber (cosmology §5).


6
Šventoji river mouth, near Palanga
Folk placing of Jūratė’s palace
Where Kastytis fished. Storm amber from here is “wall-amber” and too dangerous to work: it remembers the palace (legends §1).


7
Romuva / Romowe, Nadruvia (Prussia)
Dusburg’s sanctuary of the Criwe; location unknown; under the Order since the 13th c.
Fell in 1283; the Krivis office moved to Vilnius (master chronology). In 1382 it is a ruin under an Order chapel, and not the prologue’s location (H11, D5). Book V flashback only, flagged as a stretch.


8
Rambynas hill, on the Neman (Lithuania Minor)
Sacred hill of Lithuania Minor; its sacrificial stone was reportedly broken in the early 19th c. (verify)
In 1382 on the Order’s side of the river. Lithuanians cross at night to leave offerings; the Order’s priests know and let it happen, which is either tolerance or a trap.


9
Šatrija hill, Samogitia
In folklore the gathering place of witches (Šatrijos raganos)
A Hidden Grove after 1384 (D7). The raganos meet here because it was never part of the Pact, so the Pact’s ending cannot hurt it.


10
Medvėgalis hill, Samogitia
Besieged in the Order’s 1329 campaign with John of Bohemia; its defenders were forcibly baptised and reverted once the army left (verify)
The saga’s emblem of baptism under duress: the White Silence came, tasted, and went hungry. The local žyniai still keep the shirts as relics of a victory.


11
Kernavė, on the Neris
Early political centre with a hillfort complex; archaeology of a 13th–14th c. town; burned by the Order in 1390 (verify)
The oldest alkas of the Neris valley. Pagan lore says the first Krivis to leave Romuva rested here before Vilnius.


12
Krėva castle
Where Kęstutis died (15 Aug 1382) and where the Union of 1385 was signed
Not a holy place but an unholy one: residue of a kin-murder (magic §5.3). The White Silence settles here in 1385 (cosmology §4.2). Seers cannot sleep in the tower.


13
Puntukas boulder, near Anykščiai
Folk tale (recorded after Christianisation): Velnias meant to smash the Anykščiai church with it and dropped it at cock-crow
Saga retelling for 1382, before any church stood there: Velnias was carrying it to dam the Šventoji and drown a village that had cheated him (legends §9). After 1387 the villagers retell it with a church, because that story is safer.


14
Marienburg (Malbork), Prussia
Seat of the Grand Master from 1309; centre of the Marian cult of the Order
The Iron Saint’s forge-heart. The amber pebble goes cold here (magic §9; ch. 19). The Golden Gate’s carved virtues are sincere, and so is the furnace heat in the cellars.


15
The secret flame, Trakai island castle
—
Saga only (magic §6). Lit by Vytautas on the night of the 1387 extinguishing; it goes out at his death in 1430. Not yet a “place” in Book I, but the gazetteer should hold its slot.

title: Faiths & clergy
section: 6. Quick rules for writing faith scenes
text:
6. Quick rules for writing faith scenes

Every faith gets one decent person per book. If a chapter shows a corrupt cleric, another chapter must show an honest one of the same faith.
The gods never take creeds personally; Forces take appetites personally.
Pagan rites are shown with their cost: captives burned, children’s blood owed, people kept ignorant.
Christian rites are shown from the outside, with their beauty and their politics, and the saga never decides whether grace is real.
Use the record’s own ironies (the Assumption death, the woollen shirts, Jogaila teaching the Creed in Lithuanian) before inventing new ones.

title: Character arcs
text:
Source: books/character_arcs.md
Companion to series_arc.md. The series has one protagonist across Books I–IV: Vytautas. Each book gives him a mortal antagonist he must defeat (or be defeated by) and a mythic antagonist working behind them. Book V passes the torch (§4).

title: Character arcs
text:
1. The protagonist: Vytautas (c. 1350–1430)

1.1 The through-line
The lie he starts with: “Honour and blood will keep us safe.” (inherited from Kęstutis) The lie he adopts after Krėva: “Only cunning survives; trust is weakness.” (the Wolf) The truth he finally earns: “Cunning is a tool, faith is a choice, and some fires must be kept even at the cost of a crown.”
He is not a hero who becomes good. He is a good man who becomes effective, pays for it in people, and in the end chooses one thing to stay faithful to.


1.2 The seven forms (his “morph”)
Each form gets a name the narrative can use, a visible tell (body, objects, speech) and a trigger that ends it.











#
Form

Want

Trigger that ends it




1
Sūnus (the Son)
I, ch. 1–9

Kęstutis strangled (ch. 9)


2

Live
Shaved beard, cut hair, the maid’s dress; silent; animal
Kneels at the Order’s border (ch. 17)


3

Revenge through borrowed strength
The Order’s sword; white cloak; the dead amber; speaks German
The burned village and his friend’s death (ch. 20–21)


4

His sons poisoned (II, 1392)


5

Ruthenian robes; the Tatar court; Henė at his side; the “golden” period
Vorskla (II, 1399)

Plain armour again; the vilkatai at his back; the lantern flame on campaign

Chooses the flame; dies uncrowned (IV end)

4. Book V’s protagonist: passing the torch
Vytautas dies at the end of Book IV. Book V needs a new point of view with a clear want:

Recommended: the Flame-Keeper. An invented vilkatas of the Iron Wolves (Saga invention), a boy rescued during Book II’s Unbinding hunts and raised in the Trakai vault as the flame’s secret guard. Want: relight the flame after Vytautas’s death. Antagonists: Žygimantas (who would use him) and the unbound dead. Arc: he learns the Pact cannot be re-sworn by one man, and lets the gods become stories. That ending is the series’ last word on memory (the Law of Memory: “the land remembers”).
Narrative frame: Birutė (the Amber Queen) narrates his story as the last thing she remembers before the sea takes her statue, closing the loop opened by 00_pradzia.qmd.

title: Calendar & festivals

Source: world_rules/calendar_and_festivals.md
Canonical reference for time in the saga: how the year was counted in the 1380s, the old month names, the festival wheel, the saga’s magical zeniths, the Teutonic Order’s Christian calendar, and a season-by-season table for Book I. The zeniths follow magic_rules.md §3.3, which overrides books/1/senoves_kalba_magic_system.md. Dates follow master_chronology.md. Pronunciation of every festival name is in pronunciation_guide.md §12.

title: Calendar & festivals
text:
1. Counting time in the 1380s [Record]

1.1 The Julian calendar and the eight-day gap
Everyone who wrote dates in 1382 used the Julian calendar. In the 14th century it ran 8 days behind the sun as the modern (Gregorian) calendar measures it (for dates between 1 Mar 1300 and 28 Feb 1500, Julian + 8 = proleptic Gregorian). All dates in this file and in master_chronology.md are Julian, as in the chronicles.
The astronomical turning points of the 1380s therefore fell on these Julian dates (computed with Meeus’s formulas, ±1 day):








Event
Julian date, 1382–87
Old saying




Spring equinox
12–13 March
—


Summer solstice
13–14 June
—


Autumn equinox
14–15 September
—


Winter solstice
13–14 December
St Lucy’s Day (13 Dec) was “the shortest day” in Julian-era lore across Europe



Consequence for the saga. Christmas Eve (Kūčios, 24 Dec) fell about 11 days after the winter solstice, and St John’s Eve (Joninės, 23 June) about 10 days after the summer solstice. The folk equation “Kūčios = the solstice, Rasos = midsummer” is right in spirit, because the Church set its feasts on the old solstice festivals, but in the 1380s the days no longer matched.
Saga rule [Saga invention]: the Kalba zeniths are astronomical, because the elements watch the sky, not the Church calendar. In 1382 the pagan solstice night falls on about 13 December. Christianised households keep Kūčios on 24 December. After 1387 the feast drifts away from the zenith, and the night that families keep sacred is no longer the night the stars are strongest. It is a quiet image of the Unbinding, and Books II–V can use it.


1.2 How documents dated

Latin and German documents dated by feast days: in die Assumptionis beatae Mariae virginis (15 Aug), in vigilia Assumptionis (14 Aug), feria secunda post Michaelis (the Monday after Michaelmas). The year was Anno Domini. Chanceries in the Empire often began the year at Christmas; the Order’s practice should be checked (verify).
Ruthenian documents used the Byzantine era from the Creation. AD 1382 is 6890 (in the March-to-February reckoning common in Rus’ chronicles; verify which year-start a given source uses). A Ruthenian chronicle entry for Kęstutis’s death reads “in the year 6890”.
The Krėva Act is dated 14 August 1385, the eve of the Assumption, and so the eve of the third anniversary of Kęstutis’s death in the same castle (master_chronology).



1.3 How Lithuanians counted
Pagan Lithuania wrote nothing down. It counted by moons (mėnuo means both “moon” and “month”), by seasons, by feasts and by work: rugiapjūtė (the rye harvest), linarūtė (flax-pulling), sėja (sowing). Whether a seven-day week was in general use among pagan Lithuanians is unknown (verify). Where the week appears in older Lithuanian and in the dialects, its day names are Slavic loans [Record]: panedėlis (Monday), utarninkas (Tuesday), sereda (Wednesday), četvergas (Thursday), pėtnyčia (Friday), subata (Saturday), nedėlia (Sunday). The modern names (pirmadienis “first day” and so on) are 20th-century coinages. Kęstutis should not say penktadienis. If he names a day at all, it is a feast or a moon.

title: Calendar & festivals
text:
3. Moon and sun

3.1 The moon [Record]
Lithuanian names the phases: jaunatis (new moon, “the young one”), priešpilnis (waxing, “before full”), pilnatis (full moon), delčia (waning). Folk practice recorded in the 19th–20th centuries sows in the waxing moon, fells timber and cuts hair in the waning moon, and does not start anything at the new moon. The Moon (Mėnuo) is a warrior and a faithless husband whom Perkūnas cut in half, which is why he wanes (cosmology §3.1).


3.2 The saga’s reckoning [Saga invention]

The krivis of Šventaragis keeps the year. The year turns at the winter solstice, read from the sun’s rising point against the hills of the Neris valley. The year counts twelve moons from there.
The blind moon. Twelve lunar months fall about 11 days short of a solar year. When the twelfth moon dies too early, the krivis declares a thirteenth moon, aklasis mėnuo (“the blind moon”), in which no oath is sworn and no marriage made. (Name and rule are inventions. They give the saga a real-sounding lunisolar mechanism, since medieval Lithuania must have reconciled moons and seasons somehow, and nothing is recorded.)
After 1387 there is no krivis and no one to declare the blind moon. Peasants slowly adopt the Church calendar, and the old moon-year drifts. Another sign of the Unbinding.
The zeniths are astronomical (§1.1). The calendar of feasts is how people keep them, and the two need not coincide.

title: Calendar & festivals
section: 5. The Christian calendar overlay: the Order’s year [Record]
text:
5. The Christian calendar overlay: the Order’s year [Record]

Two Reise seasons. The Order raided Lithuania mostly in winter (December–February, when swamps and rivers froze into roads) and in late summer (August–September, after the harvest). Western “guests” (French, English, Bohemian knights) came for them. By custom the Reisen were tied to the great Marian feasts: the Purification (2 Feb) for the winter season and the Assumption (15 Aug) for the summer (verify for the 1380s). A banquet of honour, the Ehrentisch (Table of Honour), was sometimes held before a Reise.
Mud seasons. Spring thaw (March–April) and autumn rains (October–November) stopped armies. The “two muddy seasons” are why Book I’s set pieces cluster in high summer and deep winter (geography_gazetteer.md).
Marian feasts (the Order’s patroness is Mary): Purification 2 Feb, Annunciation 25 Mar, Assumption 15 Aug, Nativity of Mary 8 Sept. (The Visitation, 2 July, was only instituted in 1389; no Order knight keeps it in Book I.)
Dates that fall on feasts:

15 Aug 1382: Kęstutis found dead at Krėva on the Assumption, the feast of the Order’s own patroness. The Lithuanian name Žolinė belongs to the Christian centuries; in the saga, the peasants who later keep Žolinė half-remember it as “the day the old duke died”. (15 Aug is the traditional date used in master_chronology.md; some accounts give an earlier August date. Verify.)
21 Oct 1383: Vytautas baptised Wigand at Tapiau on St Ursula’s Day.
14 Aug 1385: the Krėva Act, on the eve of the Assumption.
18 Feb and 4 Mar 1386: Jogaila’s wedding and coronation both fall in Shrovetide, the last days before Lent (Ash Wednesday was 7 Mar 1386), when weddings were still allowed. The haste of the Kraków calendar is visible in the dates.
Feb–Mar 1387: the baptism of Lithuania falls in Lent (Ash Wednesday 20 Feb 1387; Easter 7 Apr). Jogaila’s privilege to the Catholic boyars is usually dated 20 Feb 1387, which would be Ash Wednesday itself (verify the date).
15 Jul 1410: Žalgiris, on the feast of the Dispersion of the Apostles (Długosz notes it).

title: Calendar & festivals
section: 7. Where the chapters diverge, and the cheapest fixes
text:
7. Where the chapters diverge, and the cheapest fixes

Ch. 1–3 are set at an autumn Dagotuvės; the arrest was in early August.

Where: 01_senasis_sernas.qmd:3 (“Ruduo šiemet… atslinko anksti”) and :5 (the first Dagotuvės, harvest end); 03_gintaro_sapnas.qmd:7 (Dagotuvės songs) and :13 (“nors dar ne žiema”).
Fix: make the feast the rye harvest-home (pabaigtuvės) of late July. It is still a harvest feast with Žemyna’s thanks, and it keeps every image (new bread, the women thanking Žemyna). If the author wants the name, Dagotuvės can be the saga’s name for the rye harvest-home rather than the equinox feast. In that case Žemyna’s zenith stays at the equinox, and Birutė’s ch. 3 working is off-zenith either way (magic_rules §3.3 already doubles its cost).

Ch. 2 has snow at harvest time.

Where: 02_vilko_perspejimas.qmd:81 (“šešėliai ant sniego”).
Fix: use dew, stubble or moonlight (review C13).

Ch. 6 says autumn in Vilnius.

Where: 06_geleziniai_vartai.qmd:3 (“rudens pavakarę”).
Fix: a late-summer evening, with dust and harvest smoke.

Ch. 8 says winter at Krėva, but the death on 15 Aug is a fixed date (D3).

Where: 08_krevos_pozemiai.qmd:3 (“prasidėjo tikroji pilka žiema”), with summer remembered in :9.
Fix: keep the cold and lose the season. The dungeon is cold in August: stone that never warms, “a winter that lives under the castle”. Then the ch. 8 memory of green summer becomes the summer just outside the wall.
The irony to use: Kęstutis dies on the Assumption, the great feast of the Order’s patroness, in a castle where three years later (on the eve of the same feast) Jogaila will sign the union.

Ch. 10 has autumn ice on the morning after the death.

Where: 10_saltas_rytas.qmd:7 (“rudeninį ledą”).
Fix: use a metal or stone simile, or dew. And show the cremation (H4).

Ch. 19 compresses about ten months.

The baptism (21 Oct 1383) comes in what reads as the same scene as the winter 1382 arrival.
Fix: add a date header or a time-skip line. Give the baptism its autumn (and St Ursula’s Day, if the author wants a detail the Order would note).

Ch. 20–21 are set in spring.

Where: 20_svetimi_dieviai.qmd:17, 21_pirmoji_kova.qmd:15, 29.
These chapters come after the October 1383 baptism, so they can only be spring 1384, when Vytautas was the Order’s vassal (Königsberg, Jan 1384). That works with the review’s recommended recast of ch. 22–25 as the July 1384 burnings (H7).
Fix: date them spring 1384, and move the “first battle” to a raid of that spring.

Ch. 25 is set in spring (“last year’s leaves”).

Where: 25_isdaviku_isdavikas.qmd:9.
If ch. 22–25 become the July 1384 defection, change it to midsummer.

Ch. 27 has a November simile in late summer.

Where: 27_gintaro_auka.qmd:5.
The full moon after the July 1384 reconciliation is ~2 Aug 1384 (or ~31 Aug). The simile “the first November ice on a lake” is fine as a simile, but a reader may take it as the season. Optional.

Escape timing (an opportunity, not an error). The record says only “autumn 1382”. Setting the escape on Vėlinės night (around 2 Nov 1382, in a moonless week: new moon ~6 Nov) puts Birutė’s wind and fog working at Vėjopatis’s zenith, when its cost is halved. That explains how she could reach Krėva from Palanga at all, and makes the fog the dead’s own weather. (Saga suggestion.)

text:
Source: books/1/continuity_bible.md
Compiled 2026-10-10 from a full read of books/1/prologue.qmd, 00_pradzia.qmd and 01–30 in _quarto.yml order, checked against world_rules/canon_decisions.md (D1–D9), cosmology.md, magic_rules.md, master_chronology.md, books/1/senoves_kalba_magic_system.md and books/1/story_review.md.
How to read references. 12:13 means books/1/12_gedulo_skraiste.qmd, line 13 (each paragraph is one line). P is the prologue and 00 is 00_pradzia.qmd. C/H/M codes point to items already in story_review.md. N codes are new findings from this pass, indexed in §0. Line numbers are from the 2026-10-10 text and will drift after edits.

title: Book I continuity bible
section: 0. Index of new findings (not in story_review.md)
text:
0. Index of new findings (not in story_review.md)









N
Where
Finding
Sev.




N1
17:25
Vytautas calls himself “Senojo Šerno vienintelis likęs gyvas sūnus”. Kęstutis’s sons Tautvilas (d. 1390) and Žygimantas Kęstutaitis (d. 1440, a Book V lead in master_chronology.md) were alive.
High


N2
8:3, 14:17, 17:9, 17:11, 18:5
The seasons flip back and forth: “prasidėjo tikroji pilka žiema” (8:3), then “įprasta rudeninė migla” (14:17), then “gruodu sustingusios žemės” next to “šaltoje rudeninėje saulės šviesoje” (17:9/17:11), then “žiemos šviesa” (18:5).
High


N3
10:7, 16:13, 17:27, 26:19
The amulet has no origin and no return. Vytautas “nelietė tėvo atšalusio kūno” (10:7), so he could not have taken it then. He gives up his “paskutinius bajoriškus daiktus” (16:13). The border guard takes it (“paėmė amuletą”, 17:27) and it is never handed back, yet in 26:19 he has kept it “per visą savo bėgimą”.
High


N4
24:23 → 25:7
He runs into the forest “galutinai … vienas” (24:23), and the next morning “Su juo liko nedidelis būrys žmonių” including Jonas (25:7). The bridge sentence “Jis bėgo vienas, bet jautėsi vienišas” (25:7) is garbled.
High


N5
15:27, 23:9, 23:13
Eglė’s silence breaks, and so does D5. In 15:27 she nods to “Tu esi Gintaro Šventikė” (“Mergina lėtai linktelėjo galva”), confirming the identity D5 says she must correct. In 23:9 a voice speaks to Vytautas and 23:13 says she spoke “daugiau nė vieno … žodžio”, although she is mute in ch. 15–16.
High


N6
3:69 vs 28:13
Birutė gives him the pebble as “prisiminimas apie jūrą, kurios tu dar nematei”, but Ona remembers him loving her “prie Palangos jūrų”.
Med


N7
28:3, 30:3
Internal chronology fails. 23:3 dates the siege to 1383 and ch. 26–28 follow straight on, yet 28:3 says “dar prieš kelerius trumpus metus” (about one year by the text’s own dates). 30:3 says only “metai” have passed since the division, but Jogaila already holds the Polish crown (≥1386) and Skirgaila is vicegerent (1387).
Med


N8
30:11 vs ch. 28
Henė tells Skirgaila that Vytautas has “viltį visiškai atstatyti Trakus”, although ch. 28 shows Vytautas already rebuilding Trakai. On the record, Trakai went to Skirgaila (H8), so the taunt is aimed at the wrong man.
Med


N9
7:11, 17:33, 18:11
Cosmology §2.2 is broken (“the saga never passes judgement on the Christian God”): “tam tamsiam, negailestingam pavidalui, kurį kantriai maitino Dievas” (7:11). “krikščioniškojo Geležinio Šventojo kvėpavimas” (17:33). Knights “aklai meldėsi” to the Iron Saint “Marienburgo katedroje” (18:11), and Marienburg had no cathedral.
Med


N10
21:23, 13:7, 13:35
Slips that invert the meaning: “netikėtai pamatė neapykantą, o gailestį” (21:23; it needs ne). “Jos rankos nė akimirkos netvirtėjo” (13:7) says her hands shook, the opposite of the intent. “Laukiau tavęs prie Jūros” (13:35) is past tense and should be future (Lauksiu).
Med


N11
9:19–21
Kęstutis crushes one killer’s skull (“kaukolės sutriuškinimo garsas”), yet “jų buvo trys” and all three still pin him down.
Med


N12
9:27 = 9:39
Duplicated sentence: “Pasaulis pradėjo blėsti, virsti į begalinį pilką rūką.”
Low


N13
29:5 vs 29:17
He stands “iki pat kulniukų” (ankle-deep), then “išniro iš vandens”. 29:5 treats this as his second baptism, but by 1387 he had been baptised Catholic in 1383, Orthodox (Jurgis) in 1384 (verify) and Catholic (Aleksandras) in 1386.
Med


N14
22:3
Vilnius is called Vytautas’s “gimtąjį miestą”. He was born at (Senieji) Trakai.
Low


N15
6:9
“Net paukščiai virš katedros nutilo”. There was no cathedral in pagan Vilnius in 1382 (it was founded in 1387).
Low


N16
19:27
“pirmą kartą per visus šiuos metus”: only months have passed since ch. 3. “savo karius, dabar vilkinčius baltus apsiaustus”: he arrived alone, and only professed knight-brothers wore white.
Med


N17
13:11 vs 13:17; 13:25
The maid’s dress is “pilką” and then “ruda lininę” eleven sentences later. The maid lies “nusukusi veidą į sieną”, yet Vytautas looks “į jas” (her eyes).
Low


N18
12:13
The sleeping draught is called “mirtina dovana”. A lethal sleeping draught is a contradiction, and it is never used (C5).
Low


N19
ch. 2, 6, 9
Kęstutis’s rusted sword, the big plant of ch. 2, disappears: it is never mentioned at the gate, at the arrest or at Krėva. Its metal also changes: “Žalvaris jaučia pavojų” (2:51), “ryjant sidabrinį blizgesį” (2:75), against iron rust.
Med


N20
3 → 11
Birutė is at Trakai in ch. 3 and on the Palanga shore (about 300 km) in ch. 11, days later, while Jogaila holds her husband. The journey is never accounted for.
Med


N21
9:29
Birutė appears to the dying Kęstutis. He carries no amber anchor, so under magic_rules.md §3.4 her range is line of sight. Attribute it to the Amber Queen (a Force) or to Giltinė, not to Kalba.
Med


N22
8:5 vs 14:17
The White Silence sits over Krėva (8:5). Under magic_rules.md §9 it smothers Wind, so Birutė’s Vėjopatis fog should fail or cost double. The text does not address this.
Med


N23
3:61–63
A “tau” working means the caster pays (magic_rules.md §3.1), but the only cost shown (a burn scar) lands on Vytautas, the recipient.
Med


N24
15:21, 15:33, 15:39
The swamp invocation is called “Senovės Sutartis” three times. Under magic_rules.md it is the Five-Voice invocation, and the Sutartis is the ch. 3 binding.
Low


N25
27:15
“jos Gyvybės Versmės palaiminimas”: Life Spring is the Water healing boon, not a self-sacrifice.
Low


N26
27:13
The pebble is missing at the moment of transformation. cosmology.md §3.4 says the Queen now acts only through amber Birutė touched, so the touch Vytautas feels in Vilnius should come through the pebble.
Med


N27
23:25 vs 22:9
“„Geležis dega,“ — prisiminė jis inžinieriaus žodžius”: the engineer never said it (22:9 says “Geležis ir siera … nugali akmenį ir medį”). 24:15 then spells the arrow message “Geležis degia”.
Low


N28
20:19
The copy-paste breaks the logic: “bėgančią su tėvu Kęstučiu” and then “Kęstutis stovėjo šalia … jūs abu esate man sūnūs!” Kęstutis is now both a runner and the onlooker.
Med


N29
4:55 vs 6:3/6:5; 5:47 vs 6:25
They arrive “Vėlai vakare” (4:55), but enter the gate “rudens pavakarę” in “popietės oras” (6:3/6:5). Jogaila walks to the “derybų stalo” (5:47), then watches from the top of the Gediminas tower (6:25).
Low


N30
23:15 vs 10:5
“su kuriais Vytis jį matė paskutinį kartą prie Vilniaus vartų”: he last saw his father as a corpse at Krėva (10:5). Resolved: the arrest is at the camp near Trakai, so the gate is the camp gate, and the line no longer appears in ch. 23.
Low


N31
21:25
“Tavo tėvas apsiverstų kape” depends on the ch. 10 burial. If the H4 cremation fix goes in, this line must change with it.
Low


N32
6:15, 12:19, 1:25
Kinship errors beyond C12: “savo dėdėms” (plural; Skirgaila has one uncle present, 6:15). Ona says “tėvo Kęstučio” (D9: uošvio, 12:19). The envoys bring “broliškus sveikinimus” from a nephew to an uncle (1:25).
Low


N33
4:51, 21:25; 14:19, 28:13
D4: “Vyti” is used by the beggar and by Gediminas, not only Birutė and Kęstutis. “Vyties” is a non-existent genitive (Vyčio).
Low


N34
P:17, P:23
From “Romuva” Eglė looks “tiesiai link sostinės Vilniaus akmeninių sienų”, which supports D5’s move to Šventaragis. Jogaila’s captain wears “Gediminaičių stulpais”, the emblem later tied to the Kęstutaičiai (Vytautas, Žygimantas) (verify), so they belong to the wrong house.
Low


N35
P:19
Plant: “po tūkstančio naktų” from August 1382 lands in spring to summer 1385, which is the Krėva Union (14 Aug 1385). It pays off H10 if that scene is added.
Note


N36
ch. 15–17; ch. 19–21
History: the escape route through Masovia (his sister Danutė, Duke Janusz I) is missing. The joint campaign in ch. 20–21 is set in spring, but on the record it was autumn 1383, and the baptism (21 Oct 1383) came after it. The 1383 Order Marshal was Kuno von Hattenstein (verify).
Med


N37
1:5, 1:11
master_chronology.md places the Order and Jogaila besieging Trakai in Jul–Aug 1382. Ch. 1 shows a peaceful harvest feast inside Trakai (this extends H3).
Med


N38
25:19
“atsisېdo” contains an Arabic-script letter (U+06D0). It will break the LuaLaTeX/DejaVu PDF build or render as a box.
Med (build)


N39
24:17
“paties Birutės balsas” is a gender error (pačios).
Low


N40
17:11 vs 17:35/17:39
“masyvi medinė tvirtovė”, then “juodus kryžius ant mūrų sienų” and “sušalusių vokiškų akmenų”.
Low


N41
30:19
The Vorskla prophecy has the cousins “vėl klastos vienas kitą”. Vorskla (1399) was a defeat by Edigu, not kin betrayal, and Skirgaila died in 1397.
Low


N42
12:5; 15:27
Back-to-back repeats: two veil sentences (12:5) and two “ištiesė savo ranką” sentences (15:27).
Low


N43
00
00_pradzia ends “pirmiausia … apie tą, kas nutiko Trakuose”, so in the build it must sit after the prologue (Šventaragis) and immediately before ch. 1.
Note


N44
13:5, 15:3, 28:11; 2:75, 26:27, 26:31
“vito” is not a word (virto). “klausėsi” is misused for “aidėjo / skambės” (“žingsnių, kurie klausėsi koridoriuje”, “tavo vardas klausėsi Europos žemėse”, “baimė klausėsi”).
Low


N45
17:15
“Trakų ir visos Lietuvos kunigaikštį”: Vytautas held no grand-ducal title in 1382.
Low


N46
18:21
His answer to the terms, “Priešingai nei jūs norėtumėte, magistre”, never says yes, yet ch. 19 assumes acceptance.
Low


N47
25:7
Jonas, “senasis Kęstučio ginklanešys”: a Christian name for a pagan duke’s squire in 1383, and his presence in the Order camp is never explained.
Low


N48
15:5
The horse that appears from nowhere (C4) is mourned as his “ištikimu palydovu”, which implies an old horse of his own that a prisoner could not have.
Low


N49
29:25
His double accuses him of acting “kad tavo siela liktų amžinai švaria”: the accusation contradicts itself.
Low


N50
27:5 vs 27:13
Birutė knows the union is “ką tik formaliai pasirašyta”, while in 27:13 Vytautas is still about to sign it.
Low


N51
14:17, 24:17, 25:15
Three “last gifts”: “paskutinė Birutės dovana” (14:17), the wind (24:17), and “galutinė jo motinos dovana” (25:15).
Low


N52
ch. 3 → 29
The scar from ch. 3 appears only once more (15:27). It is absent when he undresses (13:17), is bathed (18:5) and at both baptisms (19, 29), where it should react.
Opp.


N53
3:11, 3:33, 3:81
There are two ambers in ch. 3: Birutė’s large bee-amber (left glowing blue on the floor) and the thumb-sized pebble. The bee-amber is never seen again, and readers may conflate the two.
Low


N54
27:13
“skubotai kylančių naujų bažnyčių pamatų” in Vilnius in 1383–84, before the 1387 baptism.
Low


N55
9:19
Kęstutis was about 85 by tradition (b. c. 1297) and wrestles three young men. Fine for legend, but one line acknowledging his age would help.
Note
