title: Julijona Alšėniškė
text:
Summary
Julijona Alšėniškė (Uliana Olshanska; died 1448) is Vytautas’s second wife, married at Grodno in 1418 (13 November per en.wikipedia; “before Christmas” per VLE), with the Bishop of Włocławek officiating. The widow of the murdered Prince Ivan of Karachev, a clever woman who asks of every suitor whether he knows how to listen, she marries a man who does not hear what she says, and finds it good irony. Book IV makes her the old Grand Duke’s companion and the point-of-view of ch. 10 and 18: the person who sits beside him in the last twelve years and works out that he is listening to something under the floor. Ona was her aunt, and she is the aunt of Jogaila’s later queen, Sophia of Halshany. Not to be confused with Uliana of Tver (Julijona Tverietė), Algirdas’s widow and Jogaila’s mother.

title: Julijona Alšėniškė
text:
Appearance & tells
Thirty in 1418, with a silver band on her hair, a red cloak and a belt of clinking brass buckles. She crosses herself with the right hand out of habit and then, seeing the priest, with the left: the way women learn in two-faith families. At forty-one at Lutsk (1429) she wears a plain dark-blue gown without pearls, “because pearls get in the way when a hand must reach the pot”. Tells: she counts and cannot stop, she reads her husband’s face “like a map”, and she keeps vigil beside the bed.

title: Julijona Alšėniškė
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
To be heard: to marry a man who listens.


Need (internal)
To be loved by a man who is half in another world.


Lie they believe
That marriage to an old man who hears only through water will be a quiet ironic one.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
That a husband who listens to the floor lives with someone who speaks, and that his last letter is “Come back if you can; if you cannot, know that I know” (Book IV ch. 29).

title: Julijona Alšėniškė
text:
Arc by book

Book IV (1418-1430): POV of ch. 10 (Julijona): married in Vilnius, dines with the Karaim captain Elijas, finds Vytautas awake at night counting; Form 7 begins; stages the Lutsk feast and finds she can no longer count (ch. 18); helps him turn the bed against Giltinė (ch. 28); sits at his bedside through the fever and reads him letters (ch. 29, 30).
Book V (1430): asks that no one go down to the vault for three days after his death (ch. 1); chooses the burial place in the Vilnius cathedral beside Ona (ch. 2); mentioned in ch. 4, 7.

title: Julijona Alšėniškė
text:
Power & magic
Tier 0: Orthodox, with no gift and no bargain. Her power is attention. She is one of the few mortals who realises that Vytautas is listening to something other than people, and that the voice she begins to hear at the Lutsk feast counting with her (the Counter) belongs to the same world.

title: Julijona Alšėniškė
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: Uliana (Julijona) Olshanska, daughter of Ivan Olshansky, a leading ally of Vytautas; her first husband was Ivan of Karachev, who according to Posilge and Długosz was murdered so that she could marry Vytautas. After Ona (Anna) died on 31 July 1418, Vytautas married Julijona; because Ona was her aunt the Bishop of Vilnius Piotr Krakowczyk refused to officiate without papal leave, and Jan Kropidło, Bishop of Włocławek, performed the ceremony (at Grodno per VLE; 13 Nov 1418 per en.wikipedia’s Vytautas article, “before Christmas 1418” per VLE and the Uliana article); Pope Martin V granted a dispensation later. The marriage was childless. She died in 1448 (some sources 1449) and was buried at the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra. Her niece Sophia of Halshany became Jogaila’s fourth queen (1422). See Wikipedia.
[Saga invention]: Her age (30 in 1418; the record gives no birth date, and the graph’s 1370 conflicts with the book), her interior life, the voice she hears at Lutsk, and the scenes of the last winter. The Book IV handoff flags the 1370 vs c. 1388 mismatch.

title: Julijona Alšėniškė
text:
Pronunciation
ju-li-JO-na by the standard rule; the lexicon marks it ju-li-jo-NA (/jʊlʲɪjoˈnɐ/), English respelling yoo-lih-yoh-NAH, stress on the last syllable (to be verified). Russian Uliana (oo-LYAH-nuh). [world_rules/pronunciation_lexicon.json]

title: Julijona Alšėniškė
text:
Appearances
Book IV: ch. 9, 10 (POV), 12, 13, 18 (POV), 19, 22, 25, 28, 29, 30 and the afterword. Book V: ch. 1, 2, 4, 7. Another page needs care: the Julijona of the persona folder Julijona_Tveriete is Algirdas’s wife, Uliana of Tver, who is not given a wiki page.

title: Jogaila
text:
Summary
Jogaila (c. 1362 - 1 June 1434), baptised Władysław, is the nephew who kills Kęstutis, the cousin who spends fifty years half-fearing Vytautas, and the king who founds a dynasty. When the reader first meets him in Book I he is a young, anxious Grand Duke living in his father’s shadow, convinced that Lithuania must become Christian and Western to survive and that betrayal is a higher form of loyalty to the future. He is the Shadow-Seller’s first and longest-lasting customer. In the saga he is the mortal antagonist of Book I (with Skirgaila as his hands) and the man whose baptism ends the Silent Pact.

title: Jogaila
text:
Appearance & tells
Slender and frail-looking but restless, with dark intelligent eyes that never settle. He wears fine velvets and silks in the Western style against his cousins’ furs and leather, and is clean-shaven where the pagan dukes keep beards. Tells: he cannot look at Kęstutis’s silver wolf (Book I ch. 26; Book III ch. 20, where it costs him “everything he has” to hold Vytautas’s eyes); a crushing pressure on his chest in sacred groves; crows that follow him; a court burtininkas who has never cast him a bad lot. By the end, an old man with spectacles in his hand, looking at the floor in front of his feet at Vytautas’s funeral (Book V ch. 2).

title: Jogaila
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
The Lithuanian throne and a Western dynasty: to unite Lithuania and Poland into a power rivalling the Holy Roman Empire, and to keep the Order from finishing Lithuania.


Need (internal)
To trust the one man he cannot buy: to stop seeing Krėva everywhere.


Lie they believe
That baptism and the Polish crown are a cheap price: that betrayal is only a higher loyalty to the future.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
What a bargain with the Shadow-Seller really buys: a line that inherits the crown and loses the land. He half-learns it in his old age, outliving Vytautas still guilty (Book IV; Book V ch. 12).

title: Jogaila
text:
Arc by book

Book I (1377-87), antagonist: inherits the throne (1377); signs the secret Treaty of Dovydiškės with the Order (31 May 1380); is caught and freed by Kęstutis in autumn 1381 (the “mercy” that will pay off at Krėva); retakes Vilnius on 12 June 1382; seizes Kęstutis and Vytautas at his camp near Trakai (early August 1382); is haunted by Krėva (ch. 26); signs the Union of Krėva (14 Aug 1385) and is baptised, married and crowned in Kraków (1386); puts out the Šventaragis flame (1387).
Book II: the distant king; makes Ostrów (4 Aug 1392) with Vytautas (ch. 10); Jadwiga dies (ch. 21).
Book III: the reconciliation: Vilnius-Radom (1401, ch. 3), the Brest council (ch. 13), and at Grunwald beside Vytautas (ch. 18-24).
Book IV: at Lutsk (1429) he is the one who offers and then withdraws the crown (ch. 18, 19, 24, 26); outlives Vytautas.
Book V: dies at Gródek, 1 June 1434, after hearing a nightingale (ch. 12).
Book VI: seen as a boy, taught by Uliana at six to hide what he wants (ch. 15), and as Algirdas’s chosen heir at fifteen (ch. 27, 28).

title: Jogaila
text:
Power & magic
Tier 0 (Paprastas): no gift. His power is bought: the 1380 bargain with the Shadow-Seller is “the easy way” of the trap, and its price is that his line inherits the crown and loses the land (Sandėris). He holds the golden chain sent as a “gift” with the 1382 envoys. Henė’s stone for him is the last he holds in Book V. His ambition feeds the Gold-Glutton and draws the White Silence. Visible costs: four wives and sons only from the last; the grove pressure; the crows. The Root-Mother regards him as a tumour in her side.

title: Jogaila
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: Born c. 1362 (Tęgowski 1999, the post-1990 consensus; the older view is c. 1352), Grand Duke of Lithuania from 1377 (co-ruling with Kęstutis), baptised Władysław in Kraków on 15 Feb 1386, married Jadwiga on 18 Feb and crowned King of Poland on 4 Mar 1386; ruler of Lithuania until 1392, then overlord of Vytautas. He signed the Treaty of Dovydiškės with the Order on 31 May 1380, regained Vilnius on 12 June 1382, when Hanul and the townspeople handed him the city while Kęstutis was away fighting Kaributas, and had Kęstutis and Vytautas seized on 3 Aug 1382 at his camp near Trakai; Kęstutis was found dead at Krėva on 15 Aug (the official story: suicide). Union of Krėva (14 Aug 1385); baptism of Lithuania (1387); Ostrów (1392); Grunwald (15 Jul 1410); Horodło (1413); Lutsk (1429). Wives: Jadwiga (d. 1399), Anna of Celje (d. 1416), Elżbieta Granowska (d. 1420), Sophia of Halshany (m. 1422), mother of Władysław III and Casimir IV. Died 1 Jun 1434 at Gródek (Horodok) near Lviv. See Wikipedia.
[Saga invention]: The Shadow-Seller’s bargain and the golden chain used on Kęstutis; the strangulation (the record gives murder by strangulation as one side of a disagreement, suicide as the official story); the crows and the grove pressure; his inability to look at the silver wolf; the court burtininkas. The nightingale at Gródek is a historical anecdote (Długosz). The saga chooses 1362 for his birth; it never states his age except in Book I ch. 5 (four, in 1366).

title: Jogaila
text:
Pronunciation

title: Jadvyga (Jadwiga)
text:
Summary
Jadvyga (Jadwiga of Anjou, 1373/74 - 17 July 1399) is crowned King (rex) of Poland at about ten and marries Jogaila at twelve. In the saga she is the Saint-King: sincere, pious, wise beyond her years, sold into a marriage she believes is a mission from God. She is also the unwilling vessel of the White Silence, a cold Force that gathers where baptisms are bought, and whose touch makes her heal with frost. She dies at twenty-five, days after burying her newborn daughter, and her tomb on Wawel becomes the Force’s anchor in Poland.

title: Jadvyga (Jadwiga)
text:
Appearance & tells
Ethereal and delicate, with reddish-gold hair, dressed in the height of Western fashion with crowns, silks and pearls, and always carrying a small black crucifix. Her tells are the White Silence’s: a cold calm spreads from her in council so that people find it hard to lie; her touch heals but leaves a faint layer of frost; warmth and sound leave her. In Book II ch. 21 there is frost on the sheets in July. Jogaila finds the stone of her tomb frosted in March 1401 (Book III ch. 3).

title: Jadvyga (Jadwiga)
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
To christianise the north and to see Lithuania baptised; to endow schools and the poor; to defend her crown’s rights.


Need (internal)
To be loved as a girl and not only as a crown, and to be allowed to keep her childhood betrothal, Wilhelm of Habsburg.


Lie they believe
That a holy end justifies a political marriage, and that the cold calm she feels is holy.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
Eglė’s dream-warning, which she half-hears: the White Silence will freeze her heart before it saves her soul. Her death in childbirth makes it literal (Book II ch. 21).

title: Jadvyga (Jadwiga)
text:
Arc by book

Book I (1385-87): the offstage prize of the Union of Krėva (ch. 28b, where she is not present); Vytautas and Jogaila’s baptisms and the baptism of Lithuania are bought in her name (ch. 28-29).
Book II (1392-99): the sympathetic crown behind Ostrów (ch. 10, though the record has no mediation by her); POV of ch. 21, Šerkšnas ant Vavelio (22 Jun - 17 Jul 1399): she bears Elżbieta Bonifacja, who dies within weeks, and dies herself. Her warning against the steppe war is saga (ch. 21, 22).
Book III (1401-1411): her frozen tomb keeps Jogaila honest (ch. 3, 13, 18, 24, 27, 30).
Book V: the White Silence’s anchor is felt in Kraków while Žygimantas bargains for Polish overlordship (ch. 6, 12).

title: Jadvyga (Jadwiga)
text:
Power & magic
Tier 5, the White Silence’s unwilling vessel: its touch is granted, not asked. She heals with frost and holy calm (the white touch); calm, fearlessness and the inability to lie follow her into council; at her death her body becomes the Force’s anchor in the Polish heartland. She is its victim, not its servant. In a dream Eglė warns her of the Force; the Amber Queen takes up her grief for the lost betrothed and amber “pearls” appear on the Baltic shore.

title: Jadvyga (Jadwiga)
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: Born 1373 or 1374 (Buda), daughter of Louis I of Hungary and Elizabeth of Bosnia; crowned King of Poland on 16 October 1384, aged about ten. She was betrothed to Wilhelm of Habsburg and gave up the match for the crown. She married Jogaila in Kraków on 18 February 1386 (he was baptised Władysław on 15 February and crowned on 4 March). In 1387 she led the expedition that recovered Red Ruthenia. She refounded the Kraków Academy by bequest (1400) and gave birth to a daughter, Elżbieta Bonifacja, on 22 June 1399; the baby died on 13 July and Jadwiga followed on 17 July 1399. She was canonised in 1997. See Wikipedia.
[Saga invention]: The White Silence as her unwilling anchor; Eglė’s dream-warning; Jadwiga’s warning against the Vorskla campaign (Book II ch. 21, no source); frost on the sheets. The persona notes that there is no record that she mediated Ostrów (1392): Jogaila’s envoy was Henryk of Masovia.

jad-VY-ga (/jɐdˈviːɡɐ/), English respelling yahd-VEE-gah; stress on the second syllable. Polish Jadwiga (yahd-VEE-gah), Latin Hedvig. [world_rules/pronunciation_lexicon.json]

title: Günther von Hohenstein (invented Order brother)
text:
Summary
Günther von Hohenstein is a saga invention in Book VI: a young brother of the Teutonic Order (22 in 1353, about 30 in 1361), fluent in Lithuanian from a Curonian nurse of the Ragnit march, who asks to serve at Ragnit, is the third knight to take Kęstutis at Lake Ublik, carries and translates the prisoner’s meals at Marienburg, and stands at Kaunas in 1362. He is the honest enemy of the Order’s side. He is not the 1381 informant: that was Kuno von Liebenstein.

title: Günther von Hohenstein (invented Order brother)
text:
Appearance & tells
Fair-haired, with a childlike, puzzled face, “the face of people who have not yet worked out what faith costs” (Book VI ch. 14, age 22); about thirty when he takes Kęstutis (ch. 16), where the bewilderment is still on him; he speaks Lithuanian in an old, soft Curonian dialect, so gentle his voice sounds almost womanly (ch. 19). He wears the Order’s white mantle, lowers his sword like a man who has not come to kill, gives his word, and asks to carry the prisoner’s meals himself. Tells: he repeats a sentence a third time; he admires and cannot bear it.

title: Günther von Hohenstein (invented Order brother)
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
To save lives by giving terms: to receive Kęstutis’s surrender and stop the killing.


Need (internal)
To find out whether the crusade is a faith or a ledger.


Lie they believe
That the Order’s cause and its terms are honest; that one honourable enemy can be reconciled to being an enemy.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
That Kęstutis cannot be bought or trusted by any word of his, since he will never say it unless he means it: “He did not swear. I begged.” (Book VI ch. 17).

title: Günther von Hohenstein (invented Order brother)
text:
Arc by book

Book VI (1353-1362): at Kniprode’s feast he sits uneasy among the Order’s guests and says aloud that the heathen duke keeps every word (ch. 14, 1353); takes Kęstutis at Lake Ublik, offers terms and is refused (ch. 16, March 1361); asks to carry the prisoner’s meals and translates between the duke and the Grand Master (ch. 17, Marienburg); lifts Vaidotas out of the ruins at Kaunas and gives his word that women and children in the inner tower will be spared (ch. 19, Easter 1362).

title: Günther von Hohenstein (invented Order brother)
text:
Power & magic
Tier 0. No gift and no bargain: the saga uses him as proof that the Order is made of men and not only of the Iron Saint’s egregore. He is on the Order’s side of the line, and his one act of mercy is to speak Lithuanian.

title: Günther von Hohenstein (invented Order brother)
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: A real Günther von Hohenstein (c. 1310-1380) was komtur of Osterode from 1349 and later of Brandenburg; he is attested only weakly (a Russian archaeology press release) and in any case died before 1381, so he cannot have warned Kęstutis.
[Saga invention]: The young brother, his Lithuanian, his terms offered at Ublik, the meals and translation at Marienburg (Book VI ch. 14, 16, 17, 19). The old canon line that he “warned Kęstutis in 1381” is withdrawn; the afterword of Book VI says so.

title: Günther von Hohenstein (invented Order brother)
text:
Pronunciation
GÜN-ter fon HO-en-štain (/ˈɡʏntɐ fɔn ˈhoːənʃtaɪn/), English respelling GUEN-ter fon HOH-en-shtine; the saga’s Lithuanian form is Günteris fon Hohensteinas. [world_rules/pronunciation_lexicon.json]

Book VI: ch. 14, 16, 17, 19 and the afterword. Not to be confused with Kuno von Liebenstein, the real 1381 informant who appears in Book I ch. 1.

title: Jonas Goštautas
text:
Summary
Jonas Goštautas (d. 1458), the council lord who coordinates the elevation of Casimir in 1440; at the feast of Book V ch. 17 he gives a warm coin to a beggar (event).

title: Jonas Goštautas
text:
Appearance & tells
Book V paints him as heavy-set and full-faced, with a thick chain whose weight “said more than his words” (ch. 3); by 1440 grey, broad-shouldered, riding at the young Casimir’s right (ch. 23); by about 1447 changed “like well-built buildings: without visible marks, but irreversibly” (ch. 26). He stands at windows, leaning on the frame, and smiles with one corner of his mouth. At the 1437 feast he knows every brick of the floor, which came from Danzig via Riga, and the count of the sixteen that broke at the Vilnia ford. Tell: he counts.

title: Jonas Goštautas
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
To make the council lords, not Trakai’s prince, the real government of Lithuania, and to put a child on the throne against Kraków’s will.


Need (internal)
To give something once without counting it.


Lie they believe
That the realm is a ledger and that he who fears gives: “Kas bijo, tas dalija” (ch. 17).


Truth they learn (or refuse)
The warm coin, passed on to a beggar without a glance, silences the Counter for three breaths: not everything is counted (ch. 17).

title: Jonas Goštautas
text:
Arc by book

Book IV (1413): one of the 47 family names read at Horodło (ch. 2).
Book V (1430-1447): the first of the lords at Švitrigaila’s elevation (ch. 3); the soft-spoken ringleader of the Trakai conspiracy of 1432, in a fisherman’s hat that doesn’t suit him (ch. 8); present at the Ašmena night (ch. 9); POV of ch. 17 (Aukso Rijūno Puota, Feb 1437): receives forty-two villages near Ašmena from the Grand Duke, gives the warm coin to a beggar; raises twelve-year-old Casimir as Grand Duke on 29 June 1440 (ch. 23); drafts the privilege of c. 1447 that bars arrest “without trial” (ch. 26).

title: Jonas Goštautas
text:
Power & magic
Tier 0: no gift of his own. He is a man the Gold-Glutton works through: warm coins, “money that warms from someone else”, turn up in a bishop’s chest, in Daugirdas’s sleeve and in his own wife’s purse; the Counter speaks under the floor of every hall. His one act outside the ledger is the coin he gives to the beggar. Records of the family: Goštautai.

title: Jonas Goštautas
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: Captured defending Lutsk in 1431; conspirator of the 1432 coup; voivode of Trakai, then Vilnius voivode and chancellor 1443-58 (sources differ on start years); coordinated the 1440 election of Casimir. VLE calls his part in the 1440 murder uncertain; the killers are recorded as the Czartoryski brothers, Švitrigaila’s partisans.
[Saga invention]: The Counter, the warm coin, the ledger of villages (Book V ch. 17); the harness-mark in ch. 21 is an insinuation, not a claim.

title: Jonas Goštautas
text:
Pronunciation
JO-nas GOŠ-tau-tas (/ˈjoːnɐs ˈɡoʃtɐʊtɐs/), English respelling YOH-nahs GOHSH-tow-tahs; the surname is stressed on the first syllable, -tau- as in “cow”. Polish Jan Gasztołd. [world_rules/pronunciation_lexicon.json]

title: Jonas Goštautas
text:
Appearances
Book IV: ch. 2 (as a family name). Book V: ch. 3, 8, 9, 10, 17 (POV), 21, 23, 26 and the afterword. Continuity: the page’s record has him as Vilnius voivode and chancellor 1443-58; en.wikipedia gives 1443-58 for both, while some sources call him voivode of Trakai in 1440.

title: Gediminas
text:
Summary
Gediminas (c. 1275 - winter 1341/42) is the founder-figure of the dynasty, the Grand Duke who made Vilnius a capital and gave his name to the house of the Gediminids. He never speaks in the main books; he is the father of Algirdas and Kęstutis, the author of the Iron Wolf dream, and the man whose pyre opens the prequel (Book VI ch. 1). His legacy is a realm that was too large for one heir and a bloodline bound to a pact he did not live to hear.

title: Gediminas
text:
Appearance & tells
Gediminas is seen only in memory and legend. In the prequel he burns on his pyre with his horse and hounds (Book VI ch. 1); the boy Kęstutis remembers him through the Krivis’s account of the Iron Wolf dream rather than through any portrait. The saga gives him no features. His signs are objects: the grey skull of the dream-wolf that he ordered carried to the Dykra (1323), and the unanswerable authority of a name that every later Gediminid claims.

title: Gediminas
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
A realm that could not be swallowed by the Order, and a capital on the hill where the Neris meets the Vilnia.


Need (internal)
To leave a succession that would hold (he chose Jaunutis; the family broke it in 1345).


Lie they believe
That a wolf and a dynasty can share one legend without the wolf’s hundred voices tearing at each other.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
The Krivis’s half of the dream, which Lizdeika never told him: the wolf is collared, and its hundred voices are its own sons (Book VI ch. 1).

title: Gediminas
text:
Arc by book

Book VI: opens the prequel at his pyre (winter 1341/42, ch. 1); his chosen heir Jaunutis is deposed in 1345 (ch. 2-3); the Pact of ch. 4 is sworn by his sons in his absence; he lingers in the Iron Wolf’s skull (ch. 5) and in the first Amber Debt (ch. 8).
Book I: the founder whose name the cousins carry (ch. 7, 12, 29).
Books II-V: invoked as the dream behind the iron wolf, the Gediminid blood that wolves may never shed (Book III ch. 15; Book V ch. 5, 13).

title: Gediminas
text:
Power & magic
No tier: in the saga’s system he is a man of the Middle World with a legend attached. The magic is retrospective: the Iron Wolf dream (Šventaragis hunt, 1323) produces the relic, the Iron Wolf’s skull, by which the Iron Wolves later swear. His blood is the blood the Pact forbids his descendants to shed (“no Gediminid blood”). He himself is not bound, because the Pact is sworn four years after he dies.

title: Gediminas
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: Grand Duke of Lithuania c. 1315/16-1341 (born c. 1275, died probably in December 1341; the pyre is sometimes dated 1342). His letters of 1323 to Pope John XXII and the Hanseatic towns offered settlement and mention Vilnius as his seat; he fought the Order for a quarter-century, married his daughter Aldona to the future Casimir III of Poland (1325) and built an alliance web of Ruthenian and Polish marriages. The circumstances of his death are unrecorded or disputed (Order chroniclers tell of a death at the siege of Bayerburg/Veliuona). The Iron Wolf dream and Lizdeika are first told in the 16th-century Bychowiec Chronicle. See VLE.
[Saga invention]: The Iron Wolf’s skull found where the dream-wolf stood (1323); the Krivis’s lost second half of the dream; the funeral pyre of Book VI ch. 1. Whether Gediminas had one wife or several is disputed in the record, and the saga stays neutral.

title: Gediminas
text:
Pronunciation
ge-DI-mi-nas (/ɡʲɛˈdʲɪmʲɪnɐs/), English respelling geh-DIH-mih-nahs. Genitive Gedimino, dative Gediminui. [world_rules/pronunciation_lexicon.json]

title: Gediminas
text:
Appearances
Book VI: ch. 1 (his pyre), 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 13, 15, 23, 26, 29 and the afterword. Book I: ch. 7, 12, 29. Book II: ch. 5, 7, 9, 21. Book III: ch. 8, 9, 15, 18, 20. Book IV: ch. 22, 23. Book V: ch. 5, 8, 11, 13, 18, 20, 21, 22, 24, 28. In the later books he appears only as an ancestor or a name (“the Gediminid’s blood”).

title: The Flame-Keeper (Book V POV)
text:
Summary
Žiežirba, the Flame-Keeper (Book V’s point-of-view character, b. c. 1390), raised in the Trakai vault as the flame’s guard. After the flame goes out in 1430 he wanders with the silver wolf and the cracked pebble; on 12 Dec 1449, the longest night by the drifted calendar, he reaches Palanga and is named at a driftwood fire; he dies in early March 1450 and is cremated on the beach (Book V ch. 29).

title: The Flame-Keeper (Book V POV)
text:
Appearance & tells
Lean and pale from years underground, with smoke-darkened hands and a throat-mark from the wolf-christening (krikštas); he carries the ash-pot, the wolves’ most important office after 1387. After 27 Oct 1430 he is a “keeper without a flame”: the throat-scar, the empty pot, cold skin, and nights in byres (Book V). He wears the silver wolf and carries Birutė’s cracked pebble. His tells follow the quarrel between flame and name: the vault’s cold keeps him from sleeping on the bench Vytautas built; the lightning-fire from Perkūnas’s storm burns, but “keeps no names” (ch. 2). In his last winter, at Palanga, he ages his forty-five sworn years in a single season, weeps for the first time and dies.

title: The Flame-Keeper (Book V POV)
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
To relight the Last Flame after Vytautas’s death, and so to keep the Pact’s wolves alive.


Need (internal)
To let the gods become stories: to stop trying to hold up something a people never knew it had sworn.


Lie they believe
That the flame can be relit if one man is faithful enough; that the Pact belongs to its keepers.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
The Pact cannot be re-sworn by one man, and the people were never asked (Book V ch. 5, 20); the land remembers, and the sea remembers a name the dead flame let go (ch. 29).

title: The Flame-Keeper (Book V POV)
text:
Arc by book

Book II (1390s): a five-year-old pulled from a cold house in an Unbinding hunt at Šermukšniai (ch. 14, winter 1395-96) and taken to the Trakai vault.
Book III (1405-1411): sworn at fifteen in the twelve nights after Kūčios, 1405-06, whispering his true name into the secret flame and taking his skin-name Žiežirba (“Spark”) on the Iron Wolf’s skull (ch. 9); carries the flame out of the vault in a horn lantern across the Vistula bridge and to Grunwald (ch. 15, 20, 21); feeds it again at the vault on his return (ch. 28).
Book IV (1430): the vault’s keeper to the end; Vytautas spends his bought week on him, arranging that the pebble and silver wolf go to him through Pilkoji (ch. 28, 29).
Book V (1430-1450): POV. He sees the flame die as Vytautas dies (ch. 1); carries away Perkūnas’s lightning-fire (ch. 2); learns that the Pact had three parties (ch. 5); takes the silver wolf and pebble from Pilkoji (ch. 7); refuses to light the flame for Žygimantas (ch. 8-10, 18-19), tries to relight the Pact in the cathedral crypt and nothing answers (ch. 20), refuses Henė’s last deal (ch. 24), watches the last žynys die (ch. 27) and Pilkoji lie down in the bog (ch. 28), and is named at Palanga by the Amber Queen through the pebble (ch. 29, 12 Dec 1449). He dies in early March 1450 and is cremated on the beach.

title: The Flame-Keeper (Book V POV)
text:
Power & magic
Granted, not born: the Wolf-Change (Vilkų krikštas, graph tier 3; wolf-change) from the Root-Mother via the Dykra, sworn in December 1405, and Ženklai (signs, tier 2; zenklai). He sits outside the tier ladder: wolves are not casters. Artifacts: Kęstutis’s silver wolf and Birutė’s pebble, both from Pilkoji at Kūčios 1430, and the Šventaragis ember, whose ash he feeds from Kalvis’s remains. A wolf sworn twenty years or more may take wolf shape; after the flame goes out new wolves cannot be made. The cost is that he is the last sworn wolf, a name without a flame.

title: The Flame-Keeper (Book V POV)
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: No such person in the record.
[Saga invention]: All of him. Dates: arrival at Palanga 12 Dec 1449; death early March 1450 (graph: named, dies).

title: The Flame-Keeper (Book V POV)
text:
Pronunciation
Not in the JSON lexicon (the working skin-name is canon D11). Derived from the Lithuanian žiežirba (“spark”): ŽIE-žir-ba (/ˈʒʲiɛʒʲɪrbɐ/), English sound-alike ZHYEH-zhir-bah; stress on the first syllable (to be verified). Skin-name = kailio vardas.

title: The Flame-Keeper (Book V POV)
text:
Appearances
Book II: ch. 14 (Vilkų Medžioklė), 29 and the afterword. Book III: ch. 2, 9 (the Wolves’ Baptism, POV), 15 (the Bridge over the Vistula, POV), 17, 20, 21, 28. Book IV: ch. 1, 3, 16, 17, 22, 25, 27, 28, 29. Book V: the point-of-view character: ch. 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13, 16, 18-22, 24, 27-29 (the others are told by Birutė, Pilkoji, Žygimantas, Casimir). Continuity: born c. 1390 (Book III fact-check: “b. c. 1391; 14 at Kūčios 1405”); Pilkoji must be born c. 1365 to foster him (canon Q13).

title: Elena (Ona’s maid)
text:
Summary
Elena is the young maid of Ona’s household at Krėva who stays behind: a secret follower of the Root-Mother who lies in Vytautas’s bed in his old furs, face to the wall, while he walks out in her dress (Book I ch. 13). The saga names her and gives her an end; the record does neither. She is the Quiet Sacrifice of the book, and the price Vytautas learns to carry: Ona tells him her name and orders him to remember it.

title: Elena (Ona’s maid)
text:
Appearance & tells
Young (“jauna tarnaitė”, ch. 13). At Kęstutis’s funeral she walks among the mourners looking only at the ground, with a dried flax knot, the Root-Mother’s sign, in her sleeve (ch. 12). In the bed she does not move; when Vytautas looks back her eyes hold neither fear nor pity, “only a calm offering”. Her last words are “Go, prince; the roots remember me”.

title: Elena (Ona’s maid)
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
To make the escape work, so that the sacrifice is the seed of a free Lithuania.


Need (internal)
To be remembered.


Lie they believe
That a death for the roots is a seed.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
What she gets: Ona orders Vytautas to remember her name; he does, at the end of a list of the dead he carries (Book II ch. 27).

title: Elena (Ona’s maid)
text:
Arc by book

Book I (autumn 1382): among the mourners at Kęstutis’s pyre (ch. 12); the swap on the eve of Vėlinės (ch. 13); hanged on the gate the next morning on Skirgaila’s order, as Ona tells Vytautas in Masovia (ch. 17).
Book II: the last name on Vytautas’s list of the remembered dead (ch. 27); after the Vorskla Vytautas asks Ona what Elena’s eyes were like, and gets no answer (ch. 29).
Book IV (1418): dying Ona confesses that she has sent silver to Elena’s mother every year, through a man at Ašmena (ch. 9).

title: Elena (Ona’s maid)
text:
Power & magic
Tier 0, with a gesture of faith: a follower of the Root-Mother (“Šaknų Motinos pasekėja”, ch. 13) who has no craft. The wiki graph records a tier-1 užkalbėjimai (charm) in the sign she carries: the dried flax knot. Her willingness is the working.

title: Elena (Ona’s maid)
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: The oldest Lithuanian annals say that Ona persuaded one of her maids to change clothes with Vytautas; the maid stayed in the castle and he walked out (Lithuanian Chronicle). Wigand says he put on Ona’s own clothes; other accounts have him lowered from a window in a basket. The maid’s name (“Elena” or “Alena”) and her execution are a nineteenth-century addition (Narbutt) and not in the primary record.
[Saga invention]: The name Elena, her faith in the Root-Mother, her hanging on the gate and Ona’s yearly silver to her mother (Book IV ch. 9) are saga invention. The persona file and some codex pages once called them historical; the fact-check (Book I item 8) corrected that.

title: Edigu
text:
Summary
Edigu (Idegey, Lithuanian Edigėjus; c. 1352 - 1419), a Manghit emir and beglerbeg of the Golden Horde, is the Antagonist of Book II and the only mortal enemy who beats Vytautas outright. He is the Horde’s cold genius and kingmaker, ruling through khans, whom he uses as puppets, from 1396 to about 1411. His want is to keep any western power, Lithuania or Moscow, off the steppe and to hunt down Tokhtamysh and his line. At the Vorskla (12 Aug 1399) he wins the battle that ends Vytautas’s dream of an eastern empire, and then rides on to ransom Kyiv.

title: Edigu
text:
Appearance & tells
Compact and powerful, a man who lives on a horse; sharp, hawk-like features and a thin moustache; minimal armour of hardened leather and iron rings, built for speed. Book II ch. 24 is told from his point of view: at the river parley he sees “a man drunk on a horizon”, and is not himself drunk. Tells: patience, the habit of using the khan’s voice for his own demands, and a flat, unhurried manner while negotiating the terms of three days’ truce that he has no intention of keeping.

title: Edigu
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
Steppe mastery: to keep Lithuania and Moscow out of the Horde’s lands, to hunt Tokhtamysh, and to rule through any khan he chooses.


Need (internal)
To admit what he serves: whether he knows he feeds the Steppe-Hunger is left open by the canon.


Lie they believe
That cold calculation is immune to the Hunger that eats other men’s hubris.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
The Force feeds through his victory regardless: at the Vorskla the Steppe-Hunger takes its harvest of princes (Book II ch. 26).

title: Edigu
text:
Arc by book

Book II (1399): a distant force in ch. 15 and 22; POV of ch. 24 (Edigu): the river parley on the Vorskla, where he turns Vytautas’s demand that the khan call him father round and answers it with the same demand; wins the battle on 12 Aug (ch. 26) with the feigned retreat and reserves from behind; rides on to Kyiv and to Lutsk (ch. 28).
Book III (1408): his raid round Moscow in December 1408 shadows Vytautas’s Ugra negotiations (ch. 10); his name returns as the creditor paid with icon-covers stripped from Kyiv’s Pechersk (ch. 2, 25) and as the Vorskla’s feigned-retreat trick that Vytautas cannot be sure he is not seeing again at Grunwald (ch. 19).
Book IV (c. 1419): killed in the steppe wars; the Black Sea forts hold what Vytautas gained (ch. 11).

title: Edigu
text:
Power & magic
Tier 0: no craft. His patron is the Steppe-Hunger (Erdene-Chuluu), which feeds on the hubris of horizon-kings; it feeds through his victory at the Vorskla. The canon fixes only that the Force feeds there; whether Edigu serves it knowingly is an open author’s choice. He has the Golden Horde as his instrument (“the power behind the khans”, 1396-1411).

title: Edigu
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: Born c. 1352 (a Manghit mirza), killed in 1419 or 1420, most likely by a son of Tokhtamysh (en.wikipedia). The effective ruler of the Golden Horde under Temür Qutlugh from 1396 and the power behind the khans until about 1411; legendary ancestor of the Nogai Horde. With Temür Qutlugh he defeated Vytautas, Tokhtamysh and the Ruthenian-Polish coalition at the Vorskla River on 12 Aug 1399 (en.wikipedia body says 5 Aug); about 20 princes, among them Andrius of Polotsk, Dmitrijus of Bryansk and Spytko II of Melsztyn, were killed (VLE says 12). The river meeting, in which Edigu demanded the obedience owed to an elder, is the Rus’/Polish tradition. He burned the suburbs of Moscow in December 1408 and ransomed Kyiv in 1399. See Wikipedia.
[Saga invention]: His point-of-view chapter and tactics scene (Book II ch. 24; the tactics are saga, the Vorskla’s shape is not); the Steppe-Hunger’s patronage; the final exchange on the river is attested in outline only.

title: Edigu
text:
Pronunciation
Not in the JSON lexicon; the pronunciation guide gives the Lithuanian form Edigėjus (e-di-GĖ-jus, /ɛdʲɪˈɡʲeːjʊs/), English respelling eh-dih-GAY-yoos (stress to be verified); the Tatar Idegäy is closer to ee-deh-GAY. The saga’s “Edigu” is the English-scholarly spelling.

title: Edigu
text:
Appearances
Book II: ch. 15, 22, 24 (POV), 25, 26, 28 and the afterword. Book III: ch. 2, 10, 19, 25. Book IV: ch. 11 (the Black Sea forts; his death noted).

title: Danutė
text:
Summary
Danutė (baptised Anna, c. 1358 - 1448) is the daughter of Kęstutis and sister of Vytautas, wife since c. 1373 of Janusz I of Masovia. She is the Safe Harbour of Book I: the one Kęstutaitis who married into Christendom early and lived quietly. When Vytautas, shaved, starving and still wearing a maid’s dress, reaches Warsaw in late 1382, she takes him in without a word of mockery and sends him on to Prussia with Janusz’s guides.

title: Danutė
text:
Appearance & tells
Book I ch. 17 shows her only in action: she comes down the stairs and embraces her brother three times until he stops shaking, has the maid’s dress washed and mended because he will not let it be thrown away, and for several days speaks to him slowly and loudly. Only on the third day does he understand why: the cost of the Five Voices had not left him with the fog. Book VI ch. 16 gives a glimpse of her as a three-year-old clinging to her mother’s skirt in the spring of 1361. Her visible sign in the saga’s world is a candle lit in church and a splinter lit at home.

title: Danutė
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
To keep her brother alive and her husband’s small duchy safe among three larger neighbours.


Need (internal)
To be allowed one honest conversation with her blood without it being used.


Lie they believe
That she can serve both altars without choosing.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
That a house in Christendom is also a hiding place (Book I ch. 17).

title: Danutė
text:
Arc by book

Book VI (1361): a child in her mother’s arms at the Kęstutis-Birutė household (ch. 16).
Book I (late 1382): shelters Vytautas in Warsaw, tells nothing, and sends him to Prussia (ch. 17).
Books II-IV: a background ally in Masovia, whose family links the three cousins’ houses: her sister-in-law Aleksandra Algirdaitė marries Siemowit IV in 1387.

title: Danutė
text:
Power & magic
Tier 0 as written. Open question: the amber gift runs down the maternal line, and as Birutė’s daughter she could carry a latent gift that never woke or that the Church in Warsaw taught her to fear. The saga does not resolve it; she is shown as a woman whose faith is a candle in church and a splinter at home.

title: Danutė
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: Danutė (baptised Anna; the saga keeps only “Danutė” to avoid confusion with Vytautas’s wife Ona/Anna), born c. 1358, married c. 1373 Janusz I of Masovia (Warsaw, Czersk) and died in 1448 (dates approximate; see VLE). Her godfather was the Order komtur Kuno von Liebenstein, who in August 1381 warned Kęstutis of the Treaty of Dovydiškės (en.wikipedia, after Ivinskis 1978). After his escape from Krėva in autumn 1382 Vytautas went to Janusz and Danutė in Masovia before turning to the Order (Wigand; en.wikipedia).
[Saga invention]: The three embraces, the mended dress, the slow loud speech, the guides to Prussia (Book I ch. 17), and the splinter lit at home. The record says only that he stayed with Janusz; the saga adds her sympathy and her sharp ear for the hidden cost.

title: Birutė
text:
Summary
Birutė of Palanga, Kęstutis’s wife by tradition (c. 1350), mother of Vytautas; in the saga the Amber Queen’s last vessel (D1).

title: Birutė
text:
Appearance & tells
In youth she is hauntingly beautiful, with long white-blonde hair; at 27, in 1361, it is still “pale as milk” (Book VI ch. 16). In maturity she has what the persona file calls a terrible grace. Her tells follow her stages: before 1382 the shore-fire woman who smells of salt and smoke; after the widowing of August 1382 her eyes go sea-dark; after the Krėva fog (autumn 1382) her voice fails, and later costs dim her sight. From 1384 she is a statue, the amber kneeling woman on the Palanga shore, and a voice in surf that reaches the world only through amber she once touched. She calls her son “Vyti”.

title: Birutė
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth



Want (external)
To keep the Palanga flame and the letter of her vow, then to see her son live to inherit his father’s strength without his father’s fate.


Need (internal)
To let the debt of her surety fall due, all at once, rather than be paid in pieces by someone else.


Lie they believe
That the letter of a vow can protect its spirit: she let herself be ‘taken’ so that she never gave herself (Book VI ch. 11).


Truth they learn (or refuse)
The spirit of the vow was written down and does come due. She pays his whole remaining surety in July 1384 and becomes the last vessel of the Amber Queen (Book I ch. 27).

title: Birutė
text:
Arc by book

Book VI (c. 1350-1377): the Palanga vaidilutė refuses Kęstutis, is “taken” in a staged abduction (ch. 10, 11); bears Vytautas and holds the shears at bay with “not yet” (ch. 12); gives Kęstutis an amber bead for the Marienburg cell, where it goes cold (ch. 16, 17); presides at the Pact’s first payments and watches Algirdas’s pyre (ch. 23, 29 POV).
Book I (1382-84): binds Vytautas in the Sutartis and stands surety for him (ch. 3); is widowed, thrown into the Bug and refused by the sea thrice (ch. 11); covers his Krėva escape with fog at the cost of her voice (ch. 14, via the pebble); walks into the water at Palanga and leaves the statue (ch. 27). The frame narration of 00_pradzia is her post-1384 voice.
Books II-III: felt only through the pebble: it warms in Vytautas’s palm and cools when he breaks an oath (Book II ch. 2; Book III ch. 25).
Book IV: the statue is the last pagan object on the Samogitian coast; a priest asks to remove it and the fishwives refuse (ch. 8); Sofija wears her amber bead in Moscow (ch. 15).
Book V: the frame narrator; names the keeper at the driftwood fire and sinks with the statue (ch. 1, 5, 10, 20, 29).

title: Birutė
text:
Power & magic
Tier 4 Gintaro šventikė (all five elements, Senovės Kalba, Gintarystė), born to the gift down the Palanga maternal line. Canon D1 makes her a vessel of the Amber Queen: she hears the Queen (ch. 3), is changed by widowhood (ch. 11, the eyes go sea-dark) and is fully transformed at Palanga (ch. 27). Her signature workings are the Sutartis over Vytautas and the pebble, a bead of her blood-anchored amber through which she acts at a distance. She pays part of every price he pays: the fog costs her voice, later costs take her sight, and in 1384 she settles the whole surety at once. After 1384 she can act only through amber she has touched, which is why moving the statue kills at sea.

title: Birutė
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: Death date unknown. Wigand (c. 1394): Jogaila had her drowned (en.wikipedia: at Brest, with relatives Vidimantas and Butrimas, likely in answer to Vytautas’s escape; VLE: Kęstutis had sent her there in 1382). Vytautas’s 1390 letter accuses Jogaila of killing both parents; at Constance (1416) delegates said she lived long and died naturally; the Palanga burial first appears in Stryjkowski (1582). The drowning is Wigand’s, not Długosz’s.
[Saga invention]: The drowning attempt at Brest in the Bug, which she survives, then Palanga; her mortal end in July 1384 (Book I ch. 27) and her life as the Amber Queen; Marquard’s insult to her after Raciąż (1404).

title: Birutė
text:
Pronunciation
bi-RU-tė (/bʲɪˈrʊtʲeː/), English respelling bih-ROO-tay; stress on the second syllable. The instrumental Birutè is end-stressed (to be verified); elsewhere the stress stays on -RU-. Birutės kalnas (Birutė’s Hill at Palanga): bi-RU-tės KAL-nas, bih-ROO-tays KAHL-nahs. [world_rules/pronunciation_lexicon.json]

title: Birutė
text:
Appearances
Book VI: ch. 10 (POV), 11, 12 (POV), 13, 16, 21, 23, 28, 29 (POV), 30. Book I: ch. 3 (the Sutartis), 8, 9, 11 (widowed, drowning at Brest), 14 (the fog), 18, 20, 24, 25, 27 (the Amber Sacrifice), 31, 32 and the frame piece 00_pradzia. Book II: ch. 1, 2, 4, 6, 8. Book III: ch. 10, 14, 20, 21, 25. Book IV: ch. 5, 8 (the statue), 15, 27. Book V: frame narrator throughout (ch. 1, 5, 10, 20, 29). Continuity: her mortal end is July 1384 (Book I ch. 27), but the record has no date, which is why the afterwords call it invention; the Book IV ch. 5 complaint cites Wigand’s Brest drowning to the council at Constance.

title: V · Vilko Palikimas
text:
Premise
On the night Vytautas dies, the Last Flame goes out in the Trakai vault, and the young wolf who guarded it is left with cold ash, a cracked amber pebble and a silver wolf no one will honour. He wants to light it again. The heirs of the two cousins go to war, Žygimantas wants the keeper as a tyrant’s hound, the Shadow-Seller has nothing left to sell, and a century of unfed dead rise at Pabaiskas.

title: V · Vilko Palikimas
section: Protagonist arc (form at start → form at end)
text:
Protagonist arc (form at start → form at end)
Sargas be Ugnies (Keeper without a Flame) → Ieškotojas (the Seeker) → Žmogus (a Man): his true name is spoken back to him by a living fire at Palanga in 1450, he ages his sworn years in one winter, dies and is burned. Want: relight the flame. Lie: “one faithful man can hold the gods to the land”. Truth: the Pact was the people’s, and its last keeping is memory.

title: V · Vilko Palikimas
text:
Antagonists & outcomes

Žygimantas Kęstutaitis: tyrant, with Henė whispering; murdered at Trakai on 20 Mar 1440.
Švitrigaila: crushed at Pabaiskas; dies in Volhynia in 1452.
The Unbinding (the unfed dead): burned over a winter at the cost of the last wolves.
Henė: unmasked with empty hands in ch. 24, refused.

title: V · Vilko Palikimas
text:
Threads advanced (see books/series_arc.md)
All threads close. A: the Pact is folklore (ch. 27). B: the lightning-fire is not the Gediminid flame; the relighting fails because one man cannot re-swear a people’s oath (ch. 20). C: the statue dims in 1445 and is taken by the sea in 1450. D: stones one, then none. G: the last wolf; I: Sofija’s son rules Moscow; J: the four Forces become institutions.

title: V · Vilko Palikimas
section: Hands on to the next book
text:
Hands on to the next book
The series ends. For readers going on to Book VI, the last žynys has sung the Pact wrong and the keeper has seen the true oath in the pebble; the prequel shows the oath itself.

title: III · Žaliasis Miškas
text:
Premise
After the Vorskla Vytautas turns west with nothing but the forest. Samogitia, sold by every treaty, rises in 1401 and 1409 under Galminas, and the Order under Ulrich prepares its last great crusade. To win, Vytautas must ally with Jogaila, the cousin whose men strangled his father, and refuse Henė’s shortcut. On the eve of Grunwald he carries the Last Flame in a lantern and swears a thunder-oath that binds Perkūnas. The Iron Saint breaks; Samogitia comes back only for two men’s lifetimes.

title: III · Žaliasis Miškas
section: Protagonist arc (form at start → form at end)
text:
Protagonist arc (form at start → form at end)
From the broken Form 5 to Geležinis Vilkas (plain armour, Kęstutis’s recovered sword, the wolves at his back, the lantern flame) in ch. 2. It ends still in Form 6, hollowed by Thorn, with the first tell of Form 7 (half-deafness from the Five-Voice) in ch. 28. Want: to break the Order. Lie: “I can do it alone”. Truth: victory needs the cousin he hates. Cost: pride, Samogitian blood, the Root-Mother’s last strength, Galminas.

title: III · Žaliasis Miškas
text:
Antagonists & outcomes

Ulrich von Jungingen (Grand Master 1407), the Iron Saint on the field: killed at Grunwald; the Iron Saint breaks and the Riders of the Reise scream.
Secondary: Order commanders in Samogitia; Heinrich von Plauen, who holds Marienburg and signs Thorn; the White Silence at Jadwiga’s tomb, which holds.
Sigismund, allied with the Order in 1409–10. Henė advises both sides, offers a blood-price shortcut (ch. 8) and is refused.

title: III · Žaliasis Miškas
text:
Threads advanced (see books/series_arc.md)

B: the flame leaves the vault once, in the lantern (ch. 15, 17). E: Perkūnas rewards a kept oath. F: the Root-Mother spends her last great strength; Galminas becomes a grove (ch. 19, 23). G: Pilkoji sworn (1404), the boy named into the flame (1405–06), vanguard at Grunwald. I: Sofija’s Moscow as a rival (Ugra). J: the Iron Saint broken.
The pebble warms when the oath is kept. Silent Pact ended; Unbinding holds at 3.

title: III · Žaliasis Miškas
section: Hands on to the next book
text:
Hands on to the next book
Samogitia Lithuanian only for the lifetimes of Jogaila and Vytautas (it becomes permanent at Melno, 1422), pagan and waiting for the priests. The Hidden Groves are spent; Eglė begins to fade; the Order is beaten but alive; Henė keeps two stones; and a young secretary, Zbigniew Oleśnicki, has decided that ink will settle Lithuania.

title: I · Vilko Tremtis
text:
Premise
The last pagan realm in Europe is held by a Silent Pact its rulers have half forgotten. Jogaila, bought by the Shadow-Seller, and his brother Skirgaila seize their uncle Kęstutis and strangle him in the dungeon of Krėva. A Gediminid has shed Gediminid blood, and the Pact’s second clause breaks. His son has one chance to live.

title: I · Vilko Tremtis
section: Protagonist arc (form at start → form at end)
text:
Protagonist arc (form at start → form at end)
Vytautas starts as Sūnus (the Son), believing “honour and blood will keep us safe”. He passes through the Survivor (shaved, in a maid’s dress, silent; ch. 10–17) and the Tool (the Order’s sword and white cloak; ch. 18–22) and ends as the Traitor of Traitors, who burns his allies’ castles in July 1384 and lights the secret flame on the night of the 1387 baptism. The lie he adopts is “only cunning survives”. The truth he glimpses is that even the Wolf needs a pack. He pays in honour, his father, his gods (a false baptism that kills the amber), his mother’s surety and Trakai itself.

title: I · Vilko Tremtis
text:
Antagonists & outcomes

Skirgaila (the hands) with Jogaila (the will): mortal. Partial victory for Vytautas, then a deal; Skirgaila has held Trakai since 1382, so the villain keeps the land and lights the fuse of Book II.
Šešėlių Pardavėjas (Henė): mythic. Goes from Hanulas to Jogaila’s jester to Skirgaila’s stone; ends the book juggling three black stones.
Zöllner and the Teutonic Order (behind them the Iron Saint): secondary. Defeated by betrayal in July 1384. The 1381 warning of Dovydiškės came, in the record, from the komtur Kuno von Liebenstein (not from the invented Hohenstein of Book VI).

title: I · Vilko Tremtis
text:
Threads advanced (see books/series_arc.md)

A, Pact: clause 2 broken (Krėva); formally ended when the Šventaragis flame is put out (Feb–Mar 1387).
B, Last Flame: the Sutartis and flame promise (ch. 3); the flame lit in secret at the end of ch. 29.
C, Amber Queen: Birutė becomes the Queen (1384); the kneeling amber statue.
D, Shadow-Seller: three stones; E: Perkūnas’s claim on Vytautas (ch. 10); F: Eglė’s price (ch. 16).
G, Iron Wolves: seven of the hidden nine massacred in the tents at Jogaila’s camp near Trakai (ch. 7), re-formed under Jonas (ch. 25).
H, blood-debt: Krėva and the truce in the ashes; I: Ona held by the Order (1383–84); J: the Iron Saint and the White Silence (Krėva Union).

title: I · Vilko Tremtis
section: Hands on to the next book
text:
Hands on to the next book
A twice-baptised Vytautas (Wigand 1383, Aleksandras 1386) with Grodno and no father’s land, no surety, and a flame he cannot let die; a land whose spirits begin to go feral. Skirgaila rules Trakai (since 1382) and is Jogaila’s governor of Lithuania (from 13 Mar 1386); Book II opens on him there in spring 1387.

title: Henė’s three black stones
text:
Description
Three black, worn, round stones “like river pebbles, but not from a river” (Book V ch. 12). Henė juggles them in every book. Two fly true; the third always wobbles. When he is working, the bells on his cap are silent and the stones make no sound.

title: Henė’s three black stones
text:
Power
Each stone is one cousin’s bargain, tied to Jogaila, Skirgaila and Vytautas (graph: hene_stones). A stone shows that a deal is in progress; its fall marks the collection of that bargain (power_systems.md §5; magic_rules.md §8).

title: Henė’s three black stones
text:
Rule & cost
Henė keeps bargains to the letter and “never lies; I only write it down”. Each stone falls when its cousin’s deal is collected: Skirgaila’s in 1397, Vytautas’s in 1430 and Jogaila’s in 1434. Once his hands are empty, Henė has no leverage left and unmasks (Book V).

title: Henė’s three black stones
text:
Origin
[Saga] Made in 1380 (graph), the year of Dovydiškės. The first deal is with Jogaila at Krėva in 1382, “the easy way”: the crown for his line, the land lost.

title: Henė’s three black stones
text:
Arc across the books

Three, 1385-1397. First seen juggled at the Krėva union (Book I ch. 28b) and in the Trakai hall before Skirgaila (I ch. 30, with an offer of “ten good years”). At Ostrów, 1392, he holds all three while kneeling to Vytautas (II ch. 10).
Two, 11 Jan 1397. Skirgaila’s stone falls through the floor at Kyiv “like falling into water” (II ch. 16). Two are shown through Books III-IV.
One, 27-28 Oct 1430. Vytautas’s stone falls in the death chamber (IV ch. 29). Henė throws it into Lake Galvė at dawn on 28 Oct: no splash, a film of ice parts and closes (IV ch. 30).
None, 1 Jun 1434. Jogaila’s stone drops on the floor of his deathbed room and does not roll; it is an ordinary river pebble. After 52 years Henė’s hands are empty (V ch. 12). He keeps them empty in V ch. 19, 24, 26 and 30.

Graph: Henė holds the stones 1380-1434 (the hene_stones progression runs 3, 2 in 1397, 1 in Oct 1430, 0 on 1 Jun 1434); no stones after 1434.

title: Motinos gintaras (Birutė’s pebble)
text:
Description
A pea-sized lump of cloudy, honey-coloured amber from the Palanga shore, worn smooth by decades of carrying. In Book V it has a hairline crack through the middle, “visible only from one angle” (V ch. 7). It hangs on a leather thong against the chest.

title: Motinos gintaras (Birutė’s pebble)
text:
Power
An anchor between the bearer and Birutė (graph: anchors her 1382-1384). Held to the ear it carries the sea and, for those she chooses, her voice (Book III ch. 14, Book V ch. 29). It lets an ungifted bearer use the Five-Voice (power_systems.md §4) and acts as the reader’s moral barometer: warm when he tells the truth, cold when he lies to himself or the oath is false. Amber from her shore also remembers what it witnessed (V seam pass, rule 2).

title: Motinos gintaras (Birutė’s pebble)
text:
Rule & cost
It answers to truth, not belief (magic_rules.md §5.4). Consecrated stone deafens it, so costs double near Order castles and cathedrals (Book I ch. 19; Book V ch. 20). The bond needs amber, the binder’s blood, the bound person’s true name and a promise exchanged both ways (Book I ch. 3).

title: Motinos gintaras (Birutė’s pebble)
text:
Origin
Given by Birutė to Vytautas in Trakai with her blood on it, his true name spoken once and the pledge “Jo skola, mano skola” (Book I ch. 3, 1382).

title: Motinos gintaras (Birutė’s pebble)
text:
Arc across the books

Vytautas, 1382-1430. Warm (I ch. 3), a faint light in the Krėva cell (I ch. 8), dead after the false baptism at Tepliava, 21 Oct 1383 (I ch. 19), hot at the Marienwerder burning (I ch. 23-24), glowing in 1387 (I ch. 29). Neither warm nor cold at the Black Sea (II ch. 17), cold after the Vorskla, 1399 (II ch. 20), a single tremor in 1405 (III ch. 8), warm at the Grunwald oath (III ch. 17), burning at the lightning (III ch. 20). It cracks “like thin ice” at his death, 27 Oct 1430 (IV ch. 29).
Pilkoji, 27 Oct-24 Dec 1430. She takes it from his chest, as he wished (IV ch. 28).
The Flame-Keeper (Žiežirba), Kūčios 1430-1450. Handed over cold and cracked (V ch. 7; graph: Pilkoji 1430, the keeper from 1431). He first looks through the crack at Rasos, June 1432 (V ch. 9). It stays dead on the flame in the crypt (V ch. 20). Birutė’s voice through it ends at his name (V ch. 29). It burns with him at Palanga, March 1450.

title: The Lutsk crown (turned to leaves)
text:
Description
Never a real crown. For the Saga it is a gold crown in a gold-painted oak chest, carried north from Buda in summer 1430. When the chest is opened at the Noteć ford it holds dry leaves. The goldsmith’s apprentice Pál (19) swears he held real gold (Book IV ch. 21, 23).

title: The Lutsk crown (turned to leaves)
text:
Power
None, except as a lure. It is the instrument of Henė’s last bargain at Vytautas’s vault: the crown for the flame (Book IV ch. 22). Vytautas refuses and the gold turns to leaves, as Henė puts it: “my most honest bargain, and I lost it” (IV ch. 23).

title: The Lutsk crown (turned to leaves)
text:
Rule & cost
Henė never lies; the word “no” simply turns the gold to leaves (IV ch. 30: “žodis atsakė ne ir auksas virto lapais”). The price of the refusal is the crown itself.

title: The Lutsk crown (turned to leaves)
text:
Origin
[Record] The crown plan comes from the Congress of Lutsk, Jan 1429, where Sigismund of Luxembourg offered Vytautas a royal crown. A coronation was set for 15 Aug 1430, then 8 Sep, then moved by Vytautas to 29 Sep. Sigismund’s courtiers Baptista Cigala and Sigismund Roth were robbed on the Neumark or Greater Poland border by Jan Czarnkowski’s guards before 19 Aug 1430, and the crown embassy waited at Frankfurt (Oder) and turned back. The crown was never seized: “crown seized” is a later legend (Book IV hand-off, fact-check item 14).

title: The Lutsk crown (turned to leaves)
text:
Arc across the books

15 Aug 1430. On the road in the chest (Book IV ch. 21); Henė makes his offer in the vault the same night (ch. 22).
Late Aug 1430. The chest is opened at the Noteć ford before Czarnkowski and Oleśnicki’s envoy Baltramiejus Rogala (ch. 23).
Oct 1430. Vytautas postpones the coronation, falls on the Trakai road and dies uncrowned (ch. 24-29).
1 Nov 1430. An old woman tells it as a tale: he died with a crown, “only an invisible one” (ch. 30). Graph: Henė holds it in 1430 (the gold-painted chest, an illusion), until the “no” turns it to leaves.

title: Šerno kalavijas (Kęstutis’s sword)
text:
Description
A broad sword with a boar’s head on the pommel, the sword that hung over the Trakai hall stairs (Book III ch. 2). Beneath the grip is a perkūnėlis, a thunder-cross burned into the metal by Kęstutis himself.

title: Šerno kalavijas (Kęstutis’s sword)
text:
Power
A warded oath-blade. While clean, the perkūnėlis keeps the bearer’s word under Perkūnas’s eye. In Book III it is the instrument of Vytautas’s oath at Grunwald (III ch. 17). It “recognises” its bearer each morning (Skirgaila, Book II ch. 1, 11).

title: Šerno kalavijas (Kęstutis’s sword)
text:
Rule & cost
Rust spreads along the blade with every oath broken in the family: Dovydiškės, Skirgaila’s safe-conduct, Vytautas’s false baptism, the Order oath, Lyck, the Vorskla (III ch. 2). After Grunwald a thin bright silver line from guard to point survives (III notes, part 3).

title: Šerno kalavijas (Kęstutis’s sword)
text:
Origin
Forged for Kęstutis around 1330 (graph); in Book VI ch. 7 it is new and warm. Rust begins with the cracks of 1380.

title: Šerno kalavijas (Kęstutis’s sword)
text:
Arc across the books

Kęstutis, to 1382. He cleans it nightly (Book I ch. 2). Skirgaila’s men take it from him at the gate when he is disarmed (I ch. 6).
Skirgaila, 1382-1397. Hung in Kęstutis’s Trakai hall (Book II ch. 1). Vytautas lets him keep it at the 1392 handover (II ch. 11). It goes into Skirgaila’s inventory, one of twelve oak chests, at Kyiv, 11 Jan 1397 (II ch. 16).
Vytautas, spring 1400-1430. Found by the wolves in the third chest, black with rust, left unpolished: “Rūdys yra sąskaita” (III ch. 2). Blood-sworn at Grunwald on 14-15 Jul 1410 (III ch. 17); the rust stops spreading (III ch. 28). It stands by the door at his death (IV ch. 29).
After 1430. No fate is given (Book IV hand-off); Book V does not mention it. A gap.

The graph gives the Iron Wolves as holders 1397-1400 (Skirgaila’s Kyiv chests pass to the wolves; Vytautas has it from spring 1400) and notes that after 1430 its whereabouts are unknown.

title: Auksinė grandinė (the strangling chain)
text:
Description
A heavy chain of Riga gold, each link perfectly welded and colder than the last. At the clasp is a small mark: two crossed keys under a cross, the sign of Riga (Book I ch. 1). It is warm when someone wears it.

title: Auksinė grandinė (the strangling chain)
text:
Power
It carries the Breath of the Void. It strangles its victim without a mark and afterwards lets its wearer hear the dead man’s last breath. In Book V it lets Žygimantas hear Kęstutis breathe “and know that he is not alone” (V ch. 22). It also muffles sound around the wearer, which is Henė’s signature (power_systems.md §5).

title: Auksinė grandinė (the strangling chain)
text:
Rule & cost
A Henė-bargain object, always kept to the letter. It does not “exhale” until it has been in the room where the dead man died (V ch. 19). Masses said over it wash the wearer, not the gold (IV ch. 20). The wearer slowly stops sleeping.

title: Auksinė grandinė (the strangling chain)
text:
Origin
[Saga] Sent from Riga as Jogaila’s “gift” with Hanulas’s envoys, summer 1382 (Book I ch. 1); Henė made it for the cousins’ deal.

title: Auksinė grandinė (the strangling chain)
text:
Arc across the books

Jogaila’s envoys, then the mercenaries, 1382. Kęstutis weighs it and puts it back (I ch. 1). It is fitted round his neck in the Krėva cell on 15 Aug 1382 (I ch. 9). Graph: Jogaila 1382.
Skirgaila, 1383-1397. Graph holder; the books show Henė on the scene.
Henė, Jan 1397. He pockets it after Skirgaila dies at Kyiv (Book II ch. 16) and wears it openly in 1405 (III notes).
Baltramiejus Rogala, Apr 1429-Aug 1430. Given in a Buda corridor as a “gift, not a bribe” (IV ch. 20); worn silent at the Noteć ford (IV ch. 23). Graph: Rogala 1429-1430. It stays with the bishop’s people at Kraków (IV ch. 30; graph: Poland, the treasury, 1430-1438) and is eight years in the cathedral treasury (V ch. 19).
Žygimantas Kęstutaitis, 14-15 Aug 1438-20 Mar 1440. Henė fetches it, stoneless, to the Krėva cell and Žygimantas puts it on (V ch. 19). It turns to dust at his murder at Trakai (V ch. 22). The graph now has Henė 1397-1429 (to Rogala in April 1429), the Kraków treasury 1430-1438, Henė again in 1438 and Žygimantas 1438-1440.

title: Paskutinė žarija (Šventaragis ember)
text:
Description
A palm-sized yellow flame that gives no smoke and does not bend in a draught (Book II notes, Part 2). It sits on a black ring of stone, fed in pinches with live ash from the first coal. Where it burns the wolves cannot sleep, because the brotherhood may not rest under a lit roof.

title: Paskutinė žarija (Šventaragis ember)
text:
Power
The last of the Gediminid sacred flames. While it burns the Silent Pact’s remnant and the vilkatai’s oath have a living anchor. New wolves can be made only at a living flame (D10), so it also keeps the brotherhood alive. Pinches of its ash can serve as a weapon or a lamp.

title: Paskutinė žarija (Šventaragis ember)
text:
Rule & cost
It is held to Vytautas’s promise “Kol aš gyvas, paskutinė ugnis neužges” (Book I ch. 3; magic_rules.md §6). If he lets it die while he lives, the Pact’s penalties fall on him. Every pinch of ash taken is a risk to him (Book II ch. 14). Fire’s cost doubles when it is worked in spring flood or an off-zenith crossing (II ch. 2, 11).

title: Paskutinė žarija (Šventaragis ember)
text:
Origin
[Saga] Lit secretly on the night Jogaila’s priests extinguished the Šventaragis fire, Feb-Mar 1387 (record: Długosz). Vytautas lights it from the ember he carried out of the valley, in Kęstutis’s old hunting lodge beyond the Neris (Book I ch. 29; canon_decisions.md D11).

title: Paskutinė žarija (Šventaragis ember)
text:
Arc across the books

Vytautas, 1387-1430 (graph holds); in practice he is its bearer and others are its keepers (graph keeper_of: Kalvis 1387-1399, Spyglys 1399-1410, the Flame-Keeper Žiežirba c. 1405-1430). The Karaim captain Elijas keeps the vault door (graph: keeper of the flame promise, 1398-1411).
Lodge, then island foundations, 1387-1392. Kalvis, whom Vytautas spared, guards the first hearth, then the half-flooded south corner of Trakai Island (Book II ch. 2).
Island undercroft, from autumn 1392. Moved by boat on the night the keys are handed over (II ch. 11). The boy Žiežirba (b. c. 1390) tends it from c. 1396. After Kalvis dies at the Vorskla, 1399 (II ch. 26), Spyglys and the boy keep it (II ch. 29).
The lantern, 8 Jun 1410-spring 1411. Žiežirba carries it in a horn lantern to Grunwald (III ch. 15, 17, 20). It returns “like a bird on a nest” (III ch. 28).
Refused crown, 1429-1430. Henė offers the crown for the flame; Vytautas refuses (IV ch. 22).
27 Oct 1430. It goes out at the moment of Vytautas’s death (IV ch. 29); the vault replay is V ch. 1. The lightning-fire given at his funeral (V ch. 2, 7) cannot make wolves (V ch. 20).

title: Klūpančioji (amber statue, Palanga)
text:
Description
A human-sized kneeling woman of honey-coloured amber, with small insects and grains of sand suspended inside. She kneels at the tide line facing the sea. Her head is bowed and her hands are clasped (Book I ch. 27; the books now agree on this pose). Her face is “like candle wax”. Fishermen tie ribbons to her neck.

title: Klūpančioji (amber statue, Palanga)
text:
Power
The Amber Queen’s last anchor on land (graph: anchors Gintaro Karalienė 1384-1450). She calms storms along that shore. She is warm to the touch and light as a sleeping child. Her glow tracks how well she is remembered.

title: Klūpančioji (amber statue, Palanga)
text:
Rule & cost
Whoever moves her dies at sea (power_systems.md §5). Gifts of bread or fish must be left for her when amber is taken from the shore; amber taken without an offering stays cold for life (Book V ch. 25). She dims as people forget her story (V ch. 25).

title: Klūpančioji (amber statue, Palanga)
text:
Origin
Left where Birutė vanished into the sea at Palanga on the night of the Amber Sacrifice, 1384 (Book I ch. 27), the payment of the Amber Debt that bought the Hidden Groves.

title: Klūpančioji (amber statue, Palanga)
text:
Arc across the books
No one “holds” her; the graph gives only her anchor edge.

1384. The wave leaves her on the sand (Book I ch. 27).
March 1410. Vytautas visits; she pales and the Queen’s voice grows quieter (Book III ch. 14, which also has the Queen speak through the pebble).
Oct 1417. The priest Andžej Radzimski takes six men to remove her. Hammers fail; the boat sinks calmly; she is back at dawn with six crosses in her hands (Book IV ch. 8).
1445-1446. The village forgets and she goes grey (Book V ch. 25).
March 1450. She glows again the evening Žiežirba tells his stories, and is the pyre’s site (V ch. 29). The closing tide of Book V is Birutė’s own, the water reaching her chin (V ch. 29); the sea takes the statue (V ch. 29); in 1553 the mother’s talk of “the kneeling woman” is memory and tale (V ch. 30).

title: Kryžiaus kalavijas (the Order’s sword)
text:
Description
A heavy straight German sword with a cross-shaped hilt, consecrated at Marienburg; it smells of cold steel and “a new religion” (Book I ch. 19, 24).

title: Kryžiaus kalavijas (the Order’s sword)
text:
Power
It dampens Kalba around it (power_systems.md §5). While Vytautas carries it, his pebble cannot answer, his blood feels strange and his Five-Voice is closed to him. It also marks him publicly as the Order’s vassal.

title: Kryžiaus kalavijas (the Order’s sword)
text:
Rule & cost
Consecrated metal smothers amber and fire. It can be removed only by a free act: Vytautas must put it in fire himself (Book I ch. 24). As the replacement of Kęstutis’s sword it bears no history, only a debt.

title: Kryžiaus kalavijas (the Order’s sword)
text:
Origin
[Record] Konrad Zöllner von Rotenstein was Grand Master 5 Oct 1382-20 Aug 1390; Vytautas was baptised “Wigand” at Tapiau on 21 Oct 1383 and swore vassalage by the Treaty of Königsberg, 30 Jan 1384. [Saga] The sword is presented to him at the baptism by Zöllner (Book I ch. 19), made by the Order for its protégé.

title: Kryžiaus kalavijas (the Order’s sword)
text:
Arc across the books

Vytautas, Oct 1383-Jul 1384. It knocks his thigh on the Order’s march into Lithuania (Book I ch. 20). He fights his first battle against his own people with it (ch. 21).
July 1384. He unbuckles it at Marienwerder (Naujapilis) and throws it into the burning tower, whereupon the pebble lights and the silence lifts (I ch. 23-24; Marienwerder).
After. No other holder. Later Order swords at Grunwald (III ch. 18, the “two swords” of the record) are a separate matter.

title: Sidabrinis vilkas (Kęstutis’s amulet)
text:
Custody, 1345–1450



Artifact custody timeline


The silver wolf is the top lane. Editable source.

title: Sidabrinis vilkas (Kęstutis’s amulet)
text:
Description
A silver wolf a hand long, with raised snout and a worn coat. Old pagan patterns run along its flank, and under the belly is a small second mark: a wolf’s head without a collar (Book VI ch. 5). By Book V a tooth is broken and the silver is blackened in the hollows and bright only where skin touches it (V ch. 7).

title: Sidabrinis vilkas (Kęstutis’s amulet)
text:
Power
An identity token. Every sworn vilkatas recognises the brotherhood’s sign and touches the scar at his throat before it (V ch. 7). Outsiders read it too: the Order’s border guards when he shows it at the fort (Book I ch. 17), Jogaila, who cannot hold its gaze (I ch. 26, III ch. 3, 13, 24). It carries no spell of its own.

title: Sidabrinis vilkas (Kęstutis’s amulet)
text:
Rule & cost
It is not the holder’s to give away. It belongs to the brotherhood, so Vytautas cannot offer it to the Dykra himself (Book I ch. 16; iron_wolves.md §16). It must pass hand to hand “bread for bread”. Its meaning dies with the pack.

title: Sidabrinis vilkas (Kęstutis’s amulet)
text:
Origin
[Saga] Cast in the Dykra in 1345 from the silver of three drowned knights and given to Kęstutis by the Wolf-Father Kuolas after the Pact (Book VI ch. 5).

title: Sidabrinis vilkas (Kęstutis’s amulet)
text:
Arc across the books

Kęstutis, 1345-1382. Worn on a leather strap; sewn into his lining at Marienburg in 1361 (Book VI ch. 18; Book I ch. 8). He touches it before the arrest (I ch. 2).
Vytautas, 1382-1430. Passed through the gap beneath the Krėva wall (“let the wolf stay with the wolf”, I ch. 8). Jonas’s pack halts before it (I ch. 25). Worn through Books II-IV to his deathbed (IV ch. 26, 29).
Pilkoji, 27 Oct-24 Dec 1430. She keeps it until Kūčios.
The Flame-Keeper, 1430-1449. She gives it to him in the circle of fourteen wolves, who touch it one by one, Kirmėlė last (V ch. 7).
Rimgailė, Palanga, March 1450. He gives it to her “bread for bread” and she puts it under her threshold (V ch. 29). It is seen again on the keeper’s neck in a vision in 1553 (V ch. 30).

The graph’s holder edges: Kęstutis to 1382, Vytautas 1382-1430, Pilkoji 1430, the Flame-Keeper from Kūčios 1430-31 to 1450, then Rimgailė of Palanga from 1450.

title: Geležinio Vilko kaukolė
text:
Description
A skull too large to be a man’s or any wolf’s, grey as old iron, with deep empty orbits, but light enough to lift with two fingers (Book V ch. 28). In Book VI ch. 18 it is cracked, with a round hole through one eye socket. It rests on a flat stone or pine stump on a bog-island in the Dykra.

title: Geležinio Vilko kaukolė
text:
Power
The brotherhood’s oath-stone. A wolf who lays both hands on it swears the nine laws of the Pack’s Word, and every sworn wolf from the Neman to the Narew hears a lie spoken there (power_systems.md §5; Book VI ch. 5). Its keeper is the Wolf-Father, later once the Wolf-Mother.

title: Geležinio Vilko kaukolė
text:
Rule & cost
Rules sworn on it, such as “no Gediminid blood” (Book III ch. 15), bind even the guilty. The keeper is chosen by the Root-Mother in the bog (Book IV ch. 6). A wolf is laid to the bog, never burned, and the skull goes down last.

title: Geležinio Vilko kaukolė
text:
Origin
[Saga] Found by Lizdeika where the dream-wolf stood after Gediminas’s dream on the Šventaragis hunt, 1323, hard and grey as iron (iron_wolves.md §3.2). He carried it into the Dykra and the packs swore on it.

title: Geležinio Vilko kaukolė
text:
Arc across the books

Vilkatai, 1323-1450. Graph holder; Lizdeika’s hundred.
Kuolas, 1345. The Wolf-Father presides at Šešiapirštis’s oath over it (Book VI ch. 5).
Pušis, 1405-1415. It lies on a stump while Žiežirba swears (Book III ch. 9, Dec 1405) and while Pilkoji is chosen and takes it up (Book IV ch. 6, 1415-16).
Pilkoji, 1415-1449. She keeps it in the oldest bog.
2 Nov 1449. On Vėlinės she carries it to the deepest water and lies down with it on her chest. The bog closes over her (Book V ch. 28). With it goes the last office of the brotherhood.

title: II · Auksinis Šešėlis
text:
Premise
The Pact is dead and the spirits go feral. Vytautas, twice baptised and holding only Grodno, must bow in Trakai to the man who held the rope at Krėva while he keeps the last flame alive in the flooded foundations of the island castle. Ambition drives him back to the Order (1389–92), to besiege the city he once saved, and then to betray the Order again. By one late tradition (the afterword says it is only that) his hostage sons pay with their lives. Made Grand Duke at Ostrów, he builds an empire toward the Black Sea and rides it to the Vorskla.

title: II · Auksinis Šešėlis
section: Protagonist arc (form at start → form at end)

Protagonist arc (form at start → form at end)
Traitor of Traitors (burned Teutonic armour, the silver wolf worn openly) → Didysis Kunigaikštis from Ostrów (Ruthenian robes, the Tatar court, Henė at his side) → broken at the Vorskla; plain armour is the first tell of the Iron Wolf. Want: to rule as a king among kings. Lie: “the horizon belongs to the bold”. Truth: empire eats its builder. Cost: his sons (a contested tradition), about twenty princes, a body without surety (every working at full price), Ona’s regard.

title: II · Auksinis Šešėlis
text:
Antagonists & outcomes

Skirgaila (Part I): defeated at Ostrów, compensated with Kyiv, dies there on 11 Jan 1397; Henė collects, three stones become two.
Edigu (Parts II–III), behind him the Steppe-Hunger: wins the Vorskla. This is the book the protagonist loses.
Secondary: the Order (Zöllner to Konrad von Jungingen) loses Vytautas twice, takes revenge through hostages and gains Samogitia by treaty; Jadwiga dies 17 Jul 1399, her tomb the White Silence’s anchor.

B: the flame moves from the foundations to the island vault (ch. 11). D: Henė changes masters at Ostrów and collects Skirgaila. E: Perkūnas punishes the broken oaths at the Vorskla. H: second civil war. I: Sofija marries Vasily I (1391). J: Steppe-Hunger and Gold-Glutton.

A humbled Vytautas, the pebble cold, Henė with two stones; Samogitia sold (Salynas 1398) and ready to rise; Skirgaila dead; the wolves estranged; the Order under Konrad von Jungingen eyeing Samogitia. Open title question: the outline notes a README variant, Vytis ir Šešėlis.

title: IV · Nematoma Karūna
text:
Premise
Grunwald won the war and lost the gods. Samogitia is baptised and the Hidden Groves fall (1413–17) while Vytautas preaches by day and keeps the Last Flame by night. He rules from the Baltic toward the Black Sea and wants a crown so the realm will not revert to Poland. At Lutsk, Sigismund offers one. The Bishop of Kraków sets out to stop it, and the Shadow-Seller makes his last offer: the crown if the flame is allowed to die. Vytautas refuses. The embassy is blocked at the Polish border in August 1430, and he dies uncrowned; the flame goes out with him.

title: IV · Nematoma Karūna
section: Protagonist arc (form at start → form at end)
text:
Protagonist arc (form at start → form at end)
Geležinis Vilkas, its last tells fading across Part I, until Ona’s death turns him into Ugnies Sargas (Keeper of the Flame): old, half-deaf, with Julijona beside him and the vault beneath. Want: the crown. Lie: “legitimacy comes from Rome or Kraków”. Truth: it comes from what you keep. Costs: the crown, Ona, his life.

title: VI · Šventasis Miškas (prequel)
text:
Premise
In 1345 two brothers push their brother Jaunutis aside and, at night in the Šventaragis valley, swear the Silent Pact: the land will not be conquered while a Gediminid keeps the sacred flames, while no Gediminid sheds Gediminid blood, and while royal blood is paid for land lost. Kęstutis says the last clause aloud, and Algirdas never forgives him. Across thirty years Kęstutis pays the price in kin and keeps his word, marries an amber priestess by a trick the gods must accept, and buries his brother by fire in 1377. The reader learns the clauses here, so every breach in Book I lands.
