title: Algirdas
text:
Summary
Algirdas (c. 1296 - May 1377) is the elder of the two brothers who shared the Grand Duchy for thirty-two years: he held Vilnius and looked east, while Kęstutis held Trakai and looked west. When the saga’s readers meet him he is already ash. He is the dead brother of Book I, the man whose will Kęstutis keeps to his own death, and the hesitant oath-giver of the 1345 Silent Pact. In the prequel (Book VI) he is a patient, silent strategist who never says where an army is marching, and who gives the old gods the flames while his brother gives the blood. His want is the east: Kyiv, Podolia, Moscow. What he leaves behind is a divided house, because the sons of his first marriage were passed over for Jogaila.

title: Algirdas
text:
Appearance & tells
Book VI gives him few features and many habits. In his prime he is known for a calm face that betrays nothing; Jaunutis dreads that face on the morning he is deposed (ch. 3). His great tell is secrecy: he does not tell his captains where the army is going, even when it is already marching (ch. 15, ch. 20, the Blue Waters campaign). In ch. 28 he lies dying with a grey beard “like ashes” and hands thin as grass roots, a body that has shrunk to eyes and bones. At his pyre in ch. 29 a strip of black cloth shows at the edge of the fire, the sign of the Orthodox monk’s vows that Ruthenian sources claim he took at the end; the Krivis and an Orthodox priest stand on either side of the flames, and the saga lets both stories be true.

title: Algirdas
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
The east: Ruthenian lands, Kyiv, a steppe frontier that makes Lithuania safe from the Order by making it larger.


Need (internal)
To tell his brother, and the Pact’s gods, the whole truth about what he is paying and who will pay it.


Lie they believe
That an empire built eastward can be held by silence and by a younger son’s obedience.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
He learns it only at the end: he asks Kęstutis to guard Jogaila, the one promise that will be kept and the one that will kill its keeper (Book VI ch. 28).

title: Algirdas
text:
Arc by book

Book VI (1341-1377): deposes Jaunutis with Kęstutis in 1345 (ch. 3), hesitates while Kęstutis speaks the Pact’s unspoken third clause aloud (ch. 4), and never forgives him; marries Uliana of Tver (1350, ch. 12); wins at Blue Waters (1362, ch. 20), where the Steppe-Hunger first notices Lithuania; marches on Moscow (1368, 1370, 1372; ch. 22, 25); names Jogaila his heir and asks Kęstutis to protect him (ch. 28); is burned in May 1377 as the Pact weakens (ch. 29).
Book I: dead from the first page; remembered as the brother whose heir Kęstutis spared in 1381 (ch. 1, 2, 8).
Book II: his disinherited sons Andrius and Dmitrijus die at the Vorskla (1399); his eastern lands are Skirgaila’s and Vytautas’s to take.
Book V: Žiežirba sees the oath night in the cracked pebble and learns that Algirdas hesitated (ch. 5).

title: Algirdas
text:
Power & magic
Tier 0: no gift of his own, in the saga or in the record. His standing in the magic is structural. He is one of the two oath-takers of the Silent Pact (1345): he gives the sacred flames, Kęstutis the blood. He keeps the Vilnius wolf packs at the Šventaragis flame, which is the root of the 1382 schism among the Iron Wolves. His death in 1377 is the first weakening of the Pact; Kęstutis’s kin-slaying in 1382 and Jogaila’s baptism (1386-87) finish it. The Shadow-Seller watches his court only through small shapes, a black dog and a clerk with a ledger, and has no stones or mask yet.

title: Algirdas
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: Grand Duke of Lithuania 1345-77 (born c. 1296, died May 1377), ruling from Vilnius in a diarchy with his brother Kęstutis after they deposed their brother Jaunutis in 1345. Through his first wife Maria of Vitebsk (m. c. 1318) he held Vitebsk; in 1350 he married Uliana of Tver, and in 1377 her son Jogaila was preferred over Maria’s elder sons. He defeated three Tatar commanders at Blue Waters (1362; dating debated) and drew Kyiv and Podolia into the realm, and besieged Moscow in 1368, 1370 and 1372. He was cremated according to pagan custom; Ruthenian sources say he took monastic vows near the end (tradition, unverified). See VLE and Wikipedia.
[Saga invention]: The Silent Pact of 1345 and his hesitation at its third clause (Book VI ch. 4; Book V ch. 5); the black dog and the ledger clerk at his court (Book VI ch. 8, 27); the double funeral with Krivis and monk side by side (ch. 29). These are private scenes in gaps of the record and contradict no date or deed.

title: Algirdas
text:
Pronunciation
al-GIR-das (/ɐlʲˈɡʲɪrdɐs/), English respelling ahl-GIHR-dahs; stress on the second syllable. Genitive Algirdo, dative Algirdui, accusative Algirdą. [world_rules/pronunciation_lexicon.json]

title: Algirdas
text:
Appearances
Book VI (Šventasis Miškas): the dominant figure of the prequel after Kęstutis: ch. 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 15, 20 (POV), 22, 24, 25 (POV), 26, 28, 29, 30 and the afterword. Book I: ch. 1, 2, 6, 8, 10 (remembered). Book II: ch. 12, 13, 22, 28 and the afterword (as father of Andrius, Dmitrijus, Skirgaila, Švitrigaila). Book III: ch. 2, 5, 8. Book IV: ch. 12, 24. Book V: ch. 3, 5 (the oath flashback), 9, 11, 15, 19, 26. Continuity note: Book VI ch. 15 and 29 set his heir-naming and death in spring 1377; Book I treats the date as three years and some months before Jogaila’s accession scenes.

title: Danila (Vytautas’s scribe)
text:
Summary
Danila is a loyal chancery scribe and personal chamber servant to Grand Duke Vytautas throughout his later years in Vilnius and Trakai (Book IV). He handles correspondence, manages parchment and seals, and attends to the aging duke as his sight and hearing fade.

title: Danila (Vytautas’s scribe)
text:
Appearance & tells
A quiet, ink-stained clerk in modest wool robes, moving without sound between the archive chests and the duke’s table. Attentive and discreet, he knows when to read aloud, when to hold the parchment, and when to step into the shadow of the door.

title: Danila (Vytautas’s scribe)
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
To preserve the letters and records of the Grand Duchy with meticulous precision.


Need (internal)
To serve an aging titan with quiet loyalty without becoming entangled in court conspiracies.


Lie they believe
Parchment and royal seals outlast the whims of kings and princes.


Truth they learn
Crowns and charters turn to dust, but the true word spoken in private endures.

title: Danila (Vytautas’s scribe)
text:
Arc by book

Book IV (1411–1430). Serves as Vytautas’s trusted chancery scribe. Present during diplomatic correspondence across Ruthenia and the West; reads letters into Vytautas’s right ear after the duke loses his reading sight; attends the duke during his final illness at Trakai.

title: Danila (Vytautas’s scribe)
text:
Power & magic
Tier 0 (mortal). A skilled secular scribe and archivist. No supernatural gifts.

title: Danila (Vytautas’s scribe)
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: Historical clerks and notaries of Vytautas’s chancery are well-attested in the Lithuanian Metrica and diplomatic registers.
[Saga invention]: Danila as a specific named personal chamber scribe and reader is an invention.

title: Eglė (vaidilutė → Pelkių Eglė)
text:
Summary
Eglė, the last vaidilutė of the eternal flame in the Šventaragis valley, spends her last night as a mortal priestess in the prologue. After a captain of Jogaila’s insults her she leaves Vilnius on foot and, days later, walks into the Dykra and is taken by the Root-Mother, becoming Pelkių Eglė, “Eglė of the Swamps”: the swamp’s voice, the keeper of the bridge between humans and the old gods. She appears at turning points as a girl with moss-tangled hair and a yellow-cheeked žaltys (grass-snake) round her neck, and she fades as the groves fall.

title: Eglė (vaidilutė → Pelkių Eglė)
text:
Appearance & tells
A girl with dark, moss-tangled hair, green eyes and a gold- or yellow-cheeked žaltys coiled around her neck (Book I ch. 16; Book II ch. 3, 19). The snake is the last of the Šventaragis line; when it dies in Book IV ch. 7, Eglė can no longer hold a shape by day. In Book III she is “fainter than she was” (ch. 16, 23), standing in Galminas’s new grove and unable to hold her form long; her last appearance is Book IV ch. 27, where the forest presses to the lake and she sees Vytautas’s past go by in the halls.

title: Eglė (vaidilutė → Pelkių Eglė)
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
To keep the bridge between the people and the gods open, and to save the sacred snake, flame and groves from the axe.


Need (internal)
To let the gods become stories instead of keeping them as an army.


Lie they believe
That the Root-Mother’s gifts can hold a forest against axes for ever.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
The Green Wood is dying; her price, ‘never sell the forest’, falls due at Salynas (Book II ch. 19), and she fades with the groves (Book IV ch. 7, 27).

title: Eglė (vaidilutė → Pelkių Eglė)
text:
Arc by book

Prologue / Book I: the prophecy night, her last as a mortal (prologue); she is Birutė tells Vytautas to seek her at the Šventaragis flame if he is ever lost among roots and moss (ch. 3); meets Vytautas in the Dykra during his escape (ch. 16), where he misnames her “Gintaro Šventikė” and her silence corrects him: “Ne gintaro. Šaknų.”; takes his buckle on the offering stone and refuses the silver wolf; the ashes of ch. 23.
Book II: watches the bishop’s men hunt the last sacred snake (ch. 3); reads the blood-foam on the Neman for Vytautas’s hostage sons (ch. 9); appears to the Samogitian elder Gedgaudas at Salynas to say that the buckle was a pledge: her price comes due (ch. 19). The Book II outline also lists a last word from her in ch. 22; the text of ch. 22 does not mention her.
Book III: she and the žalčiai guide the scouts through “impassable” woods before Grunwald (ch. 16), stands in Galminas’s grove (ch. 23) and receives the Root-Mother’s thanks (ch. 29).
Book IV: the Medininkai bishopric falls on the last great grove, and the snake dies (ch. 7); a faint Eglė shows Pilkoji’s pack the bog road home (ch. 16); her last appearance on Trakai island (ch. 27).
Books V-VI: a memory at the frame of Book V (ch. 1, 29); in Book VI (ch. 26) a girl vaidilutė called Eglė keeps the Šventaragis flame when Vytautas and the boy Jogaila feed it.

title: Eglė (vaidilutė → Pelkių Eglė)
text:
Power & magic
Tier 3 before the prologue (vaidilutė, born to Fire; practises Senovės Kalba and herb-lore). After she walks into the Dykra she is taken: power granted by the Root-Mother, outside the tier ladder, the swamp speaking through her. She is not an amber priestess (canon D5). Costs: her mortal shape, then her daytime shape, and the price of the Dykra rescue, “never sell the forest”. She appears to Jadvyga in a dream to warn her of the White Silence.

title: Eglė (vaidilutė → Pelkių Eglė)
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: There is no historical Eglė. The name comes from the Lithuanian folk tale Eglė žalčių karalienė (Eglė, Queen of the Grass-snakes), in which a woman marries the snake-king Žilvinas and, after her brothers kill him, turns herself and her children into trees; eglė is the spruce. The Šventaragis valley was the traditional site of the sacred flame at Vilnius. The sacred fire of Vilnius is attested only by later chronicle tradition.
[Saga invention]: All of her as a character: the last Šventaragis vaidilutė, her insult by Jogaila’s captain, the Dykra walk (the graph event Eglė leads Vytautas through the Dykra), the Root-Mother’s taking, the snake, her price and her fading. The two Eglės of earlier drafts are one woman (D5).

title: Eglė (vaidilutė → Pelkių Eglė)
text:
Pronunciation
eg-LĖ (/ɛɡˈlʲeː/), English respelling eg-LAY; stress on the second syllable. Paradigm 4: accusative Ẽglę, dative Ẽglei, vocative Ẽgle stress the first syllable; the other forms stress the ending. Pelkių Eglė: PEL-kių eg-LĖ, PEL-kyoo eg-LAY. [world_rules/pronunciation_lexicon.json]

title: Eglė (vaidilutė → Pelkių Eglė)
text:
Appearances
Prologue (the prophecy night). Book I: ch. 3, 16 (the Dykra rescue), 17, 23 (the ashes), 31, 32. Book II: ch. 3, 9 (Blood-Foam), 19 (Salynas) and the afterword. Book III: ch. 16 (Forest Whispers), 23 (Galminas’s Grove), 29 (the Root-Mother’s Thanks). Book IV: ch. 6, 7, 16, 27 (her last appearance) and the afterword. Book V: ch. 1, 29 and the afterword. Book VI: ch. 26, 29.

title: Elijas, son of Mošė (Karaim guard captain)
text:
Summary
Elijas, son of Mošė, the Karaim captain of the Trakai guards (wife Rachelė), keeps the vault door; his younger son Zacharijas holds it in 1430; his elder son is Samuelis.

title: Elijas, son of Mošė (Karaim guard captain)
text:
Appearance & tells
A tall man with a grey beard and dark, quiet eyes; a warrior, not a priest (Book II ch. 18; Book III ch. 28). He stands at the vault door the way a man stands who does not know he is entitled to sit (Book IV ch. 10). His rare smile “soft as a hand’s touch”. Tells: his wife Rachelė’s small lamp on a shelf, which the Karaims keep burning in every house; the copper lamp with a three-part wick he brought from Crimea, which his son Zacharijas keeps burning day and night when the hearths of Trakai die (Book V ch. 4).

title: Elijas, son of Mošė (Karaim guard captain)
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
To settle his thirty families safely on Duke Vytautas’s land and keep their faith.


Need (internal)
To understand that a door can guard something even when it guards nothing.


Lie they believe
That a soldier need not explain what he sees on the road.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
That an empty door, held faithfully, is heavy: he never thought empty doors could be so heavy (Book III ch. 28).

title: Elijas, son of Mošė (Karaim guard captain)
text:
Arc by book

Book II (1397-98): arrives at Trakai with thirty Karaim families, sees the dust-pillar of the steppe-spirit crumble at the first pine wood (“We are no longer his”); the Franciscan offers to baptise his children and is turned away with bread; the Grand Duchess Ona visits (ch. 18); in 1399 he lets Vytautas pass with the Vorskla cloak and asks nothing (ch. 29).
Book III (1410-11): stays behind at the empty vault when the lantern goes to Grunwald (“Someone has to stand at a door with nothing behind it, so that someone can come back”, ch. 15); the lantern returns after eleven months (ch. 28).
Book IV (1418-1430): at the dinner with the new bride Julijona (ch. 10); his younger son commands Vytautas’s escort at the fall (ch. 25), and receives Jogaila (ch. 26); he himself is long in the Karaim cemetery by 1430 (ch. 29).
Book V: his sons Samuelis and Zacharijas; the copper lamp (ch. 4).

title: Elijas, son of Mošė (Karaim guard captain)
text:
Power & magic
None; a mundane warrior. His own faith keeps a lamp, and the saga goes no further than that parallel (see the Book II outline). He is the witness of the vault, not its keeper: the Karaims are the Steppe-Hunger’s refugees, never its servants. He keeps the flame promise by silence: the graph lists him as keeper of the Last Flame promise at the vault door (1398-1411).

title: Elijas, son of Mošė (Karaim guard captain)
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: The Karaims settled at Trakai in 1397-98 (tradition; numbers disputed).
[Saga invention]: Elijas himself and his role at the vault door (Book II ch. 18, 29; Book III ch. 15, 28).

title: Elijas, son of Mošė (Karaim guard captain)
text:
Pronunciation
Not in the JSON lexicon; derived from the Lithuanian spelling: e-LI-jas (/ɛˈlʲɪjɐs/), English sound-alike eh-LIH-yahs. The Karaim original Eliyah is eh-lee-YAH. His father’s name is Mošė (MO-šė, “Moses”).

title: Elijas, son of Mošė (Karaim guard captain)
text:
Appearances
Book II: ch. 18 (Trakų Naujakuriai), 29 and the afterword. Book III: ch. 15, 21 (a mention in a letter), 28. Book IV: ch. 10, 25 (his younger son), 26, 29, 30. Book V: ch. 4 (Užgesusios Krosnys). Continuity: Book V ch. 4 says the Karaims came “from Crimea 33 years before Vytautas’s death” (1397); the record’s tradition says 1397-98 and disputes the number of families (Book II afterword: about 300, Elijas’s thirty being one band).

title: Galminas
text:
Summary
Galminas is the saga’s Samogitian žynys, “the last of the old priests”, Elder of Samogitia and Lord of the Forest, who watches the false baptism of 1387 from a snowy hill under dark pines (Book I ch. 29). He is already dead and reanimated: the Root-Mother grew roots through his ribcage in place of a heart after an Iron Knight’s spear pierced it in his youth, and she acts through him. He leads the Samogitian uprisings of Book III, transforms at Grunwald into a wood-skinned beast, and becomes a grove (Book III ch. 19, 23).

title: Galminas
text:
Appearance & tells
Gnarled and weathered like the trees of his home, in leather and bone armour for mobility in the swamp; his face tattooed with old Baltic signs of protection. When he speaks, the wind in the trees provides a bass harmony. Sap, not blood, runs in him: in winter 1399-1400 he “does not eat and bleeds sap” (Book III ch. 1). Set on fire by pitch in the siege of Kaunas, he does not burn but smoulders like peat and keeps fighting. In battle rage he takes on the attributes of a bear or wolf (vilkatas, Wolf-shift) through spirits of the wood.

title: Galminas
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
The survival of the Way: to protect the sacred groves from the knights’ axes and to keep Samogitia free of both the Order and Vilnius.


Need (internal)
To let the forest take its harvest and to hand his knowledge on, since he cannot hold the groves for ever.


Lie they believe
That a wolf can be washed: ‘you can baptise a man, but the truth remains in his blood’, and that an old war can still be won.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
He becomes the grove where he falls (Book III ch. 23); his pupil, the last žynys, dies singing the Pact song with its details wrong (Book V ch. 27).

title: Galminas
text:
Arc by book

Book I (1387): watches the baptism from the hill as Vytautas lights the secret flame elsewhere (ch. 29).
Book II: listens from the far bank at Salynas (ch. 19), and in the Samogitian grove at the epilogue as Ulrich von Jungingen says “Next time we finish them” (ch. 30).
Book III (1399-1410): POV of ch. 1 (Frozen Buds), 4 (the First Rising, where the žyniai burn a captured knight on his horse and he lets them); leads the second rising in 1409 (ch. 12), guides the army through the borderlands, fights at Grunwald (ch. 17, 19) and becomes a grove (ch. 23, 26).
Book V: the last žynys of the Pact, “Galminas’s pupil”, still knows the words (ch. 11, 27).

title: Galminas
text:
Power & magic
Tier 5, vessel (host) of the Root-Mother (canon: power systems §4). Before his death he was a tier-3 žynys; the Root-Mother reanimated him and acts in full through him. Powers: the Iron-Sense (the spirits whisper the ringing of iron long before Teutonic scouts arrive); the Shifting Swamp (the ground softens beneath the Iron Knights’ chargers at his silent command); the Beast-shift. He is a tool of Perkūnas as well, and the Root-Mother’s gifts fade far from forest. Cost: he is dead and made of wood, and the transformation at Grunwald (ch. 19) spends him; the Root-Mother’s last great act is the grove (ch. 23).

title: Galminas
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: Not a historical person as drawn. The name Galminas does appear in en.wikipedia’s article on the Samogitian uprisings among five deputies (Rumbaudas Valimantaitis, Galminas, Getautas, Klausigaila, Vasibutas) whom Vytautas sent to lead the rebels in 1409; VLE (vle.lt, Galminas) identifies him as Jurgis Galminas, a nobleman who helped organise the 1409 rising, joined a Samogitian delegation to the Council of Constance in 1415, and was Samogitian elder from late 1432 to late 1434 (succeeding Stanislovas Kęsgaila). The saga’s Galminas, who dies as a grove in 1410, is a different, invented figure sharing the name (the Book III afterword says so). The uprisings are historical: the first began on 13 March 1401, the second on 26 May 1409 (en.wikipedia). The Samogitians’ groves and their last pagan priests survive in the record only as tradition; Samogitia was baptised in 1413-17.
[Saga invention]: All the rest: the reanimation, the root-heart, the shapeshift, the transformation and the grove at Grunwald, the Pact-song pupil. The graph lists him as a Saga invention; the wiki infobox’s dates (c. 1340-1410) are the saga’s. The only 1410 anchor is the Grunwald field, where the afterword says the regrowth over the graves is invention.

title: Galminas
text:
Pronunciation
GAL-mi-nas (/ˈɡaːlʲmʲɪnɐs/), English respelling GAHL-mih-nahs; stress on the first syllable. [world_rules/pronunciation_lexicon.json]

title: Galminas
text:
Appearances
Book I: ch. 29 (Krikštas). Book II: ch. 19 (Salyno Puota), 30 (epilogue). Book III: ch. 1 (POV), 4 (POV), 12, 16, 17, 19, 23, 26 and the afterword. Book V: ch. 11 (as the teacher of the beekeeper-žynys). Continuity: persona places the fire-and-no-burn scene at the siege of Kaunas; Book III keeps the 1410 transformation.

title: Hanulas (Riga merchant)
text:
Summary
Hanulas, a Riga merchant of Vilnius, led the townspeople who took the castle for Jogaila on 12 Jun 1382 and became first elder of Vilnius (1382-87); in the saga he is Henė’s first mask.

title: Hanulas (Riga merchant)
text:
Appearance & tells
A prosperous burgher in good German furs, ink-stained fingers and a merchant’s ring; a pleasant, forgettable face. People remember the voice, which sounds like their own. In Book I ch. 5 Jogaila carries silver that is “Hanulas’s promises, smelling of Western power and the new gods” and never once sees the Riga merchant and the jester Henė in one room. In Book VI ch. 27 the Shadow-Seller’s ledger lists him as a Riga silver-trader, “owing a little; still free”.

title: Hanulas (Riga merchant)
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
The Shadow-Seller’s mask: to open the gate for Jogaila and to place Riga and Order silver where it will do most harm.


Need (internal)
For the real man (Hanul): to be a respected burgher; for the mask: to find a customer.


Lie they believe
That a merchant can trade without being owned.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
That every coin he gives is warm and every gift carries a thread (the golden chain, Book I ch. 9).

title: Hanulas (Riga merchant)
text:
Arc by book

Book VI (c. 1375): a name in the Shadow-Seller’s ledger as a Riga silver-trader still free (ch. 27).
Book I (1382): takes the Vilnius castle with the townspeople and hands castle and city to Jogaila on 12 June while Kęstutis is away (ch. 1, 2); his Riga-made golden chain is the “gift” that kills Kęstutis (“Hanulas said it was worthy of your honour”, ch. 9); his silver reaches Jogaila (ch. 5).
Book II (1387): Hanulo “wagon-man” is whispered to be the jester Henė’s origin (ch. 1).
Book V: the chain-line is repeated in Žygimantas’s Krėva night, again on the lips of the hired killers (ch. 19).

title: Hanulas (Riga merchant)
text:
Power & magic
Not a mortal practitioner: he is a mask of a Force, a shard of Velnias, outside the tier ladder (Shadow-Seller / Henė; canon D2). As Hanulas he never casts; he trades. Every coin he hands over is warm. He carries the golden chain, Riga-made, which holds the Breath of the Void. Canon Q12: a real man, possessed 1380-82, who never remembers it, because the historical Hanul keeps acting after 1382.

title: Hanulas (Riga merchant)
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: Hanul of Riga (Hennecke, Hannike): took the castle and handed castle and city to Jogaila; Jogaila’s deputy in Vilnius 1382-87; took part in the missions before the Act of Krėva; died in Kraków c. 1417-18.
[Saga invention]: Henė’s possession of him 1380-82; the sack of Riga silver is only a rumour in Book I.

title: Hanulas (Riga merchant)
text:
Pronunciation
HA-nu-las (/ˈɣaːnʊɫɐs/), English respelling HAH-noo-lahs; stress on the first syllable. Also written Hannike, Hennecke or Hanco in the German sources. [world_rules/pronunciation_lexicon.json]

title: Hanulas (Riga merchant)

Appearances

title: Janusz I of Masovia
text:
Summary
Janusz I of Masovia (c. 1346 - 1429), Duke of Warsaw and Czersk, is Vytautas’s brother-in-law through Danutė. In the saga he is the small, moustached, proud neighbour who gives Vytautas refuge in Czersk castle in late 1382, and is open about it: the arrival causes him more worry than joy. He is the neutral ground of the story, a Piast squeezed between the Order, Poland and Lithuania.

title: Janusz I of Masovia
text:
Appearance & tells
Book I ch. 17: a small, moustached man, “too proud”, who has learned to survive among three stronger neighbours. He receives Vytautas in the Warsaw castle without ceremony and speaks practically: “Rest; in the meantime we will see what the world does.” His tell is caution; the Masovian house words, Między dwoma ogniami (between two fires), are the saga’s invention for the Piasts.

title: Janusz I of Masovia
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
Keep Masovia out of the cousins’ wars and on good terms with every side.


Need (internal)
To be a prince who is more than a buffer.


Lie they believe
That a small duchy is safest when it is helpful to everyone.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
That sheltering a wolf costs less than refusing him (Book I ch. 17).

title: Janusz I of Masovia
text:
Arc by book

Book I (late 1382): receives Vytautas in Czersk castle (his capital until 1406), gives him a few weeks’ rest and guides to Prussia (ch. 17).
Later books: an offstage ally and kinsman; his brother Siemowit IV marries Aleksandra Algirdaitė (1387), so the two Gediminid lines are in-laws in Masovia.

title: Janusz I of Masovia
text:
Power & magic
Tier 0. A mundane prince with no gift and no bargain.

title: Janusz I of Masovia
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: Janusz I the Elder (born c. 1346, died December 1429), Duke of Warsaw and Czersk, a Piast and from 1405 a vassal of the Polish crown. He married Danutė (Anna) of Lithuania c. 1373. Masovian troops under Janusz and his brother Siemowit IV fought on the Polish-Lithuanian side at Grunwald (1410). After Krėva, Vytautas went to Janusz’s court before going to the Order (Wigand; en.wikipedia). See Wikipedia.
[Saga invention]: His wary welcome and exact phrasing in Book I ch. 17. The record gives only the fact of the refuge.

title: Janusz I of Masovia
text:
Pronunciation
JA-nusz (/ˈjanuʂ/), English respelling YAH-noosh. Lithuanian: Janušas Mazovietis. [world_rules/pronunciation_lexicon.json]

title: Janusz I of Masovia
text:
Appearances
Book I: ch. 17 only. Mentioned in Book II (hostage and marriage networks) and in the Book III Brest council context. Masovia as a place: see Masovia.

title: Jonas (vilkų vyresnysis)
text:
Summary
Jonas, Kęstutis’s armour-bearer and pack-elder (vilkų vyresnysis) of the hidden nine, is the Loyal Hound of Book I, the oldest surviving Iron Wolf of Kęstutis’s guard. “Jonas” is a skin-name (kailio vardas): the baptismal name of an Order sergeant he killed at the gate in 1361 during Kęstutis’s escape from Marienburg, worn as a trophy, which is why a pagan wolf has a saint’s name. He serves the son because he swore to the father, leaves a horse at an oak for the fleeing Vytautas, leads the remnant band in 1384 and dies under the oak.

title: Jonas (vilkų vyresnysis)
text:
Appearance & tells
Grey-bearded, broad and quiet, in wolf-hide over quilted wool, no plate. His mark is the burned palm, the pack-elder’s brand, from carrying the pack’s single feast-day iron blade wrapped in linen. He does not drink Jogaila’s mead and will not drink from a hand that has not given bread (Book I ch. 2). Part of his soul stays wolf.

title: Jonas (vilkų vyresnysis)
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
To keep the oath he swore to Kęstutis by serving the son.


Need (internal)
To be told that the old law has an end, and that it may be broken without dying.


Lie they believe
That the Pack’s Word is the whole of the law.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
That a wolf’s law can be kept by the prince: Vytautas does not burn him but carries him to a bog (Book I ch. 25).

title: Jonas (vilkų vyresnysis)
text:
Arc by book

Book VI (1361): the young wolf who kills an Order sergeant at Marienburg’s last gate and takes his Christian name (ch. 18, POV); at Rudau (ch. 24); in the epilogue (ch. 30).
Book I (1382-84): among the hidden nine at Kęstutis’s side (ch. 2); the silver wolf goes to Vytautas; is not in the tents when the guard is slaughtered at Jogaila’s camp (ch. 7; seven of the nine die there, Jonas’s men stayed in Kęstutis’s own camp, canon D10); leaves a horse for the fleeing Vytautas at a named oak (ch. 15); leads the band at the burning of the Order’s castles in July 1384 and dies under the oak (ch. 25).

title: Jonas (vilkų vyresnysis)
text:
Power & magic
Granted, the Wolf-Change (Vilkų krikštas) from the Root-Mother via the Dykra: night-sight, scent, fast healing, the berserk “iron hour”. Vilkatai are not casters and sit outside the tier ladder; the graph gives tier 3 to the wolf-change. He lives by the Pack’s Word and by its nine laws, one of which, no Gediminid blood, is the Pact’s. Part of his soul stays wolf.

title: Jonas (vilkų vyresnysis)
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: No such person in the record. The 1361 escape is real (Kęstutis fled Marienburg on 11 Nov 1361 with a servant, Alf, who removed bricks from the cell wall; veidas.lt, VLE); the Order sergeant at the gate, and Jonas, are the saga’s.
[Saga invention]: All of him: the skin-name, the burned palm, the hidden nine, the horse at the oak, the band of 1384. Book VI ch. 18 (his POV) shows how he took the name.

title: Jonas (vilkų vyresnysis)
text:
Pronunciation
JO-nas (/ˈjoːnɐs/), English respelling YOH-nahs. Paradigm 2: instrumental Jonù and locative Jonè are end-stressed; elsewhere the stress is on JO-. [world_rules/pronunciation_lexicon.json]

title: Jonas (vilkų vyresnysis)
text:
Appearances
Book I: ch. 2, 4, 7, 8, 12, 13, 15, 25. Book VI: ch. 18 (POV), 24, 30 and the afterword. Not to be confused with Jonas Alšėniškis (Book II) or Jonas Goštautas.

title: Ulrich von Jungingen
text:
Summary
Ulrich von Jungingen (1360 - 15 July 1410), the 26th Grand Master of the Teutonic Order (elected 26 June 1407), is the mortal Antagonist of Book III: brave, proud, convinced, “the last true believer of the knightly Order”. Unlike his cautious brother Konrad, he wants one decisive battle against the “pagan-Polish hydra”. The saga lets him speak flawless Lithuanian, learned from the enemy, and shows him as a man who does not fear. He leads sixteen white banners into the field at Grunwald and dies fighting, refusing to flee.

title: Ulrich von Jungingen
text:
Appearance & tells
A mountain of a man: tall, broad-boned and wide-shouldered, with light straight hair and a face the brothers call the “holy machine”, a smooth face that carries the one emotion he allows himself (Book II ch. 30, about forty in 1399). His white mantle with the black cross is always immaculate, even in battle. He speaks Lithuanian cleanly and without accent (Book III ch. 6). At Grunwald he is about fifty, without helmet, standing on a pile of dead with a broken sword while dozens of men swirl round him “like water round a rock” (ch. 20). Tells: he asks for a lantern before descending into the Marienburg vaults, and does not flinch at the heat in the walls (ch. 11).

title: Ulrich von Jungingen
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
To finish the Order’s mission: to claim the Wild Lands for Christ and to prove the German knights superior to the “Eastern rabble” by a single decisive battle.


Need (internal)
To doubt: to learn pity, the thing the Iron Saint’s gift takes from him.


Lie they believe
That the Order is invincible and favoured by the Virgin, and that fearlessness is a virtue.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
He does not learn it. He dies on the field, and Jogaila covers his body in purple (record; Book III ch. 22).

title: Ulrich von Jungingen
text:
Arc by book

Book II (Dec 1399): at the Marienburg window he hears the frozen Nogat sing, as the brothers sing Salve Regina, and tells his brother Konrad of the map of a Samogitia that is theirs on paper: “Next time we finish them.” (ch. 30; also ch. 19 mention).
Book III (1404-1410): at Raciąż he stands at the church door and tells Vytautas in clean Lithuanian that he swears beautifully, and that he is waiting (ch. 6, 1404); is named in Henė’s offer (“Ulrich will die in his bed, in agony”, ch. 8) which time contradicts; is elected the Sunday after Konrad’s death and descends into the warm Marienburg vaults without a flinch (ch. 11, 1407); sends the two swords before the battle (ch. 18); leads sixteen banners at Grunwald and dies (ch. 20, 15 July 1410); his body is brought to Marienburg two days later (ch. 22).

title: Ulrich von Jungingen
text:
Power & magic
Tier 0, with the Iron Saint’s gift (granted; iron_gift, graph tier 3 from 1407): fearlessness and tireless marching at the price of pity. His patron is Geležinis Šventasis, who stands on the field in person behind him at Grunwald. The cost shows as the missing doubt: the walls of Marienburg sweat with heat that he alone does not mind. His death does not end the Force; the Order survives as an ordinary state (Book III ch. 22).

title: Ulrich von Jungingen
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: Born 1360; komtur of Balga 1396-1404; Grand Marshal from 1404; Grand Master from 26 June 1407 after his brother Konrad died on 30 March 1407; killed on 15 July 1410 at Grunwald (Tannenberg), where about 203-211 of c. 270 brothers died too. Długosz says he fell to a blow from Mszczuj of Skrzynno; the Cronica conflictus names Dobiesław of Oleśnica. Before the battle, two heralds brought two swords to Jogaila and Vytautas (Długosz). His body was taken to Marienburg; Długosz says that Jogaila wept over it and had it covered in purple. See Wikipedia.
[Saga invention]: His Lithuanian conversation with Vytautas at Raciąż (ch. 6) and the Iron Saint behind him on the field; the Marienburg cellar scene (ch. 11); Henė’s prophecy. The record establishes the dates, the swords, and the death in the field; the saga picks no killer.

title: Ulrich von Jungingen
text:
Pronunciation
UL-rich fon JUN-gin-gen (/ˈʊlʁɪç fɔn ˈjʊŋɪŋən/), English respelling OOL-rikh fon YOONG-ing-en; in Lithuanian text Ulrichas fon Jungingenas. [world_rules/pronunciation_lexicon.json]

title: Ulrich von Jungingen
text:
Appearances
Book II: ch. 19, 30 (the Marienburg epilogue) and the afterword. Book III: ch. 6, 8, 11, 12, 18, 19, 20 (Geležies Mirtis), 22 and the afterword. His brother Konrad von Jungingen (Grand Master 1393-1407) is also named in Book II ch. 19.

title: Kaributas
text:
Summary
Kaributas (baptised Dmitry; Dmitry Korybut) is Jogaila’s half-brother and Algirdas’s son, Duke of Novhorod-Siverskyi in the Ruthenian south-east. He is a minor figure whose single act in the saga is off stage: his 1382 revolt pulls Kęstutis away from Vilnius while the Riga merchant Hanulas takes the city for Jogaila. He returns in Book II as the tired rebel who confesses that he sold nothing, because there was nothing to sell.

title: Kaributas
text:
Appearance & tells
Book II ch. 12 gives the only portrait: about thirty-five, broad-boned, grey at the temples, walking out to meet Vytautas on foot, without a sword, with two children and his wife behind him. He speaks Ruthenian in the gentle tone one uses with an invalid. His tell is resignation: he counts his fingers where others count horsemen.

title: Kaributas
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
To keep his own principality in the south-east, free of both Vilnius and Kraków.


Need (internal)
To stop choosing the losing brother and the losing cousin.


Lie they believe
That a minor prince can rebel safely if the stronger side is slow.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
That Vytautas does not kill his rivals; he removes them one by one, like teeth (Book II ch. 12).

title: Kaributas
text:
Arc by book

Book I (1382): an offstage campaign in the Severian land draws Kęstutis away from Vilnius in June (ch. 1, 2); Vytautas names the date as the moment when the Grand Duke’s mercy was repaid with a stab.
Book II (1393): the second wave of rebellions against Vytautas; he comes out on foot, disarmed, says he sold nothing, loses Novhorod-Siverskyi and is given a quieter holding in the south (ch. 12).
Book IV and V: appears only as the father of Žygimantas Kaributaitis, the Hussite claimant, whose captivity after Pabaiskas (1435) closes the line (Book IV ch. 12; Book V ch. 13).

title: Kaributas
text:
Power & magic
Tier 0. A Ruthenian prince with no gift and no bargain; his rebellions are conventional politics. The Pact’s clause about not shedding Gediminid blood protects him from Vytautas’s sword, which is why Vytautas chooses to dismantle his principality rather than his person (Book II ch. 12).

title: Kaributas
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: Born after 1350, baptised Dmitry (c. 1380), Prince of Novhorod-Siverskyi until 1393; his revolt there in 1382 drew Kęstutis away from Vilnius and so helped Jogaila retake it (en.wikipedia). He backed Jogaila in 1381-84 and 1389-92, but after the Ostrów Agreement (1392) refused to accept Vytautas, was beaten near Lida in 1393, held for a time and then given Zbarazh, Bratslav and Vinnytsia. He is last mentioned in 1404 during Vytautas’s Smolensk campaign. His son Sigismund Korybut (Žygimantas Kaributaitis) claimed the crown of Bohemia in the 1420s. See Wikipedia.
[Saga invention]: The disarmed surrender in Book II ch. 12 and the line about being taken “like teeth”; his word to Švitrigaila at the horses. None of it contradicts the record, which is silent on the scene.

title: Kaributas
text:
Pronunciation
ka-RI-bu-tas (/kɐˈrʲɪbʊtɐs/), English respelling kah-RIH-boo-tahs. The lexicon marks the stress as still to be verified against a native speaker. [world_rules/pronunciation_lexicon.json]

title: Kaributas
text:
Appearances
Book I: ch. 1 and 2 (the June 1382 campaign, mentioned). Book II: ch. 12 (Brothers’ Rations; the 1393 meeting). Book IV: ch. 12 (as father of Žygimantas Kaributaitis) and the afterword. Book V: ch. 13 (Pabaiskas) and the afterword. Not to be confused with Karigaila, another son of Algirdas.

title: Kęstutis
text:
Summary
Kęstutis (c. 1297-15 Aug 1382), Duke of Trakai, co-ruler of Lithuania with Algirdas, then with Jogaila. Captured at Lake Ublik on 21 Mar 1361, escaped from Marienburg on 11 Nov 1361; warned in Aug 1381 by Kuno von Liebenstein, took Vilnius in autumn 1381 while Jogaila was away; lured to Jogaila’s camp near Trakai and arrested on 3 Aug 1382, found dead at Krėva on 15 Aug.

title: Kęstutis
text:
Appearance & tells
A broad, gnarled man who in Book I looks like an old oak: wide shoulders made for chain mail and for carrying the defence of the whole west, hands thickened by the saddle and scarred white by fifty years of the Order’s war. By 1382 his hair and great beard are white and braided in the old fashion; in 1361, in the Marienburg cell, they are still grey and cropped short, and a scar on the left cheek drags the corner of his eye down (Book VI ch. 17). He dresses in bear fur and wears iron perkūnėliai (thunder-amulets) of Perkūnas, with the silver wolf at his neck and the boar-tusk sword at his side. His seat at Trakai is a plain oak chair worn smooth by his grandfather’s elbows (Book I ch. 1).
He speaks little and bluntly; German only roughly, “as a border duke who dislikes being cheated by languages”. He calls his son “Vyti” in private and nobody else may. His tells are a man who will not take back a move: he never swears what he does not mean (so he refuses baptism in 1361 and the abdication in 1382), and he looks at a danger and walks toward it with his eyes open. After he gives the Beggar his coin and receives a grey stone (Book I ch. 4), he rides to Jogaila’s camp knowing the road.

title: Kęstutis
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
To keep the Order out of Samogitia and the sacred flames lit; to hold the western half of the realm his brother Algirdas left in his care.


Need (internal)
To pass on to Vytautas the true price of the Pact (the unspoken Amber Debt) and to learn that a kinsman who has sold the realm cannot be ruled by mercy.


Lie they believe
Gediminid blood keeps faith: kin do not kill kin, so Jogaila can be spared and trusted (the family lie that Vytautas inherits as “honour and blood will keep us safe”).


Truth they learn (or refuse)
Blood without faith is no shield; he accepts it at Krėva, refusing to abdicate and walking to his death without breaking his word.

title: Kęstutis
text:
Arc by book

Book VI (1341-1377, protagonist). At about forty-four he lights his father Gediminas’s pyre (ch. 1) and in 1345 helps depose Jaunutis with Algirdas; that night at the Šventaragis fire he swears the Silent Pact and, while Algirdas hesitates, speaks the fire’s unspoken third clause aloud (ch. 4). He sees the 1347 martyrs hanged (ch. 6), loses his brother Narimantas at Strėva (2 Feb 1348, ch. 7), and pays the first Amber Debt (ch. 8). He takes Birutė as his wife c. 1350, in the staged abduction she asks for (ch. 10-11), gives the ox-oath of 1351 and slips away (ch. 13). Captured at Lake Ublik in March 1361, he refuses Kniprode’s offer of freedom for baptism (ch. 16-17) and escapes from Marienburg on 11 Nov with Alf’s help (ch. 18). Kaunas falls on Easter 1362 while he is too late (ch. 19); at Rudau (1370) the keeping of faith has not kept the land (ch. 24). He ends the book old, nearly eighty, after Algirdas dies in 1377 (ch. 28-30).
Book I (July-August 1382). The old boar at Trakai, who spared Jogaila in 1381 and is now tricked by his nephew: he rides to the camp near Trakai under Skirgaila’s safe-conduct (ch. 1-6), is arrested on 3 Aug, refuses to abdicate in the Krėva dungeon (ch. 8) and is strangled on 15 Aug (ch. 9). His body is burned in Vilnius with pagan rites (ch. 10); his death breaks the Pact’s clause against kin-blood.
Books II-IV (memory). His sword and silver wolf pass to Vytautas (the wolf through the Krėva stones, Book I ch. 8). Vytautas finds the boar-tusk sword in the Trakai vault (Book III ch. 2); it stands by his door at his death (Book IV ch. 29).
Book V (1430-1450). Žiežirba sees the 1345 night in the cracked pebble: the “elder brother hesitating” and Kęstutis speaking the Amber Debt aloud (ch. 5), and the keeper rides the road where Kęstutis rode (ch. 9).

title: Kęstutis
text:
Power & magic
Tier 0 (no gift), but he is a sworn oath-taker of the Silent Pact (1345) and is claimed by Perkūnas (Perkūno Rūstybė), who keeps the oath-breakers’ accounts. His sword carries a perkūnėlis ward under the grip that fails as the family’s oaths break (see Šerno kalavijas); the silver wolf amulet is the Pact’s token, passed to Vytautas (Sidabrinis vilkas). In the consecrated cellars of Marienburg Kalba cannot reach him, and Birutė’s amber goes cold (Book VI ch. 17). By giving the Beggar his coin (Book I ch. 4) he walks to Krėva seeing the whole road, which is a gift of foresight, not a working. The Krėva silence at his death is Henė’s Breath of the Void, not his own power (canon D11). The cost he pays is his own life and, with it, the Pact’s protection of the realm (the Silent Pact’s clause against kin-slaying breaks on 15 Aug 1382, canon D7).

title: Kęstutis
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: Capture 21 Mar 1361 at Lake Ublik; escape 11 Nov 1361 with Alfas; the 1381 coup; the arrest at the camp near Trakai (3 Aug 1382); death at Krėva (strangled per VLE; Jogaila said he hanged himself); the body burned in Vilnius.
[Saga invention]: The Beggar’s coin, the Pact and the silver wolf; Hohenstein as the third knight at Ublik.

title: Kęstutis
text:
Pronunciation
kęs-TU-tis · IPA /kʲæːsˈtʊtʲɪs/ · English sound-alike “kess-TOO-tis”. Stress on the second syllable; the ę is a long open e. Patronymic Kęstutaitis: kęs-tu-TAI-tis. In prose never “Kestus” or “Kęsto” (canon D4); “Vyti” belongs only to him and Birutė.

title: Kęstutis
text:
Appearances

Book I: ch. 1-11 (strongest in ch. 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 9), then in memory in ch. 14, 20, 22, 23, 28, 30.
Book II: ch. 1, 2, 9, 11, 19 (memory, the sword, the silver wolf).
Book III: ch. 2 (the sword found), ch. 20.
Book IV: ch. 15, 16, 21, 25, 27.
Book V: ch. 2, 3, 5 (the 1345 oath), 6, 8-10, 12, 15, 19, 21, 22, 24, 29.
Book VI: protagonist in ch. 1-8, 10, 12-14, 16-22, 24-26, 28-30 (ch. 9, 11, 15, 23 and 27 follow other viewpoints).

Continuity: the 1361 capture is in March at Lake Ublik; the escape is on 11 Nov (Book VI ch. 16-18, matching Book I ch. 8). Birutė’s sons Vytautas, Žygimantas and Tautvilas are his; Vaidotas and Butautas belong to an earlier wife (canon D11).

title: Winrich von Kniprode
text:
Summary
Winrich von Kniprode (c. 1310 - 24 Jun 1382), Grand Master of the Teutonic Order from 1351 until his death, the longest-serving of all Masters and the architect of the Order’s golden age. In the saga he is Book VI’s mortal antagonist: a sincere, patient chess-player who studies Kęstutis like a problem, wins at Kaunas (1362) and Rudau (1370), and is a worthy enemy rather than a monster. He dies on 24 Jun 1382, six weeks before Kęstutis is murdered at Krėva, so he never meets Vytautas; his successor Zöllner receives the fugitive instead.

title: Winrich von Kniprode
text:
Appearance & tells
A grand master in the plain white mantle of the Order who carries his own chessboard across the Marienburg courtyard rather than let a servant jolt the pieces, “as one carries a child or a testament” (Book VI ch. 17). The game on it stands as it stood three nights earlier: a white queen on the left, black knights by the lake, six white-cloaked men on the shore and a single black king. He has read reports about Kęstutis for ten years and is surprised to find only an old man, broad, tired, scarred, with a short grey beard. His tells are courtesy and patience: he leaves a prisoner a small amber bead because “amber is a Prussian coin, not an idol”, lets the Lithuanian servant Alf speak Samogitian to the prisoner, and answers Kęstutis’s thanks for the chessboard with a calm nod. He knows he will one day lie in the chapel beside the former masters, behind the wall of the cell, and has never decided whether the thought comforts him.

title: Winrich von Kniprode
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
The Order’s golden age: the Reise turned into Christendom’s tournament, Samogitia and Lithuania subdued or baptised, the Order secure.


Need (internal)
To see that the ‘problem’ he is solving is a man, and that some opponents cannot be moved by a better position.


Lie they believe
A patient player wins every contest in the end: Kęstutis can be broken, bargained with or baptised.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
Kęstutis ‘never takes back a move’: he will not swear what he does not mean, so Kniprode’s best offer is refused, and even victory at Rudau leaves the war as it was.

title: Winrich von Kniprode
text:
Arc by book

Book VI (1352-1370). Takes over after Grand Master Dusemer; studies Kęstutis across the border and makes the Reise a tournament of English and French guests (ch. 14, POV chapter); receives Kęstutis, taken by chance in March 1361, offers him freedom for baptism and gets a refusal in the Marienburg cellars (ch. 17, POV); loses him to Alf’s escape on 11 Nov (ch. 18); takes Kaunas on Easter 1362 after a five-week siege (ch. 19); at Rudau, 17 Feb 1370, he raises a hand “like a chess player whose opponent has made an unexpected, interesting move” (ch. 24).
Book I (1382). Dead already: “the old Master Winrich von Kniprode died in the summer”, and the chapter elects Zöllner in his place (ch. 18).
Books II-III. Remembered as the standard against which the Order measures itself: Konrad von Jungingen speaks of the lands Kniprode “could only dream of” (Book II ch. 30), and the Marienburg Samogitian oak beam is “from Kniprode’s time” (Book III ch. 11).

title: Winrich von Kniprode
text:
Power & magic
Tier 0, no gift and no bargain. He commands the Order, whose consecrated halls and sword make Kalba fail: Birutė’s amber goes cold in the Marienburg cellars where he holds Kęstutis (Book VI ch. 17). The mythic antagonist of Book VI, the Geležinis Šventasis (Iron Saint), gathers around the Order’s prayers, but Kniprode is not its creature; his honesty is why he is the saga’s best portrait of a sincere enemy. He pays no magical price.

title: Winrich von Kniprode
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: Born c. 1310 at Kniprath (now Monheim am Rhein); Grand Commander before 1351; commanded with Marshal Siegfried von Dahnenfeld at Strėva (2 Feb 1348, VLE); elected Grand Master in 1351 (some sources 1352) and held the office for 31 years, the longest on record. Held Kęstutis, captured at Lake Ublik in March 1361, at Marienburg for about half a year until the escape of 11 Nov 1361; the Order under him besieged and took Kaunas (13 Mar - 17 Apr 1362); the Order won at Rudau on 17 Feb 1370 (Marshal Henning Schindekop died of his wounds), a victory credited by the Order to the Virgin Mary. He enlarged Marienburg and founded the Augustinian convent at Heiligenbeil. Died 24 Jun 1382 and was buried in the chapel of St Anne at Marienburg (en.wikipedia; VLE). Succeeded by Konrad Zöllner von Rotenstein (5 Oct 1382).
[Saga invention]: The chessboard and the cell talks with Kęstutis; the amber bead left to the prisoner; the invented young Order brother Günther von Hohenstein at his side (Book VI); his raised hand at Rudau. The English and French guests and the “Table of Honour” of the 1350s are left as flavour (not verified for the period). The record says nothing of any personal encounter between Kniprode and Kęstutis beyond the capture and escape.

title: Winrich von Kniprode
text:
Pronunciation
VIN-rikh fon KNEE-proh-deh · IPA /ˈvɪnʁɪç fɔn ˈkniːpʁoːdə/ · English sound-alike “VIN-rikh fon KNEE-proh-deh”. German; stress on the first syllable of each name. The Lithuanian text writes Winrichas fon Kniprodė.

title: Krivis of Šventaragis
text:
Summary
The Krivis of Šventaragis (Krivių Krivaitis), high priest of the Šventaragis valley at Vilnius, keeper of the eternal flame and of the Silent Pact. He is a saga invention built on a debated historical office: the saga names him Sirvydas, a name he gave to the fire the day he inherited the crooked staff (the krivulė) and has not used since (Book VI ch. 8). He binds Algirdas and Kęstutis in the Tylioji Sutartis in 1345, pays the first Amber Debt in 1348, sends the last vaidilutė Eglė to answer Jogaila’s captain in 1382, and, when the fire is put out in February-March 1387, speaks the Pact’s ending aloud (“Sutartis baigta”) and walks into the felled grove. He is an honest broker who keeps a dishonest silence: he never told the people what the Pact would cost.

title: Krivis of Šventaragis
text:
Appearance & tells
In Book VI he is grey-haired, “not old, but already one from whom the fire has taken everything not needed”: sunken cheeks, smoke-reddened eyes, hands rough as pine bark. His krivulė, a crooked staff “crooked as a river’s bend”, is black from a hundred years of touching and remembers every oath sworn while it was held. By 1382 he is very old, with white hair to his waist, a linen robe with a belt of woven perkūnėliai, and eyes red from sixty years at the fire. He asks nothing and announces nothing; he simply steps up to the logs and lifts the staff. His tell is silence: when Kęstutis asks whether the Pact demanded the hanging of the Orthodox martyrs in 1347 (ch. 6), he does not answer; when the 1369 friars are killed (ch. 23) he keeps his silence again. He is afraid of the Duke’s captain in 1382 and sends a young priestess in his place.

title: Krivis of Šventaragis
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
To keep the eternal flame lit and the Pact kept, so that the gods hold Lithuania unconquered while a Gediminid tends the fire.


Need (internal)
To say the price aloud: to tell the people, not only the two princes, what the Amber Debt is.


Lie they believe
A priest who says everything at once dies that night, so silence protects the Pact (the old Krivis’s second lesson, which Sirvydas learned better than the first).


Truth they learn (or refuse)
He does speak the last line: ‘Sutartis baigta’ at the 1387 fire, ‘so that the spirits of place hear it from a human mouth and not from a priest’, and walks into the grove without resisting.

title: Krivis of Šventaragis
text:
Arc by book

Book VI (1341-1377). The young pupil carrying the ash-pot at Gediminas’s pyre (ch. 1); inherits the staff from the old Krivis, who taught him that the fire does not ask and that a priest who tells everything at once dies the same night. In 1345 he receives the two brothers at the tall, unmoving fire and binds them in the Silent Pact; the third clause, royal blood for land lost, goes unspoken until Kęstutis says it aloud (ch. 4). He keeps silence over the martyrs of 1347 (ch. 6), names the first Amber Debt at Narimantas’s pyre in 1348 while a black dog (Henė’s small shape) sits watching (ch. 8), and again keeps silence in 1369 (ch. 23). He stands at Algirdas’s pyre in 1377 (ch. 29).
Book I (1382-1387). Offstage in 1382: sends Eglė to give Jogaila’s captain the prophecy (prologue) and is called to Kęstutis’s pyre (ch. 10). On 15 Aug 1382 he feels the Pact’s second clause break. In February-March 1387, as the king’s men pour buckets on the Gabija fire, he stays at the flame and says “Sutartis baigta” (ch. 29); then he is not seen again.
Book V (1345, 1439). Seen in the 1345 flashback in the cracked pebble (ch. 5); the last žynys (Galminas’s pupil) still knows his words (ch. 11), and Žiežirba, repeating “the last line of the Krivis” in the cathedral crypt in 1439, hears the vault answer only “girdi” (“it hears”, ch. 20; the last žynys’s song in ch. 27).

title: Krivis of Šventaragis
text:
Power & magic
Tier 4, the highest: all five elements, able to bind a Senovės Sutartis, able to speak with the Forces but not to command one (world_rules/power_systems.md). He rarely casts: his power is binding and the oath-memory of the flame and the krivulė. The fire in him, which has never wholly gone out since Vėlinės, shrinks when it counts the blood owed (Book VI ch. 8). His costs are his name (given to the fire when he took the staff), the silence on which his office rests, and, in 1387, his own disappearance with the flame. He is one of the “tier-4 practitioners” (six in 1341, falling to four by 1382).

title: Krivis of Šventaragis
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: The Lithuanian high priest is a debated figure. Peter of Dusburg describes a Prussian high priest (Criwe) at Romuva, and whether Lithuania had a single high priest is unclear; the sixteenth-century chronicles make Lizdeika high priest under Gediminas (the Lizdeika legend of the Iron Wolf dream); ethnography records the krivulė staff that summoned village assemblies. Długosz describes the Vilnius sacred fire, grove and snakes destroyed in 1387 at Jogaila’s baptism of the Lithuanians (the Vilnius bishopric was founded on 17 Feb 1387). No source names a Krivis of Vilnius.
[Saga invention]: Everything personal: the name Sirvydas, the 1345 Pact binding, the three Amber Debt clauses, his silence over the 1347 martyrs, the 1348 Debt at Narimantas’s pyre, his sending Eglė in 1382, the words “Sutartis baigta” and his disappearance in 1387. He is a Saga invention on folk ground; the open questions (lineage from Lizdeika; whether he passed the last ember to Galminas or Kalvis carried it) are in world_rules/religion_and_clergy.md.

title: Krivis of Šventaragis
text:
Pronunciation
KRI-vis · IPA /ˈkrʲɪvʲɪs/ · English sound-alike “KRIH-vis” (the title: “krivis”, Krivių Krivaitis, the Krivis of the Krivis). His private name Sirvydas is not in the lexicon; derived: SIR-vy-das · /ˈsʲɪrvʲiːdɐs/ · “SIHR-vee-dahs”. Krivulė (the staff): KRI-vu-lė.

title: Krivis of Šventaragis
text:
Appearances

Book I: ch. 10 (called to the pyre, mentioned), 29 (the extinguishing).
Book II: ch. 3 (his warning comes true, as the Unburned rise from the felled grove).
Book V: ch. 5 (the 1345 oath), 11, 20, 27.
Book VI: ch. 1, 3-8, 10, 12, 15, 23, 26, 29.

Continuity: persona says old in 1382 (“he bound the Pact thirty-seven years earlier”), while Book VI ch. 8 gives him a young grey-haired priest in 1348; the world graph dates him c. 1310-1387.

title: Marquard von Salzbach
text:
Summary
Marquard von Salzbach, komtur of Ragnit and later of Brandenburg, is Vytautas’s captive of July 1384, his adviser in 1389 and then his enemy: he signs the Treaty of Lyck (1390), helps negotiate Salynas (1398), fights at the Vorskla (1399), insults Birutė after the Peace of Raciąż (1404, not 1390) and is beheaded by Vytautas after Grunwald for refusing to apologise.

title: Marquard von Salzbach
text:
Appearance & tells
A komtur with a wind-burned face and a voice that begins to sing as soon as he has drunk his third horn. He speaks Lithuanian better than any other Order brother, a fluency earned when Vytautas held him prisoner and fed him as a guest, and he uses it as a weapon: at Lyck he raises his cup in Lithuanian, “to my old host”, before the hostages; at Raciąż he again speaks in Lithuanian “so that all who ought to understand will understand”. He wears armour “like a skin” (Book III ch. 21), is broad-shouldered, and always smiles at what he takes for a toast. His honesty is his tell: at the stump on the evening after Grunwald he neither dodges Vytautas’s eyes nor begs for mercy.

title: Marquard von Salzbach
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
To serve the Order and be proved right about Vytautas, the betrayer; to keep the Order’s hold on Samogitia.


Need (internal)
To account for his old friendship with the man he now humiliates: he is the saga’s picture of a friend turned into an enemy by the Order’s cause.


Lie they believe
Vytautas is a traitor who will never be loyal, so insulting him costs nothing.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
Refused: at the stump he answers Vytautas’s question with a flat ‘I remember’ and ‘That it’s a pity’, and pays the price without complaint.

title: Marquard von Salzbach
text:
Arc by book

Book II (1390-1399). At the Lyck feast in January 1390, as komtur of Ragnit and the old friend of his former captor, he toasts “my old host” and says he is paying back a debt: Vytautas’s wife, children and brother “will eat at my table and sleep under the Order’s keys”. Vytautas answers quietly in Lithuanian, “I will remember that” (ch. 6). In July 1399 he brings the Order’s knights to the Vorskla under the Salynas treaty, “some say one and a half thousand horse” (ch. 22), and fights openly at the eastern wagons, where the chronicler later counts nine Order dead and names Marquard among the rescued (ch. 26).
Book III (1404-1410). At the Raciąż feast he raises a cup to “the witch” who could not be swallowed by the sea, Birutė; Vytautas answers “Aš tai prisiminsiu” for the second time (ch. 6). In spring 1410, at Palanga, the Amber Queen names him through the pebble: “Marquard raised a cup for me at Raciążek” (ch. 14). After the battle, on the night of 15-16 July 1410, Vytautas has him and Heinrich Schaumburg beheaded at a stump for the insult he refuses to apologise for (ch. 21).

title: Marquard von Salzbach
text:
Power & magic
Tier 0. No gift. His fluency in Lithuanian is the only “power” he uses, to wound; the Amber Queen’s response is not his to feel. His beheading at Grunwald is the Queen’s son answering the insult on the field of the Iron Saint (Book III ch. 21).

title: Marquard von Salzbach
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: En.wikipedia (Marquard von Salzbach; Ekdahl 1992 pp. 58-59; Urban 2003): after Raciąż (1404) he insulted Vytautas by attacking his murdered mother Birutė; at Grunwald, as komtur of Brandenburg, he was beheaded with Heinrich Schaumburg. At the Vorskla he brought a force (1,600 horse is unconfirmed); Posilge lists nine of the Order dead and names Marquard among the rescued.
[Saga invention]: His velvet threat to the hostages at Lyck (“grąžinu skolą”; Book II ch. 6) and Vytautas’s “Aš tai prisiminsiu”; the toast to “the witch” Birutė at the Order’s feast after Raciąż (Book III ch. 6).

title: Marquard von Salzbach
text:
Pronunciation
MAR-kvart fon ZALTS-bakh · IPA /ˈmaʁkvaʁt fɔn ˈzaltsbax/ · English sound-alike “MAR-kvart fon ZAHLTS-bahkh”. German; the Lithuanian text writes Markvardas fon Zalcbachas. Not in the pronunciation lexicon; derived from its conventions for German names.

text:

Book III: ch. 6 (Raciąż), 14 (the Amber Queen names him), 21 (the beheading) and the afterword.

Continuity: the insult to Birutė is dated 1404 (Raciąż), not 1390; at Lyck (1390) he issues only a velvet threat to the hostages. At the Vorskla the Order fights openly under him (Posilge: nine dead).

title: Zbigniew Oleśnicki
text:
Summary
Zbigniew Oleśnicki (5 Dec 1389 - 1 Apr 1455), royal secretary, Bishop of Kraków (1423) and cardinal, is the mortal antagonist of Book IV: brilliant, devout and utterly sure that Lithuania must not become a kingdom. He is a statesman, not a cartoon: he fears two crowns, the Order, the Hussites and the Turks, and he is not wrong to stop Vytautas’s coronation, by his lights. He wins: the crown embassy is blocked at the border in August 1430 (the record), and Vytautas dies uncrowned. In Book V he is the shadow regent of Poland who swears Žygimantas in for the king at Grodno and keeps the young Jagiellonians in line.

title: Zbigniew Oleśnicki
text:
Appearance & tells
Usually in clerical robes but carrying himself like a general, with a sharp, clean-shaven face and deep-set, intelligent eyes: “the cross in his hand and the sword in his heart”. At twenty-two in the royal chancery (Book III ch. 30) he sits with his back to the wall so that he can see the door, a habit from his student years that became something else on 15 July 1410, and he brews the chancery’s ink himself (oak galls, iron sulphate, Arabic gum, “a little too much wine”). On his desk lies a coin that is always warm; it grows hotter when he is most certain, and he picked it up fourteen years earlier from the purse of a cut-open knight and long ago stopped trying to explain it. He is inflexible: once he has set a course, gold and threats do not move him.

title: Zbigniew Oleśnicki
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
Polish supremacy in the union: to keep Lithuania and Ruthenia under the Polish crown and block any independent Lithuanian kingdom.


Need (internal)
To fear less: to see that stopping a crown can be the same fear that the Order and the Hussites exploit.


Lie they believe
Lithuania must not be a kingdom: ‘I need him not to have time.’


Truth they learn (or refuse)
Left to the reader: he wins every move (1430, 1432, 1440), and the saga lets him be right on his own terms.

title: Zbigniew Oleśnicki
text:
Arc by book

Book III (1409-1411). A twenty-year-old royal secretary at the Brest council (Dec 1409, ch. 13); at Grunwald he saves Jogaila from a German knight’s charge with a broken spear (ch. 20, after Długosz); in the epilogue “Ink” (ch. 30, 1411) he sits at the chancery, a warm coin on his desk, and says to himself, “The sword did its work. Now the ink must do ours.”
Book IV (1413-1430). At Horodło in 1413 (ch. 2); Bishop of Kraków in 1423 as the king’s sons are born and the lords sell their succession for privileges, he is “devout and right on his own terms”, the coin warmest on his desk (ch. 14). At Lutsk he opposes the crown (ch. 18-19). In 1429-30 he writes, pays and argues to stop the coronation; his envoy Baltramiejus Rogala wears Henė’s golden chain and is sent to stop the crown at the Noteć ford (ch. 20, 23); he arrives in Lithuania with Jogaila in October 1430 (ch. 24). The “Gold-Glutton” works through his seals and ledgers, though he serves it unknowingly.
Book V (1430-1447). He is the king’s voice, the only one whose words reach the deaf Jogaila “whole, without holes”: beside him through Jadwiga’s death in 1431 (ch. 6) and the last illness of 1434 (ch. 12). At Grodno in 1432 he reads the king’s act in Latin and receives Žygimantas’s oath for life (ch. 10); his letters to Žygimantas are the politest ones, and the Grodno rope ends in Kraków (ch. 18). His black-wax seal (“so the council decided”) runs the childhood of Casimir (ch. 23), and at Casimir’s coronation feast in 1447 he raises a cup “like a man who has lost a game and is preparing for the next” (ch. 26).

title: Zbigniew Oleśnicki
text:
Power & magic
Tier 0; a statesman, not a sorcerer. The Gold-Glutton (Aukso Rijūnas) prospers around his ledgers, seals and the warm coin on his desk, and the golden chain from Krėva resurfaces on one of his envoys (world_rules/power_systems.md §5), but he serves neither knowingly. He believes superstition is an error, not a sin: told that the chain may be cursed, he orders it worn until September and then given to the cathedral with a Mass “for the one who wore it” (Book IV ch. 20). The cost of his skill falls on others: Vytautas’s last years, Rogala’s silent inhale, and the Lithuanian line he out-waits.

title: Zbigniew Oleśnicki
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: Born 5 Dec 1389 at Sienno; royal secretary to Jogaila; fought at Grunwald (15 Jul 1410), where Długosz makes him the rescuer of Jogaila with a broken spear; Bishop of Kraków from 9 Jul 1423 (consecrated 19 Dec 1423), appointed cardinal on 18 Dec 1439 by Eugene IV (the antipope Felix V also named him in 1440); died 1 Apr 1455 at Sandomierz. Leading opponent of Vytautas’s coronation, present at Lutsk (Jan 1429), sent with Mikołaj Białucha to Vytautas at Grodno in the autumn of 1429, and came to Lithuania with Jogaila in October 1430; Szybkowski places him elsewhere at the Łęczyca council in August 1430. He opposed the Hussites and invited Capistrano to Kraków; in the 1430s he fought Spytko III of Melsztyn (d. 4 May 1439 at Grotniki); effective regent for Władysław III, whom he backed in taking the Hungarian crown and the crusade that ended at Varna (10 Nov 1444); then managed Poland while Casimir IV was in Lithuania. At Grodno (15 Oct 1432) he received Žygimantas Kęstutaitis’s oath in the king’s name. Sources: Catholic-Hierarchy; en.wikipedia (cardinal); VLE; Długosz; Szybkowski 2010, Bar 2017.
[Saga invention]: The warm coin, the “Polish fear” speech (“I need him not to have time”), the golden chain that reaches him through Rogala, the ink-brewing and door-watching tells, and his private conversation with Vytautas at Lutsk in which he says he prays for the duke’s long life because he fears what follows him. The record does not say who intercepted the crown or how: the saga’s chest of dry leaves and Rogala are invention.

title: Zbigniew Oleśnicki

Pronunciation
ZBIG-nyef o-lesh-NEETS-kee · IPA /ˈzbʲiɡɲɛf ɔlɛɕˈɲit͡skʲi/ · English sound-alike “ZBEEG-nyef oh-lesh-NEETS-kee”. Polish. In Lithuanian text Zbignevas Olesnickis (the standard form, VLE).

title: Pilkoji (the Grey One, Vilkų Motina)
text:
Summary
Pilkoji (the Grey One), last Mother of the wolves (Vilkų Motina), born c. 1365 (Q13), the first sworn woman; keeps the silver wolf and the pebble from Vytautas’s body from 27 Oct to Kūčios (24 Dec) 1430, then gives both to the Flame-Keeper Žiežirba. She lies down in the oldest bog of the Dykra with the Iron Wolf’s skull on Vėlinės, 2 Nov 1449 (Book V ch. 28).

title: Pilkoji (the Grey One, Vilkų Motina)
text:
Appearance & tells
A village woman called Pilkoji, “the Grey One”, not for her hair but for the ash she has carried in her apron pocket since childhood, a fistful from her mother’s hearth renewed each spring from her own. At thirty-eight, when we first see her (Book III ch. 7), her palms are grey to the wrists and her scarf and clothes are grey; she knew the weight of everyone in Kalniškės, having lifted nearly all of them from bed to bench and bench to bier. Sworn into the wolves, she is shorter than the men, with grey hair cropped at the neck and a wolf pelt not cut for her, her palms grey to the elbow as if she had dipped them in an ash-pot and never taken them out; she does not speak, her eyes do not turn away where the men’s do, and she blinks only when the fire blinks (ch. 9). At seventy she sits on a fallen trunk with a bag of ash and watches Pabaiskas “as a midwife watches a birth that is not hers” (Book V ch. 13). At eighty-four she has become what the wolves call šaknis, root: hard, dried, dark, with joints that no longer bend and hair “white as a layer of ash”, the same pelt she has worn for forty-five years on her shoulders, “no longer her size, but no longer foreign” (Book V ch. 28). She lays a table at Vėlinės for the dead, with a place for each, and her gesture of mourning is to put out bread, a clay bowl of oat kisiel and a cup of black bog water.

title: Pilkoji (the Grey One, Vilkų Motina)
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
In 1404: to feed and keep company with her dead. Later: to keep the wolves alive and the flame’s promise kept, and to carry the names of those who are gone.


Need (internal)
To let go of the carrying: to name the dead to the bog and lie down with them.


Lie they believe
Someone has to keep remembering, or the dead are lost: she carries Eglė’s four names, Pušis’s and Kirmėlė’s, and the lost face of her sister Dalia.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
The bog asks ‘who are they?’ and she answers; when the last of her people are named she lies down with the Iron Wolf’s skull and is released (Book V ch. 28).

title: Pilkoji (the Grey One, Vilkų Motina)
text:
Arc by book

Book III (1404-1411). The village midwife of Kalniškės (b. c. 1365-66): her husband drowned in the Dubysa seven years earlier and her fourteen-year-old daughter died that September; on Vėlinės 1404 she lays a table for three, opens the door, and the village’s dead rise and walk the frost-white street. She follows them into the Dykra and the Root-Mother takes her into the krikštas against all custom: the first woman sworn (ch. 7). She stands at Žiežirba’s baptism in 1405 (ch. 9), runs with the wolves in the Grunwald vanguard (ch. 15-21) and sits at the Rasos fire in 1411 (ch. 29).
Book IV (1415-1430). After the baptised wolves split off, the bog chooses her as the first Vilkų Motina, Mother of the wolves: she lies in the bog with Spyglys and Šiurpas and names every name she carries until the bog lets them all go (ch. 6). She burns the unburied dead with the pack and sees a faint Eglė show them the bog road home (ch. 16); at the vault door with feast-day iron she nearly “enters” (ch. 22) and runs west as a wolf to the Polish border, the ford and the dry leaves of the crown chest (ch. 23); Eglė, losing her last names, leaves them with her (ch. 27), and Vytautas wills her the silver wolf and pebble for Žiežirba (ch. 28).
Book V (1430-1450). On Kūčios 1430 she lays the fifteenth bowl for Vytautas and gives Žiežirba the silver wolf and the cracked pebble (ch. 7). She holds a bog for a day and a week at Pabaiskas and then lets go (ch. 13), spends the winter burning the unburned dead with the last dozen wolves (ch. 16), and on Vėlinės, 2 Nov 1449, aged 84, lies down in the oldest bog of the Dykra beside the Iron Wolf’s skull, after naming the wolves buried there (ch. 28).

title: Pilkoji (the Grey One, Vilkų Motina)
text:
Power & magic
A vilkatė of the Iron Wolves, sworn through the bog baptism (the krikštas) in 1404; she can take wolf shape (sworn twenty years or more, per canon D10), carries the names of the dead, and holds a marsh against horsemen by the Root-Mother’s leave. Her office is the Vilkų Motina, the only one: the bog chooses her, and she alone can say the dead’s names to it. Costs paid: her sister Dalia’s face, lost while carrying Eglė’s names; a burn on her palm from the feast-day iron at the vault door; the Mother’s cold each time she lies down; and finally her life, for the pack she buries. She keeps the silver wolf and the pebble from Vytautas’s body from 27 Oct to Kūčios 1430 (world_rules/iron_wolves.md).

title: Pilkoji (the Grey One, Vilkų Motina)
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: No such person in the record.
[Saga invention]: Everything: her village’s dead rose in 1404; she carries Eglė’s four names; she is 84 in 1449.

title: Pilkoji (the Grey One, Vilkų Motina)
text:
Pronunciation
pil-KO-ji · IPA /pʲɪlˈkoːjɪ/ · English sound-alike “pil-KOH-yih”. Not in the pronunciation lexicon; derived from its conventions. Pilkoji is the definite adjective “the grey one”. The names she carries from Eglė (Book IV hand-off) include the Šventaragis valley, Mantas, Vykintė and the pine Žalioji.

title: Rimgailė (Palanga fisherwoman)
text:
Summary
Rimgailė, a Palanga fisherwoman (about sixty in 1450), receives the silver wolf from the dying keeper “bread for bread” and puts it under her threshold; her granddaughter Gedvilė’s line sweeps the statue’s stone (Book V ch. 25, 29, 30).

title: Rimgailė (Palanga fisherwoman)
text:
Appearance & tells
A grey-haired fisherman’s wife, wrapped in a shawl, with a small knife in her hand and a loaf under her arm; her face has barely changed in twenty years, only tightened a little round the eyes, attentive and waiting “as if she already knew that now it would not be as before” (Book V ch. 25). She wipes her hands on her apron after kneading, kneels on the sand with a palm on the amber where the kneeling woman’s breast would be, and says little. She lays the Kūčios table for twelve dishes, with hay under the cloth, and always one more place than there are guests: an empty plate, a spoon and a small knife with a bent handle (ch. 29). She is about sixty in 1450 (b. c. 1390). Her kitchen knife is smith’s iron, the kind the wolves burn with; she does not know it.

title: Rimgailė (Palanga fisherwoman)
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
To keep her family and her village fed and safe, and to keep the old courtesies to the dead (the extra place at Kūčios).


Need (internal)
To tell someone what her mother taught her: that Vytautas was the kneeling woman’s son and that it cost her.


Lie they believe
A fisherman’s wife’s knowledge is only a mother’s saying: ‘my mother knew’, but it can’t change anything.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
Her bread-for-bread keeping of a stranger’s wolf, and the stone that Gedvilė sweeps every morning ‘and no one will know why’, are how the knowledge survives without being understood.

title: Rimgailė (Palanga fisherwoman)
text:
Arc by book

Book V, ch. 25 (1445). At Palanga, when the fishermen find the amber kneeling woman no longer glowing and the news of Varna and of Vasily II’s blinding arrives, she speaks to her husband Dargis about the woman at the shore: “My mother said Vytautas was her son, and that he never found out how much it cost her.”
Book V, ch. 29 (Dec 1449 - Mar 1450). When the dying keeper (Žiežirba) comes to Palanga, she finds him at the fire with the white line on his throat, takes him in and watches him age in a day and a night. At Kūčios she lays places for the wolves, for Vytautas (“their prince”, to whom no one set a place), and, at his request, for his unnamed mother, the one who called him Žiežirba; she accepts the silver wolf “bread for bread” (“I will not take it” - “You will; that is how wolves do it”) and lays it under her threshold. He dies in early March, as the ice breaks, with his warm hand in hers.
Book V, ch. 30 (1553). The wolf worn under a shirt by her great-grandson and her granddaughter Gedvilė’s sweeping of the stone are her legacy.

title: Rimgailė (Palanga fisherwoman)
text:
Power & magic
Tier 0, no gift. She keeps the old courtesies without knowing their source and carries the silver wolf under her threshold, which makes her the unwitting last holder of the Pact’s token, until Gedvilė’s line carries it on (Book V ch. 29-30). The one magical sign near her is that Gedvilė’s stone is swept every morning and the sweeper never knows why.

title: Rimgailė (Palanga fisherwoman)

[Saga invention]: All of her.
