title: Skirgaila
text:
Summary
Skirgaila (c. 1354-11 Jan 1397), Duke of Trakai from 1382 (until 1392), Jogaila’s governor (regent) of Lithuania from 13 Mar 1386, took Polotsk in April 1387, held Kyiv from 1395; died in Kyiv, circumstances unclear.

title: Skirgaila
text:
Appearance & tells
A strong, martial man who is seen in armour even off the field, with a cold, calculating face, “the look of a man who knows where the bodies are buried, because he put them there”, and a prominent scar across his knuckles. At five he is a small, thin, dark-haired boy staring distrustfully at Vytautas and talking about armour (Book VI ch. 26); at twenty-eight he is the family’s “iron hand”, loyal, brutal and never thanked. In Book II he is red-faced and wet with drink, hands that do not know where to put themselves, drunk on Trakai and on being the regent; he feasts in Kęstutis’s hall with Kęstutis’s rusting sword on the wall (Book II ch. 1).
His tells are the oath and the cup: the safe-conduct he swears on Perkūnas in Book I and breaks, and the alternating bouts of drinking, explosive violence and deep depression. Once Henė holds his stone he juggles it, or is juggled, in dreams (Book III ch. 27).

title: Skirgaila
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
Security and recognition: to make Jogaila’s throne absolute and be seen as more than ‘the hands’; Trakai is the prize he finally gets.


Need (internal)
To be valued without having to earn it with another man’s crimes, and to act for himself rather than as someone’s instrument.


Lie they believe
The survival of the dynasty justifies any crime, and a loyal servant will be rewarded for it.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
He is a tool the Shadow-Seller will use and discard: the price of his bargain is to be used up, and Henė collects it in Kyiv in January 1397.

title: Skirgaila
text:
Arc by book

Book VI (prequel). A five-year-old at Kęstutis’s fire in 1359, boasting about armour (ch. 26); Algirdas’s son and Jogaila’s elder brother, brought up in the Orthodox, Ruthenian court of Uliana of Tver.
Book I (1382-1387), the hands. He gives the safe-conduct oath on Perkūnas under which Kęstutis and Vytautas ride to Jogaila’s camp near Trakai (ch. 5-6) and breaks it by seizing them on 3 Aug 1382; his men massacre the loyal guard in the tents (ch. 7) and he is believed to have ordered the strangling (ch. 8-9). He releases Ona to track Vytautas, hunts him through the Dykra (ch. 12-15), and at the 1384 settlement keeps Trakai (ch. 28-28b), “the villain wins the land”. In the Krėva cell in 1387 he meets Henė with three stones, one wobbling (ch. 30).
Book II (1387-1397), Henė’s puppet. Regent and Duke of Trakai, drunk and jealous in Kęstutis’s hall (ch. 1); he holds Vilnius against Vytautas and the Order in 1390 (ch. 7), loses Trakai and the regency at Ostrów in August 1392 (ch. 10), is compensated with Kyiv (ch. 13) and dies there on 11 Jan 1397 (ch. 16). Henė drops the first stone (three become two).
Book III-IV (afterlife). His Kyiv court hides Kęstutis’s sword among twelve identical chests (Book III ch. 2); his shade stands in Jogaila’s guilty dream and speaks with Henė’s voice (Book III ch. 27); the Krėva secret is finally said aloud in Henė’s voice through “Skirgaila’s mouth” in Book IV ch. 26.
Book V: a memory in the Krėva guilt (ch. 12, 15, 19).

title: Skirgaila
text:
Power & magic
Tier 0; his power is bought. At Krėva in 1387 he bargains with the Shadow-Seller, and the price is “to be used and discarded”; one of Henė’s three blackened stones is his (world_rules/power_systems.md §5). The cost shows in his drinking and his moods, and when the bargain is collected in Kyiv (11 Jan 1397) Henė’s hand count falls from three stones to two. His broken safe-conduct oath (sworn on Perkūnas, August 1382) draws the god’s enmity to his line (power_systems.md §2.6). The poisoning rumour around his death is mundane herb-lore if true (§2.4); the saga never says who did it.

title: Skirgaila
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: Duke of Trakai 1382-92 (VLE); governor from 13 Mar 1386 (Frost 2015; VLE gives 1387); Polotsk Mar/Apr 1387; lost to Vytautas at Ostrów (1392); died 11 Jan 1397 (infobox 8 Jan), ill after a hunt, “some sources” poison; no chronicle names a monk.
[Saga invention]: The safe-conduct oath on Perkūnas, the book of names, Henė’s stone, the monk Pachomijus (Book II).

title: Skirgaila
text:
Pronunciation
skir-GAI-la · IPA /skʲɪrˈɡɐɪɫɐ/ · English sound-alike “skihr-GUY-lah”. Stress on the second syllable (the diphthong ai as in “guy”). Orthodox name Ivan; baptised Catholic Kazimierz in 1386.

title: Skirgaila
text:
Appearances

Book I: ch. 1-10, 12, 13, 15-19, 21, 28, 28b, 30.
Book II: ch. 1, 5-7, 9-13, 15-17, 20, 29 and the afterword.
Book III: ch. 2, 5, 8, 24, 27.
Book IV: ch. 21, 24, 26, 29.
Book V: ch. 6, 12, 15, 19, 24 (memory and Henė’s reckoning).
Book VI: ch. 15, 26, 29.

Continuity: in Book I he holds Trakai from 1382 (the record), not from the 1384 settlement; the 1387 date for “regent” in Book II follows VLE, while the 13 Mar 1386 date (Frost 2015) is in the fact-check notes (books/2/notes/fact_check.md).

title: Spyglys (young ash-bearer)
text:
Summary
Spyglys, young ash-bearer, tends the Trakai vault flame after Kalvis; his hands shake and he stays behind when the lantern leaves on 8 Jun 1410. He finds Kęstutis’s sword by scent (Book III ch. 2). Dead by Vėlinės 1449.

title: Spyglys (young ash-bearer)
text:
Appearance & tells
A young ash-bearer (pelenininkas): lean, with slow eyes, who carries a clay pot with a lid pressed to his chest and touches the lid every evening with his palm, as if testing whether it is still warm. In 1387 he is a boy-faced helper rowing with Kalvis to the island foundations at Trakai; by September 1399 his face, which four years earlier was still childlike, “looks too old for his years” (Book II ch. 29); by 1410 his hands tremble as the hands of one who has carried a fire-pot too many years, so badly that he cannot lift them (Book III ch. 15). At the 1415 gathering he is still “young and lean, with slow eyes” (Book IV ch. 6). He bites his lip when the older wolves will not move (Book II ch. 11), says little, and sits beside others in silence: when the new boy learns that his mother set the last plate before him, Spyglys, his vilktėvis (wolf-father) in 1430, can only rest a hand on his shoulder (Book V ch. 7).

title: Spyglys (young ash-bearer)
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
To keep the Trakai vault flame alive and carry its ash safely wherever the Duke needs it.


Need (internal)
To be told why his hands shake, and to be allowed to put the pot down.


Lie they believe
A flame can be tended without cost if the bearer is careful and obedient.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
Every pinch of ash taken from the Flame is a risk to its keeper; the cost falls on the carrier, and he carries it silently until the bog takes him.

title: Spyglys (young ash-bearer)
text:
Arc by book

Book II (1387-1399). The ash-bearer at the night rowing to the half-flooded foundations of the island castle (ch. 11): “She is going out”, he says when the ember dwindles, and he holds the open ash-trough as Vytautas kneels to feed it at the Trakai vault; one of the five wolves who kneel at the first lighting. In the wolf hunt (ch. 14) he carries the ash pot four nights from Trakai, lightening it with every hearth lit, and helps burn the Unburned dead. In September 1399 he tells Vytautas that the flame, after days of trembling, “simply stopped trembling” (ch. 29).
Book III (1400-1410). Carries Vytautas’s plain black armour from Trakai to Kyiv, finds Kęstutis’s sword by scent among twelve identical chests (ch. 2) and tells Vytautas, as he counts its rust-stains of broken oaths, “it is sick”; tells the boy Žiežirba how the wolf-rite goes and stands at his baptism in 1405 (ch. 9); his hands tremble so that he cannot lift them (ch. 15); he stays behind when the lantern leaves on 8 Jun 1410.
Book IV (1415-1417). One of three who lie down in the bog with Pilkoji so that the dead’s names can be said (ch. 6).
Book V (1430-1449). Alive in the dozen of Kūčios 1430 (ch. 7), 1432 (ch. 9) and 1435, one of four still living in 1436 (ch. 16); dead by 1449 and buried in the oldest bog, named by Pilkoji at the middle stone (ch. 28).

title: Spyglys (young ash-bearer)
text:
Power & magic
A vilkatas of the Iron Wolves, sworn through the bog baptism; his office is the pelenininkas, the ash-bearer who carries ash from the Last Flame (ash is taken only a pinch at a time, “for a ring”) to relight hearths and for the Duke’s workings. Every pinch taken from the flame is a risk to its keeper (world_rules/iron_wolves.md); his cost is the shaking of his hands. He can take wolf shape only if sworn twenty years (canon D10). The cost of holding a fire falls on a man who never asked for it.

title: Tautvilas Kęstutaitis (Kondrat)
text:
Summary
Tautvilas Kęstutaitis (baptised Kondrat, 21 Oct 1383), younger brother of Vytautas, fights on the Order’s side and is killed at the siege of Vilnius in 1390.

title: Tautvilas Kęstutaitis (Kondrat)
text:
Appearance & tells
A man of the family’s face: Henry Bolingbroke, watching from the Order’s side, sees that the red-cloaked Karigaila under the burning gate has “the same cut of face” as Tautvilas and Wigand (Vytautas), a family face (Book II ch. 7). Tautvilas fights on the Order’s side in a white cloak, as his brother does, and the saga’s one picture of him is at the gate of the Crooked Castle in September 1390: he reaches it first, speaks a few words to the red-cloaked Karigaila under the arch and falls on his knees, his white cloak darkening, with a crossbow bolt in him. The shooter is never named. He is remembered kindly: he twice held little Sofija on his knee and taught her a German song, of which she can no longer recall the words (Book II ch. 8).

title: Tautvilas Kęstutaitis (Kondrat)
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
A place and an honour under the Order’s banner, as Kęstutis’s youngest surviving fighting son, and to take Vilnius for his brother or with him.


Need (internal)
To be reconciled with his own blood instead of fighting it from the opposite side of the wall.


Lie they believe
The Order’s baptism (Kondrat, 21 Oct 1383) and arms will give him back his family’s place.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
The gate is the same for both sides: Gediminid blood shed by Gediminids, three years after the Pact that forbade it was dead, brings no god’s punishment and no one’s justice.

title: Tautvilas Kęstutaitis (Kondrat)
text:
Arc by book

Book II, ch. 7 (Sep 1390). Dies at the gate of the Crooked Castle during the siege of Vilnius, “believed killed by a crossbow bolt”; Karigaila dies the same hour when the arch collapses. His death is the proof that, with the Pact dead, no god intervenes when Gediminids kill Gediminids.
Book II, ch. 8 (winter 1390-91). Ona’s letter tells Sofija on the road to Moscow that he is dead, killed at the Crooked Castle.
Elsewhere. In the record he is baptised Kondrat on 21 Oct 1383, the autumn Vytautas is baptised Wigand, and fights with the Order; the books show none of this.

title: Tautvilas Kęstutaitis (Kondrat)
text:
Power & magic
Tier 0. He has no gift and no bargain. His death is the saga’s demonstration of what the death of the Pact means: a Gediminid dies by a Gediminid’s gate and no Force responds (Book II ch. 7, master_chronology.md).

title: Tautvilas Kęstutaitis (Kondrat)
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: Son of Kęstutis and Birutė (VLE, Tautvila 1). Killed besieging the Crooked Castle at Vilnius in September 1390, “believed killed by a crossbow bolt” (Wigand / Marburgietis; en.wikipedia, Siege of Vilnius 1390). VLE’s “9-10 June” is nonsensical: the siege ran 11 Sep - 7 Oct. Fought on the Order’s side, not as a hostage at Lyck.
[Saga invention]: The shooter is unknown in the book (Book II ch. 7 replaced the axe duel with a bolt at the gate); Sofija’s letter in ch. 8 reports it so.

title: Tautvilas Kęstutaitis (Kondrat)
text:
Pronunciation
TAUT-vi-las · IPA /ˈtɐʊtvʲɪɫɐs/ · English sound-alike “TOWT-vih-lahs”. Stress on the first syllable. His baptismal name Kondrat (Conrad) was given on 21 Oct 1383.

title: Uliana of Tver (Julijona Tverietė)
text:
Summary
Uliana of Tver (Lith. Julijona Tverietė, c. 1325 - 17 Mar 1391) is Algirdas’s second wife, Orthodox, and the mother of Jogaila, Skirgaila, Švitrigaila and Kaributas. She is the dynast of the Algirdaičiai who sees to it that her sons, not Maria of Vitebsk’s, inherit in 1377. In Book VI she is called Uliana and learns to count horses in her first winter at Vilnius.

title: Uliana of Tver (Julijona Tverietė)
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: Daughter of Alexander of Tver, married to Algirdas in 1349, died on 17 March 1391 aged about 65; Jan Tęgowski gives her eight sons and seven daughters, the birth order disputed. Sources conflict on whether she took the veil, at the Holy Spirit monastery in Vitebsk or at the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra (en.wikipedia, Uliana of Tver). Algirdas’s 1377 will favoured her sons.
[Saga invention]: Her private conversations and the persona’s Moscow marriage-brokering in 1384 (the offer itself is attested; the bride’s name is not secure).

title: Uliana of Tver (Julijona Tverietė)
text:
Not to be confused with
Julijona Alšėniškė, Vytautas’s second wife (married 1418), a different woman. The persona folder was renamed Uliana_Tveriete for that reason.

title: Uliana of Tver (Julijona Tverietė)

title: Vasily I of Moscow
text:
Summary
Vasily I Dmitrievich (30 Dec 1371 - 27 Feb 1425), Grand Prince of Moscow and Vladimir from 1389, son of Dmitry Donskoy, marries Sofija, Vytautas’s only recorded child, on 9 Jan 1391. He is a patient, wary son-in-law who fights Vytautas in 1406-08 and then makes peace on the Ugra, and names Vytautas guardian of his son Vasily II in his testament. In the saga he is a man who learned in the Horde that any morning might be his last, and sleeps with a knife under his pillow.

title: Vasily I of Moscow
text:
Appearance & tells
Tall, broad-shouldered, patient to the point of stubbornness, and unwilling to be pressed (Book III ch. 10). He grew up four years as a hostage among the Tatars, “among people who smiled at dinner and found their neighbours dead in the morning”, and since then sleeps like an animal in its den: his right hand lies under the pillow on the grip of a narrow, long knife with a blackened handle worn to the shape of his palm. His wife never asks why; she finds the knife on his deathbed in 1425 and lays it on his chest (Book IV ch. 15). When he dies the news goes first to the metropolitan, not to his wife.

title: Vasily I of Moscow
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
To enlarge Moscow (Nizhny Novgorod, Murom) and stay out from under both the Horde and his Lithuanian father-in-law.


Need (internal)
To be able to sleep without his hand on a weapon, that is, to trust one man not to turn on him.


Lie they believe
Every morning can be the last, and the people who smile at your table are the ones who will kill you.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
Peace with Vytautas can be made across the water: after the Ugra he trusts him enough to name him his son’s guardian.

title: Vasily I of Moscow
text:
Arc by book

Book II (1388-1391). Weighed as a match at Grodno (ch. 4); marries Sofija in the Kremlin in January 1391 (ch. 8), a pawn’s match for both families.
Book III (1406-1410). Three wars with his father-in-law, ended when the two meet on opposite banks of the Ugra (ch. 10); in December 1409 his wife promises Vytautas that Moscow will not move while he fights the Order (ch. 13).
Book IV (1411-1425). Dies in the late winter of 1425 and tells the metropolitan first (ch. 15); his testament places Vasily II under Vytautas’s protection, and Sofija becomes regent.

title: Vasily I of Moscow
text:
Power & magic
Tier 0. No gift, no bargain and no contact with the Forces. His only “tell” is mortal fear, which is the Horde’s legacy; the saga uses Moscow as the cold stone city where Sofija’s amber bead chills, not as a place of magic. His line, through Vasily II, is where the Kęstutaičiai blood survives.

title: Vasily I of Moscow
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: Born 30 Dec 1371; Grand Prince 1389-1425. Held as a hostage at Tokhtamysh’s court from 1383, escaped in 1386 and returned to Moscow. Married Sofija Vytautaitė on 9 Jan 1391 (Trinity Chronicle, after Grala citing Posilge; en.wikipedia’s “1392” is not followed) with Metropolitan Cyprian officiating. Took Nizhny Novgorod-Suzdal in 1393 and Murom; fought Vytautas 1406-08, ending in the stand-off on the Ugra (1408); Edigu burned Nizhny Novgorod and other towns in December 1408 but failed to take Moscow while Vasily was at Kostroma; resumed submission to the Horde in 1412. His 1423 testament named Vytautas guardian of Vasily II (b. 10 Mar 1415). He died on 27 Feb 1425, aged 53, leaving nine children by Sofija.
[Saga invention]: The knife under the pillow, the metropolitan told first, and the Ugra meeting as the two riders facing each other across the river (Book III ch. 10); Sofija’s marriage as a “pawn” and Moscow’s cold cathedral stone. The record says nothing of his sleeping habits or of his reaction to Vytautas’s offer of peace.

title: Vasily I of Moscow
text:
Pronunciation
va-SI-lij · IPA /vɐˈsʲilʲɪj/ · English sound-alike “vah-SEE-lee”. Not in the pronunciation lexicon; this is the Russian form (Vasily Dmitrievich); the Lithuanian text writes Vasilijus. Stress on the second syllable.

title: Vasily I of Moscow
text:

Book II: ch. 4, 8, 20 and the afterword.
Book III: ch. 10 (the Ugra, strongest), 13, 28 and the afterword.
Book IV: ch. 1, 15 (his death) and the afterword.

He does not appear in Books I, V or VI; his son Vasily II does in Book V ch. 25.

title: Vytautas’s sons Jurgis and Ivanas (hostages; contested)
text:
Summary
Vytautas’s two hostage sons, Jurgis and Ivanas, are a contested tradition: the saga adopts it, but they are not in the record.

title: Vytautas’s sons Jurgis and Ivanas (hostages; contested)
text:
Appearance & tells
Two boys at the Grodno court in 1388-89, brought home from Marienburg half a year earlier: Jurgis, eleven, serious and upright, eats as the Order’s brothers taught and makes the sign of the cross from left to right as in Marienburg; Ivanas, nine, who sits on one of his own boots humming a wordless German song (Book II ch. 4). Their mother tells them in the evenings about their grandmother, “not a witch, but a woman who could talk to water”; Ivanas asks whether the water answered, Jurgis says nothing and looks at the window (ch. 6). They are not on the Order’s written hostage list (“the household’s escort, nobody writes those down”).

title: Vytautas’s sons Jurgis and Ivanas (hostages; contested)
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
Two children’s wishes: to be at home, to be at their parents’ table, and not to be watched by the Order’s brother Dietrich.


Need (internal)
To be known as something other than a pledge.


Lie they believe
Vytautas will come for them in time; he always does.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
He does not come in time: the poison reaches them first, and Eglė reads it off the Neman foam (‘milk foam if alive, blood foam if dead’).

title: Vytautas’s sons Jurgis and Ivanas (hostages; contested)
text:
Arc by book

Book II ch. 4 (1388-89). At the Grodno court; Vytautas has brought them from Marienburg half a year earlier, as promised. Their names are the tradition’s (Grunau’s “Iwan and Georg”).
ch. 5-6 (1389-90). Hostages again with Ona; Brother Dietrich eavesdrops on their evening stories.
ch. 9-10 (1392). After Vytautas’s break with the Order the cook vanishes and the boys sicken at Balga; the wolf-father Šešiapirštis goes into Prussia, takes their hair to a coastal ragana who offers a price (the child of the Order, “blood for poison”), and Vytautas will not pay it. Eglė reads the boys’ deaths in the foam of the Neman. Ona looks at her husband “as if she were seeing him for the first time” and then looks away, the first time she does.
Afterwards. Vytautas remembers them at Grunwald, “not on guard, not lying with fever, but children one evening by Trakai Lake” (Book III ch. 20), and Ona mourns them to the end (Book IV ch. 9).

title: Vytautas’s sons Jurgis and Ivanas (hostages; contested)
text:
Power & magic
Tier 0. Their deaths are herb-lore (poison), not sorcery, as the saga insists: “men need no magic for the worst things” (power_systems.md §2.4). The poison in the saga is drignė, kietis and German sugar, slow, stolen from the Balga kitchen. The offered cure is the one forbidden way of the water-craft: someone has to take the poison into themselves, and the ragana’s own old body cannot carry two children’s worth; the other price, a child of the Order, Vytautas refuses. Their deaths end his Form 4 (the Traitor of Traitors) and cost him Ona’s regard.

title: Vytautas’s sons Jurgis and Ivanas (hostages; contested)
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: Simon Grunau (16th c.) alone: “Iwan and Georg” poisoned by a knight to avenge the betrayal. En.wikipedia (Ostrów Agreement, after Jonynas 1984): a false rumour, no reliable source. Sofija is the only child in the record; Vytautas’s letters never accuse the Order. A “Jurgis and Jonas” on the 1390-92 hostage list were kinsmen who came back alive.
[Saga invention]: The boys’ temperaments, Šešiapirštis’s errand, the ragana’s offer (Book II ch. 6-10). They are not on the Order’s written hostage list in the book (“the household’s escort”).

title: Vytautas’s sons Jurgis and Ivanas (hostages; contested)
text:
Pronunciation
JUR-gis and i-VA-nas · IPA /ˈjʊrɡʲɪs/ and /ɪˈvɐnɐs/ · English sound-alikes “YUR-gis” and “ih-VAH-nahs”. Not in the pronunciation lexicon; derived from its conventions. The tradition’s forms are Jurgis (Georg) and Ivanas (Iwan).

title: Vytautas’s sons Jurgis and Ivanas (hostages; contested)
text:
Appearances

Book II: ch. 4 (Jurgis eleven, Ivanas nine), 5, 6, 9 (the poisoning and the foam), 10 and the afterword (“Vytauto sūnūs”).
Book III: ch. 20 (Vytautas’s memory at Grunwald).
Book IV: ch. 9 (Ona’s death).

Continuity: not on the Order’s hostage list in the book; Sofija is the only child in the record; “Jurgis and Jonas” on the real 1390-92 hostage list were Alšėniškis and Narimantaitis kinsmen who came home alive.

title: Konrad Zöllner von Rotenstein
text:
Summary
Konrad Zöllner von Rotenstein (c. 1325 - 20 Aug 1390), 23rd Grand Master of the Teutonic Order from 5 Oct 1382, is Vytautas’s host and the secondary mortal antagonist of Book I: a devout, patient chess-player who believes honestly in the fugitive’s conversion, which makes Vytautas’s lie at the baptismal font cost something. He receives Vytautas in Prussia in late 1382, baptises him “Wigand” at Tapiau (21 Oct 1383), binds him as a vassal at Königsberg (30 Jan 1384), and is betrayed when Vytautas burns Marienwerder and Georgenburg in July 1384. He dies weeks before the siege of Vilnius in the autumn of 1390.

title: Konrad Zöllner von Rotenstein
text:
Appearance & tells
Old but with clear, dangerous eyes “like a freshly forged knife”, tall, spare and bent, with a close-cut grey beard in the Order’s fashion and a plain white brother-knight’s mantle worn thin. He wears a rosary of consecrated amber beads (confiscated amber) and always keeps a chessboard set up in his chamber. His study is stark and exact: perfectly drawn maps, thick parchment books and a huge oak crucifix. His voice is calm and as dry as old parchment; his smile is the satisfaction of a chess-player seeing an opponent step onto a prepared square (Book I ch. 18). He looks at Vytautas “not as a tragic man or even a duke in need, but as a chess problem to be solved with the least loss to the Order”. He is not cruel by nature, which is why he is more dangerous: he sincerely believes his mission is to civilise a “wild pagan land”, even if that means destroying it. A sincere opponent, never a cartoon.

title: Konrad Zöllner von Rotenstein
text:
Want · Need · Lie · Truth







Want (external)
The baptism of the last pagans and Samogitia joined to the Order’s lands between Prussia and Livonia, and a useful, baptised Vytautas as his vassal.


Need (internal)
To see Vytautas as a man and not a piece, and to accept that a baptised Lithuania would leave the Order without a reason to exist.


Lie they believe
A conversion that is demanded in the right place and form is real; a man who kneels has changed.


Truth they learn (or refuse)
Vytautas’s July 1384 burnings show he never did: Zöllner’s one moment of rage, and a price on Vytautas’s head.

title: Konrad Zöllner von Rotenstein
text:
Arc by book

Book I (1382-1384). Elected after Kniprode’s death and meets Vytautas in the dim, exact study at Marienburg (ch. 18): his four conditions are baptism “where and when we choose”, Samogitia to the Order, vassalage and the surrender of Vytautas’s wife and children as “guests” (hostages). Vytautas answers “I agree, Master”. He waits through a year for the right moment, baptises Vytautas as Wigand in October 1383 and hands him a heavy German sword (ch. 19). After Vytautas burns the Order’s forts in July 1384, the Order seeks him “as the Grand Master’s personal enemy” and Zöllner posts a reward for his head (ch. 25).
Book II (1388-1390). Brings the household home “to show good will” (ch. 4); receives Vytautas a second time in 1389-90 and takes the family as hostages at Lyck (ch. 6); dies four weeks before the Vilnius siege, “an old, devout man who liked chess”, the Order’s brothers lowering their heads and the English guests kneeling with them (ch. 7).

title: Konrad Zöllner von Rotenstein
text:
Power & magic
Tier 0. His chamber is full of consecrated stone and the Order’s sword, which damp Kalba: the amber pebble that warmed in the Dykra goes silent in his office (Book I ch. 18). The Iron Saint (Geležinis Šventasis) gathers around the Order’s prayers and watches the negotiation “with a quiet, steel satisfaction”, but Zöllner is not its creature: he can still pity, which makes him dangerous to lie to. He pays no magical price.

title: Konrad Zöllner von Rotenstein
text:
Record vs saga

[Record]: Born c. 1325 (uncertain), probably at Birkenfeld in Franconia; elected Grand Master on 5 Oct 1382, succeeding Kniprode (d. 24 Jun 1382); died 20 Aug 1390 at Christburg (en.wikipedia; the Civil War 1389-92 article instead places his death at the Jurbarkas siege, so sources disagree) and was buried at Marienburg. His reign saw the Order’s treaty with Jogaila at Dubysa (31 Oct 1382; baptism within four years, Samogitia to the Dubysa; never ratified), the war with Jogaila in 1383, Vytautas’s baptism as Wigand at Tapiau (21 Oct 1383), the Treaty of Königsberg (30 Jan 1384), and the Treaty of Lyck (19 Jan 1390), signed for the Order by Marquard von Salzbach, Arnold von Bürglen and Thomas Survila. He died weeks before the siege of Vilnius (11 Sep - 7 Oct 1390), which was run by the Order’s marshal and Grand Commander during the vacancy; Konrad von Wallenrode was elected in 1391.
[Saga invention]: The chessboard, the amber rosary, the four-condition scene and the personal reward on Vytautas’s head after July 1384; his sincere belief in Vytautas’s conversion and his single moment of rage. No source describes his character or says anything about his sincerity.

title: Konrad Zöllner von Rotenstein
text:
Pronunciation
KON-rad TSÖL-ner fon RO-ten-shtine · IPA /ˈkɔnʁaːt ˈtsœlnɐ fɔn ˈʁoːtn̩ʃtaɪn/ · English sound-alike “KON-raht TSURL-ner fon ROH-ten-shtine”. German; the ö as in “fur” with rounded lips. The Lithuanian text writes Konradas Zöllneris fon Rotenšteinas.

title: Konrad Zöllner von Rotenstein
text:
Appearances
