title: Book I review
text:
0. Verdict in one paragraph
The spine works: trust, then betrayal, then a death in prison, an escape in disguise, a deal with the enemy, a second betrayal, an uneasy truce, a baptism. Birutė’s arc (seer, then widow, then amber statue) is the strongest thread, and the amber pebble works well as a moral barometer (dead after the Marienburg baptism, warm again when Vytautas turns on the Order). Four things hold the book back. (1) Length and pacing: 28,000 words across 30 chapters averages about 750 words a chapter, which is novella length. The big set pieces (battle, siege, truce) get a single page each, while internal monologue gets repeated. (2) Two magic systems that never meet: the five-element Senovės Kalba and the “Meddling Forces” pantheon run side by side with no rules connecting them. (3) A handful of loud historical errors (Kniprode was already dead, Polish gold arrives three years early, Vytautas becomes Marshal of the Order, Jogaila is baptised in Vilnius in 1387). (4) Continuity drift in names, objects and identities (two Eglės, a golden chain that was never given, an amulet that survives after “the last noble items” were given up, Henne serving two masters).

title: Book I review
text:
1. Pacing & structure

1.1 Word budget by part










Part
Chapters
Words
Story time
Notes




Prologue + I “Nuosmukis”
P, 1–10
~10.3k
~2 weeks (autumn 1382)
Slow and atmospheric. Ch. 5 and 6 repeat Jogaila’s “am I a traitor?” beat. Ch. 7–8 are vignettes under 500 words.


II “Pabėgimas”
11–19
~6.8k
~2 months (late 1382)
Best momentum in the book. The escape, swamp, border and Marienburg sequence flows. Ch. 18→19 rushes the negotiation and the baptism into what feels like a single day.


III “Karas ir Tvarka”
20–30
~8.5k
~5 years (1383–1387+)
Badly compressed. Ch. 23 says 1383 and ch. 29 says 1387, but nothing between them (the 1384 reconciliation, Krėva Union 1385, Jogaila’s Kraków coronation 1386) appears on the page. Time jumps carry no signposts.



Recommendations

Pick a target of 90–120k words (about 3–4k per chapter) if this is meant to read as an epic. Grow scenes, not adjectives.
Merge or differentiate ch. 5 and 6. Both stage Jogaila’s doubt plus a childhood flashback. Keep the flashback in one chapter and give the other Skirgaila’s POV.
Write the interrogation. The outline’s ch. 8 (“Kęstutis refuses to abdicate”) is missing, so the murder has no stated in-scene motive. One scene where Skirgaila demands abdication and Kęstutis refuses would fix it.
Add date or season headers to Part III chapters, or one bridging chapter covering 1384–1386 (Vytautas’s reconciliation and the Krėva Union).
Ch. 25 → 26: Vytautas is a hunted fugitive with a dying band, then in the next chapter he is negotiating as an equal. Show the arrow message being answered, or show Jogaila’s envoy finding him.



1.2 Repetition and copy-paste artefacts (fix these first)

Ch. 20 reuses Ch. 5 verbatim. “Staiga, kaip visada, kai jo siela buvo susiskaldžiusi…”, the childhood run (“bėgančią… Lėčiau, lėčiau, jūs abu esate man sūnūs!”), “Ar aš parduodu savo kraują už tuščią karūną?”, and “plyšys, iš kurio pradeda tekėti šalta, juoda kraujo upė” all appear word for word. Ch. 29 uses the same template a third time.
Ch. 1 has a duplicated sentence: “Medis nusitrynė nuo laiko… Medis per dešimtmečius nusitrynė…”
Ch. 3 has two consecutive near-identical dialogue tags (“o jos balsas nuskambėjo lyg tūkstančiai pamirštų giesmių”).
Ch. 15 and 16 both stage Eglė silently pointing the path, as if the same scene was written twice.
Ch. 30 repeats a paragraph (“Tai buvo ne tiesiog rytas. Tai buvo visų amžių sutrūkimas…”).
Ch. 1 has a garbled markdown artefact: **iš rytų** — **iš Bizantijos**…



1.3 Prose (noted, not the focus)
Adjective stacking (“mirtinai”, “neįtikėtinai”, “negailestingai” sometimes three to a sentence) flattens the intensity. Grammar slips are frequent: “Neik į jų irklas!” (ch. 2), “Vyras, kuris laivą valdo” for a guard captain (prologue), “Tai tikra žodis”, “klykojo galva” (ch. 6), and gender agreement errors (“bėgančią” for Jogaila, “Vyties”). A human Lithuanian line edit is needed after the structural fixes.

title: Book I review
text:
2. Logic & continuity









#
Where
Problem
Suggested fix




C1
Prologue vs ch. 15–16, 23
Two Eglės. The prologue’s Eglė is “vyriausioji vaidilutė” tending the Eternal Flame at Romuva. Later Eglė is a silent swamp spirit wearing a žaltys. Ch. 15 calls her “Gintaro Šventikė”, while the magic doc files her under Forest Whisperers.
Rename the prologue priestess (e.g. Krivė Daiva), or make the identity explicit: Eglė was the priestess and gave up her mortality to the Root-Mother.


C2
Ch. 9 vs ch. 1
Kęstutis is strangled with “the same golden chain Jogaila’s envoys brought as a gift”, but ch. 1’s gifts were sables, perfume and Italian candles, with no chain.
Add the chain to the ch. 1 gifts. It is a great plant.


C3
Ch. 16 vs ch. 17, 26
Vytautas gives the swamp “his last noble items” (a buckle and silk), then produces his father’s silver wolf amulet at the border and again at the truce.
Have him keep the amulet hidden in ch. 16 and refuse to give it, or make it the offering that Eglė returns.


C4
Ch. 14 → 15
Vytautas escapes on foot through a refuse gate, then rides for “two days” on a horse that came from nowhere.
Ona’s people leave a horse at a named place (historically, horses were arranged).


C5
Ch. 12
Ona carries a sleeping draught for the guard, and it is never used.
Use it in ch. 13 or 14 (e.g. the guards at the fire are drugged), or cut it.


C6
Ch. 12
Skirgaila greets Ona as “Našlė… apraudoti savo… vyro”. Ona is Vytautas’s wife and her husband is alive; the widow is Birutė.
Make it “atvykai apraudoti savo uošvio?”


C7
Ch. 19 vs ch. 20
Vytautas leaves the chapel “as the Order’s new Marshal”, then in ch. 20 a separate Order Marshal commands him.
Cut “maršalas” from ch. 19 (it is also ahistorical, see H5).


C8
Ch. 24, 25
“Jis išdavė savo tėvą Krėvoje, kad išgyventų.” He did not; he was imprisoned and his father was murdered.
Make it “Jis paliko tėvo kūną Krėvoje…”


C9
Ch. 26
“po Krėvos mūšio”: there was no battle at Krėva. The meeting place also shifts from “medinės kapinės” to “akmeninis kiautas” to “sudegusi bažnyčia”.
Pick one: a burnt church on the old Šventaragis grove site is thematically perfect.


C10
Ch. 28
Ona “returned from long hostage in German lands”. This is never set up; ch. 13 has her staying at Krėva with “meet me at the Sea”.
Add one line in ch. 17–19 (the Order keeps Ona and the children as surety). This is historically accurate.


C11
Ch. 5 vs ch. 30
Henne is Jogaila’s court jester in ch. 5 and “the cousin’s personal jester” (Vytautas’s) in ch. 30.
Either is fine, but say he changed masters. That is the Shadow-Seller’s nature.


C12
Ch. 1, 5, 6, 10
Kinship errors: Kęstutis calls Jogaila “pusbrolis” (he is his nephew); Jogaila calls Kęstutis “tėvas”; Vytautas sees “dėdės bruožų” in his own reflection.
Fix kinship terms everywhere.


C13
Ch. 2
“šešėliai ant sniego” during the Dagotuvės harvest.
Change to frost or leaves.


C14
Ch. 21
Vytautas’s childhood friend is named Gediminas, the same as his grandfather and the dynasty founder.
Rename (e.g. Daumantas).


C15
Ch. 10
Vytautas, a prisoner, stands freely in the courtyard over his father’s body, and later “scouts reported” Ona’s arrival.
Have him brought out under guard to see the body (as a threat), and have a jailer gossip instead of scouts.


C16
Naming
The outline and README say the fictional names are Vytis / Jagelis / Kestus / Anna, and the persona folders use them. The prose uses Vytautas / Jogaila / Kęstutis / Ona, with leftovers “Vytis”, “Kestutis” (ch. 10) and “Kęsto” (ch. 1). Henne appears as “Jene”, “Jenė”, “Henė” and “Jester Henne”. “Vytis” is also the coat of arms in ch. 28, so the two collide.
Pick one convention. Recommended: real names in prose, with “Vyti” only as Birutė’s and Kęstutis’s pet name. One spelling for the jester: Henė.


C17
Build
00_pradzia.qmd, 31_senoves_kalba.qmd and 32_redakcines_pastabos.qmd are not in _quarto.yml. 00_pradzia has Birutė narrate “I am the one they call the Amber Queen…”, which conflicts with ch. 3 (see M4).
Decide whether Birutė frames the book. If she does, add it to the build and have her return at the end of ch. 30.


C18
Docs
hidden_immortals.md says Birutė “drowns” in Book II and Lutsk is in Book V. Book I ch. 27 already transforms her, and the series outline places Lutsk in Book IV. The Book II title is “Auksinis Šešėlis” in the series outline but “Vytis ir Šešėlis” in the README and teaser. The Book II outline has no chapter 12.
Update the docs to match the book.

title: Book I review
text:
3. History check (1377–1387)
Fantasy may bend history. The project’s own conceit (mythic_gaps.md), though, is that magic explains history’s gaps without contradicting its record. These items contradict the record:









#
Text
Actual record
Severity / fix




H1
Ch. 18–19, 25: Grand Master Winrich von Kniprode receives Vytautas
Kniprode died 24 June 1382, before Kęstutis’s death (15 Aug 1382). Vytautas’s host was Konrad Zöllner von Rotenstein (GM 1382–1390).
High. Swap the name; the characterisation (old, devout, a chess player) can stay.


H2
Ch. 5, 7, 9: Polish gold, a Polish monk, a strangling chain “ordered from Kraków”
In 1382 Poland was ruled by Louis of Hungary (died Sept 1382). Polish courting of Jogaila began in 1384–85. Jogaila’s 1380–82 partner was the Teutonic Order (the Dovydiškės treaty).
High: it misplaces Jogaila’s whole motive. Make the money and the chain Order silver, or Riga merchant silver via Hanul, the Vilnius merchant who historically opened the gates. Polish interest can arrive in Part III.


H3
Ch. 1–6: Kęstutis is still in power and is lured to Vilnius
1381: Kęstutis learned of Dovydiškės, seized Vilnius and deposed Jogaila. 1382: Jogaila retook Vilnius while Kęstutis was in Samogitia. Kęstutis and Vytautas came to parley at Jogaila’s camp near Trakai and were seized there.
Medium. Skipping the 1381 coup makes Jogaila’s betrayal look like pure ambition and turns Kęstutis from usurped usurper into a naive old man. At least have Vytautas mention “last year we took Vilnius from him and let him go”. The mercy Kęstutis showed, letting Jogaila live, is the tragic irony the book is missing.


H4
Ch. 10: Kęstutis is buried “like a dog, without rites”
Jogaila gave Kęstutis a full pagan cremation in Vilnius, with horses and hounds.
Medium, and an opportunity: the honoured funeral of a man he had murdered is a far more chilling Jogaila.


H5
Ch. 19: Vytautas becomes the Order’s Marshal
The Marshal was a professed monastic knight. A newly baptised foreign duke could not hold the office.
High. Make him a vassal or ally with knights “lent” to him.


H6
Ch. 19: baptism at Marienburg in the same scene as the oath
Vytautas was baptised Catholic in Tapiau (Tapiava), 21 Oct 1383, as Wigand. The Treaty of Königsberg (Jan 1384) ceded Samogitia to the Nevėžis.
Low/medium. Marienburg is fine for drama; date it 1383 and name him Wigand. It is a delicious detail.


H7
Ch. 22–24: Vytautas and the Order besiege Vilnius with bombards in 1383, and Vytautas burns their siege tower
The 1383 campaigns took Trakai. Vytautas defected in July 1384, burning the Order’s castles he held (Jurbarkas/Georgenburg, Marienwerder/Naujapilis). The bombarded siege of Vilnius with Vytautas was 1390, during his second alliance with the Order.
High for series planning. Book I uses up the 1390 siege, so Book II has nothing left for 1389–92. Either (a) recast ch. 22–24 as the 1384 burning of the Order’s Neman castles, or (b) keep the fictional 1383 siege and drop the 1390 one in Book II. Option (a) is stronger and historically exact.


H8
Ch. 28: Vytautas rebuilds Trakai and “splits Lithuania” with Jogaila in 1384
In 1384 Vytautas got only Grodno, Brest and Podlasie. Trakai went to Skirgaila, which is Vytautas’s core grievance until 1392 (Ostrów).
High. This grievance is the engine for Book II. Give Trakai to Skirgaila on the page.


H9
Ch. 29: Jogaila baptised in the Neris in 1387 alongside Vytautas
Jogaila was baptised in Kraków on 15 Feb 1386 (as Władysław), married Jadwiga three days later, and was crowned on 4 Mar 1386. Vytautas was re-baptised there too (as Aleksandras). In 1387 in Vilnius, Jogaila (already king) presided over the mass baptism of ordinary Lithuanians and founded the cathedral and bishopric.
Medium. Keep the icy Neris scene, but have Jogaila presiding as king and Vytautas witnessing (he is already baptised twice).


H10
Missing
The Krėva Union (14 Aug 1385) was signed in the same castle where Kęstutis died.
Big missed thematic beat. One scene: Jogaila signs away Lithuania’s independence in the room above his uncle’s death cell.


H11
Prologue: Jogaila’s captain visits Romuva
Romuva (Nadruvia, Prussia) had been under the Order for about a century.
Move to Šventaragis valley (Vilnius) or a Samogitian grove. Keep Romuva for Book V’s 1345 flashback, where it is also a stretch.


H12
Narrative similes and terms
“giljotina” (ch. 6), “Baltarusijos miškai” (ch. 8), “Graikiška ugnis” (ch. 22), “milimetras” (ch. 10).
Low. Swap for period terms.


H13
Book II outline
Skirgaila’s death (1397) is placed in Part 3 (1399–1401). Vytautas’s second civil war and Ostrów 1392, when he actually becomes Grand Duke, are absent.
Fix before drafting Book II.

title: Book I review
text:
4. Magic system and cosmology consistency

4.1 The core problem: two systems, no bridge

System A: Senovės Kalba (senoves_kalba_magic_system.md, appendix ch. 31). Five elements with deities (Praurimė, Gabija, Bangpūtys, Žemyna, Vėjopatis), zeniths, incantations, boons, costs, three Laws and the Senovės Sutartis.
System B: the Meddling Forces (meddling_forces.md, hidden_immortals.md). These are the Root-Mother, Perkūnas, the Shadow-Seller, the White Silence, the Amber Queen, the Iron Saint, the Steppe-Hunger and the Gold-Glutton, some walking as avatars.
The text mixes them freely: “Eglė, Žemynos, Šaknų Motinos pasiuntinė” (ch. 16) treats Žemyna and the Root-Mother as the same being. Perkūnas acts directly three times (ch. 10, 19, 21) but has no element. The Amber Queen speaks from amber to Birutė (ch. 3) while other docs say Birutė is her.
Fix: one cosmology with layers. A gods layer (old high gods), a Forces layer (what the gods become when they meddle), and a craft layer (Senovės Kalba, which is how mortals ask). See world_rules/cosmology.md.



4.2 Rule violations in the text










#
Where
Rule
What happens
Fix




M1
Ch. 3
Law of Balance and element cost. Praurimė costs temporary blindness.
Birutė feels the blindness “begin”, then walks to Vytautas and reads his face the same night.
Show her blind: she finds him by touch and voice. It makes the scene better.


M2
Ch. 3
Senovės Sutartis requires amber, the caster’s blood, a true name and an unbreakable promise.
Only amber is present. No blood, no name, no promise. Who is the “caster”, Birutė or Vytautas?
Add Birutė cutting her palm, speaking Vytautas’s true (child/secret) name, and demanding a promise. That promise becomes the debt that comes due.


M3
Ch. 11, 14, 24, 25
Every spell has a cost; Vėjopatis costs vertigo and loss of voice.
Birutė sends fog and wind across about 400 km several times at no visible cost.
Show the bill: she loses her voice after ch. 14, and by ch. 27 she can only sing, not speak. That earns the sacrifice.


M4
00_pradzia, ch. 3, 11, 27, hidden_immortals.md
Who is Birutė?
Variously: the Amber Queen herself, a priestess the Queen speaks to, and a woman who “galutinai tapo” the Queen.
The book reads best as vessel becoming goddess. Update hidden_immortals.md to match (decision required).


M5
Mythic gaps #2 vs Law of Truth
“Magic cannot create lies or illusions.”
mythic_gaps.md explains the Krėva escape with fog “reflecting their expectations”, which is an illusion.
The book’s version (real fog that hides) is correct. Fix the doc.


M6
Ch. 6, 8
White Silence is the Order’s saint-force.
It smothers sound in Jogaila’s Vilnius and at Krėva, helping a pagan duke’s coup.
Use the Shadow-Seller’s “Breath of the Void” (per mythic_gaps.md), or explain that the White Silence goes wherever a baptism is being bought.


M7
Ch. 10
Vytautas feels “Perkūno prisilietimas”.
Perkūnas is outside the five elements, and the doc says his “key” is Krėva survival plus his mother’s sacrifice, which happens in ch. 27.
Define Perkūnas’s mark as a separate, unasked-for Force claim, not Kalba.


M8
Ch. 15
Element costs.
Vytautas pays dulled sight, hearing and memory, a mix of costs from no single element.
Name it: invoking all five at once costs a little of each. Make that the rule (the “Five-Voice” invocation).


M9
Ch. 7, 28
Glossary.
“Auksinis Smauglys” appears undefined; the docs say Gold-Glutton / Mercator-Rex.
Use one name. Recommended: Aukso Rijūnas (Gold-Glutton).


M10
Ch. 30
Shadow-Seller identity.
Henė unmasks as “neither pagan god nor Christian devil, the essence of time and fate”. Docs: a shard of Velnias.
Decision required. Recommended: keep the shard of Velnias. The unmasking should show Velnias’s void (Velnias rules the dead, and the dead are the past).


M11
Ch. 3
Zenith timing.
Praurimė’s zenith is the winter solstice, but she is invoked at Dagotuvės with a handwave.
Fine if stated as a rule: off-zenith casting doubles the cost. That also justifies M1’s blindness.


M12
Ch. 27
New limits introduced.
“She could see only through amber, call winds only through waves, heal only through her blood” appear here for the first time.
Move these to Birutė’s profile and seed them in ch. 3 and 11.





4.3 What works and should become canon

The amber pebble as a fidelity barometer (warm, then dead at the baptism, cold, then hot when he betrays the Order, then glowing at the 1387 baptism). Make it an explicit rule: it answers to the bearer’s truth, not his faith.
The tarnaitė who stays behind (ch. 13) as a secret Root-Mother devotee. A real historical echo (the maid Elena was executed) given mythic weight.
Birutė’s ring returned three times by the sea (ch. 11). A perfect folk-rule beat.
The amber kneeling woman on Palanga shore (ch. 27). A physical relic for Books II–V to return to.
Henė juggling three black stones (the three cousins). Keep it consistent; the docs say “balls”.

title: Canon decisions
section: D1. Birutė is a vessel who becomes the Amber Queen
text:
D1. Birutė is a vessel who becomes the Amber Queen
Decided 2026-10-10 by the author.

Birutė is born mortal, the last of the Palanga amber-priestess line (vaidilutės of the shore flame). The Amber Queen (Gintaro Karalienė) is not a person but an office of grief and memory first held by the sea goddess Jūratė (see cosmology.md §3.4). It needs a living vessel to act in the Middle World.
Book I traces her becoming: she hears the Queen (ch. 3), is changed by widowhood (ch. 11, the eyes go sea-dark), and is fully transformed at Palanga (ch. 27, the amber kneeling woman).
00_pradzia.qmd (“I am the one they call the Amber Queen, though my true name was Birutė”) is her post-transformation voice. It is canon as a frame narration.
Must change: hidden_immortals.md §1 (no longer “never mortal”; no “drowning in Book II”); persona/Birute/divine_origin.md.

title: Canon decisions
section: D2. Henė (the Shadow-Seller) is a shard of Velnias
text:
D2. Henė (the Shadow-Seller) is a shard of Velnias
Decided 2026-10-10 by the author.

Šešėlių Pardavėjas is a splinter of Velnias, lord of the dead, of wealth and of bargains. He wears mortal masks. His best known is Henė the jester, and his first mask in the saga is Hanulas, the Riga-born Vilnius merchant who historically opened Vilnius to Jogaila in 1382 (Saga invention: the names echo).
He changes masters: Jogaila’s court (1382), Skirgaila (1387–97), Vytautas’s court (from 1392), Sigismund of Luxembourg (1429–30). He always serves the deal, never the man.
The void beneath his mask (ch. 30) is the realm of the dead seen from inside, all of the past at once. Fix the ch. 30 line “neither pagan god nor Christian devil, the essence of time and fate” to “not a man, but the hollow where the dead keep the past”.
His props are three blackened stones (the three cousins). The docs’ “three black balls” are corrected to stones.
Must change: ch. 30 wording; hidden_immortals.md §2 (Lutsk is Book IV, not V).

title: Canon decisions
section: D3. History is the record plus mythic gaps
text:
D3. History is the record plus mythic gaps
Decided 2026-10-10 by the author.

Fixed: real dates, real names of office-holders, real outcomes of battles, treaties, deaths and baptisms (see master_chronology.md).
Free: private conversations, motives, unrecorded minor characters, how something happened when the chronicles are silent or contradictory, and anything supernatural.
Magic may explain a gap (how Kęstutis died silently, how Vytautas passed the guards). It may not contradict a fact (Kniprode alive in late 1382, Jogaila baptised in Vilnius).
When chronicles disagree (e.g. Birutė drowned at Brest in 1382 per the Order chronicler Wigand of Marburg (whether Długosz repeats it: verify) vs. lived to about 1416 per Lithuanian tradition), the saga may pick either and say why in-world. Our pick: both are true. Jogaila’s men tried to drown her in 1382, and the sea refused her (the ring-thrice motif). She “died” a second time by choice in 1384 (ch. 27).
Must change: see books/1/story_review.md §3 (H1–H13).

title: Canon decisions
section: D4. Real names in prose and docs
text:
D4. Real names in prose and docs
Decided 2026-10-10 by the author.

Prose and docs use Vytautas, Jogaila, Kęstutis, Ona, Skirgaila, Birutė, Švitrigaila, Jadvyga (Jadwiga).
“Vyti” survives only as the intimate vocative used by Birutė and Kęstutis. In narration, “Vytautas” always. “Vytis” in narration means the coat of arms (the mounted knight), never the man.
The jester is spelled Henė in Lithuanian text and Henne in English docs.
Must change: persona folders renamed (Vytis → Vytautas, Jagelis → Jogaila, Kestus → Kestutis, Anna → Ona); books/1/outline.md name table; stray “Kestutis”/“Kęsto” in ch. 1 and 10.

title: Canon decisions
section: D5. The two Eglės are one woman
text:
D5. The two Eglės are one woman
Recommended by the reviewer 2026-10-10; the author may override.

Eglė is the last vaidilutė of the eternal flame in the Šventaragis valley (Vilnius), not Romuva (Romuva lay in Order-held Prussia by 1382). The prologue’s prophecy night is her last night as a mortal priestess.
After the captain’s insult she leaves the city on foot and, days later, walks into the Dykra and is taken by the Root-Mother, becoming Pelkių Eglė, the swamp’s voice. Her žaltys is the folk-tale inheritance of Eglė žalčių karalienė (see legends_and_songs.md).
She is not an amber priestess. Ch. 15’s “Tu esi Gintaro Šventikė” becomes Vytautas’s mistake, and Eglė’s silence corrects him: “Ne gintaro. Šaknų.”
Must change: prologue location; ch. 15 line; senoves_kalba_magic_system.md lineage examples (fine as is: Forest Whisperers).

title: Canon decisions
text:
D6. One cosmology, three layers
Reviewer decision 2026-10-10, required to make D1 and D2 coherent.
The five-element Senovės Kalba and the Meddling Forces are one system seen from two sides. Gods are the source, Forces are gods hungry and meddling in history, and Kalba is the mortal craft of asking. Full rules are in cosmology.md and magic_rules.md.

title: Canon decisions
section: D7. The Silent Pact is the series engine
text:
D7. The Silent Pact is the series engine
Reviewer decision 2026-10-10, unifies Books I–V.

In 1345, when Algirdas and Kęstutis took power, they swore the Tylioji Sutartis with the old gods. The gods would keep Lithuania unconquered while a Gediminid kept the sacred flames, and they would take royal blood for land lost (the “Amber Debt”).
Kin-slaying breaks the Pact’s protection (Kęstutis, 1382). Jogaila’s baptism (1386–87) ends it formally. Birutė’s sacrifice (1384, ch. 27) buys a remnant: the Hidden Groves, the gods’ last foothold (Samogitia, until 1413–17).
Books II–V are the unwinding of the remnant. Book V’s flashbacks show the oath itself.

section: D9. Kinship terms (applies to all prose)

D9. Kinship terms (applies to all prose)

Kęstutis → Jogaila, Skirgaila, Švitrigaila: dėdė (uncle), and they are his sūnėnai.
Vytautas ↔︎ Jogaila, Skirgaila: pusbroliai (cousins).

title: Canon decisions
section: D10. The Iron Wolves serve two masters
text:
D10. The Iron Wolves serve two masters
Proposed 2026-10-10 in iron_wolves.md; the author must confirm.

The vilkatai are the Root-Mother’s servants (cosmology.md §3.2) and are sworn to whoever keeps a Gediminid sacred flame. They may never shed Gediminid blood.
In 1382 this splits the brotherhood: the Vilnius packs owe Jogaila and stand aside during the ch. 7 massacre at Jogaila’s camp near Trakai (seven of the hidden nine die there; Jonas’s men stayed in Kęstutis’s own camp). After 1387, Vytautas’s secret flame is the only one left, so every surviving wolf answers to him. New wolves can be made only at a living flame, so the brotherhood dies when the flame goes out in 1430.
Only wolves sworn twenty years or more can take wolf shape. The folk belief that all vilkatai shape-shift is half wrong.

title: Canon decisions
section: D11. Choices made while realigning the outlines and revising Book I (2026-10-10; the author may override)
text:
D11. Choices made while realigning the outlines and revising Book I (2026-10-10; the author may override)

Where the Last Flame is: lit in 1387 in Kęstutis’s old hunting lodge beyond the Neris (Book I ch. 29); moved by Vytautas to the half-flooded foundations of the Trakai island castle while Skirgaila holds Trakai (Book II); in the finished island-castle vault after Ostrów (1392 →).
Who carries the 1387 ember: Vytautas himself (Book I ch. 29). The Book II outline’s mention of Kalvis (iron_wolves.md) is to be read as Kalvis guarding the lodge flame.
The flame goes out at the moment of Vytautas’s death (IV ch. 29); Book V ch. 1 replays the same night from the vault.
Galminas becomes a grove at Grunwald (1410); the “last žynys” of Book V is his pupil.
The silver wolf passes Kęstutis → Vytautas (through the Krėva stones, Book I ch. 8) → Pilkoji → the Flame-Keeper (Kūčios 1430–31).
The tier-4 count from 1387 to 1410 is one: “the Medvėgalis žynys”, who dies at Grunwald.
Eglė’s price is “never sell the forest”, which falls due at Salynas (1398).
Vaidotas and Butautas are sons of an earlier, unnamed wife of Kęstutis (they are too old for a c. 1350 marriage to Birutė).
The Krėva silence in 1382 is Henė’s Tuštumos Kvėpavimas (Breath of the Void); the White Silence first touches Krėva as frost in Nov 1382 (ch. 14) and settles over it at the 1385 union (ch. 28b).
Krėva escape date: the eve of Vėlinės (late Oct/early Nov 1382): Wind’s zenith halves the fog’s cost.
Ona was released by Skirgaila (to track Vytautas), fled via Brest to Masovia, and became the Order’s surety at Königsberg (1383–84); released by exchange in 1384; the sons stay at Marienburg.
The Flame-Keeper’s working skin-name is Žiežirba.
Ages of the two fosterlings (settled by the books): Pilkoji is born c. 1365 (38 in 1404, 84 in 1449; this answers Q13). Žiežirba is born c. Oct 1390 – Mar 1391 (5 in winter 1395–96, 14 and nearly 15 at Kūčios 1405). He is sworn at that Kūčios, below the usual age of 16 (iron_wolves.md §4): the single exception to the rule, because he already lives at the flame. He tends the vault flame as a boy from 1399.

For future story edits, use the shared constraints and intentional exceptions in the bilingual alignment record (docs/LITHUANIAN_ALIGNMENT.md), together with the final case-closure report (docs/FINAL_CASE_CLOSURE.md). These record the current revised manuscripts, including the ordinary midnight-name rite versus Pilkoji’s exceptional initiation, painful brief entry versus forbidden hearth sleep, the 1387 flame rescue versus the 1392 dry cellar, amber’s cold interval, and Henė’s exact offers. title: Cosmology
text:
Source: world_rules/cosmology.md
Canonical. Reconciles the five-element Senovės Kalba (books/1/senoves_kalba_magic_system.md) with the Meddling Forces (meddling_forces.md) and Hidden Immortals (hidden_immortals.md). Mechanical rules for mortal magic are in magic_rules.md.

title: Cosmology
text:
1. The World Tree (Pasaulio Medis)
The world is an oak (sometimes sung as a linden or a silver birch). Each layer is real and reachable, though rarely by the living.









Layer
Name
Who dwells there
How mortals reach it




Crown
Dangus (the Sky), the Stiklo Kalnas (Glass Mountain) at its summit
Dievas, Saulė, Mėnuo, Aušrinė and the star-children; Perkūnas rides between
Only the dead climb the Glass Mountain, and only those with long nails (hence the custom of burying nail-clippings and lynx or bear claws with the dead)


Bridge
Paukščių Takas (the Birds’ Way, the Milky Way)
Souls (vėlės) migrating as birds; Vėjopatis’s winds
Dying. Dreaming, rarely, for seers


Trunk
Žemė (the Middle World)
Mortals, beasts, the spirits of place (dvasios)
Born here


Roots
Anapilis / Požemis (the Under-Castle), Velnias’s realm
The dead who will not climb, wealth, bargains, the past
Swamps, wells, river-bottoms, graves, crossroads at midnight, and under the mask of the Shadow-Seller


The waters around the tree
Marios (the Baltic) and every lake, which are its eyes
Bangpūtys; the drowned palace of Jūratė; the Amber Queen
Drowning, which is not always death (see Birutė)



Dausos, the afterlife meadow, lies past the Glass Mountain. Cremation is the correct funeral because fire is the fastest road up. A buried pagan climbs slowly or not at all and may linger as a vėlė that must be fed at Vėlinės. This is why Kęstutis’s honoured cremation matters (H4 in the review), and why the Order’s ban on burning the dead is, to pagans, an atrocity against the soul.

title: Cosmology
text:
2. The Three Layers of Power
This is the bridge between the two magic documents.
   LAYER I — THE GODS (Dievai)            source, ancient, mostly indifferent
          │  when a god's attention is fed by human history, it hardens into…
          ▼
   LAYER II — THE FORCES (Galios)         hungry, partisan, meddling in events
          │  both layers can be *asked* — politely, at a price — through…
          ▼
   LAYER III — THE CRAFT (Senovės Kalba)  mortal words, mortal blood, mortal cost

2.1 Gods are indifferent; Forces are partisan
A god is a fact of nature: Perkūnas is thunder and Žemyna is soil. Gods do not care who rules Vilnius. A Force forms when a god’s attention is fed long enough by human worship, war, grief or greed that it develops appetite and agenda. The Root-Mother is what Žemyna becomes after a century of watching the forests cut. Perkūno Rūstybė is Perkūnas after a thousand sworn oaths. The Shadow-Seller is a splinter of Velnias that learned to enjoy the trade.
A god can be petitioned. A Force must be bargained with, and it remembers every bargain.


2.2 The Vulture Gods are egregores
The invading Forces (Iron Saint, White Silence, Steppe-Hunger, Gold-Glutton) are not the Christian God, Tengri or any real faith’s deity. The saga never passes judgement on the Christian God. These Forces are egregores: spirits fed by institutions, by crusade, purchased baptism, conquest and ledger. They grow wherever those appetites gather, including in Lithuanian hearts (Jogaila’s ambition feeds the Gold-Glutton as surely as any Hanseatic counting-house). Honest Christians in the saga (the Franciscan martyrs of Vilnius, Jadvyga at her best) are not their servants and are often their victims.


2.3 Spirits are local
Below both layers are the dvasios: laumės, kaukai, aitvarai, žalčiai, vėlės, the spirits of particular groves, wells and households. They are bound by custom, the reciprocal courtesy of offering and respect. See bestiary.md.

title: Cosmology
text:
3. Pantheon and Force mapping

3.1 The Gods










God
Domain
Element (Kalba)
Force-face (when meddling)
Notes




Dievas (Dievas Senelis)
Sky, order, the distant father
none
none; walks as the Beggar
Never bargains. Tests with requests (bread, coin, a story). Those who give are not saved, but seen (see §5).


Perkūnas
Thunder, oaths, justice, war
none (he cannot be asked)
Perkūno Rūstybė
Acts through claims (marks) and signs (lightning on oaks and banners). Punishes broken oaths and cowardice, including in his own.


Velnias
The dead, the underworld, wealth, cattle, bargains, cleverness
none
Šešėlių Pardavėjas (a shard)
Not evil. Hungry and fair: every deal is kept to the letter. Folk tales show him regularly cheated by clever peasants, which is the only defence.


Laima (with Dalia and Giltinė)
Fate, share, death
none
none
Spins every fate at birth. Dalia allots fortune; Giltinė, her sister, cuts the thread (see bestiary). Laima’s spinning is why Praurimė’s sight shows possibilities, never certainties.


Žemyna
Earth, fertility, oaths sworn on soil
Earth (“Žemė tau laikys”)
Šaknų Motina (Root-Mother)
Oaths sworn by kissing the earth are binding physically: the oath-breaker’s land rejects him.


Saulė
The Sun, mother of life
none directly
none
Her tears are amber. Every piece of amber is a drop of solar grief, which is why amber stores memory.


Mėnuo
The Moon, warrior, faithless husband (he left Saulė for Aušrinė and Perkūnas cut him in half, hence the phases)
none
none
Governs tides and therefore Bangpūtys’s zenith.


Gabija
The hearth, sacred fire
Fire (“Ugnis tau degs”)
none; she does not hunger, she guards
Every household fire is a small shrine. Spitting into fire or stepping over it is sacrilege.


Bangpūtys
Sea, storms, waves
Water (“Vanduo tau teks”)
none
Bound in an old feud with Perkūnas over Jūratė (§3.4).


Vėjopatis
The four winds, messenger between worlds
Wind (“Vėjas tau neš”)
none
Carries the vėlės along the Birds’ Way. Speech with the dead goes through him.


Praurimė (doubtful: known mainly from 19th-century mythographers, Narbutt; authenticity disputed)
The fire of the stars, the sky-twin of the eternal flame
Stars (“Žvaigždės tau švytės”)
none
Folk memory remembers her as a goddess of sacred fire; the saga’s seers know her as the fire above, the stars read as fate-threads lit by Laima’s spinning. Both are true.


Medeina
Forests, the hunt, wild beasts
none
merged into the Root-Mother
Medeina and Žemyna’s grief fused during the 13th-century crusades. The Root-Mother speaks with both voices.





3.2 The native Forces

Šaknų Motina (Root-Mother): Žemyna and Medeina’s wild grief. Wants the forest kept and the iron and plough stopped. Takes the “Amber Debt”, royal blood for land lost (D7). Servants: Pelkių Eglė, the vilkatai (iron_wolves.md), Galminas.
Perkūno Rūstybė: justice without mercy. Wants oaths kept and cowards punished. Takes claims on warriors. Marked Vytautas in 1382 (ch. 10).
Šešėlių Pardavėjas (Shadow-Seller): Velnias’s splinter. Wants deals, and through deals the dead (the past) to outweigh the living (the future). Takes “threads”, small obligations that compound. See D2.
Gintaro Karalienė (Amber Queen): see §3.4. Wants memory kept. Takes the vessel’s mortality.



3.3 The Vulture Forces (egregores)

Geležinis Šventasis (Iron Saint, Ferrum Sanctum). Fed by: crusade, the Reise season, forced baptism. Signs: furnace heat in winter, the smell of quench-water, crosses that ring like anvils. Grants: tireless marching, absence of pity.
Baltoji Tyla (White Silence). Fed by: purchased purity, baptisms bought or sold for land and crowns. Signs: frost flowers on blades, sound dying, lilies on frozen fields. Grants: fearlessness, early winters (the “Crusader’s Winter”). Note: it gathers wherever a baptism is being bought, which is why it settles over Jogaila’s Vilnius in 1382 (he is already pricing a crown) and over Krėva (where the 1385 union will be signed). This resolves review item M6.
Stepių Alkis (Steppe-Hunger, Erdene-Chuluu). Fed by: conquest-without-end and the hubris of horizon-kings. Signs: dust devils, horse-hair in wells. Grants: the vision of an endless empire, which is its lure. Book II.
Aukso Rijūnas (Gold-Glutton, Mercator-Rex). Fed by: ledgers, tolls, land sold by the furlong. Signs: coins that are always warm, a counting voice in quiet rooms. Grants: prosperity that empties people out. Present from Book I (Hanseatic envoys, ch. 28) and dominant in Book IV.



3.4 The Amber Queen: an office, not a goddess

Jūratė, a sea goddess, lived in an amber palace beneath the Baltic. She loved Kastytis, a mortal fisherman, against the law that gods may not love the dying.
Perkūnas, keeper of oaths, shattered the palace with lightning, killed Kastytis, and chained Jūratė to the ruins. The amber that washes up at Palanga after storms is her palace, and the sea’s moaning is her grief. (Folk legend; see legends_and_songs.md.)
Her grief did not die. It became the Amber Queen: the sea’s memory of everything gods and men have destroyed. It needs a mortal vessel to act on land. Vessels are drawn from the Palanga amber-priestess line, and each vessel ends by giving her mortality back to the sea.
Birutė is the last vessel (D1). Her transformation in 1384 (ch. 27) is the last time the Queen walks; after it, she can act only through amber already touched by Birutė (Vytautas’s pebble, the kneeling statue).
Why Perkūnas “punishes” Vytautas (mystical_connections.md): he is the Queen’s vessel’s son, and the feud with Jūratė is unfinished.

title: Cosmology
section: 4. The Silent Pact and its unwinding
text:
4. The Silent Pact and its unwinding

4.1 The Pact (1345)
When Algirdas and Kęstutis overthrew their brother Jaunutis and divided the realm (Algirdas east from Vilnius, Kęstutis west from Trakai), the Krivis of Šventaragis bound them to the gods in the Tylioji Sutartis:

The gods give: Lithuania will not be conquered. The Order may raid and burn but never hold the heartland.
The princes give: (1) the sacred flames (Šventaragis, Palanga, the Samogitian alkai) are never extinguished; (2) no Gediminid sheds Gediminid blood; (3) the Amber Debt: for every land lost to the plough-and-cross, royal blood is owed.
Witnesses: every spirit of place. The Pact is what keeps the dvasios courteous. It is a treaty between the land’s people and the land’s spirits.

Historical anchor: the GDL in fact remained the last unconquered pagan state in Europe through constant crusade (1283–1387). The Pact is the saga’s reason why.


4.2 The breaking








Year
Event
Effect on the Pact




1377
Algirdas dies; cremated with horses (historical)
One oath-taker gone; the bond weakens to Kęstutis alone


1380
Treaty of Dovydiškės (Jogaila secretly abandons Kęstutis to the Order)
First crack: a Gediminid plots against Gediminid blood


1382
Kęstutis murdered at Krėva by his nephew’s men
Clause 2 broken. The gods’ protection lapses. The Shadow-Seller, who brokered it, collects


1383–84
The Order holds Samogitia by treaty (Königsberg 1384)
Amber Debt comes due


1384
Birutė’s sacrifice at Palanga (ch. 27)
Pays the debt partially: buys the Hidden Groves, a remnant protection over Samogitia and the deep Dykra


1385
Krėva Union signed in the castle where Kęstutis died
The White Silence settles over the realm


1387
Jogaila extinguishes the Šventaragis flame, fells the grove and has the sacred grass snakes killed (historical, per Długosz)
Clause 1 broken. The Pact formally ends.


1413–17
Samogitia baptised
The Hidden Groves fall one by one (Books III–IV)


1430
Vytautas dies
The last flame he secretly kept (see magic_rules.md §6) goes out (Book V, ch. 1)





4.3 The Unbinding (Atsaistymas)
The saga’s equivalent of a world-changing cataclysm; it drives the later books’ monster-haunted, grey tone.
The Pact made the spirits courteous. As it unwinds, they become unbound:

Before 1382: spirits follow custom. Feed the žaltys and it guards the house; honour the laumės and they weave for you. Folk rules work as advertised.
1382–1387 (Book I): the first unbound appear at the margins. Pelkių Eglė’s swamp eats Skirgaila’s trackers (ch. 16); the forest is “silent” (ch. 1, 20) because the spirits are listening for the Pact to break.
After 1387 (Books II–V): with no flames and no Krivis, spirits are no longer owed courtesy and no longer give it. Abandoned groves breed ravenous vėlės (the unburned dead of the crusades). Aitvarai turn from thieves to arsonists. Laumės who once swapped babies now drown them. Priests cannot see them, holy water is useless against things it does not believe in, and the peasantry turns, quietly, to whoever still knows the old ways: the last žyniai, the hedge-raganos, and the feared vilkatai (iron_wolves.md).

This is the moral engine: the baptism saves Lithuania from the Order and damns it to its own unfed dead. Neither choice was clean.

title: Cosmology
text:
5. Signs, Whispers, and the Beggar
(Supersedes mystical_mechanics.md, which remains as a quick reference.)

Whispers reach mortals between waking and sleep. Velnias’s whisper sounds like your own voice (the Echo). The Root-Mother’s is leaves, the Wind-Talk. The Amber Queen’s is surf, and it comes only through amber.
Signs are a Force’s only direct action outside vessels: lightning (Perkūnas), sap turning red (Root-Mother, before a massacre), frost-shapes (White Silence), crows leading armies (Root-Mother or Perkūnas), coins turning to stone (Dievas: what you pay for truth is worth nothing as money).
The Beggar (Dievas Senelis) appears at turning points and asks a small thing. Rule: those who give are not rescued, they are seen: their path becomes clear to them, even if it leads to death. Kęstutis gave the coin (ch. 4) and walked to Krėva knowing. Those who refuse are not punished; they are left blind to their own road. (Revises hidden_immortals.md §3.)

title: Cosmology
text:
6. What the gods cannot do

Act directly in the Middle World except through vessels, claims, signs, answered Kalba, or spirits they command.
Undo a death. Even the Amber Queen only keeps the dead (in memory, in amber).
Break their own word. A god’s bargain is iron; this is what makes Velnias beatable by the clever.
Hold a baptised land by right. They hold it only by custom, people still leaving offerings. This is why the later books’ battleground is habit, not territory.

title: Geography
text:
Source: world_rules/geography_gazetteer.md
World-bible reference for Geležinio Vilko Saga. It sits below canon_decisions.md, cosmology.md, magic_rules.md and master_chronology.md, and does not override them. Where this file and the chronology disagree, the chronology wins.
Labels. [Record] means attested in sources or archaeology, or the scholarly consensus. [Saga invention] is ours. (verify) means the claim is uncertain, contested, or a reconstruction; check it before it goes into prose. Distances are straight-line estimates from modern coordinates with a route factor added. They are planning numbers, not survey data.
Naming convention. Lithuanian name first, then the German or Polish form (and Belarusian or Ukrainian where it helps) in parentheses. Prose in Lithuanian uses the Lithuanian form. Order characters may think in German forms, which is a cheap and effective way to mark point of view.

title: Geography
text:
Part A. The realm in 1382

A.1 The shape of power
In 1382 the Grand Duchy of Lithuania (Lietuvos Didžioji Kunigaikštystė) is the largest state in Europe and the last pagan one. It is less a state than a pagan Baltic core holding a far larger Orthodox Ruthenian empire by kinship, tribute and fear. The core is small, perhaps the size of modern Lithuania with a strip of north-western Belarus. The Ruthenian lands are vast, Christian and literate, and are ruled by Gediminid princes who are often Orthodox themselves. [Record]
Since 1345 the core has been run as a diarchy [Record]. The senior grand duke (Algirdas, and after 1377 his son Jogaila) rules from Vilnius and looks east. The junior (Kęstutis) rules from Trakai and looks west, at the Order. In 1381–82 that diarchy breaks: Kęstutis seizes Vilnius in autumn 1381, Jogaila retakes it in spring–June 1382, and in August 1382 Kęstutis dies at Krėva (see master_chronology.md). Book I opens in the last weeks of the diarchy.


A.2 Status table, 1382









Land
Status in 1382
Ruler / holder
Notes




Vilnius duchy (Aukštaitija east; Vilnius, Kernavė, Krėva, Ašmena, Medininkai)

Jogaila (Krėva is his patrimony)
The heart of Book I’s betrayal


Trakai duchy (Trakai, Kaunas, Grodno, Brest, Podlasie, and overlordship of Samogitia)

Lithuanian, self-governing and contested. Ruled by its own elders under the Trakai duke. Promised to the Order on paper (Dovydiškės 1380 to the Dubysa; Dubysa treaty 31 Oct 1382; Königsberg 1384 to the Nevėžis)

The land bridge between Prussia and Livonia that the Order wants above all [Record]

Vassal, contested

Vitebsk
Vassal

Jogaila was released “to Krėva and Vitebsk” in 1381


Kyiv
Vassal, since c. 1362 (after Blue Waters)
Vladimiras (Volodymyr) Algirdaitis
Still partly tributary to the Horde (verify)


Chernihiv–Siveria (Novhorod-Siverskyi, Bryansk)
Vassal, unstable
Kaributas (Dmitry Koribut); Bryansk’s Dmitry Algirdaitis defected to Moscow in 1379 and fought at Kulikovo
Kęstutis is campaigning against Kaributas in spring 1382 (chronology)


Volhynia (Lutsk, Volodymyr)
Vassal, contested with Poland–Hungary
Liubartas (Lubart), Gediminas’s son, died c. 1383–85 (verify)
Galicia (Lviv) held by Hungarian garrisons until 1387 [Record]


Podolia (Kamianets)
Vassal
The Karijotaičiai (Koriatovichi) brothers
Frontier with the steppe


Smolensk
Independent Rurikid principality in the Lithuanian orbit
Sviatoslav Ivanovich (verify), killed fighting Skirgaila in 1386 (verify)
Annexed by Vytautas in 1395, and again in 1404 [Record]





A.3 The neighbours in 1382

The Teutonic Order in Prussia (Deutscher Orden, Lith. Kryžiuočių ordinas). Its capital is Marienburg. Grand Master Winrich von Kniprode died on 24 June 1382; Konrad Zöllner von Rotenstein is elected that autumn [Record]. It is the richest, best-administered power on the Baltic: brick castles, a cash economy, an amber monopoly, Hanseatic towns (Danzig, Elbing, Thorn, Königsberg) and an annual flow of Western crusader-guests for the Reise. Hostile; at war with Lithuania since 1283.
The Livonian Order (Livländischer Orden), the Order’s autonomous northern branch, holds Courland and Livonia. Its Landmeister is Wilhelm von Friemersheim (verify, 1364–85). It is in chronic feud with the Archbishop and city of Riga. Its raids come down into Samogitia from the north. Hostile.
Masovia (Pol. Mazowsze, Lith. Mazovija). A cluster of Piast duchies on the middle Vistula, Narew and Bug, formally within the Polish orbit. Janusz I (Warsaw and Czersk) is married to Vytautas’s sister Danutė (Anna). Siemowit IV (Płock) is a candidate for the Polish throne in 1382–83 (verify) and later marries Jogaila’s sister Aleksandra (1387). Kin, wary, neutral. It is Vytautas’s first refuge after Krėva [Record: the chronology; see D.3].
The Kingdom of Poland (Korona Królestwa Polskiego). Ruled until 10–11 September 1382 by Louis of Hungary, who rarely visits; then an interregnum and a civil war in Greater Poland (verify) until Jadwiga is crowned on 16 October 1384 [Record]. In 1382 Poland is not yet courting Jogaila (review H2).
The Golden Horde (Aukso Orda). Tokhtamysh has just reunited it after Mamai’s defeat at Kulikovo (1380). He sacks Moscow in late August 1382 [Record], in the same fortnight as Kęstutis’s death, which makes a useful “meanwhile in the east” beat. Distant overlord of the steppe; tribute-taker from Ruthenian borderlands.
Muscovy (Maskvos kunigaikštystė). Dmitry Donskoy, victor of Kulikovo, humbled by Tokhtamysh in 1382. A rival for the “gathering of the Rus’ lands”, and a magnet for Gediminid defectors. Rival.
Novgorod the Great (Didysis Naugardas). A merchant republic with a Hanseatic Kontor (the Peterhof) [Record]. It sometimes hires Lithuanian princes to defend its frontier (Lengvenis/Lugvenij from 1389, verify). Trading partner, occasional client.
Pskov (Pskovas). Novgorod’s junior sister-republic facing the Livonian Order, with a tradition of Lithuanian princes. Wary friend.
The Hanseatic towns (Riga, Danzig, Lübeck, Visby). Not a state but a web of merchant law, they reach Lithuania through Riga (Daugava–Polotsk), through Königsberg and Kaunas (Nemunas), and through Novgorod. A Riga merchant, Hanulas, opens Vilnius to Jogaila in 1382 [Record]; in the saga he is Henė’s first mask (D2).

title: Geography
section: Part B. Terrain, climate and nature
text:
Part B. Terrain, climate and nature

B.1 The lie of the land
The Baltic lands are young glacial country: low rolling moraines, thousands of lakes (the Trakai and Švenčionys lake districts), eskers, boulder fields, raised bogs and river valleys cut through sand. Nothing is high. The tallest hills in Lithuania barely reach 300 m. Every hill that matters has been shaped by people: piliakalniai (hillforts), terraced and palisaded, crown the river bends [Record]. In the saga a hillfort is always a place where the living and the dead share a roof.
Three landscape belts matter for the books:

The lake-and-forest core (Aukštaitija around Vilnius, Trakai and Kernavė). Pine on the sands, oak and linden in the valleys, cleared fields around hillforts, rye and flax. Settled, but the forest is never more than an hour’s walk away.
Samogitia (Žemaitija). Higher, wetter, more heavily wooded uplands west of the Nevėžis, cut by the Dubysa, Venta, Jūra and Minija, with sacred groves (alkai) and very few roads. People live in scattered homesteads under elders. This is the Order’s Samaiten and the saga’s last pagan heartland (the Hidden Groves, cosmology §4.2).
The great wilderness (the Wildnis, the saga’s Dykra). See B.2.

To the south-east the Ruthenian lands open into the Pripet marshes (Polesė), then the forest-steppe and finally the open steppe (the Dykra of the Tatars, the “Wild Fields”). Book II’s horizon.


B.2 The Wildnis and the Dykra
[Record] The Wildnis (Old German Wiltnis; Lithuanian historiography calls it dykra (verify usage)) was a deliberately depopulated border belt between the Order’s Prussia and Livonia on one side and settled Lithuania on the other. It formed after the Order’s conquest of Prussia (completed 1283) and Sudovia (1277–83), and through a century of raid and counter-raid. It ran:

south of the Nemunas, over old Sudovia–Yotvingia (modern Suvalkija and north-east Poland), where it was up to c. 150 km deep;
along the western and northern edge of Samogitia (towards Memel and Courland), c. 60 km deep; and
in patches along the Livonian border north of Aukštaitija [Record, per the Lithuanian encyclopedia VLE, “Dykra”].

It was not empty. Some old Baltic population survived in it, paying tribute to both sides or to neither. Historians still argue how many (verify). It was forest and bog, crossed by known trails that both sides’ guides kept in their heads. The Order wrote them down in the Wegeberichte (Die Littauischen Wegeberichte), about 100 route reports compiled between 1384 and 1402 by scouts (Lithuanian and Prussian guides) for winter and summer raids. They list fords, night camps, villages and sometimes sacred groves [Record]. They are the best ground-truth source the saga has for “how long from A to B in 1390”.
[Saga] Canon (D8) defines the Dykra as “the wild swamp-forest belt between Krėva and the Neman”, and master_chronology.md says the Wildnis “becomes the Dykra, the Root-Mother’s own country”. Both hold, because the saga’s Dykra is larger than the historical Wildnis:

The western Dykra = the historical Wildnis. Sudovia south of the Nemunas, the Prussian border forests, the Samogitian marches. Order raiders and Lithuanian Wegeleute (guides) cross it.
The eastern Dykra = the swamp-forests of the upper Nemunas. The Naliboki forest (Lith. Nalibokų giria, Bel. Nalibockaja pušča) and the Nemunas floodplain bogs that lie south and south-west of Krėva, then westward past Lida to the Grodno forests and the Biebrza marshes on the Masovian border. This belt really exists and really is “between Krėva and the Neman” [Record for the terrain]. Calling it part of one wilderness is [Saga invention].
Mythic logic: wherever war has emptied the land, the Root-Mother has taken it back. The Dykra is the map of what the crusade cost, and it grows as the books go on. It is the one country the Pact still fully protects after 1384 (the Hidden Groves, cosmology §4.2). Inside it, distances are unreliable: Eglė’s paths are shorter than they should be for those she favours and endless for those she does not. The rule is that it never lies about where you end up, only about how long it takes (consistent with the Law of Truth, magic_rules.md).

For Vytautas’s escape (ch. 15–17) this means the Dykra starts within a day’s ride of Krėva. That fits the two days of riding in ch. 15 (see D.3).


B.3 Rivers: the real roads
There are no paved roads [Record]. Rivers are highways in summer and, frozen, even better ones in winter.

Nemunas (Germ. Memel; Pol. Niemen; Bel. Nioman). The great river. It rises in Belarus south-west of Minsk, flows west past the Naliboki forest and Grodno, then turns north to Kaunas, then west again past Jurbarkas, Ragnit and Tilsit into the Curonian Lagoon through a delta. The Order’s road into Lithuania. Its lower course is Order-held: Memel, Tilsit, Ragnit. Its middle course (Jurbarkas to Kaunas) is a castle-studded no man’s land, the most fought-over water in the saga.
Neris (Pol. Wilia; Germ. Wilia). Rises in Belarus, flows past Vilnius and Kernavė, and meets the Nemunas at Kaunas. The road from the capital to the war, and, frozen, the road the Order uses to strike Vilnius.
Vilnia (Pol. Wilejka). The small river that joins the Neris under Vilnius’s castle hill. Šventaragis valley lies at the confluence.
Dubysa. A Samogitian tributary joining the Nemunas from the north. The treaty line: Dovydiškės (1380) and the Dubysa treaty (31 Oct 1382) both promise the Order Samogitia up to it [Record]. In the saga the Dubysa is a “lying border”, drawn in ink on a river that never agreed to it.
Nevėžis. Flows south through central Lithuania to the Nemunas below Kaunas. The 1384 Königsberg line: Vytautas promises the Order everything west of it [Record]. It is the real boundary between Aukštaitija and Samogitia.
Pregel (Lith. Prieglius; Pol. Pregoła). Prussia’s main river: Insterburg, Tapiau, Königsberg. At Tapiau the Deime (Lith. Deimena) branches north to the Curonian Lagoon, so a boat can go Kaunas → Nemunas delta → lagoon → Deime → Tapiau → Pregel → Königsberg without touching land. This matters for Vytautas’s 1383 movements [Record for the hydrography].
Daugava (Germ. Düna; Rus. Zapadnaya Dvina). Polotsk and Vitebsk to Riga: the Ruthenian–Hanseatic trade artery.
Vistula and Nogat (Pol. Wisła, Germ. Weichsel). Masovia (Warsaw) down to Thorn, Marienburg (on the Nogat arm) and Danzig. Dnieper (Kyiv), Bug (Brest), Narew (Masovia) and Vorskla (the steppe) for Books II–V.



B.4 Seasons and the war calendar
[Record] The climate is continental-maritime. Winters are long, with lake and river ice usually solid from December to March. Summers are short, warm and wet. The two muddy seasons (spring thaw March–April, autumn rains October–November) make the land nearly impassable to armies and miserable for travellers. The 14th century sits at the onset of the Little Ice Age (verify severity for the 1380s specifically).
Hence the two Reise seasons of the Order [Record]: the winter Reise (roughly Candlemas, 2 Feb, on frozen rivers and bogs, sleighs and fast cavalry) and the summer Reise (around the Assumption, 15 Aug, after the harvest, when the ground is driest). Lithuanian raids into Prussia and Livonia follow the same logic in reverse. Autumn and spring are seasons of diplomacy, intrigue and murder, which is exactly where Book I’s betrayal falls.









Season
Lithuanian life
War and travel
Saga resonance




Deep winter (Dec–Feb)
Threshing in the jauja, weaving, Kūčios and Kalėdos (solstice)
Best travel: ice roads, sledges, 40–60 km/day on rivers; winter Reise
The White Silence’s season; Praurimė’s zenith (solstice)
