7. Characters: saga figures [Saga invention unless marked]
Invented people, and legendary figures whose names the saga uses.










Lithuanian spelling
Stress
IPA
Sounds like
Notes




Eglė
eg-LĖ
[ɛɡˈlʲeː]
“eg-LAY”
Last vaidilutė of Šventaragis, then the swamp’s voice (D5). The word means “spruce”. Stress the end. Avoid “EGG-lee” and “EG-lay”. Accusative and vocative stress the first syllable (Ẽglę, Ẽgle).


Pelkių Eglė
PEL-kių eg-LĖ
[ˈpʲælʲkʲuː ɛɡˈlʲeː]
“PEL-kyoo eg-LAY”
“Eglė of the Swamps”, her name after the Root-Mother takes her.


Henė
HE-nė (verify stress)
[ˈɣʲæːnʲeː]
“HEH-nay”
The jester, mask of the Shadow-Seller (D2). English docs spell it Henne (German [ˈhɛnə], “HEN-uh”). The name is invented, so the stress is the author’s choice. First-syllable stress keeps the echo of German Henne; the alternative Henė̃ (“heh-NAY”) would follow Eglė̃.


Galminas
GAL-mi-nas (verify stress)
[ˈɡaːlʲmʲɪnɐs]
“GAHL-mih-nahs”
Samogitian elder, host of the Root-Mother. No dictionary stress exists for this name. GAL-mi-nas is recommended; gal-MI-nas is also possible.


Daiva
DAI-va
[ˈdɐɪvɐ]
“DYE-vah”
Proposed name for the prologue priestess (review C1, superseded by D5). A 20th-century revival name, not attested as a 14th-century personal name.


Jonas
JO-nas
[ˈjoːnɐs]
“YOH-nahs”
Kęstutis’s old arms-bearer (ch. 25); “Jonas” is his Iron Wolf skin-name (iron_wolves.md). The stress moves to the ending in the instrumental and locative (Jonù, Jonè).


Daumantas
dau-MAN-tas
[dɐʊˈmɐntɐs]
“dow-MAHN-tahs”
Suggested replacement name for Vytautas’s friend in ch. 21 (review C14). dau- “much” + -mant- “mind”.


Lizdeika
liz-DEI-ka
[lʲɪzˈdʲɛɪkɐ]
“liz-DAY-kah”
[Record: 16th-century chronicle legend] The high priest who read Gediminas’s Iron Wolf dream, found as a baby in an eagle’s nest (lizdas “nest”).


Sovijus
SO-vi-jus (verify stress)
[ˈsoːvʲɪjʊs]
“SOH-vih-yoos”
[Record: 1261 Malalas gloss] Hero of the legend of why the dead are burned.


Elgeta
el-ge-TA
[ɛlʲɡʲɛˈtɐ]
“el-geh-TAH”
“The Beggar”, Dievas Senelis in disguise (cosmology §5).

title: Pronunciation guide
text:
8. Foreign figures
Native form first. The stressed syllable is given in the native language. Lithuanian forms are listed in the notes.










Lithuanian spelling
Stress
IPA
Sounds like
Notes




Konrad Zöllner von Rotenstein
KON-rad TSÖL-ner fon RO-ten-štain
[ˈkɔnʁaːt ˈtsœlnɐ fɔn ˈʁoːtn̩ʃtaɪn]
“KON-raht TSURL-ner fon ROH-ten-shtine”
Grand Master 1382–90, Vytautas’s host 1382–84. German z is “ts”, and ö is a rounded “e”. Lithuanian Konradas Ciolneris fon Rotenšteinas (verify the Lithuanian form).


Winrich von Kniprode
VIN-rich fon KNI-pro-de
[ˈvɪnʁɪç fɔn ˈkniːpʁoːdə]
“VIN-rikh fon KNEE-proh-deh”
Grand Master 1351–82; died 24 June 1382, before Kęstutis (review H1). Sound the k in Kn-. Lithuanian Vinrichas fon Kniprodė (the chapters write Winrichas).


Ulrich von Jungingen
UL-rich fon JUN-gin-gen
[ˈʊlʁɪç fɔn ˈjʊŋɪŋən]
“OOL-rikh fon YOONG-ing-en”
Grand Master 1407–10, killed at Žalgiris. Lithuanian Ulrichas fon Jungingenas.


Konrad von Wallenrode
KON-rad fon VA-len-ro-de
[ˈkɔnʁaːt fɔn ˈvalənʁoːdə]
“KON-raht fon VAH-len-roh-deh”
Senior Order officer in the 1380s, Grand Master 1391–93; Mickiewicz’s Konrad Wallenrod.


Günther von Hohenstein
GÜN-ter fon HO-en-štain
[ˈɡʏntɐ fɔn ˈhoːənʃtaɪn]
“GUEN-ter fon HOH-en-shtine”
The saga’s invented young Order brother (not the 1381 informant, who was Kuno von Liebenstein, komtur of Osterode).


Wigand von Marburg
VI-gant fon MAR-burk
[ˈviːɡant fɔn ˈmaʁbʊʁk]
“VEE-gahnt fon MAR-boork”
Order herald and chronicler (Chronica nova Prutenica, 1394), a key source for 1382. Lithuanian Vygandas Marburgietis.


Peter von Dusburg
PE-ter fon DUS-burk
[ˈpeːtɐ fɔn ˈdʊsbʊʁk]
“PAY-ter fon DOOS-boork”
Order priest-chronicler (Chronicon terrae Prussiae, 1326). Lithuanian Petras Dusburgietis.


Toktamyšas
tok-ta-MY-šas (verify stress)
[toktɐˈmʲiːʃɐs]
“tok-tah-MEE-shahs”
Tokhtamysh, Khan of the Golden Horde, Vytautas’s ally 1397–99. Kipchak Toqtamış [toqtɑˈmɯʃ], “tokh-tah-MUSH”, stressed on the last syllable. Lithuanian texts also write Tochtamyšas and Toktamišas; pick one and use it everywhere.


Edigėjus
e-di-GĖ-jus (verify stress)
[ɛdʲɪˈɡʲeːjʊs]
“eh-dih-GAY-yoos”
Edigu (Tatar Idegäy [idɛˈɡæj], “ee-deh-GAY”), emir and victor at the Vorskla in 1399.


Timūras
ti-MŪ-ras (verify stress)
[tʲɪˈmuːrɐs]
“tih-MOO-rahs”
Timur (Tamerlane).


Zigmantas Liuksemburgietis
zig-MAN-tas liuk-sem-bur-GIE-tis (verify stress)
[zʲɪɡˈmɐntɐs lʲʊksʲɛmbʊrˈɡʲiɛtʲɪs]
“zig-MAHN-tahs lyook-sem-boor-GYEH-tis”
Sigismund of Luxembourg (German Sigismund [ˈziːɡɪsmʊnt], “ZEE-gis-moont”; Hungarian Zsigmond [ˈʒiɡmond]), King of Hungary and Emperor; offered Vytautas a crown at Lutsk in 1429.


Zbigniew Oleśnicki
ZBIG-niew o-leś-NIC-ki
[ˈzbʲiɡɲɛf ɔlɛɕˈɲit͡skʲi]
“ZBEEG-nyef oh-lesh-NEETS-kee”
Bishop of Kraków from 1423, cardinal 1439; the enemy of Vytautas’s crown. Polish stress always falls on the next-to-last syllable. Lithuanian Zbignevas Olesnickis (verify). The docs’ Olesnicki drops the ś.


Spytek z Melsztyna
SPY-tek z mel-ŠTY-na
[ˈspɨtɛk z mɛlʂˈtɨna]
“SPIH-tek z mel-SHTIH-nah”
Two men: Spytko II (killed at the Vorskla in 1399) and Spytko III (Hussite leader, killed at Grotniki in 1439). The persona file is Spytko III. Lithuanian form uncertain (verify).


Jadwiga
jad-VI-ga
[jadˈvʲiɡa]
“yahd-VEE-gah”
Polish form of Jadvyga. Polish w is “v”.


Władysław Jagiełło
wła-DY-sław ja-GIEŁ-ło
[vwaˈdɨswaf jaˈɡʲɛwwɔ]
“vwah-DIH-swahf yah-GYEH-woh”
Jogaila’s Polish regnal name. Polish ł is English w.


Jan Długosz
JAN DŁU-gosz
[ˈjan ˈdwuɡɔʂ]
“YAHN DWOO-gosh”
Polish chronicler (1415–80), source for Birutė’s drowning in 1382 and the 1387 extinguishing of the flame. Lithuanian Janas Dlugošas.


Janusz I
JA-nusz
[ˈjanuʂ]
“YAH-noosh”
Duke of Masovia, husband of Danutė. Lithuanian Janušas Mazovietis.


Liudvikas Vengras
LIUD-vi-kas VEN-gras (verify stress)
[ˈlʲʊdvʲɪkɐs ˈvʲæːŋɡrɐs]
“LYOOD-vih-kahs VEN-grahs”
Louis the Great of Hungary and Poland (died Sept 1382); Hungarian Lajos [ˈlɒjoʃ].


Dmitrijus Donskojus
DMIT-ri-jus don-SKO-jus (verify stress)
[ˈdmʲɪtrʲɪjʊs donˈskoːjʊs]
“DMIT-rih-yoos don-SKOH-yoos”
Dmitry Donskoy, Grand Prince of Moscow (Russian [ˈdmʲitrʲɪj dɐnˈskoj]); victor at Kulikovo, 1380.


Wilhelm von Habsburg
VIL-helm fon HAPS-burk
[ˈvɪlhɛlm fɔn ˈhaːpsbʊʁk]
“VIL-helm fon HAHPS-boork”
William of Austria, Jadwiga’s first betrothed. Lithuanian Vilhelmas Habsburgas.

title: Pronunciation guide
text:
9. Gods and Forces
Gods are [Record] in name (sources vary in date and reliability). Forces are [Saga invention] (cosmology §3).










Lithuanian spelling
Stress
IPA
Sounds like
Notes




Dievas
DIE-vas
[ˈdʲiɛvɐs]
“DYEH-vahs”
The sky god; also the ordinary word for (the Christian) God. ie is one gliding vowel, “ee-eh”, never two syllables.


Dievas Senelis
DIE-vas se-NE-lis
[ˈdʲiɛvɐs sʲɛˈnʲælʲɪs]
“DYEH-vahs seh-NEH-lis”
“Old Man God”, the wandering Beggar.


Perkūnas
per-KŪ-nas
[pʲɛrˈkuːnɐs]
“per-KOO-nahs”
Thunder, oaths, justice. Latvian Pērkons, Old Prussian Perkūns; related to Slavic Perun. Avoid “PER-koo-nas”.


Perkūno Rūstybė
per-KŪ-no rūs-TY-bė
[pʲɛrˈkuːno ruːsˈtʲiːbʲeː]
“per-KOO-noh roos-TEE-bay”
[Saga invention] “Perkūnas’s Wrath”, his Force-face.


Velnias
VEL-nias
[ˈvʲælʲnʲɐs]
“VEL-nyahs”
Lord of the dead, wealth and bargains. The name is usually connected with vėlė “soul of the dead”. In modern Lithuanian it simply means “devil”. Two syllables only.


Laima
LAI-ma
[ˈɫɐɪmɐ]
“LYE-mah”
Fate; laimė is “luck, happiness”.


Dalia
DA-lia (verify stress)
[ˈdaːlʲɛ]
“DAH-lyah”
Fortune’s allotter; dalia “share, lot”. The modern given name is Dãlia; the stress of the goddess name needs checking.


Giltinė
gil-TI-nė
[ɡʲɪlʲˈtʲɪnʲeː]
“gil-TIH-nay”
Death, Laima’s sister; from gilti “to sting”.


Žemyna
že-MY-na
[ʒʲɛˈmʲiːnɐ]
“zheh-MEE-nah”
Earth; from žemė. Attested in 16th–17th-century sources (verify which).


Saulė
SAU-lė
[ˈsɐʊlʲeː]
“SOW-lay”
The Sun. Her tears are amber.


Mėnuo
MĖ-nuo
[ˈmʲeːnʊɔ]
“MAY-nwoh”
The Moon, and the word for “month” (cognate with English moon and month). Also Mėnulis (mė-NU-lis).


Aušrinė
auš-RI-nė
[ɐʊʃˈrʲɪnʲeː]
“owsh-RIH-nay”
The Morning Star (Venus); from aušra “dawn”, cognate with Latin aurora.


Gabija
ga-BI-ja
[ɡɐˈbʲɪjɐ]
“gah-BIH-yah”
Hearth fire (Fire element). Possibly from gaubti “to cover”, for banking the embers (uncertain).


Bangpūtys
bang-PŪ-tys
[bɐŋkˈpuːtʲiːs]
“bahng-POO-tees”
Sea and storms (Water element); banga “wave” + pūsti “to blow”. The g is devoiced before p.


Vėjopatis
vė-JO-pa-tis (verify stress)
[vʲeːˈjoːpɐtʲɪs]
“vay-YOH-pah-tis”
The winds (Wind element); vėjas “wind” + patis “lord”.


Praurimė
prau-RI-mė (verify stress)
[prɐʊˈrʲɪmʲeː]
“prow-RIH-may”
Fire of the stars (Stars element). Known mainly from 19th-century mythographers (Narbutt); authenticity is doubtful (verify). Etymology unknown.


Medeina
me-DEI-na (verify stress)
[mʲɛˈdʲɛɪnɐ]
“meh-DAY-nah”
Forest and hunt. [Record] Named in the Hypatian Chronicle under 1252 among Mindaugas’s gods. From medis “tree, forest”.


Jūratė
JŪ-ra-tė
[ˈjuːrɐtʲeː]
“YOO-rah-tay”
The sea goddess of the amber palace; from jūra “sea”. The legend is 19th-century and literary [Record as folklore].


Kastytis
kas-TY-tis
[kɐsˈtʲiːtʲɪs]
“kahs-TEE-tis”
Jūratė’s mortal fisherman.


Gintaro Karalienė
GIN-ta-ro ka-ra-LIE-nė
[ˈɡʲɪntɐro kɐrɐˈlʲiɛnʲeː]
“GIN-tah-roh kah-rah-LYEH-nay”
[Saga invention] The Amber Queen, an office rather than a goddess (D1).


Šaknų Motina
šak-NŲ MO-ti-na
[ʃɐkˈnuː ˈmoːtʲɪnɐ]
“shahk-NOO MOH-tih-nah”
[Saga invention] The Root-Mother. Not a synonym for Žemyna (D8).


Šešėlių Pardavėjas
še-ŠĖ-lių par-da-VĖ-jas
[ʃɛˈʃeːlʲuː pɐrdɐˈvʲeːjɐs]
“sheh-SHAY-lyoo par-dah-VAY-yahs”
[Saga invention] The Shadow-Seller, a shard of Velnias (D2).


Geležinis Šventasis
ge-le-ŽI-nis šven-TA-sis
[ɡʲɛlʲɛˈʒʲɪnʲɪs ʃvʲɛnˈtaːsʲɪs]
“geh-leh-ZHIH-nis shven-TAH-sis”
[Saga invention] The Iron Saint.


Baltoji Tyla
bal-TO-ji ty-LA
[bɐɫˈtoːjɪ tʲiːˈɫɐ]
“bahl-TOH-yih tee-LAH”
[Saga invention] The White Silence.


Stepių Alkis
STE-pių AL-kis
[ˈstʲæːpʲuː ˈɐlʲkʲɪs]
“STEH-pyoo AHL-kis”
[Saga invention] The Steppe-Hunger.


Aukso Rijūnas
AUK-so ri-JŪ-nas
[ˈɐʊkso rʲɪˈjuːnɐs]
“OWK-soh rih-YOO-nahs”
[Saga invention] The Gold-Glutton (D8 replaces “Auksinis Smauglys”).


Erdene-Chuluu
ER-de-ne CHO-luu
[ˈɛrdəɴ ˈtsʰɔɮʊː]
“ER-deh-neh CHOH-loo”
Mongolian “jewel stone”, the Steppe-Hunger’s steppe name. Mongolian, not Lithuanian.


Ferrum Sanctum
FER-rum SANC-tum
[ˈfɛrrʊm ˈsaŋktʊm]
“FER-room SAHNK-toom”
The Iron Saint’s Latin epithet. Corrected from Sanctus Ferrum, which did not agree: Latin ferrum is neuter. Ferrum Sanctum means “holy iron”; Sanctus Ferreus means “iron saint” (see languages_and_naming.md).


Mercator-Rex
MER-ca-tor REX
[mɛrˈkaːtɔr ˈrɛks]
“mer-KAH-tor REX”
The Gold-Glutton’s Latin epithet, “merchant-king”. Classical stress is mer-CA-tor.

title: Pronunciation guide
text:
10. Spirits and creatures
[Record] folk beings unless marked. Plurals are given because the prose uses them.










Lithuanian spelling
Stress
IPA
Sounds like
Notes




laumė
LAU-mė
[ˈɫɐʊmʲeː]
“LOW-may”
Bird-footed fairy woman, weaver and changeling-thief. Plural laumės (LAU-mės). Etymology uncertain.


aitvaras
AIT-va-ras
[ˈɐɪtvɐrɐs]
“ITE-vah-rahs”
Fiery rooster-dragon that steals wealth for its keeper. Plural aitvarai.


kaukas
KAU-kas
[ˈkɐʊkɐs]
“KOW-kahs”
Small household or field sprite bringing prosperity. Plural kaukai (kau-KAI).


žaltys
žal-TYS
[ʒɐlʲˈtʲiːs]
“zhahl-TEES”
Sacred grass snake, guardian of the house. Final stress; avoid “ZHAL-tis”. Plural žalčiai (žal-ČIAI). Often linked to žalias “green”.


vilkatas
vil-KA-tas
[vʲɪlʲˈkaːtɐs]
“vil-KAH-tahs”
Werewolf; from vilkas “wolf”. Plural vilkatai. Used in the saga for the Iron Wolves (iron_wolves.md).


vilkolakis
vil-KO-la-kis
[vʲɪlʲˈkoːɫɐkʲɪs]
“vil-KOH-lah-kis”
The other werewolf word, borrowed from Slavic vlkolak. The docs’ “Vilkakis” is not a Lithuanian word; use vilkatas or vilkolakis.


vėlė
vė-LĖ
[vʲeːˈlʲeː]
“vay-LAY”
Soul of the dead. Plural vėlės stresses the first syllable: VĖ-lės, “VAY-lays”.


ragana
RA-ga-na
[ˈraːɡɐnɐ]
“RAH-gah-nah”
Witch or seer; commonly derived from regėti “to see”. Plural raganos.


dvasios
DVA-sios
[ˈdvaːsʲos]
“DVAH-syohs”
Spirits of place (singular dvasia, dva-SIA).


Eglė žalčių karalienė
eg-LĖ žal-ČIŲ ka-ra-LIE-nė
[ɛɡˈlʲeː ʒɐlʲˈtʃʲuː kɐrɐˈlʲiɛnʲeː]
“eg-LAY zhahl-CHOO kah-rah-LYEH-nay”
[Record: folk tale, recorded from the 19th century] “Eglė, Queen of the Grass Snakes”; Žilvinas is the serpent-husband.


Žilvinas
ŽIL-vi-nas (verify stress)
[ˈʒʲɪlʲvʲɪnɐs]
“ZHIL-vih-nahs”
The serpent-prince of the Eglė tale.


Galios
GA-lios
[ˈɡaːlʲos]
“GAH-lyohs”
[Saga invention] “the Forces” (singular galia, “power”).

title: Pronunciation guide
text:
11. Places
Lithuanian form first; German, Polish, Belarusian or Ukrainian forms in the notes (as in geography_gazetteer.md).










Lithuanian spelling
Stress
IPA
Sounds like
Notes




Vilnius
VIL-nius
[ˈvʲɪlʲnʲʊs]
“VIL-nyoos”
Two syllables. The i after n is not a vowel; it only softens the n. Avoid “VIL-nee-us”. From the river Vilnia (vilnis “surge, wave”).


Trakai
tra-KAI
[trɐˈkɐɪ]
“trah-KYE”
Plural noun, stressed on the ending; from trakas “forest clearing”. German Traken, Polish Troki.


Senieji Trakai
se-NIE-ji tra-KAI
[sʲɛˈnʲiɛjɪ trɐˈkɐɪ]
“seh-NYEH-yih trah-KYE”
Old Trakai, Kęstutis’s older seat and Vytautas’s birthplace.


Galvė
gal-VĖ (verify stress)
[ɡɐlʲˈvʲeː]
“gahl-VAY”
Lake of the Trakai Island Castle.


Krėva
KRĖ-va (verify stress)
[ˈkrʲeːvɐ]
“KRAY-vah”
The castle where Kęstutis died. Belarusian Kreva, Polish Krewo. The docs mix Kreva, Krewa and Krewo; use Krėva in English docs too.


Palanga
pa-lan-GA
[pɐɫɐŋˈɡɐ]
“pah-lahn-GAH”
Birutė’s shore. End-stressed in the nominative.


Birutės kalnas
bi-RU-tės KAL-nas
[bʲɪˈrʊtʲeːs ˈkaːɫnɐs]
“bih-ROO-tays KAHL-nahs”
Birutė’s Hill at Palanga [Record as tradition].


Šventaragis
šven-ta-RA-gis
[ʃvʲɛntɐˈraːɡʲɪs]
“shven-tah-RAH-gis”
The sacred valley at Vilnius under the castle hill, named for the legendary prince Šventaragis (šventas “holy” + ragas “horn”). 16th-century chronicle legend.


Gedimino kalnas
ge-DI-mi-no KAL-nas
[ɡʲɛˈdʲɪmʲɪno ˈkaːɫnɐs]
“geh-DIH-mih-noh KAHL-nahs”
Vilnius castle hill.


Kreivoji pilis
krei-VO-ji pi-LIS
[krʲɛɪˈvoːjɪ pʲɪˈlʲɪs]
“kray-VOH-yih pih-LIS”
The Crooked Castle of Vilnius, burned in 1390.


Kaunas
KAU-nas
[ˈkɐʊnɐs]
“KOW-nahs”
Destroyed by the Order at Easter 1362. The locative is end-stressed: Kaunè.


Kernavė
ker-na-VĖ (verify stress)
[kʲɛrnɐˈvʲeː]
“ker-nah-VAY”
Old ducal centre on the Neris.


Žemaitija
že-MAI-ti-ja
[ʒʲɛˈmɐɪtʲɪjɐ]
“zheh-MYE-tih-yah”
Samogitia, “the lowland” (žemas “low”). People: žemaičiai (že-MAI-čiai).


Aukštaitija
aukš-TAI-ti-ja
[ɐʊkʃˈtɐɪtʲɪjɐ]
“owksh-TYE-tih-yah”
“The highland” (aukštas “high”), the Lithuanian core east of the Nevėžis.


Dubysa
du-by-SA
[dʊbʲiːˈsɐ]
“doo-bee-SAH”
River; Treaty of Dubysa, 31 Oct 1382. Often linked to dubus “deep, hollow”.


Nevėžis
ne-VĖ-žis
[nʲɛˈvʲeːʒʲɪs]
“neh-VAY-zhis”
River; the 1384 Königsberg border.


Nemunas
NE-mu-nas
[ˈnʲæːmʊnɐs]
“NEH-moo-nahs”
The Neman (German Memel).


Neris
ne-RIS
[nʲɛˈrʲɪs]
“neh-RIS”
Vilnius’s river (Belarusian Viliya). Often linked to nerti “to dive”.


Vilnia
VIL-nia (verify stress)
[ˈvʲɪlʲnʲɛ]
“VIL-nyah”
The small river that gives Vilnius its name (also Vilnelė).


Jurbarkas
JUR-bar-kas
[ˈjʊrbɐrkɐs]
“YOOR-bahr-kahs”
German Georgenburg (“George’s castle”); burned by Vytautas in July 1384.


Ragainė
ra-gai-NĖ (verify stress)
[rɐɡɐɪˈnʲeː]
“rah-guy-NAY”
Order castle Ragnit on the Nemunas.


Marienburgas
ma-ri-en-BUR-gas (verify stress)
[mɐrʲɪɛnˈbʊrɡɐs]
“mah-ryen-BOOR-gahs”
German Marienburg [maˈʁiːənbʊʁk], “Mary’s castle”; Polish Malbork [ˈmalbɔrk]. Lithuanian also Malborkas.


Tepliava
TEP-lia-va (verify stress)
[ˈtʲæːplʲɛvɐ]
“TEP-lyah-vah”
German Tapiau [ˈtaːpi̯aʊ], where Vytautas was baptised on 21 Oct 1383.


Karaliaučius
ka-ra-LIAU-čius
[kɐrɐˈlʲæʊtʃʲʊs]
“kah-rah-LYOW-chyoos”
Königsberg, “the king’s town”; Treaty of Königsberg, 30 Jan 1384.


Įsrūtis
įs-RŪ-tis (verify stress)
[iːsˈruːtʲɪs]
“ees-ROO-tis”
German Insterburg.


Klaipėda
KLAI-pė-da
[ˈkɫɐɪpʲeːdɐ]
“KLYE-pay-dah”
German Memel, the Order’s castle at the Curonian Lagoon’s mouth.


Rambynas
ram-BY-nas
[rɐmˈbʲiːnɐs]
“rahm-BEE-nahs”
Sacred hill on the lower Nemunas (German Rombinus).


Šatrija
ŠAT-ri-ja (verify stress)
[ˈʃaːtrʲɪjɐ]
“SHAHT-rih-yah”
Samogitian hill, in folklore a witches’ gathering place.


Medininkai
me-di-NIN-kai
[mʲɛdʲɪˈnʲɪŋkɐɪ]
“meh-dih-NIN-kye”
Two places: a castle east of Vilnius, and Samogitian Medininkai (Varniai).


Varniai
VAR-niai
[ˈvarʲnʲɛɪ]
“VAR-nyay”
Samogitian bishop’s seat after 1417.


Dovydiškės
do-VY-diš-kės (verify stress)
[doˈviːdʲɪʃkʲeːs]
“doh-VEE-dish-kays”
Treaty of Dovydiškės, 31 May 1380 (Dovydiškių sutartis). The site is not securely identified.


Astravas
AS-tra-vas (verify stress)
[ˈaːstrɐvɐs]
“AHS-trah-vahs”
Polish Ostrów: the Agreement of 4–5 Aug 1392 (Astravo sutartis). The brief’s Ostrovas is a Slavic-shaped variant; standard Lithuanian historiography writes Astravas.


Vorskla
VOR-skla
[ˈvoːrsklɐ]
“VOR-sklah”
River in Ukraine (Ukrainian [ˈwɔrsklɐ]); battle on 12 Aug 1399.


Žalgiris
žal-GI-ris
[ʒɐlʲˈɡʲɪrʲɪs]
“zhahl-GIH-ris”
Grunwald (Polish [ˈɡrunvalt]; German Tannenberg), 15 July 1410. Lithuanian calque of “green wood” (žalia giria).


Luckas
LUC-kas
[ˈɫʊtskɐs]
“LOOTS-kahs”
Lutsk (Ukrainian Lutsk [ɫut͡sʲk]; Polish Łuck); the Congress of 1429.


Ašmena
AŠ-me-na (verify stress)
[ˈaːʃmʲɛnɐ]
“AHSH-meh-nah”
Belarusian Ashmyany, Polish Oszmiana; Žygimantas’s coup of 1 Sep 1432.


Naugardukas
nau-gar-DU-kas (verify stress)
[nɐʊɡɐrˈdʊkɐs]
“now-gahr-DOO-kahs”
Navahrudak, Black Ruthenia.


Lyda
LY-da (verify stress)
[ˈlʲiːdɐ]
“LEE-dah”
Lida, castle south-west of Vilnius.


Gardinas
GAR-di-nas
[ˈɡaːrdʲɪnɐs]
“GAHR-dih-nahs”
Grodno, Vytautas’s seat from 1384.


Brasta
BRAS-ta
[ˈbraːstɐ]
“BRAHS-tah”
Brest.


Polockas
PO-loc-kas (verify stress)
[ˈpoːɫɔtskɐs]
“POH-lots-kahs”
Polotsk.


Vitebskas
VI-tebs-kas (verify stress)
[ˈvʲɪtʲɛpskɐs]
“VIH-teps-kahs”
Vitebsk.


Smolenskas
smo-LENS-kas (verify stress)
[smoˈlʲænskɐs]
“smoh-LENS-kahs”
Smolensk.


Kijevas
KI-je-vas
[ˈkʲɪjɛvɐs]
“KIH-yeh-vahs”
Kyiv.


Krokuva
kro-ku-VA
[krokʊˈvɐ]
“kroh-koo-VAH”
Kraków (Polish [ˈkrakuf]).


Ryga
ry-GA
[rʲiːˈɡɐ]
“ree-GAH”
Riga.


Prūsija
PRŪ-si-ja
[ˈpruːsʲɪjɐ]
“PROO-sih-yah”
Prussia.


Livonija
li-VO-ni-ja
[lʲɪˈvoːnʲɪjɐ]
“lih-VOH-nih-yah”
Livonia.


Mazovija
ma-ZO-vi-ja (verify stress)
[mɐˈzoːvʲɪjɐ]
“mah-ZOH-vih-yah”
Masovia.


Romuva
RO-mu-va (verify stress)
[ˈroːmʊvɐ]
“ROH-moo-vah”
Peter von Dusburg’s Romowe in Nadruvia; under the Order since the 1270s–80s. Not a Book I location (review H11).


Ukmergė
UK-mer-gė
[ˈʊkmʲɛrʲɡʲeː]
“OOK-mer-gay”
Polish Wiłkomierz.


Pabaiskas
pa-BAIS-kas
[pɐˈbɐɪskɐs]
“pah-BICE-kahs”
Battle of 1 Sep 1435.


Šventoji
šven-TO-ji
[ʃvʲɛnˈtoːjɪ]
“shven-TOH-yih”
“The holy (river)”; its mouth lies near Palanga.


Strėva
STRĖ-va (verify stress)
[ˈstrʲeːvɐ]
“STRAY-vah”
Battle of Strėva, 2 Feb 1348.


Salynas
sa-LY-nas (verify stress)
[sɐˈlʲiːnɐs]
“sah-LEE-nahs”
Treaty of Salynas, 12 Oct 1398.

title: Pronunciation guide
text:
12. Terms of the saga
Magic, cosmology, ranks and kinship.










Lithuanian spelling
Stress
IPA
Sounds like
Notes




Senovės Kalba
se-NO-vės kal-BA
[sʲɛˈnoːvʲeːs kɐɫˈbɐ]
“seh-NOH-vays kahl-BAH”
[Saga invention] “The Ancient Speech”, the craft of asking.


Senovės Sutartis
se-NO-vės su-tar-TIS
[sʲɛˈnoːvʲeːs sʊtɐrˈtʲɪs]
“seh-NOH-vays soo-tahr-TIS”
[Saga invention] The Ancient Pact rite (magic_rules §6).


Tylioji Sutartis
ty-LIO-ji su-tar-TIS
[tʲiːˈlʲoːjɪ sʊtɐrˈtʲɪs]
“tee-LYOH-yih soo-tahr-TIS”
[Saga invention] The Silent Pact of 1345 (D7).


Atsaistymas
at-SAIS-ty-mas (verify stress)
[ɐtˈsɐɪstʲiːmɐs]
“aht-SICE-tee-mahs”
[Saga invention] The Unbinding (cosmology §4.3).


slaptas vardas
SLAP-tas VAR-das
[ˈsɫaːptɐs ˈvarˑdɐs]
“SLAHP-tahs VAR-dahs”
[Saga invention] The true name a mother whispers at birth (languages_and_naming.md §5).


Penkių Balsų Šauksmas
pen-KIŲ bal-SŲ ŠAUKS-mas
[pʲɛŋˈkʲuː bɐɫˈsuː ˈʃɐʊksmɐs]
“pen-KYOO bahl-SOO SHOWKS-mahs”
[Saga invention] The Five-Voice invocation (magic_rules §4.2).


Žymė
žy-MĖ
[ʒʲiːˈmʲeː]
“zhee-MAY”
[Saga term] A Force’s claim, “mark”.


Sandėris
san-DĖ-ris
[sɐnˈdʲeːrʲɪs]
“sahn-DAY-ris”
[Saga term] A bargain with the Shadow-Seller.


laidas
LAI-das
[ˈɫɐɪdɐs]
“LYE-dahs”
[Saga term] Surety in a Sutartis (magic_rules §4.3).


Prigimtis
pri-gim-TIS
[prʲɪɡʲɪmʲˈtʲɪs]
“prih-gim-TIS”
“Nature, birth”: the born path to Kalba.


Pažymėtas
pa-žy-MĖ-tas
[pɐʒʲiːˈmʲeːtɐs]
“pah-zhee-MAY-tahs”
“Noticed”: the second path to Kalba.


Surištas
SU-riš-tas
[ˈsʊrʲɪʃtɐs]
“SOO-rish-tahs”
“Bound”: the third path to Kalba (Vytautas’s).


Dagotuvės
da-go-TU-vės
[dɐɡoˈtʊvʲeːs]
“dah-goh-TOO-vays”
Harvest-end feast; Žemyna’s zenith in the saga. See calendar_and_festivals.md on the name’s age.


Rasos
RA-sos
[ˈraːsos]
“RAH-sohs”
Midsummer, “the dews” (rasa “dew”). Gabija’s zenith.


Joninės
JO-ni-nės
[ˈjoːnʲɪnʲeːs]
“YOH-nih-nays”
St John’s Eve, the Christian name for Midsummer.


Kūčios
KŪ-čios
[ˈkuːtʃʲos]
“KOO-chohs”
Christmas Eve supper; the saga’s winter-solstice night (Praurimė’s zenith). From kūčia, the ritual grain dish (Slavic kutia).


Kalėdos
ka-LĖ-dos
[kɐˈlʲeːdos]
“kah-LAY-dohs”
Christmas; from Slavic koliada (from Latin calendae).


Vėlinės
VĖ-li-nės
[ˈvʲeːlʲɪnʲeːs]
“VAY-lih-nays”
Feast of the dead (All Souls, 2 Nov); Vėjopatis’s zenith in the saga.


Ilgės
IL-gės (verify stress)
[ˈɪlʲɡʲeːs]
“IL-gays”
Old name for the autumn commemoration of the dead (verify the earliest source).


Užgavėnės
už-ga-VĖ-nės
[ʊʒɡɐˈvʲeːnʲeːs]
“oozh-gah-VAY-nays”
Shrovetide, “before the fast”.


Pusiaugavėnis
pu-siau-ga-VĖ-nis
[pʊsʲæʊɡɐˈvʲeːnʲɪs]
“poo-syow-gah-VAY-nis”
Mid-Lent.


Velykos
ve-LY-kos
[vʲɛˈlʲiːkos]
“veh-LEE-kohs”
Easter; from Slavic velikŭ dĭnĭ “great day”.


Jorė
JO-rė (verify stress)
[ˈjoːrʲeː]
“YOH-ray”
Spring greening feast near St George’s Day; a modern Romuva name (verify how old it is).


Jurginės
JUR-gi-nės
[ˈjʊrɡʲɪnʲeːs]
“YOOR-gih-nays”
St George’s Day, 23 Apr.


Sekminės
SEK-mi-nės
[ˈsʲækʲmʲɪnʲeːs]
“SEK-mih-nays”
Pentecost.


Žolinė
žo-LI-nė
[ʒoˈlʲɪnʲeː]
“zhoh-LIH-nay”
The Assumption, 15 Aug, “the herb feast” (žolė “grass, herb”). Kęstutis died on this day.


Šilinė
ši-LI-nė
[ʃɪˈlʲɪnʲeː]
“shih-LIH-nay”
Nativity of Mary, 8 Sept.


Grabnyčios
grab-NY-čios
[ɡrɐbˈnʲiːtʃʲos]
“grahb-NEE-chohs”
Candlemas, 2 Feb; from Slavic gromnica “thunder candle”.


Mykolinės
MY-ko-li-nės
[ˈmʲiːkolʲɪnʲeːs]
“MEE-koh-lih-nays”
Michaelmas, 29 Sept.


Lygiadienis
ly-GIA-die-nis
[lʲiːˈɡʲæːdʲiɛnʲɪs]
“lee-GYAH-dyeh-nis”
Equinox (“equal day”).


Saulėgrįža
sau-LĖ-grį-ža
[sɐʊˈlʲeːɡrʲiːʒɐ]
“sow-LAY-gree-zhah”
Solstice (“sun’s return”).


Pusiaukojis
pu-SIAU-ko-jis (verify stress)
[pʊˈsʲæʊkojɪs]
“poo-SYOW-koh-yis”
The magic doc’s name for the spring equinox. It is not an attested Lithuanian word. Its stress is a guess. Consider Pavasario lygiadienis.


Dausos
DAU-sos
[ˈdɐʊsos]
“DOW-sohs”
The afterlife meadow beyond the Glass Mountain.


Anapilis
a-na-PI-lis (verify stress)
[ɐnɐˈpʲɪlʲɪs]
“ah-nah-PIH-lis”
“The castle beyond”, the underworld.


Požemis
PO-že-mis
[ˈpoːʒʲɛmʲɪs]
“POH-zheh-mis”
The under-earth.


Pasaulio Medis
pa-SAU-lio ME-dis
[pɐˈsɐʊlʲo ˈmʲædʲɪs]
“pah-SOW-lyoh MEH-dis”
The World Tree.


Dangus
dan-GUS
[dɐnˈɡʊs]
“dahn-GOOS”
The sky, heaven.


Stiklo Kalnas
STIK-lo KAL-nas
[ˈstʲɪkɫo ˈkaːɫnɐs]
“STIK-loh KAHL-nahs”
The Glass Mountain the dead must climb.


Paukščių Takas
PAUKŠ-čių TA-kas
[ˈpɐʊkʃtʃʲuː ˈtaːkɐs]
“POWKSH-choo TAH-kahs”
The Milky Way, “the Birds’ Way”.


Sietynas
sie-TY-nas
[sʲiɛˈtʲiːnɐs]
“syeh-TEE-nahs”
The Pleiades (“the sieve”), folk astronomy for the Star-Readers.


Grįžulo Ratai
GRĮ-žu-lo RA-tai
[ˈɡrʲiːʒʊlo ˈraːtɐɪ]
“GREE-zhoo-loh RAH-tye”
The Plough or Big Dipper, “the wagon of the returner”.


Vakarinė
va-ka-RI-nė
[vɐkɐˈrʲɪnʲeː]
“vah-kah-RIH-nay”
The Evening Star.


Marios
MA-rios
[ˈmaːrʲos]
“MAH-ryohs”
The lagoon or sea (Kuršių marios, the Curonian Lagoon).


alkas
AL-kas
[ˈaːɫkɐs]
“AHL-kahs”
Sacred grove or hill. Plural alkai.


krivis
KRI-vis (verify stress)
[ˈkrʲɪvʲɪs]
“KRIH-vis”
High priest; Dusburg’s Criwe. Also Krivė. Krivių Krivaitis (verify stress) is “krivis of krivises”.


krivulė
kri-VU-lė
[krʲɪˈvʊlʲeː]
“krih-VOO-lay”
The krivis’s crooked staff, sent round as a summons.


žynys
žy-NYS
[ʒʲiːˈnʲiːs]
“zhee-NEES”
Priest or seer, “knower” (žinoti “to know”). Plural žyniai (žy-NIAI).


vaidila
vai-DI-la (verify stress)
[vɐɪˈdʲɪɫɐ]
“vye-DIH-lah”
Pagan priest-bard (Prussian Waidelotte in Order sources).


vaidilutė
vai-di-LU-tė
[vɐɪdʲɪˈɫʊtʲeː]
“vye-dih-LOO-tay”
Priestess of the eternal flame. Plural vaidilutės. The word is largely a 19th-century romantic coinage (verify).


burtininkas
bur-TI-nin-kas
[bʊrˈtʲɪnʲɪŋkɐs]
“boor-TIH-nin-kahs”
Diviner, caster of lots (burtai). Plural burtininkai.


Dykra
dyk-RA (verify stress)
[dʲiːkˈrɐ]
“deek-RAH”
The wild swamp-forest belt (D8); from dykas “empty”. Historians’ German term: Wildnis.


Amžinoji Ugnis
am-ži-NO-ji ug-NIS
[ɐmʒʲɪˈnoːjɪ ʊɡˈnʲɪs]
“ahm-zhih-NOH-yih oog-NIS”
The Eternal Flame.


Šventasis akmuo
šven-TA-sis ak-MUO
[ʃvʲɛnˈtaːsʲɪs ɐkˈmʊɔ]
“shven-TAH-sis ahk-MWOH”
The holy stone.


piliakalnis
pi-LIA-kal-nis
[pʲɪˈlʲæːkɐɫnʲɪs]
“pih-LYAH-kahl-nis”
Hillfort mound. Plural piliakalniai.


Geležinis Vilkas
ge-le-ŽI-nis VIL-kas
[ɡʲɛlʲɛˈʒʲɪnʲɪs ˈvʲɪlʲkɐs]
“geh-leh-ZHIH-nis VIL-kahs”
The Iron Wolf of Gediminas’s dream.


Vytis
VY-tis
[ˈviːtʲɪs]
“VEE-tis”
The mounted knight of the arms. In narration, never the man (D4).


Gedimino stulpai
ge-DI-mi-no STUL-pai
[ɡʲɛˈdʲɪmʲɪno ˈstʊlʲpɐɪ]
“geh-DIH-mih-noh STOOL-pye”
The Columns of Gediminas, the dynastic sign.


kunigaikštis
ku-ni-GAIKŠ-tis
[kʊnʲɪˈɡɐɪkʃtʲɪs]
“koo-nih-GUYKSH-tis”
Duke, prince. Didysis kunigaikštis (di-DY-sis) is “Grand Duke”.


bajoras
ba-JO-ras
[bɐˈjoːrɐs]
“bah-YOH-rahs”
Boyar, noble. Plural bajorai.


dėdė
DĖ-dė
[ˈdʲeːdʲeː]
“DAY-day”
Uncle (paternal), D9. A masculine noun ending in -ė.


sūnėnas
sū-NĖ-nas
[suːˈnʲeːnɐs]
“soo-NAY-nahs”
Nephew (brother’s son). Plural sūnėnai.


pusbrolis
PUS-bro-lis
[ˈpʊsbrolʲɪs]
“POOS-broh-lis”
Cousin, “half-brother” in form. Plural pusbroliai.


uošvis
UOŠ-vis
[ˈuɔʃvʲɪs]
“WOHSH-vis”
Father-in-law (spouse’s father).


anyta
a-NY-ta
[ɐˈnʲiːtɐ]
“ah-NEE-tah”
Mother-in-law (husband’s mother).


Gintaro Šventikai
GIN-ta-ro šven-TI-kai
[ˈɡʲɪntɐro ʃvʲɛnˈtʲɪkɐɪ]
“GIN-tah-roh shven-TIH-kye”
Amber Priests lineage (magic doc). Ch. 31 calls it Gintaro Žyniai, so the name needs unifying.


Miško Šnibždeliai
MIŠ-ko šnibž-DE-liai (verify stress)
[ˈmʲɪʃko ʃnʲɪbʒˈdʲæːlʲɛɪ]
“MISH-koh shnibzh-DEH-lyay”
Forest Whisperers lineage. Šnibždeliai is a coinage; the stress is a guess.


Vėjo Kalbėtojai
VĖ-jo kal-BĖ-to-jai
[ˈvʲeːjo kɐɫˈbʲeːtojɐɪ]
“VAY-yoh kahl-BAY-toh-yigh”
Wind Speakers lineage.


Ugnies Gynėjai
ug-NIES gy-NĖ-jai
[ʊɡˈnʲiɛs ɡʲiːˈnʲeːjɐɪ]
“oog-NYES gee-NAY-yigh”
Fire Guardians lineage.


Žvaigždžių Skaitovai
žvaigž-DŽIŲ skai-TO-vai
[ʒvɐɪɡʒˈdʒʲuː skɐɪˈtoːvɐɪ]
“zhvighzh-JOO skye-TOH-vye”
Star Readers lineage.


Regėjimo Aiška
re-GĖ-ji-mo AIŠ-ka (verify stress)
[rʲɛˈɡʲeːjɪmo ˈɐɪʃkɐ]
“reh-GAY-yih-moh ISH-kah”
Clear Sight (Stars boon). Aiška is not a standard noun (standard aiškumas). It reads as an archaic coinage.


Sielos Šarvas
SIE-los ŠAR-vas
[ˈsʲiɛlos ˈʃarˑvɐs]
“SYEH-lohs SHAR-vahs”
Soul Armour (Fire boon).


Gyvybės Versmė
gy-VY-bės vers-MĖ
[ɡʲiːˈvʲiːbʲeːs vʲɛrsʲˈmʲeː]
“gee-VEE-bays vers-MAY”
Life Spring (Water boon).


Nepajudinamoji Valia
ne-pa-JU-di-na-mo-ji va-LIA
[nʲɛpɐˈjʊdʲɪnɐmojɪ vɐˈlʲæ]
“neh-pah-YOO-dih-nah-moh-yih vah-LYAH”
Unmovable Will (Earth boon).


Šešėlio Greitis
še-ŠĖ-lio GREI-tis
[ʃɛˈʃeːlʲo ˈɡrʲɛɪtʲɪs]
“sheh-SHAY-lyoh GRAY-tis”
Shadow Speed (Wind boon).


Saulutė
sau-LU-tė
[sɐʊˈɫʊtʲeː]
“sow-LOO-tay”
Sun-wheel sign (power_systems).


Perkūnėlis
per-kū-NĖ-lis
[pʲɛrkuːˈnʲeːlʲɪs]
“per-koo-NAY-lis”
Thunder-cross sign. Use this, not the Latvian Pērkonkrusts.


Laimos medis
LAI-mos ME-dis
[ˈɫɐɪmos ˈmʲædʲɪs]
“LYE-mohs MEH-dis”
Laima’s tree sign.


Žirgeliai
žir-GE-liai
[ʒʲɪrˈɡʲæːlʲɛɪ]
“zhir-GEH-lyay”
Carved horse-heads on the roof ridge.


Mėnulio pjautuvas
mė-NU-lio PJAU-tu-vas
[mʲeːˈnʊlʲo ˈpjɐʊtʊvɐs]
“may-NOO-lyoh PYOW-too-vahs”
Moon-sickle sign.

title: Pronunciation guide
section: 13. The five incantations, the Laws and the vows
text:
13. The five incantations, the Laws and the vows
[Saga invention]. The formula is [Element] tau/man [verb] (magic_rules §3.1). Tau and man are unstressed clitics; give them no weight.










Lithuanian spelling
Stress
IPA
Sounds like
Notes




Žvaigždės tau švytės
ŽVAIGŽ-dės tau švy-TĖS
[ˈʒvɐɪɡʒdʲeːs tɐʊ ʃvʲiːˈtʲeːs]
“ZHVIGHZH-days tow shvee-TAYS”
Stars (Praurimė). “The stars will shine for you.” Self-cast: Žvaigždės man švytės.


Ugnis tau degs
ug-NIS tau DEGS
[ʊɡˈnʲɪs tɐʊ ˈdʲɛks]
“oog-NIS tow DEKS”
Fire (Gabija). “Fire will burn for you.” Final -gs is devoiced to “ks”. Self-cast: Ugnis man degs.


Vanduo tau teks
van-DUO tau TEKS
[vɐnˈdʊɔ tɐʊ ˈtʲɛks]
“vahn-DWOH tow TEKS”
Water (Bangpūtys). Teks is the future of tekti “to fall to one’s lot”, not of tekėti “to flow” (future tekės). Literally “water shall be your portion”. Self-cast: Vanduo man teks.


Žemė tau laikys
ŽE-mė tau lai-KYS
[ˈʒʲæːmʲeː tɐʊ ɫɐɪˈkʲiːs]
“ZHEH-may tow lye-KEES”
Earth (Žemyna). “Earth will hold (it) for you.” Self-cast: Žemė man laikys.


Vėjas tau neš
VĖ-jas tau NEŠ
[ˈvʲeːjɐs tɐʊ ˈnʲɛʃ]
“VAY-yahs tow NESH”
Wind (Vėjopatis). “Wind will carry (it) for you.” Self-cast: Vėjas man neš.


Kiek paimi, tiek atiduok
kiek pai-MI, tiek a-ti-DUOK

Do not record these until the stress (or, for foreign names, the Lithuanian form) has been confirmed against a dictionary or by a native speaker. Most come from four groups. The first is rarer historical names absent from everyday dictionaries (Kaributas, Tautvilas, Butautas). The second is names the saga invented (Henė, Galminas), where the author decides. The third is place names whose accent paradigm I could not confirm (Krėva, Galvė, Ragainė). The fourth is Lithuanian adaptations of foreign names, where usage varies (Toktamyšas, Edigėjus).

title: Pronunciation guide
text:
19. Notes for the audiobook pipeline

pronunciation_lexicon.json holds 351 entries with these fields:

text: canonical spelling.
variants: inflected Lithuanian forms that occur in prose.
ipa, respelling_en and stress: as in this guide.
category: character, foreign, deity, spirit, place, term, incantation, saying or title.
verify: true means do not trust the stress yet.
ascii (where it differs): the diacritic-stripped forms the current pipeline produces (Kestutis, Shvitrigaila, Zhemyna), so that they can still be matched.
stress_notes (on names whose stress moves): which case forms shift.

The English pipeline currently destroys the information it needs. audiobook/1_preprocess_with_ollama.py (lines 200–205) tells the model to strip ą ę į ų ū ė and turn š č ž into sh ch zh. After that, ę and ė (different vowels) both become e, and nothing marks stress. The prompt also contradicts itself: line 204 says “zh for ž”, but line 205’s example gives Žemyna → Zemyna. Better: keep the Lithuanian spelling through translation, then substitute from the lexicon. Use SSML <phoneme alphabet="ipa" ph="…"> where the TTS engine supports it, or the respelling_en text where it does not. Match longest strings first, so that Šešėlių Pardavėjas wins over Pardavėjas.
Variants matter mostly for a Lithuanian narration. The English translation will mostly contain nominatives (and English possessives, Vytautas’s). For a Lithuanian voice, every form in variants keeps the nominative’s stressed syllable, except where stress_notes says otherwise.
Respellings are for English voices. For a Lithuanian voice, feed the IPA (or the dictionary accent marks from §3), not the respelling.

title: Series arc
text:
Source: books/series_arc.md
The braid that runs through all the books. Each book’s outline must advance every thread below, or deliberately rest it. Canon sources: world_rules/canon_decisions.md, cosmology.md, magic_rules.md, master_chronology.md.
The saga’s one-sentence spine: A pagan realm survives a century of crusade by a pact with its gods; one family’s kin-murder breaks it; the murdered man’s son spends fifty years building a Christian empire with his left hand while secretly keeping the old fire alive with his right, and the moment he dies the fire goes out and the gods become folklore.

title: Series arc
section: 2. Book by book: what each must hand to the next
text:
2. Book by book: what each must hand to the next

Book VI (optional prequel): Šventasis Miškas, 1345–1377

Delivers: the oath scene of the Silent Pact; Kęstutis and Birutė’s meeting; Kęstutis’s 1361 Marienburg escape (the template for his son’s); Algirdas’s cremation.
Hands on: the reader knows the Pact’s three clauses, so every breach in Book I lands.



Book I: Vilko Tremtis, 1377–1387 (written; under revision)

Must plant: Pact clause 2 broken (Krėva); Birutė’s Sutartis with surety and the flame promise (ch. 3); Perkūnas’s claim (ch. 10); Eglė’s price (ch. 16); Henė’s three stones; the Iron Wolves massacred (ch. 7) and re-forming (ch. 25); Trakai given to Skirgaila (ch. 28); Ona as hostage; the flame lit in secret at the end of ch. 29.
Hands on: a Vytautas who is twice baptised, without his father’s land, with no surety, carrying a flame he cannot let die, and a land whose spirits are starting to go feral.



Book II: Auksinis Šešėlis, 1387–1399

Arc: ambition. From Skirgaila’s Trakai, through the second defection and Ostrów (where he becomes Grand Duke), to empire and then the Vorskla.
Must include (currently missing): the 1389–92 second civil war, the 1390 siege of Vilnius (the Crooked Castle and Bolingbroke), the poisoning of his sons (the moral price of defection), Ostrów 1392, and Skirgaila’s death in 1397, not in Part 3.
The Unbinding reaches the countryside; first vilkatai hunts.
Hands on: a humbled Vytautas who has seen what empire-hunger costs; Samogitia sold (Salynas 1398) and burning to rise.



Book III: Žaliasis Miškas, 1399–1411

Arc: atonement through alliance. Reconciled cousins; Samogitia’s uprisings; Grunwald.
Threads: the Root-Mother’s last great act; the Iron Saint broken; Perkūnas rewards a kept oath; the flame carried in a lantern on campaign (its one public moment, seen by a single žynys).
Hands on: victory that changes nothing for the gods: Samogitia will still be baptised.



Book IV: Nematoma Karūna, 1411–1430

Arc: the temptation of legitimacy. The crown offered by Sigismund; the flame as the price.
Threads: Ona’s death (1418); the Hidden Groves felled; Henė’s final bargain; the crown turned to leaves. Vytautas refuses to let the flame die, and so he dies uncrowned. Make that refusal the secret meaning of the historical mystery.
Hands on: a land with one flame left, in a dying man’s vault.



Book V: Vilko Palikimas, 1430–1450

Arc: the ghosts. The flame goes out; the civil war of the heirs; the Unbinding peaks at Pabaiskas; the gods become folklore.
Frame: Birutė (the Amber Queen) narrates. This connects to 00_pradzia.qmd, which becomes the series frame, not just Book I’s.
Ends: the Iron Wolf’s last howl over Trakai; the amber statue taken by the sea.

title: Series arc
section: 3. Rules for keeping the braid tight
text:
3. Rules for keeping the braid tight

Each book opens with a thread from the last book’s final chapter (Book I ends with Henė and Skirgaila, so Book II opens with Skirgaila in Trakai).
Every magic use spends something that matters later (magic_rules.md §4). Costs accumulate across books.
Henė appears at least once per book, always at a deal, juggling three stones (later two, then one, as the cousins die).
The amber pebble’s state is the reader’s moral compass. Track it in each book’s continuity bible.
Historical anchors are non-negotiable (D3). The myth explains why, never whether.
Keep the grey. Every book must give one sympathetic Order brother, one decent Pole, one monstrous Lithuanian and one choice where the pagan option is worse.

title: Series arc
section: 4. Open design questions for the author
text:
4. Open design questions for the author

Does the flame have a keeper other than Vytautas (an Iron Wolf? a Karaim at Trakai?), so Book V can stage its going-out from a witness’s POV?
Is Book VI written before or after Book V’s flashbacks? (If after, Book V can quote it as a “song”.)
How much of Birutė’s frame narration should each book carry: a prologue only, or interludes?

title: Aitvaras (fire-tailed thief)
text:
Folk source [Record]
A spirit that brings its keeper wealth stolen from neighbours. It hatches from the egg of an old rooster (seven or nine years old) kept warm by its owner, or is bought from a merchant. Outdoors it flies as a fiery streak; indoors it is a black cockerel or cat. It is fed scrambled eggs, and when offended it burns the farm. Named in 16th-century church writings against peasant superstition; Christian-era tales make it a devil’s gift paid for with the keeper’s soul.

title: Aitvaras (fire-tailed thief)
section: In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
text:
In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
A hatchling of Velnias’s root-wealth that hungers for fire. It does not make wealth, it moves it: every grain it brings is a grain a neighbour lost. The folk are right that it steals and burns, and wrong that it serves the devil: it serves the trade, and anyone who feeds it. “A soul for an aitvaras” is true: the keeper goes down to Velnias’s roots at death, and in life the household slowly stops being able to give anything away freely.

title: Aitvaras (fire-tailed thief)
text:
Signs & habitat
Fiery streaks at dusk from a poor farm to a rich one; a neighbour who prospers in a bad year; eggshells by the oven; a smell of singed feathers.

title: Aitvaras (fire-tailed thief)
text:
Before / after the Unbinding
Before: a nuisance kept in bounds by custom. After: aitvarai turn arsonist; near Hanseatic towns the Gold-Glutton courts them and they carry warm coin instead of grain, which starts quarrels wherever it is spent.

title: Aitvaras (fire-tailed thief)
section: Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
text:
Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
Feed it and it stays loyal (cost: the neighbours’ enmity, eventually a lynching). Sell it on, or set it an impossible count such as a sack of poppy seed (while it counts it is still yours). Spoiling its dish makes it burn the house; some families burn their own farm to be free. Cursing or baring yourself at a flying aitvaras makes it drop its load on your land, so the stolen goods are in your barn when the owner comes.

title: Aitvaras (fire-tailed thief)
text:
Danger level
II hazard → IV deadly.

title: Aitvaras (fire-tailed thief)
text:
Story hooks
Book II: Jogaila’s Vilnius and its new Magdeburg merchants crawling with aitvarai fed by the Gold-Glutton. Book IV: a fire in Trakai’s town blamed on Vytautas’s enemies, really an aitvaras abandoned by a bankrupt Hanseatic factor.

text:

Small underground beings attested in 16th-century accounts of Prussian and Samogitian belief. In the Prussian material they serve an earth-god, Puškaitis, who lives beneath the elder bush (šeivamedis), and people left bread and beer under the elder for them. Whether they are the same beings as kaukai or barzdukai, or whether the words are even related, is debated; regional variants differ.

title: Barstukai (under-elder miners)
section: In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
text:
In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
Not house-spirits at all: the Root-Mother’s diggers, miners of bog-ore and buried amber in the roots of elder thickets and under hill-forts. They hate smelted iron and the plough, but they trade: bog-iron for bread, amber for beer, a safe path for a promise. Every old-school smith had a barstukas bargain, and the vilkatai’s bog-iron comes from them. A kaukas is your dead; a barstukas is nobody’s.

title: Barstukai (under-elder miners)
text:
Signs & habitat
Elder thickets on old hill-forts and by bogs; lumps of bog-iron left on a stump; hammering underground at night.

title: Barstukai (under-elder miners)
text:
Before / after the Unbinding
Before: honest traders. After 1387 the Order and then Polish and Lithuanian lords drain and mine the land by the furlong, and the barstukai stop trading and begin to collapse wells and mine-shafts.

title: Barstukai (under-elder miners)
section: Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
text:
Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
Bread and beer under the elder at dusk, never watched (watching ends the bargain for the whole family). Never cut an elder without asking three times (the ground under your house goes hollow). Smith’s iron drives them down; feast-day iron kills them, and with it your bog-iron.

title: Barstukai (under-elder miners)
text:
Danger level
I nuisance → III dangerous.

title: Barstukai (under-elder miners)
text:
Story hooks
Book III: barstukai helping Samogitians tunnel under an Order stockade. Book IV: a Kraków mining venture in Podlasie collapses and the survivors swear the earth spoke.

title: Bebalsiai (the Voiceless)
section: In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
text:
In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
The White Silence’s hollowed ones. The White Silence gathers wherever a baptism is bought; the bought baptism is the opening, and it settles into the empty place where neither old custom nor new faith lives. Not monsters but victims: over months a bebalsis loses voice, then shadow, then warmth. They are harmless themselves, but the White Silence listens through them, and where several gather, sound dies, Wind workings fail and Water workings freeze.

text:
Signs & habitat
Frost flowers in their footprints; people who stop speaking after a mass baptism; villages along the Neris where nobody sings.

title: Bebalsiai (the Voiceless)
text:
Before / after the Unbinding
Before: almost none (Mindaugas’s bought baptism of the 13th century produced a few, long dead). After 1387: many, around Vilnius first; after 1413 in Samogitia.

section: Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
text:
Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
Real belief in anything, old or new, closes the opening; an honest Christian or honest pagan cannot become one (belief cannot be forced, and that is the whole problem). Speaking the victim’s old name by a living fire returns the voice for a night, and the White Silence notices who did it.

title: Girinis / miškinis (grove-keepers)
text:
Folk source [Record]
Lithuanian tradition knows forest guardians under several names (girinis, miškinis, medinis), less sharply personified than the Slavic leshy. Pre-Christian Lithuanians venerated sacred groves (alkai) and particular trees, above all oaks, and cutting them was taboo; legends tell of trees that bled or took revenge. A stray-herb (klystžolė) makes whoever steps on it lose the way. Hunters made offerings for game.

title: Girinis / miškinis (grove-keepers)
section: In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
text:
In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
A girinis is the local face of the Root-Mother: the spirit of one grove, wood or ancient oak. It cares about people only as they affect the trees. It gives game and safe paths to those who ask and repay, and leads the greedy in circles until they die. The oaks of the alkai are the Pact’s pillars; each one felled loosens it.

title: Girinis / miškinis (grove-keepers)
text:
Signs & habitat
Silence where there should be birdsong (Book I ch. 1, 20); paths that return to the same stump; a branch that falls exactly where you stood.

title: Girinis / miškinis (grove-keepers)
text:
Before / after the Unbinding
Before: a stern host. After a grove is felled (Šventaragis 1387, and hundreds more) its girinis does not die: it becomes a homeless hunger attached to the family of the man who swung the axe, following them for generations.

title: Girinis / miškinis (grove-keepers)
section: Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
text:
Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
Bread and salt on a stump before hunting or cutting, and “Leisk, medi” (“Permit me, tree”); never take more than you asked. Turn your clothes inside out if lost (it may let you go but will remember your face). The axe that felled a sacred oak must be thrown into running water.

title: Girinis / miškinis (grove-keepers)
text:
Danger level
II hazard → IV deadly.

title: Girinis / miškinis (grove-keepers)
text:
Story hooks
Book I: the silence in ch. 1 and 20 is the girinis listening for the Pact to break. Books II–V: the bishop’s woodcutters who cleared Šventaragis, and their haunted grandchildren.

title: Kaukas / barzdukai (field-luck)
text:
Folk source [Record]
Small (thumb- to knee-high), often bearded household and field spirits (the barzdukai, “little beards”). A kaukas brings grain and plenty, usually by multiplying what is already there rather than stealing, and must be fed. Giving it clothes makes it leave. Named with aitvarai in 16th-century church writings; in some regions kaukai are the souls of unbaptised infants. Folklorists draw the line this way: the aitvaras brings from elsewhere, the kaukas increases what is here. Regional variants differ widely.

title: Kaukas / barzdukai (field-luck)
section: In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
text:
In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
The kaukai are the unnamed dead: infants who died before their mother spoke their secret name (see magic rules §6). With no name they cannot climb the Glass Mountain, so Žemyna keeps them in the soil to tend the fields. “Unbaptised” is a distorted memory of “unnamed”. A kaukas is a family’s own dead child working the family’s field; most families half know it and never say it. Folk often confuse them with the barstukai, which is useful in fiction.

title: Kaukas / barzdukai (field-luck)
text:
Signs & habitat
A grain-bin that stays fuller than it should; tiny footprints in flour; the threshing floor and granary corners.

title: Kaukas / barzdukai (field-luck)
text:
Before / after the Unbinding
Before: they tend and multiply, asking porridge and a place. After: with no courtesy owed, the unnamed dead turn hungry and eat the grain they once multiplied; granaries rot from the inside.

title: Kaukas / barzdukai (field-luck)
section: Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
text:
Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
Porridge on the threshing floor at harvest (minimal cost, which is why the bargain lasted). Giving clothes is, in the saga, a funeral: a clothed kaukas is released to climb, and the field’s luck goes with it. A mother may speak a name over the threshing floor and burn a lock of her hair; the kaukas goes up to Dausos, and she loses the memory of that child’s face (Law of Balance).

title: Kaukas / barzdukai (field-luck)
text:
Danger level
I nuisance → III dangerous.

title: Kaukas / barzdukai (field-luck)
text:
Story hooks
Books III–V: a Samogitian widow names her three kaukai one after another as the Hidden Groves fall, choosing her children’s peace over her family’s bread.

title: Laumiukai (changelings)
text:
Folk source [Record]
In Lithuanian tradition laumės (and other water-beings) steal unattended infants and leave their own: an ugly, big-headed, ever-hungry, never-growing child. Remedies resemble those across Europe: mistreating the changeling so the laumė returns the stolen child, or provoking it to reveal its great age. Infants were protected by never being left alone and by iron, a knife or a broom near the cradle.

title: Laumiukai (changelings)
section: In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
text:
In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
The swap is real, and it is a bargain enforced without consent. Laumės take children whose mothers broke courtesy, or who were born on a laumės’ night, to raise as weavers. What they leave is sometimes their own sickly child, but often a dying human child from another house that the laumė is trying to save. The cruel folk remedies work because they offend custom so badly that the laumė returns the child, which means torturing a child who might be someone else’s.

title: Laumiukai (changelings)
text:
Signs & habitat
A baby who changes overnight: eyes too old, appetite too great, never crying at the right times; wet hen-tracks by the cradle.

title: Laumiukai (changelings)
text:
Before / after the Unbinding
Before: swaps happen, and the child is often returned at seven, trained and strange. After: laumės leave nothing; the cradle is empty or holds a linen-wrapped log.

title: Laumiukai (changelings)
section: Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
text:
Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
Never leave an unnamed infant alone; a knife or broom under the cradle (a mother cannot work the fields). Carve Laimos medis on the cradle and feed it a thread of the mother’s hair. Whisper the child’s secret name into its ear at birth (the elements, and anyone who overhears, now know it). The cruel remedy: you may be beating somebody else’s baby.

title: Nedegintieji (the Unburned)
text:
Folk source [Record]

title: Nedegintieji (the Unburned)
section: In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
text:
In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
The crusade dead: Lithuanians killed in Order raids and buried in pits rather than burned, and the Order’s own dead buried in pagan ground far from any church. With no fire to lift them, no kin to feed them, and a century of crusade fervour soaked into them, they rise in abandoned groves after 1387: hungry vėlės crossed with the Iron Saint’s appetite, so they march as well as hunger. Cold, silent, they walk in the formation they died in, pagan and Christian side by side, and take warmth hearth by hearth rather than eat.

title: Ragana (seer-witch)
text:
Folk source [Record]
The Lithuanian witch. The word is commonly linked to regėti, “to see”. Raganos gather on the Šatrija hill in Samogitia and other hills on Midsummer night; spoil cows’ milk and steal “milk-luck” with dew gathered on Rasos morning; cause illness and turn people into animals; and in tales threaten or devour children. They also heal. The figure blends a wise woman, a seer and a dangerous neighbour.

title: Ragana (seer-witch)
section: In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
text:
In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
A woman born with Kalba (prigimtis) outside the priestly lines: no vaidilutė training, no shrine, only gift and need. The folk are right that she sees and can harm, and wrong that she serves Velnias, at least before 1387. After the Krivis and the vaidilutės are gone, Velnias’s small shapes are the only teachers left and many raganos learn from them. They pay their own costs (blindness, voicelessness, thirst) and pass them on in their prices.

title: Ragana (seer-witch)
text:
Signs & habitat
A woman alone at the edge of the village whom everyone visits and no one invites; dew-marks dragged through the rye on Rasos morning; cows dry for no reason.

title: Ragana (seer-witch)
text:
Before / after the Unbinding
Before: the village’s healer and occasional scapegoat. After: needed and hunted at once, the only defence against the hungry dead and the first one blamed for them.

title: Ragana (seer-witch)
section: Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
text:
Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
Against a hostile ragana: rowan over the cowshed, iron in the churn, juniper smoke (she will know you did it). Hiring one is expensive: she works by Kalba and pays the price herself, so she charges what she asks, plus your silence, plus the risk you will need her again.

title: Ragana (seer-witch)
text:
Danger level
II hazard → III dangerous.

title: Ragana (seer-witch)
text:
Story hooks
Book I: the prologue’s captain calls Eglė raganos dukteri, a half-right insult to a vaidilutė. Book II ch. 9: a ragana offers to buy the boys back with an Order child’s blood and Vytautas refuses. Books II–V: a ragana and a vilkatas working together, each despising the other’s methods.

In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
A spirit of the Gold-Glutton, formed wherever ledgers, tolls and land sold by the furlong gather: tollhouses, counting-rooms, the Order’s commanderies, Hanseatic factories. A voice, never a body, that counts: the coins in the room, then the goods, then the people, then the years each person has left, in a soft monotone. Those who listen too long begin to see one another as sums. It does not kill; it empties people out, leaving them prosperous and hollow.

Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
An unmeasured gift: giving something away without counting it (the reverse of the laumė’s linen) silences the Counter in that room, though it makes counting feel like breathing. Fill the room with song, since counting and singing cannot share a room.

title: Smakas (the dragon under the cathedral)
text:
Folk source [Record]
The usual Lithuanian folk dragon is the slibinas, often many-headed, which demands tribute (often maidens) and is slain by a hero in the international dragon-slayer pattern. Smakas is a Slavic borrowing (smok). The folk dragon overlaps with the fiery-flying aitvaras and with serpents generally.

title: Smakas (the dragon under the cathedral)
section: In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
text:
In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
A smakas is a žaltys that grew wrong: a snake-king fed on blood instead of milk, with the žaltys’s link to a household’s luck swollen into a link with a whole town’s. After the sacred snakes of Šventaragis are killed (Book I ch. 29) their bodies are thrown unburned into the trench for the new cathedral; snake-blood in the ground breeds snakes, and blood spilled in hatred breeds a single smakas beneath the bishop’s floor. Its demand for maidens is the folk memory of towns paying daughters to keep their prosperity. Eglė’s žaltys remains the last living snake of the old line; the smakas is the line’s revenant.

title: Smakas (the dragon under the cathedral)
text:
Signs & habitat
Under hill-forts, cathedrals and old cellars; cattle vanishing; a town that prospers inexplicably while its girls disappear.

title: Smakas (the dragon under the cathedral)
text:
Before / after the Unbinding
Before: very rare, put down by the Krivis’s people. After 1387: one beneath the Vilnius cathedral, feeding on the city’s wealth; the Gold-Glutton and the Root-Mother both want it.

title: Smakas (the dragon under the cathedral)
section: Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
text:
Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
Fire and smith’s iron (it lives deep; digging it out means digging up the town). Tribute, as towns have always paid. Starve it of luck: if the town stops prospering it weakens, and the town stops prospering.

title: Smakas (the dragon under the cathedral)

title: Vaiduokliai (apparitions)
text:
Folk source [Record]
Ghosts and apparitions: the visible return of the dead, especially those who died violently or left something undone, haunting a place or a person.

title: Vaiduokliai (apparitions)
section: In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
text:
In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
A vaiduoklis is not a soul. It is the land’s memory replaying (the Law of Memory, magic rules §5.3): a residue of something so strongly felt that the place keeps showing it. The folk confuse vaiduokliai with vėlės, which is half right: a vėlė can use a vaiduoklis as a mask, but most apparitions have no one inside, which is why most ghosts cannot be fed or bargained with. Amber shows them most clearly, because amber stores memory.

title: Vaiduokliai (apparitions)
text:

The same figure at the same hour; places of great working or great grief (the Krėva cell, the Palanga stone).

title: Vaiduokliai (apparitions)

Unchanged in nature, but more of them: the Unbinding is a century of grief, and grief leaves pictures.

title: Vaiduokliai (apparitions)
section: Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
text:
Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
None needed; most do no harm (mistaking one for a vėlė wastes offerings and raises false hope). To lay one, change the place (burn the room, fell the tree) and the memory goes with it.

Book I ch. 23: Kęstutis after an honoured cremation is not his vėlė but a vaiduoklis carried by Birutė’s amber, which is why the scene smells of sea salt. Book IV: Vytautas, near death, sees his younger self in the Trakai halls.

title: Vėlės (the fed dead)
text:
Folk source [Record]
The souls of the dead. In the autumn season of the dead (Vėlinės; in Samogitia also Ilgės) families set food on the table overnight, left doors ajar and heated the bathhouse (pirtis) for their dead. At Kūčios a place was kept for them, and kisielius (oat jelly) was their food. Souls were imagined as birds, migrating along the Milky Way (the Birds’ Way); a bird knocking at the window foretold a death.

title: Vėlės (the fed dead)
section: In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
text:
In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
Exactly as the cosmology has it: cremation is the fastest road up the Glass Mountain to Dausos, and slower-climbing dead linger as vėlės who must be fed. Fed vėlės are the land’s memory and first line of defence: they warn their kin, guard the threshold and sometimes fight. A family with well-fed dead has a hidden army of grandparents. A fed vėlė can be asked for help through Vėjopatis; it will ask in return to be remembered by a child who has forgotten it.

Before / after the Unbinding
Before: honoured, content, protective. After: the Church moves the feast to All Souls and forbids the old offerings, and families that convert in earnest stop feeding them; their dead turn hungry (see Alkanosios vėlės).

Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
Feed them at Vėlinės and Kūčios, heat the pirtis, say their names (a family’s best food, every year).

Vilkatas / vilkolakis (cursed werewolf)
Cursed shape · Samogitian folk belief, saga-true

Origin [Record] werewolf belief (Olaus Magnus 1555; Herodotus 4.105) · [Saga] two things under one word
Tier Bought power · Velnias's craft sold through raganos (the cursed vilkolakis, not the sworn brotherhood)

title: Vilkatas / vilkolakis (cursed werewolf)
text:
Folk source [Record]
Lithuanian werewolf belief has two strands: a witch or sorcerer turns people into wolves (a whole wedding party in some tales) with a belt, hoop or spell; or a person turns himself by somersaulting over a stump with a knife stuck in it, and if someone pulls the knife he cannot change back. A werewolf is restored by bread on the tip of a knife, or by being called by name. Olaus Magnus (1555) describes werewolves gathering on Christmas night in Prussia, Livonia and Lithuania to drink cellars dry; Herodotus (4.105) says the Neuri became wolves for a few days each year.

title: Vilkatas / vilkolakis (cursed werewolf)
section: In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
text:
In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
One word covers two things. (1) The cursed vilkolakis: an ordinary person changed by a bargain, real flesh-change, Velnias’s craft sold through raganos; the victim keeps a human mind for a season, then loses it. (2) The sworn vilkatai, the wolf-brotherhood of the Dykra, who are men and do not change shape (see Vilkatai (Iron Wolves)). Bread-on-a-knife cures the cursed, because bread is courtesy and iron reminds the flesh it was human; it only offends a sworn vilkatas. Galminas’s beast-rage is a third thing, the Root-Mother’s possession, and should not be called vilkolakis.

title: Vilkatas / vilkolakis (cursed werewolf)
text:
Signs & habitat
A wolf that hangs around one village and will not attack its people; a wolf with human eyes; a stump with a knife in it at a crossroads.

title: Vilkatas / vilkolakis (cursed werewolf)
text:
Before / after the Unbinding
Before: rare, a ragana’s worst curse. After: with raganos learning from Velnias, curse-belts multiply and whole hamlets of runaways and debtors are turned.

title: Vilkatas / vilkolakis (cursed werewolf)
section: Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
text:
Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
Bread on the tip of a knife offered to the wolf (you must stand within reach of its jaws). Call the person by name (if you are wrong, you have just told a hungry wolf your name). Burn the belt that made it (you must take it from the ragana). Pulling the knife from the stump traps the self-changer as a wolf forever: someone’s son.

Žaltys (household grass snake)
Household guardian · Baltic folk belief, saga-true

Origin [Record] household grass snake, fed with milk (Jerome of Prague via Piccolomini; Długosz, 1387) · [Saga] the children of Žilvinas's spilled blood
Tier Dvasia · the Root-Mother's ear inside the house
Danger I nuisance before 1387 → III dangerous after
Habitat Under the threshold, warm straw by the oven, the cowshed
Wants Milk in a clay bowl at the threshold, daily; to be left alive

They are wrong that it is harmless: it cannot hurt anyone directly, but it can withdraw, and a house it leaves goes sick, barren and quarrelsome within a year. The priest who calls it a demon is wrong too.Žilvinas's blood. When Eglė's brothers cut Žilvinas down, his blood went into the ground and the grass snakes of the land were born from it. The living owe them. Eglė's own žaltys is the eldest.

title: Žaltys (household grass snake)
text:
Folk source [Record]
The grass snake (Natrix natrix), marked by yellow patches behind the head, was kept and fed in Lithuanian homes for health, fertility and luck; killing one brought misfortune. Late-medieval visitors report snake veneration (the account of Jerome of Prague’s mission, retold by Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini), and Długosz records sacred snakes being killed at the 1387 baptism. The tale Eglė žalčių karalienė is the great žaltys story; folk tales also know a crowned snake-king.

title: Žaltys (household grass snake)
section: In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
text:
In the saga (where the folk are half-wrong)
The žalčiai are the children of Žilvinas’s spilled blood, which is why the living owe them. Each is a real guardian, but it is the Root-Mother’s ear inside the house: it keeps the luck and tells the forest what it hears. Feeding it is a tax. The folk are right that killing it kills the luck and wrong that it is harmless: it cannot hurt anyone directly, but it can withdraw, and a house it leaves goes sick, barren and quarrelsome within a year. Eglė’s žaltys is the eldest of them.

title: Žaltys (household grass snake)
text:
Signs & habitat
Under the threshold, in the warm straw by the oven, in the cowshed. A healthy household’s žaltys is seen often and fearlessly; a žaltys that hides is a warning.

title: Žaltys (household grass snake)
text:
Before / after the Unbinding
Before: milk and respect keep it loyal for generations. After the sacred snakes are slaughtered at Šventaragis (Book I ch. 29) the survivors are unbound: many leave houses in a body, snakes crossing a road in a long line toward the forest; those that stay drink cows dry and coil in cradles.

title: Žaltys (household grass snake)
section: Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
text:
Banes, wards, bargains, and their cost
Milk in a clay bowl at the threshold, daily (in a hungry spring it is the baby’s milk). To move one, carry it to the forest edge in clean linen with a crust of bread and ask it aloud; it may refuse. Juniper smoke and feast-day iron drive it off, and the luck goes with it. Taking a snake-king’s crown brings wealth for life and every žaltys in the parish hunting the thief’s kin.

title: Žaltys (household grass snake)
text:
Danger level
I nuisance before 1387 → III dangerous after (it withdraws or turns on the household).

title: Žaltys (household grass snake)
text:
Story hooks
Book I: the 1387 snake-killing on the page, with Vytautas quietly saving one. Later: a crowned žaltys-king beneath Vilnius (see Smakas); a Samogitian village that keeps its žalčiai and is the only one spared a plague.

title: Algirdas dies; cremated
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Algirdas died in late May 1377 (the exact day and place are not secure; Maišiagala is suggested). Lithuanian tradition has him cremated on a pyre with his best horses, traditionally eighteen, and this is the usual reading of the pagan rite; the horse count and the site are traditional, not documented. Ruthenian sources, followed by later Orthodox writers (Kojałowicz, Macarius, Antonovych), say he took monastic vows a few days before his death and was buried in Vilnius under the name Alexius. The two accounts contradict each other and the sources do not decide between them. Shortly before his death he named Jogaila, his son by Uliana of Tver, as heir over the sons of his first wife, having earlier favoured Fiodor. Jogaila became Grand Duke in 1377 and Kęstutis stayed on as co-ruler. See the Wikipedia article on Algirdas.

title: Algirdas dies; cremated
text:
What really happened [Saga]
The saga keeps both versions, and says so: both are true. Algirdas takes the black Orthodox cowl the night before, speechless, with a lifted hand, and is burned on a hill above the Neris with the pagan rite beside a Ruthenian monk reading prayers. “Ugnis neklausia, ko prašei” (the fire does not ask what you asked), he had said. The first log is laid by Jogaila, the youngest son leading the father, following the Sovijus rule of the old legend. Eglė, seventeen, carries the Šventaragis flame in a clay pot, and the fire hesitates three breaths before it catches. Birutė feels one thread of the Silent Pact slip and another tremble. Earlier, at the deathbed, Algirdas makes Kęstutis swear to protect Jogaila, and Kęstutis, who cannot give a promise he will not keep, swears only that no hair will fall by his own hand or order. That narrow oath is the gap through which Skirgaila later walks.

title: Algirdas dies; cremated
text:
Consequences
The graph records no outgoing ‘causes’ edge for this event. In canon it is the first loss among the oath-takers of 1345: the Pact weakens until Kęstutis alone holds it. Jogaila’s accession (1377) leads directly to the secret treaty of Dovydiškės in 1380, the breach that becomes the civil war and Krėva. The 1345 oath itself is here.

title: Algirdas dies; cremated
text:
Dramatisation
Book VI ch. 28 “Algirdo Valia” (Kęstutis, spring 1377, first thunder), ch. 29 “Algirdo Laužas” (Birutė, May 1377, the hill above the Neris), ch. 30 “Epilogas: Senasis Šernas” (Kęstutis, autumn 1377, Trakai). It ends Book VI and hands over to Book I ch. 1.

title: Battle of Ašmena: Žygimantas defeats Švitrigaila
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Fought on 8 December 1432 near Ašmena (Oshmiany), not in 1433 as an older outline had it (VLE; Wikipedia, Battle of Ashmyany). Švitrigaila marched from Polotsk with Tatar help, took Minsk, Krėva and Ašmena, and was beaten by Žygimantas Kęstutaitis. Długosz gives about 10,000 dead, a figure that should be treated with caution. This was one battle, not two: a “second battle in December 1433” in the outline does not exist.

title: Battle of Ašmena: Žygimantas defeats Švitrigaila
text:
What really happened [Saga]
Pilkoji sees it from the roads. The Root-Mother courts Švitrigaila with a promise to restore the old realm; trees fall across roads and the wolves attack only riders carrying foreign seals. On 8 December the field is Žygimantas’s, with about a thousand or two dead, some with Tatar colours, and the dead lie unburned: the first rehearsal of what the saga calls the Unbinding at its height at Pabaiskas. Pilkoji takes the keeper to the last žynys, Galminas’s pupil, who still knows the Pact’s words.

title: Battle of Ašmena: Žygimantas defeats Švitrigaila
text:
Consequences
The graph shows this as an effect of Žygimantas’s coup at Ašmena and records no outgoing edge: Švitrigaila falls back to Polotsk and the war drags on to Pabaiskas in 1435.

title: Birutė’s Amber Sacrifice
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Not in the record. What the sources do say about Birutė conflicts. The Order’s chronicler Wigand of Marburg is cited (via Wikipedia’s civil-war article) for a drowning at Brest, probably in autumn 1382 after Vytautas’s flight; no other source confirms it, and it is unclear whether Długosz repeats it (verify). Lithuanian tradition, by contrast, has her return to Palanga, where she kept the shrine until her death, a date given as about 1389 in one popular summary and about 1416 in canon D3 (verify). A Samogitian delegation at the Council of Constance (1415–16) is said to have denied the story of her murder, which fits the long-life version.

title: Birutė’s Amber Sacrifice
text:
What really happened [Saga]
Birutė’s drowning at Brest is the in-world attempt on her life in 1382, which the sea refused three times (the ring returned thrice, ch. 11). Her second “death”, by choice, is this one. At the full moon of Bangpūtys, after the cousins’ truce in the burnt church, she walks into the sea and becomes the amber kneeling woman on the Palanga shore. It pays Vytautas’s surety in full (Sutartis, “Jo skola yra mano skola”) and buys the Hidden Groves, the gods’ last foothold in Samogitia, a remnant of the Pact’s protection. The cost is shown: her mortal form, her voice (lost since the fog at Krėva) and her failing sight. After it the Amber Queen can act only through amber she has touched.

title: Birutė’s Amber Sacrifice
text:
Consequences
Caused by the truce in the ashes. It makes the Klūpančioji amber statue at Palanga, which later books use as the Queen’s anchor and as a target of Polish clergy.

title: Birutė’s Amber Sacrifice
text:
Dramatisation

title: Vytautas burns Order castles; turns on the Order
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
In July 1384 Vytautas abandoned the Teutonic Order and reconciled with Jogaila. Wikipedia’s civil-war article (Urban, Ivinskis, Kiaupa) records that he burned the Order’s new castles on the Neman, including Georgenburg (Jurbarkas), and that the joint forces of Jogaila and Vytautas besieged New Marienwerder (Naujapilis) for six weeks until it fell; Vytautas captured Marquard von Salzbach. The Order had begun building New Marienwerder in May 1384 and he had reconfirmed the Königsberg terms there in June and July (the Wikipedia article on the treaty gives 14 June and 16 July; they differ and need checking). Earlier in 1384 Jogaila had offered Volhynia with Lutsk, which Vytautas refused, demanding his Trakai patrimony.

title: Vytautas burns Order castles; turns on the Order
text:
What really happened [Saga]
The book recasts a fictional 1383 Vilnius siege as these July 1384 events (canon Q9). Vytautas sees the Order’s bombards trained on the city he intends to defend; his father’s shade and Eglė’s ashes come to him in the camp; he cuts a rope, kills a young sentry and fires the siege tower “Lietuvos griovėjas”, sends an arrow with the message “Geležis degia” and flees. Next day the Order’s soldiers hunt him through the forest; he loses Jonas, Birutė’s weak fog saves him (cost implied), and the ‘Geležinis Vilkas’ legend is born. Henė calls him Išdavikų išdavikas, the traitor of traitors.

title: Vytautas burns Order castles; turns on the Order
text:
Consequences
Caused by the Treaty of Königsberg; leads to the truce in the ashes. With it Vytautas is the Order’s most dangerous apostate and the surety of the Pact (Birutė’s sacrifice) falls due.

title: Vytautas burns Order castles; turns on the Order

title: Kęstutis seizes Vilnius, spares Jogaila
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
In autumn 1381 (August to December in the sources; VLE says November) Kęstutis learned of the secret treaty of Dovydiškės from the Order’s komtur of Osterode, Kuno von Liebenstein (Ivinskis, via the English Wikipedia). Vytautas denied knowing. Jogaila was away putting down the Polotsk revolt; Kęstutis took Vilnius, which opened without a fight, and was proclaimed Grand Duke. Jogaila was caught on his way back, swore loyalty, and was freed with Krėva and Vitebsk. The sources are the Order’s chroniclers (Wigand of Marburg) and later Lithuanian chronicles.

title: Kęstutis seizes Vilnius, spares Jogaila
text:
What really happened [Saga]
Liebenstein’s warning (the saga keeps the historical informant; Hohenstein of Book VI is a different, invented man, and he does not warn anyone) sends Kęstutis to Vilnius with a band; he rides in three days, the city opens, and when Jogaila is brought back to the Lower Castle with two servants, sweating, the Dovydiškės parchment lies in his chest under his blanket. He spares him: “Kraujas yra kraujas.” This is his tragic hinge: the mercy that will kill him in 1382.

title: Kęstutis seizes Vilnius, spares Jogaila
text:
Consequences
Caused by Dovydiškės; leads to Jogaila’s retaking of Vilnius.

title: Kęstutis seizes Vilnius, spares Jogaila
text:
Dramatisation

title: Crown intercepted; Vytautas refuses Henė
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
The crown was never intercepted. Sigismund of Luxembourg sent two couriers ahead of the embassy, the jurist Baptista Cigala and Sigismund Roth. They were robbed and beaten before 19 August 1430 on the Neumark and Greater Poland border by royal guards under Jan Czarnkowski, who took letters, horses and valuables worth about a thousand ducats. The main embassy (Archbishop Günther of Magdeburg, Dukes Přemek of Opava and Ludwig of Brzeg-Liegnitz, Hungarian and Bohemian lords) waited at Frankfurt an der Oder and turned back; the crowns, made by Nuremberg goldsmiths, were with it. Jogaila read the captured letters and ordered every road watched. The Komtur of Schlochau wrote on 19 August that the crown had not been taken because the couriers did not have it. The coronation had been planned for 15 August, then 8 September, then 29 September, in Vilnius. Vytautas’s letter of 13 October makes it clear he wanted the crown only with Polish consent. Zbigniew Oleśnicki was the leading opponent but was not at the Łęczyca council of August 1430 (Szybkowski 2010; Bar 2017).

title: Crown intercepted; Vytautas refuses Henė
text:
What really happened [Saga]
On the Assumption, 15 August 1430, Henė comes down into the vault at Trakai and offers the last deal: the crown will arrive if the flame is allowed to die. Vytautas refuses. Pilkoji waits at the door with feast-day iron, deciding whether to break the second rule of the Pack. Late in August Pilkoji’s wolves, sent to bring the crown through, find the Polish border guards cursing over a gold-painted trunk at the Noteć ford: inside, to the rim, dry leaves. A jester sits on the verge watching. The crown that was never meant for the mortal world has turned to leaves (mythic_gaps §4).

title: Crown intercepted; Vytautas refuses Henė
text:
Consequences
Caused by the Congress of Lutsk, where the crown was offered. It turns the crown to leaves (the Lutsk crown). The graph names Zbigniew Oleśnicki as participant. The failure frames Vytautas’s last weeks and his death.

title: Crown intercepted; Vytautas refuses Henė
text:
Dramatisation
Book IV ch. 21 “Karūnos Kelionė” (Henė, 15 August 1430), ch. 22 “Paskutinis Sandėris” (Vytautas, the same day, the Trakai vault), ch. 23 “Lapai Pakelėje” (Pilkoji, late August, the Noteć ford). Seasonal tag: Žolinė, high summer.

title: Pontoon bridge over the Vistula at Czerwińsk
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
The allied army crossed the Vistula at Czerwińsk on a pontoon bridge prepared near Kozienice in winter and spring 1410 (the timber from the Radom Forest, master Jarosław of Kozienice), floated downstream about 29 June and assembled in roughly half a day on 30 June. The king and most of the Lesser Poland troops crossed that day, the Lithuanians arrived the same day; the crossing lasted until 2 July (a Polish source says 3 July). The exact spot above the monastery is uncertain (en.wikipedia, Czerwińsk Floating Bridge).

title: Treaty of Dovydiškės
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
A secret treaty of 31 May 1380 between Jogaila and Grand Master Winrich von Kniprode, directed against Kęstutis. The clauses are convoluted: the two sides promised not to attack each other, and Jogaila promised not to help Kęstutis or his children against the Order; helping in a way that avoided suspicion would not breach the treaty. Its purpose was Teutonic neutrality in Jogaila’s struggle with his rivals. The Order covered the signing with a five-day hunt. The place name appears only in Wigand of Marburg and in German texts, and the village is not securely identified (Wikipedia; VLE, Dovydiškių sutartis). In August 1381 the Order told Kęstutis of the treaty. The informant is Kuno von Liebenstein, komtur of Osterode and godfather of Danutė (Ivinskis 1978, via the English Wikipedia; VLE and Wigand name no one). The saga’s Günther von Hohenstein is not the informant: he is an invented young brother of Book VI (the real Günther von Hohenstein of Osterode died in 1380). Vytautas, asked for advice, said no such treaty existed.

title: Treaty of Dovydiškės
text:
What really happened [Saga]
It is the first crack in the Silent Pact: a Gediminid plotting against Gediminid blood. Henė takes his first thread of Jogaila here. The saga leaves the place unidentified, in the border country, which the record’s silence permits (the graph no longer pins it to the Dykra).

title: Treaty of Dovydiškės
text:
Consequences
Leads to Kęstutis’s seizure of Vilnius in autumn 1381 and so, through the retaking of Vilnius and the arrest, to the death at Krėva. Jogaila’s accession is Algirdas’s death three years earlier.

title: Treaty of Dovydiškės
text:
Dramatisation
Not dramatised. Book I ch. 1 “Senasis Šernas” (Kęstutis, Trakai, late summer 1382) and ch. 2 “Vilko Perspėjimas” (Vytautas, the same evening, arguing with his father and showing the Dovydiškės parchment, “1380-ieji”) carry the backstory. It is mentioned again in ch. 4 and 8.

title: Vytautas secretly lights the Last Flame
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Nothing in the record. Długosz reports that when Jogaila came to Vilnius in 1387 he put out the sacred fire, felled the sacred groves and had the sacred snakes killed (the details are of disputed accuracy). Whether any ember survived the extinguishing is not asked in the sources; that is the gap the saga fills.

title: Vytautas secretly lights the Last Flame
text:
What really happened [Saga]
That night Vytautas rides out alone to the wet black ashes of the Šventaragis hearth, kneels where the fire burned the day before, and finds in the ashes one red grain, no larger than a pea, that never went out. He carries it in a clay cup under his cloak to Kęstutis’s old hunting lodge beyond the Neris, a windowless hut that no one in Jogaila’s service knows of. He lights it with birch bark. “Kol aš gyvas, paskutinė ugnis neužges.” The scar over his heart warms. If it dies while he lives, the debt of the Sutartis falls on him. The wolves answer from the forest, from several sides.
The flame moves later: to the half-flooded foundations of the Trakai island castle (Book II ch. 2), and after Ostrów to a dry vault (ch. 11); it goes out at his death in 1430 (the Last Flame ember).

title: Vytautas secretly lights the Last Flame
text:
Consequences
Caused by the baptism of Lithuania. It creates the ember and makes Vytautas the keeper of the only flame the vilkatai can still serve (D10). The graph places the event at Kęstutis’s hunting lodge beyond the Neris (canon D11), not at Trakai; the moves to Trakai come in Book II. Kalvis guards the lodge flame; later keepers are Spyglys and the Flame-Keeper Žiežirba.

title: Vytautas secretly lights the Last Flame
text:
Dramatisation
Book I ch. 29 “Krikštas” (Vytautas; the night after the baptism in the Neris, February 1387) and Book II ch. 2 “Salos Pamatai” (Vytautas; the following spring, the flame moved to the island foundations).
