title: Grodno: Žygimantas sworn Grand Duke before Oleśnicki (Jogaila absent)
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
A Polish delegation under Bishop Zbigniew Oleśnicki received Žygimantas Kęstutaitis’s oath at Grodno on 15 October 1432 (VLE; the English Wikipedia gives an act of 25 October) and proclaimed him Grand Duke for life. Jogaila was not there: he issued his own act at Lwów on 30 October 1432 and confirmed Grodno on 3 January 1433. Terms: the Union of Vilnius and Radom of 1401 was confirmed; Jogaila’s supremacy was recognised; after Žygimantas’s death Lithuania was to return to Jogaila and his heirs; Trakai was to go to Mykolas; Podolia was ceded to Poland; most of Volhynia was left to Lithuania until Žygimantas’s death; no crown for Žygimantas. See Oleśnicki and Wikipedia, Union of Grodno (1432).

title: Grodno: Žygimantas sworn Grand Duke before Oleśnicki (Jogaila absent)
text:
What really happened [Saga]
On the empty oak throne lie the king’s seal and a folded parchment. A shaking line in a different hand under the king’s letter reads “Tu turi tėvo akis”, followed by the first two letters of a word struck out: Kr, for Krėva. Žygimantas swears kneeling, with the sense of something invisible sitting on the cushions and watching. Henė stands among the Lithuanian lords with one stone in his fingers, looking at the empty throne like a buyer whose seller has not come. That night the new Grand Duke asks the keeper again to relight the flame, and the keeper says no.

title: Grodno: Žygimantas sworn Grand Duke before Oleśnicki (Jogaila absent)
text:
Consequences
Caused by the coup at Ašmena; it leaves no outgoing graph edge. Its succession clause is the knot that civil war and the Vilnius council later cut.

text:

title: Union of Horodło; Samogitian baptism begins
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
The Union of Horodło was signed on 2 October 1413 at Horodło on the Bug. Forty-seven Lithuanian noble families were adopted into Polish heraldic clans; Catholics alone could hold the new offices of voivode of Vilnius (Albertas Manvydas) and of Trakai, closing high office to the Orthodox (Wikipedia, Union of Horodło). In November 1413 Jogaila and Vytautas baptised Samogitians for about a week near the Dubysa, Vytautas preaching in the local tongue (Długosz); the process was complete in 1417 with the bishopric of Medininkai. Some scholars think the 1413 mission was modest. The young Oleśnicki at the ceremony is plausible but unattested.

title: Union of Horodło; Samogitian baptism begins
text:
What really happened [Saga]
For the saga it is a heraldry ceremony that is a declaration of civil war twenty years early. The Samogitian baptism that follows fells the first Hidden Grove, and the Quenched multiply in the hearths. By day Vytautas preaches; by night he thinks of the vault. The Riders of the Reise take to the Samogitian roads.

title: Union of Horodło; Samogitian baptism begins
text:
Consequences
Caused by Grunwald; it has no outgoing graph edge. The Hidden Groves then fall one by one until the founding of the bishopric (1417). The event now sits at its own place node, Horodło on the Bug (no longer the Lutsk placeholder).

title: Jogaila dies
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Jogaila died on 1 June 1434 at Gródek near Lviv, in the forty-eighth year of his reign. According to Długosz he caught a cold in a late-April frost at Medyka (the chill), listening to nightingales at night, was ill for weeks and was taken to Gródek; the day before he died he summoned loyal knights and entrusted his sons to them. Queen Sophia was in Kraków; Oleśnicki and the chancellor, bound for Basel, turned back at Poznań. The body reached Kraków on 11 June and the funeral was at Wawel on 18 June (historia.org.pl, 11 October 2024). His birth year is c. 1362 on current scholarship (Tęgowski 1999), so about 72; an older view gives c. 1352 (verify). The graph now places the death at Gródek; the body was taken to Kraków.

title: Jogaila dies
text:
What really happened [Saga]
His death ends the cousins’ feud, and Henė loses his last stone, Jogaila’s: it drops and his hands are empty. Jogaila, who had dreamed of a jester turning a black stone, sees Kęstutis at the foot of the bed and pretends not to. The last confession is invention (the record is silent).

title: Jogaila dies
text:
Consequences
The graph records no outgoing edge. Žygimantas’s Orthodox-rights privilege follows on 6 May 1434, and the war of the heirs moves to Pabaiskas.

title: Kęstutis escapes Marienburg
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
The captured prisoner who walked out of the Order’s capital is one of the better-attested episodes of the century. Kęstutis, over sixty, and Algirdas had taken Eckersberg and Johannisburg; a small band of knights returning from another raid fell on his camp by Lake Ublik (Wobel) in Masuria. Wigand dates the capture 21 March 1361 (Wartberge: 13 March). He was held at Marienburg about half a year and escaped on 11 November 1361 (Baronas: around 11 or 17–18 November) with the help of Alfas (Adolfas), a servant of Lithuanian origin, who removed bricks from the cell wall over months and carried out the rubble; Kęstutis broke through the wall, crossed the empty terrace, dropped into the dry moat where Alfas waited with horses and a Teutonic knight’s cloak, and rode out through the outer gate as a knight, toward Liebstadt; he hid in a bog, freed the horses and went on foot over the Drwęca to Mazovia. Alfas’s fate is not recorded. The main source is Wigand of Marburg, whose chronicle survives only through a Latin translation and fragments; Baronas (2004) notes that Wigand knew details only a participant could. See Baronas, “Kęstučio pabėgimas iš Marienburgo” (Lietuvos istorijos studijos), and Wikipedia, Kęstutis.

title: Kęstutis escapes Marienburg
text:
What really happened [Saga]
No magic. In the consecrated cellars Birutė’s amber bead goes cold (Kalba cannot reach into a consecrated place) and the Order lets him keep it. The escape is wit and loyalty: Kniprode, Grand Master for ten years, offers freedom for baptism and Kęstutis, bound by his thunder-mark, cannot promise what he will not keep. The invented young brother Hohenstein (the third knight who took him at Ublik; not the real Osterode komtur) carries his meals and translates; the young wolf Jonas, taken in the same column, kills a sergeant at the last gate and takes his Christian name (saga). Alfas’s fate is left open. It becomes the template for his son’s escape in 1382.

title: Kęstutis escapes Marienburg
text:
Consequences
Caused by the capture at Lake Ublik. The graph attaches no outgoing ‘causes’ edge. The escape is the pattern Vytautas repeats at Krėva twenty-one years later (Kęstutis tells it to him at Krėva, Book I ch. 8).

title: Kęstutis escapes Marienburg
text:
Dramatisation
Book VI ch. 16 “Paimtas” (Kęstutis; March 1361, Lake Ublik), ch. 17 “Marienburgo Požemis” (Kniprode; September), ch. 18 “Alfo Raktas” (Jonas; 11 November 1361, the eve of the saga’s Vėlinės mood). Told again by Kęstutis to Vytautas in Book I ch. 8 (the wall dug out, the white knight’s mantle, the horses).

title: Jogaila baptised, married, crowned in Kraków
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Jogaila arrived in Kraków on 12 February 1386 and was baptised three days later, on 15 February, taking the name Władysław. He married Jadwiga on 18 February and was crowned King of Poland jure uxoris on 4 March. Pope Urban VI did not confirm the marriage; Boniface IX later declared it valid (Wikipedia, Union of Krewo). Vytautas was re-baptised Catholic in Kraków, as Aleksandras, according to the saga’s canon (the sources for his presence and the name are thin; verify). Jadwiga had been crowned “king” on 16 October 1384.

title: Jogaila baptised, married, crowned in Kraków
text:
What really happened [Saga]
Offstage. The White Silence, which has been settling over the realm since Krėva, finds its vessel crowned: the child-king’s marriage to a pagan prince buys the baptism of a nation. Jogaila’s hands stop trembling. Skirgaila is left as regent in Lithuania.

title: Jogaila baptised, married, crowned in Kraków
text:
Consequences
Caused by the Union of Krėva; it leads to the baptism of Lithuania and the quenching of the Šventaragis flame a year later.

title: Jogaila baptised, married, crowned in Kraków
text:
Dramatisation
Offstage in Book I: ch. 28 “Nauja Tvarka” (autumn 1384; a merchant tells Jogaila the Poles have crowned Jadwiga, and his hands stop trembling) and ch. 29 “Krikštas” (Vytautas recalls Kraków and the name Aleksandras). Winter 1386.

title: Union of Krėva
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
The Act of Krėva (Krewo) was issued by Jogaila at Krėva castle on 14 August 1385 and addressed to the Polish delegation; it was guaranteed by the seals of his brothers Skirgaila, Kaributas and Lengvenis and his cousin Vytautas. In exchange for marriage to Jadwiga he promised to convert Lithuania, to pay 200,000 florins to William of Austria to end her betrothal, to recover Poland’s lost lands and free Polish prisoners, and to “attach” (applicare) the Lithuanian and Ruthenian lands to the Polish Crown. Historians disagree on applicare: it meant incorporation as a province (Koneczny, Łowmiański, Kolankowski), a fief (Adamus, Paszkiewicz) or only a personal union (Šapoka, Ivinskis). Only Jogaila made binding promises, so Kiaupienė argues it was not a final international treaty. The document was found in 1835 in the Kraków chapter archive; no contemporary chronicle mentions the meeting, and Dainauskas’s 1975 challenge to its authenticity has found little support (Wikipedia, Union of Krewo).

title: Union of Krėva
text:
What really happened [Saga]
It is signed in the upper hall, directly above the cells where Kęstutis was strangled, one day short of three years after his death. Poles on one side and Lithuanian lords on the other, with a red cloth on the table; the guard spears along the well wall are rimed with white frost in August: the White Silence settles over the realm. Skirgaila, drunk, says he cannot sleep in this castle, it is too quiet. Vytautas, who knows he will have to refuse only once and has decided what to save the refusal for, goes down to the cell, finds the stone where the body lay a different colour, and sees his breath turn to winter. Henė sits on the stairs; his breath does not show.

title: Union of Krėva
text:
Consequences
The graph lists no cause. It leads to the baptism and coronation at Kraków in February 1386 (the marriage and baptism it promised).

title: Union of Krėva
text:
Dramatisation
Book I ch. 28b “Krėvos Sutartis” (Vytautas; 14 August 1385, harvest heat; a scene added by the author for review item H10).

title: Congress of Lutsk: the crown offered
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
A gathering of princes at Lutsk castle from about 9 to 29 January 1429 (6 January in some accounts). Jogaila arrived first with the Poles; Sigismund of Luxembourg arrived late, on 20 January, with Queen Barbara. Guests included Eric of Denmark, a papal legate (a Dominican), Byzantine envoys, Moscow (Vasily II, Metropolitan Photius), Tver, Ryazan, the Masovian princes, envoys of the Livonian and Prussian Orders, the Moldavian hospodar Alexander the Good and the men of Tatar khans; Oleśnicki, Jan of Tarnów and Wojciech Jastrzębiec were there on the Polish side. Švitrigaila is mentioned by no source. Sigismund proposed a crown for Vytautas; Jogaila first agreed and then withdrew under pressure from his lords, with Oleśnicki, Oporowski and Tarnów-Szafraniec opposing. Sigismund wanted a Lithuanian kingdom to weaken the union. See Wikipedia, Congress of Lutsk; lt.wikipedia, Lucko suvažiavimas; Litwa za Witolda (1429).

title: Congress of Lutsk: the crown offered
text:
What really happened [Saga]
Henė has left Vytautas’s court with two stones and the golden chain and appears at Sigismund’s table, serving the deal, never the man. The gathering feeds the Gold-Glutton: feasts beyond counting that the Counter numbers, including the gems of a crown not yet made. In the offer Laima’s old sentence comes true in Vytautas’s ear: a crown will travel toward him all his life.

title: Congress of Lutsk: the crown offered
text:
Consequences
Leads to the crown embassy being blocked in August 1430. The reversion clause of Vilnius and Radom is the fuse; the offered crown is the price the saga will make Vytautas refuse.

title: Vytautas before Zöllner at Marienburg
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
After the escape from Krėva (autumn 1382) and the stop in Masovia, Vytautas went to the Order in Prussia. Winrich von Kniprode had died on 24 June 1382; Konrad Zöllner von Rotenstein was elected Grand Master in 1382. The saga’s audience itself is not in the record.

title: Vytautas before Zöllner at Marienburg
text:
What really happened [Saga]
In the austere negotiating room Zöllner offers recognition for a price: baptism when and where the Order chooses, Samogitia, and Ona and the children as “guests” (hostages). The Iron Saint, fed by the prayers of the Marienburg church, watches with steel satisfaction. Vytautas: “Sutinku, magistre.” The two voices in him split.

text:

title: Vytautas shelters with Janusz I in Masovia
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
After the escape from Krėva (autumn 1382) Vytautas sought help from his sister Danutė and her husband Janusz I of Warsaw, then from Siemowit IV of Masovia, and finally from the Teutonic Knights (Wikipedia, Lithuanian Civil War 1381–84). Louis of Hungary and Poland died in September 1382, leaving Poland without a king; on 31 October 1382 Jogaila agreed the Treaty of Dubysa with the Order (never ratified). Danutė died in 1424.

title: Vytautas shelters with Janusz I in Masovia
text:
What really happened [Saga]
Janusz receives him in Warsaw without ceremony: a small, moustached prince who has learned to survive between three stronger neighbours and does not hide that a fugitive is more worry than joy. Danutė comes down the stairs and embraces her brother three times. She has the maid’s dress washed and mended because he will not let her throw it away. For some days she speaks slowly and loudly; on the third day he understands that the cost of the Five-Voice did not leave with the fog.

title: Vytautas shelters with Janusz I in Masovia
text:
Consequences
Caused by the escape from Krėva. It leads to the audience with Grand Master Zöllner at Marienburg: from Masovia he goes to the Order.

text:

title: Agreement of Ostrów
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
The Ostrów Agreement, 4 August 1392. The place is uncertain (Ostrów Lubelski, or a manor near Lida); talks had begun at Ritterswerder near Kaunas. Henry of Masovia, bishop-elect of Płock, was Jogaila’s secret envoy; to avoid the Order’s suspicion he married Vytautas’s sister Rymgajla. Jogaila handed the government of Lithuania to Vytautas as regent, Grand Duke in all but name under Jogaila as supreme duke. In the summer Vytautas had invited the Knights to a feast at Ritterswerder, taken most of the guests prisoner and destroyed Ritterswerder, Metenburg and Neugarten. Skirgaila was moved from Trakai to Kyiv (1395). (Wikipedia, Ostrów Agreement; Koncius, Ivinskis, Urban.)

title: Agreement of Ostrów
text:
What really happened [Saga]
Jogaila’s hands shake as they always do when he has to sign. Henė changes masters in front of everyone and bows to Vytautas, Skirgaila’s stone still in his hand. Ona will not look at her husband after the boys (by the contested tradition). Trakai is Vytautas’s again, and the flame moves from the flooded foundations to the dry vault. A new phase of his arc begins (Form 5 in the arc notes).

title: Agreement of Ostrów
text:
Consequences
Caused by the break at Ritterswerder (summer 1392) and so, through it, by the siege of Vilnius. The graph no longer makes Ostrów cause the poisoning of the hostage sons: in the book (and in Grunau’s contested tradition) the boys die first, in the Order’s revenge. Ona, released by the Order in May, confirms Ostrów in two letters, to Jogaila and Jadwiga.

title: Agreement of Ostrów
text:
Dramatisation
Book II ch. 10 “Astravo Sutartis” (Jogaila; 4–5 August 1392, summer), ch. 9 “Kraujo Puta” (the spring and summer lead-up) and ch. 11 “Trakų Raktai” (Vytautas, autumn 1392).

title: Silent Pact sworn
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Not in the record, which gives only the 1345 co-rule of Algirdas and Kęstutis (the diarchy). A sacred fire in the Šventaragis valley at Vilnius is known from Długosz’s report of its extinguishing in 1387, and the founding legend of Šventaragis, Lizdeika and the Iron Wolf’s dream survives in the later Lithuanian chronicles (Bychowiec chronicle). The historical anchor is that the Grand Duchy remained pagan, and unconquered, through a century of crusade until 1387. The saga builds its engine on that fact.

title: Silent Pact sworn
text:
What really happened [Saga]
Sworn on All Souls’ Night 1345 in the Šventaragis valley by Kęstutis, Algirdas and the Krivis alone. The fire stands taller than men and the spirits of place gather. Each brother whispers his true name into it. The Krivis cuts his palm and casts a Palanga amber bead into the flame; it hangs blue and never falls. Algirdas gives the flames: Vilnius, Palanga and the Samogitian groves, “kol vienas mano kraujo vaikščios šia žeme”. Kęstutis gives the blood: no Gediminid shall shed a Gediminid’s blood. The fire adds a third clause by pressure: royal blood for every furrow the cross ploughs, the Amber Debt. Kęstutis says it aloud while Algirdas’s raised hand hangs; Algirdas never forgives him. Algirdas demands silence, and the Krivis: “Tai ir bus tylioji sutartis.” The gods promise that the heartland will not be conquered as long as the word is kept. Wolf-Father Kuolas gives Kęstutis the silver wolf in December.

title: Silent Pact sworn
text:
Consequences
Caused by the diarchy. The graph shows it creating the Silent Pact. Clause 2 is broken by the murder of Kęstutis in 1382 and clause 1 by the baptism of Lithuania in 1387.

title: Silent Pact sworn
text:
Dramatisation

title: Polish lords seize Podolia after Vytautas’s death
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Immediately after Vytautas’s death (October–November 1430) Polish lords seized Podolia, Kamianets castle among the places taken (Polish sources: the Podolian lords took it, by one account in agreement with the starosta); the truce required Kamianets, Smotrych and Červonogrod to be returned to Lithuania, and the Poles did not return them (lt.wikipedia, Švitrigaila). Podolian forces retook Kamianets only in 1433 (en.wikipedia, Battle of Murafa). Švitrigaila had been raised Grand Duke unilaterally by the Lithuanian lords against the Horodło clauses; Jogaila, who was in Vilnius for the funeral, announced his approval on 7 November 1430 and then withdrew under pressure from the Polish lords. Jogaila lodged in Vilnius castle as a virtual hostage until just before Christmas.

title: Polish lords seize Podolia after Vytautas’s death
text:
What really happened [Saga]
The news arrives in late November “when the roads were already freezing”. The saga treats it as the first deal of the new reign: Švitrigaila promises the east a return to the old realm and finds the west moving before he sits.

title: Polish lords seize Podolia after Vytautas’s death
text:
Consequences
Caused by the death of Vytautas. It leads, via the Polish invasion of Volhynia, to the truce of Czartorysk and the treaty of Christmemel.

title: Peace of Raciąż; Marquard insults Birutė
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Peace of Raciąż, 22-23 May 1404 (en.wikipedia 22 May; VLE 23 May), on an island in the Vistula at Raciążek, at the confluence of the Drwęca and the Vistula; talks from September 1403 through Vytautas’s plenipotentiaries. The 1398 Salynas borders were kept; the Order regained Samogitia and part of Sudovia and ended support for Švitrigaila; Poland could buy back Dobrzyń; Vytautas might move 250 Samogitian noble families into Lithuania. Smolensk was retaken in July 1404. Marquard von Salzbach had nearly derailed the talks by accusing Vytautas of treachery; after the peace he insulted Vytautas by attacking his murdered mother Birutė (en.wikipedia, after Ekdahl 1992). Ulrich von Jungingen (marshal from 1404) is plausibly present.

title: Peace of Raciąż; Marquard insults Birutė
text:
What really happened [Saga]

At Grunwald he keeps the promise. The Amber Queen later names Marquard (Book III ch. 14: “Raciążeke”).

title: Treaty of Salynas
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Treaty of Salynas, 12 October 1398 (a preliminary treaty was signed at Grodno on 23 March 1398), on an islet of the Nemunas, probably between Kulautuva and the mouth of the Nevėžis. Vytautas ceded Samogitia to the Order roughly up to the Nevėžis; the Order received part of Sudovia; the spheres of influence were Novgorod for Vytautas and Pskov for the Order; the Knights promised help against the Tatars; hostages including Sigismund Kęstutaitis (Žygimantas, hostage 1390–98) were released. Konrad von Jungingen signed; Marquard von Salzbach helped negotiate. Posilge alone says the Lithuanian nobles may have proclaimed Vytautas king at the feast; Polish historians doubt it (Wikipedia, Treaty of Salynas). Vytautas needed his western front quiet for the campaign against the Golden Horde that ended at the Vorskla.

title: Treaty of Salynas
text:
What really happened [Saga]
A Samogitian elder, Gedgaudas, sixty-two, brings twelve elders as witnesses without knowing why. Henė pours; the Hidden Groves now lie under the Order’s flag; Galminas watches from the far bank. Eglė’s price comes due: the price of the 1382 rescue was “never sell the forest”.

title: Treaty of Salynas
text:
Consequences
Leads to the Vorskla: the western peace frees Vytautas for the steppe. The place is an island in the Nemunas, no longer the Dykra.

title: Treaty of Salynas
text:
Dramatisation
Book II ch. 19 “Salyno Puota” (Gedgaudas, a Samogitian elder; 12 October 1398, autumn) and ch. 20 “Stepių Alkis” (Vytautas; winter 1398–99).

What the chronicles say [Record]
Skirgaila died in Kyiv in January 1397, on 11 January in the body of the Wikipedia article and 8 January in its infobox; he was buried in the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra. The circumstances of his death are not entirely clear. He had been Duke of Trakai (1382–92) and Jogaila’s regent in Lithuania (1386–92), was moved to Kyiv after Ostrów, and held it from 1395. The Wikipedia article gives no cause; poison is rumoured in later accounts (verify the source).

What really happened [Saga]
Thunder in January over the Dnieper: Perkūnas’s verdict on the safe-conduct broken in 1382. Skirgaila dies after a feast. Henė, who sees four storeys of Kyiv at once, reclaims the golden chain; a stone drops, three to two. The sword is lost in the dead man’s estate. Everyone suspects Vytautas, who did not do it and is not sorry.

title: Birutė binds Vytautas (Sutartis, surety, flame promise)
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Not in the record. The chronicles say nothing of a binding at Trakai in 1382; they note only that Vytautas was with Kęstutis in Trakai that summer and that Birutė later vanishes from them (see her sacrifice).

title: Birutė binds Vytautas (Sutartis, surety, flame promise)
text:
What really happened [Saga]
On the night after the Dagotuvės harvest songs, in a tower shrine at Trakai, Birutė hears the Amber Queen and sees in Praurimė’s fire a black Ship. She gives Vytautas an uncut amber pebble, charmed before sunrise, “warm, pulsing”, and binds him with five lines of the Five-Voice. The cost falls on him: a scar on his chest, nothing on the caster. She cuts her palm over the amber (ch. 27 recalls it): “Jo skola yra mano skola”, making herself his surety. Vytautas answers with a promise of his own, a flame he must keep. The five-voice working tonight is both a vow and a debt, which the book tracks through the pebble’s warm, cold and dead states.

title: Birutė binds Vytautas (Sutartis, surety, flame promise)
text:
Consequences
Creates Birutė’s Senovės Sutartis and the Last Flame promise. Its surety is paid in full at Palanga; its promise is fulfilled and then ended at Vytautas’s death.

title: Trakai granted to Skirgaila (1382)
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Trakai fell to Jogaila and the Order on 20 July 1382. Skirgaila was Duke of Trakai from 1382 to 1392 (VLE), the reward for helping imprison Kęstutis and Vytautas. In spring 1384 Jogaila offered Vytautas Volhynia with Lutsk, which Vytautas refused, demanding Trakai; Jogaila promised Trakai once Skirgaila was settled in Polotsk (taken in April 1387). Skirgaila was Jogaila’s governor of Lithuania from 13 March 1386 (VLE gives 1387). After the reconciliation of July 1384 Vytautas received Grodno, Brest and Podlasie. Under Ostrów in 1392 Trakai returned to Vytautas.

title: Trakai granted to Skirgaila (1382)
text:
What really happened [Saga]
The grant itself is backstory in Book I: Skirgaila has held Trakai since the summer of 1382 and says so. In the autumn of 1384, at the settlement in Vilnius’s rebuilt Lower Castle, Jogaila does not give Trakai; he says Skirgaila has held it since last summer and Trakai will be discussed again. Vytautas gets Grodno, Brest and Podlasie. He thinks one sentence he does not say: Skirgaila has my father’s castle. The Vytis emblem is hung over the gate; Ona returns from hostage; Henė greets him coldly.

title: Trakai granted to Skirgaila (1382)
text:
Consequences
Caused by Jogaila’s retaking of Vilnius and the fall of Trakai (the 1384 truce in the ashes only reaffirms it). It leads to Vytautas’s second flight to the Order in 1389.

title: Trakai granted to Skirgaila (1382)

Dramatisation

title: Union of Vilnius and Radom
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
After the Vorskla defeat and rebellions in Smolensk, Pskov and Novgorod, negotiations began at Grodno in late December 1400. On 18 January 1401 Vytautas and the Lithuanian nobles issued their act in Vilnius, the first political act issued by Lithuanian nobles in their own name; Jogaila issued a separate act (the original is lost), and on 11 March 1401 the Polish royal council issued the third at Radom. Vytautas was recognised as Grand Duke, with Jogaila holding the rights of overlord (in effect co-regents, with Jogaila dominant); on Vytautas’s death the Grand Duchy would pass to Jogaila or his heir and be bound to the Crown; neither side would elect a king without consulting the other. Historians disagree whether it was a diplomatic failure for Vytautas (the road to a crown blocked), a Polish concession or a codification of existing relations (Wikipedia, Union of Vilnius and Radom).

title: Union of Vilnius and Radom
text:
What really happened [Saga]
Jogaila, widowed, prays at Jadwiga’s tomb in Kraków and finds the stone frosted: the White Silence holds. The reversion clause is a fuse. Henė is at the table. Vytautas, who puts on plain armour in Book III ch. 2, is now Grand Duke by consent of Poland, and the saga sets up the Book IV conflict: a crown that Poland has agreed in advance he will never wear.

title: Union of Vilnius and Radom
text:
Consequences
Caused by the Vorskla. It leads to Grunwald: the cousins’ reconciliation of 1401 is the alliance that wins 1410.

title: Union of Vilnius and Radom
text:
Dramatisation
Book III ch. 3 “Vilniaus ir Radomo Aktai” (Jogaila; 18 January and 11 March 1401, winter into spring; Vilnius, Radom, Kraków).

title: Siege of Vilnius; Crooked Castle burned
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
The Order and Vytautas besieged Vilnius from 11 September to 7 October 1390 (a Vilnius University historian dates the arrival to the end of August). The attackers took and burned the wooden Crooked Castle on the Bald Hill (it fell on 16 September and was never rebuilt) and burned the town, killing about a thousand townspeople and taking two thousand, but the Lower and Upper Castles held; supply shortages and expiring mercenary contracts forced the withdrawal. Karigaila, Jogaila’s brother, who defended the Crooked Castle, died in its fall on 16 September; Jogaila charged that he was captured and beheaded (his head was carried on a stake round the Lower Castle), the Order said he was killed in the fighting. Tautvilas Kęstutaitis (baptised Kondrat), Vytautas’s brother, fighting on the Order’s side, was killed besieging the Crooked Castle, believed by a crossbow bolt (VLE’s “9–10 June” is wrong). Skirgaila defended the city. Henry Bolingbroke, Earl of Derby, the future Henry IV, took part with 70 or 80 household knights according to Wikipedia, 300 men according to Posilge. Zöllner died on 20 August 1390 at Christburg (the civil-war article places his death at the siege of Jurbarkas; the sources disagree). See Wikipedia, Siege of Vilnius (1390).

title: Siege of Vilnius; Crooked Castle burned
text:
What really happened [Saga]
A Gediminid kills a Gediminid: Karigaila dies when the arch falls, Tautvilas dies attacking, hit at the gate by a bolt whose shooter is unknown. No god intervenes and no one is punished: the Pact that forbade it died three years earlier. Vytautas besieges the city he saved in 1384 and has to live with it. Bolingbroke, twenty-three, is happier each morning at the siege than he ever was in England and cannot decide whether that is sin.

title: Siege of Vilnius; Crooked Castle burned
text:
Consequences
Caused by the Treaty of Lyck (and so by the second defection). It leads to the break of 1392 and, through it, Ostrów, when Jogaila sought a compromise.

title: Siege of Vilnius; Crooked Castle burned
text:
Dramatisation
Book II ch. 7 “Kreivoji Pilis” (Henry Bolingbroke; 11 September to early October 1390, Vilnius, Bald Hill). The Order’s guest as narrator, in the first non-Lithuanian POV. Sofija’s letter in ch. 8 reports Tautvilas’s death as the book has it.

title: Vytautas dies at Trakai; the Last Flame goes out
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Vytautas (born c. 1350; a minority puts it at 1354–55) died on 27 October 1430 at Trakai Island Castle, uncrowned. He had been well until a sudden decline after a fall from his horse on the road from Vilnius to Trakai about 15–16 October, while escorting Jogaila (Długosz, written c. 30 years later; Petrauskas doubts details; Kraszewski adds an ulcer between the shoulder blades). On 21 October he issued a testamentary donation to Vilnius cathedral naming his burial place, St Michael’s altar beside Ona. He was bedridden about eleven days. He died “in Jogaila’s arms” (pl.wikipedia, Kraszewski), with Julijona and Bishop Matthias hearing confession; Švitrigaila was already acting as lord at Trakai (Kraszewski). He was buried in Vilnius cathedral about eight days later (Kraszewski: 7 November). The crown embassy had been blocked in August (the crown intercepted). Whether the fall was an accident, a fever, a plot (some later writers suspected one; there is no evidence) or all three is unrecorded. Sources: pl.wikisource, Litwa za Witolda (1430); en/pl Wikipedia on Vytautas; the 15min.lt summary of Petrauskas’s argument.

title: Vytautas dies at Trakai; the Last Flame goes out
text:
What really happened [Saga]
On the morning of 27 October he feels better, eats soup and sees the lake through the window with a thin film of ice and cranes going south. He has turned Giltinė once, buying a week, which he spent on Žiežirba: the pebble and the silver wolf will go to him through Pilkoji. He dies as one promise is kept: “Neužgeso.” The pebble cracks and a small hard round thing falls on the floor and rolls: Henė’s stone, two to one. In the vault below, the Last Flame goes out, “like a pot taken off the fire”. He hears with both ears at last, and his mother says his true name, the one she whispered once in the tower at Trakai forty-eight years before. He waits for thunder. There is none: Perkūnas holds his storm, not from anger but out of respect. The vilkatai feel their true names go up the last smoke. Jogaila sits in the corridor outside, not asking to be let in.

title: Vytautas dies at Trakai; the Last Flame goes out
text:
Consequences
Mirrors the graph: the death ‘ends’ the Last Flame promise and leads to Žygimantas’s coup at Ašmena (the war of the heirs) and to the seizure of Podolia. The vilkatai die with the flame: new wolves can be made only at a living flame.

title: Vytautas dies at Trakai; the Last Flame goes out
text:
Dramatisation
Book IV ch. 24 “Vilniaus Laukimas” (Jogaila), ch. 25 “Kritimas” (Vytautas; mid-October), ch. 26 “Paskutinis Susitikimas” (Jogaila), ch. 27 “Šaknų Motinos Atsisveikinimas” (Eglė; the night of 19–20 October), ch. 28 “Giltinė prie Lovos” (20–26 October), ch. 29 “Vilko Mirtis” (Vytautas; 27 October 1430, evening; the Trakai island castle) and ch. 30 “Epilogas: Nematoma Karūna” (Henė; Lake Galvė, late autumn). The same night is replayed from the vault in Book V ch. 1 “Paskutinis Atodūsis” (Birutė frame; Žiežirba).

title: Žygimantas assassinated at Trakai
text:
What the chronicles say [Record]
Žygimantas Kęstutaitis was murdered at Trakai on 20 March 1440, which was Palm Sunday (Easter 1440 fell on 27 March). The conspirators were boyars led by Aleksandras and Jonas (Ivan) Czartoryski, supporters of Švitrigaila, who then returned Lutsk to him (VLE; Wikipedia says possibly led by Alexander Czartoryski). The complicity of Jonas Goštautas is flagged as uncertain by the VLE. He had been Grand Duke since 1432 and had turned increasingly suspicious, executing boyars and negotiating with Albert II of Habsburg in 1438–39. Casimir was proclaimed Grand Duke on 29 June 1440.

title: Žygimantas assassinated at Trakai
text:
What really happened [Saga]
The last Kęstutaitis to rule dies in his father’s castle. The wolves heard the Czartoryskis’ plan and were too few to stop it, and the keeper decided not to save a tyrant and is not sure he is right. When he dies the Iron Wolf’s last howl rises from the lake: the pack of the dead mourning the last of the prince they were first sworn to. The ice breaks round the island in one circle, from shore to shore, as if cut by a knife, and the castle stands in black water as if built anew. Palm Sunday bells ring on the Trakai belfry.

title: Žygimantas assassinated at Trakai
text:
Consequences
The graph attaches no outgoing ‘causes’ edge. The saga’s consequence is the elevation of Casimir in June 1440 and the council’s rule; Henė appears to the keeper on the ice in the winter.

title: Algirdaičiai (Algirdas’s line)
text:
Overview
[Record] The sons of Algirdas (d. May 1377) and Uliana of Tver: Jogaila, Skirgaila, Kaributas, Lengvenis, Karigaila, Vygantas and Švitrigaila. They hold Vilnius and the eastern appanages. Jogaila signed Dovydiškės (31 May 1380), retook Vilnius on 12 Jun 1382 and was baptised at Kraków in 1386 as King of Poland. Skirgaila governed Lithuania for him (1387-92) and died at Kyiv on 11 Jan 1397. Švitrigaila ruled 1430-32 and died in 1452. Jogaila’s Jagiellonian sons, Władysław III and Casimir, carry the line into the next century.

title: Golden Horde
text:
Overview
[Record] The Mongol khanate of the western steppe, tributary master of the Rus’ lands. Tokhtamysh reunited it in 1380, burned Moscow in Aug 1382, and was broken by Timur in 1391 and 1395. He then fled to Vytautas. The beglerbeg Edigu, kingmaker for Temür Qutlugh, crushed Vytautas’s coalition at the Vorskla on 12 Aug 1399. Edigu raided Moscow in 1408, and died in 1419 (some say 1420), probably killed by a son of Tokhtamysh. Tokhtamysh’s son Jalal ad-Din led Tatars at Grunwald. After the 1420s the Horde fractured, and Crimea broke away under Hacı Giray with Lithuanian support.

title: Kęstutaičiai (Kęstutis’s line)
text:
Overview
[Record] Kęstutis held the western half of the realm from Trakai (1345-82); he was captured and escaped from Marienburg in 1361, and died at Krėva on 15 Aug 1382 (strangled, per most accounts). His sons: Vytautas (c. 1350-27 Oct 1430), Tautvilas (killed Sep 1390 at the Crooked Castle, per Wigand of Marburg) and Žygimantas (hostage c. 1389/90-1398; Grand Duke 1432-20 Mar 1440, murdered at Trakai). Their allies: Samogitia and the Masovian husbands of their sister Danutė. The line ends with Žygimantas’s son Mykolas, exiled and dead in 1452.

title: Pagan clergy (Krivis, žyniai, vaidilutės)
text:
Overview
[Record] Little is certain. Długosz describes the Vilnius sacred fire, grove and snakes destroyed in Feb-Mar 1387. Peter of Dusburg describes a Prussian high priest, the Criwe at Romuva. Whether Lithuania had a single Krivis is debated; the title Krivių Krivaitis is mostly 16th-century and later. Lizdeika, Gediminas’s dream-reader, is a chronicle legend. Žynys and vaidilutė survive as folk terms, and the Palanga amber-priestess is shaped by 19th-century Romanticism.

title: Žemaičiai (Samogitians)
text:
Overview
[Record] The western lowland between Prussia and Livonia, the land bridge the Order needs. Samogitians beat the Sword Brothers at Saulė (22 Sep 1236). They govern themselves through elders and owe the Grand Duke service, not obedience. The land is ceded on paper at Dubysa (1382), Königsberg (1384), Lyck (1390), Salynas (12 Oct 1398) and Raciąż (1404), and held by the Order only about 1404-09. They rose in 1401 and in 1409, which began the Great War. Thorn (1 Feb 1411) gave it to Lithuania for the lifetimes of Jogaila and Vytautas; Melno (27 Sep 1422) permanently. Baptism came in 1413, with the diocese of Medininkai on 24 Oct 1417. A Samogitian delegation testified at Constance (the Proposicio Samaytarum, Feb 1416) that the Order wanted conquest, not conversion.

title: Žiniuoniai (village charm-healers)
text:
Overview
[Record] Lithuanian folk healers (žiniuoniai, užkalbėtojai, žolininkės, midwives and layers-out of the dead) kept a large oral tradition of spoken charms against snakebite, bleeding, fright, toothache and fire, whispered three or nine times over water, bread or salt. The tradition is documented chiefly in 19th-century collections; whether specific 14th-century practices were the same is unknown. The Church condemned charms, and many village priests used them anyway.

title: Žiniuoniai (village charm-healers)
text:
Patron Force
No canonical patron. [Saga] A tier-1 craft (power_systems.md §2.2 and §4): no gift is needed, only exact words from a living teacher and a medium. After the Unbinding, charms are the peasantry’s main defence against unbound spirits, and from the 1387 collapse of the clergy the žyniai become healers.

title: Žiniuoniai (village charm-healers)
text:
Internal tensions
A charm told to the wrong person dies; a charm said for money works at half strength; a healer who charms too much grows strange and takes a trace of what she removes. They are condemned by priests and sought by the same priests at night.

title: Žiniuoniai (village charm-healers)
text:
Notable members
No wiki character. The books name Pilkoji, a layer-out and midwife before she is sworn a wolf (III ch. 7), and Gedvilė, the Palanga midwife (V ch. 25, 29). See also Užkalbėjimai and the Dykra.

title: Aukso Rijūnas (Mercator-Rex)
text:
Nature
Egregore (cosmology §2.2): Aukso Rijūnas, Latin Mercator-Rex. It is fed by ledgers, tolls, land sold by the furlong, and counting-houses, including the Hanseatic ones and, from 1411, Poland. It grows wherever appetite gathers, including in Lithuanian hearts.

title: Aukso Rijūnas (Mercator-Rex)
text:
Wants
Profit: the landscape as a resource, men as ledger entries. It lends and asks for a pledge, usually a word not yet spoken.

title: Aukso Rijūnas (Mercator-Rex)
text:
Takes (its price)
A prosperity that “empties people out”. It gives gold on pledge, and the pledge is the other side of the crown: “Vytautas’s word, not yet spoken” (Book IV ch. 21). It drives the sale of Samogitia for silver and the theft of the crown.

title: Aukso Rijūnas (Mercator-Rex)
text:
Signs & manifestations
Coins that are always warm; a counting voice in quiet rooms: the Counter (Skaičiuotojas), soft and pleasant, counting geese, barrels, pearls, wheel-turns;. The warmest place in Olesnicki’s chamber is not the stove but the coin he never touches (ch. 20). Each murder in Vilnius in 1382 goes “into the Gold-Glutton’s chest” (Book I ch. 7).

title: Aukso Rijūnas (Mercator-Rex)
text:
Vessels, servants, claims
Patron of Olesnicki (from 1411), Skaičiuotojas as the voice. Fed by the Hanse and Poland; servant: the Counter. Vytautas hears the voice for thirty years and learns to carry it “like a pebble in the boot” (Book IV ch. 16). A servant girl tells Goštautas that Aukso Rijūnas eats no bread but is calmer when fed (Book V ch. 17).

title: Aukso Rijūnas (Mercator-Rex)
text:
Weaknesses
It can only count what exists. At Lutsk the crown is turned to leaves and the Gold-Glutton writes a zero on his account (Book IV ch. 30). It cannot buy a word that has not been spoken, and Vytautas’s refusal to let the Last Flame die is the one entry it cannot enter. Henė calls the Counter fond of showing numbers, never asking if you want to know (Book II ch. 13).

title: Aukso Rijūnas (Mercator-Rex)
text:
Arc across the books
I: present from the start, at the massacre and the merchants (ch. 7, 28). II: the Counter named (ch. 13). IV: dominant: Sigismund’s debts (ch. 17), the crown with the borrowed third (ch. 21), “the last bargain” (ch. 22), the zero (ch. 30). V: the feast and the voice among the lords (ch. 17, 21).

title: Geležinis Šventasis (Sanctus Ferrum)
text:
Nature
Egregore (cosmology §2.2): Geležinis Šventasis, Latin Ferrum Sanctum. It is fed by the Reise season, crusade, indulgence and forced baptism, and by thousands of prayers in the Marienburg church of the Virgin (Book I ch. 18). It is not the Christian God, which the saga never judges. It is institutional appetite wearing faith’s clothes.

title: Geležinis Šventasis (Sanctus Ferrum)
text:
Wants
Total homogeneity: the wild and pagan as a sickness to be purged, the world made orderly and silent.

title: Geležinis Šventasis (Sanctus Ferrum)
text:
Takes (its price)
It grants fearlessness, tireless marching and absence of pity (the Iron Saint’s gift): knights with faces “of people who feel nothing” (Book VI ch. 7). The price is pity, and such knights cannot weep.

title: Geležinis Šventasis (Sanctus Ferrum)
text:
Signs & manifestations
Furnace heat in winter; the smell of quench-water; crosses that ring like anvils; ice melting on shields; snow turning black and round where steel steps (Book VI ch. 24). “The breath of the Iron Saint” along the Prussian border: metal, peat smoke, forests that stand silent as dead (Book I ch. 17). Marienburg’s cellars stay warm for a hundred years (Book III ch. 11, 22).

title: Geležinis Šventasis (Sanctus Ferrum)
text:
Vessels, servants, claims
Patron of the Order’s leaders: Zöllner (1382–90) and Jungingen (1407–10). Servants: the Reise riders and the Nedegintieji. Its oaths on relics bind the Order’s men.

title: Geležinis Šventasis (Sanctus Ferrum)
text:
Weaknesses
Earth’s Unmovable Will and Fire’s terror find no grip on its knights, but consecrated stone is its home ground, and Kalba costs double there. It is broken at Grunwald, when the white-cloaked knights lay down their swords and weep (Book III ch. 20, “Geležies Mirtis”), and “all that was warm in him went out with his god” (Book V ch. 14).

title: Geležinis Šventasis (Sanctus Ferrum)
text:
Arc across the books
VI: first met at Strėva (1348, ch. 7) and Rudau (1370, ch. 24), where Kęstutis recognises its signs. I: Marienburg and Zöllner (ch. 17–18, 20). III: the warm cellars (ch. 11), the siege (ch. 22), its death at Grunwald (ch. 20). V: silenced in the North, among the dying Order (ch. 14).

The three layers of power

title: Šaknų Motina (Root-Mother)
text:
Nature
Native Force: the wild grief of Žemyna and Medeina, fused during the 13th-century crusades (cosmology §3.1; canon D8: she is not a synonym for Žemyna). She took shape when the Order emptied Sudovia (1277–83) and made the Dykra her body (Book VI ch. 9).

title: Šaknų Motina (Root-Mother)
text:
Wants
The forest kept; plough, axe and iron stopped. She hates the knights’ iron and the cities’ stone, and chooses not a prince but “what a prince can give her” (Book V ch. 11).

title: Šaknų Motina (Root-Mother)
text:
Takes (its price)
The Amber Debt: royal blood for land lost (canon D7). Her servants pay in parts: Eglė’s price, “never sell the forest”, falls due at Salynas (Book II ch. 19); wolves leave part of the soul in the bog (rite in the Iron Wolves §4); Galminas’s body. “Kas neiškils, tas liks”: whoever does not rise from the mud stays (Book III ch. 9).

title: Šaknų Motina (Root-Mother)
text:
Signs & manifestations
Groans in the earth, roots shifting, sap turning red before a massacre, crows leading columns, a whisper that is leaves. She arrives from all sides at once, and the mouth fills with soil that smells of rain (Book III ch. 29).

title: Šaknų Motina (Root-Mother)
text:
Vessels, servants, claims
Host: Galminas, the dead žynys she reanimated, who becomes a grove at Grunwald. Servants: Eglė (Pelkių Eglė, taken in the prologue, Book I ch. 16), the Iron Wolves, the žaltys, barstukai, and devotees such as Elena, who carries her tow-knot sign (Book I ch. 12–13). Claim: Vytautas, contested with Perkūnas.

title: Šaknų Motina (Root-Mother)
text:
Weaknesses
She cannot follow onto the steppe: “no forest, no bog” at Vorskla (Book II ch. 23). Consecrated stone and the axe that comes with the priests defeat her; by 1411 she says she has nothing left to stop them (Book III ch. 29). She fades as groves are felled.

title: Šaknų Motina (Root-Mother)
text:
Arc across the books
Book VI: the Dykra is born (ch. 9). I: Elena, Eglė and the swamp (ch. 12–16). II: the debt of the forest at Salynas (ch. 19); absent on the steppe (ch. 23). III: Pilkoji, Galminas and Grunwald (ch. 7–29), her last great act. IV: she sleeps (ch. 6) and says farewell through Eglė (ch. 27). V: she returns and courts Švitrigaila (ch. 11), reclaims the abandoned groves (ch. 28).

title: Dievas (Senelis)
text:
Folk sources [Record]
Dievas (Latvian Dievs) is the common Baltic name of the sky god, from Proto-Indo-European *deiwos, “the shining one”; in Lithuanian it is also the ordinary word for God. Almost everything written about him comes from Christian-era texts (Mažvydas, 1547, already uses it for the Christian God), so the pre-Christian figure is hard to isolate. Beresnevičius called him a deus otiosus, a remote god whose cult is doubtful, while others (Gimbutas) stress the sky-father of folklore. His name was often avoided in favour of epithets (Aukščiausiasis, Visagalis, Praamžius; Łasicki’s Auxtheias Vissagistis).
Dievas Senelis (“Old Man God”) is folk-tale material, recorded in the 19th and 20th centuries: God walks the earth as an old man or beggar, tests households’ hospitality and teaches chores. Folk tellers already blend him with the Christian God.

title: Dievas (Senelis)
text:
In the saga
Domain: sky, order, the distant father. Element: none. Force-face: none. He never bargains and cannot be asked (cosmology §3.1). Instead he walks as the Beggar (§5) and tests with small requests. Those who give are not rescued but seen: their road becomes clear to them, even if it leads to death. Those who refuse are not punished, only left blind to their own road.
In Book I ch. 4 an old beggar in grey rags sits at the roadside in a whirl of wind that stirs no other leaf. Kęstutis throws him a silver coin, and the beggar opens his palm on a grey pebble (the coin): what is paid for truth is worth nothing as money. Kęstutis then walks to Krėva knowing. The beggar calls Vytautas “Vyti” (canon Q7: a god may use the intimate name). A beggar at Goštautas’s door in Book V ch. 17 may be the same figure. Weakness: none that matters; he does not act. He only sees.

title: Dievas (Senelis)
text:
Offerings & taboos
No cult is recorded or invented. The only observance is custom: give bread, coin or a story to the stranger at the door, since in the tales the beggar may be God.

title: Giltinė
text:
Folk sources [Record]
Giltinė (from gilti, “to sting”) is the personification of death, usually an old or tall woman in white, with the owl as her bird in later lore. She is late-attested: the earliest named source is Prätorius (1690s); she is not in the 13th–14th-century chronicles or, as far as the standard lists show, in Łasicki. Her kinship as Laima’s sister is a folk tradition recorded in the 19th–20th centuries. The best-documented material is the “Godfather Death” tale type, common in Lithuanian collections. Giltinė stands at the head of a sickbed (the patient dies) or at the foot (he recovers), and a cunning man turns the bed around to win time.

title: Giltinė
text:
In the saga
Domain: death. Element: none. Force-face: none. She is Laima’s servant and sister who cuts the thread, and the one being unaffected by the Unbinding, because death owes no courtesy and was never bound by the Pact (bestiary §18). She cannot be bribed and does not bargain, but she can be tricked once.
In Book I ch. 9 she is glimpsed, unnamed, “tall and grey, with shears”, at Kęstutis’s cell door on 15 Aug 1382, not entering. She is named only in Book IV. In ch. 28 (“Giltinė prie Lovos”) a tall woman in white appears in the glass behind the dying Vytautas; he knows the bed-turning tale, and he and Julijona turn the bed so the woman moves from his head to his feet. In ch. 29 she comes to his head anyway, her palm “dry as ash”, gentler than the other woman a week before. The trick bought days, not years, and the debt was collected, as in the tale. In Book VI ch. 12 the tall grey sister with the shears is almost certainly her, unnamed. Canon gap: the bestiary says she should be glimpsed at Krėva in Book I ch. 9; the text does not name her there.

title: Giltinė
text:
Offerings & taboos
None are possible: she is not asked, fed or appeased. The only counsel in the tales is the bed-turning trick, which works once per family, and she returns when the trickster’s house is at its height. The saga adds a smell of cut grass in winter and a silent cuckoo.

gil-TIH-nay (IPA [ɡʲɪlʲˈtʲɪnʲeː]), stress gil-TI-nė.

title: Jūratė
text:
Folk sources [Record]
Jūratė (from jūra, “sea”) is the queen of the amber palace under the Baltic. She is not attested as a goddess in any medieval or early-modern list. The legend of Jūratė and the fisherman Kastytis was first written by Liudvikas Adomas Jucevičius in 1842 and made famous by Maironis’s 1920 poem. Perkūnas, enraged that a goddess loved a mortal, shatters her amber castle and kills Kastytis, or chains her to the ruins; the amber washed up after storms is her palace, and the sea’s moan is her grief. Scholars generally read the tale as literary-romantic, assembled from folk amber lore, and Polish tradition knows a “Jurata” on the Hel peninsula. Amber itself is ancient: Tacitus (Germania 45) says the Aestii gathered it, and the Order later monopolised the Prussian trade.
The saga keeps it as folklore of the 19th century and lets it circulate orally in 1382 (a deliberate anachronism, see the legends).

title: Jūratė
text:
In the saga
Domain: the sea’s amber court and grief. Element: none. Force-face: the Amber Queen, an office born of her grief and first held by her (canon D1), later passed to a vessel, finally Birutė. She feuds with Perkūnas, who shattered her palace, and the feud is unfinished, which is why he marks Birutė’s son. Her drowned court survives as the sea-maidens (vandenis).
In the books: in Book III ch. 14 the Queen’s voice says, “the sea remembers all that gods and men broke; Perkūnas won against my palace”. In Book IV ch. 8 a Vilnius bishop’s letter orders “the idol they call Jūratė” removed, meaning the amber kneeling woman. In Book VI ch. 10 the young Birutė tells Kęstutis the tale and he judges, “Perkūnas acted like a prince”. Weakness: she is chained to the ruins, and a god who loves a mortal steals a death from Laima and Giltinė.

title: Jūratė
text:
Offerings & taboos
Amber taken from the shore after a storm without an offering goes cold; wall-amber from the Šventoji mouth is too dangerous to work, since it remembers the palace. The law: dievai nemyli mirtingųjų, gods do not love the dying.

title: Medeina
text:
Folk sources [Record]
Medeina (Medeinė), from medis “tree” or medė “forest”, is the Baltic goddess of forest and hunt. A deity usually read as Medeina is among the gods Mindaugas still worshipped, according to the Volhynian Chronicle’s entry for 1252 (the form is corrupt; the reading is conventional). Jan Łasicki lists “Modeina et Ragaina” as forest and hunting goddesses (c. 1582), Długosz and Stryjkowski compare her to Diana, and Daukša names her. She is often equated with Žvorūna (“wild beast”), glossed “the bitch” in the Malalas insert (c. 1261), but the identification is common and uncertain. Greimas portrays an unmarried, alluring huntress with divine and demonic sides who guards the forest rather than aids hunters; the hare, the she-wolf and wolf packs are her animals in later reconstruction.

title: Medeina
text:
In the saga
Domain: forests, the hunt, wild beasts. Element: none. Force-face: merged into the Root-Mother: in the saga Medeina’s and Žemyna’s grief fused during the 13th-century crusades, and the Root-Mother speaks in both voices (cosmology §3.1, canon D8). That fusion is why the Root-Mother’s servants are wolves, the Iron Wolves, who were first men who lay down in the Dykra mud after the Order emptied Sudovia (1277–83).
She is never named in the books. She exists only in the Root-Mother’s wild, partisan grief: the swamp that eats Skirgaila’s trackers (Book I ch. 16), the woods that guide Lithuanian scouts (Book III ch. 16), the wolves that attack only riders with foreign seals (Book V ch. 11). Gap noted: no scene names or invokes her; a single naming (a hunter’s offering) would anchor her. Weakness: the forest she guards is felled, and she has no distinct voice left.

title: Medeina
text:
Offerings & taboos
No offering to her is attested in detail, and the saga assigns none separately: what the Root-Mother is owed (the forest kept, the axe stopped) is what Medeina was owed. The one recorded taboo nearby is the hare: the 1252 chronicle says Mindaugas would not enter a grove if a hare crossed his path.

title: Perkūnas
text:
Folk sources [Record]
Perkūnas (Latvian Pērkons, Old Prussian Perkūns) is the best-attested Baltic god; his name is also the word for “thunder”. The earliest datable mention is the Lithuanian insert (usually dated c. 1261) in the Ruthenian Malalas chronicle, glossing Perkun as “thunder”. The Volhynian Chronicle’s list of Mindaugas’s gods (1252) does not, as usually read, name him. Later witnesses: Mažvydas (1547), Jan Łasicki’s De diis Samagitarum (c. 1582, printed 1615), Stryjkowski (1582) and Prätorius (1690s).
Treat as later or reconstructed: the oak and thunderstone axes, the chase of Velnias through trees, the cleaving of Mėnuo (songs in Rhesa’s Dainos, 1825) and the shattering of Jūratė’s palace (Jucevičius, 1842). His role as oath-keeper rests on comparison with Slavic Perun, by whom the Rus’ swore in 944 and 971, and on Gimbutas, Greimas and Vėlius; medieval Lithuanian treaties do not name him.

title: Perkūnas
text:
In the saga
Domain: thunder, oaths, justice, war. Element: none; he cannot be asked. Force-face: Perkūno Rūstybė. He acts only through claims and signs, patronises Priesaika, and feuds with Bangpūtys and Jūratė.
Skirgaila swears the safe-conduct “by Perkūnas” and breaks it (Book I ch. 1, 2, 8). The god marks Vytautas at Krėva (ch. 10, the mark) and warns him through the cracked window of the false baptism (ch. 19). He audits Vytautas’s oaths at Vorskla (Book II ch. 26), accepts the renewed oath over the rusted sword (Book III ch. 17), is silent in Book IV and thunders at the funeral (Book V ch. 2). In Book VI Kęstutis swears to him over an ox (ch. 13). Weakness: he punishes his own as readily as others, so those he claims can only keep faith.

title: Perkūnas
text:
Offerings & taboos
Oak groves and lightning-struck trees; the stone axe treated as a thunderbolt (Book VI ch. 1); an ox or goat for oaths, as in Kęstutis’s historical 1351 oath to Louis of Hungary. Thursday as “Perkūno diena” is later folk reckoning (Book III ch. 26 leaves him bread). Folk taboos: shelter under no tree in a storm, put black cats out, and shut doors so Velnias cannot hide.

title: Perkūnas
text:

per-KOO-nahs (IPA [pʲɛrˈkuːnɐs]), stress per-KŪ-nas; never “PER-koo-nas”. Force-face: per-KOO-noh roos-TEE-bay.

title: Saulė
text:
Folk sources [Record]
Saulė (Latvian Saule) is the Sun, a goddess in Baltic myth. The record is thin and mostly folkloric. The Lithuanian insert in the Ruthenian Malalas (c. 1261) says the smith Teliavelis forged the Sun and threw it into the sky. Jerome of Prague, reported in later Humanist retellings, described Lithuanians worshipping the Sun and an iron hammer used to free it from a tower (the zodiac legend). The Battle of Saule (1236) bears her name, though its link to sun-cult is unproven. The bulk comes from dainos (folk songs, many Latvian), collected from the 17th–19th centuries: Saulė’s golden clothes, her horses and boat; Mėnuo as her husband; Aušrinė and Vakarinė as daughters or servants; and a daughter Žemyna in some variants. Greimas and Beresnevičius give the framework.
Amber and tears: the saga says amber is Saulė’s tears. That is an overlay. The folk record ties amber to Jūratė’s shattered palace, and the Greek parallel is the Heliades’ tears (Ovid), not a Baltic source.

title: Saulė
text:
In the saga
Domain: the Sun, mother of life. Element: none directly. Force-face: none. She is patron of Gintarystė: every piece of amber is a drop of solar grief, which is why amber stores memory (cosmology §3.1; magic rules §5.3). Her husband Mėnuo left her for Aušrinė, and her tears gathered in the sea became Jūratė’s palace.
She never acts, speaks or appears as a character. Her presence is the amber: Book I’s prologue is titled “Gintaro Ašaros” (“Amber Tears”); Birutė’s pebble and the kneeling statue carry it; and in Book VI ch. 29 Birutė throws a piece of Palanga amber into the fire at Algirdas’s death and the smell of “the warmth of the sun” fills the hill, “Saulės ašaros”. Weakness: none; she is indifferent, and the grief she left outlives her notice.

title: Saulė
text:
Offerings & taboos
Amber taken from the shore after a storm without an offering goes cold for its whole life (Palanga’s law, power systems). Sun-wheels (saulutės) carved on lintels and vault keys are her sign: Book II ch. 11, Book V ch. 20. Fed with milk at dawn.

Velnias
Lord of the dead, wealth and bargains · a pre-Christian god is argued, the folk devil is firm

Domain The dead, the underworld, wealth, cattle, bargains, cleverness
Layer God (Layer I) · the Roots, Anapilis. A shard of him became the Force Šešėlių Pardavėjas
Force-face The Shadow-Seller (Henė), a splinter, not the whole god (D2)
Offerings None attested. The dead are owed their feast at Vėlinės
Taboos Naming him lightly; giving him shelter in a storm; a pact at a crossroads at midnight; shaking his hand
Signs A gentleman in green or black with a goose-foot; black cats and dogs; warm coins; sounds that die; three blackened stones; a stranger who laughs a great deal by the fire

AnswersThe deal. Anything, worded precisely. He drafts, never cheats, and keeps every deal to the letter. Free at first; the thread comes later.The dead and the past. He keeps them, and with them every broken oath he has bought as a debt.
RefusesBreaking his word. A god's bargain is iron, which is what makes him beatable by the clever.Perkūnas. He flees him, hiding in trees, stones and animals.
CostsInterest. Paid later, with something worth more than you thought.The aitvaras. A keeper's soul goes down to his roots at death.Cleverness. Beaten only by wit (the crop-division tale): turnips and rye. Nobody has beaten the neighbours.

title: Velnias
text:
Folk sources [Record]
Velnias (Latvian Velns) means “devil” in every Lithuanian Christian text. Whether a pre-Christian god lies behind the devil is argued. The name is usually linked with vėlė, “soul of the dead”, though some linguists doubt the link, as they doubt the equation with Slavic Veles. Greimas and Vėlius reconstruct an old god of the dead, cattle and wealth, the antagonist of Perkūnas (the Ivanov–Toporov combat-myth model, which has critics). Sceptics read a Christian devil that gathered pagan traits. Seventeenth-century lexicography (Sirvydas) records a Velinas. No medieval chronicle names him among the Lithuanian gods.
What is solid is folklore collected in the 19th–20th centuries: Perkūnas chases Velnias, who hides in trees, stones and animals, which is why lightning strikes them; and Velnias is the dupe of clever peasants, as in the crop-division tale (ATU 1030) with its turnips and rye.

title: Velnias
text:
In the saga
Domain: the dead, the underworld, wealth, cattle, bargains, cleverness. Element: none. Force-face: a shard, the Shadow-Seller (canon D2). Not evil but hungry and fair: every deal is kept to the letter, and he can only be beaten by cleverness. He is patron of Sandėris.
Book I ch. 19 is titled for his bargain, and the void beneath the jester’s mask (ch. 30) is “the hollow where the dead keep the past”. Book IV ch. 21 states that he never offers more than he has, and an old woman repeats the saying that Velnias fears only Perkūnas and women at the river (ch. 30). In Book V ch. 19 he gives Žygimantas the golden chain. Book VI shows the older face: the Krivis recognises his “small thing” at a pact (ch. 8), and the Sovijus tale is told in a forge at Algirdas’s death (ch. 29). Servants: aitvaras, žaltvykslės, pinčiukas.

title: Velnias
text:
Offerings & taboos
Folk custom: never name him lightly, give him no shelter in a storm, and make no pact at a crossroads at midnight. The dead are owed their feast at Vėlinės. Weakness: he is bound to his own words, so the clever peasant wins by planting turnips and rye.

title: Velnias
text:
Pronunciation
VEL-nyahs (IPA [ˈvʲælʲnʲɐs]); two syllables only.

Julijona Alšėniškė married Vytautas on 13 Nov 1418; Sophia (Sonka) of Halshany (c. 1405–1461) married Jogaila on 7 Feb 1422 and bore Władysław III and Casimir IV. title: Alšėniškiai (Holszański, princes of Halshany)
text:
Fate across the books

IV: Julijona enters in ch. 10 (1418), clever enough to see Vytautas listening to something under the floor; Vytautas picks Sophia for Jogaila (ch. 13, Melno year) and her sons become the heirs (ch. 14).
V: Casimir, Sophia’s son, is raised Grand Duke by the council in 1440, and the family’s blood sits on two thrones.

title: Gediminaičiai (House of Gediminas)
text:
House card



Seat
Vilnius (Upper Castle, Lower Castle, the wooden Crooked Castle, burnt 1390); older seats Kernavė and Trakai. [Record]


Arms / sigil
The Vytis, an armed rider, on princely seals from the later 14th century; which duke used it first is debated. The Columns (Gediminaičių stulpai) are a 19th-century name for a sign first attested on Vytautas’s coins and seals in the late 14th century (c. 1397 is often cited), plausibly a family tamga of the Kęstutaičiai. [Record, dating to verify] Saga sigil: the Iron Wolf howling on the hill. [Saga invention]


Words
Kol staugia vilkas, stovi miestas. “While the wolf howls, the city stands.” [Saga invention]


Patron / burden

title: Gediminaičiai (House of Gediminas)
text:
Lineage
Gediminas (c. 1275 – winter 1341/42) became Grand Duke c. 1316 and wrote to the Pope and the Hanse in 1323, the first time Vilnius is named as capital. His sons: Manvydas and Narimantas (d. 1348), Algirdas, Kęstutis, Karijotas, Liubartas and Jaunutis; his daughters married Casimir III of Poland (Aldona-Ona, 1325) and Simeon of Moscow (Aigusta, 1333). [Record; his wife or wives are disputed]
Branches in this wiki: Algirdaičiai, Kęstutaičiai, Jogailaičiai and Čartoriskiai. Lesser lines: the Karijotaičiai (Podolia), Liubartaičiai (Volhynia), Jaunutaičiai (Zasławski) and Olelkaičiai (Kyiv). The house’s genius was the appanage: every son got a city, and every city got a son who might rebel.

title: Gediminaičiai (House of Gediminas)
text:
Feuds & alliances

1345: Algirdas and Kęstutis depose their brother Jaunutis, the first Gediminid wronged by Gediminids. [Record]
Algirdaičiai against Kęstutaičiai: 1380–1392 (Jogaila and Skirgaila against Kęstutis and Vytautas) and again 1432–1440 (Švitrigaila against Žygimantas).
Maria’s sons against Uliana’s sons: the elder, Orthodox Algirdaičiai were passed over in 1377.
The Order and Poland court one branch against another; Masovia and Moscow marry into both.

title: Gediminaičiai (House of Gediminas)
text:
Fate across the books

VI: the Pact is sworn (1345); Algirdas’s pyre (1377) weakens it.
I: Krėva, 15 Aug 1382: clause 2 broken by Jogaila and Skirgaila. II: Karigaila and Tautvilas die on opposite sides of the Vilnius walls (1390); the Vorskla (1399) takes Andrius and Dmitrijus.
III–IV: a reconciled house wins Grunwald; Vytautas dies without a male heir (1430); his blood survives in Moscow through Sofija.
V: Žygimantas is murdered at Trakai (1440). The Iron Wolf’s last howl follows. [Record] The Jagiellonian male line ended with Sigismund II Augustus in 1572.

Lineage
Mykolas Kęsgaila (Kieżgajło, d. 1450), son of Valimantas, was elder of Samogitia 1412–32, 1440–41 and 1443–50 (terms to verify). His brothers the Valimantaičiai, among them Rumbaudas Valimantaitis, were Vytautas’s men in Samogitia c. 1409–11 and the bridge between Vilnius and the Samogitian assemblies. Kęsgaila was Švitrigaila’s man, imprisoned by Žygimantas after 1432 and restored in 1440. [Record, verify offices]

title: Kęsgailos (Kieżgajło)
text:
Fate across the books

III: Rumbaudas Valimantaitis is POV in ch. 12 of the second Samogitian rising (1409).
IV: the Samogitian baptism (1413–17) and Melno (1422) fix the land’s fate.
V: the Kęsgailos are one of the council houses in ch. 17 and share in the power that unmakes Žygimantas. As the groves fall, the family is a man between two orders. [Record, saga framing]

title: Masovian Piasts
text:
Lineage
A cadet line of the Piasts, small, proud and squeezed between the Order, Poland and Lithuania. Janusz I (c. 1346–1429) married Danutė Kęstutaitė, and his brother Siemowit IV (c. 1352–1426) married Aleksandra Algirdaitė in 1387, so the two brothers married both Gediminid lines. Henryk, bishop-elect of Płock, married Rimgailė Kęstutaitė in 1392 and was dead within a year. [Record; details marked verify in the world bible]

title: Masovian Piasts
text:
Feuds & alliances
Steady allies of Vytautas through Janusz. Siemowit was a failed candidate for the Polish crown in 1382–84, which makes him a quiet rival of Jogaila; Henryk carried Jogaila’s offer to Vytautas before Ostrów (1392). The Order’s borders press on the duchy from the north.

title: Masovian Piasts
text:
Fate across the books

I: after the escape from Krėva, Vytautas runs first to Janusz and Danutė in Masovia (the refuge). II: Henryk’s embassy opens the road to Ostrów.
III–IV: the duchy stays between the two powers; Danutė outlives her brother’s era in the record.
V: the Masovian dukes remain neighbours at the edge of the cousins’ war. [Saga, minor]

title: Rurikids of Moscow
text:
Lineage
Rurikids ruling Moscow: Dmitry Donskoy (1350–89), victor of Kulikovo (8 Sep 1380); his son Vasily I (1371–1425), who married Sofija Vytautaitė on 9 Jan 1391 (day to verify); and Vasily II (1415–62), Vytautas’s grandson, blinded in 1446. [Record] Algirdas’s daughter Elena married Vladimir of Serpukhov, and his son Lengvenis married Dmitry’s daughter. Vasily I has his own page.

title: Rurikids of Moscow
text:
Feuds & alliances
Rival of Tver (the home of Uliana) and of Lithuania for the Rus’ lands. Dmitry negotiated with Uliana in 1384 over an Orthodox alternative to Krėva. Algirdas’s elder sons Andrius and Dmitrijus fought for Moscow at Kulikovo. Three wars between Vasily and his father-in-law (1406–08) end in the stand-off on the Ugra.

title: Rurikids of Moscow
text:
Fate across the books

II: Sofija is sent north as a pawn (1391); the Kęstutaičiai blood takes root in Moscow. III: Sofija rides between the camps at the Ugra (1408).
IV: Vasily I dies and ten-year-old Vasily II is placed under Vytautas’s protection; Sofija is regent.
V: Vasily II is blinded (1446). The blood the Order tried to wipe out sits on the Muscovite throne, the series’ bitterest irony.

title: Žymė (claim)
text:
What it is
A Žymė (claim): a god or Force marks a mortal as its instrument, without consent. It is granted power, not asked, and the Force’s own nature binds it, not the Three Laws.

title: Žymė (claim)
text:
Who can use it (path & tier)
No one chooses it. The claimed is an instrument, not a caster (no tier, though a vessel is tier 5). Patron: Perkūno Rūstybė. Examples: Kęstutis and Vytautas (Perkūnas), contested with the Root-Mother.

title: Žymė (claim)
text:
How it works (medium, words, timing)
The mark is felt: a rhythm in the fingers, a smell of ozone or sap, eyes that catch lightning; sometimes seen as a scar. At Krėva it is a heavy, slow beat “not his own pulse”, asked for by no one (Book I ch. 10, the mark). The Force acts through the claimed at moments of its choosing; he is not empowered at will.

title: Žymė (claim)
text:
Costs
Obedience to the Force’s nature. Perkūnas’s claimed must keep oaths; breaking them brings a blow (Book II ch. 5, 11, 26). At the right moment a claimed hand “knows which tree will be struck” before the lightning (Book IV ch. 1). The mark is release, too: it lets go when the work is done.

title: Žymė (claim)
text:
Limits & counters
A claim can be contested (Perkūnas and the Root-Mother both want Vytautas). It does not make a sorcerer; his power is political, not magical. A žynys reads it for him: Perkūnas set a mark at Krėva, and an oath sworn by a name the Force has marked binds the Force too (Book III ch. 17).

title: Žymė (claim)
text:
Folk basis [Record]
[Record]. There is no Baltic record of a “claim” system. Later folk belief treats lightning-struck trees and stones as holy and the person struck or spared as marked by Perkūnas. The saga turns that into a mechanism.

title: Žymė (claim)
text:
Notable practitioners
Kęstutis (Book VI ch. 13, 24, 28: “Perkūnas knows you”); Vytautas (Book I ch. 10, 19, 21; Book II ch. 5, 26; Book III ch. 17; Book IV ch. 1; Book V ch. 1). Pilkoji’s wolf-krikštas is a claim by the Root-Mother taken “against all custom” (Book III ch. 7).

title: Ugnis (Fire)
text:
Deity & zenith
Deity: Gabija, the hearth and sacred fire. Incantation: Ugnis tau degs (“Fire for you shall burn”), man for oneself. Medium: living fire. Zenith: Rasos, summer-solstice noon (~13–14 June in 1382), when the cost is halved and Gabija’s fire is deadly to unholy things; doubled in rain or floods.

title: Ugnis (Fire)
text:
Boon
Soul Armour and strength: warming, kindling, bracing the spirit against the dark half of the year. At its simplest it keeps a dying flame alive. It is also the craft of the vaidilutės who tend the sacred flames.

title: Ugnis (Fire)
text:
Minor / major cost
Minor (a candle’s length): exhaustion. Major (a night, an army, a life): soul-chill: empathy gone for days; the caster can kill without feeling. On the page the chill is physical and climbs from the fingers: legs, elbows, shoulders, and “a gap where something was” (Book II ch. 2, 11; Book IV ch. 3).

title: Ugnis (Fire)
text:
Limits
Doubled in rain and floods. The Iron Saint’s knights are immune to Fire’s terror. Consecrated stone doubles the cost. A sacred flame cannot guard itself: killed flames throw off užgesilės.

title: Ugnis (Fire)
text:
Uses in the books
Book II ch. 2: in the island castle’s wet foundations Vytautas whispers Ugnis tau degs to the failing Last Flame; the spring damp doubles the cost, the chill climbs to his elbow, and Birutė is no longer there to share it. Ch. 11: a one-candle working in the rain on the lake, the cost doubled, his legs going first. Book IV ch. 3: he lights Samogitian hearths with a pinch of vault ash “with an iron tint”. Book I ch. 29 and the secret flame: the baptism.

title: Vanduo (Water)
text:
Deity & zenith
Deity: Bangpūtys, with Mėnuo setting his tides. Incantation: Vanduo tau teks (“Water for you shall flow”), man for oneself. Medium: running or sea water. Zenith: full moon or high tide, strongest at the spring ice-break: cost halved; doubled away from living water.

title: Vanduo (Water)
text:
Boon
Life Spring: healing, and the pull of a soul back from the gate. It can carry a thirst away or draw poison out through hair and blood across distance. It is also the sea-craft of the amber priestesses, scrying in a bowl of water with amber.

title: Vanduo (Water)
text:
Minor / major cost
Minor: raging thirst. Major: the caster takes the patient’s wound in part. Book II ch. 27: after Vorskla Vytautas casts Vanduo man teks on a wounded Ruthenian boyar; the thirst vanishes, and “a side that was not his” passes into him, and though he pushes it away, part of the pain stays. Book II ch. 9: a Lagoon witch will draw the poison from the poisoned hostage boys “over any distance”, but her old body cannot carry it, so the poison must go into a younger body: an Order child’s. “Blood for poison; I only say what it costs.” Moving a healing’s cost into another body is a forbidden, costly working: “the debt finds its owner” (magic_rules.md §4.1); Vytautas refuses it (“Ne”).

title: Vanduo (Water)
text:
Limits
It cannot heal a mortal wound (the village woman’s charm and herb poultice can). The White Silence freezes Water workings. Doubled in caves and at distance from living water. At the sea, a Palanga priestess’s wedding ring is refused thrice by the waves (Book I ch. 11).

title: Vanduo (Water)
text:
Uses in the books
Birutė’s ring thrown into the Baltic (Book I ch. 11); her full-moon sacrifice (ch. 27, the whole surety paid); the amber bowl at the ice-break “when the cost is lower” (Book VI ch. 10–11). The poisoned boys and the witch (Book II ch. 9); Vytautas’s own working (ch. 27). See the poisoning.

title: The Last Flame promise
text:
Terms
[Saga invention]: Vytautas’s half of the Sutartis in Book I ch. 3, “Kol aš gyvas, paskutinė ugnis neužges” (“while I live, the last fire will not go out”). After Jogaila puts out the Šventaragis flame in 1387, Vytautas secretly keeps one sacred flame burning: lit in Kęstutis’s old lodge beyond the Neris (Book I ch. 29, lit), carried to the half-flooded foundations of the Trakai island castle (Book II ch. 2), and from 1392 in the island castle’s deepest vault.

title: The Last Flame promise
text:
Parties & witnesses
Binds: Vytautas, who made the promise in return for Birutė’s surety. Witness: the flame itself, and a keeper: the Karaim guard Elijah, who “guarded nothing” for eleven months (Book III ch. 28), and later the Flame-Keeper Žiežirba, who carries the vault ash (Book IV ch. 3). The flame is also Gabija’s (Gabija).

title: The Last Flame promise
text:
Breaches
If the flame goes out while he lives, the Pact’s penalties fall (madness, then death). The Book IV temptation: Henė offers him the crown in exchange for letting it die; at Lutsk the offer comes with a pledge, his word not yet spoken (Book IV ch. 21–22). He refuses, and the crown, which “never existed as gold”, turns to leaves (Lutsk; the crown).

title: The Last Flame promise
text:
Consequences
Vytautas dies uncrowned on 27 October 1430. At that instant the flame “went quiet, as a pot taken from the stove goes quiet”, after forty-three years (Book IV ch. 29, his death). Book V ch. 1 replays the night from the vault, and a cold fills Trakai (Book V ch. 4). The Iron Wolves can make no new wolves, so the brotherhood dies out; the pebble cracks; the gods become folklore.

title: Senovės Kalba
text:
What it is
The Ancient Tongue: asked power, the mortal craft of petitioning the gods (and, riskier, the Forces) through five elements. It is the rarest and strongest school, and the only one that reaches across distance (through amber). Bound by the Three Laws: Balance, Truth, Memory. Full rules: Magic rules.

title: Senovės Kalba
text:
Who can use it (path & tier)
Three paths: born (prigimtis, usually down the maternal line, as the Palanga priestesses), noticed (pažymėtas, after a great deed) or bound (surištas, into another’s Sutartis: Vytautas’s path). Tier 3 (žynys, vaidilutė) casts one or two elements; tier 4 (Krivis, amber priestess) all five; Vytautas is “bound tier 2”. The baptised can use it.

title: Senovės Kalba
text:
How it works (medium, words, timing)
A line of Old Lithuanian naming an element, a recipient and a verb of giving (Ugnis tau degs). Tau is cast on another, man on oneself, at lighter cost. It needs a sacred medium, the words aloud (a whisper will do; the Order gags captured žyniai) and true intent. Each element’s zenith halves the cost; off it, the cost doubles.

title: Senovės Kalba
text:
Costs
Every working shows its bill (elements). The Five-Voice (Penkių Balsų Šauksmas) calls a little of every boon and costs a little of every price, permanently: dimmer sight and hearing, frayed memory (Book I ch. 15). A surety pays part of another’s prices (Birutė, until ch. 27).

title: Senovės Kalba
text:
Limits & counters
No illusions, no raising the dead, no creating love, no changing the past, no winning wars; at most a castle for a night. Consecrated stone doubles the cost; the Iron Saint’s knights are fearless; the White Silence smothers Wind; the Order’s sword dampens it. It fails against one who knows their true name better than you do.

title: Senovės Kalba
text:
Folk basis [Record]
A saga system (Book I ch. 31, appendix) built on real folk practice (charms, oaths, sacred fires, herbs, amber), with god-names from Baltic sources of uneven reliability: Praurimė, Bangpūtys and Vėjopatis are late or doubtful. No Baltic source describes a five-element craft.

title: Senovės Kalba
text:
Notable practitioners
Birutė (tier 4: the Praurimė vision, ch. 3; the Krėva fog, ch. 14; the sacrifice, ch. 27), the Krivis (4), Eglė (3), Vytautas (the Five-Voice, ch. 15; Book II ch. 2, 11, 27).

title: Tylioji Sutartis (Silent Pact)
text:
The Pact at a glance



The Silent Pact: parties, clauses and the Unbinding


Editable source.

title: Tylioji Sutartis (Silent Pact)
text:
Terms
[Saga invention], sworn on Vėlinės night, 1345, in the Šventaragis valley, when Algirdas and Kęstutis overthrew their brother Jaunutis and divided the realm (Book VI ch. 4, the oath). The gods give: Lithuania will not be conquered; the Order may raid and burn but never hold the heartland. The princes give: (1) the sacred flames (Šventaragis, Palanga, the Samogitian alkai) are never extinguished; (2) no Gediminid sheds Gediminid blood; (3) the Amber Debt: royal blood for every land lost to plough and cross. Historical anchor: the Grand Duchy remained the last unconquered pagan state in Europe, under constant crusade, until 1387; the Pact is the saga’s reason why.

title: Tylioji Sutartis (Silent Pact)
text:
Parties & witnesses
Binds: Algirdas, Kęstutis, the pagan clergy and the Gediminid line. The Krivis is no envoy but a witness: “the gods will not bargain with you, and give nothing for free”. Rite: iron laid on a stone; each prince whispers his secret name to the fire; blood on a Palanga amber bead (“the sea will witness”); each states what he gives. Witnesses: every spirit of place (laumės stand surety), which is why the dvasios are courteous. Its quiet nature is the line “Niekas nėra klausiamas”: no one asked the children.
