title: Tylioji Sutartis (Silent Pact)
text:
Consequences
The Unbinding (Atsaistymas): spirits that were owed courtesy are no longer owed or giving it. Samogitia’s swamps eat trackers; groves breed ravenous vėlės; aitvarai turn arsonists; laumės who swapped babies now drown them. Priests cannot see them and holy water means nothing to them. The baptism saves Lithuania from the Order and damns it to its own unfed dead. Costs fall on the line: kin-blood for land lost.

title: Užkalbėjimai (charms)
text:
What it is
Spoken charms: Kalba’s humble cousin, folk word-magic that needs no gift, only the exact words learned from a living teacher and a medium (water, bread, salt, linen thread, a knife).

title: Užkalbėjimai (charms)
text:
Who can use it (path & tier)
Tier 1: the žiniuonis or herb-woman, the midwife, the village healer. Thousands in 1382. Patron: Laima. Learned only from a living teacher.

title: Užkalbėjimai (charms)
text:
How it works (medium, words, timing)
Whispered three or nine times, often over water, bread or salt. It works on one person and one ailment or danger at a time: stopping bleeding, drawing snake venom, calming a horse, taking away fright, warding a house from fire for a night.

title: Užkalbėjimai (charms)
text:
Costs
Small but personal: the charmer takes a trace of what they remove (a headache, a cold hand, a nightmare); healers who charm too much grow strange. A charm said for money works at half strength, since payment is already “giving back”.

title: Užkalbėjimai (charms)
text:
Limits & counters
A charm told to the wrong person dies for the teller; charms fail against someone who does not believe they are being helped (Law of Truth). After the Unbinding they are the peasantry’s chief defence against unbound spirits, condemned by the priests, quietly used by village ones. They cannot work a mortal wound alone; a bleeding-charm plus a Rasos-herb poultice saves wounds that Water cannot.

title: Užkalbėjimai (charms)
text:
Folk basis [Record]
[Record]. Lithuanian užkalbėtojai and žiniuonys kept a large oral tradition of charms against snakebite, bleeding, fright (išgąstis), toothache, fire and the evil eye, whispered three or nine times over water, bread or salt, and traditionally passed to a younger person of the opposite sex, or lost. The texts survive from folklore archives of the 19th–20th centuries, often Christianised.

title: Užkalbėjimai (charms)
text:
Notable practitioners
Village healers generally; Elena, the Root-Mother’s devotee who carries her tow-knot sign (Book I ch. 12–13). Thin on the page: no scene performs a charm by name, so the school survives as background and as Ona’s and Eglė’s herb-craft (Žolės).

title: Vilkų krikštas (wolf-change)
text:
What it is
Vilkų krikštas, the Wolves’ Baptism: granted power from the Root-Mother through the Dykra. It makes a man a vilkatas: night-sight, scent, sight of the dvasios, the Root-Mother’s healing and the berserk “iron hour”. It is not shape-change.

title: Vilkų krikštas (wolf-change)
text:
Who can use it (path & tier)
Unmarried men of 16 to 25, sponsored by a sworn wolf (his vilktėvis). Only wolves sworn twenty years or more (the Seniai) can put on the wolf; the folk belief that all vilkatai shape-shift is half wrong. Examples: Jonas (tier 3) and the Flame-Keeper Žiežirba (Book III ch. 9).

title: Vilkų krikštas (wolf-change)
text:
How it works (medium, words, timing)
Held in the twelve nights after Kūčios at a sacred flame: a wake as if he had died, his true name whispered to the fire, a throat-cut rubbed with live ash, nine nights without fire, then pressed under the mud of the oldest bog until the Root-Mother decides (“Kas neiškils, tas liks”, Book III ch. 9), and an oath on the Iron Wolf’s skull. Full rite: the Iron Wolves.

title: Vilkų krikštas (wolf-change)
text:
Costs
Taken: his true name, the road up (laid in the bog, never burned, never climbs to Dausos), his hearth, part of his soul, a little memory each iron hour, and his tears. Given: the pack, the sight, the iron hour. He can leave once, if someone who knew his true name speaks it at a living flame and offers bread on a knife-point (Book V ch. 29).

title: Vilkų krikštas (wolf-change)
text:
Limits & counters
No hearth under a roof; feast-day iron burns them; consecrated stone sickens them; the unfed dead hunt them. New wolves can be made only at a living flame, so the brotherhood ends when the last flame goes out in 1430 (canon D10). Bound by the Root-Mother’s nature, not the Three Laws.

title: Vilkų krikštas (wolf-change)
text:
Folk basis [Record]
[Record]. The wolf-warrior band is an Indo-European pattern (Männerbund, Old Norse úlfheðnar). Herodotus (4.105) has the Neuri becoming wolves for days each year; Olaus Magnus (1555) has werewolves gathering at Christmas in Prussia, Livonia and Lithuania. The Iron Wolf dream is a 16th-century chronicle legend.

title: Vilkų krikštas (wolf-change)
text:
Notable practitioners
Jonas; the Flame-Keeper; Šešiapirštis, wolf-father (Book II ch. 9); Pilkoji, taken “against all custom” after her village’s dead rise (Book III ch. 7, 9); Kęstutis’s silver wolf (Book VI ch. 5).

title: Žolės (herb-lore)
text:
What it is
Herb-lore: brews, smokes and poisons. It is power anyone can carry, with no gift and no Law of Balance (the graph marks it laws: false), which is exactly why it is the most dangerous. It is mundane chemistry in a mythic world.

title: Žolės (herb-lore)
text:
Who can use it (path & tier)
Tier 1: the žolininkė, the herb-woman, the midwife; also anyone who can gather and measure: Ona, the Lagoon witch, the Order’s poisoners. Eglė practises it at tier 3.

title: Žolės (herb-lore)
text:
How it works (medium, words, timing)
Herbs gathered at Rasos (Midsummer) before dawn, in silence, are double potency and keep a year. Effects: sleep, truth-loosening, fever-breaking, wound-cleaning, and the seer’s smoke (henbane and amber dust) that lets a Kalba seer see further.

title: Žolės (herb-lore)
text:
Costs
There is no magical cost: the price is the moral one. The seer’s smoke costs a terrible headache. A poison needs no sorcery at all (Book II ch. 16: “no spell, no god, no pact; only henbane seeds and root, a human hand’s work”).

title: Žolės (herb-lore)
text:
Limits & counters
It is mundane, so it can be undone by mundane means: knowledge, a physician, an antidote. In the saga’s moral design it is where the worst crimes are done, because the horror is how little magic the world needs. A charm plus a Rasos-herb poultice heals what Water cannot.

title: Žolės (herb-lore)
text:
Folk basis [Record]
[Record]. Lithuanian folk medicine was rich in wormwood (kietis), St John’s wort (jonažolė), sweet flag (ajeras), mugwort, linden, chamomile, valerian, henbane (drignė) and poppy; herbs gathered on Joninės night were held strongest, and the Assumption (Žolinė, 15 August) is the herb-blessing feast.

title: Žolės (herb-lore)
text:
Notable practitioners
Ona’s sleeping draught for the guards at Krėva (Book I ch. 12); Ona’s herb list “kietis, chamomile, jonažolė, and drignė, keep that one apart” (Book II ch. 4, 6); the slow poison in the hostage sons’ food, drignė, kietis and sugar (Book II ch. 9); Skirgaila’s death in 1397 (ch. 16). The historical poisoning of 1392 rests on weak evidence (Simon Grunau), as canon Q11 notes.

title: Brześć Kujawski
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
Brześć Kujawski, on the Zgłowiączka river in Kuyavia, was a stronghold of the Dukes of Kuyavia from the 13th century and the capital of a small duchy from 1267 under Władysław the Elbow-high, who was crowned king in 1320. The Order occupied it in 1332 until the Treaty of Kalisz (1343) restored it to Poland; from the 14th century it was a royal town and the seat of a voivodeship, and Casimir III the Great expanded its brick royal castle. The last crusader siege failed in 1431. The Peace of Brześć Kujawski, 31 December 1435, ended the Polish-Teutonic war of 1431-35: the Order stopped backing Švitrigaila and agreed to support only dukes chosen jointly by Poland and Lithuania. The nobility’s demands that became the neminem captivabimus privilege were drawn up here in 1425. The council of early December 1409 that planned the Grunwald campaign is placed by some sources at Brześć Kujawski and by others at Brest-Litovsk on the Bug (the place is disputed). Do not confuse it with Brasta on the Bug. Sources: VLE (Bresto taika); en.wikipedia (Brześć Kujawski, Czerwińsk Floating Bridge).

title: Brześć Kujawski
text:
Sensory sketch
Flat Kuyavian grain country: black soil, low willow-lined streams, long rows of rye and wheat stubble in autumn, brick church towers visible for miles, a royal castle of red brick beside a small town of timber houses. The air smells of manure, straw and wood smoke; carts crunch on frozen ruts. On the last day of December it is dark by four, the snow is dry, and sound carries a long way: bells, geese, a distant mill.

title: Brześć Kujawski
text:
In the saga
A paper end to the Order’s war: the peace the saga treats as the Iron Saint’s retreat from Lithuania’s quarrels, observed from Vilnius in Book V ch. 15. Nothing mythic happens here: the Order signs because it can no longer pay for a war it does not win, and the saga lets the news arrive as a receipt.

title: Brześć Kujawski
text:
Getting there
Brześć Kujawski is about 50 km from Toruń and 45 km from Raciążek on the Vistula, and about 160 km from Marienburg (c. 200 km by road, five to six days). From Kraków it is about 290 km (eight to ten days); from Vilnius some 480 km straight, c. 600 by road (two to three weeks). Envoys from the Order and the Crown met here on neutral Polish ground a few days from either capital.

title: Brześć Kujawski
text:
Scenes set here
Book V ch. 15 Švitrigailos žlugimas (the peace of 31 Dec 1435, recalled as news at Polotsk and Lutsk); Book III ch. 13 Brastos pasitarimas (December 1409; the book places the council at Brasta on the Bug, a disputed identification); Book IV ch. 14 (the nobles’ demands of 1425).

title: Czartorysk (Volhynia)
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
Czartorysk (now Staryi Chortoryisk) is a village on the Styr in Volhynia, first mentioned in the Hypatian Chronicle in 1100; by the late 14th century it was the seat of Constantine (Kostiantyn), son of Algirdas, whose son Vasili Konstantinovich founded the princely house of Czartoryski. A 13th-century stone tower stands there. The truce of Czartorysk ended the brief Lutsk war of 1431: Poland invaded Volhynia from 25 June, the king crossed on 21 July, Švitrigaila was beaten on the Styr on 31 July, Lutsk castle was besieged from c. 1 August and a Polish assault repulsed on 13 August; an agreement was reached on 26 August and the truce of 1 September 1431 ran to 24 June 1433 (sources vary by a few days). Sources: en.wikipedia (Staryi Chortoryisk, Lithuanian Civil War 1431-35); VLE (Švitrigaila).

title: Czartorysk (Volhynia)
text:
Sensory sketch
A riverside village in Volhynia’s forest and marsh: slow Styr water with reeds and alder, a stone tower older than any wooden house, Orthodox bells, wet meadow, and in late August or early September the first cold mornings, smoke over the harvest, geese on the pasture. Armies camped at the water’s edge make the place noisy: horses, wagons, the pounding of tent stakes and trumpet calls.

title: Czartorysk (Volhynia)
text:
In the saga
A truce on the edge of Švitrigaila’s war, signed in the family seat of the men who will kill his rival. The saga uses the place mostly by what it will bear: the Czartoryski brothers, both Gediminids, are the knives of the Trakai murder of 1440 (Book V ch. 21-23).

title: Czartorysk (Volhynia)
text:
Getting there
Czartorysk is some 60 km north of Lutsk (a day and a half on horse). Brest on the Bug is about 140 km west; Horodło about 180 km; Vilnius about 440 km straight (c. 550 km by road, two weeks). The Styr is navigable, and the river is the natural road from Lutsk to Czartorysk and on toward Pinsk.

title: Czartorysk (Volhynia)

Book V ch. 3 Švitrigailos pakilimas (the Volhynian war and the truce of September 1431, offstage); ch. 21 Bajorų sąmokslas, ch. 22 Kraujas ant Trakų akmenų and ch. 23 Vaikas soste (the Czartoryski brothers Aleksandras and Ivanas).

title: Dovydiškės (unidentified)
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
The place of the secret treaty of 31 May 1380. The name appears only in Wigand of Marburg and German texts; the village is not securely identified.

title: Dovydiškės (unidentified)
text:
Sensory sketch
Because no map shows it twice in the same place, the saga’s Dovydiškės has to be built from what the treaty itself needed: a manor or hunting camp deep in the pine and bog border country, far from any road a Lithuanian official would use. The Order covered the meeting with a five-day hunt, so the air is horn calls, wet hounds, smoke from roasting game, and the smell of horse sweat and spruce resin. Late May in this country means cold nights and pale, long evenings, birdsong at three in the morning, mosquitoes by the water, and mud on the tracks from the spring thaw. Inside the hall, the sound is quills and low German, and then the long silence after the seals are pressed.

title: Dovydiškės (unidentified)
text:
In the saga
The saga leaves it in the border wilderness.

title: Dovydiškės (unidentified)
text:
Getting there
The site is unknown, so every figure is a planning number. Theories place it somewhere between Kaunas and Insterburg, which puts it on the Order’s side of the Dykra or at its edge; another identifies it with a village called Šiaudiniškė. From Vilnius, Jogaila’s party reaches Kaunas in about 2.5 days on horseback (c. 100 km), and a further few days across the border belt would bring them to a hunting lodge in the Order’s march. From Marienburg, Grand Master Kniprode’s delegates would ride roughly two weeks (Vilnius to Marienburg is 13-16 days by envoy). The hunt was a perfect screen: a company of mounted men, hounds and servants travelling openly in the forest raised no questions. Kęstutis’s scouts could not reach it quickly. In the saga it is, deliberately, a place you can be told about but cannot find again.

In the 1380s [Record]
Gródek (Horodok) near Lviv, where Jogaila died on 1 Jun 1434, after catching a cold at Medyka in a late-April frost (event).

title: Gródek (Horodok near Lviv)
text:
Sensory sketch
A small Ruthenian-Polish market town on low ground west of Lviv, with a wooden parish church of Jogaila’s own foundation (1372), a ducal-royal manor, and a ring of earth ramparts left from the Galician-Volhynian fortress. The soundscape of the last days of May 1434 is the nightingale at night (the saga’s “first sound without holes”), church bells and psalms, the hush of servants carrying water, the rattle of litters on the road. The air smells of damp meadow, new rye, wax, and the herbs strewn on the floor of the sickroom. Late spring there is green and cool, with frost still possible at night in late April, which is how the cold that killed the old king began.

title: Gródek (Horodok near Lviv)
text:
In the saga
The nightingale that is “the first sound without holes”.

title: Gródek (Horodok near Lviv)
text:
Getting there
Gródek lies about 30 km west of Lviv (Lwów), on the road toward Przemyśl; Medyka, where Jogaila caught his chill, is near Przemyśl, a further ~80 km west. From Vilnius it is about 550 km in a straight line and 700 km by road, roughly three weeks for a normal mounted party (Vilnius to Kyiv, 750-800 km by route, is three to four weeks). From Kraków the road is some 330 km, about ten days with a sick man in a litter, which fits the record: the body left Gródek and reached Kraków on 11 June, and the Wawel funeral was held on 18 June. A courier with remounts (80-100 km per day) can carry the news from Gródek to Kraków in four days and to Vilnius in under a week.

title: Žalgiris (Grunwald)
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
The battlefield of 15 July 1410 lies between the villages of Grunwald, Stębark (Tannenberg) and Łodwigowo (Ludwigsdorf) in the Osterode district of the Order’s Prussia, about 95 km south-east of Marienburg. The allied army of Poland and Lithuania crossed the Vistula on a pontoon bridge above Czerwińsk on 30 June, reached the Order’s land, burned Gilgenburg on 11 July, and met the Order’s army under Ulrich von Jungingen after a stormy night. Two heralds brought two swords before noon; Jogaila delayed for two Masses; the Lithuanian light cavalry attacked the Order’s left and withdrew (feigned or real: historians disagree), while Polish banners held. Jungingen was killed with his leading commanders, and Vytautas had Marquard von Salzbach and Heinrich Schaumburg beheaded. The allies besieged Marienburg from 26 July to 19 September. The Lithuanian name “Žalgiris” (žalia giria, green forest) is a 19th-century coinage, from the 1880s-90s; 15th-century sources say Grunwald, Tannenberg or the Ruthenian Griunvaldas. Sources: en.wikipedia (Battle of Grunwald); VLE; a Vilnius University article on the name.

title: Žalgiris (Grunwald)
text:
Sensory sketch
Open, gently rolling farmland between three villages, with scattered woods, lakes, rye in the fields and a heavy July heat after the previous night’s storm. Before the clash there is the noise of two armies waiting: banners, trumpets, Latin hymns, horses stamping, the knights’ Christ ist erstanden and the Polish Bogurodzica. Afterwards the dominant smells are trampled grain, blood, horse sweat and burnt powder; flies come with the sun. The ground is dry and dust-choked, the stubble flattened for a mile.

title: Žalgiris (Grunwald)
text:
In the saga
Book III’s climax, the one day the Root-Mother’s forest and the Iron Saint’s open ground meet on equal terms. The Order’s cannon, the Lithuanians’ feigned retreat, the Law of Cost: Galminas becomes a grove here, and the “last žynys” tier-4 dies at Grunwald. The Iron Saint screams when the Grand Master falls. The name is handled with care: characters say Griunvaldas (ch. 24), but the chapter datelines of ch. 20, 21 and 23 still read “Žalgirio laukas”, the narrator’s modern name, which a strict reading of the record would not use in 1410.

title: Žalgiris (Grunwald)
text:
Getting there
Marienburg is about 95 km north-west (110 km by road, three days on horse, four to five on foot); this is the road the allies took after the battle (arriving 26 July). Czerwińsk (the bridge) is about 120 km straight to the south (150 km by the allies’ route, 30 June to 11 July with rest days). Osterode lies about 25 km to the north-east; Gilgenburg a day’s march. From Vilnius the distance is about 360 km straight; from Kraków about 380 km.

title: Žalgiris (Grunwald)
text:
Scenes set here
Book III ch. 15 Tiltas per Vyslą (Czerwińsk, 30 Jun-2 Jul), ch. 16 Miško šnabždesiai (border forests), ch. 17 Žibintas (the night camp by burned Gilgenburg), ch. 18 Du kalavijai (the field between Grunwald, Stębark and Łodwigowo), ch. 19 (Tannenberg field), ch. 20 Geležies mirtis, ch. 21 Kruvini laužai, ch. 23 Galmino giraitė (autumn, the field), ch. 25; later recalled in Book IV (ch. 1, 4, 9, 26, 29) and Book V ch. 11, ch. 25.

title: Jurbarkas (Georgenburg)
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
Jurbarkas (Germ. Georgenburg, Jurgenburg) was the Order’s castle on the middle Nemunas, on Bišpiliukai (Kalnėnai) hill about 3 km west of the present town; the dating (1343-1403) is disputed against a “1259” tradition. It was the Order’s outpost in the “castle-studded no man’s land” of the Jurbarkas-Kaunas stretch. On 9 July 1384 Vytautas took it by deception and burned it, capturing the vice-komtur Dietrich von Gruste and ten knights. It was rebuilt in 1387 and destroyed again in 1403; in 1392 the Order let Vytautas lodge relatives there. Zöllner is variously said to have died (20 Aug 1390) at Christburg or at the siege of Jurbarkas; sources disagree. Sources: VLE (Jurgenburg); en.wikipedia (Konrad Zöllner, Lithuanian Civil War).

title: Jurbarkas (Georgenburg)
text:
Sensory sketch
A castle on a hill over the Nemunas, with timber and earth works, a gate with watchers, woods on the slope. July heat; the river broad and brown. In the saga’s night: warm stone, torches, a gate swung open for a vassal, men who have been drinking, and then the smell of burning pitch and the sound of the gate-bar dropped from the wrong side.

title: Jurbarkas (Georgenburg)
text:
In the saga
The second fire after Kaunas, lit not in rage but by a lord’s key: the “Išdavikų išdavikas” in its purest form. The Order believed the messenger from Naujapilis, and the gate opened to a lie that travelled faster than the river. The mythic residue is thin; the saga’s weight is moral.

title: Jurbarkas (Georgenburg)
text:
Getting there
From Kaunas 75 km straight, about 85 km by the Nemunas (two days by horse, two days downstream by boat). Vytautas rode “along the Nemunas, ahead of the news, which travelled only by river” and reached it on 9 July. Ragnit is about 60 km further downstream; Königsberg lies about 150 km west (c. 190 km by road, four to six days). Skirsnemunė (Christmemel) lies about 9 km away.

title: Jurbarkas (Georgenburg)
text:
Scenes set here
Book I ch. 24 Pasirinkimas (9 July 1384), ch. 25 Išdavikų išdavikas (the fire seen from the forest); Book II ch. 30 (a name on Marienburg’s map).

text:

title: Kęstutis’s hunting lodge beyond the Neris
text:
Sensory sketch
A low, windowless log hut in deep pine, on sand, across the Neris and away from every track. The inside smells of mould and old horn: antlers hang on the wall, and in the middle there is a stone hearth pit that has been cold for years. In the Lithuanian forest, February and March mean snow crust, leaden light, and the creak of pines in cold wind; there are black grouse in the dark, and the only other sounds are wolves, far off, and the small crack of birch bark taking fire. For a first flame it is almost unbearably quiet, which is the point.

title: Kęstutis’s hunting lodge beyond the Neris
text:
In the saga
Saga place (D11): Kęstutis’s old hunting lodge across the Neris in the pines, a windowless hut known to none of Jogaila’s men. Vytautas lights the Last Flame there on the night of the 1387 baptism (the flame); Kalvis guards it. It is moved to the flooded foundations of the Trakai island castle in Book II.

title: Kęstutis’s hunting lodge beyond the Neris
text:
Getting there
The saga does not fix a distance, only that the lodge lies beyond the Neris, in pinewoods deep enough that no one of Jogaila’s household knows it. Vilnius sits at the confluence of the Neris and the Vilnia, so any ride across the river from the baptism site goes out of the city’s built-up bank within an hour. Planning figure: roughly half a day by horse from the Šventaragis valley, a morning on foot in snow (Foot: 25-30 km per day; halve it in deep snow). From Trakai the lodge is around 30 km, about half a day on horse (the Trakai-Vilnius figure of 28-32 km). It was a hunting seat of Kęstutis, so it lies within a day of both of his capitals. Moving the flame from here to the island castle vault in Book II is about a day’s work.

title: Kraków
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
Kraków (Lith. Krokuva) was the royal seat of Poland, with the royal castle and Gothic cathedral on the Wawel hill above the Vistula. Jadwiga was crowned rex of Poland there on 16 October 1384. Jogaila was baptised as Władysław on 15 February 1386, married Jadwiga on 18 February and was crowned on 4 March; VLE says Vytautas was baptised again (as Aleksandras) here in the same year. Jadwiga gave birth to a daughter, Elżbieta Bonifacja, on 22 June 1399 and died on 17 July (the child died on 13 July and was buried in her arms); her will bequeathed jewels to refound the Kraków University, which reopened in 1400. After Grunwald Jogaila returned in triumph in autumn 1410. His second wife Sophia of Halshany bore Władysław (31 Oct 1424) and Casimir (late November 1427); Jadwiga Jagiellonka died in Kraków on 8 December 1431. Jogaila died at Gródek on 1 June 1434 and was buried on Wawel on 18 June; his youngest son Casimir was crowned here on 25 June 1447 by Archbishop Wincenty Kot. Sources: VLE; en.wikipedia (Jogaila, Jadwiga, Sophia of Halshany, Casimir IV).

title: Kraków
text:
Sensory sketch
A Gothic city of brick and limestone rising above a wide river: the Wawel’s towers, a market square with stalls and the Cloth Hall, a cathedral with golden Gothic vaults, and a royal court of Polish nobles in colourful dress. Bells of dozens of churches, Latin chant, the clatter of carts on cobbles and wood-block lanes, the smell of coal smoke, tallow, fur and spiced wine, and the Vistula’s barges. Autumn and spring mean mud and fog off the river; the cold of winter in the castle is only softened by tiled stoves.

title: Kraków
text:
In the saga
The White Silence’s cathedral. The crown that Jogaila takes is the instrument of the Shadow-Seller’s long bargain: Jadwiga is the Silence’s “vessel”, a mortal queen whose crowning and death mark the first and last beats of its reign. In Book II Jadwiga’s death scene is also the saga’s farewell to the old century; in Book V Jogaila’s burial and Casimir’s coronation turn the page. The Polish court is where Oleśnicki’s scheming lives; the cathedral’s golden chain (Book IV) comes to rest here.

title: Kraków
text:
Getting there
From Vilnius 750-850 km, three to four weeks on horse, six on foot; embassies and the king’s winter journey of 1387 took that long. From Lutsk about 390 km straight (c. 480 km by road, two weeks). From Lublin about 230 km straight; from Horodło on the Bug 340 km (ten to twelve days). From Warsaw about 250 km. From Buda about 290 km straight (c. 400 km by road, ten to twelve days). From Gródek near Lviv 330 km (ten days with a litter; Jogaila’s body took ten days, 1-11 June 1434).

title: Kraków
text:
Scenes set here
Book I ch. 29 (offstage: the baptisms of 1386 recalled); Book II ch. 21 Krokuva, Vavelio pilis (Jadwiga’s death, 22 Jun-17 Jul 1399); Book III ch. 3 (after Radom), ch. 24, ch. 27 Jogailos sielvartas, ch. 30 (the royal chancery); Book IV ch. 14 (1424-27), ch. 20 Lenkų baimė (1429-30); Book V ch. 6 (December 1431), ch. 12 (the old king’s death, recalled), ch. 26 (the 1447 coronation).

title: Kyiv
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
Kyiv, the mother city of the Rus’, was sacked by the Mongols in 1240, after which its princes only nominally controlled it. Gediminas’s army took it in the 1320s (a traditional date); Algirdas incorporated it into the Grand Duchy in 1362 after the Battle of Blue Waters (1362 or 1363, historians debate), and Vladimir Olgerdovich, Algirdas’s son, ruled from the castle on Zamkova hill until 1394, when Vytautas removed him. Skirgaila governed Kyiv from 1395 and died there on 11 January 1397 (VLE; en.wikipedia gives 8 Jan in its infobox; poison is rumoured, the cause is unclear). After the defeat on the Vorskla (12 Aug 1399) the Tatars besieged Kyiv, which paid a ransom, and raided as far as Lutsk. The Caves Monastery and St Sophia remained the city’s great churches; the town core had moved to the lower Podil. Kyiv stayed a Lithuanian principality until abolished in 1470. Sources: VLE; en.wikipedia (Kyiv, Skirgaila, Battle of the Vorskla River).

title: Kyiv
text:
Sensory sketch
Gold domes dulled by weather above a hill-city of ruins and gardens, with the wide Dnieper below: timber lanes in the riverside Podil, Orthodox chant from the cave monastery, the smell of beeswax, incense, fish, smoke and damp earth. In winter the river is ice, wolves come near the walls, and the cold gets into the stone of St Sophia. In summer the road south is dust and flies; steppe wind carries the smell of hay and horse.

title: Kyiv
text:
In the saga
Book II’s Kijevo šešėliai: the Steppe-Hunger’s door. A half-ruined capital whose ruins make a lord feel like a guest in his own house. Skirgaila is Henė’s discarded tool, and his death on 11 January 1397 is the collection of the bargain. Book II ch. 28 returns after Vorskla to the Pechersk Monastery and the city that paid its ransom.

title: Kyiv
text:
Getting there
From Vilnius 590 km straight, 750-800 km by road: three to four weeks on horse, the last leg by the Dnieper. From Vorskla about 300 km south-east (twelve to twenty days for an army), from Lutsk about 380 km, from Smolensk about 480 km. The Dnieper is the road south, though the rapids below the city block simple through-traffic to the Black Sea.

title: Kyiv

title: Lutsk
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
Lutsk (Lith. Luckas, Pol. Łuck) is the capital of Volhynia, on the Styr, with a stone castle on an island of the river. Liubartas (Lubart), Gediminas’s son and last ruler of united Galicia-Volhynia, held it; after he lost Vladimir in 1366 he made it his capital, and its masonry was built mostly in the second half of the 14th century (second building period ending with his death, c. 1383-85). It had an Upper Castle and a Lower or “Okolnyi” castle. Vytautas held it from c. 1387-88 (verify). In March 1418 Švitrigaila was freed from Kremenets and took Lutsk. The Congress of Lutsk met in January 1429, from about 9 to 29 January (accounts differ; some say 6 Jan and 13 weeks); Jogaila arrived first with the Poles and Sigismund came late (20 Jan) with Queen Barbara; guests included Eric of Denmark, a papal legate, Byzantine envoys, Moscow, Tver, Ryazan, Masovian princes, the Livonian and Prussian Orders and the Moldavian hospodar; Švitrigaila is mentioned by no source, and Oleśnicki led the Polish opposition to a crown. In 1431 the Poles besieged the castle (assault repulsed 13 Aug). The Czartoryski brothers restored Lutsk to Švitrigaila after the murder of Žygimantas in 1440; he died there on 10 Feb 1452. Sources: VLE; en.wikipedia (Congress of Lutsk, Lutsk); lt.wikipedia.

title: Lutsk
text:
Sensory sketch
A stone castle with a dam on the Styr: a drawbridge, tall entry tower, two baileys, and a town crowded to bursting in the winter of 1429, with kings’ retinues in tents and cellars. January mud and ice, horses steaming in lanes, trumpets, bells, torches. Smells: wet wool, roasted venison, wax, ink, stable dung, spiced wine. Inside the great hall, a roar of languages, Latin, Polish, German, Ruthenian, Greek, and Tatar.

title: Lutsk
text:
In the saga
Henė’s crown bargain: the Shadow-Seller offers a crown for the flame at Lutsk. Book IV ch. 18-19: Sigismund’s offer is made, Jogaila and Vytautas bargain, and the Poles’ fear grows. Švitrigaila is absent at Lutsk in Book IV (the record is silent) while Book V ch. 15 puts him there, which is pure invention. In Book V the castle is where Goštautas defends the walls and where the war of 1431 is fought.

title: Lutsk
text:
Getting there
Lutsk is about 440 km south of Vilnius in a straight line (c. 550 km by road, two weeks on horse); about 380 km from Kyiv (two to three weeks), about 390 km from Kraków (c. 480 km by road), 100 km from Horodło on the Bug, and 190 km from Brest. Czartorysk is some 60 km north. A sledge on the frozen Styr could do 40-60 km a day.

title: Lutsk
text:

Book II ch. 15 Benamis chanas (Kyiv and Lutsk, 1395-96); Book IV ch. 18 Lucko suvažiavimas and ch. 19 Zigmanto pasiūlymas (January 1429); Book V ch. 3 (the Volhynian war of 1431), ch. 15 (Polotsk and Lutsk, 1435-37), ch. 18 (1438).

title: Marienburg (Malbork)
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
Marienburg (Pol. Malbork; Lith. Marienburgas), on the Nogat arm of the Vistula, was the seat of the Grand Master from 1309, when the Order moved its headquarters here. It is a vast brick complex in three parts: the High Castle (convent and St Mary’s church), the Middle Castle with the Grand Master’s Palace, and the Lower Castle. Work ran from the 1270s to about 1406. The Palace was rebuilt in the Kniprode-Zöllner years (roughly c. 1380-96, interiors painted by 1397). It is among the largest brick buildings in Europe.
Grand Master Winrich von Kniprode died on 24 June 1382; Konrad Zöllner von Rotenstein was elected that autumn and ruled to 1390, followed by Konrad von Wallenrode (1391-93) and Konrad von Jungingen (1393-1407). Kęstutis was held here after his capture on 21 March 1361 and escaped on 11 November 1361: a servant, Alf (Adolfas), removed bricks from the cell wall, Kęstutis broke through, dropped into the dry moat and rode out in a knight’s cloak (Wigand of Marburg; Baronas 2003). Vytautas was received by the Order’s leadership after his flight in 1382-83 (the saga stages the audience at Marienburg); in January 1402 Švitrigaila came here disguised as a merchant and signed a treaty with the Order on 2 March. After Grunwald (15 July 1410) Heinrich von Plauen held the castle: the allied army arrived on 26 July, and the siege was lifted on 19 September. Ulrich von Jungingen’s body was brought here on 19 July. Sources: VLE; en.wikipedia (Malbork Castle).

title: Marienburg (Malbork)
text:
Sensory sketch
A mountain of red brick above a flat green delta: the Nogat running slow and wide under walls, geese and swans in the meadow, mud and reed. Inside, the smell of beeswax, incense, cold stone, boiled cabbage, hot iron and wet wool. The sound is the Order’s day: bells for the canonical hours, boots in corridors, a smith in the lower ward, Latin chant, German orders, the heavy shutting of doors. Winter fills the vaulted halls with stove smoke; summer brings heat off the brick and flies from the river. The Palace’s star vaults and the Grand Master’s own stove-warmed rooms are the only luxury.

title: Marienburg (Malbork)
text:
In the saga
The Iron Saint’s capital. Consecrated stone dampens Kalba: Vytautas’s amber is silent inside these walls (Book I ch. 18), which is why this is where he negotiates and is received, not where he is baptised (Tapiau). It is the place where Kęstutis’s escape, told by him at Krėva (Book I ch. 8), originally happened, and in Book VI the dungeon where Kęstutis is held; in Book III the place where Švitrigaila and the Order plot (ch. 5, 11) and the target of the failed siege of 1410. The map room in Book II’s epilogue is where the Order plans how to hold the land it won at Salynas.

title: Marienburg (Malbork)
text:
Getting there
From Vilnius 550-650 km (via Kaunas, Insterburg, Königsberg and Elbing): 13-16 days for envoys on horse, and part of the way by the Nemunas, the lagoon and the Pregel. From Czersk in Masovia 280-320 km (seven to eight days; five to six days down the Vistula). From Grunwald (Tannenberg) 95 km straight, 110 km by road: three days on horse, four to five on foot, which is the route the allied army took after the battle (26 July). Elbing is about 25 km north; Danzig about 55 km north-west. From Königsberg about 165 km straight (c. 200 km by road).

Book I ch. 18 Geležinis magistras (Vytautas’s reception), ch. 22 (Ona and the children moved here after the Königsberg treaty); Book II ch. 30 (Marienburg map, December 1399); Book III ch. 5 (Švitrigaila, 1402), ch. 11 Marienburgo šešėliai (June 1407), ch. 22 Marienburgo apgultis (26 Jul-19 Sep 1410); Book VI ch. 14 (1353-60), ch. 17 Marienburgo požemis, ch. 18 Alfo raktas (the escape, 11 Nov 1361).

title: Masovia (Płock / Warsaw)
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
Masovia (Pol. Mazowsze; Lith. Mozūrija) was a cluster of Piast duchies on the middle Vistula, Narew and Bug, in the Polish orbit and bordering both the Order and Lithuania. Janusz I (c. 1347-1429), Duke of Warsaw from 1373/74 and full ruler of the Warsaw-Czersk lands from 1381, married Vytautas’s sister Danutė (Anna) c. 1371-73. His capital was Czersk until 1406, then Warsaw; he gave German (Kulm) law to 24 towns from 1383. In 1382 he seized Podlachian towns as her dowry. When Vytautas fled in late 1382, Janusz refused him shelter and sent him on to the Order. Siemowit IV of Płock was a candidate for the Polish throne in 1382-83 and married Jogaila’s sister Aleksandra in 1387. His brother Henry of Masovia, bishop-elect of Płock, was Jogaila’s secret envoy to Vytautas in 1392 (Ostrów). The Order captured Janusz in 1393 and 1404. The allied army crossed the Vistula on a pontoon bridge above Czerwińsk on 30 June 1410, and Janusz fought at Grunwald. Płock was the see of the bishopric. Sources: VLE; en.wikipedia (Janusz I, Ostrów Agreement).

title: Masovia (Płock / Warsaw)
text:
Sensory sketch
Sandy plains and pine forest, slow rivers, drained meadows, timber towns with a brick castle or two, and a mixed Polish-Mazovian-Lithuanian crowd. The Vistula at Płock is wide, brown and slow; in spring floods fill the low ground. Roads are tracks; carts sink in mud in March and October. German colonists’ villages with Kulm law bring new wells and field strips. In the saga the warmth of Danutė’s hearth is a rare thing in this cool, careful borderland.

title: Masovia (Płock / Warsaw)
text:
In the saga
Danutė’s hall: the first warm room after Krėva and the first refusal. A sister who weeps three times as she embraces him, and a brother-in-law who calculates. The ch. 17 border post is the Masovian-Prussian border (Soldau/Działdowo or Neidenburg sector), with the Order’s stone behind it. Masovia is also where the border forests whisper in 1410 (Book III ch. 16), and the seat of Bishop Henry, Jogaila’s secret envoy.

title: Masovia (Płock / Warsaw)
text:
Getting there
From Krėva about 300 km to the Narew/Biebrza frontier and 420 km to Warsaw/Czersk (480-520 km by road; ten to twelve days on horse, four to five weeks on foot through bog). From Czersk to Marienburg 280-320 km (seven to eight days, five to six down the Vistula). Czerwińsk (the 1410 bridge) is some 50 km down the Vistula from Warsaw. Płock is about 100 km north-west of Warsaw. From Kraków to Warsaw is about 250 km straight, eight to ten days by road.

title: Masovia (Płock / Warsaw)
text:
Scenes set here
Book I ch. 17 Pasienis (Janusz I in Czersk castle; Danutė; Ona and the children in a small room); Book II ch. 9 Kraujo puta and ch. 10 Astravo sutartis (Henry of Masovia); Book III ch. 15 Tiltas per Vyslą (Czerwińsk), ch. 16 Miško šnabždesiai (the border forests, July 1410).

title: Ostrów
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
The Agreement of Ostrów was signed on 4 August 1392 between Jogaila and Vytautas, ending the Lithuanian civil war of 1389-92. Vytautas became Jogaila’s regent (viceroy for life, a Grand Duke in all but name) and Trakai was restored to him; Skirgaila received compensation (Kyiv, in 1395). Henry of Masovia, bishop-elect of Płock, had been Jogaila’s secret envoy; Vytautas’s wife Anna and Jogaila’s wife Jadwiga ratified it in separate letters. The site is unknown. The most likely place is Ostrów Lubelski near the Polish-Lithuanian border; the alternative is the Ostrovo manor near Lida in modern Belarus, possibly near the Dzitva river east of Yantsavichy. The saga uses the Lida manor. Sources: en.wikipedia (Ostrów Agreement); VLE (Vytautas, Skirgaila).

title: Ostrów
text:
Sensory sketch
A wooden manor on a river island: two timber towers, a long hall smelling of smoked beams, tallow and wet dogs, a bridge to the mainland, hay in the yard. Early August: storks on the roofs, harvest heat, midges at dusk, the tiny sounds of cups on a table when no one wants to speak first. The treaty is plain on the page: “Vytautas shall rule Lithuania as Jogaila’s lieutenant, for life”, and the silence afterwards is long.

title: Ostrów
text:
In the saga
Henė changes masters: after Ostrów the Shadow-Seller serves Vytautas instead of Skirgaila. The manor is a plain place for a very large peace; the saga treats it as an unmagical room. After Ostrów the Last Flame can be moved into the finished vault at Trakai.

title: Ostrów
text:
Getting there
If Ostrovo near Lida is meant: Lida is about 90 km south of Vilnius (c. 110 km by road, two to three days on horse), 90 km from Trakai, about 100 km from Grodno, and 100 km south-west of Krėva. From Warsaw about 340 km. If Ostrów Lubelski: about 380 km from Trakai and a few days from Lublin. The saga makes the manor reachable by both courts in about a week.

title: Palanga
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
A coastal settlement in the Curonian-Samogitian borderland, about 25 km north of the Order’s Memel (Klaipėda) and near the Livonian frontier on the Šventoji. Birutė’s hill is a dune with a hillfort and settlement of the 10th-13th centuries, a defensive wall of the late 14th or early 15th century, and a pagan sanctuary or observatory (late 14th-15th century) found by excavation in 1989; dates vary by source. A St George chapel was built on the summit in 1506 to counter the cult of Birutė’s grave. The tradition that Birutė was a vaidilutė here, taken by Kęstutis c. 1350, buried on the hill, is first set down by Stryjkowski (1582); the Order chronicler Wigand says she was drowned at Brest in 1382, and Polish-Lithuanian delegates at Constance (1416) said she lived long and died naturally. The Treaty of Melno (27 Sep 1422) left Lithuania a coast from Palanga to Šventoji. A church is documented c. 1540. Sources: VLE (Palanga, Birutė), en.wikipedia.

title: Palanga
text:
Sensory sketch
A dune coast under pine: pale sand, bent pines, sea fog, the smell of iodine and weed, smoke from drying fish, resin heating in the sun. After storms amber washes up in the wrack line, and the beach-combers know it by its warm, light weight. The Baltic is cold, grey and loud in autumn gales, glassy in summer evenings; in winter the shore ice grates. At night the only lights are hill fires and, on clear days, smoke from Memel to the south. Gulls, cormorants; wind is the main sound.

title: Palanga
text:
In the saga
The Amber Queen’s shore. The last of the priestess line watches here; the Šventasis akmuo and the kneeling amber woman stand on the hill (Book I ch. 11, ch. 27). Birutė’s Amber Sacrifice at the full moon in 1384 buys the Hidden Groves of Samogitia, and the sea refuses to keep her (the ring thrice). Memel’s smoke is the Order’s presence on the horizon: the refuge is a front line. In 1449-50 it is where the keeper, Žiežirba, is named at the fire and cremated on the beach (Book V ch. 29). Correction on the page: there is no castle at Palanga, only the hill, a palisade and the priestesses’ house.

title: Palanga
text:
Getting there
From Trakai 340-380 km, eight to ten days on horse (four with relays; this is Birutė’s own route after the arrest). From Krėva 470-520 km, ten to thirteen days (five to six with relays). From Vilnius 350-400 km. Memel is only about 25 km south: half a day’s ride, one day on foot. The Šventoji and the Livonian border lie a few km north. Between Palanga and the Nemunas lie the Samogitian uplands, with few roads; most travel follows the coast and sandy tracks.

title: Palanga
text:
Scenes set here
Book I ch. 3 (in memory), ch. 11 Našlė, ch. 27 Gintaro auka; Book III ch. 14 Jūros balsas (March 1410); Book IV ch. 8 Klūpančioji (Oct 1417); Book V ch. 1 (the 1450 beach), ch. 25 (1445-46), ch. 29 Vardas prie ugnies, ch. 30 (a farmstead beyond Palanga, 1553); Book VI ch. 10 Palangos ugnis, ch. 11 (1349).

In the 1380s [Record]
Not a named road in the sources: the way from the pine hill where Kęstutis’s army stood to Jogaila’s camp by Trakai.

title: Road to Jogaila’s camp (from Kęstutis’s pine hill beyond the Trakai lake)
text:
Sensory sketch
A forest track through sandy pine ground between the lakes, in the heat of an August afternoon: resin, dry needles, warm sand and horse sweat, a dull buzzing of flies. The pace is slow, with a ducal retinue strung out in single file where the trees close in. Birds go silent; the camp ahead is audible only as a wall of nothing. Ruts are baked hard, with a thin dust that sticks to sweat. A roadside beggar under the pines is the only person in the landscape who is not part of the procession.

title: Road to Jogaila’s camp (from Kęstutis’s pine hill beyond the Trakai lake)
text:
In the saga
The Beggar meets the retinue at the roadside in the afternoon of 3 August 1382 (the coin).

title: Road to Jogaila’s camp (from Kęstutis’s pine hill beyond the Trakai lake)
text:
Getting there
A ride of a few hours, an afternoon at most: from the pine hill beyond the lake (where Kęstutis stood after Trakai fell on 20 July) round the lakes to the camp near Trakai. If the hill was a few kilometres from the camp, the party covered it at the walking pace of a ceremonial retinue, perhaps 4-5 km an hour. Trakai-Vilnius is only 28-32 km by road (half a day), so the party was close to the capital throughout. The forest track is unnamed in every source: the route is the saga’s.

title: Šventaragis valley
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
The valley is the flat ground at the Neris-Vilnia confluence below Gediminas hill, around today’s cathedral. The founding story (in the 16th-century Lithuanian chronicles) is that the prince Šventaragis was cremated here and a perpetual flame kept burning; later dukes were burned here too. That is legend, not contemporary record. What is recorded: the cathedral site shows layers of earlier brick buildings, perhaps Mindaugas’s 13th-century church and, some argue (the Kitkauskas hypothesis, contested), a pagan sanctuary phase. Algirdas died in 1377 and was cremated by pagan rite, and Kęstutis’s body was burned in Vilnius in 1382 (sources). In 1387 Jogaila, according to Długosz, extinguished the eternal fire, felled the sacred grove and killed the sacred snakes. A Gothic cathedral went up in 1387 and burned in 1419; Vytautas replaced it with a larger church. Sources: VLE; en.wikipedia (Vilnius Castle Complex).

title: Šventaragis valley
text:
Sensory sketch
Before 1387: a grove of old oak and lime on level ground by two rivers, a stone altar blackened by smoke, the smell of burned fat, juniper and wax, the dry crackle of a fire never allowed to go out, and thin pipe-smoke in river mist. After 1387: stumps, churned earth, scaffolding, lime pits and brick kilns, ringing hammers, and a new bell. In winter the Neris carries black ice floes past the valley; in summer meadow and mosquitoes. The valley is quiet because the hill blocks the wind.

title: Šventaragis valley
text:
In the saga
The holiest place in the realm. The Silent Pact was sworn here in 1345 (Vėlinės night, Book VI and Book V ch. 5), Eglė tended the flame, and Kęstutis’s pyre burned here in August 1382. The valley’s extinguishing in 1387, the end of Pact clause 1, begins the Unbinding. It is used in every book as a changing sign: the grove (1382), the stump field (1387), the cathedral (1390s), the cathedral crypt (Book V). The ember artifact (Paskutinė žarija) is made here, and the Last Flame survives only because Vytautas carries a spark away.

title: Šventaragis valley
text:
Getting there
It is inside Vilnius, a few minutes’ walk from the Lower Castle and the confluence. From Trakai it is 28-32 km (half a day), from Krėva 90-105 km (two days), from Kernavė about 35 km up the Neris. The valley is the reference point for the saga’s road distances: to Palanga 350-400 km (eight to ten days), to Kraków 750-850 km, to Marienburg 550-650 km.

title: Trakai
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
Trakai (“New” Trakai, Pol. Troki) was Kęstutis’s capital, on the neck of land between Lakes Galvė and Luka, with the older seat of Senieji Trakai a few kilometres east. Two castles stood here in the saga’s period. The Peninsula Castle, a brick-and-stone enclosure with towers, is dated to Kęstutis’s mid-14th-century building. The Island Castle on Lake Galvė was begun under Kęstutis in the second half of the 14th century; the Order’s attack of 1377 and the civil war of 1381-84 interrupted it, and the main works were completed under Vytautas around 1409 (an Order-trained mason is said to have supervised during a truce). Its walls were later thickened and a moat dug. Historians still argue about the early phases (Trakai History Museum; en.wikipedia, Trakai Island Castle).
Trakai fell to Jogaila and the Order on 20 July 1382; Skirgaila was made duke of Trakai (1382-92), and the Agreement of Ostrów (4 Aug 1392) restored the duchy to Vytautas. Tradition places the settling of Karaim families here in 1397-98, though the number is disputed. Ona died at Trakai on 31 July 1418; Vytautas died in the island castle on 27 October 1430; Žygimantas Kęstutaitis was murdered here on 20 March 1440 (which castle is not certain). Trakai became a voivodeship seat in 1413. Sources: VLE (Trakai, Skirgaila, Vytautas), en.wikipedia.

title: Trakai
text:
Sensory sketch
Water on three sides. Fog lifts off Galvė at dawn and wraps the towers; in summer the lakes smell of reeds, fish and warm mud, and gulls and swans move on the water. Before 1400, a working castle: wood smoke, tar, cattle and horses in the bailey. After 1400, hammering and the dry smell of lime, brick dust and kiln smoke from the island, where masons stacked red brick under scaffolds. Boat traffic, fishermen, the bells of Senieji Trakai. Winter closes the lakes with thick ice, sledge runners hiss across them, and the island castle can be reached on foot. Karaim and Tatar voices and horse markets appear after 1397.

title: Trakai
text:
In the saga
Trakai is the wolf’s lair: Kęstutis’s hall, Birutė’s tower shrine, and for Book I the last warm house before the arrest. Its mythic centre moves as the castles change. In 1387 the saga leaves the island as half-flooded foundations and an abandoned building site, where Vytautas hides the Last Flame in the lowest water-logged vault while Skirgaila holds the peninsula castle; a house-silence settles over Skirgaila’s Trakai. From 1392 the rising island castle houses the secret flame in its deepest vault until it goes out on 27 October 1430, the night Vytautas dies. Henė watches from an overturned boat on the south shore of Galvė; the Iron Wolf dissolves into mist above the Duke’s tower. In 1440 the murder of Žygimantas stains the same stones.

title: Trakai
text:
Getting there
Trakai is about 25 km west of Vilnius (28-32 km by road), half a day on horseback, one day on foot. To Krėva it is about 90 km (110-125 km by road), two and a half days on horse; the arrested Kęstutis reached it in roughly three. To Palanga it is 340-380 km, eight to ten days (four with relays). To Kaunas it is about 70 km in a straight line (85-90 km by road), two days by horse. In winter the lakes make a straight shortcut, but a sledge on river ice makes 40-60 km a day, so the lake is a stage, not a road. To Marienburg the Order’s envoys’ route from Vilnius (550-650 km) takes about two weeks.

title: Trakai
text:

title: Vorskla river
text:
In the 1380s [Record]
The Vorskla is a left tributary of the Dnieper near Poltava, in the forest-steppe. On 12 August 1399 Vytautas’s coalition (Lithuanians, Ruthenians, Poles, Moldavians, Wallachians, a Teutonic contingent under Marquard von Salzbach, and the exiled khan Tokhtamysh) was crushed by Edigu and Temür Qutlugh. en.wikipedia’s body text also gives 5 August, and the army figures vary (about 38,000 against 90,000 in one count). Vytautas built a wagon-fort with cannon; Temür Qutlugh asked for a three-day ceasefire while Edigu’s reserves came up, then feigned a retreat, drawing the army out; Edigu’s units appeared behind them. Tokhtamysh fled. Perhaps 20 of about 50 princes died, among them Andrius of Polotsk, Dmitry of Bryansk and Spytko II of Melsztyn; Posilge lists nine Order members dead. The Tatars besieged Kyiv (which paid) and raided to Lutsk. Lithuania lost the steppe; Smolensk, Novgorod and Pskov rebelled. Sources: en.wikipedia (Battle of the Vorskla River); VLE (Vytautas).

title: Vorskla river
text:
Sensory sketch
Open steppe in August: feather grass and wormwood, white dust, burned yellow plain to every horizon, with the Vorskla a green line of willows and reeds. Heat that shimmers, horseflies, locusts, the taste of dust in water. The sounds are scale: tens of thousands of hooves, kettledrums, the creak of wagon-fort chains, the cannon’s bang. No hill, no wood, no shadow; the day ends in orange dust.

title: Vorskla river
text:
In the saga
Book II’s atrocity. The land is “alien, endless”: no forest, so the Root-Mother cannot follow. The Steppe-Hunger feeds, and Velnias’s vision is collected. It is the saga’s clearest case of the Law of Cost: Vytautas’s pride is paid for in thousands of unburied names. The Order’s contingent fights under Marquard, who is among the rescued.

title: Vorskla river
text:
Getting there
Kyiv is about 300 km north-west (twelve to twenty days for an army at 15-25 km a day); Poltava is a few tens of kilometres south. Vytautas’s army left Vilnius on 18 May 1399 and fought on 12 August: roughly twelve weeks for about 1,000 km by road, including waits. Tokhtamysh fled north-west and was pursued as far as Lutsk, some 700 km away. A survivor’s road home ran through Kyiv, then the Dnieper to Lutsk and Vilnius, three to four weeks.

title: Vorskla river
text:
